setup: A real estate agent is writing a commentary on the local market for brokerage blog and local paper readers.

a.text:
The Spring Slowdown Isn’t a Crash. It’s Stubborn Sellers.

Last spring, the median home in our zip sat eight days. This spring it’s 34. Showings per listing have been cut in half. List prices are still up 6 percent year over year. Those numbers are real, and they feel like a punch if you’re a seller who expected last year’s frenzy.

They are not a crash.

I have three listings right now that have been on the market more than 60 days. The owners will not drop the price. They keep telling me the house next door sold for X last June, so theirs is worth Y. They are watching the calendar, not the showings. Buyers have noticed. They walk through, they like the house, they wait. Then they make an offer on the one down the street that came on last week at a number that actually matches today’s demand.

The homes that are priced to the current market—not last spring’s market—are still going under contract in under two weeks. I closed two of them this month. Both had multiple offers. Both sellers listened when I said the days of 15 percent over asking in 48 hours are over.

What we have is a timing problem, not a value problem. Inventory is still tight. Rates are higher. Buyers are more deliberate. They will pay a fair price. They will not overpay for a seller’s memory of 2021. The agents who keep telling their clients “just wait, it’ll pick up” are doing those clients no favors. The market has already picked a new pace. Catch up to it or sit.

That’s the whole story. Price it right and it sells. Pretend it’s still last year and it doesn’t.

b.text:
# The Market Didn't Crash. Some Prices Are Just Stuck in Last Spring.

Last spring, the median home in our zip code spent 8 days on the market. Eight. This spring it's 34.

I've heard what people are saying about that number. I've heard "crash" at the grocery store, at closings, from buyers who think they should wait it out and from sellers who think the whole game is rigged against them. I've been selling homes here for ten years, and I'll tell you plainly: this is not a crash. This is a pricing problem. And it's fixable, house by house, price by price.

Here's the whole story in two numbers. Showings per listing in our area have dropped by half since last spring. Meanwhile, list prices are still up 6% year over year. And I said *list* prices — what sellers are asking, not necessarily what they're getting.

Put those together. Sellers are asking more money for less attention. Buyers no longer have to compete with a crowd of strangers for every listing, so they've stopped doing it. They're looking carefully, they're being picky, and when a home is priced right, they still buy it fast. When it isn't, they scroll right past it.

I'll be honest about my own listings, because I'm not pointing fingers from a distance. I have three sellers right now who've been on the market over 60 days. Three good homes, three owners I genuinely like, three price tags set for a market we don't live in anymore. I've sat at their kitchen tables with the showing data, the days-on-market counts, and the list of what's actually closing versus what's just sitting. They're holding anyway, anchored to what a neighbor got last spring.

I understand the instinct. But a home is worth what a buyer will pay this month — not what the guy down the street got a year ago. Every one of those three homes will sell. They'll just sell for today's number, after weeks of sitting and a price cut that could have been the starting price in March.

And here's the proof this isn't a crash: the homes priced to *this* market are still going under contract in under two weeks. Sometimes with multiple offers, sometimes with one strong one. If demand had collapsed, nothing would sell at any price — that's what a crash looks like. Instead, well-priced homes move in under two weeks while overpriced ones sit at 34 days and counting. That's not a demand problem. That's a math problem.

A little perspective, because we all got spoiled. Eight days on market was never a real market. That was a frenzy — inventory so thin that buyers waived inspections and paid tens of thousands over asking on houses they'd walked through for twelve minutes. Prices rode the back of that desperation. The desperation is gone. Buyers have choices now, room to negotiate, and the freedom to sleep on a decision. But a lot of sellers — and, frankly, some listing agents — never updated the spreadsheet.

The market didn't crash. It just stopped being a seller's auction.

So, some straight talk for both sides.

**If you're selling:** the first two weeks are everything. That's when your listing is new, when the buyers with alerts set come through, when you have leverage. Price too high and you burn that window, and after that you're negotiating against buyers who know exactly how long you've been sitting. Chasing the market down in small cuts — always a step behind — costs you more than pricing right the first time. A stale listing doesn't get stronger with age. It gets negotiable.

**If you're buying:** you're holding the best hand you've held in years. You can ask for closing costs. You can keep the inspection you should never have waived in the first place. You can walk away without feeling sick about it. But don't confuse patience with a crash. The well-priced homes are still gone in two weeks, and the one you love at a fair number is not going to wait around for a collapse that isn't coming.

I'm not bracing for a crash, and you shouldn't either. Our market isn't broken — it's normalizing, and normal feels like a crash to anyone who got used to frenzy.

Thirty-four days on market isn't the sound of the market collapsing. It's the sound of some sellers — a few of them my own clients — catching up to reality. The ones who already have are closed and moved. The rest will get there eventually. It's just a lot cheaper to get there first.

setup: A small dog grooming salon owner is writing a how-to for dog owners about preventing coat matting between grooming visits.

a.text:
How to Keep Your Dog's Coat From Matting Between Grooming Visits

If your dog has a double coat or one of those wonderful curly coats, you already know they need a little more attention at home than a short-haired breed does. And the number one thing I want you to take away from this post is: brush before the bath, never after. I cannot stress this enough. So many owners come in and tell me they bathed their dog first because they figured the water and shampoo would help loosen up any tangles. It does the exact opposite. Wet fur, especially wet matted fur, basically felts itself together, like actual felting, the kind you'd do on purpose with wool and a needle. Once that happens, you're not dealing with a tangle anymore, you're dealing with a mat that's bonded to the skin, and that's a much bigger problem.

So brush first, every time, before any water touches the coat.

When you're brushing, grab a slicker brush and use short strokes, almost like little flicking motions in a line, not circles. Circular brushing just pushes the loose undercoat around and tangles it into itself instead of pulling it out. Short line strokes actually lift the loose hair out and away from the coat.

Work in sections rather than just running the brush over the whole dog in one go. I always tell people to pay special attention behind the ears and under the front legs, because that's where mats show up first, almost every single time. There's friction there, less airflow, and the fur is often finer in those spots, so it tangles faster than anywhere else on the body. If you're only going to spot check two areas between full brush-outs, make it those two.

And if you do find a mat that's already started, please don't just grab a comb or brush and start yanking at it. Work some conditioner into it with your fingers first, gently, until it softens up a bit. Let the product do some of the work before any tool touches it. Pulling a dry or half-formed mat with a brush usually just tightens it and makes it more painful for your dog, and honestly more frustrating for you too.

Keep up with this in between visits and you'll notice a real difference, less time on the table for your dog, less stress for both of you, and a coat that stays in much better shape overall.

b.text:
Keeping your dog’s coat mat-free between grooming visits does not have to mean a full grooming session at home. A little regular maintenance in the spots that tangle first can make a huge difference—especially for curly coats and double-coated breeds.

The biggest thing I want clients to remember is this: **brush before the bath, never after.** If there are tangles or small mats in the coat, getting them wet can tighten them into dense, felt-like pads. Water makes the hair shrink and bind together, and shampooing over mats usually locks them in even more. What may have been a manageable tangle before the bath can become something that needs to be shaved out afterward.

Before bathing, take a few minutes to check the areas that mat first. Behind the ears, under the front legs, around the collar area, under harness straps, and along the back of the legs are common trouble spots. For dogs with curly coats, also check where the legs meet the body and around the tail. These areas get friction from movement, sleeping, collars, and harnesses, so mats can form there quickly even when the rest of the coat looks fine.

A slicker brush is usually the best tool for regular at-home brushing. Use short, gentle line strokes rather than big circles over the top of the coat. Brushing in circles can tangle the hair more and may only smooth the outer layer while mats hide close to the skin. Work in small sections, parting the coat so you can see down toward the skin. If the brush cannot get through a section easily, there is likely a tangle forming underneath.

Start with the places that tend to mat first instead of just brushing the easy areas your dog enjoys. Behind the ears and under the front legs are usually where I find mats earliest. A few minutes spent there several times a week is much easier—and more comfortable for your dog—than trying to tackle a large mat later.

If you find a mat starting, do not immediately go at it with a brush or comb. Work a little dog-safe conditioner or detangling spray into it with your fingers first. Gently pull the mat apart from the ends, using your fingers to loosen the hairs before brushing. Once it starts to separate, use the slicker brush in small strokes from the ends upward. Pulling a brush straight through a tight mat can hurt, and a painful brushing experience can make dogs understandably nervous about being groomed.

For double-coated dogs, regular brushing is especially important during shedding seasons. Loose undercoat gets trapped in the outer coat and can quickly turn into compacted areas if it is not removed. For curly-coated dogs, consistency matters even more because the coat naturally twists and wraps around itself as it grows.

If you are not sure whether you are dealing with a tangle or a true mat, try to gently separate it with your fingers. If you cannot get your fingers between the hairs near the skin, or if your dog is uncomfortable when you touch the area, it is best to call us before bathing. Please do not use scissors to cut mats out at home—mats often pull the skin up into them, and accidental cuts happen much more easily than people realize.

A quick brush-out before every bath, plus regular attention to the ears, armpits, collar area, and harness lines, will help keep your dog more comfortable between visits and make each grooming appointment easier on everyone.

setup: A general contractor is writing a short X thread to contractors, homeowners, and architects about a hidden joist problem and the lesson learned.

a.text:
1/4
Maple Ave kitchen. Opened the subfloor after demo: three consecutive 2x10s cut clean through at midspan for an old 4" stack. Previous “repair” was 2x4s toenailled on the sides. 3/4" sag right where the island was going.

2/4
Sistered them full length with 2x10s, added blocking, hangers, and a short LVL. Three extra days for our crew. Extra cost to the owner: $2,850 in labor and material. Cabinets and stone were already in the warehouse.

3/4
Homeowners see the cabinets. We see whether the floor can actually hold them. That’s the gap.

4/4
Lesson: don’t lock the finish package until you’ve seen the structure. If you’re bidding a kitchen without looking at the joists, you’re not pricing a remodel. You’re guessing.

b.text:
1/ Pulled up the subfloor on the Maple Ave kitchen job yesterday and found three joists that had been notched halfway through by whoever ran the original plumbing. Probably 40 years ago. Someone just kept going and nobody ever fixed it.

2/ Notched joists are a structural problem that gets worse over time. Floor gets bouncy, tile cracks, cabinets go out of level. The fix was sistering new 2x10s alongside each one, full length, glued and through-bolted. Took a day and a half with two guys.

3/ Cost the homeowners about $1,100 in labor and material they weren't expecting. Could've been a lot worse. If we'd tiled over that floor without looking, it would've failed within a year and the repair would've been triple once everything was finished.

4/ The lesson isn't "always expect the worst." It's pull the subfloor before you commit to a tile scope. Ten minutes with a pry bar tells you what you're actually working with. Every old kitchen has a story underneath it and you want to know before you're four weeks in.

setup: A small coffee shop owner is writing testimony to city council opposing a parking meter rate increase.

a.text:
Testimony to the City Council Regarding the Proposed Parking Meter Rate Increase

My name is [Name], and I own [Coffee Shop Name] on Main Street. I'm here today because I believe this proposed increase—from 50 cents to a dollar fifty an hour—will do real damage to the businesses this council has spent years trying to support, and I don't think it will accomplish what it's meant to.

I want to start with the city's own numbers, because they matter more than anyone's gut feeling about parking. According to the city's own budget report, meter revenue currently accounts for just 4% of the downtown budget. That is not a rounding error we can ignore, but it's also not a crisis that justifies tripling the rate overnight. If the goal is to shore up downtown finances, a 4% line item is not where that fight should be fought—not at the expense of the small businesses that make Main Street worth visiting in the first place.

I didn't just want to speculate about what this increase might do, so I looked for real evidence. In 2019, [Neighboring Town] raised their downtown meter rates in a very similar jump. I tracked my own register during a comparable six-week stretch after their increase went into effect, because I have a second location there and wanted to understand what we might be facing. Foot traffic dropped 18% over that period. That's not a guess or a worst-case scenario—that's what actually happened when a neighboring town made this exact kind of change. People didn't stop wanting coffee. They stopped wanting to pay more to park for it.

I also want to speak to something more specific to my own shop: the actual behavior of my customers. I've tracked visit times, and the average customer at my counter is in and out in 22 minutes. That means the current 50-cent hour-minimum already comfortably covers their visit, with time to spare. Tripling the rate doesn't change how long someone sits with a coffee—it just triples what they pay for the same 22 minutes. For a customer buying a $4 latte, a $1.50 parking charge on top of that hourly rate starts to feel less like a convenience fee and more like a reason to just stay home.

I understand the city needs revenue, and I'm not asking this council to pretend that budgets balance themselves. But I am asking you to weigh a 4% revenue line against an 18% drop in foot traffic for businesses like mine—businesses that employ your neighbors, pay property taxes, and rely on people being willing to stop downtown for twenty minutes at a time. The data from a nearly identical increase next door tells us plainly what happens when parking gets more expensive than the errand it's meant to serve.

I'd ask the council to consider a smaller, incremental increase, or at minimum, a trial period with real tracking of foot traffic and receipts—not just meter revenue—before committing to a full jump from 50 cents to a dollar fifty. Main Street businesses can adapt to gradual change. We cannot easily recover from an 18% drop in customers over a few short weeks.

Thank you for your time and for considering the people who will actually feel this decision on the ground, one 22-minute visit at a time.

b.text:
# Testimony on the Proposed Downtown Parking Meter Rate Increase

Members of the City Council,

My name is [NAME], and I own [BUSINESS NAME], a small independent coffee shop on Main Street. I am submitting this testimony in opposition to the proposed increase in downtown parking meter rates from 50 cents to $1.50 per hour. I want to be clear that my opposition is not based on general worry. It is based on numbers, including some I collected myself, and I ask the Council to consider them seriously before voting.

First, I want to talk about what a rate hike like this actually does to foot traffic, because we do not have to guess. The town next to ours implemented a nearly identical increase back in 2019. When they did, I started tracking my own register receipts for six weeks to see whether the effect would spill over or give me any indication of what to expect. In the town that raised its rates, foot traffic to comparable Main Street businesses dropped 18 percent. That is not a projection or a scare figure. That is what happened when a neighboring community tripled its meter rate, exactly as this proposal would do here.

An 18 percent drop is the difference between a small business making payroll and a small business cutting hours. For a shop like mine, operating on the margins that independent coffee shops operate on, that is not a rounding error. It is survival.

Second, I want to address the argument that higher rates encourage turnover and free up spaces. My customers average a 22-minute visit. They come in, order, sit for a few minutes or grab their coffee to go, and leave. The current one-hour minimum already covers them nearly three times over. There is no turnover problem at the businesses that rely on quick visits. Raising the rate does not open up a single additional space for my customers, because they are already gone long before their paid hour is up. What it does instead is add a psychological and financial deterrent to people deciding whether to stop downtown at all, when a $1.50 minimum feels like a penalty for a five-minute errand.

Third, and this is the part I most want the Council to sit with: this increase does not actually solve the problem it claims to solve. According to the city's own report, meter revenue covers only 4 percent of the downtown budget. Even a dramatic increase to that revenue stream leaves the overwhelming majority of the budget untouched. We would be tripling the rate, risking an 18 percent decline in foot traffic that we have already watched happen next door, in exchange for a marginal bump to a line item that represents 4 percent of the whole. That is a poor trade. We would be absorbing a real, measurable harm to local businesses in return for a financial impact the city itself describes as minor.

I understand the Council is looking for revenue, and I respect that you have hard budget decisions to make. But this particular lever costs downtown businesses far more than it gains the city. The 18 percent figure is real. The 22-minute average visit is real. The 4 percent budget contribution is your own number. I am asking you to weigh those three facts together and reject this increase.

Thank you for your time and for entering this testimony into the record.

Respectfully,
[NAME]
[BUSINESS NAME], Main Street

setup: A high-school senior is writing a personal essay for college admissions readers about working at her family's Vietnamese restaurant.

a.text:
Every Saturday, I tie on my apron at 10:45 a.m. and check the rice cooker, the tea containers, and the stack of takeout menus by the register. My family’s Vietnamese restaurant opens at eleven. By eleven-thirty, someone is usually asking for extra bean sprouts, no onions, or “that noodle soup with the meatballs.”

I have worked there every weekend since sophomore year. At first, I mostly carried waters and wiped tables. Now I take orders, pack takeout, answer the phone, train new employees, and sometimes explain to customers that yes, the pho broth really does take that long to make.

One Saturday, our register system died during the lunch rush.

The screen froze halfway through an order, then went black. The card reader stopped working. The receipt printer made one long unhappy noise and quit too. My dad stared at it for about ten seconds before walking back to the kitchen because there were tickets waiting.

I found a pad of paper, a pen, and the old carbon-copy receipt book we normally ignored. For the next three hours, I wrote every order by hand.

“Two P1, one with no cilantro. One spring roll. One Vietnamese iced coffee.”

I wrote the table number, repeated the order back, tore off the ticket, and ran it to the kitchen. When customers came to pay, I added prices with a calculator and wrote down the last four digits of their card numbers so we could charge them later. A few people were annoyed. Most were patient once I explained what happened. One man said, “You’re doing great,” while I was trying to remember whether he had ordered the beef noodle salad or the grilled pork rice plate.

By the end of the shift, my handwriting had gotten worse, and there were stacks of paper all over the counter. But nobody’s order was lost. The kitchen kept moving. My mom found the register manual after closing, and we spent an hour entering the day’s sales.

The restaurant has taught me that there is always something that needs doing, even when the plan falls apart.

Sometimes that something is small. Last summer, we hired a new server who had never made spring rolls before. My grandma stood beside her at the prep table with a bowl of warm water, rice paper wrappers, shrimp, noodles, lettuce, and herbs.

My grandma does not give long explanations. She dipped one wrapper in water, laid it flat, and placed the filling in the middle. “Not too much,” she said. Then she folded in the sides and rolled it tightly.

The new server’s first few rolls looked loose and uneven. One split open when she picked it up. My grandma laughed, not in a mean way, and showed her again. I translated when needed, but mostly I watched their hands. My grandma’s fingers moved quickly from years of practice. The new server slowed down, pressed the wrapper more firmly, and tried again.

After twenty minutes, she made one that stayed together.

My grandma held it up, inspected it, and nodded once. “Good.”

At school, I am used to being evaluated with numbers: grades, test scores, percent correct. At the restaurant, improvement is more obvious. A spring roll either opens in the fryer or it does not. An order either reaches the right table or it does not. A new employee starts answering the phone without looking frightened. My grandma notices these things without making a speech about them.

During the school year, I usually bring homework to the restaurant. There is a small table in the back near the walk-in cooler, and when business slows down, I sit there with my backpack between cases of soda and boxes of noodles. The cooler is louder than people expect. It hums constantly, and cold air escapes every time someone opens the door.

I have done calculus homework there while listening for the bell above the front door. I have worked through derivatives with the smell of broth and grilled pork coming from the kitchen. Sometimes I get halfway through a problem before my mom calls my name because a customer wants to split a check or the phone is ringing.

I do not always finish as much homework as I planned. My notebook has stains from iced coffee and sauce. Once, I found a piece of cilantro pressed between two pages of my textbook.

Still, I like that table in the back. It is the place where my school life and restaurant life overlap. I can be thinking about a limit problem one minute and carrying bowls of pho the next. Neither part feels separate from me anymore.

On Saturday nights, after the last customers leave, we sweep under the tables, refill sauce bottles, and count the cash drawer. My feet hurt, and my hair smells like fryer oil. My family talks about what we ran out of, who forgot to ring in a drink, and whether we should add another dessert to the menu.

Then we lock the door and go home, knowing we will do it again next weekend.

b.text:
# Working Weekends

The register died on a Saturday in March.

I was refilling water glasses when my coworker frantically waved me over. The screen was black. The keyboard wouldn't respond. We had forty people in the restaurant and no way to ring anything up.

My manager looked at me like I might fix it. I didn't. But I grabbed a notepad and started writing orders by hand instead—table numbers, items, prices that I'd memorized years ago. I wrote fast and small so the tickets would fit. The kitchen staff knew my handwriting by then. They didn't need me to clarify when I scribbled "gỏi cuốn" or "bánh mì thịt nạc."

I did this for five hours. My hand cramped. I got the math wrong twice and had to recalculate totals while customers waited. It wasn't efficient. It wasn't good. But the restaurant kept running.

This is what I think about when I'm working: I notice things that break and try to fix them. Not always successfully. When Linh started in the kitchen last year, she kept tearing the spring roll wrappers. My grandma showed me how to fold them first—the way you have to be gentle but firm, how the rice paper gets stronger when you wet it just enough. I stood next to Linh on a Friday night and folded five rolls while she watched, then handed her the wrapper and stepped back. She got three right before messing one up. We didn't talk about it. The next week she was better.

Some nights I do calculus homework in the walk-in cooler. It's the only quiet place. I sit on a milk crate between boxes of frozen shrimp and bok choy, working through integrals with my hands getting cold. My manager thinks it's funny. My mom thinks I should rest instead. But I like being in there—surrounded by ingredients, knowing the restaurant is running ten feet away, doing something for college while I'm still here.

I've worked weekends since sophomore year. That's ninety-some Saturdays and Sundays, probably more. I don't think this makes me special. Lots of people work. I think it just means I know how to show up when something needs doing, even if I don't know how to do it yet. The register will get fixed by someone else. I'll write the tickets. Linh will learn to fold the spring rolls. That's how this works.

setup: You're Frank and Bethany Choi. The general manager is sending June numbers, shortfall reasons, and a July promo update.

b.text:

setup: A home baker is reviewing the Corlane SM6 mixer for blog readers deciding whether to buy it.

a.text:
# Corlane SM6 Stand Mixer Review: 8 Months of Near-Daily Sourdough Use

**Verdict: Buy the Corlane SM6 if you regularly make heavy bread dough. Skip it if your baking is mostly cookies, cakes, and occasional soft doughs.** At $429, it costs about $80 more than the comparable KitchenAid, but for weekly sourdough, bagels, pizza dough, or other stiff mixes, the stronger performance has been worth the premium in my kitchen.

I’ve used the Corlane SM6 almost every day for the past eight months, mostly for the sourdough loaves I sell at the farmers market on weekends. It has mixed everything from standard country dough to high-hydration sourdough to double batches of stiff bagel dough, and the motor has been the standout feature.

A double batch of bagel dough is where many home mixers start to complain: the head bounces, the motor strains, the dough climbs the hook, or the machine simply stalls. The SM6 has not stalled on me once. It works through stiff dough steadily without sounding like it is about to give up, even when I’m mixing enough dough to make a serious market bake. For someone who kneads heavy dough every week, that reliability matters more to me than having a long list of attachments or a prettier countertop appliance.

That said, it is not a flawless machine.

The bowl-lift lever squeaks. Mine started doing it early on, and now I give it a quick shot of WD-40 about once a month. It is a minor maintenance issue rather than a functional problem, but at $429, I think the lever should operate smoothly without regular lubrication.

My bigger complaint is the included dough hook. The bowl is deep, but the hook is too short to do its job well at the bottom of the bowl, especially with smaller dough batches. It tends to leave dough sitting low in the bowl instead of fully engaging and kneading it. I eventually bought a third-party dough hook, which improved the mixer substantially. Once I swapped hooks, it became much more effective and consistent.

That is frustrating because a stand mixer marketed toward serious dough mixing should come with a dough hook that actually reaches the dough properly. Factoring in the cost of a replacement hook makes the Corlane’s already-higher price harder to swallow.

Still, after eight months of hard use, I would buy it again for bread baking. The motor is strong, it has handled my market production without stalling, and it gives me confidence when I need to mix a heavy batch quickly. The monthly squeak and replacement hook are annoyances, but they have not outweighed the performance.

For $429, the Corlane SM6 is not the best value for every baker. If you mostly make cookies, cake batter, frosting, muffins, or one-off weekend loaves, save the $80 and buy the equivalent KitchenAid. You do not need this much mixer for soft batters.

But if your regular routine includes sourdough, bagels, pizza dough, enriched bread, or any stiff dough that makes lesser mixers struggle, the Corlane SM6 is worth buying. Just plan on replacing the dough hook—and keeping a little WD-40 nearby.

b.text:
# Corlane SM6 Stand Mixer: 8 Months of Near-Daily Market Baking

I've had the Corlane SM6 on my counter for eight months now, and unlike most of the gear that passes through my kitchen for a review, this one has earned its spot by actually working for a living. I bake sourdough for the farmers market most weekends, which means this machine gets fired up almost every day. Here's what I've learned.

## The Motor Is the Real Deal

This is where the SM6 justifies itself. I regularly run a double batch of stiff bagel dough through it, which is the kind of dense, low-hydration dough that makes lesser mixers whine, walk across the counter, or shut off entirely to protect themselves. The Corlane doesn't flinch. No stalling, no burning smell, no motor overheating cutoff. If you knead heavy dough, this is the headline feature, and it delivers.

## The Annoyances

Two of them, and I want to be honest about both.

First, the bowl lift lever squeaks. It started a couple months in, and I now hit it with a shot of WD-40 about once a month to keep it quiet and smooth. It's not a dealbreaker, but at this price point I shouldn't have to babysit a moving part on a schedule.

Second, and more irritating: the included dough hook is too short for the depth of the bowl. It doesn't reach the bottom well, so flour and shaggy dough get left behind and you're scraping constantly. I bought a third-party hook that fits properly, and it fixed the problem entirely. Frustrating that I had to spend extra to make the machine do its main job, but the fix is cheap and easy.

## The Price

It's $429. That's $80 more than the comparable KitchenAid. There's no getting around the fact that you're paying a premium, and you should know that going in.

## The Verdict

**Buy it if you knead heavy dough every week.** If you're running stiff bagel, bagel-adjacent, or high-volume sourdough batches the way I do, the extra $80 buys you a motor that won't quit, and that's worth every penny over the life of the machine. Budget another twenty bucks for a proper dough hook and expect to keep a can of WD-40 in the drawer.

**Skip it if you're mostly baking cookies and cake batter.** The SM6's whole advantage is its muscle, and you'll never use it. For lighter work, the cheaper KitchenAid does the same job, comes with a hook that actually fits, and doesn't squeak. Save your $80.

setup: A parent of two middle-schoolers is writing an op-ed to local readers urging an 8:45am middle-school start time.

a.text:
**Our Kids Aren't Lazy. They're Exhausted.**

If you've ever tried to wake a 13-year-old at 6:15 in the morning, you know it's less like waking a child and more like negotiating with a hibernating bear. I have two middle-schoolers, so I run this gauntlet twice every morning, and I'm writing to support the proposal to move our middle schools to an 8:45 start.

This isn't about coddling kids. The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends that middle and high schools start no earlier than 8:30, because adolescent biology genuinely shifts: teenagers don't get sleepy until later at night, and they still need 8.5 to 9.5 hours of sleep. Our 7:30 start means buses at 6:15, kids up by 6. Do the math on bedtime. You can put a 13-year-old in bed at nine o'clock. That doesn't mean a 13-year-old brain can fall asleep.

And this isn't just theory — we have our own evidence. Lincoln Middle piloted a later start, and the results were hard to argue with: attendance went up, and first-period grades went up. First period — the one our kids currently spend in a fog. When Lincoln's students started school at a time their bodies could handle, they showed up more and learned more. That's our district, our kids, our results.

The objection I keep hearing at meetings is buses. Won't a later middle school start wreck the bus schedule? Here's the thing: the proposal already re-tiers the routes. That work is done. It's in the plan the board will be voting on — the routes get rearranged and everyone still gets where they need to be. The loudest argument against this proposal is one the proposal itself already answers.

So what's actually left to decide? The AAP recommends it. Lincoln tested it, and it worked. The logistics are solved. The only thing standing between every middle schooler in Millbrook and a start time that matches their biology is a vote.

The board votes next month. I'd ask them — as a parent who has watched two bright, hardworking kids drag themselves to a bus stop in the dark, yawning into their jackets — to pass it.

Our kids aren't lazy. They're thirteen, and they're running on fumes. Let's stop scheduling the school day as if that's their fault.

— [Your name], parent of two Millbrook middle schoolers

b.text:
**An 8:45 Start Is the Right Choice for Millbrook**

As the parent of two Millbrook middle-schoolers, I know that getting teenagers out the door in the morning can feel like a daily test of endurance. But the debate over an 8:45 school start is about more than making mornings easier. It is about giving students a better chance to arrive at school awake, ready to learn and able to succeed.

The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends that middle and high schools start at 8:30 a.m. or later. Adolescents generally need eight to ten hours of sleep each night, yet their changing body clocks make it difficult for many of them to fall asleep early. Telling a 13-year-old to “just go to bed sooner” sounds reasonable, but it often does not match the biology of adolescence.

We also have evidence close to home. In the Lincoln Middle School pilot, attendance improved and first-period grades went up after the school adopted a later start. Those are not abstract benefits. They mean more students in their seats and more students learning during a period that too often begins with tired faces and half-open eyes.

The most common objection I hear is about buses. That concern is understandable. Families depend on reliable transportation, and changing one school’s schedule can affect the entire system. But the proposal before the board does not ignore that problem. It already re-tiers the bus routes to accommodate the 8:45 start. Any new system will require adjustment, but bus logistics should be something we solve—not a reason to reject a schedule that better serves students.

There will undoubtedly be complications involving sports, after-school activities and family routines. Our household will have to adjust, too. Still, the current early schedule also has costs: rushed mornings, missed breakfasts, late arrivals and children trying to learn while exhausted. We should not treat those costs as unavoidable simply because we are used to them.

This proposal is not a cure-all, and it will not turn every teenager into a cheerful morning person. But the AAP recommendation, the Lincoln pilot and plain common sense all point in the same direction.

When the school board votes next month, I hope its members choose the 8:45 start. Millbrook’s students deserve a school day built around when they are most able to learn.

setup: A high school girls' soccer and track coach is writing an op-ed urging turf funding for the girls' field.

a.text:
I coach girls’ soccer and track at the high school. I do it for the stipend and because I like the kids. I don’t write columns, and I don’t have patience for long speeches. But the school board is voting on next year’s facilities budget, and they need to hear something the athletic director already knows: the girls’ soccer field is a mess, and it’s dangerous.

In the last two seasons, rain has killed or moved nine of our games. Nine. The grass field floods every time a storm rolls through, and it doesn’t drain. It turns into a mud pit where the ball stops dead and kids slip and stutter-step around ruts. Last October, one of my defenders planted to make a cut and her foot caught in a rut carved out by the rain. She tore her ACL. She’s a junior who’s still not back to full speed.

Meanwhile, the football team has been playing on turf since 2019. Their games don’t get washed out. Their players don’t step in sinkholes. I’m glad they have a good surface. I’m not glad our girls are still stuck competing on a field that’s half a step above a bog.

The board needs to put turf on the girls’ soccer field in this budget. Not next year. Not after another study. Now. We’re talking about safety, we’re talking about equal treatment, and we’re talking about nine games that didn’t happen because the field was underwater. Fix the field.

b.text:
I don’t have time for metaphors. The field floods, games get canceled, and kids get hurt. Next Tuesday, the school board votes on next year’s facilities budget. Put the girls’ soccer field on turf. That’s all this comes down to.

Over the past two seasons, weather and poor drainage have forced us to cancel or relocate nine games. Nine. The field saturates, sits under water, and turns into uneven terrain. We lose valuable practice windows. We scramble to secure host schools. We spend evenings coordinating bus routes and managing parent complaints while the clock ticks toward Friday nights. And it’s not just an administrative headache. Last October, one of my players stepped into a deep rut during warmups, twisted her knee, and tore her ACL. That’s not bad luck. It’s a documented hazard disguised as normal spring weather.

In 2019, the boys’ football program received an artificial turf upgrade. There was no multi-month feasibility study. No competing bids debated into oblivion. They got the surface. They kept their schedule. Now it’s our turn. This isn’t a gender issue. It’s a baseline equity issue. These athletes sign waivers, adhere to strict attendance policies, and sacrifice weekends for the program. We don’t honor that commitment by demanding they perform safely on ground that actively works against them.

Artificial turf requires capital. I know how budget meetings work. But compare that to the recurring costs of maintaining a failing grass field: ER visits for ligament tears, coaching hours burned on rescheduling, transportation fees for makeshift venues, and a team that can’t develop offensive or defensive schemes because we never know if we’ll actually play. Turf is a fixed investment. It drains consistently. It provides uniform traction. It stops the bleeding—financially and athletically.

The board has a straightforward choice ahead. Approve the turf line item. End the seasonal uncertainty. Give the girls’ soccer program the same functional playing environment the district already installed six years ago. Don’t make me justify another flooded matchup or explain another preventable injury. Fund the surface. Get it done.

setup: You're everyone at the startup. Yesterday's 40-minute outage was caused by a bad database migration during deploy.

a.text:
Hi team,

First and foremost: the system is fully recovered, stable, and yesterday's outage is completely resolved. 

As you know, we experienced a 40-minute outage yesterday around 2:00 PM. I know this was a stressful experience, especially for those of you fielding customer complaints, so I want to share a quick breakdown of what happened and how we are preventing it from happening again.

What happened:
During a routine software update, we ran a change to our database structure. Normally this happens instantly in the background, but this specific change ended up "locking" a core part of the database. While it was locked, our system couldn't access the data it needed to function, which caused the app to go down.

How we fixed it:
We reversed the update to the previous stable version, which immediately unlocked the database and brought everything back online.

How we prevent it going forward:
To avoid this in the future, we are changing our process. Any database changes that carry a risk of locking the system will no longer be bundled with our normal daytime updates. Instead, they will be run during scheduled, off-hours maintenance windows when traffic is low.

Thank you all for your patience and for helping manage the customer impact while we worked on the fix. Please let me know if you have any questions!

Thanks,

b.text:
Everything is back to normal, and has been since about 2:40pm yesterday. No data was lost, and nothing customers had saved or submitted was affected. If anyone is still hearing about problems from a customer, send it my way and I'll dig in.

**What happened**

Around 2pm we pushed a routine update to the app. Part of that update included a change to how one of our database tables is structured — normally a quick, invisible thing. This time it took far longer than expected and, while it was running, it effectively blocked anything else from reading or writing to that table. Because that table sits in the middle of a lot of what the product does, most of the app stopped responding.

We caught it quickly, but undoing a change like this safely takes some care, so total downtime was about 40 minutes.

**Impact**

For roughly 40 minutes, customers trying to use the app would have seen errors or pages that never loaded. Anything they tried to do during that window didn't go through, so some may have needed to redo an action. Nothing was corrupted or lost.

Thank you to everyone who fielded customer messages while we were heads-down on the fix — that made a real difference.

**What we're changing**

Changes of this type won't run during regular deploys anymore. They'll happen in a scheduled maintenance window, which means we can watch them closely, communicate ahead of time if we expect any disruption, and stop them safely if something looks wrong. We're also adding a check that flags this category of change before it ships, so it can't slip into a normal deploy by accident.

Happy to go deeper on the technical details with anyone who's curious — just ask. And if you're talking to a customer who wants an explanation, feel free to use the "what happened" section above word for word.

setup: A fourth-generation soybean and corn farmer is writing a newsletter commentary on crop insurance costs and SB 214 for county readers and state legislators.

a.text:
# The 22% That Came Out of My Pocket

The USDA raised the prevented planting base premium rate 22% this year for our region. For my operation, that worked out to roughly $46,000 in additional cost, and that's on top of a spring where I could only get 60% of my acres in the ground before the late May deadline.

I want to walk through the numbers, because I think most of us felt the pinch but haven't sat down and added it all up.

When the rain finally let up enough to plant, the calendar had already decided my season for me. Prevented planting coverage is exactly what it's for—it's the safety net that keeps a bad spring from becoming a lost year. But the 22% rate increase means that safety net costs dramatically more to hold onto right when we needed it most.

Here's the part that stings worse, and it's the reason I'm writing this: the way the acreage caps are structured, family operations like mine absorb this increase at a higher effective rate than the larger operations nearby. A big operation can spread its planted and prevented acres across a larger base, so the cap doesn't bind the same way it does for us. When you're farming a family-sized footprint, the cap hits earlier, and every percentage point of premium increase lands on fewer acres to carry it. The 22% isn't evenly distributed, even though the announcement reads like it is.

I've farmed my whole life on ground my great-grandfather broke. I'm not looking for sympathy—wet springs come with the territory. What I'm asking is that the rules be fair when the wet spring arrives. Right now, they aren't.

Senate Bill 214 would fix the acreage cap so that family operations aren't paying a disproportionate share of these premium increases. It's a targeted fix. It doesn't cost the state much, and it doesn't change anyone's coverage—it just makes the cap reflect the reality of how mid-sized family farms are structured.

Our state legislators read this newsletter, and I hope they read this piece. Call their offices. Write them. Tell them you support SB 214, and tell them why: not because farming is hard—everybody knows that—but because a 22% premium increase that falls hardest on family operations is a policy choice, and policy choices can be changed.

I paid my $46,000 this year. I'd rather pay for a wet spring than for an unfair rule. Right now I'm paying for both.

b.text:
## A $46,000 Increase for One Wet Spring

This spring, I was able to plant only 60% of my soybean and corn acres by the late-May deadline. The rain kept coming, and the fields stayed too wet to work. That left a large share of my operation facing prevented planting coverage.

At the same time, USDA raised the base prevented-planting premium rate in our region by 22%. For my farm, that increase adds approximately $46,000 to this year’s costs—before accounting for lost production, machinery expenses, input commitments, and the income we will not receive from those acres.

The acreage cap makes that increase even harder on family operations. The cap does not affect every farm in the same way. For a farm like mine, where each acre represents a larger share of the operation’s total revenue, the added premium cost takes a bigger proportional bite. Larger operations nearby may absorb the same rate increase across more acres and more production. Family farms do not have that same cushion.

This is not about avoiding responsibility or asking taxpayers to cover every bad outcome. We pay premiums, manage risk, and make planting decisions based on the best information available. But when a federally determined rate jumps 22% in a year when weather prevents planting, the acreage cap can turn an already difficult situation into a disproportionate financial burden for farms like mine.

Senate Bill 214 would fix the acreage-cap problem and make the program more equitable for family-sized operations. It would not eliminate the risks of farming or guarantee a profit. It would simply ensure that the program’s limits do not penalize smaller operations more severely than larger ones.

I encourage farm bureau members and other producers to contact their legislators and support SB 214. A $46,000 increase is not an abstract policy number for my farm. It is a real cost tied directly to a wet spring and a program structure that needs to be corrected.

setup: A solo SaaS founder is posting a thread to indie hackers and customers about a pricing mistake and the fix.

a.text:
I made a massive pricing mistake with Tallyup.

I raised our prices by 40% on everyone overnight.

In just one week, I lost 30 of our 140 customers.

Here is what went wrong, why it blew up, and what I changed: 🧵

1/ The background:

Every advice thread for indie SaaS founders says the same thing: "Charge more."

As a solo founder building Tallyup (a retention tool for gym owners), I knew the value was there. So I decided it was time to adjust our pricing up by 40%.

2/ The mistake wasn't the price increase itself—it was how I rolled it out.

- I applied the 40% hike to existing users overnight.
- I gave zero advance notice.
- I didn't grandfather the early users who supported the product from day one.

3/ The fallout was fast.

In 7 days, 30 out of our 140 customers canceled. 

In a close-knit niche like gym owners, trust matters. Forcing a sudden 40% jump on existing users broke that trust, and the cancellations poured in.

4/ What I changed to fix it:

- Reverted the price hike for all impacted existing users and reached out directly to explain.
- Grandfathered existing accounts at their original rate.
- Applied the new 40% higher pricing ONLY to new sign-ups moving forward.

5/ Lessons learned the hard way:

- Protect your early supporters. Grandfather existing users when making big leaps.
- Test new pricing on new traffic, not your existing base.
- If you ever do change rates for current customers, give plenty of advance notice and clear reasoning.

Building in public means sharing the bad decisions alongside the wins. Hopefully, this saves another solo founder from making the same mistake.

b.text:
1/ I made a pricing mistake at Tallyup.

I raised prices 40% on everyone overnight.

Within a week, we lost 30 of our 140 customers.

Here’s what happened, and what I changed:

2/ The mistake wasn’t just the increase.

It was the surprise.

Customers had signed up under one expectation, then woke up to a different one.

No warning. No transition. No chance to ask questions.

3/ When you raise prices on existing customers without context, it can feel like a broken promise.

Especially with gym owners. Retention is personal to them, and Tallyup is supposed to help with that.

4/ What I changed:

- No more overnight pricing decisions
- Separate new customers from existing customers
- Give advance notice
- Explain the reason before the change
- Make it easy for customers to reach out and talk

5/ The lesson: pricing is not just a spreadsheet decision.

It’s trust, timing, and communication.

A price change can be reasonable and still be delivered badly.

6/ I’m building Tallyup in public, and this is part of it.

I’d rather share the mistake than pretend we got everything right.

If you’re thinking about raising prices, don’t surprise the people who already believed in you.

setup: A high school girls' soccer and track coach is writing an op-ed urging turf funding for the girls' field.

a.text:
# The Girls' Soccer Field Needs Turf. Here's Why.

I coach girls' soccer and track at our high school. I'm writing this because our soccer field is a problem the school board can fix, and next year's budget is the time to do it.

Start with the games we've lost. Over the last two seasons, nine of our games have been rained out or moved off-site because the grass field floods. It doesn't take much. A steady rain the night before, and we're playing in standing water or not playing at all. That's nine times our girls trained all week for nothing, or got bused somewhere else to play a "home" game. Rescheduling isn't free either. It costs officials' fees, transportation, and the goodwill of every family trying to plan around it.

Now the part that matters most. Last October, one of my players tore her ACL. She stepped in a rut in that field and her knee went. That's a torn ligament, surgery, months of rehab, and a season—maybe a career—gone. The field is uneven because it floods and gets torn up, and grass fields that get overused and waterlogged don't heal right. This isn't bad luck. It's a predictable result of playing on a field that isn't safe.

Turf drains. Turf is flat. Turf doesn't develop ruts that blow out a 16-year-old's knee. This isn't complicated.

And here's the other thing I'll say plainly: the boys' football field got turf in 2019. So the district already knows turf is worth the money, already knows how to budget for it, already made the case that our athletes deserve a safe, playable surface. The boys got that answer five years ago. The girls are still waiting, still getting rained out, still stepping in ruts.

I'm not asking for something new or extravagant. I'm asking the board to do for the girls exactly what it already did for the boys. Same standard. Same safety. Same respect.

I coach for the stipend, not because I love writing op-eds. But I've watched enough canceled games and carried enough girls off that field to know this needs saying. Put turf on the girls' soccer field in next year's budget. It's overdue, it's fair, and it will keep our players safe.

*[Name], girls' soccer and track coach*

b.text:
Nine girls’ soccer games have been rained out or moved in the last two seasons because our grass field floods. The boys’ football field got turf in 2019.

The school board is about to vote on next year’s facilities budget. It’s time to put turf on the girls’ soccer field—with the drainage and maintenance plan needed to make it work.

I coach girls’ soccer and track at our public high school. I’m not asking for a showpiece. I’m asking for a field we can count on using.

When a game gets moved, families have to rearrange rides and work schedules. When it gets canceled, players lose a chance to compete after putting in the work to prepare. Coaches can adjust. So can kids. But nine games in two seasons is not an occasional inconvenience. It is a facilities problem.

Last October, one of my players tore her ACL stepping in a rut on our field. I’m not going to claim that turf prevents ACL injuries. It doesn’t, and the board should look carefully at the safety, heat and maintenance requirements of any surface it considers. But we cannot talk about the drawbacks of replacing this field while ignoring the condition of the field our girls use now.

Keeping what we have is also a decision. Our players live with that decision every season.

Then there is the fairness question.

The district invested in turf for boys’ football in 2019. I’m glad those athletes have it. This is not an argument for taking anything away from them. It is an argument for giving girls’ soccer the same serious attention when its field repeatedly fails.

Our girls practice, compete and represent this school. They deserve more than being told to make do with a flooded field while another program has had turf for years.

I know facilities money is limited. Classrooms need repairs. Other teams have needs. A responsible board has to weigh all of that. It also has to account for the full cost of turf, including upkeep and eventual replacement—not just installation.

So get solid bids. Require proper drainage. Ask hard questions about player safety and long-term costs. Then fund the project instead of pushing it into another budget year.

I expect my players to show up prepared and take care of their responsibilities. They should be able to expect the district to take care of its responsibilities, too.

They have put in the work. Give them a field that does.

setup: A retired Army staff sergeant is writing about coming home after his second deployment for readers of the veterans' writing workshop anthology.

a.text:
The carousel stopped. Luggage spilled out in uneven waves. I stepped off the rubber mat and waited by the arrival gate. My wife found me first. She looked tired. Her hair was pulled back in a frayed scrunchie, sleeves rolled up past her elbows. Behind her, my daughter stepped forward. She didn’t recognize me. Not right away. She just pressed herself against her mother’s leg. Her hands gripped the hem of my wife’s shirt. I stood up straight. Nodded once. My duffel felt heavier than it should. We walked out to the parking lot. She didn’t speak in the car. Just watched the highway blur past the window. I kept my hands at ten and two. Same way I had for eleven months.

This was the second time I’d come home. The first time, everything felt loud. This time, it felt thin. Like I was walking through glass.

A few days later, we went to the grocery store. The automatic doors slid open and pushed warm air across my ankles. Fluorescent lights hummed overhead. I pushed the cart down the main aisle, then turned toward breakfast foods. Cereal boxes lined the shelves. Cheerios. Corn Flakes. Shredded Wheat. Raisin Bran. Honey Oats. Cinnamon Crisp. Apple Cinnamon Clusters. Fourteen brands alone, each with five variations. Forty kinds. Forty different promises. I hadn’t seen a full pantry in over a year. In Helmand, breakfast was a foil packet of powdered eggs and instant coffee stirred with boiling water from a canteen cup. You ate it standing up, before sunrise. Here, I reached for a box of corn flakes. Set it down. Pulled down a granola blend. Read the back. Put it back. Checked the price. Tapped my thumb against the plastic handle. People walked around me. A kid dropped a juice box. A cart squeaked near the dairy case. Twenty minutes went by. I realized I hadn’t moved from that spot. My wife called from the cleaning supplies aisle. Asked if I needed sponges. I grabbed the first cereal I’d touched. Walked to checkout. Didn’t look back at the shelf.

At night, the house was quiet. Too quiet. I climbed into bed and rolled onto my left side. Back to the door. Always back to the door. After the first deployment, I started doing it. When the world changes direction, you learn to orient yourself to the exit. You sleep facing the door. You rest light. For a year, that’s what my body did. Even on leave. Even in my own house. The sheets cooled against my spine. My breathing stayed shallow. At 3 a.m., I woke up dry-mouthed and tense. Same every night.

My wife left the bedroom door open. Said it helped with airflow. Said it made the place feel less like a barracks. For a while, I kept turning toward it anyway. Muscle memory doesn’t read memos. So I started practicing. I’d lie on my back. Eyes on the ceiling tile directly above the headboard. Count the seams. Feel the mattress shift under my weight. Force my shoulders down. Unclench my jaw. It took a week before I stopped waking up scanning the hallway. It took another two before I could leave the door open and actually drift off. The fan clicked on high. It kicked cool air across the room. Dust motes drifted in the blue nightlight glow. I didn’t think about what happened out there. I just let the noise fill the space. Breathing matched the rotation. In. Out. In. Out. Morning came. Sun stripped across the floorboards. I swung my legs over the edge of the bed. Feet hit carpet. Door was still open. House was still here. I stood up. Got ready for the day.

b.text:
I got off the plane and walked out into the terminal. My wife was there with our daughter. The girl was six. She saw me and ducked behind her mom's leg. Held on tight. Wouldn't look up. I stood there with my bag, waiting. After a minute she peeked out, then hid again. My wife said her name and pulled her around a little. She stared at my face like she was trying to match it to something. Finally she let go and took a step. I picked her up. She was stiff at first.

We drove home. The house looked the same. Same couch, same pictures on the wall. That night I went to bed and pushed the door almost shut the way I always had over there. Then I remembered and opened it all the way. Lay down facing the open doorway. Couldn't sleep. Kept checking it. Next night same thing. Took a week before I could leave it open and turn my back to it.

A couple days later I went to the store for milk and cereal. Stood in the aisle looking at the shelves. There must have been forty kinds. Boxes of all colors, some with cartoons, some with fruit, some claiming to be healthy. I picked one up, put it back. Picked another. Stood there twenty minutes. A woman with a cart asked if I needed help finding something. I said no. Finally grabbed a plain box of corn flakes and left. 

That was the first week home.

setup: You're everyone at the startup. Yesterday's 40-minute outage was caused by a bad database migration during deploy.

a.text:
Hi everyone,

Quick summary up front: yesterday's outage is fully resolved. Service has been stable since we fixed it yesterday afternoon, and we've changed our process so this specific issue can't happen the same way again. Details below for anyone who wants them.

**What happened**

Starting around 2pm yesterday, the product was unavailable for about 40 minutes. During a routine deploy, a database change we were rolling out locked one of our main data tables for far longer than it should have. The closest analogy: imagine a delivery truck parking across the only road into a warehouse — nothing could move in or out until it was cleared. Once we identified the cause, we rolled the change back and service came back up.

**Impact**

- Product unavailable for roughly 40 minutes, starting around 2pm
- No action needed from anyone — this is informational only
- For those of you who fielded customer questions during the window, thank you. If it's helpful, feel free to reuse this with customers: "We experienced a brief service interruption yesterday afternoon. The issue has been fully resolved, and we've made changes to prevent it from happening again."

**What we're changing**

Database changes like this one will no longer run as part of regular deploys. They'll run during scheduled maintenance windows — low-traffic times where we can watch them closely and react quickly if anything looks off.

I know a few of you were dealing with frustrated customers in real time while this was happening, and I'm sorry for the scramble. This one's on us, and I appreciate how quickly everyone jumped in.

If you have questions or want the more technical writeup, just reply here or grab me directly.

Thanks,
[Your name]

b.text:
Hi everyone,

First and foremost: the application is fully operational and the issue from yesterday is completely resolved. 

I know several of you had to field customer complaints during the downtime, so I want to provide a quick explanation of what happened and what we are doing to prevent it from happening again.

**What happened**
Yesterday around 2:00 PM, the platform went down for about 40 minutes. 

**The cause**
This downtime occurred during a routine daily update. We were applying a structural change to our database (a migration), which unexpectedly "locked" a critical data table for much longer than normal. Because the application couldn't access that table, the whole system froze. 

**The resolution**
Once we pinpointed the issue, we immediately canceled the database update and rolled our systems back to their previous state to bring everything back online. 

**Next steps**
To make sure this doesn’t cause daytime disruptions in the future, we are changing our process. From now on, any updates that involve these heavier database changes will be scheduled to run during an off-hours maintenance window, rather than during our regular daytime deployments.

Please let me know if you have any questions or need any specific details to share with affected customers.

setup: A bakery owner is writing a warm blog and newsletter post to regular customers explaining why wedding cake orders are ending.

a.text:
**A note about wedding cakes**

I've started this post a few times now, so I'll just say it plainly: we're no longer taking custom wedding cake orders.

First, the part that's easy. We have loved making them. Being even a small part of someone's wedding day is one of the best things about this job, and some of my favorite mornings in this kitchen have been delivery mornings — carrying a cake out the door and hoping it makes somebody cry in the good way. To everyone who trusted us with yours over the years: thank you, truly. We never took that lightly.

Here's the harder part, but I think you deserve the honest version. Every custom wedding cake, before we ever turn the ovens on, takes about fourteen hours of consultations, tastings, sketches, and back-and-forth emails — all of it unpaid. We're a three-person shop, and I'm already up at four most mornings. Those fourteen hours have to come from somewhere, and where they've been coming from is the case.

And the case is the whole point. The croissants, the morning buns, the bread you grab on your way home, the thing you pick up with your coffee on a Tuesday — that's what pays our rent and keeps our lights on. It's what this bakery actually is. This year there were weeks when I looked at the case and it was thinner than I wanted it to be, because our attention was somewhere else. That didn't sit right with me.

The other piece of it: we had three couples cancel at the last minute this year, after we'd already bought ingredients — special-order things we couldn't return or use anywhere else. I'm not angry about it. Plans change, weddings fall apart, life happens to good people. But three in one year made the math impossible to ignore. On a custom order, nearly all of the risk sits with us, and we're too small to keep carrying it.

So that's the news. Nothing else is changing. The case will be full, we'll be here same as always, and honestly we'll probably be happier, because this is us getting back to the thing we're actually built for. And if you're planning a wedding and need a cake — come talk to me anyway. I know some wonderful bakers who do this work full-time and do it beautifully, and I'm glad to point you their way.

Thank you for being the kind of customers I can write a letter like this to. Most businesses would send out something polished and vague. I get to just tell you the truth, and that's because of who you are.

See you at the counter.

— [Your name]

b.text:
It’s a little past noon here at the bakery, which means my 4 am alarm is finally starting to catch up with me, but I wanted to sit down with a cup of coffee and share a quick update with you all before we dive into the weekend rush. 

We’ve been taking a hard look at how we spend our time in the kitchen lately, and we’ve made the bittersweet decision to step away from taking on custom wedding cakes. 

I know this might be disappointing for those of you planning your big days, but I always want to be totally transparent with the community that supports us. setup: A fourth-generation soybean and corn farmer is writing a newsletter commentary on crop insurance costs and SB 214 for county readers and state legislators.

a.text:
# The Math on This Spring Doesn't Add Up

By the time the late May planting deadline arrived, I had 60% of my acres in the ground. The rest were underwater or too wet to touch. That's just how this spring went — I'm not here to complain about the rain.

I'm here to talk about what happened next.

USDA raised the prevented planting base rate 22% for our region this year. On my operation, that works out to about $46,000 in additional premium costs. Forty-six thousand dollars, not for seed or fertilizer or land — for an insurance bill on ground I couldn't plant.

Here's what makes it harder to swallow: the way the acreage caps are structured under the current formula, that 22% hits smaller family operations at a higher proportional cost per acre than it does the larger operations nearby. I'm not naming names. We all know the operations I'm talking about, and most of them are good people. But the math is the math. When you scale up enough, the cap structure softens the blow in a way that just doesn't apply to a farm my size. The 22% increase lands differently depending on where you sit on the acreage curve, and fourth-generation operations like mine are sitting in the worst spot.

My great-grandfather broke ground on this ground. My grandfather held it through the '80s. My father put in the drainage tile that's now overflowing. I'd like to hand it to my kids without a mortgage note tied to an insurance premium I couldn't control.

There's a fix sitting in the legislature right now. Senate Bill 214 addresses the acreage cap formula that's driving this disparity. It doesn't eliminate the premium increase, and it's not a handout. It adjusts the cap structure so that family-scale operations aren't carrying a disproportionately heavier load per acre than the operations that already have more room to absorb these hits.

I'd ask you to do two things. First, call your state senator and tell them to support SB 214. Second, show up at the farm bureau meeting next month and make sure this stays on our legislative priority list. The newsletter reaches a lot of mailboxes in this county. Let's make sure the people opening them know the numbers — and know that there's something we can do about them.

The rain will do what the rain does. But the cap formula is something we wrote, and it's something we can fix.

b.text:
This spring I got 60% of my acres planted by the late May deadline. The other 40% sat underwater while the rain kept coming. That’s not a new story—what’s new is the bill.

USDA jacked the prevented planting base rate 22% in our region this year. For my operation, that means roughly $46,000 in additional premium costs for coverage I didn’t choose to need. I’ll absorb it because the alternative is worse, but I’m not writing about the weather. I’m writing about the math.

Here’s what the numbers don’t show on the rate sheet: the acreage cap. Because of how the subsidy structure is built, that 22% increase hits family operations like mine harder proportionally than the bigger spreads nearby. We carry a heavier load per acre, and when you’re only planting 60% of what you planned, every capped dollar stings worse.

There’s a fix sitting in the legislature. SB 214 would adjust the acreage cap so family farms aren’t shouldering a disproportionate share of a federal rate hike we had no hand in setting. If you’re reading this, you’re likely in the same boat—literally, this spring. Call your state senator and representative. Tell them to pass SB 214. We’ve got enough unpredictability to manage without the policy stack working against us too.

setup: A parent of two middle-schoolers is writing an op-ed to local readers urging an 8:45am middle-school start time.

a.text:
My kitchen at 6:15 feels less like a home and more like a dispatch center. Me, pouring cereal with one hand, shoving backpacks with the other, while my two middle-schoolers in Millbrook shuffle past like zombies. I stopped saying “hurry up” months ago. I just accepted that their bodies haven’t gotten the memo that seventh grade begins before sunrise.

You know the board’s ask: push middle school bells to 8:45 a.m. I’ve read the full proposal closely, because this isn’t just a calendar tweak. It’s about whether our kids can actually wake up enough to learn. The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends middle schools start no earlier than 8:30 a.m. It’s not convenience. It’s biology. Puberty shifts adolescent sleep cycles, making pre-dawn classes physiologically brutal. Cramped schedules don’t build grit. They build burnout.

We don’t have to wonder if later starts help. Last year, Lincoln Middle piloted an 8:45 start. The results speak for themselves: attendance rose, and first-period grades climbed. Teachers noted sharper focus and fewer glazed stares before anyone’s coffee had kicked in. Real kids showing up, not just names on a spreadsheet. These weren’t marginal bumps. They were measurable improvements.

Then comes the bus worry. I hear it constantly at pickup lines and over backyard fences. No one wants stranded families or extra miles in the dark. But the proposal already solves this through route re-tiering. By staggering dismissals across different start windows, the district mapped a practical transit fix. They’ll run later, but smarter. Parents, teachers, and drivers will adjust. That’s how communities work. The logistics are already on the table; we just need to adopt them.

Next month, when the board votes, look past the clock change to what’s actually at stake. Align our schedule with how kids actually develop. Prioritize rest so learning can happen. Trust the evidence over outdated routine. Please support the 8:45 start. Vote yes. For the sake of our kids, and for the sake of surviving the morning rush.

b.text:
**To the Editor: Let Them Sleep. Then Send Them to School at 8:45.**

I read the school board's 8:45 start-time proposal at my kitchen table last Tuesday, after my seventh-grade daughter had finally closed her laptop and my sixth-grade son had finally gotten out of the shower. I read it carefully, because I care about how this town runs its schools. And I'm writing to ask you to support it.

I'll start with the part that isn't really controversial. The American Academy of Pediatrics says kids aged 11 to 14 need eight to ten hours of sleep a night. The same AAP advisory notes that middle-schoolers who go to bed before they're actually sleepy are *wired*, not tired—hormones, circadian shift, all of it. Our kids aren't lazy. They're biology going public.

I'm not a researcher, so I lean on what our own district can already see. The Lincoln Middle pilot ran the later start for a full semester. Attendance ticked up. First-period grades—the one everyone worries about—went up too. Not by a little. Enough that Lincoln's principal noted fewer "first-ten-minutes-of-homeroom zombie" reports from teachers. You don't need a peer-reviewed journal to know what that looks like at our kitchen table at 6:45 a.m., when I'm coaxing two humans into socks while they moan like they've been drafted.

Now, the bus question. I get it—I get it. You're a commuter, a nurse with a night shift, a single parent who needs that 7:15 yellow line at the corner. You looked at the old schedule and thought, *if high school starts later, what happens to me?* I did the same math, cross-eyed, with a coffee. But the proposal already re-tiers the routes. Elementary moves first, middle next, high school last. Three runs, staggered so the buses actually make every stop. It's not a science project. It's logistics the district has already modeled, and the numbers close.

I'm not asking you to love the change. I'm asking you to let the kids sleep seventy-five more minutes and then walk into a building where a teacher can start the day with an actual, present, half-awake human being instead of a body in a desk.

The board votes next month. If you're reading this over morning coffee, please call or email them. Tell them a parent in your kid's building thinks 8:45 is right.

We'll get our commute sorted. Let's not sort our kids at the cost of their sleep.

—A parent of two, Millbrook

setup: A real estate agent is posting one specific observation about early block walks and happier buyers to LinkedIn buyers, agents, and lenders.

a.text:
Twelve years into selling homes in Asheville, I've started to believe I can predict which buyers will still love their house five years from now. It's not the ones who found the best kitchen or won the bidding war. It's the ones who walked the neighborhood at 7am before we ever wrote an offer.

I started giving this advice because of the Pruitts. First-time buyers, pre-approved, and torn between two houses. One photographed beautifully. The other was a plainer place over on Sycamore Street. On a hunch, I told them: before you decide, go stand on both streets at seven on a weekday morning. See what wakes up. See who drives through.

The pretty house sat on a street that turned into a commuter cut-through at about 6:45, cars idling at the stop sign, headlights sweeping the bedroom windows. Sycamore Street at 7am was a school bus, three dog walkers, somebody's wood stove going, and a neighbor who saw them standing on the sidewalk, crossed the street, and said, "If you buy the blue house, I'll see you at the block party." They bought the blue house.

The Pruitts still text me a photo from that porch every year on their closing anniversary. I don't think they ever fell in love with the house, honestly. They fell in love with the street at 7am, and the house just came with it.

So if you're touring right now: a showing tells you about the house. Seven in the morning tells you about the street, and you're buying both. Go walk it before you sign anything.

b.text:
After twelve years of selling homes here in Asheville, I’ve developed a rule of thumb for first-time buyers that sounds overly simple, but it rarely fails: walk the neighborhood at 7:00 AM on a Tuesday before you put in an offer.

Open houses are staged theatre. At 2:00 PM on a Saturday, the sunlight is flattering, soft music is playing, nobody is rushing to work, and every street feels peaceful. Real life, however, happens at 7:00 in the morning on a weekday.

A few years back, I was working with the Pruitts on a bungalow over on Sycamore Street. It checked every box on their spreadsheet, but it was at the very top of their budget, and they were agonizing over the decision. I told them to grab a thermos of coffee, park two blocks away, and just walk the loop around Sycamore before the workday started.

They watched where the sun actually hit the front porch. They saw which direction the commuter traffic backed up trying to turn onto the main road. They ran into an older neighbor walking his hound, who warned them that the bottom curve of the road tends to hold black ice for three days after a freeze, but that the neighborhood potluck in October was not to be missed. 

They made the offer that afternoon. Not because the neighborhood was flawless, but because the romanticized version in their heads had been replaced by the real thing, and they still loved it. 

Four years later, they’re still on Sycamore, and whenever I run into them at the grocery store, they talk about that morning walk. The buyers who take the time to see a street at its most mundane, groggy hour are almost always the ones who are still in love with their choice five years down the road.
