setup: A wedding photographer is posting that couples who ditch rigid shot lists get better photos, using the rained-out Barrera wedding as an example.

a.text:
In my 8 years shooting weddings full-time, I’ve noticed a consistent trend: the couples who ditch the rigid "shot list" always end up with the best photos. 

When you hire a photographer, you’re hiring them for their eye, instinct, and experience—not their ability to check boxes on a clipboard. A strict list often forces a photographer to hunt for manufactured moments rather than capturing the authentic magic of the day as it actually unfolds.

Take the Barrera wedding, for example. Out of nowhere, the Texas Hill Country weather turned on us and the outdoor ceremony got completely rained out. If we had been tied to a pre-planned list of locations and specific poses, the timeline pivot would have been an absolute disaster. 

Instead, the couple completely let go of expectations and trusted the vendor team. We moved everything under a massive, sprawling pecan tree to wait out the worst of the weather. The rain shifted the light, creating an incredibly romantic, moody atmosphere. Because I was free to just observe and shoot, I was able to capture the raw, unscripted joy of the couple laughing together under those branches while their guests huddled nearby. 

Those ended up being some of the most powerful images I’ve ever delivered. 

To engaged couples currently planning: do your research, hire a vendor team whose vision you completely trust, and then give them the freedom to do their best work. The magic happens in the moments you can't plan for.

To my fellow wedding professionals: here is to the couples who embrace the pivot! 

What’s the best unscripted moment you’ve experienced at an event?

b.text:
I've photographed weddings in the Texas Hill Country for 8 years and around 35 a year.

One thing I've learned: the couples who throw out the shot list always end up with the better photos.

The Barrera wedding is my favorite example.

It rained. Not a drizzle — a real Hill Country downpour.

The whole timeline was shot. The ceremony backdrop was unusable. The portrait spot we'd scouted was a puddle.

So we moved everything under this massive pecan tree on the property. Old thing. Had probably been standing longer than anyone at the wedding.

Family photos under the pecan tree. Bride and groom portraits under the pecan tree. Quiet moments between them under the pecan tree.

The couple had come to me with a classic shot list. Specific groupings, specific poses, the whole nine yards.

By the end of the night, none of it mattered.

What they wanted was each other. Under that tree. In the rain. With everyone they loved huddled around them.

That's the photo they tell me is still their favorite.

The shot list would've given them a checklist. The storm gave them something real.

If you're planning a wedding right now, my honest advice: hire a photographer you trust, then actually trust them. The best images don't come from a list. They come from the moments no one planned for.

setup: An in-house recruiter is posting a contrarian observation about candidates asking about the team’s last failed project in interviews to recruiters, hiring managers, and job seekers.

a.text:
After sitting in ~200 interviews, I’ve noticed a pattern:

The best candidates ask about our last failed project.

Not in a “gotcha” way. They’re trying to understand how the company handles reality.

One candidate asked me:

“What’s something the team tried, learned didn’t work, and then changed because of that?”

I told her about a warehouse staffing model we rolled out that looked great on paper but struggled during peak season because we hadn’t tested it against the way supervisors actually assign daily work.

Her next question was even better:

“Who was responsible for pulling it back, and what changed before the next rollout?”

That’s when I knew she was serious.

She wasn’t trying to catch us off guard. She was trying to figure out whether leaders here admit mistakes, how quickly teams course-correct, and whether lessons actually stick.

A lot of candidates ask about growth, culture, and expectations.

The ones who stand out ask about failure.

Because every company has it. The good ones don’t hide it.

b.text:
After ~200 interviews, here's a pattern I can't unsee:

The strongest candidates ask about the projects that didn't work.

Most people ask about growth, roadmap, "what does success look like in this role." Fine questions. Safe questions.

But every so often someone asks: "Tell me about a project that failed recently. What happened?"

Had one last month. When I brought up a warehouse routing rollout we'd scrapped, most candidates would nod and move on. This one asked why we scrapped it, who made that call, and whether we'd try again with a different approach.

That's not a candidate trying to impress me. That's someone figuring out how we handle being wrong—because they're deciding if they want to work here as much as I'm deciding if I want to hire them.

The failed-project question tells them more than any polished win story ever could. How we talk about failure is how we'll talk about theirs.

If you're interviewing soon, ask it. And pay attention to how long it takes us to answer.

setup: A general contractor is writing a short X thread to contractors, homeowners, and architects about a hidden joist problem and the lesson learned.

a.text:
1/ Opened up the kitchen ceiling on the Maple Ave job Tuesday. Three joists notched more than halfway through for an old cast iron drain line that got abandoned decades ago. Nobody ever sistered them. Floor above had a sag the homeowner thought was "just old house charm."

2/ Fix was 6 sistered joists, new blocking, and a half day of plumbing rerouting we didn't plan for. About $2,800 and pushed the schedule 3 days. Homeowner wasn't thrilled but I'd flagged the possibility in writing before demo, so the conversation was easy.

3/ The lesson isn't "old houses have surprises." Everybody knows that. It's that the change order conversation happens at contract signing, not when you're standing under a cut joist. I put a line in every proposal: concealed conditions = documented, photographed, priced before we proceed.

4/ 15 years in and the jobs that go sideways are almost never about the framing. They're about expectations nobody set. The joists were a Tuesday problem. Bad paperwork would've made them a lawsuit.

b.text:
Framing the Maple Ave kitchen took a turn when we started laying out the main span joists. Driven two nails through the pantry ceiling and hit solid timber where there should’ve been open space. Old beam from a demolished interior wall sitting right in our joist path.

Had to modify the layout, add structural hangers, and sister three joists around it. Came out to roughly $1,800 in materials and a full day of labor. Change order issued, signed, and we kept the timeline intact. Old Pittsburgh homes don’t read the blueprints, and neither should you wait to find out.

Real lesson from 15 years on site: never finalize joist layouts or final bids without poking a few diagnostic holes first. Transparency beats assumptions every time. Homeowners hiring remodelers, insist on exploratory inspections before breaking ground. Contractors, lock in your surprise-structural workflow early. Clean scopes start with clean discovery.

The job, day to day:

- Answering tickets from dispatchers running small fleets. Mostly email, some phone. They're busy, direct, usually not software people, and often writing in because something in their day just broke. Your job: fix it, or find out who can and own the follow-up.

- The recurring questions: rescheduling a load that changed, a driver who didn't get a notification, setting up a recurring route, billing, "is it down or is it me." A lot of these repeat — which means you'll get good fast.

- When something's actually broken: reproduce it, collect the details, hand us a clean writeup, and keep the customer updated until it's fixed. You don't need to code. You do need to not vanish on someone.

- Onboarding new customers — a setup call, a walkthrough, and honest answers to "can it do X" (sometimes the answer is no).

setup: A real estate agent is writing a commentary on the local market for brokerage blog and local paper readers.

a.text:
## The Market Didn't Break. The Clock Just Changed.

I've had three separate conversations this month that went almost word for word the same way. Seller sitting at the kitchen table, sixty-some days on market, maybe four showings total, and they look at me and say some version of: "We're not giving it away."

Nobody's asking you to give it away. I'm asking you to price it like it's 2025.

Here's what's actually happening in our zip code. Last spring, the median days on market was eight. Eight. You listed on a Thursday, you had offers by Sunday night, and half of them were waiving inspection and throwing in an appraisal gap. This spring, that number is thirty-four. That's not a rounding error. That's a different market wearing the same clothes.

And yet list prices are up six percent year over year. Six percent, while showings per listing have been cut clean in half. Read that sentence again, because it's the whole story. Sellers are asking more money from fewer buyers who are taking four times as long to decide. That math doesn't work, and it's not going to start working because we want it to.

So let me say the thing everyone's dancing around: this is not a crash. I've been doing this ten years, I remember what a bad market smells like, and this isn't it. Homes are still selling. Good homes, priced right, are going in under two weeks — I've closed three like that since February. Buyers are out there. They're employed, they're pre-approved, they toured your house on a Saturday and they liked it.

They just didn't like it *that* much.

What we have is a pricing problem dressed up as a demand problem. And the reason it's so hard to shake is that sellers are anchored to a nine-week window in 2022 when their neighbor's split-level went thirty grand over ask to a guy who'd never seen it in person. That was the anomaly. That was the fever. We all knew it at the time and said so out loud, and then somehow it became the baseline against which every listing since has been judged.

I have a seller right now — good people, lovely house, genuinely one of the nicer kitchens on their street — who has been on the market since early March. We've had two showings in the last three weeks. I brought them a comp analysis showing three comparable homes that sold in the same window, all of them priced eight to twelve thousand below where we are. Their response: "Those houses don't have our lot."

Maybe not. But the market doesn't price your lot. Buyers price your lot, and right now buyers are pricing your lot at less than you are.

Here's what I wish more sellers understood about the mechanics of this. In an eight-day market, overpricing costs you almost nothing. The market is moving so fast it catches up to your mistake in two weeks and you sell anyway, and you tell yourself you were smart to hold firm. In a thirty-four-day market, overpricing is expensive and the expense compounds. You burn your first two weeks — the only two weeks when every buyer with a saved search gets an alert with your address on it — talking to nobody. Then you sit. Then the days-on-market counter starts doing your negotiating for you, badly. Then when you finally do cut, buyers don't read it as a deal. They read it as a question: what's wrong with it?

The price drop you refuse to make in week three is almost always smaller than the price drop you'll accept in week ten. I have watched this play out enough times that I'd put money on it.

The flip side, and this is the part I want to shout from the parking lot: the sellers who *are* getting it are doing great. Not surviving. Doing great. Price it at what the last three comps actually closed at, not what your neighbor listed at and later withdrew. Clean it out. Fix the thing you've been meaning to fix for four years. Take the pre-listing inspection seriously. Those houses are going pending in ten, twelve days, at or near ask, with normal contract terms and buyers who show up to closing happy. There is nothing wrong with this market for people who are willing to meet it where it is.

So no, I'm not going to tell you the market is complicated and depends on many factors. It depends on one factor right now, and that factor is whether the seller has updated their internal calendar. The buyers already have. Rates did that for them. They're methodical now. They tour four houses instead of one. They go home and think about it. They come back for a second showing before they write. That's not weakness — that's what a normal market has always looked like, and we're just out of practice.

The pace changed. The price expectations didn't. That gap is where the thirty-four days lives.

Close the gap and you'll be moving by summer. Don't, and I'll see you in September, taking less than I'm telling you to take today.

b.text:
# The Market Didn't Crash. Some Sellers Just Haven't Caught Up.

If you've been watching our local market and reading the headlines, you might think we're headed off a cliff. Days on market nearly quadrupled. Showings have been cut in half. And yes, those numbers are real — they're happening right here in our zip codes. But before you start panicking or waiting for a massive price correction, let me tell you what's actually going on.

**This is not a crash. It's a correction in expectations.**

Last spring, a well-priced home in our area was getting multiple offers in under a week. Eight days on market was the median, and sellers were in the driver's seat. That pace has slowed to about five weeks. Some people look at that shift and see collapse. I look at it and see a market that's returning to something more balanced — something that's actually healthy.

Here's the piece that's getting lost in the conversation: list prices are still up six percent year over year. Six percent. That's not the sign of a market in freefall. That's a market where sellers are still confident — perhaps too confident in some cases.

And that's where the problem actually lives. I have three sellers right now who have been on the market for more than sixty days and are refusing to adjust their price. They're looking at last spring's numbers and expecting last spring's results. But last spring's buyer who would've lined up for that house with minimal negotiation doesn't exist anymore — at least not at that price point. Those buyers have either adjusted their expectations, gotten more selective, or in some cases, stepped back entirely.

Meanwhile, the sellers who are pricing it right — really pricing it to the current market, not the market of twelve months ago — are still selling in under two weeks. That tells you everything you need to know about where the demand actually is. The buyer is still there. They're just not willing to overpay anymore.

I get it. Nobody wants to hear that they need to come down in price. When you've watched your home's value climb the way it has over the past several years, it feels like a loss to ask for less. But asking for less than you wanted isn't the same as losing money. Those sellers who are holding firm on overpriced listings aren't protecting their equity — they're watching their homes grow stale, losing leverage with every passing week.

The market didn't change overnight. It shifted. And the agents and sellers who adapt to that shift — who price smart, who market effectively, who trust the data over their gut — are still getting deals done quickly and at strong numbers.

So if you're selling right now and you're frustrated because the phone isn't ringing the way it did last spring, you're not alone. But the answer isn't to hold your ground and hope. The answer is to look at what's actually happening and make the smart move. The market will reward you — if you meet it where it is.

*If you're thinking about listing and want an honest conversation about where your home falls in this market, I'm always happy to talk.*

setup: A third-year electrical apprentice is writing an argumentative essay for the union newsletter against a 15% cut to apprenticeship funding.

a.text:
**Don’t Pull the Plug on What Works**

Right now, there’s a proposal in the state budget to slash apprenticeship funding by 15%. That’s a bad idea, and I’ve got the numbers to prove it.

I’m a third-year apprentice with the IBEW. When my class started, there were 24 of us. Twenty-one finished and are out on the job today working as journeymen electricians. That’s an 88% completion rate. We’re earning good wages, paying taxes, and keeping the lights on across this state—literally.

Here’s what the path looked like for us. Apprentices start at around $19 an hour. It’s a living wage from day one, and every year we get a raise as our skills grow. By the time we top out, we’re making around $46 an hour as journeymen. Nobody in my class had to lean on food stamps or housing aid for long. Most of us were off any kind of public assistance within the first year or two, because the paychecks actually covered life. That means the state’s investment in us pays itself back fast.

Now let’s talk about what that investment actually costs. The total public money put into each apprentice who completes the program runs about $14,000. That’s it. Compare that to the average taxpayer subsidy for a student who finishes a four-year college degree: over $48,000. For nearly three and a half times the cost, you often get a graduate with debt, a degree that might not lead straight to a job, and no guarantee they’ll stay in-state. With apprenticeships, taxpayers get a skilled, licensed worker bolted directly into the local economy. We’re not moving away—we’re wiring your hospitals, schools, and factories.

A 15% cut hits the pipeline hard. Fewer slots open up. Fewer folks get a shot at a career that doesn’t require student loans or a trust fund. That means fewer journeymen a few years down the road, right when our state needs every set of skilled hands it can get to rebuild infrastructure and handle the energy transition. It’s shortsighted and it doesn’t save money in the long run. You’re just pushing people toward paths that cost the public more and deliver less.

Legislators talk a lot about “workforce development” and “return on investment.” Well, here’s the real deal: $14,000 for a near-guaranteed job with zero debt and a good wage. That’s a deal any business would take. The state should too.

Brothers and sisters, if you’re reading this, don’t just shake your head. Call your state rep and your state senator tomorrow. Tell them to reject the 15% cut and fully fund apprenticeship programs. Tell them my story. Tell them our numbers. And if you’re a legislator holding this newsletter: come ride with us for a day. I’ll show you what your dollars build. Don’t cut the one thing that’s working exactly the way it’s supposed to.

b.text:
# Why Cutting Apprenticeship Funding Makes No Sense

The state is looking at cutting apprenticeship funding by 15%. I'm in my third year as an IBEW apprentice, and I want to be straight with you about why that's a bad idea.

Let's talk money, because that's what this is really about.

I started my apprenticeship at $19 an hour. When I finish, I'll be making around $46 an hour as a journeyman. That's a real jump in two years. My cohort started with 24 people. Twenty-one of us finished and are working now. That means 21 people who went from entry-level wages to middle-class jobs without student debt hanging over our heads.

Think about what that means. Twenty-one apprentices who are no longer drawing on assistance programs. Twenty-one electricians paying taxes instead of needing help. Twenty-one people who can afford rent and buy things in their communities.

The state spent about $14,000 per apprentice who finishes. That's it. Compare that to the average four-year degree program—the state puts in about $48,000 per student who graduates. We're getting people to good jobs for a third of the cost.

If the state cuts this program 15%, they're not saving much money. They're losing it. They're losing the tax revenue from journeymen. They're losing the work we do. They're losing apprentices who would have made $46 an hour and bought houses and supported their families.

I've seen this work. I'm living proof it works. Don't cut it.

setup: A small HVAC company owner is writing a how-to for homeowners on bleeding air from hot water baseboard radiators before winter.

a.text:
1. Shut off the circulator pump and boiler at the control switch or breaker. Bleeding a pressurized, running system forces fresh air back in, wastes time, and can damage the pump seals.

2. Find the bleeder valve on each baseboard unit. It’s a small brass fitting, usually half an inch across, located on the end cap where the supply and return pipes meet. Every unit in the loop gets one.

3. Cup a small container directly underneath the valve. Keep a shop rag folded over the rim to catch drips. You’re only going to release a few ounces per unit.

4. Open the valve slowly using a dedicated bleeder key or a flathead screwdriver. Turn counter-clockwise just enough to break the seal. You’ll hear air hiss out, followed by sputtering water. Keep it cracked until the stream runs completely steady and silent—that means the air pocket is gone.

5. Close the valve by turning clockwise until it stops, then tighten it firmly with one additional quarter-turn. Snug is all it takes. Overtightening shears the rubber washer or cracks the valve seat, which turns a three-minute maintenance task into a leaky fixture replacement.

6. Work your way through every unit in the loop, always starting with the baseboard closest to the boiler and moving outward to the farthest room. Water carries air as it circulates, so purging from the source pushes trapped pockets cleanly out through each valve.

The single biggest reason I show up to houses for cold radiator calls is that homeowners only bleed the upstairs units and completely ignore the basement loop. Air rises with the heat and migrates with the water flow, which means it consistently settles in the lowest part of the system—the basement circuit. Skip that loop and the rest of your house will stay cold regardless of what you do upstairs. Purge the basement first or treat it equally, and your zones will balance fast.

Once you’ve run through every unit, verify the system pressure on the gauge. It should read 12 to 15 psi when the boiler is cold. Top off with a filling loop or garden hose adapter if needed, restart the boiler, and let each zone pull hot. 

If you complete this entire process and still get lukewarm floors or major temperature swings, the culprit is usually a worn circulator, partially closed zone valves, or sediment buildup in the piping. Call us out, and we’ll diagnose it properly before the first hard freeze.

b.text:
# How to Bleed Air Out of Your Baseboard Heating

Air trapped in your baseboard loops is the number one reason we get "my radiator's cold" calls this time of year. The good news is you can usually fix it yourself in an afternoon. Here's how we do it.

## 1. Shut Down the System First

Turn off the boiler and the circulator pump before you touch anything. You want the water still, not moving. If the system's running while you bleed, you'll fight against the circulator and never get a clean result. Give it a few minutes to settle.

## 2. Find the Bleeder Valve

Look at the end cap of each baseboard unit. The bleeder valve is a small fitting, usually round with a square nub or a slot for a flathead. Some take a special bleeder key (they're a couple bucks at any hardware store), others open with a screwdriver.

## 3. Cup Underneath It

Hold a cup or rag under the valve before you open it. Water is going to come out, and it can be dirty. Protect the floor and the wall behind it.

## 4. Open It Slow

Crack the valve open slowly with your key or flathead. You'll hear air hissing out first — that's exactly what you're after. Keep it open until the hissing stops and water runs out in a steady stream with no sputtering. That steady flow tells you the air is gone from that unit.

## 5. Close It Snug — Don't Crank On It

Once the water's running clean, close the valve. Snug is enough. If you muscle it down hard, you can crack the valve seat, and now you've got a leak on top of a cold radiator. Firm, not forced.

## 6. Work Unit by Unit, Boiler to Farthest

Start with the unit closest to the boiler and work your way out to the farthest one. Doing it in order pushes the air through the system the right direction instead of trapping it.

## The Mistake That Causes Most of Our Cold Radiator Calls

People bleed all the upstairs units, feel good about it, and skip the basement loop entirely. That basement loop is almost always where the air actually is. If your upstairs is fine but a room stays cold, or if you did all the visible units and still have a problem, get down to the basement and bleed that loop too. Nine times out of ten, that's the fix.

---

Once you've bled everything, turn the boiler and circulator back on, let it run, and check your pressure gauge — you may need to top off the water. If units are still cold after all this, or if you can't find a bleeder valve on a unit, give us a call and we'll come take a look.

setup: A first-year nursing student is writing a scholarship essay about her first ER rotation for scholarship committee readers.

a.text:
**Four Tries**

Before my first week in the emergency room, I had a picture in my head of what I would be doing. I would be moving fast. I would be needed. Nobody told me how much of it would be standing there.

The first day, a man came in with a cut across his forearm from a piece of sheet metal at work. It wasn't life-threatening, but it was deep and it needed to be cleaned out before they could close it. The nurse told me to stand on his other side. That was my whole assignment. Stand there.

He kept looking at the door. His wife was coming from across town and she was stuck on the highway. He said she'd be here any minute, and then he said it again, and then the nurse started irrigating the wound and he grabbed my hand without asking. I don't think he even knew he did it. He squeezed hard enough that my fingers went white. I didn't know what to say to him, so I asked him what his wife drove, and he told me, and then he told me about the traffic on that road and how they should have widened it years ago. He talked about that road for ten minutes. When his wife walked in he let go of my hand and I stepped back and I don't think he ever really looked at me. That was fine. I wasn't the point.

On the third day there was a code. I was standing at the nurses' station and everything changed at once, people moving toward one bay, someone pulling the cart. My preceptor looked at me and said, "Go restock gauze in bay six." I knew what that meant. It meant get out of the way. I went.

Bay six shared a curtain with where they were working. I stood there with my hands full of packages and I could hear them counting compressions. Twenty-eight, twenty-nine, thirty. Then a pause, then somebody's voice, then counting again. Nobody was yelling. I had expected yelling. It was steady, almost boring, the way you'd count out change. I put the gauze in the drawer very slowly so I'd have a reason to stay. I don't know what happened to that patient. Nobody told me and I didn't ask. I think about the counting more than anything else from that week.

The last day I was supposed to draw blood on a man in his sixties with diabetes. He had been stuck a lot in his life. His veins rolled, they were scarred, and I could barely feel them. I missed. I apologized. He said don't worry, everybody misses on him. I missed again. My face was hot. My preceptor asked if I wanted her to take over and before I could answer he said, "No, let her go again." I missed the third time and I wanted to leave the room. He said, "You're close." I don't know how he could tell.

The fourth time I got it. Blood came into the tube and he said, "There you go," like I'd done him a favor. I hadn't. I had hurt him four times. But he had decided I was going to get it, and he was willing to wait for me to catch up to him.

I thought my first week would tell me whether I was cut out for this. It didn't. Most of what I did was stand there, get sent away, and fail three times before something worked. What it told me is that I want to go back. I want to be the person doing the counting, not the one listening through the curtain. That is going to take a lot more school and a lot more misses. I'm ready for both.

b.text:
My first week in the ER, I mostly tried to stay out of the way.

I'm in my first year of nursing school. I don't know much yet. I know how to wash my hands right and check blood pressure and not touch stuff I'm not supposed to. That first week was the first time I was around real sick and hurt people, not just class stuff.

The first day, there was a man with a bad cut on his leg that they had to clean out. It hurt and he was scared. His wife was trying to get there but she was stuck in traffic. The nurse said I could stand with him. I held his hand while they cleaned it. He squeezed so hard. He was my dad's age, but he just held on and looked at the wall. I didn't really know what to say, so I just said you're doing good, almost done. His wife walked in right when they finished. I was glad she made it, but I'm glad I was there for the part she missed.

Another day there was a code. I wasn't supposed to go in the room. They sent me to the back to restock the gauze. I was in the supply room stuffing gauze into the bins and I could hear them through the curtain. I could hear them counting, one, two, three, real steady for the chest pushes. Someone calling out what to do next. I just stood there and listened and kept stacking. I felt pretty useless. I kept thinking I should be doing more. But somebody has to make sure the gauze is there when they yell for it. That stuck with me.

The one I still think about was a blood draw. He was a diabetic guy and his veins were bad, they roll and they're hard to find. I missed three times in a row. Three sticks and no blood. He didn't get mad, which almost made it worse. My face was hot and my hands were shaking. I wanted to quit and tell the nurse to just do it. She told me to take a breath and try one more time. On the fourth try I got it. Blood came back in the tube and I almost couldn't believe it. He smiled and said, see, you got it. I said sorry about ten times and he just said it's okay.

I know I'm just starting. I have a lot to learn. But that week showed me what the job really is. It's holding someone's hand when their person can't be there yet. It's getting the gauze ready when you can't be in the room. It's saying sorry and trying again when you mess up.

This money would help me a lot. I work part time now and school costs a lot with gas and books and everything else. It would help me work less and focus more on school so I can finish and be good at this. Thank you for reading this.

setup: A real estate agent is posting one specific observation about early block walks and happier buyers to LinkedIn buyers, agents, and lenders.

a.text:
After twelve years of selling homes here in Asheville, I’ve developed a rule of thumb for first-time buyers that sounds overly simple, but it rarely fails: walk the neighborhood at 7:00 AM on a Tuesday before you put in an offer.

Open houses are staged theatre. At 2:00 PM on a Saturday, the sunlight is flattering, soft music is playing, nobody is rushing to work, and every street feels peaceful. Real life, however, happens at 7:00 in the morning on a weekday.

A few years back, I was working with the Pruitts on a bungalow over on Sycamore Street. It checked every box on their spreadsheet, but it was at the very top of their budget, and they were agonizing over the decision. I told them to grab a thermos of coffee, park two blocks away, and just walk the loop around Sycamore before the workday started.

They watched where the sun actually hit the front porch. They saw which direction the commuter traffic backed up trying to turn onto the main road. They ran into an older neighbor walking his hound, who warned them that the bottom curve of the road tends to hold black ice for three days after a freeze, but that the neighborhood potluck in October was not to be missed. 

They made the offer that afternoon. Not because the neighborhood was flawless, but because the romanticized version in their heads had been replaced by the real thing, and they still loved it. 

Four years later, they’re still on Sycamore, and whenever I run into them at the grocery store, they talk about that morning walk. The buyers who take the time to see a street at its most mundane, groggy hour are almost always the ones who are still in love with their choice five years down the road.

b.text:
Twelve years in, you stop guessing and start noticing patterns.

One that’s held up every time: the buyers who walk the neighborhood at 7 a.m. before we tour the house are the ones who still love the place two years later. Not because the house changes, but because they actually know what they’re buying into.

I learned that with the Pruitts. They were under contract on a little craftsman just off Sycamore Street, and the inspection was clean, the numbers worked, everything looked good on paper. But I’d watched enough buyers grow quiet six months after closing to know that paper isn’t the whole story. So I told them to grab coffee at the shop on the corner, walk the full length of Sycamore at 7 a.m. on a Tuesday, and then call me.

They did. They saw the retired guy three doors down who hoses off his driveway every morning and waves whether you wave back or not. They heard the school bus stop at the end of the block, which meant kids, which meant the Pruitts—who were expecting their first—wouldn’t be the only young family on the street. They realized the “quiet” street they’d driven through at 5 p.m. on a Saturday was actually alive in a way they liked at 7 a.m. on a weekday.

They closed three weeks later, and last I checked they were still happy. Not because the house was perfect, but because Sycamore Street felt like home before they ever walked through the front door.

I don’t have a statistic for this. I just know that when buyers fall in love with the context around the house, the house itself tends to stick.

setup: A high school girls' soccer and track coach is writing an op-ed urging turf funding for the girls' field.

a.text:
**It’s Time to Level the Field for Our Girls**

For the past two seasons, my girls’ soccer team has lost nine games—not to opponents, but to rain. The field floods, the schedule gets wrecked, and our athletes are left scrambling for make-up dates or, worse, watching their season shrink because the grass can’t handle the weather. Last October, one of my players tore her ACL stepping in a rut that never should have been there. That’s not bad luck; that’s neglect.

Meanwhile, the boys’ football field got turf in 2019. No more rainouts, no more dangerous divots, no more second-class treatment. The message to our girls? Their safety and their season don’t matter as much.

Turf isn’t a luxury—it’s a necessity. It drains properly, it’s playable in all weather, and it reduces injuries. The football team got it. The girls’ soccer team deserves it. The school board votes on next year’s budget soon. This isn’t about keeping up with the latest trends; it’s about fairness, safety, and giving our athletes a field they can actually play on. Let’s get it done.

b.text:
# The Girls Deserve a Field That Doesn't Hurt Them

We've had nine games rained out or relocated in the last two seasons. Nine. That's not bad luck or a rough patch. That's a field that doesn't work.

Our girls soccer field sits at the bottom of a slope and floods anytime we get more than a drizzle. The grass turns to mud, the mud turns to puddles, and the puddles sit there until someone cancels the game or moves it to a campus we have to bus to. Our girls end up playing "home" games twenty minutes away while their parents and classmates stay home. Last October, one of my sophomores planted her foot in a rut left from a previous flooding and tore her ACL. She's had surgery. She missed the rest of the season. She'll miss track this spring. A rut in the grass did that.

The boys football field got turf in 2019. I'm not going to pretend that doesn't matter to these girls, because it does. They walk past that field every day on their way to practice on a surface that floods, wears unevenly, and actively injures them. They're not asking for anything the boys don't already have. They're asking for the same.

I've coached girls soccer and track at this school for eleven years. I do it for the stipend and because I care about these kids, not because I want to write op-eds. But I've watched two seasons of games wash out, watched a girl get hurt on a field we knew was a problem, and watched the school board approve turf for football while the girls play in mud. Something's wrong with that math.

The facilities budget vote is coming up. Turf for the girls soccer field is in the proposal. I'm asking the board to approve it. Not as a luxury, not as a "nice to have if we can afford it," but as the bare minimum for giving these girls a safe place to play the sport they signed up for.

Nine rained-out games. One torn ACL. One field that doesn't work. The fix is sitting in the budget. Approve it.

setup: A high-school senior is writing a personal essay for college admissions readers about working at her family's Vietnamese restaurant.

a.text:
At 5:17 on a Saturday night, our register system went black.

There were already people waiting by the door, and the printer in the kitchen had stopped spitting out orders. My dad pressed the power button three times, as if the third time would be different. My mom stood at the counter holding a bowl of pho she did not know where to take.

I pulled a stack of guest checks from under the register and started writing.

T12: two pho tai, one no onions.  
T7: bun bo hue, extra spicy.  
Pickup: four spring rolls, one grilled pork banh mi.

I made a copy of each ticket, handed one to the kitchen, and kept the other beside me. I wrote totals with a calculator and called out orders when they were ready. My handwriting got worse as the line grew. At one point, I charged a table for three iced coffees instead of two and had to run after them in the parking lot with five dollars.

The system came back almost two hours later. By then, the counter was covered in scraps of paper, and my left hand was stained blue from the pen. My dad wanted to enter every order into the register. My mom looked at the pile and said, “Tomorrow.”

Every weekend since sophomore year, I have worked at my family’s Vietnamese restaurant. I usually arrive before the lunch rush and leave after we stack the chairs. My jobs change depending on who is busy. I take orders, refill water, pack takeout containers, wipe tables, and translate when my parents need help with a customer or a delivery driver. I know which regular wants extra basil and which one will ask if the broth is really made that morning.

Some jobs take longer to learn. When we hired a new kitchen worker, I showed her how my grandma folds spring rolls. The wrapper has to be tight enough to keep the filling in but not so tight that it tears in the fryer. First fold the bottom over the filling. Then bring in both sides. Roll once, brush the edge with egg, and finish.

My first few rolls were crooked when my grandma taught me. She would unwrap them without saying anything and push the wrapper back toward me. Now I do the same thing, except I usually explain why.

“Not too much filling,” I told the new hire. “It looks small now, but it expands.”

She tried again. The next roll was still uneven, but it held. We lined it up on the tray with the others. By the end of the afternoon, hers looked almost like mine. None looked exactly like my grandma’s.

The restaurant is also where I do a lot of homework. During busy shifts, the dining room is too loud, and someone always needs the table I am using. The walk-in cooler is quieter. On breaks, I sometimes sit on an upside-down bucket between boxes of herbs and containers of broth, wearing my work apron over my school clothes.

That is where I finished a calculus problem set on derivatives. I balanced my notebook on my knees and set a ten-minute timer because staying longer would make my fingers stiff. Every few minutes, the compressor turned on and covered the sound of the kitchen. When the timer rang, I took a picture of the last problem, put my phone in my pocket, and went back out to refill sauces.

My weekends do not have much separation between school, work, and family. My mom might ask about an English assignment while sealing takeout bags. My dad might quiz me about college deadlines while chopping cilantro. Sometimes I am annoyed that I cannot spend Saturday the way my friends do. Sometimes I am relieved to have somewhere I already know what to do.

At closing, I sweep rice from under the tables and count the cash drawer. The kitchen smells like fried garlic, dish soap, and broth that has been simmering all day. Before we leave, I check the next morning’s reservations and make sure there are blank guest checks under the register.

We still use the computer. I just keep a pen beside it now.

b.text:
The register went black around two on a Saturday. The dining room was full enough that the floor had become a maze of chairs and trays. My father pressed buttons that should not have been pressed. My mother looked at the line by the door and said, “Write it down.”

I took order slips. I knew which ones were for dine-in and which ones were for pickup, because I have done this since sophomore year. I started writing. Pho no beef. Bun cha, grilled pork, less carrot pickle. Spring rolls, six, no peanut sauce. Two plates of broken rice with egg.

setup: A high school junior is writing an argumentative essay to her English teacher and classmates arguing for open campus lunch for juniors and seniors.

a.text:
**Open Campus Lunch for Juniors and Seniors**

Lunch is supposed to give students a break in the middle of the school day, but right now it is also one of the most crowded and stressful parts of the schedule. Our school should allow juniors and seniors to have open campus lunch because it would reduce cafeteria overcrowding, reflect what students actually want, and follow the example of nearby districts where the policy has worked. Allowing older students to leave campus for lunch would be a reasonable change that benefits both students and the school.

The most immediate reason to consider open campus lunch is overcrowding. Our cafeteria only seats 220 people, but one lunch wave has 340 students. That means there are more students than seats before even considering how long lines move or how much space people need to actually eat comfortably. When the cafeteria is that full, students have trouble finding seats, the noise level increases, and lunch becomes rushed. If juniors and seniors were allowed to leave campus, fewer students would need to eat in the cafeteria at the same time. This would make lunch more manageable for the students who remain and for the staff supervising them.

Students also strongly support the idea. In a survey I conducted with 80 students at our school, 71 said they were in favor of open campus lunch for juniors and seniors. That is almost 89 percent, which shows that this is not just a small preference but a clear opinion among the student body. Students are the ones most affected by lunch policies, and their views should matter when the school is deciding how to improve the daily schedule. Juniors and seniors are also older and more experienced students, so they can be trusted with a limited privilege like leaving campus for lunch.

Another reason to support open campus lunch is that similar schools have already tried it successfully. Nearby districts such as Fairmont, West Linn, and Cascade already allow open campus lunch, and their published statistics show no rise in tardiness. This is important because one of the biggest concerns about open campus lunch is that students will not return to class on time. However, the evidence from other districts suggests that students are able to handle the responsibility. If those schools can make the policy work without creating a tardiness problem, our school can do the same with clear expectations and consequences.

Some people may argue that open campus lunch is a bad idea because students might leave the allowed area, return late, or make poor choices while off campus. Those concerns are understandable, but they do not mean the policy should be rejected. Instead, the school can create rules to prevent problems. For example, open campus lunch could be limited to juniors and seniors who have signed permission forms. Students could also lose the privilege if they are late or break the rules. Since nearby districts have not seen an increase in tardiness, it seems likely that these concerns can be managed.

Open campus lunch for juniors and seniors would be a practical solution to a real problem. It would reduce overcrowding in the cafeteria, give students more independence, and follow the successful example of nearby schools. The evidence shows that students support it and that it does not have to create the problems people fear. Our school should consider open campus lunch as a responsible and reasonable change.

b.text:
# Open Campus Lunch for Juniors and Seniors

At our school, 340 students share a lunch wave in a cafeteria that seats only 220. That leaves 120 students without a cafeteria seat if everyone tries to eat there at once. Lunch should be a chance to eat and take a break, not a daily struggle to find space. Allowing juniors and seniors to leave campus during lunch would give students more choices while helping address this overcrowding. Our school should adopt an open campus lunch policy for upperclassmen, with clear expectations for returning on time.

The strongest reason for this change is the cafeteria’s limited capacity. The school assigns 340 students to the same lunch wave but cannot seat all of them in the cafeteria. An open campus policy would allow some juniors and seniors to eat elsewhere, reducing the number of students competing for the available seats. It would not guarantee that overcrowding disappears, since we do not yet know how many students would leave each day. Still, giving upperclassmen that option is a practical way to ease the pressure on a space that is already too small for the group assigned to it. Students who choose to stay would benefit as well.

Student opinion also supports considering a change. In a survey I conducted of 80 students at our school, 71 favored open campus lunch—nearly 89 percent of those surveyed. That result does not prove that every student supports the policy, and popularity alone is not enough to make a school rule worthwhile. However, it shows substantial interest among the students who responded. A policy meant to improve students’ lunch experience should take their views seriously, especially when those views align with a clear problem such as overcrowding.

One reasonable objection is that students who leave campus might return late and disrupt afternoon classes. However, nearby districts offer evidence that open campus lunch does not necessarily cause that problem. Fairmont, West Linn, and Cascade already allow it, and their published statistics show no rise in tardiness. Their results do not guarantee that our school would have exactly the same experience, but they weaken the argument that allowing students to leave will inevitably lead to more late arrivals. Rather than rejecting the idea based on that prediction, our school should examine how those districts manage the policy.

Our school could also address concerns by introducing open campus lunch as a trial for juniors and seniors. Students would still be responsible for arriving at their next class on time, and repeated late returns could result in losing the privilege. During the trial, administrators could track afternoon tardiness and cafeteria use to see whether the policy is working. This would give the school evidence from its own students instead of forcing it to make a permanent decision based only on expectations.

Open campus lunch would not solve every problem in the school day, but it offers a reasonable response to an overcrowded cafeteria. The survey shows strong student interest, and the experience of nearby districts suggests that the policy can work without increasing tardiness. With clear rules and a trial period, our school can give juniors and seniors greater independence while holding them accountable. Students should have the opportunity to show that they can handle that responsibility.

setup: A retired Army staff sergeant is writing about coming home after his second deployment for readers of the veterans' writing workshop anthology.

a.text:
The plane got into Fort Campbell late. I don't remember the flight. I remember the walk out into the hangar, and the noise, and how bright it was. Somebody's mother was screaming. Not a bad scream. People were holding signs with names on them and a lot of the names were spelled with glitter.

My wife was maybe twenty feet in. She had our daughter by the hand. Emma was six. She'd had a birthday while I was gone and I had seen the cake on a video call, a little lopsided thing with a horse on it, and I had told her it was the best cake I'd ever seen and I meant it.

I put my bag down and got down on one knee, which is what you do, and I said her name.

She went behind her mother's leg.

Not a joke, not a game. She got behind that leg and put her face into the denim and held on with both hands. My wife's face did something I don't have the words for. She said, Emma. She said, honey, it's Daddy.

I stayed down on the knee. Some guys nearby were getting picked up off the floor by their kids and I could hear it happening around me. I stayed down because I figured if I stood up I'd be tall and that seemed worse. I said, hey. I said, that's alright.

Here's the thing I didn't think about until later. I had lost about fifteen pounds. I had a beard from the last few weeks and I hadn't shaved because we came out of there fast. My voice was rough from the dust and it had been rough for a year. Somebody had taken a photograph of me two months before that and my wife told me later she almost didn't send it to Emma, because I looked like a different person in it. Emma had a picture of me on her nightstand from before. Clean-shaven. Heavier in the face. Laughing at something.

So a stranger got off a plane and knelt down and used her name.

It took maybe four minutes. My wife crouched down and talked to her low, the way you talk to a horse, and Emma looked at me sideways around the leg for a while. Then she let go of the denim and came out about a foot. She looked at my hands. I don't know why the hands. Then she came the rest of the way and put her arms around my neck and I picked her up and she was heavier than I remembered and that was the part that got me, that she was heavier. She said, you got skinny. I said, I know it.

She would not let go of my collar in the truck. She had two fingers hooked in it the whole ride home.

---

Four days later my wife sent me to the store for milk and cereal. It was a Tuesday morning. She had a list on the back of an envelope.

I got the milk fine.

Then I went to the cereal aisle and I stopped, and then I kept standing there.

I want to be plain about this because I've heard guys make it into a funnier story than it was. There were forty kinds of cereal. Maybe more. There were four kinds of Cheerios. There was a cereal with a cartoon dog on it that I had never seen in my life. The boxes went up over my head and down the aisle both directions and every one of them was yellow or red or orange and every one of them was shouting at me.

For a year I ate what was in front of me. That's not a complaint. That's a relief, is what that is, and I didn't know it was a relief until I was standing in that aisle. Somebody else decided. You went through the line and you took what was there and you sat down and you ate it and it was fine, and then you got up.

I stood there and I could not choose. It wasn't that I was scared. It wasn't a flashback, none of that. My chest was going a little but mostly it was just that the decision would not come. Every time I reached toward a box a voice in my head said, why that one. And I didn't have an answer, so my hand came back down.

A woman came in with a cart and a toddler in the seat and she said excuse me and I said sorry and moved, and she got two boxes off the shelf in about six seconds and left. I watched her do it. Six seconds. I remember thinking, how does she know.

A kid in an apron came by and asked if I was finding everything alright. I said yeah. He went away.

I looked at my watch when I finally left and it had been a little over twenty minutes. I came out with nothing. I sat in the truck in the parking lot for a while and then I went back in and got the box with the cartoon dog on it, because Emma had pointed at that one on TV, and I want to say I felt good about that but really I just wanted to be out of the store.

I told my wife they were out of the kind she wanted. That was the first lie I told her after I got back, and it was about cereal.

---

The sleeping took longer than anything.

Over there I slept facing the door. Not because anybody told me to. You just do. You lie on your right side with your face toward the door and your boots where your hand falls and you sleep like that for a year, and it stops being a choice, it becomes the shape your body makes.

At home the bedroom door was on the other side of the room. My wife's side. So the first two weeks I slept turned toward her, which she thought was sweet and which was not that. I was looking past her at the door.

She noticed the door thing before I did. She sleeps with it open. She always has, since Emma was born, so she can hear down the hall. I had been getting up after she went to sleep and closing it. I didn't remember doing it. She said, you keep shutting the door.

One night she asked me straight out to leave it open. Just asked. She didn't make it a whole conversation, which I appreciated.

So we left it open, and I lay there and looked down the hall. There's a nightlight in the bathroom, one of those little plug-in ones with a seashell on it. It throws a yellow line on the hall floor. I lay there and looked at that line and every hour or so I got up and walked down and checked on Emma and came back. I did that for a long time. Weeks. My wife knew I was doing it and didn't say anything about it.

Somewhere in there I started sleeping. Not straight through, but sleeping. And I got turned around at some point, I don't know when, so I was facing her instead of the door, and I only figured that out because one morning I woke up looking at the back of her head and I had to think about where the door was.

The door was open. It's still open. Emma's fourteen now and shuts hers, which is how it should be.

b.text:
# The Cereal Aisle

The flight from Germany was long but quiet. I slept some, which surprised me. When we landed at Dallas-Fort Worth, I carried my bag through the terminal and saw my wife standing near baggage claim with our daughter. Lily had just turned six. She was wearing a purple dress and her hair was done up in braids I didn't recognize. My wife saw me first and smiled and started to wave, but Lily stepped back and hid behind her mother's leg. She peeked around at me with one eye like she was deciding whether I was safe.

I stopped walking.

I'd talked to her on the phone almost every week. Sent her drawings I'd done of her dog, of our house, of things she'd recognize. But I'd been gone a year, and I guess a man in uniform with a shaved head and a bag over his shoulder wasn't quite what she had pictured. She stayed behind that leg until my wife knelt down and pointed at me and said something I couldn't hear. Then Lily came forward slow, looking up at me with her mouth open a little, and I knelt down too. She touched my face with her hand like she was checking if I was real. Then she grabbed me around the neck and I picked her up and she was heavier than I remembered. I held her for a while. My wife put her hand on my back. People moved around us with their roller bags.

The first week home, I drove to the grocery store for milk and eggs. My wife had made a list. I found the eggs fine. The milk was fine. Then I turned down the cereal aisle.

I stood there for what must have been twenty minutes. There were forty kinds of cereal. Maybe more. Cereal with marshmallows in it. Cereal with flakes and clusters. Cereal in a box with a cartoon on it. Cereal in a bag. Cereal with a label that said it was good for your heart. I'd been eating eggs and toast and whatever else they had at the chow hall, and before that, MREs, and the idea of choosing between forty kinds of cereal was something I couldn't get my arms around. It wasn't that I couldn't read the boxes. I just couldn't make the decision. A woman with two kids in her cart came through the aisle and grabbed a box of Cinnamon Toast Crunch without slowing down and kept walking. I watched her do it like she'd performed a trick.

I left without the cereal. I told my wife they were out of the kind she wanted.

The sleeping took longer to sort out. For a year I'd slept on my side, facing the door. It wasn't something I decided to do. My body just did it. In the barracks you slept a certain way, and in a sleeping bag you slept a certain way, and after a while it wasn't a choice anymore. Back home, my wife slept on the left side of the bed, and I'd sleep on the right, which put my back to the door. I'd lie there and feel it. Nothing was wrong. I knew nothing was wrong. But I'd turn over and face the door anyway, and my wife would roll over too in her sleep and put her hand on my arm.

After about a month, she said to me one morning, "Do you want to leave the door open?"

I said sure. She'd started leaving it cracked, then open a little more each night, like she was helping me get used to it. The first night it was all the way open, I lay there listening to the house. The dishwasher running. The furnace clicking on. Lily coughing once down the hall. I could hear everything. I lay on my back and stared at the ceiling and listened to the house make its sounds and eventually I slept.

Some nights I still turn over and face the door. But most nights now I sleep on my side with my back to it, and my wife's hand on my arm, and the door open, and the house quiet.

setup: A general contractor is writing a short X thread to contractors, homeowners, and architects about a hidden joist problem and the lesson learned.

a.text:
1/3
Maple Ave kitchen job last week. Pulled up three layers of subfloor and found four consecutive 2x8 joists notched about 70% through so a plumber in 1982 could run a 3” drain line. 

The previous owner had a 400 lb cast iron range sitting directly over the cut. Pure friction and prayer keeping it up.

2/3
The fix: shore up the basement, engineer-approved sistering with LVLs back to the center carrying beam, and re-routing the waste line correctly. 

Total cost to the homeowner: $3,800 and a 4-day schedule hit before we could even start setting new cabinets. 

3/3
The lesson: A 15-20% contingency on pre-1950s Pittsburgh homes isn't contractor fluff. It’s an insurance policy against the guy who worked on the house forty years ago with a Sawzall and zero supervision. Always budget for what's hiding under the subfloor.

b.text:
Pulled up the kitchen subfloor on the Maple Ave job yesterday and found two joists notched almost halfway through their depth. Someone ran a drain line through them 20+ years ago and just hogged out whatever they needed. Floor had a noticeable bounce right over it.

Notch that deep in the middle third of a joist is basically cutting its strength in half. You're allowed a notch, but there are rules about depth and location for a reason. Whoever did this either didn't know or didn't care.

Fix was sistering both joists full length and rerouting the drain properly. Added about $1,400 and a day and a half to the schedule the client wasn't planning on.

The lesson: that bounce in your floor is rarely "just how old houses feel." It's usually something structural someone hid behind finishes. Open it up before you tile over it, not after.

setup: A solo SaaS founder is posting a thread to indie hackers and customers about a pricing mistake and the fix.

a.text:
1/ I made a pricing mistake at Tallyup.

I raised prices 40% for everyone overnight.

Within a week, we lost 30 of 140 customers.

2/ The mistake wasn’t raising prices.

We needed to charge more to keep building a sustainable product.

The mistake was treating existing customers the same as new customers — with no warning, no context, and no choice.

3/ For a gym owner, Tallyup is another operating expense.

A sudden increase doesn’t feel like “we’re improving the product.”

It feels like: “this tool I rely on just got more expensive without asking.”

That’s on me.

4/ What I changed:

- Existing customers are grandfathered or moved gradually
- Price changes get communicated before they happen
- New pricing applies to new customers first
- I explain what’s changing and why

5/ The lesson:

Pricing is not just a number on a checkout page.

It’s a trust decision.

Especially when you’re a small SaaS asking customers to bet on you long-term.

6/ I still believe Tallyup should be priced sustainably.

But I won’t make another “overnight” decision that asks customers to absorb the cost of my learning curve.

b.text:
1/  
I made a pricing mistake with Tallyup.

I raised prices by 40% for everyone overnight.

Within a week, 30 of our 140 customers had left.

Here’s what happened—and what I changed.

2/  
The mistake wasn’t raising prices.

Tallyup had changed since many customers first subscribed. The old pricing no longer reflected the value we were providing.

The mistake was treating a pricing change like a switch:

Old price → new price  
No transition. No context. No room for customers to adjust.

3/  
I underestimated how the change would feel to customers.

A 40% increase might be reasonable on paper.

But to a gym owner receiving an unexpected bill, it’s still a 40% increase overnight.

The math made sense to me. The rollout didn’t.

4/  
The churn was immediate:

30 of 140 customers left in one week.

That’s roughly 21% of the customer base.

It was painful, but it made the problem impossible to ignore.

5/  
The biggest lesson:

Pricing isn’t just a number.

It’s also timing, communication, trust, and whether customers understand the value they’re paying for.

I focused too much on the first part.

6/  
What I changed:

I stopped thinking about pricing as a one-time decision.

It needs to be treated as an ongoing product decision—something to revisit carefully, communicate clearly, and roll out deliberately.

7/  
I also became much more cautious about making a broad pricing change all at once.

When you’re a small SaaS, it’s easy to make a decision in a spreadsheet and forget that every row represents a real customer relationship.

8/  
I’m still glad I looked at pricing.

Tallyup needs to be a sustainable business, and pricing has to reflect the value the product creates.

But sustainable pricing shouldn’t come at the cost of surprising the people who helped build the business.

9/  
The uncomfortable version of the lesson:

A pricing increase can be “correct” and still be handled badly.

The 40% increase wasn’t the only issue.

The overnight rollout was.

10/  
For other indie founders:

Don’t only ask, “What should we charge?”

Also ask:

- How will customers experience this?
- How much notice do they need?
- How can we explain the value?
- What would make the transition feel fair?

11/  
I lost 30 customers in a week because I optimized for the new price instead of the long-term relationship.

That’s a mistake I don’t plan to repeat.

Pricing is part of the product. Treat it that way.

setup: A first-year nursing student is writing a scholarship essay about her first ER rotation for scholarship committee readers.

a.text:
My first week in the emergency room did not go the way I expected.

I thought I would spend most of my time watching nurses, learning where supplies were kept, and trying not to get in the way. I did learn those things, but I also learned that nursing is often about staying present during moments that are difficult, rushed, or uncertain.

One of the first patients I met needed a wound cleaned. His wife was on her way, but she was stuck in traffic. He was nervous and kept looking toward the door. Since she could not be there yet, I sat beside him and held his hand while the nurse worked. I did not have the experience to fix the problem or make the pain go away. All I could do was stay with him. I realized that sometimes a patient does not need a long explanation or a perfect answer. Sometimes they need to know they are not alone.

Another moment happened during a code. I was sent to restock gauze, so I was outside the room when I heard the team counting through the curtain. The voices were quick and steady. I could hear how focused everyone was. Even though I was not directly involved, I understood that every person in that room had a job, and every second mattered. I returned with the supplies and saw how the nurses moved with purpose. They were calm because they had practiced, studied, and learned how to work together. That moment showed me the responsibility that comes with this profession.

The hardest moment for me was a blood draw on a diabetic patient with difficult veins. I missed three times. Each time, I felt more embarrassed and more nervous. I knew the patient was already dealing with enough, and I did not want to make things harder for him. After the third attempt, I took a breath and tried again. On the fourth try, I got the draw.

I was relieved, but I also knew that getting it on the fourth try did not make the first three attempts disappear. The patient was patient with me, and I was grateful for that. The experience taught me that being a good nurse does not mean getting everything right the first time. It means being honest, paying attention, learning from mistakes, and continuing to treat the patient with respect.

That first week made nursing feel more real to me. In class, we learn skills and procedures. In the ER, I saw how those skills affect real people. I saw fear, pain, urgency, and trust. I also saw how much patients depend on nurses to be prepared and present.

I left that week tired, but more certain that I had chosen the right path. I still have a great deal to learn, and I know there will be more difficult days ahead. But I am ready to keep learning. My first week in the ER reminded me that nursing is not only about knowing what to do. It is also about showing up, staying calm, and caring for people when they need it most.

b.text:
I finished my first clinical rotation in the ER last week. As a first-year nursing student, I thought class had prepared me. It hadn’t.

One of the first things that hit me was holding a stranger’s hand. A man came in with a wound that needed cleaning. It was deep and he was hurting bad. His wife was stuck in traffic and couldn’t get there. While the nurse cleaned it, I just held his hand. He squeezed hard every time the pain hit, and I squeezed back. I told him it was okay to squeeze as much as he needed. We didn’t talk much. I just stayed there until it was over.

Later they called a code. Everyone moved fast. They sent me to restock the gauze because I was still learning the ropes. I stood by the supply cart filling it, and through the curtain I could hear them counting. One, two, three. Over and over. I knew what that sound meant. Someone’s heart had stopped and they were trying to bring them back. My side of the curtain was quiet. Their side wasn’t.

Then there was the blood draw. An older diabetic guy with veins that just wouldn’t cooperate. I stuck him once and missed. Twice and missed. Three times and still nothing. I felt terrible. Kept apologizing. He just looked at me and said it was fine, keep going, he’d been through worse. On the fourth try I got it. The tube started to fill and I finally breathed again.

None of those moments were big or dramatic from the outside. Holding a hand because someone else’s wife was stuck in traffic. Hearing the count through a curtain while I restocked gauze. Missing a simple stick three times before I got it right. But they stuck with me. They showed me that nursing is mostly about showing up when people are scared or hurting or waiting, even when you’re new and your hands shake and you don’t get it perfect the first time.

I want to keep learning how to do this. A scholarship would take some of the money pressure off so I can focus on becoming the kind of nurse those patients needed that week.

setup: A third-year electrical apprentice is writing an argumentative essay for the union newsletter against a 15% cut to apprenticeship funding.

a.text:
**Keep Our Apprenticeships Funded: Why a 15% Cut is Bad Math for Our State**

As a third-year electrical apprentice with our local IBEW, I see every day how much this program changes lives. That is why the state’s proposed 15% cut to apprenticeship funding is so concerning. I’m not an English professor, and I’m not going to use fancy political talk to make my point. I’m just going to use the real numbers, because the numbers don’t lie.

Let’s start with how successful these programs actually are. In my own cohort, 24 of us started the program together. Out of that group, 21 finished and are working as journeyman electricians right now. That is a massive success rate. We aren’t just sitting in a classroom; we are out on job sites building our communities, keeping the lights on, and powering our state's economy.

The financial impact on the state is also immediate. We start out making around $19 an hour, and we top out around $46 an hour once we become journeymen. Because we earn a solid living wage from day one, apprentices get off state assistance programs fast. We don’t need taxpayer help to buy groceries or pay rent because our careers give us the independence to support ourselves. Instead of taking from the system, we are paying into it through taxes right away.

Now let’s talk about what we cost the taxpayers compared to other paths. The total public cost for an apprentice who finishes their program is about $14,000. Compare that to a four-year college graduate, where the average public subsidy is about $48,000. 

For less than a third of the cost of a college degree, the state gets a highly skilled, licensed professional who is ready to work on day one without a mountain of student debt. You won't find a better return on investment anywhere. 

To our state legislators: cutting our funding by 15% is not saving money. It is hurting a program that actually works, costs the taxpayers very little, and puts people directly into the middle class. We are the ones building our schools, hospitals, and power grids. 

Please don’t cut the funding that keeps our state running. Leave our apprenticeship budget alone so we can keep doing our jobs.

b.text:
**Keep Funding Apprenticeships—They Work**

The state wants to cut apprenticeship funding by 15%. That’s a bad idea, and here’s why.

My cohort started with 24 apprentices. Twenty-one of us finished, and now we’re all working as journeymen. That’s a 90% success rate—people who came in with no experience, learned a trade, and are now making good money. Apprentices start at around $19 an hour, and by the time we’re journeymen, we’re making $46 an hour. That’s enough to support a family, buy a house, and get off any kind of public assistance fast.

Here’s the kicker: the public cost per apprentice who finishes is about $14,000. Compare that to the average $48,000 in public subsidies for a four-year college grad who actually finishes. We’re not just cheaper—we’re putting skilled workers into the economy without saddling them with debt.

Cutting this funding won’t save money. It’ll just mean fewer apprentices, fewer skilled workers, and more people stuck in low-wage jobs. The state should be investing in programs that work, not gutting them. Keep the funding—it’s a smart deal for everyone.

setup: A real estate agent is writing a commentary on the local market for brokerage blog and local paper readers.

a.text:
# The Market Hasn’t Crashed—Sellers Just Haven’t Adjusted Yet

If you’re judging the local real estate market by headlines, you might think we’ve gone from bidding wars to a full-blown collapse.

That’s not what I’m seeing.

What I’m seeing is a market that has changed pace—and sellers who haven’t changed their expectations with it.

In my ZIP code, the median time on market has climbed from just eight days last spring to 34 days this spring. That is a meaningful shift. Buyers have more choices, they’re taking longer to decide, and they’re no longer assuming they need to waive every protection or pay far above asking price to win a home.

At the same time, list prices are still up 6% compared with last year. That matters. Prices have not fallen off a cliff. The market is not in a crash. It is correcting from an unusually fast, unusually aggressive period when nearly every reasonably priced home attracted immediate attention.

The clearest sign of that adjustment is showings. Showings per listing have dropped by half. That tells sellers something important: buyers are being more selective. They are not automatically walking through every new listing, and they are not willing to overlook an inflated price simply because inventory is limited.

Yet some sellers are still pricing their homes as if it were last spring.

I currently have three sellers who have been on the market for more than 60 days and are refusing to reduce their prices. I understand why. A home is personal, and most sellers believe their property is worth what the neighbor’s—or the house down the street—sold for during the peak of the frenzy.

But the market does not pay for what a seller believes a home should be worth. It pays for what today’s buyers are willing to pay.

The homes that are priced correctly are still moving. In fact, the right listings are selling in under two weeks. That is the part of the market some sellers are missing. Buyers have not disappeared. They are simply passing on homes that feel overpriced.

A home that sits for 30, 45 or 60 days sends a message, whether the seller intends it or not. Buyers begin to wonder what is wrong with it. They watch for a price reduction. They assume the seller may eventually become more negotiable. By refusing to respond early, sellers can turn a small pricing problem into a stale-listing problem.

The new market requires a different strategy. Pricing slightly ahead of the competition and waiting for the “right buyer” is no longer a reliable plan. The strongest launch price is the price that makes buyers feel they need to act—not the price that tests how much optimism the market will tolerate.

That does not mean sellers should give their homes away. It means they need to price according to current buyer behavior, not last year’s memories.

The local market is not collapsing. It is normalizing. Buyers have regained some leverage, and sellers have lost the luxury of being dramatically overpriced without consequences.

The agents and sellers who recognize that shift are still getting homes sold quickly. Those who refuse to recognize it are sitting on the market, waiting for the old market to come back.

It isn’t coming back—not in the same form. The sooner sellers accept that, the sooner they can compete in the market we actually have.

b.text:
**The Spring Market Reality Check We Can’t Ignore**

Ten years in this job teaches you that real estate has seasons—not just weather seasons, but mood seasons. And right now? The mood has shifted, but the data tells a more interesting story than the headlines might suggest.

Let’s start with the numbers from my own zip code. Last spring, the median days on market was a blistering 8 days. This spring, it’s 34. That’s a quadrupling of time on market, and it’s real. Showings per listing have been cut in half. You’d think that would send prices tumbling, right? But here’s the thing: list prices are still up 6% year over year. That’s not a typo. Buyers are more selective, and sellers aren’t budging—at least not yet.

I’m living this tension right now. I have three sellers who’ve been on the market for over 60 days, and none of them will drop their price. They’re anchored to comps from a year ago when bidding wars were the norm and “sight unseen” offers landed in my inbox. That market is gone. But here’s the twist: homes that are priced accurately from day one are still selling in under two weeks.

So what’s really happening? This isn’t a crash. I’ve seen crashes—foreclosures stacking up, prices in freefall, panic. This is something different. This is a seller pool that hasn’t caught up to the new pace. Sellers are flying blind on old expectations, thinking a “For Sale” sign is a magic wand. It’s not. Buyers have more options now, and they’re using them. They’ll look at three more houses before pulling the trigger, and they’ll notice when your price feels like a relic from last year’s frenzy.

The 6% year-over-year price growth is proof that the market is still fundamentally sound. Values are holding because demand isn’t gone—it’s just being smarter. The sellers who get that, who price for today’s buyers instead of yesterday’s bidding wars, are the ones cleaning out their garages and moving on. The ones who don’t? They’re the reason the median days on market shot up to 34.

If you’re thinking of listing, don’t let the slower pace scare you. Let it focus you. Price aggressively for the market we’re in, not the one we wish we had. That doesn’t mean giving your house away—it means respecting the buyer’s reality. Because the market hasn’t stopped; it’s just stopped waiting for you.
