setup: An in-house recruiter is posting a contrarian observation about candidates asking about the team’s last failed project in interviews to recruiters, hiring managers, and job seekers.

a.text:
In roughly 200 interviews for logistics roles, the best candidates almost always ask a version of the same question:

“Tell me about your last failed project.”

At first, it can feel like a strange question in an interview. Not “what’s your culture like?” or “what’s the biggest opportunity?” — but failure.

When a strong candidate asks it, though, it usually means they’re not trying to perform. They’re trying to understand the job.

The good ones don’t ask it as a trap. They ask it plainly:

“Did the WMS migration go well?”

And if I’m honest, I say no.

Then the conversation gets much better:

Candidate: “Was it the tech, the timelines, or the adoption on the floor?”

Me: “Mostly the timelines. We underestimated how much time the warehouse crews needed to trust and adapt to the new process.”

Candidate: “Fair. So for the person stepping into this role, what’s the first thing they’d need to fix?”

That’s the moment they stand out.

They’re not just asking what went wrong. They’re asking what they’d actually have to deal with after day one.

For hiring managers: that question is a signal.

For recruiters: let the conversation go that deep. The right candidates often want the truth more than they want polish.

For candidates: asking about failure isn’t rude. It’s due diligence.

b.text:
I've sat in on roughly 200 interviews over 9 years. The candidates who impress me most almost always ask some version of the same question.

"What was the last project here that failed?"

Not "what's the culture like." Not "what does success look like in this role." They want the failure story.

Had one a few months ago. Senior ops candidate, second round, going well. She asks: "What's the last initiative that didn't work here — and what happened to the people who ran it?"

That second half. That's the actual question.

I told her about a route optimization tool we rolled out two years back. Big vendor, big promises. Dispatchers hated it, adoption collapsed within a few months, and we quietly went back to the old process.

She didn't nod and move on. She asked: "Whose idea was it, and where is that person now?"

Honest answer: the director who championed it is still here. He ran the post-mortem himself. One thing that came out of it — dispatchers now sit in on every pilot before we buy anything — is standard practice.

She told me that was the answer she'd been hoping for. Her last employer had a failed rollout and pinned it on one analyst, who was gone within a month. She left shortly after.

That's what I've figured out about this question: candidates aren't testing whether you fail. Everyone fails. They're testing what failure costs the person attached to it.

If you're interviewing somewhere, ask it. Pay attention to whether the interviewer hesitates, and whether the failure story has a villain.

And if you're on my side of the table: the quality of your answer tells them more about working here than anything on the careers page. If your honest answer ends with "and we fired them," expect the best candidates to politely finish the process and take another offer.

setup: A parent of two middle-schoolers is writing an op-ed to local readers urging an 8:45am middle-school start time.

a.text:
**Later Starts Mean Better-Rested Kids—and Better Days at School**

As a parent of two middle-schoolers in Millbrook, I’ve watched the school board’s 8:45 start-time proposal with more than casual interest. I’ve read it carefully. And I’m writing to urge the board—and my neighbors—to support it when they vote next month.

Like a lot of parents, I’ve seen the morning scramble: kids who stayed up late fighting biology, not laziness, then dragging themselves out the door half-asleep. The American Academy of Pediatrics has been clear for years that middle- and high-school students need 8–10 hours of sleep and that later start times are one of the most effective ways to help them get it. An 8:45 bell finally lines up with what science and common sense already tell us.

We don’t have to guess how this might work here. The Lincoln Middle pilot already gave us a local look. Attendance improved. First-period grades went up. Kids were more present—literally and mentally—when the day started later. That matches what I’ve noticed in my own house on delayed-start days: fewer arguments, clearer heads, and a lot less “I can’t keep my eyes open” at the breakfast table.

I know the bus-schedule worry is real. Changing start times can ripple through routes and family logistics. But the proposal already addresses this head-on by re-tiering the bus routes. The plan isn’t “start later and hope the buses figure it out.” It’s a coordinated adjustment so elementary, middle, and high school runs still fit together without leaving families stranded or forcing impossible early pickups.

This isn’t about making mornings perfect. It’s about giving our kids a fairer shot at being awake, healthy, and ready to learn. Middle school is hard enough without starting the day already behind on sleep. The board has done the homework—reviewed the research, run a local pilot, and built the bus piece into the plan. Now it’s our turn to back them.

I’m not a policy expert. I’m just a Millbrook parent who wants my kids, and everyone else’s, to walk into school a little more rested and a little more ready. An 8:45 start is a practical step toward that. I hope the board votes yes, and I hope other parents will speak up too.

—A Millbrook parent of two middle-schoolers

b.text:
# A Later Start Is the Right Call for Millbrook's Kids

I have two kids at Millbrook Middle, and like a lot of parents in this town, I've spent more mornings than I can count trying to pry a groggy 12-year-old out of bed before sunrise. So when the school board proposed moving our middle school start time to 8:45, my first reaction wasn't about policy. It was relief.

Here's the thing I didn't fully understand until I read the proposal closely: this isn't about kids being lazy. The American Academy of Pediatrics has been clear for years that adolescents are biologically wired to fall asleep later and wake later than the rest of us. Their bodies literally don't produce the sleep hormones on the same schedule ours do. Asking a middle-schooler to be alert at 7:30 a.m. is like asking me to be sharp at 4:00 in the morning. It's not attitude. It's chemistry.

We don't have to guess whether a later start helps, either. Lincoln Middle, one county over, ran a pilot with a later bell. Their attendance went up. Their first-period grades went up. These are the exact numbers our board is looking at, and they point in one direction. Kids who sleep more show up more, and they learn more once they're there. As a parent, that's the whole ballgame.

I know the objection I'll hear at the coffee shop, because I had it myself: what about the buses? You can't just move one school's clock without the whole system going sideways. But if you actually read the proposal, the board already thought this through. The plan re-tiers the bus routes so the elementary and middle schedules swap slots. The younger kids, who are up at dawn anyway, catch the earlier runs. The buses don't need to multiply. They just need to run in a different order. It's a logistics fix, not a dealbreaker, and pretending otherwise is an excuse to do nothing.

I'm not a writer or an expert. I'm a parent who's tired of watching my kids drag through the school day running on too little sleep, when there's real evidence we could do better.

The board votes next month. If you've got kids in this district, or grandkids, or you just care about how our schools do, tell them you support the 8:45 start. Our kids have earned the chance to show up rested.

setup: A high-school senior is writing a personal essay for college admissions readers about working at her family's Vietnamese restaurant.

a.text:
I haven’t had a Saturday off since October of my sophomore year. While my classmates are at football games or sleeping in, my weekends belong to my family’s Vietnamese restaurant. I start at 10:00 AM, just as the broth from the day before is reaching a rolling boil, and I don't leave until the chairs are stacked on the tables at ten at night.

My breaks are twenty minutes long, and I spend them in the walk-in cooler. It is the only place in the restaurant where nobody is shouting in Vietnamese or clattering stainless steel bowls. I sit on an overturned five-gallon bucket of pickled carrots, my winter coat zipped to my chin, and do my AP Calculus homework. The pages of my textbook always curl from the humidity, and after fifteen minutes, my fingers get too stiff to grip my mechanical pencil. But the quiet is absolute. I solve for limits while staring at crates of cilantro and boxes of beef bones, finding a weird kind of peace in the cold.

If the walk-in is where I find quiet, the front counter is where I learn how to handle chaos. Last November, during our prime Saturday dinner rush, our digital register system went completely black. Twenty active orders vanished from the kitchen screen, and a line of hungry customers began to stretch out the door. My dad was already sweating over four gas burners in the back, and my mom was frantically trying to reboot the router. 

I didn't have time to panic. I grabbed a stack of green guest checks and a black pen. I took orders by hand, writing down "P1" for beef pho and "E2" for spring rolls in my own shorthand. I ran the physical tickets to the kitchen, shouting modifications over the hiss of the exhaust fan, and did the math for the tax and change in my head. I kept a metal lockbox under the counter for cash. By the time the rush ended, my thumb was calloused from the cheap pen, but we hadn’t missed a single order, and the cash drawer balanced to the penny. 

When I am not running the register, I am training the new hires. Most of them are high school kids who have never had a job before. Last month, I taught a junior named Marcus how to roll spring rolls using my grandmother’s technique. The rice paper is temperamental—if you wet it too much, it turns to mush; if you don't wet it enough, it cracks. 

I showed him how to lay down the pork, the noodles, and the mint, and then how to tuck the sides in tight, like making a small sleeping bag. The trick is getting the shrimp to lay flat against the translucent wrapper so it looks good when served. 

"If you roll it too loose, it falls apart in the peanut sauce," I told him. "If you roll it too tight, the paper rips. You just have to feel the tension." I watched him tear six wrappers before he got one clean roll. I didn't get frustrated; I just cleared the sticky rice paper away and handed him another sheet. 

I am not going to say that working at the restaurant taught me the secret to life. The truth is, my feet hurt every Sunday, my clothes always smell like star anise, and I have missed a lot of high school events that I probably would have enjoyed. But this is my reality. I know how to work under pressure, I know how to teach people, and I know how to find quiet in a busy room. When I start college, I won't just be bringing my textbooks. I’ll be bringing the work ethic I built twelve hours at a time.

b.text:
The register died at 11:40 on a Saturday in October, twenty minutes into lunch rush. The screen froze on order #34, two bowls of pho, and my dad smacked the side of it twice, which is his fix for everything. Nothing. He called the company from the kitchen and the company said Monday. The dining room had six tables eating and two more walking in the door.

He tore a to-go pad off the stack under the counter and handed it to me. "You write."

So I wrote. Table numbers, dishes, prices off the menu I've had memorized since I could see over the host stand. I did the tax in the margin — 8.25 percent, I've done that math enough times that I trust it — and kept a running total on the back page. My dad unlocked the cash drawer with the little emergency key he keeps in his shirt pocket. I counted change back to people the old way, ones on top of the fives. At four o'clock I added everything up against the cash in the drawer. We were off by $2.25. I found it in twenty minutes: I'd written a 3 that looked like an 8 on table twelve. After that I did every ticket twice. The register came back Monday, and there's a stack of order pads in my locker at school in case it ever dies again.

I've worked at my family's Vietnamese restaurant every weekend since sophomore year. Friday nights, Saturdays, Sundays. I host, run food, work the takeout counter, and fill in on whatever station is short, which is usually all of them. The restaurant is in a strip mall between a nail salon and a phone store. It seats forty-two. I know that number because I've pushed the tables into party arrangements more times than I can count.

Last month we hired a new kid, Marcus, seventeen, first job. My dad handed him to me for the spring rolls, because spring rolls are mine. My grandma taught me the fold at this same counter when I was ten, by saying "Again" every time one came out wrong. You dip the rice paper for two seconds — longer and it goes soft and sticky. Filling goes in the bottom third, not the middle. Fold the bottom edge up over it, fold the sides in, roll forward, seam down. Grandma's test was to hold it by one end and shake it. If anything moved, again. Marcus's first five fell apart in his hands. His ninth held. He looked up at me like he'd passed something, which I guess he had. Last Saturday he rolled sixty for a birthday party and nobody at the party could tell whose were whose.

Breaks are thirty minutes when it's slow and ten when it's not. There is exactly one quiet room in the building: the walk-in cooler. I keep a plastic stool in there between the bean sprouts and the crates of Thai chiles, and I do my calculus homework sitting on it, jacket zipped, breath showing. Last year the chapter on related rates and the lunch rush happened at the same time, so I worked the ladder-against-the-wall problem in eleven-minute pieces, with the door sliding open — "Two more spring rolls, table five" — between part b and part c. My notebook has a soy sauce stain in the shape of Michigan. I have not tried to get it out.

People ask what it's like, working weekends, and I never know what to say, because it's not like anything. It's just what my Saturdays are. I know the 12:30 church crowd orders number five by habit. I know the front door sticks when it's humid. I know which regulars pay in exact change and which ones tip in fives because fives are what the ATM gives. When my friends post pictures from the lake I'm usually in the same apron, and honestly, some Saturdays I wish I were at the lake. Then a party of ten walks in and I don't think about the lake again until we close.

Next Saturday I'll be there at ten to open. If the register works, fine. If it dies, the order pads are in my locker and I already know the tax.

setup: A co-founder is posting a LinkedIn hiring announcement for a first customer support hire to potential applicants and customers.

a.text:
The three of us co-founders at Ridgepoint are officially drowning in support tickets. So, we’re hiring our first support person. 

Since day one, the founders have answered every single ticket. It was the best way to learn our users' pain points, but as we've grown, this system is falling apart. We need someone to take the wheel.

Ridgepoint is a scheduling tool for small trucking dispatchers. Our users are busy, no-nonsense logistics pros who just need to get their loads scheduled and trucks moving. 

I’m not going to sell you on our "amazing startup culture" or ping-pong tables. Instead, here is exactly what you’ll be doing day-to-day:

• Triage the inbox: You’ll be the first line of defense when a dispatcher is stuck, frustrated, or in a rush. 
• Translate tech to logistics: Explain software features without using SaaS jargon. Speak their language and respect their time.
• Bug hunting: Figure out if an issue is user error or a real software bug. If it's a bug, write clear reproduction steps for our dev team.
• Build the knowledge base: Notice when you answer the same question three times? You'll write and update help docs so dispatchers can self-serve.
• Own the queue: You will have full autonomy to organize, prioritize, and clear the inbox. The founders will get out of your way.

You won't be a cog in a massive machine. You will be building the support foundation for a 3-person SaaS from the ground up, and our customers are already looking to you for guidance.

If you have high empathy, extreme patience, and don't mind rolling up your sleeves, we want to talk to you. 

Apply here: [Link] or send me a DM if you want to chat about the role first.

b.text:
We're hiring our first support person at Ridgepoint.

Some honesty about why: there are three of us, and we've been splitting every support ticket between founder work, sales calls, and shipping product. It worked at 20 customers. It doesn't work anymore. Response times are slipping and that's not fair to the dispatchers who rely on us.

What the job actually looks like day to day:

- Answering tickets from small trucking dispatchers, mostly via email and chat. Common stuff: load scheduling questions, driver assignment confusion, billing issues, "why isn't this syncing"
- Getting on the occasional screen share when written back-and-forth isn't cutting it
- Reproducing bugs and writing them up clearly enough that we can fix them without asking you ten follow-up questions
- Building out our help docs, which are currently thin because we've been the docs
- Telling us bluntly which parts of the product confuse people most, because you'll see the patterns before we do

What you should know going in:

- Our customers are dispatchers. They're busy, sometimes stressed, and they need answers fast. Patience and clarity matter more than technical depth.
- You don't need trucking experience, but you'll need to learn how dispatching works. We'll teach you.
- It's a three-person company. There's no support team to join, no manager above you in a support org. You'd be defining how support works here, with a lot of direct access to the people building the product.
- Some days will be repetitive. Some days will be chaotic. That's the honest version.

If answering the same question the 40th time with the same care as the 1st sounds like something you're actually good at, send me a message or comment here. Happy to answer questions about the role openly in the comments too.

setup: A wedding photographer is posting that couples who ditch rigid shot lists get better photos, using the rained-out Barrera wedding as an example.

a.text:
The Barrera wedding almost fell apart.

Rain came out of nowhere about an hour before the ceremony. The outdoor venue they'd planned around for months was suddenly off the table.

We moved everything under this massive old pecan tree near the property line. Not the plan. Not what anyone picked out during the planning meetings.

And here's the thing — they didn't panic. They didn't start trying to reshoot the timeline or hand me a list of "must-have" poses to make up for what they were losing. They just let it unfold.

The first look happened under wet branches, light filtering through in a way no venue would have given us. The dancing started early because why wait. The toasts happened in a circle of lawn chairs on wet grass.

Those photos are some of my favorites from 8 years of full-time shooting.

Here's what I've seen over and over: the couples who show up with a rigid shot list tend to get photos that look exactly like their shot list. Fine. Safe. Done.

The couples who trust the day — who let their photographer respond to what's actually happening in front of them — those are the ones who end up with images nobody else has.

The Barreras didn't get the wedding they planned. They got the one that happened. And it was better.

If you're planning your wedding right now, my advice is simple: pick a photographer whose work you trust, then let them work. Bring a short list of non-negotiables if you need to. But leave room for the pecan tree.

b.text:
After 8 years and 300+ weddings, here's something I've learned: the couples who hand me a rigid shot list rarely get my best work.

The Barrera wedding is the perfect example.

We had everything planned. Then the rain came, and the whole outdoor ceremony we'd mapped out was suddenly impossible. So we moved everything under the big pecan tree on the property.

No shot list could have accounted for that. And honestly? It gave us the best photos of the entire day.

The light coming through the branches. The way the whole wedding party crowded in close because the space was smaller. The genuine laughter when the plans fell apart and everyone just rolled with it.

That's the thing about a shot list. It's built for the wedding you imagined, not the one that actually happens. And the real moments almost never show up on a list.

I'm not saying don't communicate what matters to you. Tell me about your grandmother who traveled across the country. Tell me the tradition your family does every year. Those things I want to know.

But the magic? You can't script it. You just have to trust the person holding the camera to catch it when it comes.

The Barreras trusted me under that pecan tree. I'll never forget it.

If you're planning a wedding in the Hill Country, my advice is simple: plan less, trust more. The photos will thank you.

#WeddingPhotography #TexasHillCountry #WeddingPlanning

setup: A freelance wedding photographer is writing a blog post for couples about why to book a winter wedding.

a.text:
I Used to Chase June Weddings. Now I Actually Prefer November.

Six years of shooting weddings in this area, and I’ll be straight with you: I used to treat winter dates like something couples settled for. Then I started looking at the proof. In the last two years, I’ve shot 11 winter weddings, and they’ve changed my mind entirely.

Here’s the part your budget will care about: winter bookings run about 30% cheaper than peak-season dates. That’s real money that can go back into your experience—or your pocket.

But here’s the part I care about: the light.

A flat overcast day in June is genuinely a harder portrait situation than a clear November afternoon at 3pm. In June, that gray sky turns into a giant, boring softbox. In November, the sun sits lower and cuts through bare trees, giving me directional light with depth and texture. I’m not trying to be poetic. Side-by-side, the November portraits from this area have more dimension and drama than the flat June ones. The light is honestly better.

And the logistics actually work. In June, I’m regularly sharing the venue parking lot with three or four other vendors, unloading gear around each other, and competing for the same shady spot during cocktail hour. Winter weddings give me room to breathe, set up without obstruction, and focus on you instead of the timeline traffic jam.

You’ll need a coat. The sun will set earlier. But if you’re browsing photographers and trying to decide whether an off-season date is a compromise, I want you to hear it from someone who’s been in the parking lot: it’s not.

I still have limited winter availability for next season. If you’re considering a November or winter date, reach out before the spring rush starts.

b.text:
# Why I Actually Like Photographing Winter Weddings Now

I’ll admit it: I used to think of winter weddings as the off-season.

After photographing 11 of them over the last two years, I’ve changed my mind. Winter weddings aren’t simply a backup option for couples who couldn’t get a June date. In some ways, they’re easier to photograph—and often easier on a wedding budget.

## The portrait light can be better

One of my favorite kinds of wedding light happens around 3 p.m. in November.

With the leaves gone, sunlight passes cleanly through the bare trees instead of breaking into uneven patches. It creates soft, directional light that gives portraits depth without feeling harsh. Honestly, I’ll take that over flat, overcast June light more often than I expected.

Winter does mean working with an earlier sunset, so the timeline matters. If portraits are important to you, we’ll usually plan them before the ceremony or immediately afterward. But when we make that window around 3 p.m. work, the results can be beautiful.

## Popular locations are actually usable

In June, I can arrive at a favorite portrait location and find three or four other wedding vendors sharing the same parking lot. That means crowded paths, people waiting for the same photo spots, and less flexibility if we need to adjust the schedule.

Winter is different.

The same locations are quieter, which gives us room to move and more freedom to use the best light. You’re less likely to have another wedding party just outside the frame, and we don’t have to rush through a spot because several other groups are waiting behind us.

That breathing room makes the portrait portion of the day feel calmer.

## Winter dates can cost about 30% less

For the couples I work with, winter bookings run about 30% cheaper. That can leave more room in the budget for an album, extra coverage, or another part of the wedding that matters to you.

Winter availability is also usually less competitive than peak-season availability. You still shouldn’t wait until the last minute—especially if you have a specific photographer or venue in mind—but you may have more options than you would for a Saturday in June.

## So, when should you book?

For a peak spring, summer, or fall date, booking as early as possible is still the safest choice. Those dates fill quickly in our area.

For a winter wedding, you may have more flexibility, but I’d still recommend reaching out once your venue and date are confirmed. An earlier booking gives us time to build the photography timeline around the limited daylight rather than trying to squeeze portraits into whatever time is left.

After 11 winter weddings in two years, I no longer see winter as the season couples settle for. The light can be better, locations are less crowded, and the savings are real. If you’re open to an earlier portrait schedule—and possibly bringing a warm coat for the walk between locations—it may be one of the smartest times of year to get married.

I drove Route 4 for twenty-two years, every gravel driveway and washed-out culvert of it, before I retired last year. So when I say I know this town, I mean I know the mailboxes and the people behind them. That's why I'm writing about the counter service closure the district office has proposed.

The USPS says the branch is losing $40,000 a year. What they don't say plain enough is that the loss came after they cut the counter hours from 8 to noon last spring. Cut a service down to four hours a day and of course fewer people use it. Then they turn around and point at the low traffic like it proves something. It doesn't. It proves you can starve a thing and then blame it for going hungry.

I think of Mrs. Halloran up on Kettle Hill. She's in her eighties, gets her heart medication by mail, and depends on that counter for money orders since she doesn't do the online banking business. Close the counter here and her nearest option is twenty minutes away in Fairview, on roads that aren't kind to an old car in the winter. She's not the only one out that way in the same boat. Route 4 is full of Mrs. Hallorans.

I'm not a writer and I don't have a lot else to say except this: if you care about this town keeping something as basic as a post office counter, show up on July 28 at the Grange Hall. That's when the district manager is holding the public forum. These decisions get made by people looking at spreadsheets in an office somewhere else. They ought to have to look at some faces too.

Bill Corbin
Kettle Falls

b.text:
To the Editor:

I drove Route 4 for 22 years before I retired last year, so I know this town and the people in it. I want to say something about the plan to close counter service at our post office.

The USPS says the branch loses $40,000 a year. What they don't say is that they already cut the counter hours from a full day down to 8 to noon. Of course business dropped after that. Working people can't get to the counter before noon. So they cut the hours, watched the traffic fall off, and now they're pointing at the drop as the reason to close. That's a problem they made themselves, and it isn't right to hang it on us.

I'll tell you who this hurts. Mrs. Halloran up on Kettle Hill is in her eighties and gets her heart medicine by mail. She still handles some of her bills with money orders because that's how she's always done it. She cannot drive twenty minutes to Fairview and twenty minutes back for a money order. There are more folks like her on every route out of this town. I delivered to them for two decades. I know their mailboxes and I know their situations.

A post office counter isn't just a place to buy stamps. It's where people who don't do everything on a computer can still take care of their business. Take that away and you've cut some of our neighbors off, plain and simple.

The district manager will be at a public forum on July 28 at the Grange Hall. If this counter matters to you, show up and say so. Empty chairs will tell them nobody cares. I don't believe that's true of this town, and I plan to be there to say it.

I'm no writer, just a retired mail carrier. But I know that when the mail matters to people, somebody ought to speak up.

Kettle Falls

a.text:
Hi everyone,

I wanted to tell you this myself instead of putting up a sign or hoping the word just got around.

We're not taking custom wedding cake orders anymore.

I have loved making them. There's a particular kind of quiet pride in watching a cake leave the shop knowing it's going to sit in the middle of someone's wedding day. We've done some beautiful ones, and I'm grateful for every couple who trusted us with that.

But I also have to be honest about what it actually takes in a shop this size.

Each of those cakes eats about fourteen hours of consults and tastings and emails and sketches before we even turn the mixer on. None of that time is paid. With three of us here and me starting at four most mornings, those hours come straight out of the day we need for everything else.

This year we had three last-minute cancellations. Plans change, I understand that completely. We'd already bought the ingredients, though, and for a little bakery that cost just sits there.

The part that finally settled it is that the wedding work was pulling us away from the case. The muffins and cookies and loaves and simple cakes you all actually come in for, day after day. That's what pays the rent. That's what keeps this place open for you in the morning.

So we're going back to that. We'll still have cake. We'll still do what we can for smaller celebrations if you come in and talk to us. But the big custom wedding cakes are something we have to set down.

Thank you for understanding. Thank you for walking through the door. It means more than I can say.

See you soon.

b.text:
I’ve been baking since four in the morning most days now, so I spend a lot of quiet hours alone with dough rising and ovens warming up. Those early minutes are where I get to think things through, which is exactly when I realized I needed to make some hard choices about what stays on our counter and what doesn’t. One of those decisions is stepping back from custom wedding cakes.

We used to take them because we genuinely loved helping you plan something beautiful, and honestly, listening to people’s stories about their upcoming day is one of my favorite parts of running this shop. But somewhere along the way, the reality of running a three-person team against modern expectations started to show its limits. Every single wedding cake order asks for roughly fourteen hours of free consultation, design sketching, and tastings. Those hours don’t come from a separate budget or an extra staff member—they come right out of the time I could be mixing your morning bread, frosting your favorite slice cakes, or just being behind the counter when you walk in.

This year tested us in a way we simply didn’t anticipate. Three last-minute cancellations hit close together, and between the perishable specialty ingredients already baked into those designs and the lost booking windows, we had to absorb every bit of that cost ourselves. It adds up fast when you’re a tiny crew trying to keep the counters full and the bills paid. Wedding cakes are meaningful work, but they’re also incredibly resource-heavy, and honestly, they’ve been slowly pulling us further away from the everyday case—the loaves, pies, pastries, and simple desserts that show up on our shelves daily and actually pay this rent.

So, going forward, we won’t be accepting any more custom wedding cake commissions. I want to be clear that this isn’t about turning our backs on your big celebrations; it’s about making sure we can keep showing up reliably for all of you who stop by after the school drop-off, who know exactly which flavor hits home on a rainy Tuesday, and who support this neighborhood spot week after week. If you’re planning a reception and need something sweet, we’d still love to help with grazing tables, sheet cakes, or curating a gorgeous selection of our existing pastries. 

Thank you for reading this during whatever spare moment you have between emails and errands. I’m so grateful to share this kitchen with you, and I’ll keep showing up at 4 a.m. to make sure your usuals are always ready. See you soon, probably over a cup of coffee and a warm slice of cake.

setup: A remote software engineer is writing a 6-month standing desk review for blog readers researching standing desks.

a.text:
# Jarvis L2 Standing Desk: My 6-Month Review

I’ve used the Jarvik L2 as my primary work desk for six months, working remotely as a software engineer. It has gone through daily height changes, long typing sessions, video calls, and the general abuse of a desk that is actually used—not just photographed in a minimalist office.

My verdict is straightforward: **buy it at the $549 sale price. Do not buy it at $749.** At the lower price, it’s a good, practical standing desk with a quiet and fast motor. At the regular price, the wobble and terrible cable tray are harder to excuse.

## The motor is the best part

The Jarvik L2’s motor has been consistently quiet and quick. Height adjustments don’t interrupt calls, and I can move from sitting to standing without waiting around or listening to a loud mechanical whine.

After six months, the motor still sounds and feels the same as it did when I installed the desk. There’s no grinding, hesitation, or noticeable slowdown. For a desk I adjust multiple times a day, that reliability matters more to me than having a long list of extra features.

## It wobbles at full height

The desk is stable enough at sitting height and at moderate standing heights. The problem appears when I raise it near its maximum height.

If I type aggressively—especially during a fast coding session—the monitor and desk surface wobble. It isn’t unusable, but it is noticeable and irritating. Light typing is fine. Resting my forearms on the desk is fine. Hard, rapid typing makes the desk move.

This is not a dealbreaker for me because I don’t spend the entire day at maximum height. However, if you’re tall, plan to keep the desk fully raised, or are particularly sensitive to monitor movement, you should take this seriously. The L2 is not rock-solid at full height.

## The memory presets drift

The memory presets are convenient, but they aren’t perfectly consistent. After six months, the saved positions can drift by roughly a centimeter.

That’s enough to notice if you’re trying to switch between a carefully tuned sitting height and standing height. I don’t have to recalibrate constantly, but I do occasionally find myself adjusting the desk manually after using a preset.

A one-centimeter difference isn’t catastrophic, but it undermines the point of having presets. I expected better repeatability.

## The cable tray is garbage

The included cable tray is the weakest part of the desk.

It doesn’t provide a clean or flexible way to manage cables, and it feels like an afterthought rather than a properly designed component. Once you add a monitor, laptop charger, peripherals, and a power strip, the tray becomes difficult to use effectively. Cables still hang awkwardly or require your own clips and ties to keep organized.

I ended up treating the tray as optional and using separate cable-management hardware. If clean cable routing matters to you, budget for a replacement or plan to improvise. I would not choose this desk because of its cable-management setup.

## Six-month durability

So far, the frame and lifting mechanism have held up well. There are no obvious signs of mechanical degradation, and the motor remains as quiet and fast as it was on day one.

The desk’s shortcomings are mostly design and stability issues rather than failures. It works every day, but it is not as polished as the price suggests when sold for $749.

## Final verdict

**At $549: worth buying.** The Jarvik L2 gives me a quiet, fast motor and a generally good sit-stand experience. The wobble at full height is manageable, the preset drift is annoying but minor, and the cable tray can be replaced or ignored.

**At $749: not worth it.** At that price, I expect better stability at maximum height, more accurate memory presets, and a cable tray that does its job. The L2 is a solid midrange desk, not a premium one.

If you can get it for **$549 or around that price**, I’d recommend it. If the price is **$749**, I’d keep shopping.

b.text:
# Jarvik L2 Standing Desk: 6-Month Review

**TL;DR:** Good motor, mediocre stability at height, sloppy presets, embarrassing cable management. Worth $549. Not worth $749. Buy it on sale or buy something else.

I bought the L2 in [month], paid the $549 sale price with my own money, and have used it 8+ hours a day, five days a week, ever since. No affiliate links in this post — nobody makes money if you buy this thing, including me. My setup: two 27" monitors on a gas-spring arm, mechanical keyboard, and a standing height of about 42.5". I switch positions 4–6 times a day, so the motor and presets have had a real workout — somewhere north of 700 cycles at this point.

## The motor is the best part of this desk

Genuinely. Sit-to-stand takes about 17 seconds under full load, it's smooth, and it's quiet enough that I've adjusted it mid-meeting with my mic unmuted and nobody noticed. There's a low hum, not a whine, and no grinding or hesitation at the top of travel. After 700+ cycles it sounds identical to day one.

This is the thing cheap desks get wrong — my previous budget frame started stuttering under two monitors within a year. The L2's motor has given me zero problems and I expect that to continue.

## Stability: fine sitting, wobbly standing

At sitting height, it's a rock. No complaints.

At my standing height (42.5"), there's front-to-back wobble when I type hard — and I type hard, because mechanical keyboard, because programmer. The monitors on my desk-mounted arm visibly sway for a second or two after I really get going. It's not alarming, nothing's going to fall, but it's noticeable and it's the kind of thing that bugs you more in month six than month one.

Two things made it better: torquing every frame bolt again after the first month (they settle), and moving my monitor arm's clamp closer to a leg. If you type gently or use a laptop, you may never notice. If you hammer a keyboard like you're mad at it, you will.

## The memory presets drift

There are four presets. Great. Except they drift by about a centimeter. I'll hit preset 2, the display says 42.5", and I can feel it's wrong — measure it, and it's at 41.6" or 43.1". It's not consistent in which direction it misses, which honestly offends me more. A centimeter doesn't sound like much until your elbows are slightly wrong for three hours.

I've done the factory recalibration (hold the down button, let it bottom out) three times. It helps for a week or two, then the drift creeps back. My fix is dumb but effective: I use the presets to get close, then nudge with the manual buttons and watch the readout. It works, but "the memory buttons get you within a centimeter" is a sad sentence to write about a desk that costs this much.

## The cable tray is garbage

I don't use that word lightly. It's a shallow stamped-metal trough that attaches to the underside of the desktop with four short screws into particle board. Here's what happened, in order:

1. I loaded it with one surge protector and the usual cable bundle. It sagged in the middle within a week.
2. The rear two screws loosened themselves from the desk's vibration. I re-seated them. One stripped the hole.
3. It's too shallow to close over a standard surge protector anyway, so the lid has been off since month one.

I ripped it out in month three, mounted a $15 under-desk cable raceway from [generic], and my cable situation is now better than the desk deserves. Budget for that. Plan on throwing the included tray directly in the trash and saving yourself the intermediate steps.

## Smaller stuff

- **The desktop** is laminate over particle board and it's fine. Edges haven't chipped, it wipes clean, and my monitor arm clamp hasn't dented it. Not premium, not a problem.
- **The controller** display is bright enough to read in a dark room, which also means it's bright enough to annoy you in a dark room. No way to dim it. I put a strip of electrical tape over half of it.
- **Assembly** took me about 50 minutes alone. Instructions were clear, hardware was labeled, nothing was missing. Genuinely good experience.
- **Anti-collision** works. It stopped on my chair arm once and reversed. Tested it deliberately a second time because I didn't trust it. It passed.

## The verdict

At **$549**, this desk is a good deal. The motor alone justifies it — quiet, fast, and proven over six months of daily abuse — and the flaws are livable if you know about them going in. Recalibrate occasionally, re-torque your bolts, replace the cable tray immediately, and you've got a desk that does its job.

At **$749**, it's overpriced. At that number you're in range of frames with better lateral stability and controllers that remember where 42.5 inches actually is. The wobble and the preset drift are forgivable at $549. They are insults at $749.

Jarvik runs sales constantly — I've seen it at $549 three separate times since I bought mine. So the advice is simple: if you want this desk, set a price alert and wait. Do not pay full price. Full price is for people who don't read reviews, and you just read 800 words about a cable tray.

412 copies in seven days. For about six hours it sat on the front page of a small subreddit, then traffic went back to normal.

# One Week After Launch

The game launched last week, after three years of nights-and-weekends work, and somehow 412 people bought it in the first seven days.

That number still feels strange to look at. I’d spent so long thinking about the game as a folder on my PC that seeing hundreds of actual players show up was a little surreal.

Launch day itself was mostly me refreshing dashboards, answering messages, and checking that nothing had caught fire. A post about the game also reached the front page of a small subreddit for about six hours, which caused the biggest spike in traffic. Watching it climb was exciting. Watching it disappear again was probably good for my blood pressure.

The reviews so far have been encouraging, along with a few useful criticisms. One review said the movement feels floaty, and honestly, they’re right. It’s one of those things I got used to after playing the game for hundreds of hours, but it’s much more obvious when someone new picks it up.

I’m working on that now. Version 1.1 is planned for next month and will include tighter movement, some smaller balance changes, bug fixes, and a few quality-of-life improvements based on player feedback.

For now, I’m reading every report, watching playthroughs when people post them, and making a list of everything that needs attention. Thanks to everyone who bought the game, left a review, shared the launch post, or sent me a message.

setup: A home baker is reviewing the Corlane SM6 mixer for blog readers deciding whether to buy it.

a.text:
**Corlane SM6 Stand Mixer Review: 8 Months of Daily Sourdough Duty**

I’ve put the Corlane SM6 through nearly every weekend market load for eight months now—double batches of stiff bagel dough, high-hydration country loaves, and the occasional rye that fights back. This is the mixer that lives on my counter and earns its keep.

The motor is the reason I keep it. A double batch of 65% hydration bagel dough (about 2.2 kg of stiff, dense stuff) goes in without drama. No stalling, no thermal cutoff, no high-pitched whine. It just grinds through the knead cycle at speed 2 like it’s bored. For market volume, that reliability matters more than pretty attachments.

Two real-world annoyances showed up fast. The bowl-lift lever started squeaking after about six weeks. A quick shot of WD-40 once a month keeps it quiet; ignore it and it gets embarrassing during a Saturday morning bake. More annoying: the stock dough hook is too short for the deep bowl. It rides high and leaves a thick collar of dough unworked at the bottom. I swapped in a third-party spiral hook ($28) and the problem disappeared. Plan on that extra purchase.

Price: $429. That’s eighty bucks more than the comparable KitchenAid. You’re paying for the extra torque and the deeper bowl, not for luxury features.

**Verdict:** Buy the Corlane SM6 if you knead heavy dough every single week. Skip it if most of your mixing is cookies and cake batter—those jobs don’t need this much muscle, and the cheaper options will treat you fine. For serious bread bakers who load the bowl hard and often, the SM6 has already paid for itself in my kitchen.

b.text:
# Corlane SM6 Stand Mixer Review: 8 Months of Nearly Daily Use

**Quick take:** The motor is worth the money. The accessories aren't. Full verdict at the bottom.

---

I've been running the Corlane SM6 for eight months now, and it gets used almost every day. I bake sourdough for a weekend farmers market stall, so this isn't a "unboxed it and made two batches of banana bread" review — this machine has mixed hundreds of batches of dough since it landed on my counter. Here's what eight months of hard use looks like.

## The motor is the whole reason to buy this mixer

The test that kills most home stand mixers is stiff, low-hydration dough — and I run the SM6 through that test constantly. A double batch of bagel dough, stiff enough that plenty of consumer mixers would stall out or walk themselves across the counter, runs through this machine without hesitation. No stalling, no straining, no standing there with my hand on the bowl waiting for it to recover. I can walk away and weigh out the next ingredient while it kneads.

If you've ever heard a mixer bog down in the middle of a bread dough, you know how quickly that becomes a dealbreaker. In eight months of near-daily bread work, the motor has never done that to me once. That is the entire case for this mixer.

## Two real problems

**The bowl lift lever squeaks.** Not a catastrophic issue, but it's a monthly maintenance item — I hit it with WD-40 about once every four weeks or it gets genuinely annoying. For a machine at this price, it shouldn't squeak out of the box, and it shouldn't squeak eight months later either.

**The included dough hook is too short for the bowl.** This is my biggest complaint. The SM6's bowl is deep, and the stock hook doesn't reach far enough down — dough at the bottom of the bowl just sits there, not getting worked in. I ended up buying a third-party hook, which solved the problem completely, but it means the hook that ships with the mixer is effectively useless for exactly the kind of dough this machine is built for. Factor that into the price.

## Speaking of price

The SM6 is $429. The comparable KitchenAid is $349. So the real math is: an $80 premium over KitchenAid, plus the cost of a replacement dough hook on top.

## Verdict

**If you're kneading heavy dough every week — bread, bagels, low-hydration anything, double batches — buy it.** The $80 premium buys you a motor that genuinely doesn't stall where other mixers in this class will, and after eight months I trust it with my market bread. Deal with the hook swap, keep a can of WD-40 under the sink, and it earns its spot on the counter.

**If your mixer mostly sees cookie dough and cake batter, skip it.** You'd be paying an $80 premium, plus a new dough hook, for a motor you'll never stress. Buy the KitchenAid and put the savings toward something else.

That's not a hedge — there's exactly one question that determines the answer, and it's whether stiff dough is a weekly event in your kitchen. For me it is, and I'd buy the SM6 again tomorrow.

setup: A small dog grooming salon owner is writing a how-to for dog owners about preventing coat matting between grooming visits.

a.text:
# How to Keep Your Dog’s Coat From Matting Between Grooming Visits

The biggest mistake I see owners make is bathing a matted dog because they think the water will loosen everything up. Unfortunately, it does the opposite. Once matted fur gets wet, it tightens as it dries and can turn into a felt-like pad against the skin.

Always brush your dog thoroughly **before** a bath at home, not after the mats have been soaked and set tighter. This is especially important for curly-coated dogs and double-coated breeds, whose loose undercoat can quickly become packed.

Use a slicker brush and work in small sections so you reach all the way through the coat instead of just smoothing the top. I recommend short, gentle “line brushing” strokes rather than brushing in circles. Circular brushing can twist the hair and contribute to tangles.

Start behind the ears and under the front legs. Those are two of the first places mats tend to form because of friction, movement, collars, and harnesses. Then work through the rest of the coat section by section, including the chest, belly, legs, tail, and areas where equipment rubs.

If you notice a mat beginning to form, don’t immediately pull at it with a brush or comb. First, work a little dog-safe conditioner or detangling product into the mat with your fingers. Gently separate the outer edges before using your slicker brush in short strokes. Hold the hair close to the skin while you work so you aren’t tugging on your dog.

If the mat is tight against the skin, covers a large area, or your dog seems uncomfortable, stop and call your groomer. Don’t try to cut it out with scissors—dog skin is thin and can easily be pulled up into the mat.

A few minutes of section-by-section brushing several times a week can make a huge difference. It keeps your dog more comfortable and makes the next grooming visit easier for everyone.

b.text:
**How to Keep Your Dog's Coat from Matting Between Grooming Visits**

If I could give every dog owner one piece of advice, it's this: never put a matted dog in the bathtub. I see it all the time — someone gives their pup a bath at home thinking the water will loosen the tangles, and by the time they come in to me, what started as a few small knots has dried into a solid felt pad against the skin. Water doesn't loosen mats. It locks them in tighter, and once that happens there often isn't a humane option besides clipping them out.

So the rule at home is simple: always brush before the bath, never after. Get the coat completely tangle-free first, then bathe.

When you brush, grab a slicker brush and use short line strokes — little strokes in one direction — not circles. Brushing in circles just winds the hair around itself and tightens whatever's already tangled. Work in small sections instead of going over the whole dog at once, and start behind the ears and under the front legs. That's where mats almost always begin, because of the friction from collars, harnesses, and all that leg movement. If those spots are clear, the rest of the coat usually follows pretty easily.

This matters even more with double-coated breeds — goldens, huskies, shepherds — where the soft undercoat tangles down at the skin where you can't see it, and with curly coats like poodles and doodles, where the hair seems to knot itself overnight. For those coats especially, a few minutes of brushing every couple of days beats an hour-long battle once a month.

And if you run your fingers through and feel a mat already starting, don't reach for the brush or comb first. Work a little conditioner into it with your fingers and gently tease the hairs apart with your fingertips. Once it loosens up, then you can ease through it with the brush. Going straight in with a tool pulls at the skin, hurts your dog, and teaches them to dread brushing — which makes everything harder next time.

Brush before the bath, keep an eye on those trouble spots, and your dog stays comfortable between visits. And if you're ever not sure about your technique, just ask at your next appointment — I'm happy to show you on your own dog. It's a lot easier to learn hands-on than from reading about it.

setup: A small coffee shop owner is writing testimony to city council opposing a parking meter rate increase.

a.text:
**Testimony Submitted for the Public Record**
**Re: Proposed Parking Meter Rate Increase from $0.50 to $1.50 Per Hour, Downtown Commercial District**

Council members, good evening. My name is on the sign above the door of a two-person coffee shop on Main Street, third from the corner. I'm here because I'm asked, as a small business owner, to comment on the proposal to triple our parking meter rate from fifty cents an hour to one dollar fifty. I'll keep this grounded, because small businesses don't get to speculate. We deal in what we actually count, and that's what I brought.

In 2019, the town eleven miles north of here passed a comparable parking rate increase. I don't mean a comparable in principle. I mean the same kind of neighborhood commercial strip, the same kind of metered storefronts, and I'll go a step further: I went to their Main Street equivalent for six weeks after their meters switched over and tracked my own register against my own register from the prior six weeks. Same hours, same menu, same staff. Foot traffic at my neighboring-town location dropped eighteen percent. Not two percent. Not "a noticeable decline." Eighteen percent of the people who walked through the door simply did not walk through the door. I have the receipt tallies. I will produce them into the record if asked. That eighteen percent was not an industry-wide trend. That town's surrounding businesses were fine. Mine wasn't. The variable was the meter.

Now I'll talk about the people who do walk through my door here on Main Street. I have been pulling time-stamped data off my own point-of-sale system for the better part of three years. The average visit at my shop is twenty-two minutes. Twenty-two minutes. A customer parks, walks in, orders a drip and maybe a scone, sits down with a book or a laptop or a friend, and leaves. The current one-hour meter minimum already covers that entire visit with nearly forty minutes of buffer. These people are not overstaying. They are not "hogging spaces." They are spending twenty-two minutes on a street you are asking them to pay three dollars and fifty cents for. Before my coffee gets cold. Before their scone is finished. Three-fifty for twenty-two minutes of being a person in a town.

And if the argument being made in this chamber tonight is that the increase is necessary to fund downtown maintenance, I'd gently point everyone at your own document. The city's published parking authority report, the one attached to this very agenda item, states that meter revenue accounts for four percent of the downtown operating budget. Four. Percent. Tripling the rate from fifty cents to a dollar-fifty does not close a ninety-six percent gap. It does not fix a sidewalk in three years. What it does, in concrete dollars-and-cents, is add one dollar to every twenty-two-minute visit my customers make, every single time, and it does so on top of a change I have watched cost an independent shop eighteen percent of its foot traffic in a town with otherwise identical conditions.

I am not here to tell you downtown maintenance doesn't matter. I am here to tell you that four percent is not a budget fix and eighteen percent is not an abstraction, and that the people on your committee drafting this have not stood behind a counter at 6 a.m. counting receipts against the prior six weeks while a meter ticks over into its second hour.

I am asking you to vote no. Or if not no, then to set the rate at seventy-five cents, to cap single-visit meter time at ninety minutes so that a twenty-two-minute customer isn't paying for an hour they won't use, and to return to this body with a plan that actually addresses the ninety-six percent of the budget that meters were never going to cover in the first place.

My name is [Name]. I run [Shop Name], 217 Main Street. My phone number and my six weeks of register data are available to any council member who wants them.

Thank you.

b.text:
Council Members,

I own a small independent coffee shop on Main Street, and I am asking you to reject the proposed increase in downtown parking meter rates from 50 cents to $1.50 per hour. Tripling the rate would impose a noticeable new cost on short visits while doing little to address the city’s broader downtown budget.

My customers stay an average of 22 minutes. The current one-hour minimum already more than covers the typical visit to my shop. Raising the hourly charge to $1.50 would not create more turnover for these customers; it would simply make a brief stop for coffee three times as expensive to park.

I have also seen evidence that higher parking prices can reduce downtown activity. In 2019, after a similar meter-rate increase in the next town over, I tracked my own register data for six weeks and observed an 18% drop in foot traffic. That is not a vague concern about what might happen. It is a measurable decline that I documented following a comparable change. For a small independent business, losing nearly one in five customer visits can affect staffing, inventory, operating hours, and the ability to remain open.

The city’s own report further indicates that meter revenue covers only 4% of the downtown budget. Increasing the rate from 50 cents to $1.50 an hour therefore does not appear to solve the underlying budget problem. Instead, it risks discouraging the customers whose spending supports downtown shops, restaurants, employees, and tax revenue.

Downtown businesses depend on convenience and repeat visits. A customer deciding whether to stop for a 22-minute coffee, pick up an order, or visit another Main Street business may choose a location with free or less expensive parking. Each decision may seem small, but together they can produce the kind of 18% decline I have already observed.

I respectfully urge the council not to triple the downtown parking rate. Please consider alternatives that address the budget without placing a disproportionate burden on short-term visitors and small businesses. At minimum, the city should conduct a clear economic-impact analysis and consider short-term parking options before approving an increase.

Thank you for considering this testimony and for entering it into the public record.

setup: A third-year electrical apprentice is writing an argumentative essay for the union newsletter against a 15% cut to apprenticeship funding.

a.text:
**Don’t Cut a Program That Works**

I’m a third-year electrical apprentice with the IBEW. I’m not writing this as somebody who’s against education. I’m writing this because I’m in the middle of a system that works, and the state is talking about cutting it.

The proposed 15% cut to state apprenticeship funding is a bad move. It’s bad for apprentices, bad for workers, bad for taxpayers, and bad for the future of the skilled trades.

Let me keep this simple: apprenticeship works. I’ve seen it work.

My cohort started with 24 apprentices. Twenty-one of us finished, and those 21 are working journeyman jobs now. That’s not a small number. That’s a success rate most programs would be proud of. We didn’t just sit in a classroom and collect debt. We showed up, worked, learned, got paid, and became skilled workers.

That’s the difference with apprenticeship. From day one, apprentices start around $19 an hour. By the time they become journeymen, they can top out around $46 an hour. That means people are getting on their feet fast. They’re paying rent. They’re buying groceries. They’re paying taxes. They’re getting off public assistance programs instead of staying on them.

That matters. A lot.

When somebody starts an apprenticeship, they’re not waiting four years to begin earning a paycheck. They’re earning while they’re learning. That means less student debt, less financial stress, and a faster path to a stable life. For a lot of people, that path is the only reason they were able to build a career at all.

Now look at the cost to the public.

The total public cost per apprentice who finishes is about $14,000. Compare that to something like $48,000 in average public subsidy for a four-year college graduate who finishes. That’s a huge difference. Apprenticeship is training workers at a fraction of the cost, while still producing highly skilled people who fill jobs the state actually needs.

So why would we cut a program that gives this kind of return?

A 15% cut might sound small to somebody sitting in an office. But in real life, cuts like this mean less support for training. They can mean fewer classes, fewer instructors, fewer resources, and fewer opportunities for the next group of apprentices. If the state cuts funding, it doesn’t make apprenticeship go away overnight. It just makes it harder. And when you make something harder, you lose people.

That would be a mistake.

We need more electricians, not fewer. We need more skilled workers, not less. Every year, more journeymen retire. Every year, more work comes in—construction, maintenance, infrastructure, energy projects, upgrades, repairs. The demand is real. If we want trained, licensed, safe electricians doing that work, then we need to keep investing in the system that produces them.

This isn’t a handout. Apprentices put in the work. Contractors put in the work. The union puts in the work. The state’s role is to support a training model that already proves itself. Cutting funding now would slow down a pipeline that is already delivering results.

To state legislators: if you’re looking for a smart use of public money, this is it. You’re not throwing money at a program that sounds good on paper. You’re supporting a proven path from training to employment. You’re helping people become taxpayers instead of dependents. You’re helping build a skilled workforce that keeps communities safe and functioning.

And to my fellow union members: this is why we need to speak up. This program changed our lives, and it can change more lives after us. But only if we defend it.

I’m a third-year apprentice. I’m not finished yet. But I’ve seen enough to know what this system does. It takes people who are willing to work and turns them into professionals. It gives people a fair shot. It builds careers, families, and futures.

A 15% cut to apprenticeship funding isn’t savings. It’s short-sighted. It weakens one of the best workforce programs we have.

The state should not cut it. The state should protect it.

b.text:
**Cutting Apprenticeship Funding Is the Worst Deal in the State Budget**

I'm a third-year electrical apprentice with this local. I didn't plan on writing for the newsletter, but the state is proposing a 15% cut to apprenticeship funding, and somebody who is actually living this program should say something before that vote happens.

Here's what I know from the inside.

My cohort started with 24 apprentices. Twenty-one of us finished. That's a completion rate of 87.5%. All 21 are working journeyman jobs right now. Not "looking." Not "in the field they studied." Working, with tools in their hands, on jobs in this state, paying taxes.

Compare that to a four-year college. Roughly six out of ten students who start finish within six years. Of the ones who finish, plenty are working jobs that have nothing to do with their degree, and a lot of them are carrying debt they'll be paying on for twenty years.

Now look at the money, because that's what this cut is really about.

The total public cost for an apprentice who finishes the program is about $14,000. The average public subsidy for a student who finishes a four-year degree is around $48,000. That's more than three times as much per person, for a program that loses more people along the way and delivers less certain results.

I'm not knocking college. Some jobs need it. But if the state is trying to decide where each dollar does the most good, this isn't close. Apprenticeship is the cheapest way this state has to turn somebody into a skilled worker with a career. And it's the one they're proposing to cut.

Here's the other piece legislators need to understand. Apprentices don't sit in a classroom for four years and then hope to get hired. We get paid from the first week. Starting wage is around $19 an hour. By the time you top out as a journeyman it's around $46 an hour, plus health insurance and a pension.

Think about what that does. A first-year apprentice at $19 an hour is already off most assistance programs. A journeyman at $46 an hour is buying a house, paying property taxes, and raising kids who don't need help either. The state stops spending on that person and starts collecting from them, fast. Nobody in my cohort is on assistance. Not one.

So when you cut apprenticeship funding by 15%, you're not saving money. You're spending more later. Fewer apprentices means fewer journeymen. Fewer journeymen means more people stuck in $12-an-hour jobs, still on Medicaid, still on SNAP, still not paying much in taxes. The state pays for that. It just pays for it in a different line of the budget, and it pays for it every year instead of once.

And it's not like the work is going away. Every contractor in this local is short on hands. Data centers, hospitals, schools, solar, EV chargers, grid work — all of it needs licensed electricians and there aren't enough of us. Cut the pipeline now and in four years the state is either paying out-of-state contractors premium rates or watching projects sit unfinished.

I want to be clear about one more thing. A 15% cut doesn't mean the program gets 15% worse. It means fewer seats. Someone who would have gotten into the next cohort doesn't. That person is real. He's probably 20 years old, working retail or warehouse, wants something better, and the state just told him no. Not because he wasn't qualified. Because the state decided the cheapest, most successful training program it funds was the one to trim.

If you're a member of this local, call your representative. Tell them what you make, what you started at, and what you'd be doing if this program hadn't been there. Keep it short. They need to hear it from working people, not just from staff.

If you're a legislator reading this: 21 out of 24. $14,000 versus $48,000. $19 an hour to $46 an hour. Those are the numbers. Cut something else.

setup: A bakery owner is writing a warm blog and newsletter post to regular customers explaining why wedding cake orders are ending.

a.text:
A little note about wedding cakes

I’ve been putting off writing this one, because I don’t want anyone to feel like we’re letting them down. But I also believe in being straight with you, so here it is: we’re not taking on custom wedding cake orders anymore.

It’s not because we stopped loving weddings. We haven’t. I still get a little teary when someone tells me they got engaged at our counter or when a regular brings in photos of a cake we made years ago. Wedding cakes were a joy in a lot of ways.

But the honest truth is, they don’t work for a bakery our size. There are only three of us. I’m up at 4am most days, and by the time a wedding cake is done—the emails back and forth, the tasting, the sketching, the scheduling, the hunting down exactly the right ribbon or flower—it’s usually about 14 hours before I even turn on the oven. That’s 14 hours I’m not spending on the things that keep our doors open: the morning buns, the bread, the cookies, the case full of everyday stuff you actually come in for.

This year we also had three wedding cakes cancel on us at the last minute. I don’t blame anyone—big life plans change, things fall apart, I get it. But by then the ingredients were ordered, some of the prep was already done, and for a business this small, those losses stung. It’s hard to bounce back from that when you’re also trying to make payroll and keep the lights on.

And honestly, the wedding cake work was pulling us away from the everyday case, which is what actually pays rent. That case is our heartbeat. It’s what you count on when you come in for a coffee and a croissant, or a last-minute birthday cake, or just something good after a long week. I don’t want to lose that. I don’t want to be too busy with a five-tier cake to make sure the sourdough is right.

So we’re making the call to focus on what we do best, and to do it really well. If you’re already on our calendar or mid-conversation with us about a wedding cake, we’ll honor that. We’ll still have cakes in the case, and if you need something for a smaller gathering, come talk to us—we’ll do what we can. If you’re looking for a wedding cake, I’m happy to point you toward some local bakers I truly trust.

Thank you for understanding. Thank you for being the reason we get to do this at all. And thank you for still coming in for the daily stuff—that’s the part I never want to lose.

See you at the counter.

b.text:
We’ve decided to stop taking orders for custom wedding cakes. It’s a hard thing to write, because being asked to bake for someone’s wedding is a lovely kind of trust, and we’re grateful to everyone who’s let us be part of their day.

But there are three of us here, and we’ve had to be honest about how much we can fit into a week.

A custom wedding cake takes a lot of work before we even turn on the oven. Between consultations, tastings, and working through the details, we spend around 14 hours on each order that we don’t charge for. We’ve also had three last-minute cancellations this year after ingredients were already bought, leaving us to absorb those costs. Neither of those things is easy for a shop our size.

The bigger thing, though, is that the wedding work has been pulling us away from the everyday case. That’s the baking most of you come in for, and it’s what keeps the rent paid. It deserves our time and attention—not whatever we have left after a big custom order.

Most mornings I’m baking by 4 a.m., and lately I’ve been reminded that starting early doesn’t make the day any longer. We can love making something and still decide it doesn’t fit the bakery anymore.

So we’re making a little more room for the daily baking, and for doing it well. I’m sad to let the wedding cakes go, but I’m also looking forward to giving more of our energy to the things you stop in for on an ordinary morning.

Thank you for making those ordinary mornings enough to build a little bakery around. We’re very glad to be here.

setup: A solo indie game developer is writing a devlog recap for subscribers about his game's launch week sales, subreddit attention, review feedback, and upcoming 1.1 patch.

a.text:
**Devlog #48: Launch Week**

Well, it’s out. After three years of nights, weekends, and staring at the same collision bugs until my eyes crossed, the game actually launched last Tuesday. 

Here is how the first week went, by the numbers and otherwise.

We sold 412 copies in the first seven days. For context, I had no publisher, zero ad spend, and a wishlist count that was modest at best. It’s not quit-your-day-job money, but seeing 412 people actually pay money to play something I built at my kitchen table feels surreal. 

Most of the initial spike came on Wednesday when a post I made hit the front page of a small genre subreddit and stayed there for about six hours before sliding down. That brought in a sudden wave of traffic, a handful of streams, and my first batch of written reviews.

Speaking of reviews: sitting at mostly positive right now, but one negative review specifically called out the movement controls, saying the character feels "way too floaty and unresponsive on hard landings." 

Honestly? They’re completely right. When you spend three years tuning physics values by yourself, you just get used to the weird momentum quirks and stop noticing them. Reading that critique stung for about two seconds, and then I went back into the engine, played with fresh eyes, and immediately saw what they meant. 

So, that’s being reworked. I’m overhauling the air deceleration and coyote time for the 1.1 patch, which I'm planning to push out sometime next month alongside a few keybind fixes people asked for.

Right now, the plan is pretty simple:
* Fix two minor crash reports that came in over the weekend (patch 1.0.3 drops tomorrow).
* Tighten up the movement physics for 1.1.
* Catch up on some sleep.

Thanks to everyone here who bought a copy, dropped a review, or just followed along with these posts over the last three years. I'll have another update in a couple of weeks with a look at the revised movement.

b.text:
# Devlog #47: It's Out

Okay. So the game is out. It's been out for a week. I keep typing that sentence and deleting it because it still feels fake.

Here's what actually happened.

**412 copies.** That's the number after week one. I don't have anything to compare it to and I'm not going to pretend I know if that's good or bad. It's more than my mom and my three friends, which is the only threshold I'd actually set for myself out loud. Three years of nights and weekends and it's a real number on a real dashboard now.

For about six hours I was on the front page of a small subreddit. I watched the concurrent player count tick up in real time like an idiot, refreshing everything. Then it fell off the front page and things went quiet again, which is how these things go. But for those six hours it was genuinely happening.

**The floaty movement thing.** One reviewer said the movement feels floaty. I read it, got a little defensive for about ninety seconds, and then went and played my own game with fresh eyes and — yeah. They're right. It's floaty. I've played this build so many thousands of times that I stopped feeling it. So that's getting fixed. Reworking the acceleration and the fall curves, tightening the jump. That's the big thing in **1.1, coming next month.** Also cleaning up a couple of collision spots people flagged.

That's it. That's the update. Game's out, some people bought it, one person was right about the jumping, and I'm patching it.

More when 1.1 is close.
