setup: A family plumbing company owner is writing a blog post for Minneapolis homeowners about winterizing outdoor pipes.

a.text:
**How to Winterize Your Outside Spigots (And Avoid a Costly Burst Pipe)**

Frozen outdoor pipes are one of the most common—and preventable—winter plumbing disasters. Here’s how to protect your spigots before temperatures drop:

1. **Shut off the interior valve** – Locate the shutoff valve inside your home (usually in the basement or utility room) and turn it clockwise to close it. This stops water from flowing to the outdoor spigot.

2. **Drain the spigot** – Go outside, open the spigot, and let any remaining water drain out. Leave it open to prevent pressure buildup if any water is left behind.

3. **Disconnect all hoses** – This is the biggest mistake we see. A connected hose traps water, which freezes and expands, cracking the pipe. Store hoses indoors for the winter.

4. **Install a foam cover** – Pick up a $3 insulated cover from any hardware store and snap it over the spigot for extra protection.

**Don’t have an interior shutoff?** Some older homes lack this valve, making winterization trickier. If that’s the case, give us a call—we can install one or recommend other solutions to keep your pipes safe.

A few minutes of prep now can save you from a messy (and expensive) cleanup later. Stay warm, Minneapolis!

b.text:
# How to Winterize Your Outdoor Spigots Before the Minneapolis Freeze

If you leave water sitting in your exterior sillcocks when the ground freezes solid in Hennepin County, that copper pipe will split open. You won’t notice it when it happens—you’ll notice it during the first spring thaw when water starts pouring into your finished basement or crawl space.

Here is the exact step-by-step process we tell our customers to follow every October. It takes ten minutes.

---

### Step 1: Disconnect all hoses, splitters, and timers immediately

If you only do one thing on this list, do this. 

Leaving a garden hose connected to an outside spigot is responsible for roughly 80% of the burst-pipe calls we run in January and February. Even if you have a modern "frost-free" spigot, leaving a hose attached traps water inside the barrel of the valve. The water cannot drain out. It freezes, expands, and splits the brass tube wide open inside your wall. 

Unscrew the hose, drain it, roll it up, and put it in the garage. Take off brass splitters and plastic timers, too.

### Step 2: Locate and close the interior shutoff valve

Head into your basement, utility room, or crawl space. Look at the wall roughly where the outdoor faucet sits outside, and follow that copper line inward. 

You’re looking for a shutoff valve. It will usually be either:
* **A round wheel handle (gate valve):** Turn it clockwise until it stops tight.
* **A lever handle (ball valve):** Turn it a quarter-turn so the handle sits perpendicular across the pipe.

### Step 3: Drain the trapped water (Don't skip the bleeder cap)

Turning off the interior valve only stops incoming water; you still have water sitting between the shutoff and the outside spigot. You need to get that water out.

1. **Go outside:** Turn the spigot handle all the way open. Let whatever water is inside run out. Leave this tap open all winter.
2. **Go back inside:** Grab a small bucket or a rag. On the side of your interior shutoff valve, you’ll usually see a tiny brass cap—that’s the bleeder port. Unscrew that cap with a pair of pliers. A cup or two of water will drain out into your bucket. 
3. Once it stops dripping, screw the tiny bleeder cap back on hand-tight.

If you don't open that bleeder cap, an airlock keeps the water trapped in the line, defeating the whole purpose of shutting off the valve.

### Step 4: Install a $3 foam faucet cover

Run down to your local hardware store and buy an insulated foam faucet cover—they usually cost less than five bucks. Hook the rubber loop over the spigot handle and slide the foam dome tight against the exterior siding. 

While this won't save an undrained pipe from twenty below zero, it blocks cold Minneapolis drafts from creeping directly through your foundation rim joist.

---

### What if you don't have an interior shutoff valve?

A lot of older homes in Minneapolis—especially in South Minneapolis, Northeast, and older parts of St. Paul—never had dedicated interior shutoff valves installed for the hose bibbs. Or, the old gate valve is corroded and won't turn without snapping.

If you can't find an interior shutoff, **give us a call.** We can get out to your house quickly, sweat in a reliable quarter-turn ball valve with a bleeder, or upgrade you to a true commercial frost-free hydrant before the hard freeze sets in. It costs far less to install a shutoff today than it does to remediate water damage in mid-winter.

setup: A high-school senior is writing a personal essay for college admissions readers about working at her family's Vietnamese restaurant.

a.text:
On Saturdays I’m at the restaurant by ten. I tie an apron over my jeans and start cutting carrots into matchsticks while my mom argues with the produce delivery. The dining room smells like bleach and last night’s fish sauce.

The register died one Saturday in October. A power blink killed the screen, and my dad hit the side of it like it owed him money. The line stretched to the door. I grabbed a pad of guest checks and a pen. For the next three hours I wrote every order by hand: two large pho tai, no onion for table six; one bun thit nuong, extra peanuts, table four. My handwriting got worse. I asked people to repeat themselves over the steam and a baby crying. By the end my palm was gray from ink. When the register came back on around two, I typed in the stack of tickets while my dad watched. The numbers matched. He nodded once and went back to the kitchen. That was the whole thing.

Another Saturday, a new hire named Keisha stood over a tray of spring roll skins looking panicked. She said she’d watched the training video twice but her rolls came out lumpy. I told her the video was useless. I took half the filling and showed her how my grandma does it: let the rice paper soften, fold the bottom up tight, tuck the sides like making a bed, roll forward without pushing. “Don’t squeeze,” I said. “Just guide it.” Her first one still looked a little pregnant on one side, but the second was better. By closing she’d done a whole tray and her fingertips were pruned from the water. She said her mom would be proud. I said mine wouldn’t care as long as they didn’t fall apart.

The walk-in cooler is where I do calculus homework. Between rushes I drag a milk crate inside, sit against the wire shelf of Thai basil and cilantro, and balance my textbook on my knees. It’s forty degrees. The compressor kicks on and drowns out my mom calling for me. I get maybe fifteen minutes before my hands go stiff. Last Saturday I finished a whole worksheet in there. I came out smelling like cold herbs, and my dad asked if I was getting sick. I said no, it was just derivatives.

I’ve worked every weekend since sophomore year. I know the menu by heart and can carry four bowls without a tray if they’re not too full. I know which customers want extra sriracha before they ask and which ones will complain the Thai tea is too sweet no matter what we do. I know the register’s moods and the exact sound of the back door when my dad goes out to smoke. The restaurant needs hands, and I have hands. Some weekends are boring, some are a disaster, most are both by closing. I do my homework in the cold and roll spring rolls and write down what people want to eat. That’s the job. I do it.

b.text:
By the time I got my driver’s license, I already knew how to take an order for pho, carry three hot bowls at once, and tell when my dad was about to get mad just by the way he held the ticket pad.

I have worked every weekend at my family’s Vietnamese restaurant since sophomore year. It is not fancy work. It is loud, hot, and repetitive. The floor gets sticky. My apron always smells like fish sauce by the end of the night. Most Saturdays, I am at the front counter, the register, or running food between tables while my parents and grandmother move around the kitchen like they are part of a machine that has been running for years.

One Saturday, the register system died in the middle of lunch rush.

At first everyone kept pressing the screen like that would fix it. Then the screen stayed frozen, the line kept growing, and my mom called my name in the way that means she is trying not to panic. I grabbed a stack of blank receipts and started writing every order by hand. Appetizers, no onions, extra noodles, one egg roll, two iced coffees, one banh mi to go. I wrote fast enough that my wrist hurt. I copied table numbers onto the tickets and called them out to the kitchen. I could hear my dad behind me saying, “What table? What table?” and I kept answering without looking up.

It took longer than usual, and customers had to wait. Some were patient. Some were not. I just kept writing. There was no fixing it. The restaurant still had to keep moving.

Another day, my grandmother showed a new hire how to fold spring rolls. She does it fast, with the same careful motion every time, tucking the sides in so the filling stays tight. The new girl kept making them too loose, and my grandmother kept shaking her head and starting over without saying much. I watched for a minute, then showed the new hire how my grandma likes it done: not too much stuffing, fold once, tuck in, roll tight. “Like this,” I said, pressing the wrapper flat on the tray. She copied me, and the next one looked right.

Most of my homework got done in pieces. I did calculus problems during slow hours, sometimes standing in the walk-in cooler because it was the only quiet place in the whole restaurant. I would lean against a crate of produce with my notebook open on top of a box and work through derivatives while the cold made my fingers stiff. Every few minutes someone would open the door and call my name. Then I would go back out, wipe my hands on my jeans, and take another order.

I used to think of weekends as the part of the week that belonged to everyone else. Now they are the part I know best. I know the sound the fryer makes when it is too full. I know which customers sit by the window every Saturday. I know how to read my grandmother’s face when she is tired and still keeps cooking. I know how to hand-write a ticket so the kitchen can still keep going when the system stops.

Working there did not make me special. It just became part of who I am: someone who shows up, keeps track of what needs to be done, and does it even when my hands are tired and my homework is still unfinished.

setup: A parent of two middle-schoolers is writing an op-ed to local readers urging an 8:45am middle-school start time.

a.text:
**An 8:45 Start Time Is a Better Start for Millbrook Students**

As a parent of two middle-schoolers in Millbrook, I have seen firsthand how hard it is for adolescents to be fully awake, focused, and ready to learn early in the morning. This is not about laziness or poor habits. Teenagers’ bodies are wired differently: as they enter adolescence, their natural sleep cycles shift later.

That is why I support the school board’s proposal to move the middle school start time to 8:45 a.m.

The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends that middle and high schools start no earlier than 8:30 a.m. so students can get the sleep they need. That recommendation is not based on a preference for sleeping in. It is based on what we know about adolescent health, learning, mood, and safety. Well-rested students are better able to pay attention, retain information, regulate emotions, and participate in class.

We do not have to look far for evidence that a later start can make a difference. At Lincoln Middle, the pilot program produced encouraging results: attendance improved, and first-period grades went up. Those may sound like simple measures, but they matter. A student who is present, alert, and able to learn during first period has a better chance of succeeding throughout the day.

Some residents have raised understandable concerns about buses. Transportation is complicated, and families rely on schedules that work. But the proposal already addresses that issue by re-tiering bus routes. In other words, the board is not ignoring the practical details; it has built a transportation plan into the proposal rather than treating buses as an afterthought.

No schedule change will be perfectly convenient for every household. As parents, we all juggle work, child care, activities, and family routines. But we should ask what inconvenience is worth accepting if it gives our children a healthier and more productive school day.

An 8:45 start time is not a cure-all. Students will still have homework, sports, phones, and busy lives. But it is one meaningful step the district can take to align school with what we know about how middle-school students learn best.

The school board has an opportunity next month to put student well-being ahead of an outdated schedule. I hope they vote yes on the 8:45 start time.

b.text:
Why Our Kids Need That 8:45 Start Time

I'm not a doctor, a teacher, or a school board member. I'm just a Millbrook mom with two middle-schoolers, a coffeemaker that works overtime, and a minivan that smells like soccer practice.

Our mornings go like this: alarm at 6:15, lights on, snooze, snooze again, then me begging two half-asleep kids to get dressed, eat something, find their shoes. They make it to homeroom by 7:30, but I wouldn't say they're really there. First period is a fog.

That's why I'm writing in support of the proposal to move our middle school start time to 8:45, which the board votes on next month. I've read the whole thing, highlighter and all, and I think it's the right call for our kids.

This isn't about letting kids be lazy. It's biology. The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends that teens ages 13 to 18 get 8 to 10 hours of sleep a night, and that middle and high schools start no earlier than 8:30. Our current 7:30 start makes that math almost impossible. For my 13-year-old to get nine hours, she'd need to be fully asleep by 9:30. With homework, shower, and just being a kid who needs to unwind, that doesn't happen in real life.

And we don't have to guess whether later would work here in Millbrook. We already saw it. Last year Lincoln Middle piloted the 8:45 start, and attendance went up and first-period grades went up. Teachers said kids were more alert, less tardy. As a parent, that rings true. When my kids actually sleep, everything is easier — mood, homework, even how they treat each other.

I know the number one worry is buses. I've heard it at soccer, at the grocery store: how will this work without chaos? I worried about that too. But if you read the proposal, it already handles it by re-tiering the routes. Middle school, high school, and elementary would each get their own staggered window, so the same buses and drivers can cover everyone without buying a whole new fleet. Will the first week be bumpy? Probably. But it's not unplanned.

We're always telling our kids to make healthy choices and work hard in school. Giving them a start time that lets them sleep and show up ready to learn is how we back that up.

Please join me in telling the school board: vote yes on 8:45.

setup: A real estate agent is posting one specific observation about early block walks and happier buyers to LinkedIn buyers, agents, and lenders.

a.text:
After 12 years helping people buy homes in Asheville, I’ve noticed something: the buyers who walk the neighborhood at 7 a.m. before we tour tend to be happier with their choice later. Not a statistic—just a pattern I keep seeing, especially with first-time buyers.

I always think of the Pruitts on Sycamore Street. [Insert what they noticed on their early-morning walk, how it affected their decision, and what they told you after living there.]

A showing gives you a good look at the house. That morning walk gives you a glimpse of what it might feel like to live there. You hear the traffic when people are actually leaving for work. You find out whether the route you pictured walking with your coffee is somewhere you’d enjoy spending time.

I still want you to take your time in the kitchen and make sure your furniture fits. But before you commit, spend a little time outside the property line, at an hour that looks like your real life. You’re buying the house, but the neighborhood will be part of your day, too.

b.text:
The best advice I give buyers after twelve years in Asheville real estate has nothing to do with interest rates or contingencies. It's this: before you tour the house, walk the neighborhood at 7am.

I made it a standing suggestion after the Pruitts. First-time buyers, terrified of making a mistake, and they'd fallen hard for a listing on Sycamore Street. Great photos, cute porch, and they were half ready to write an offer before we'd even stepped inside. I told them what I tell everyone now: get there early, park a few streets over, and just walk.

At 7am on a Tuesday in October they met the actual street. A neighbor walking an arthritic old lab. A woman sweeping her porch. Somebody's coffee drifting out an open window, cold enough that they could see their breath, and the kind of quiet you can't judge from inside a car. The lab's owner stopped to chat, told them about the fall cookout at the end of the block, which houses had kids, and — almost as an aside — that the back corner of the yard they were about to stand in turns to soup after a hard rain.

We toured the house at 8:30. They still loved it. But they made their offer knowing the whole street, not just the kitchen, and they asked the sellers about the drainage directly instead of finding out in year one.

Three years later they're still on Sycamore. When that corner ponds up after a storm, they don't call me in a panic. They know their neighbors by name, somebody feeds their cat when they travel, and the soggy corner is just a Tuesday.

Here's the pattern I've noticed over twelve years of this: buyers who see a house at 10am and drive off fall in love with the finishes. Buyers who walk the block at 7am fall in love with the life they're actually buying. Every house eventually does something disappointing. The 7am buyers shrug it off. The others call me wondering if they made a mistake.

If you're buying, ask your agent to build the walk into your day. If you're an agent, steal it. It's free, it takes an hour, and it's the most honest showing your buyers will ever get.

setup: You're everyone at the startup. Yesterday's 40-minute outage was caused by a bad database migration during deploy.

a.text:
Hi team,

I wanted to give you an update on yesterday's outage.

**Status: Fixed.** Our service was down for about 40 minutes yesterday around 2 PM. We've identified the cause, rolled back the change, and everything is back to normal.

**What happened:**
During our routine deployment yesterday, we ran a database update that accidentally locked up a critical table in our database for much longer than expected. This made it impossible for customers to access the service. We caught it quickly, reversed the change, and service came back online.

**Why it happened:**
The database update was supposed to be a quick operation, but the way it was written caused it to hold a lock on that table for the full 40 minutes instead of releasing it immediately. We didn't catch this in testing because it depends on the exact size of our production database.

**What we're doing about it:**
Going forward, any database updates like this one will run during our scheduled maintenance windows (when we've already notified customers to expect potential disruptions) instead of during regular deployments. This gives us more control and means updates won't accidentally impact live customer traffic.

I know some of you fielded customer questions and concerns yesterday—thanks for handling those. If anyone has follow-up questions, I'm happy to discuss.

b.text:
**Current Status:** All systems are fully operational and stable. The issue from yesterday is completely resolved.

Hi team,

I want to give everyone a clear update on yesterday’s 40-minute outage around 2:00 PM. I know several of you were on the front lines handling customer complaints during that time, so I appreciate your patience and quick communication while we sorted it out. Here is what happened, how we fixed it, and how we are preventing it in the future.

**What Happened**
During a routine code deploy, we ran a background update to our database. That update unexpectedly locked up a key database table for much longer than anticipated, which blocked the rest of our application from loading and caused the downtime.

**How We Fixed It**
Once we identified the lockup, the engineering team immediately cancelled and rolled back the update. This released the lock and brought the entire system back online.

**What We’re Changing**
To ensure this doesn't happen again, we are changing how we handle database updates. Going forward, any database changes with the potential to lock tables will only be run during scheduled, off-peak maintenance windows, rather than during normal daytime deployments.

setup: A solo indie game developer is writing a devlog recap for subscribers about his game's launch week sales, subreddit attention, review feedback, and upcoming 1.1 patch.

a.text:
# Launch week: 412 copies, six hours on a front page, and one very fair review

The game launched last week. After three years of nights and weekends, I don't have a clever way to describe that, so I'll just say it plainly: it's out, people can buy it, and I've been refreshing the sales dashboard more than I'd like to admit.

Numbers, since that's what most of you are here for: **412 copies in the first week.** Before launch I told myself that 100 would make it worth doing and 500 would be a miracle, so I'm landing somewhere in the middle, and I'll take it. It's not quit-the-day-job money. It's "the last three years weren't for nothing" money, which is what I was actually hoping for.

Mid-week, a post about the game hit the front page of a small subreddit and stayed there for about six hours. I watched it happen in real time. Traffic spiked, a good chunk of the week's sales came out of that one window, and then it slid off the page and everything went back to normal. Six hours of internet fame, gone by dinner. It was fun while it lasted.

Now the reviews. They've been mostly kind so far. One of them said the movement feels floaty, and I sat with that for about a minute before admitting they're right. I've played this game for three years and somewhere along the way I lost the ability to feel it — you tune something a hundred times and your hands just adapt. Fresh eyes caught in an afternoon what I couldn't catch in three years.

So: **patch 1.1 is coming next month**, and the headline item is movement tuning. Tighter acceleration, faster stops, less sliding around. If the floatiness bugged you, it's being fixed. There's also a short list of bugs people reported that I've been able to reproduce, and those are going in too.

After that, I'm going to keep supporting the game for a while and see how sales settle before deciding on anything bigger.

Thanks to everyone who bought it, everyone who wishlisted it forever ago and actually showed up, and everyone who's been following along with this devlog. 412 of you took a chance on it.

Back to work.

b.text:
**Launch Week**

Game went live last Tuesday. Sold 412 copies in the first week, which is more than I expected and less than I hoped, which I think is the most honest way to put it.

It hit the front page of r/indiegaming for about six hours on launch day. I refreshed the page way too many times. The traffic spike drove a decent chunk of those sales and the rest seemed to come from wishlists converting. Steam's algorithm did its thing for a day or two after, then settled back down to the usual trickle.

One review mentioned the movement feels floaty. They're right. I felt it in the last few weeks of testing and kept telling myself I'd tune it after launch, which is exactly the kind of thing you shouldn't do. Patch 1.1 is in the works for mid-next month — tightening the gravity, the air control, the whole feel. There are also a couple of crash bugs I'm chasing that only seem to show up on certain hardware, so if that's been happening to you, hang in there.

What's next: 1.1 ships next month, then I'm going to sit with it for a bit and decide whether a content update is worth the time or whether I should start moving on the next thing. Haven't decided yet.

Thanks to everyone who picked it up, posted about it, or sent me a message that first week. Means a lot.

setup: A family plumbing company owner is writing a blog post for Minneapolis homeowners about winterizing outdoor pipes.

a.text:
## How to Winterize Your Outdoor Spigots (Minneapolis Homeowners, Do This Before Halloween)

Four steps. Twenty minutes. Do them both — front and back of the house, plus the garage if you've got a hose bib out there.

### 1. Shut off the interior valve

Every outdoor spigot should have a shutoff valve inside the house on the pipe that feeds it. In most Minneapolis homes that's in the basement, along the rim joist, near where the pipe runs out through the wall. Older houses in Nokomis, Longfellow, Northeast — it's usually a small gate valve or a ball valve within a few feet of the exterior wall.

Turn it off. Gate valve, that's clockwise until it stops. Ball valve, quarter turn so the handle sits crosswise to the pipe.

### 2. Drain the spigot

Go outside and open the spigot all the way. Let it run until it stops dripping. This is the step people skip, and it's the whole point of the exercise — the interior valve keeps new water out, but whatever's already sitting in that pipe is what freezes and splits it.

Leave the outdoor spigot open all winter. Nothing's feeding it, and an open valve gives any leftover moisture somewhere to expand.

If your interior shutoff has a small bleeder cap on the side, put a bucket under it, unscrew it a turn or two, and let the rest drain out. Snug it back down when it quits dripping.

### 3. Disconnect your hoses

Read that again, because this is the one that costs people money.

### 4. Put a $3 foam cover on it

Hardware store, insulation aisle, styrofoam dome with a rubber strap. Loop the strap over the spigot handle, tighten it, push the cover flat against the siding. It's not doing the heavy lifting — steps 1 and 2 did that — but it buys you a margin when we hit a stretch of below-zero nights and it cuts down on wind chill hitting that pipe where it passes through the wall.

## The mistake that keeps us busy every January

A garden hose left attached to the spigot holds water. That water freezes and backs pressure up into the spigot and the pipe behind it. Even a frost-free hose bib — the long ones designed to shut off inside the heated part of the wall — can't drain if there's a hose hanging on the end of it. That's the part homeowners don't know. People install a frost-free bib and figure they're covered, then leave the hose on and split the pipe anyway.

Here's how it plays out: the pipe cracks in December, but it's holding no water, so nothing happens. Nobody notices. Then in May somebody hooks up a hose to water the tomatoes, turns on the interior valve, and water comes pouring into the basement through the rim joist. Or worse — it cracked on the interior side of the wall and it's been running down inside the wall cavity since the first thaw.

Coil your hoses, drain them, hang them in the garage. Takes five minutes.

## What if you don't have an interior shutoff?

A lot of Minneapolis houses don't — especially anything pre-war where a spigot got added at some point without a dedicated valve, or where a previous owner's remodel buried the valve behind finished basement wall.

If you go down to the basement and can't find a shutoff for that line, don't guess and don't just cover the spigot and hope. **Give us a call.** Adding an interior shutoff valve is a small job — usually an hour or two — and it's a lot cheaper than the drywall, insulation, and framing repair after a burst line lets go behind a finished wall.

Same goes if the valve is there but seized, or if you shut it off and the spigot outside is still dripping steady after ten minutes. That means the valve isn't holding, and it needs to be replaced before it gets cold.

We're a family business and we've been pulling apart frozen hose bibs in this city for a long time. We'd rather set you up in October than cut open your ceiling in January.

**Call us or book online — we'll get someone out.**

b.text:
Here’s a quick, no-nonsense guide to winterizing your outdoor spigots. If you do nothing else, take this seriously: the biggest mistake we see every January is a hose left connected. That one oversight is behind most of our frozen-pipe calls — and it’s completely avoidable.

**Step 1: Disconnect every hose**
Start here. Unscrew hoses, splitters, spray nozzles — anything attached to the spigot. Water trapped inside a hose or a fitting freezes and pushes back into the pipe inside your wall. That’s the burst you dread. Remove it all and store hoses indoors or at least drain them completely.

**Step 2: Shut off the interior water valve**
Head to the basement, crawl space, or utility closet. You’re looking for a valve on the pipe leading directly to the outside faucet. It might be a lever or a round handle. Turn it all the way off (clockwise). If you’ve never done this and aren’t sure which valve controls which spigot, now’s the time to label them.

**Step 3: Drain the spigot**
Go back outside and open the faucet fully. Let any remaining water dribble out. Leave it open — this gives any trapped water room to expand if a little freeze happens. Don’t close it again until spring.

**Step 4: Cover it with a foam insulator**
Pick up a rigid foam spigot cover at any hardware store — they cost about $3. Slip it over the faucet, tighten the cord or clip, and you’re done. This isn’t just a plastic cap; it insulates against wind and holds a bit of warmer air. It’s cheap insurance that actually works.

**What if you don’t find an interior shutoff valve?**
Some older Minneapolis homes don’t have them. Don’t guess and don’t just skip it. Give us a call at [your phone number]. We can install a proper shutoff valve inside, or help you winterize safely. It’s a small job that prevents a massive mess.

A frozen spigot doesn’t just break outside — the split often happens inside your wall. Come January, you won’t know until water’s gushing into your basement or living room. Do these four steps now, before the real cold hits, and you’re set.

b.text:

setup: A small coffee shop owner is writing testimony to city council opposing a parking meter rate increase.

a.text:
# Testimony Regarding Proposed Parking Meter Rate Increase

**To the City Council:**

My name is [your name], and I am the owner of [coffee shop name], a small independent coffee shop on Main Street. I am writing to oppose the proposed parking meter rate increase from 50 cents to $1.50 per hour downtown.

I understand the city is looking for revenue solutions, but I want to share some specific data that I hope will give you pause before voting on this increase.

In 2019, a neighboring town implemented a similar meter rate hike. Concerned about what it might mean for my own business, I tracked my register traffic for six weeks following that change. My foot traffic dropped by 18% during that period. Customers who used to come in three or four times a week started coming once. Some stopped coming altogether. These are not abstract numbers to me. They represent real people who decided that the added cost and hassle of parking was enough to change their habits. When someone is deciding whether to spend four dollars on a coffee, adding another dollar fifty to the cost of just being there tips the scale more than you might expect.

I also want to point out that my customers average a 22-minute visit. They come in, order, sit for a few minutes, and leave. Under the current rate structure, where parking is purchased in one-hour increments at 50 cents, they are already paying for far more time than they actually use. The current system already covers them fine. Raising the rate to $1.50 per hour means a customer who stays 22 minutes is paying three times as much for the same unused 38 minutes. That is a 200% increase for zero additional benefit to the customer.

Finally, I would direct the council's attention to the city's own report on downtown parking revenue. Meter revenue currently covers only 4% of the downtown budget. Even if this rate increase doubles revenue, which is optimistic given the behavioral response I have observed firsthand, you are still talking about a marginal gain that will not meaningfully close any budget gap. This increase is not actually solving the problem it is being presented as solving. What it will do, based on the evidence I have seen, is reduce foot traffic to businesses like mine by something in the range of 15 to 20%, which in turn reduces the sales tax revenue the city collects from us.

I ask the council to consider whether a revenue strategy that risks an 18% decline in downtown commerce in exchange for a modest improvement in a budget line that represents 4% of downtown costs is sound fiscal policy. I do not believe it is, and I urge you to vote no on this increase.

Thank you for your time and for the opportunity to submit this testimony.

**Respectfully submitted,**
[your name]
Owner, [coffee shop name]
Main Street

b.text:
**Testimony on the Proposed Downtown Parking Meter Rate Increase**

My name is [Name], and I own [Shop Name] on Main Street. I've been open [X] years. I'm here because the council is considering raising downtown meter rates from 50 cents an hour to a dollar fifty an hour, and I want to put three specific numbers on the record before you vote.

The first number is 18 percent.

In 2019, the next town over raised its meter rates by a similar amount. I was paying attention because I knew the same conversation would eventually reach us, so I kept a count. For six weeks after that increase took effect, I tracked register transactions against the same six-week window from the year before. Foot traffic was down 18 percent. Not sales dollars, which can swing with a big catering order or a price change—transactions. Bodies through the door. Nearly one in five customers stopped coming in during the period right after parking got more expensive.

Some of those people came back eventually. Some found a drive-through on the highway with a free lot and never thought about downtown again. A shop like mine runs on margins thin enough that an 18 percent drop over six weeks isn't a rough patch. It's a question of whether I make payroll.

The second number is 22 minutes.

That is the average length of a visit to my shop. I know this because I've timed it, and because anyone who has bought a coffee knows it. People come in, order, sit for a few minutes or take it to go, and leave. Almost nobody stays an hour. Under the current system, a customer pays 50 cents for an hour minimum and uses about a third of that time. They're already paying for parking they don't use, and they've accepted that as the cost of coming downtown.

Tripling the rate doesn't change how long they stay. It changes the math. A dollar fifty on a three-dollar coffee is a 50 percent surcharge for the privilege of parking within sight of my door. On a busy corner in a big city, maybe people shrug at that. On Main Street, where the alternative is a free parking lot three miles away, they do the arithmetic and they drive.

The third number is 4 percent.

That figure is not mine. It comes from the city's own report on downtown finances. Meter revenue covers 4 percent of the downtown budget. I want to be careful here, because I'm not saying that money doesn't matter. I'm saying that if the goal is to close a budget gap, this proposal is asking Main Street businesses to absorb a very real risk—I've measured that risk at 18 percent—in exchange for moving a line item that accounts for one twenty-fifth of the total. Even if you triple the rate and lose no traffic at all, which the 2019 data says you won't, you've gone from 4 percent to something like 12 percent. That doesn't solve the problem. It just relocates it from the city's ledger to mine.

And once traffic drops, the city loses on the other side too. Fewer customers means less sales tax collected downtown, fewer people walking past the other shops on the block, and a Main Street that looks emptier than it did the year before. Empty storefronts don't pay meters at all.

I'm not asking the council to freeze rates forever. Costs go up, and I understand that. If a smaller increase is genuinely necessary, I'd rather see something phased and modest, with the city tracking downtown foot traffic before and after so we're deciding on evidence rather than guessing. What I'm asking is that you not triple the rate in one step on the basis of a revenue source that your own report says is a rounding error in the downtown budget.

I've given you the numbers I have. I'd ask that anyone supporting this increase bring numbers of their own showing that Main Street won't lose customers, because in six weeks in 2019, one town over, I watched it happen.

Thank you for your time.

setup: A solo SaaS founder is posting a thread to indie hackers and customers about a pricing mistake and the fix.

a.text:
1/  
I made a pricing mistake with Tallyup.

I raised prices by 40% for everyone overnight.

Within a week, 30 of our 140 customers had left.

Here’s what happened—and what I changed.

2/  
The mistake wasn’t raising prices.

Tallyup had changed since many customers first subscribed. The old pricing no longer reflected the value we were providing.

The mistake was treating a pricing change like a switch:

Old price → new price  
No transition. No context. No room for customers to adjust.

3/  
I underestimated how the change would feel to customers.

A 40% increase might be reasonable on paper.

But to a gym owner receiving an unexpected bill, it’s still a 40% increase overnight.

The math made sense to me. The rollout didn’t.

4/  
The churn was immediate:

30 of 140 customers left in one week.

That’s roughly 21% of the customer base.

It was painful, but it made the problem impossible to ignore.

5/  
The biggest lesson:

Pricing isn’t just a number.

It’s also timing, communication, trust, and whether customers understand the value they’re paying for.

I focused too much on the first part.

6/  
What I changed:

I stopped thinking about pricing as a one-time decision.

It needs to be treated as an ongoing product decision—something to revisit carefully, communicate clearly, and roll out deliberately.

7/  
I also became much more cautious about making a broad pricing change all at once.

When you’re a small SaaS, it’s easy to make a decision in a spreadsheet and forget that every row represents a real customer relationship.

8/  
I’m still glad I looked at pricing.

Tallyup needs to be a sustainable business, and pricing has to reflect the value the product creates.

But sustainable pricing shouldn’t come at the cost of surprising the people who helped build the business.

9/  
The uncomfortable version of the lesson:

A pricing increase can be “correct” and still be handled badly.

The 40% increase wasn’t the only issue.

The overnight rollout was.

10/  
For other indie founders:

Don’t only ask, “What should we charge?”

Also ask:

- How will customers experience this?
- How much notice do they need?
- How can we explain the value?
- What would make the transition feel fair?

11/  
I lost 30 customers in a week because I optimized for the new price instead of the long-term relationship.

That’s a mistake I don’t plan to repeat.

Pricing is part of the product. Treat it that way.

b.text:
1/
I raised Tallyup prices by 40% overnight for every existing customer.

In one week, we lost 30 of our 140 customers.

Not because the product was bad.
Because I handled pricing like a switch, not a relationship.

2/
The mistake wasn’t charging more.

The mistake was changing the deal for loyal users without giving them context, choice, or time.

For existing customers, that feels like being punished for trusting you early.

3/
Customers who pay you first are not an inventory of seats to reprice.

They are proof your product matters.

When they leave, you don’t just lose revenue.
You lose trust.

4/
What I changed:

No more overnight price hikes for existing users.

If pricing changes, existing customers get:
- notice
- a reason
- a choice
- time to adjust

5/
New pricing applies to new customers first.

Existing customers get grandfathered or given a transition path.

They can still cancel.
But they shouldn’t feel forced out.

6/
I stopped assuming the value explains itself.

If Tallyup helps gym owners track member retention, I need to communicate why that matters before asking existing customers to pay more for it.

7/
I made leaving easier, not harder.

No guilt trips.
No traps.
No extra friction.

If someone can’t stay at the new price, I want them to remember Tallyup as something that treated them fairly.

8/
For indie SaaS founders:

Raising prices is often necessary.

But how you raise prices can cost you the customers who made the company possible.

9/
I’m not pretending I got this perfect.

I got it wrong fast.

Now I’m rebuilding trust the slow way: one customer at a time.

setup: A small HVAC company owner is writing a how-to for homeowners on bleeding air from hot water baseboard radiators before winter.

a.text:
# How to Bleed Air Out of Baseboard Heating Before Winter

Switch the circulator off or set the boiler to **Off** so water isn’t being pushed through the system while air is escaping.

1. **Shut off the circulator or boiler first.**  
   If the pump has its own switch, turn it off there. If not, turn the boiler control to Off or power off the boiler circuit.

2. **Find the bleeder valve on each baseboard unit.**  
   Look at the end cap of the baseboard run. The valve is usually small, threaded, and may need a radiator key or a flathead screwdriver.

3. **Place a cup underneath the valve.**  
   Air will sputter out first, then water. A small coffee cup or plastic container catches it neatly.

4. **Open the valve slowly with the key or flathead screwdriver.**  
   Turn it just enough to hear the hiss of air. Don’t open it wide right away. Let the air come out gently.

5. **Wait until the water runs steady with no hissing air.**  
   You’ll usually get a few short bursts of air, then a smooth, continuous stream of water.

6. **Close the valve snug, but don’t overtighten.**  
   Once the water is steady, turn the valve closed. Overtightening can crack the valve seat and cause a slow leak.

7. **Go unit by unit, starting closest to the boiler and working outward.**  
   Bleed each baseboard loop in sequence so air doesn’t get trapped farther out in the system.

The mistake that causes most of our cold radiator calls is people only bleed the upstairs units and skip the basement loop. In many homes, the basement loop is where the air actually collects. If you miss it, the upstairs baseboards may still heat poorly even after bleeding them.

b.text:
If your baseboards are cold, you likely have air trapped in the lines blocking the hot water from circulating. You can fix this yourself in about fifteen minutes with a cup and a flathead screwdriver or radiator key. 

**1. Shut off the boiler and circulator.** Don't try to do this while the system is running. Shut the power off at the emergency switch so the water settles and the pump isn't pushing more air through the lines.

**2. Start at the unit closest to the boiler.** You need to go unit by unit, starting at the boiler and working your way out to the end of the line. The mistake that causes most of our "cold radiator" service calls is when people only bleed the upstairs bedrooms and entirely skip the basement loop. Don't skip the basement—that is usually where the air actually is.

**3. Find the bleeder valve.** Pull the cover off the end of your baseboard unit. You'll see a small brass valve on the pipe with a slotted screw head or a square fitting for a radiator key. 

**4. Open the valve slowly.** Hold your cup right underneath the valve. Turn the screw or key counter-clockwise just a little bit until you hear air hissing out. 

**5. Wait for a steady stream of water.** Let it hiss and spit until the air is gone. Once the water flows out into your cup in a solid, steady stream with no sputtering or hissing, the air is cleared from that unit.

**6. Close it snug, but don't overtighten.** Turn the valve clockwise until the water stops. Make it tight enough to seal, but do not crank down on it hard. If you overtighten it, you will crack the valve seat and you'll be calling me to come out and solder in a replacement.

Work your way through every baseboard in the house. Once you're done, flip the boiler back on and let it run. The heat should distribute evenly now, but if you still have dead spots after bleeding the entire system, you might be dealing with a stuck zone valve or a failing circulator pump. Give us a call and we'll come get it sorted out.

setup: A wedding photographer is posting that couples who ditch rigid shot lists get better photos, using the rained-out Barrera wedding as an example.

a.text:
The couples who ditch the shot list always seem to end up with the best photos.

Not because planning doesn’t matter—it does. I still want the family groupings, meaningful details, and moments you don’t want missed.

But an exhaustive list of poses can pull everyone out of the day they’re actually living.

The Barrera wedding is a perfect example. Rain changed the plan, and we moved everything under the pecan tree. Instead of trying to force the original vision, they trusted the moment, embraced the weather, and stayed present.

That flexibility created photographs that felt like them—not a checklist.

Give your photographer the must-haves. Then leave room for the unexpected.

That’s often where the best images are hiding.

b.text:
The couples who hand me a five-page shot list from Pinterest rarely end up with the photos they actually wanted. 

The ones who throw the list away? They get magic.

After eight years and nearly 300 weddings in the Texas Hill Country, I’ve seen this play out over and over: you can either perform for your wedding gallery, or you can live your wedding day. You can’t do both.

Take the Barrera wedding, for example. 

Thirty minutes before their outdoor ceremony, the sky opened up. Total downpour. The manicured lawn, the timeline, the planned backdrop—all gone. 

Instead of stressing over a checklist of missed photo ops, they looked at each other, laughed, and pivoted. We moved the entire setup under a massive, dripping pecan tree. 

Because they weren’t mentally tracking whether we got "Pose #14 by the arbor," they were completely dialed into the moment. When the hem of her dress soaked through with mud, she didn't care. When the wind blew the rain sideways during their vows, he just pulled her closer. 

The gallery from that afternoon remains one of my absolute favorites. Not because it was technically perfect—none of the original lighting setups worked—but because every single frame captured genuine, unfiltered emotion. 

To the couples currently planning: by all means, list out your family formal groupings so we don’t miss Grandma. 

Beyond that? Trust the vendor team you hired. 

When you free your photographer to watch for moments instead of hunting down clipboard items, and when you give yourself permission to just live the day as it unfolds, that’s when the real art happens. 

Ditch the list. Live the day. The photos will take care of themselves.

setup: A small coffee shop owner is writing testimony to city council opposing a parking meter rate increase.

a.text:
To the Members of the City Council:

My name is [Name], and I am the owner of [Coffee Shop Name], a small independent coffee shop on Main Street. I am submitting this testimony in opposition to the proposed increase in downtown parking meter rates from fifty cents to one dollar and fifty cents per hour.

The evidence that this increase will hurt small businesses is not theoretical. In 2019, when the neighboring town enacted a similar parking rate hike, I tracked my own register sales for six weeks to see how foot traffic would respond. The result was an eighteen percent drop in customer visits. That figure comes from six weeks of actual transaction data, not from speculation. Nearly one in five customers simply stopped coming through my door after parking became significantly more expensive.

This proposal is particularly misaligned with businesses like mine because of how our customers actually use downtown parking. The average visit to my shop lasts twenty-two minutes. Under the current rate, a customer pays fifty cents for a one-hour minimum, which already covers their stay with nearly forty minutes to spare. If this increase passes, that same twenty-two-minute visit will cost one dollar and fifty cents. We are asking our customers to triple their parking cost for time they do not use.

Furthermore, the city’s own report states that parking meter revenue covers only four percent of the downtown budget. This increase will not meaningfully address our fiscal needs. It will simply triple the burden on short-term parkers for a revenue stream that, by the city’s own accounting, contributes just four cents of every dollar in the downtown budget.

An eighteen percent decline in foot traffic is a proven consequence, not a possibility. A twenty-two-minute visit should not carry a one-dollar-and-fifty-cent parking fee. And a policy that impacts only four percent of the budget is not a financial solution. I respectfully urge the council to reject this proposed rate increase.

Respectfully submitted,  
[Name]  
Owner, [Coffee Shop Name]  
Main Street

b.text:
**To Members of the City Council and the Downtown Community:**

My name is [Your Name], and I am the owner of [Name of Coffee Shop], located on Main Street. I am submitting this written testimony for the official public record to formally oppose the proposed parking meter rate increase from $0.50 to $1.50 per hour in our downtown district. 

I do not write this out of an instinctive resistance to city revenue adjustments, nor do I rely on abstract warnings that this policy "might hurt small business." I am writing because the cold, hard numbers—from my own sales logs, from regional precedent, and from the city’s own fiscal reports—demonstrate that a 200% rate hike will disproportionately damage the downtown retail ecosystem while delivering negligible fiscal return to the municipality.

First, consider the direct economics of a downtown visit. Over the past year, my point-of-sale logs show that the average visit length for a customer in my shop is precisely 22 minutes. These patrons are not long-term parkers occupying spots for an entire workday; they are residents popping in to grab a coffee, pick up a pastry, or meet a colleague briefly before moving on. Under the current structure, the 60-minute minimum charge of $0.50 easily covers their stay while remaining an afterthought. Tripling that rate to $1.50 introduces immediate transactional friction. When a customer buys a $4.75 latte, adding a mandatory $1.50 parking fee represents an effective 31.5% surcharge on their purchase. For short-stay errands, parking cost shifts from an incidental expense into a deterrent. Drivers will simply reroute to suburban strip malls and drive-throughs where surface parking remains free.

Second, we already have empirical data on what happens when a municipality implements this exact change. In 2019, when our neighboring municipality instituted an identical tripling of their downtown meter rates, I closely tracked foot traffic and customer frequency over a six-week control period using our register data. During those six weeks, foot traffic across comparable merchant categories dropped by 18%. In an industry operating on 5% to 8% net margins, an 18% decline in foot traffic is not a minor inconvenience; it is the difference between retaining staff and cutting shifts, or between breaking even and shutting our doors entirely. The downtown core relies on compounded micro-trips. When you disincentivize the casual, spontaneous visit, the entire retail block absorbs the loss.

Finally, the justification that this increase will meaningfully shore up municipal finances collapses under the city’s own accounting. According to the Downtown Mobility and Budget Report released last month, parking meter revenue accounts for exactly 4% of the downtown operating budget. Even if one were to assume—unrealistically—zero decline in parking utilization after tripling the fee, this rate hike does not resolve the structural challenges facing downtown infrastructure or transit maintenance. Balancing a municipal deficit requires substantive fiscal planning, not nickel-and-diming the foot traffic that generates downtown property tax, sales tax, and economic vitality in the first place. Sacrificing nearly a fifth of Main Street foot traffic to manipulate a revenue source that constitutes only 4% of the ledger is bad math and worse governance.

Downtown businesses have spent years rebuilding steady, dependable foot traffic. Replacing that stability with a 200% parking hike will extract revenue from local patrons while failing to meaningfully move the needle on city finances. I strongly urge the Council to reject the proposed increase from $0.50 to $1.50 and to pursue revenue alternatives that do not penalize the residents patronizing our local businesses.

Respectfully submitted,

[Your Name]  
Owner, [Name of Coffee Shop]  
[Address / Main Street Location]

setup: A real estate agent is posting one specific observation about early block walks and happier buyers to LinkedIn buyers, agents, and lenders.

a.text:
After 12 years selling homes in Asheville, mostly to first-time buyers, I’ve noticed something quiet but consistent: the buyers who walk the neighborhood at 7 a.m. before we even step inside a house? They almost always end up happier down the road.

The Pruitts taught me that on Sycamore Street.

They were relocating from out of state, nervous about picking the right spot. We had a full Saturday of showings lined up, but they insisted on driving over before sunrise. I met them at the corner at 6:45, coffee in hand, and we just walked. No phone screens, no listing sheets—just the street waking up. A neighbor waved from their porch with a dog leash in one hand, and another called out a hello by name. We heard kids laughing from a backyard before the school bus came. A woman walking her lab mentioned the block party in June, the way the sycamores drop giant leaves every fall, and how safe she felt jogging alone in the half-light. By the time we actually toured the house, the Pruitts weren’t just seeing square footage anymore. They were already picturing Saturday mornings retrieving their newspaper from the driveway, or grabbing pie from the bakery three blocks over because we saw the baker opening up.

That house wasn’t the most updated. But they made an offer before lunch, and six years later they still send me a Christmas card from that same Sycamore Street front porch.

I’m not a fan of made-up stats or generic advice, so I won’t tell you that an early-morning walk guarantees anything. But the feeling of a neighborhood when it’s just beginning its day—before the noise, before the rush—that’s a piece of truth you can’t get from a Zillow scroll or a Saturday open house. If you’re looking this spring, give it a try. Your future self might thank you from the front porch.

b.text:
After 12 years of helping people buy homes in Asheville, I’ve noticed something simple: buyers who walk the neighborhood early in the morning—before we even tour the house—tend to feel much more confident about their decision later.

The Pruitts taught me this on Sycamore Street.

They loved a house we were scheduled to see on a Saturday afternoon. Great kitchen, sunny back porch, enough room for their growing family. But before the showing, they drove over around 7 a.m. with coffee and walked the block.

They noticed parents loading kids into cars, a neighbor walking two old dogs, someone opening up a small business nearby, and how the morning light came through the trees. They also noticed the traffic pattern at that hour and a train they hadn’t considered.

None of it was a dealbreaker. It was just real life.

By the time we toured the house, they weren’t only evaluating countertops and closets. They had a clearer picture of what a Tuesday morning might feel like there. They bought the home, and later told me that early walk was the moment the neighborhood started to feel like theirs.

A house can show beautifully for an hour. A neighborhood reveals itself over time—and 7 a.m. is often a pretty honest introduction.

setup: An in-house recruiter is posting a contrarian observation about candidates asking about the team’s last failed project in interviews to recruiters, hiring managers, and job seekers.

a.text:
I've sat through roughly 200 interviews over the last few years, and there's a pattern I can't unsee.

The strongest candidates don't ask about career progression. They don't ask about "culture." They ask what failed recently.

Specifically: "Tell me about the last project that didn't go the way you expected."

Here's what happened a few months ago. A candidate we were interviewing for an ops coordinator role asked me this about 25 minutes in. I paused because honestly, most people just want to talk about the role and get out. I told them about a warehouse routing rollout we did last spring that was supposed to cut loading times by 15%. Took three months to implement. Net result was maybe 4%, and that was generous. The vendor setup didn't account for how our drivers actually behaved during peak, and we over-customized the config to the point where nobody wanted to touch it after launch.

This candidate nodded, asked two follow-ups. "Who owned the post-mortem?" and "Did the drivers get a say in the config before launch?" That was it. Didn't lecture me about what we should have done. Didn't try to pitch themselves as the person who would have done it better.

But those two questions told me more about how they think than any behavioral question I had on my list. They understood that failure has an ownership question and a process question, and they're separate things.

We hired them. They're doing well.

The thing I keep thinking about is that most candidates treat the Q&A at the end like a courtesy round. The ones who don't are almost always the ones we end up wanting.

b.text:
I've sat in on roughly 200 interviews at our company. The candidates who end up being the strongest hires almost always ask some version of the same question:

"Tell me about a project here that didn't work out."

Not "what's the culture like." Not "what does success look like in 90 days." Those are fine. But the failed-project question changes the whole conversation.

Recent example. We were interviewing for an ops analyst role, and near the end the candidate asked our hiring manager about the last initiative that got shelved. The manager paused, then told her about a warehouse slotting overhaul we'd rolled out too fast — pilots looked great, full rollout fell apart because we hadn't accounted for how differently our seasonal sites run.

Her follow-up: "When it started going sideways, how long before someone said so out loud?"

The manager laughed and gave her an honest answer (longer than it should have been). They spent ten minutes talking about how the team handles bad news now. That was the moment he decided to hire her.

Here's why the question works. Anyone can vet a company on its wins — that's what the careers page is for. Asking about failure tells you how the company actually behaves under pressure. Do they blame a person or examine a process? Do they get cagey or get specific?

And it tells us something too. This candidate isn't shopping for a place where nothing goes wrong. She's checking whether it's safe to be the one who flags a problem.

If you're interviewing anywhere right now, ask it. The answer — and how comfortable they are giving it — will tell you more than the entire job description.

setup: A real estate agent is writing a commentary on the local market for brokerage blog and local paper readers.

a.text:
If you’ve spent five minutes talking to anyone looking to buy or sell a house in our area this spring, you’ve probably heard the panic. The frenzy of the last few years is gone, and the sudden quiet has people on edge. 

Let’s look at the numbers. Last spring, the median days on market in our zip code was a blistering eight days. You put a sign in the yard on Thursday, and by Monday, you were sifting through multiple offers. This spring? Our median days on market has stretched to 34. 

Naturally, people are whispering about a housing crash. 

Let me stop you right there. We are not in a crash. What we are experiencing right now is a stubborn standoff, driven by sellers who absolutely refuse to accept that the pandemic-era real estate market is over. 

Here is the reality on the ground: List prices in our area are still up 6% year-over-year, but showings per listing have dropped by exactly half. Buyers are still out there, but they are no longer willing—or, thanks to interest rates, able—to tolerate wildly speculative pricing. The foot traffic simply doesn't support the sky-high price tags anymore. 

I see it on the front lines of this market every single day. Right now, I have three different sellers who have been sitting on the market for over 60 days, flat-out refusing to drop their prices. They are waiting for a 2021 buyer to walk through the door. But that buyer is gone, and no amount of holding out is going to bring them back. 

For the better part of a decade, and especially over the last three years, sellers got used to dictating the terms, the timeline, and the price. They haven't caught up to the new pace. They are confusing a normalized market with a crashing one. 

How do I know the market isn't crashing? Because the sellers who actually listen to the data are doing just fine. The homes that are prepped well and priced accurately for *today's* reality are still going under contract in under two weeks. Buyers are ready to pull the trigger, but they are completely ignoring listings that are priced like it's still last spring.

The bottom line is this: If your house is sitting at day 45 with crickets in the driveway and empty open houses, the local market isn't broken. Your price is. It’s time to stop chasing the ghosts of the boom market and start pricing for the reality of right now.

b.text:
**It's Not a Crash. It's a Lag.**

I've spent the last ten years selling houses in the same five zip codes, and I can tell you when the market shifts by how my weekends feel. Last spring, my weekends were 12 showings, a line out the door at the open house, and an offer deadline on Sunday night. This spring feels different.

The numbers back it up. In our zip, median days on market went from 8 days last spring to 34 days this spring. Showings per listing have dropped by about half. And yet list prices are still up 6% year over year.

If you just read those headlines, you'd think we're heading off a cliff. We're not.

What we're in is a standoff, and sellers are losing it.

For two years, sellers got to name their price. Whatever number you put on it, someone would beat it. That muscle memory is hard to break. Right now I have three sellers, all great houses, all well-kept, all sitting 60+ days because they will not take a price drop. I get it. Your neighbor got $40k over asking last May. Zillow still says your home is worth X. You don't want to "give it away."

But you're not giving it away. You're pricing it for a market that doesn't exist anymore.

Buyers didn't disappear. They're still looking, they're still approved, they're still writing offers. They just aren't panicking anymore. When they see a house priced like it's May of 2022, they don't rush to offer — they scroll past it. Half the showings means you get half the chances to make an impression, and at the wrong price, you get zero second chances.

Here's the part that isn't making the headlines: The houses priced right are still gone in under two weeks. I listed a three-bed on the west side last month at a number that made my sellers nervous. We had 11 showings in four days and two solid offers by Monday. No bidding war frenzy, no waived inspection horror story — just a clean, fair market sale.

That's the actual market right now. Not crashing. Not booming. Normalizing.

If you price for last year's headlines, you'll sit and you'll end up chasing the market down with a cut anyway. If you price for today's buyers — who are still out there, just choosy — you'll sell.

Sellers haven't caught up to the new pace yet. When they do, that days-on-market number will come right back down.

setup: A parent of two middle-schoolers is writing an op-ed to local readers urging an 8:45am middle-school start time.

a.text:
If your house is anything like mine around 6:30 every morning, it isn't pretty. As the parent of two middle-schoolers here in Millbrook, my day starts with dragging two half-conscious kids out of bed, nagging them to find their shoes, and shoving breakfast into their hands before they stumble out the door in the dark. 

It’s exhausting, and it turns out, it’s completely unnecessary.

Next month, our school board will vote on whether to move our middle and high school start times to 8:45 a.m. I’ve read through the board’s proposal carefully, and I believe voting "yes" is the single most common-sense move we can make for our kids’ health and education.

This isn't about letting teenagers be "lazy." The American Academy of Pediatrics has pointed out for years that biological shifts during puberty make it nearly impossible for teens to fall asleep before 11:00 p.m. Pre-teens and teens need between 8.5 and 9.5 hours of sleep for healthy brain development. Forcing them awake at dawn directly undermines their physical and mental well-being.

We don’t have to guess whether a later bell works—we already have local proof. When Lincoln Middle ran their pilot program with an 8:45 start, the results spoke for themselves. Attendance improved, morning tardiness dropped significantly, and first-period grades went up. Teachers reported that students were actually awake and participating, rather than resting their heads on their desks. 

I know some neighbors have valid concerns, particularly about how this impacts family logistics and busing. I was worried about the transportation puzzle myself. But the proposal specifically solves this by re-tiering the district’s bus routes. By staggering the pick-ups between the different grade levels, the district can make the 8:45 start happen using our current fleet, without blowing up the budget or stranding younger students. The logistics are already figured out.

Change is rarely easy, and adjusting morning routines takes effort. But our current schedule is asking our children to fight their own biology every single morning just to make the opening bell. 

When the board votes next month, I urge them to listen to the medical experts, look at Lincoln Middle's success, and approve the 8:45 start time. Our kids deserve to walk into first period alert, healthy, and ready to learn.

b.text:
# Let Our Teenagers Sleep: Why 8:45 Is Right for Millbrook

My kids are exhausted. Not the "I stayed up too late" tired—the bone-deep, adolescent-body tired that no amount of willpower fixes. And I'm not alone. Every parent with a middle or high schooler knows this struggle.

Next month, our school board will vote on moving start times to 8:45 a.m., and I'm urging them to say yes.

Here's the science: the American Academy of Pediatrics recommends that middle and high school students get 8-10 hours of sleep on school nights. Our current 7:30 start time makes that nearly impossible. When my daughter has to be out the door by 7, she's getting up around 6:15. Even if she's in bed by 9:30—which rarely happens with homework and activities—that's nine hours in bed, maybe eight of actual sleep.

The research isn't theoretical. Lincoln Middle School ran a pilot program last year with a later start time. The results? Attendance went up. First-period grades improved. We're not talking about transforming education overnight, but these are real gains for real kids, right here in Millbrook.

I know the immediate objection: bus schedules. But I've read the proposal carefully. It already includes a re-tiered route plan. Yes, there will be adjustments. Yes, the district and transportation department have work to do. But "it's complicated" isn't a reason to leave teenagers chronically sleep-deprived.

My son's bus comes at 7:15 a.m. Under the new plan, it would come later. That's not a crisis. That's actually solving a problem we've lived with for years.

The pushback I hear most is about sports and after-school activities. I get it—I'm driving my kids to soccer and debate club. But here's what I know: a well-rested kid performs better at everything. School. Sports. Everything. One parent told me she was worried about evening activities ending later. They do. But the alternative—having kids wake up when their bodies are literally wired to sleep—isn't working.

This isn't about mollycoddling teenagers. It's about basic biology. Adolescent circadian rhythms shift around age 13. This is established science, not opinion. An 8:45 start time aligns school with how teenagers' brains actually work.

The Lincoln pilot showed it works. The proposal addresses logistics. The science is clear.

Our school board has a chance next month to give our kids something their bodies desperately need: sleep. I hope they take it.

setup: A local sports columnist is writing an opinionated season-ending commentary for readers of the local paper's sports section.

a.text:
# Second-Round Exit Still Leaves Questions

Eight and two. School record for passing yards. A playoff win. By most measures around here, that's a season you frame and put on the wall.

I'm not sure that's how the kids will remember it, though. And I think that matters.

Let's talk about Friday night. The Raiders lost to Central Valley by a touchdown, 24-17. Same Central Valley team they beat by 20 back in week 3. Same quarterback, same scheme, same field — different result.

Here's what I can't get past: they ran the ball in the first half and it worked. Kowalski was terrific all year, and 2,340 yards is nothing to shrug at, but Friday wasn't about whether Dez could throw. Friday was about whether the staff trusted the run enough to grind out a close one.

They didn't.

Second half, they came out throwing on first down. Three-and-out. Next drive, same thing. The lead was three points. Three. That's not a situation where you panic and start sprinting out on every snap.

I understand the instinct. You've got a record-setting quarterback, you want to let him cook. But the run was getting five yards a pop, and every incomplete pass was a dead clock. By the time they went back to it, Central Valley had already flipped the field position.

Coaches always say the loss is on them. This one actually was.

Still — 8-2, a home playoff win, and a kid who rewrote the record book. That's a good season. It just didn't have to end when it did.

b.text:
# One Game Away From Something Special

There's a difference between a disappointing loss and a frustrating one. Friday night's playoff exit was both.

The 8-2 season will look fine in the record book. Dez Kowalski's 2,340 passing yards are legit—a school record that reflects a kid who worked for it. But we all know what this team could've been, and that's what stings.

They beat Riverside 34-14 in week three. Riverside came into Friday's rematch as a two-seed, and our guys had every reason to believe they could do it again. They were down three at halftime. They had momentum. They had a running game that was moving the ball.

And then they got cute.

In the second half, the offense abandoned the run almost entirely. I watched them abandon what was working—what *was winning*—to let Kowalski sling it around. Maybe the coaches got spooked. Maybe they thought Riverside had figured something out. Whatever the reason, it looked like panic, not adjustment.

The kids fought back and made it close, but you don't recover from that kind of self-inflicted wound against good teams.

This group had the talent to make a deep run. They proved it in week three. They proved it most of the season. But making the state tournament and making a run are two different things, and on Friday night, they chose the wrong identity when it mattered most.

That's the one that'll stick around.

setup: A real estate agent is writing a commentary on the local market for brokerage blog and local paper readers.

a.text:
**The Market Didn’t Crash—Sellers Just Haven’t Caught Up**

After 10 years selling in this suburb, I’ve learned that the most dangerous words in real estate are “let’s just see what happens.” Last spring, that phrase was harmless. Median days on market in our zip code was 8. Eight days. You could overprice a house by five or ten grand and still have multiple offers before the weekend was over. The market moved so fast that mistakes didn’t matter.

This spring is different. Median days on market has stretched to 34. Showings per listing have dropped by half. And yet list prices are still up 6 percent year over year. So sellers look at that number and think the old rules still apply. They don’t.

I currently have three sellers who have been on the market for over 60 days. All three have refused to lower their price. All three are getting a handful of showings, no offers, and the same feedback on repeat: “Nice house, but it’s priced too high.” These aren’t bad houses. They aren’t in bad locations. They are priced for a market that no longer exists.

This is not a crash. Let me say that clearly, because I know the headlines love that word. A crash is when prices fall hard and demand disappears. That is not what is happening here. Prices are still up year over year. Buyers are still out there. The problem is tempo. Last spring, the market was so fast that an overpriced listing could still get saved by a buyer who was tired of losing. This spring, buyers are slower. They are seeing more inventory. They compare. They negotiate. They don’t panic. An overpriced house now sits while the correctly priced one down the street goes under contract in under two weeks.

I’ve watched it happen all spring. The houses priced at or just below recent comparable sales are still moving in 10 to 14 days. The houses priced 5 to 10 percent above the comps are sitting, collecting days on market like a stain that gets harder to wash out.

Here is the hard truth for sellers: your list price is not a statement of what your house was worth last spring. It is a statement of what a buyer is willing to pay this week. The market does not owe you last year’s momentum. If you have been on the market for more than 30 days without an offer, the problem is not your photos, your staging, or your agent’s marketing. The problem is the price. Buyers are telling you with their silence.

I know price reductions feel like defeat. They aren’t. They are catching up to reality. A price cut after 45 days often costs you more than pricing honestly from day one, because buyers start to wonder what’s wrong with the house. The longer you sit, the more leverage you hand to the buyer who eventually does make an offer. The best time to reduce your price was two weeks ago. The second-best time is today.

For buyers, this is not a fire sale, but it is a moment of opportunity. The desperation is gone. You can read the inspection report without being told to waive it. You can negotiate on closing dates, repairs, and some contingencies. You have room to breathe. After three years of bidding wars, that is a real shift. But do not expect prices to fall off a cliff. The fundamentals here have not changed: good schools, steady jobs, limited new construction. What changed is the speed.

The agents telling their sellers to “wait for the right buyer” are doing them a disservice. The right buyer is not coming at the wrong price. This spring is separating the honest actors from the wishful thinkers. My advice to sellers is plain: if you want to sell in this market, price like you actually want to sell. If you want to list high and hope, don’t be surprised when you are still on the market in August.

This is not a crash. It is a correction in expectations. The sellers who understand that are still selling. The ones who don’t are still on the market.

b.text:
Sellers Are Still Pricing Like It's Last Spring

I've been selling houses in this suburb for ten years. I've done the bidding wars, the 2 a.m. offers, the lines out the door at open houses. And I'm telling you straight: this is not a crash.

Here's what's actually happening.

Last spring, the median days on market in our zip was 8 days. Blink and it was gone. This spring, it's 34 days. List prices are still up 6% from last year, but showings per listing have dropped by half.

Buyers didn't disappear. They just stopped playing along.

Right now I have three sellers sitting at 60-plus days on market who refuse to take a price cut. Good houses. Good streets. Dead listings. Every week it's the same conversation: "Let's just give it another week." Another week isn't going to fix a price from 2023.

Because the homes that are priced for 2026? They're still gone in under two weeks. I just saw it happen last month — clean, well-priced ranch, three offers by day ten. Not 30 offers like the old days, but three real ones. That's a healthy market.

The problem isn't interest rates or the economy or some mystery factor. The problem is sellers who haven't caught up to the new pace. You can't list 6% higher than last year for a market that's taking four times as long to move and expect buyers to chase you.

If you're selling: Price it for the buyers who are here today, not the ones who were here two years ago. The first two weeks are everything. Miss that window and you're just paying your mortgage while everyone scrolls past your listing.

If you're buying: Stop waiting for a crash that isn't coming. You finally get to breathe, get an inspection, actually think. The well-priced homes are still moving fast, so don't sleepwalk, but you don't have to beg anymore.

This market rewards honesty. Price it right and it sells. Price it like last spring and it sits.
