setup: A bakery owner is writing a warm blog and newsletter post to regular customers explaining why wedding cake orders are ending.

a.text:
It’s just past five in the morning as I write this, sitting at the little table by the window while the first batch of croissants of the day is baking. It’s my favorite hour in the bakery—quiet, warm, and smelling of caramelized butter. Usually, my mind is spinning with the day’s bake list, but today I wanted to sit down and share a big decision we’ve made about the shop. 

Starting next season, we’ve decided to step away from doing custom wedding cakes. 

This wasn’t an easy choice to make. Being a small part of someone's wedding day is an incredible honor, and we have loved bringing those sweet visions to life. But as a tiny three-person team, we’ve had to take a hard, honest look at where our time and energy go, and how we can best keep serving this community we love so much.

The truth is, custom wedding cakes are a massive undertaking behind the scenes. By the time we sit down for initial tastings, exchange dozens of emails, sketch out designs, and source specialized decorations, we’ve easily poured about fourteen hours of work into a single cake before we even crack the first egg. When there are only three of us running the entire show, those hours have to come from somewhere, and lately, it has felt like we’re constantly running on empty.

We also had a tough run of luck this year with three last-minute wedding cancellations. While we completely understand that life happens and plans change, for a business of our size, absorbing the cost of expensive, specialty ingredients that we’ve already purchased—and can't reuse—is a really heavy blow. 

Most importantly, we realized that pouring so much of our limited time into these massive, one-off custom projects was pulling us away from the heart of our bakery: our daily pastry case. It’s the morning buns, the sourdough loaves, the chocolate chip cookies, and the casual birthday cakes that actually pay our rent and keep our doors open. More than that, it’s the daily connection with you—our regulars who pop in on your way to work or bring your kids in for a weekend treat. You are the reason we get up at 4:00 AM, and we want to make sure our pastry case is always packed with the very best we have to offer.

We will absolutely still be baking our signature cakes, and we'd still love to be a part of your birthdays, anniversaries, and casual celebrations—we'll just be sticking to our set menu of favorite flavors and styles rather than doing fully custom, bespoke wedding commissions. 

Thank you all so much for your warmth, your understanding, and your incredible support as we navigate what it means to grow and stay sustainable as a neighborhood bakery. The timer on the oven is buzzing, so I have to run—but I hope to see you at the counter later this week.

b.text:
# A Little Change Around Here

I've been putting off writing this one, which is usually a sign I should just sit down and do it. So here I am, coffee in hand, flour probably still on my sleeve.

We're not going to be taking custom wedding cake orders anymore.

I want to tell you why, because you've been good to us and you deserve more than a line on the order form. The truth is that wedding cakes, as much as I've loved making them, were quietly pulling the shop in a direction we couldn't keep up with. Every cake starts long before I ever turn on the oven — the consultations, the tastings, the back-and-forth about buttercream shades and how many tiers and whether the flowers should be real. By the time a single cake is done, we've usually put somewhere around fourteen hours into it that no one ever sees. And with three of us running this place, those are hours that have to come from somewhere.

Where they came from was the everyday. The morning loaves, the case full of scones and tarts, the thing you grab on your way to work. That's the part of the bakery that actually keeps our lights on, and it's the part I love most — the regulars, the small daily rhythm of it. When I was buried in wedding planning, that case suffered, and so did I.

I'll be honest about the other piece too. This year we had three weddings cancel at the last minute, and each time we'd already bought the ingredients and blocked the time. That kind of thing happens, I understand it, life is complicated and weddings especially so. But for a shop our size, absorbing that a few times over is a real hit, and it made me look hard at whether this was something we could keep doing well.

So we're stepping back from it, at least for now. If you've got a wedding coming up, I'm genuinely happy to point you toward a few people I trust who do beautiful work and have the setup for it. Just ask.

And please know — we're not going anywhere, and neither is the sweet stuff. We'll still do birthday cakes and the smaller celebration cakes you order ahead. We'll still have the case full every morning. If anything, pulling back on the big commitments means we get to do the everyday things better, which was always the whole point.

Thanks for reading this far, and for being the reason there's a shop to write about. See you at the counter.

— Maggie

*(and the whole crew)*

setup: A high-school biology teacher is writing a cover letter to a customer success hiring manager at the edtech company.

a.text:
For two years, [Product Name] ran my biology classroom. I graded quizzes with it, built labs with it, and spent more time in the analytics dashboard than I did with my gradebook. So when I say I'm applying to your Customer Success team, I'm not flipping through a brochure—I'm the user who called support at 11 p.m. in March begging you to fix a broken LMS sync before finals.

Eight years as a high-school biology teacher was, among other things, a masterclass in customer success. Every August I onboarded thirty students who'd never touched the platform, walked them through a login, and then spent October troubleshooting why one kid's iPad kept logging him into his *sister's* account. That's onboarding, training, and tier-one support, repeated every semester, whether the class was into biology or would rather be at a lacrosse practice.

Handling parents is its own discipline. I de-escalated phone calls about a "D" that was really a missing quiz, talked a furious mom through how the product actually calculates her son's participation grade, and once got a grandparent to stop emailing the district superintendent and just email me instead. I learned to translate "this app is broken" into "here's what's happening and here's how we fix it," which sounds a lot like a CS call log.

For two of those eight years I served as our campus administrator for [Product Name]—managing licenses, coordinating PD sessions for colleagues, logging tickets, and feeding feature requests upstream. I was, in practice, your de facto implementation contact for a 900-student school. I know your roadmap conversations, your seasonal crunches, and the specific questions a first-year science teacher asks in September.

I'm not leaving the classroom because I'm done with kids or with this product. I'm leaving because I realized the work I loved most wasn't the lab—was the moment a reluctant teacher said, "Okay, maybe I'll actually use this thing next period," and I'd helped them get there. I want to do that at scale.

I'd love ten minutes to talk about what your next cohort of onboarding schools looks like and where I can help you keep them.

Thank you for your time.

[Name]
[Email] · [Phone]

b.text:
Dear Hiring Manager for Customer Success,

For the past two years, your platform has run my biology classroom every single day. Not as a demo I saw once — as the tool my freshmen used for labs, quizzes, and review.

I'm a high-school biology teacher with eight years in the classroom, looking to move into Customer Success and help other educators get what I got from your product.

At my school, I became the unofficial campus admin for your tool. Every semester I onboarded 30 new students, most of whom had never used anything beyond Google Classroom. I trained three other science teachers on building assignments and reading the mastery data, and I was the person they texted when logins failed or a lab submission disappeared during 4th period.

That's also where I learned the human side of this work. I walked frustrated parents through grade sync issues at Back-to-School Night, translated dashboards into plain English in IEP meetings, and turned a lot of angry emails into collaborative conversations.

I know exactly what teacher churn looks like: overwhelm in week two, frustration after an update, silence when no one checks in. I’d love to be the person who prevents that.

Thanks for considering a teacher’s perspective on your team.

Warmly,
Maya Torres

setup: A small dog grooming salon owner is writing a how-to for dog owners about preventing coat matting between grooming visits.

a.text:
The single most common thing I see on my table is a dog who got a bath at home last weekend, and now has a coat that feels like a car mat. The owner did everything with good intentions. That's what makes it worth writing about.

Here's the thing nobody tells you: water is what turns a loose tangle into a mat. Wet fur swells, then it shrinks as it dries, and every one of those little knots cinches down on itself like a wet shoelace. Add shampoo, which strips the slip right out of the hair, and you've essentially wet-felted your dog. It's the same process people use on purpose to make wool hats. So when you bathe a matted dog hoping the suds will loosen things up, you get the exact opposite. That mat is now denser, tighter, and closer to the skin than it was an hour ago. On a really bad one, I can't get a comb under it at all, and my only honest option is to shave it out.

So: brush first. Always. Before the bath, on a dry coat, top to bottom. Then bathe. Never the other way around.

**Brushing a dry coat, the way it actually works**

Get yourself a decent slicker brush — the flat rectangular kind with the fine bent wire pins. If you have a doodle, a Poodle, a Bichon, a Cocker, anything curly, you'll want a metal greyhound comb too, because that's your only real way to know if you got all the way down. On a Husky, Pomeranian, Golden, Aussie, or any of the other double coats, the slicker plus an undercoat rake will do most of the heavy lifting.

Use short, straight strokes in a line, and lift the brush off the coat at the end of each one. Little flicking strokes, an inch or two long. What you don't want is that big sweeping circular motion people naturally fall into — circles push hair around and tangle it against itself, and they only skim the surface anyway. You end up with a coat that looks brushed on top and is packed solid underneath. Straight lines, off and back, off and back.

Work in sections instead of wandering all over the dog. I like to part the coat with my free hand, brush the hair right at the part line, then move my hand up a half inch and do it again. It's slow the first few times and then it becomes second nature.

Start behind the ears and under the front legs. That's where mats show up first on nearly every dog I touch, and it's where most people brush last, if at all. Behind the ears the hair is fine and it rubs against the ear leather all day. Under the front legs and in the armpit it's constant friction from walking, plus harness straps. Same story around the collar, the base of the tail, and the back of the hind legs where they brush together. If you only have five minutes, spend them in those spots and you'll prevent most of your problems.

**If you can already feel a mat**

Don't attack it with a brush. Dry mats are welded together and dragging a slicker through one hurts — that's the tug that teaches a dog to hate being brushed, and once they've learned that, everything gets harder for both of us.

Instead, put a little conditioner or a detangling spray right on it and work it in with your fingers. Squish it, roll it, pull it apart into smaller pieces, hair by hair if you have to. Give it a minute to actually soak in. Conditioner works by coating the strands so they slide past each other instead of gripping, and that's a chemical job, not a mechanical one. Only once it feels softer and you can see some separation should the comb or slicker come near it. Work from the outside edge of the mat inward, holding the base of the hair with your other hand so you're not pulling on skin.

And be honest with yourself about size. A mat bigger than a quarter, or one that's flat against the skin and won't lift, is a phone call, not a project. There can be moisture and irritation trapped under there, sometimes a hot spot, and forcing it out at home usually means a stressed dog and a nick in the skin. I'd much rather see you early with two or three tangles than three months later with a coat that has to come off.

Ten minutes, two or three times a week, in the spots I listed. Dry coat, straight strokes, sections. That's genuinely the whole thing — and it's the difference between your dog leaving here with the haircut you wanted and leaving with a summer shave.

b.text:
The easiest way to prevent painful mats is to catch them before bath day. Once fur is wet, any small tangles can tighten into dense, felt-like pads that are much harder to remove.

This is especially important for double-coated and curly-coated dogs. Areas like behind the ears, under the front legs, around the collar, and along the belly tend to tangle first because they get a lot of rubbing and movement.

Before bathing your dog at home, make sure the coat is completely brushed out. Don’t rely on the bath to loosen knots. That’s a mistake I see constantly, and it usually has the opposite effect: water pulls the tangled hairs together and can lock the mats in even tighter.

Use a slicker brush and work with short, gentle line strokes. Think of brushing a small section at a time, moving the brush away from the skin and then checking your progress. Avoid scrubbing in circles, since circular brushing can twist the hair and create more tangles.

Start behind the ears and under the front legs, then work through the rest of the coat in sections. Part the hair with your fingers so you can see down toward the skin instead of only brushing over the surface. For a double-coated dog, you’ll need to work through the outer coat and the undercoat. For a curly-coated dog, take your time so the brush reaches all the way through each curl.

If you notice a mat beginning to form, don’t immediately attack it with a brush or comb. First, work a little dog-safe conditioner into the mat with your fingers. Gently loosen the outside edges before trying to separate the hairs. Never yank or force a brush through a tight mat, especially if your dog is uncomfortable.

A quick brush before the bath is much kinder and more effective than trying to deal with a tightened, wet coat afterward. If you find mats close to the skin, large areas of matting, or a dog who is painful or upset when you touch the coat, stop and contact your groomer. Some mats need to be safely clipped out rather than brushed out, and trying to remove them at home can injure your dog’s skin.

setup: A family plumbing company owner is writing a blog post for Minneapolis homeowners about winterizing outdoor pipes.

a.text:
# How to Winterize Your Outdoor Spigots (And Avoid a January Burst Pipe)

Every January, our phone blows up with emergency calls for burst pipes inside basement walls. Nine times out of ten, the culprit is an outdoor hose spigot that wasn't properly shut down before the ground froze. 

Freezing water expands with incredible force. If water gets trapped in your spigot or the line feeding it, it will split the copper pipe inside your wall, and you won't know it until gallons of water are pouring into your basement.

Here is the exact step-by-step process we tell all our Minneapolis customers to follow every autumn.

---

### Step 1: Disconnect Your Hoses (The #1 Mistake Homeowners Make)
If you only do one thing on this list, do this. Leaving a garden hose connected to the spigot is the single biggest cause of frozen pipes we fix in the winter. 

When a hose stays attached, it prevents water from naturally draining out of the spigot body. That trapped water freezes, expands backwards into your home, and cracks the pipe inside the wall. Disconnect all hoses, drain them, and roll them up for the winter. 

### Step 2: Shut Off the Interior Valve
Go inside your home—usually in the basement, utility room, or crawlspace directly behind where the outdoor spigot sits—and locate the shutoff valve for that specific line. Turn the handle clockwise until it is completely closed. 

### Step 3: Drain the Line and Spigot
Once the inside valve is shut, head back outside. Turn the outdoor spigot completely on and let any remaining water drain out into the yard. 

Next, go back inside to that interior shutoff valve. Most modern ball valves or gate valves have a small brass cap on the side called a bleeder cap. Hold a small cup under it, unscrew the cap, and let the small amount of trapped water drain out. Once it stops dripping, screw the bleeder cap back on hand-tight. 

**Pro-tip:** Leave the outdoor spigot turned *open* all winter long. If any tiny amount of moisture freezes inside the pipe, leaving the faucet open prevents pressure buildup.

### Step 4: Install a $3 Foam Cover
Head down to the local hardware store and grab an insulated foam spigot cover. They cost about three bucks. Slip the rubber loop over the spigot handle, push the foam dome tight against your exterior siding, and pull the plastic slider tight. This blocks drafty winter winds from blowing straight into the brass fixture.

---

### Can’t Find an Interior Shutoff Valve?
Some older homes in Minneapolis don't have interior shutoff valves for outdoor plumbing, or a previous owner remodeled and covered them up. 

If you look behind the spigot inside your house and there is no valve, do not just leave it to chance. Give our team a call. We can come out, install a dedicated interior shutoff valve or a modern frost-free sillcock, and make sure your home is completely protected before the deep freeze hits.

b.text:
# How to Winterize Your Outdoor Spigots (Advice from a Minneapolis Plumber)

Every January, a big share of our burst-pipe calls trace back to the same thing: an outdoor spigot that didn't get winterized. The whole job takes about ten minutes and costs three bucks. Here's exactly how to do it.

Do this by mid-October. Around here the first hard freeze can hit early, and it only takes one cold night to split a pipe.

## 1. Disconnect your hoses

Start here, because everything else depends on it. Unscrew every hose, splitter, and timer from every outdoor faucet. Drain the hoses, coil them, and put them in the garage or shed — they'll last longer anyway.

This matters even if you have a frost-free spigot. A frost-free only works if water can drain out of it. A connected hose traps water inside, and then it's no better than the old-style faucet.

## 2. Shut the interior valve

Go down to the basement and find where the pipe runs from the spigot through the wall. There should be a shutoff valve on that line, usually within a few feet of where it exits the house. Turn it clockwise until it stops.

One valve per spigot — if you have faucets on multiple sides of the house, each one has its own shutoff.

## 3. Drain the spigot

Go back outside and open the spigot. Let it run until the water stops — that's the water trapped between the shutoff and the faucet, and it's the water that would otherwise freeze.

If your interior valve has a little bleeder cap on the side, open that too (hold a cup under it). It lets air into the line so it drains completely.

Leave the outdoor spigot in the open position all winter. If any water is left in there, it has somewhere to go when it expands.

## 4. Put on a foam cover

The hard foam faucet covers are about $3 at any hardware store. It slips over the spigot and cinches tight against the siding. It's cheap insurance against wind chill hitting the pipe where it comes through the wall.

## The mistake that causes most of our January burst-pipe calls

Leaving the hose connected. That's it — that's the big one.

Here's what happens. The hose traps water in the spigot, and because the hose is still on, most people never shut the interior valve either. So you've got a pressurized line, full of water, sitting against an exterior wall. January rolls around, we get a real cold snap — the minus-twenty kind Minneapolis does every year — and that water freezes, expands, and splits the pipe. Often it splits *inside* the wall, where you can't see it.

Then you've got water pouring into your wall cavity or basement, and a ten-minute job just became an emergency call, a plumbing repair, and drywall work.

Take the hoses off. It's the single most important step on this list.

## Don't have an interior shutoff?

A lot of older Minneapolis homes don't — the spigot line runs straight out through the wall with no way to isolate it. If that's your setup, don't try to get through winter with just a foam cover and good intentions.

Give us a call at [phone number]. We can install an interior shutoff valve, or swap the spigot for a frost-free sillcock that drains itself every time you turn it off. Either one is a quick, inexpensive job — and it's a whole lot cheaper than the burst-pipe version of the same visit.

setup: A retired rural mail carrier is writing a letter to the Kettle Falls Courier urging residents to oppose the post office counter closure at the July 28 forum.

a.text:
To the editor:

I drove Route 4 here in Kettle Falls for 22 years before retiring last year. Same 38 miles, day after day. I’m not much of a writer, but I know this town, and closing our post office counter is a bad idea.

USPS says the branch loses $40,000 a year. But they already cut the counter hours to 8 a.m. to noon. Of course traffic dropped. People who work mornings can’t get there. Now USPS is pointing to that drop as a reason to close the counter altogether. They ought to account for what their own cuts did before telling us the town doesn’t use its post office.

I think of Mrs. Halloran up on Kettle Hill. She’s in her 80s and gets her heart medicine by mail. Closing the counter isn’t the same as stopping delivery, but that counter is still a service she needs. She can’t just drive twenty minutes to Fairview when she needs a money order. Neither can plenty of other folks around here.

A post office serves people, not just a balance sheet. Before the district manager takes our counter away, I’d like to hear what restoring useful hours would do for that $40,000 figure.

Please come to the public forum July 28 at the Grange Hall. Tell the district manager what you use the counter for and what losing it would mean. We need the people making this decision to hear from the people who have to live with it.

b.text:
To the Editor:

I drove Route 4 out of the Kettle Falls post office for 22 years. Thirty-eight miles, six days a week, in mud season and in January. I retired last year. I am not a writer, so I will say this plainly.

The Postal Service wants to close our counter service. The reason they give is that the branch loses about $40,000 a year. I would like people to think about where that number comes from.

A few years back they cut the window hours from a full day down to eight to noon. Anybody who has ever run a business could tell you what happens next. Folks who work days can't get in. Folks who used to mail a package on their lunch hour go to Fairview instead, or they order a label online, or they just quit bothering. Traffic dropped. Of course it dropped. Then the receipts dropped with it.

So now they hold up the low numbers as proof the counter isn't needed. That is pointing at a problem they made themselves. It is like cutting a man's hours to half time and then firing him for not getting enough done.

I want to say something about what the counter actually does, because a report in an office somewhere does not show it.

Mrs. Halloran lives up on Kettle Hill. She is in her eighties. Her heart medication comes by mail, and it has come by mail for years, and I carried it up that hill more times than I could count. She does not drive to Fairview. Twenty minutes each way on that road is not a small thing when you are her age and the weather turns. When she needs a money order — and she does, she pays some bills that way, the way a lot of older people around here still do — she walks into our post office and a person she knows helps her. There is no website that replaces that. There is no cluster box that replaces that.

She is not the only one. There are dozens of people on that route in the same position, and most of them will not write a letter to the paper about it.

The district manager is coming to the public forum on July 28 at the Grange Hall. I am asking people to show up. Not to yell at anybody — the folks who work in our office are our neighbors and this is not their doing. Just show up, so the man from the district can see the room is full and can hear it from people who live here.

Numbers on a page are easy to close. A room full of your customers is harder.

Please come.

— [Name], Kettle Falls
Retired rural carrier, Route 4

setup: A high school junior is writing an argumentative essay to her English teacher and classmates arguing for open campus lunch for juniors and seniors.

a.text:
# Open Campus Lunch: A Reasonable Privilege for Upperclassmen

Every school day at noon, 340 students crowd into a cafeteria built to seat 220. The math does not work, and neither does the policy behind it. Our school should allow juniors and seniors to leave campus during lunch. An open campus lunch would ease a real overcrowding problem, reflect what nearby districts have already proven safe, and give students the responsibility they are ready for.

The most immediate reason to adopt open campus lunch is that our current setup is physically overcrowded. Our cafeteria seats 220 people, but 340 students share the same lunch wave. That leaves more than a hundred students without a real place to sit, forcing them into hallways, stairwells, and the floor. Overcrowding like this is not just uncomfortable; it makes the space harder to supervise and harder to keep clean. Letting upperclassmen leave for lunch would relieve the pressure directly, freeing up seats for the students who stay.

Critics might argue that letting students leave campus would cause them to come back late, disrupting afternoon classes. This is a fair concern, but the evidence from nearby districts suggests it is unfounded. Fairmont, West Linn, and Cascade all allow open campus lunch for juniors and seniors, and their published statistics show no rise in tardiness after the policy took effect. These are not distant, unfamiliar schools; they are districts right next to ours, with similar students and similar schedules. If open campus lunch worked without increasing tardiness for them, there is little reason to believe our students would behave differently.

Beyond the practical benefits, open campus lunch is also something students want and are ready for. When I surveyed 80 students at our school, 71 said they were in favor of the policy. That is nearly nine out of ten. Juniors and seniors are sixteen and seventeen years old, many of them working jobs, driving cars, and preparing for college, where they will manage their own time entirely. A short window to leave for lunch is a modest, age-appropriate step toward that independence.

Some may still worry that open campus lunch treats a privilege as if it were a right, or that not every student will use the freedom responsibly. But the policy would apply only to upperclassmen, and it could be tied to conditions like good standing or timely returns, just as it is in neighboring districts. A privilege can be earned and, if abused, taken away.

The case for open campus lunch is straightforward. Our cafeteria cannot hold the students assigned to it, nearby districts have shown the policy causes no increase in tardiness, and the overwhelming majority of students support it. Allowing juniors and seniors to leave campus for lunch is not a risky experiment. It is a practical, proven solution that our school should adopt.

b.text:
Stepping Outside the Gates: Why Open Campus Lunch Works for Upperclassmen

Every day at fourth period, the bell triggers an uncoordinated sprint toward the cafeteria. The rush is not just about getting food; it is about securing a place to sit. For juniors and seniors who are months or a year away from living independently in college or entering the workforce, this daily routine feels less like preparation for adulthood and more like an overcrowded holding pattern. While our closed-campus policy was designed with safety and discipline in mind, it fails to meet the practical realities of our school today. Granting off-campus lunch privileges to juniors and seniors would resolve severe logistical strain on our facilities, encourage personal responsibility, and align our policy with proven regional standards.

The most immediate argument for an open campus is not philosophical; it is physical. Our cafeteria was built to seat 220 students, yet our current lunch wave serves roughly 340. The result is a daily bottleneck where over a third of the student body is displaced. Students are forced to eat sitting on the floor against locker banks, crowd onto stairwells, or spend twenty minutes in a line only to rush through their meal before the bell rings. Allowing juniors and seniors to leave during lunch would immediately draw down those numbers, freeing up seats and table space for freshmen and sophomores. It solves a physical capacity problem without requiring school renovation or additional staff supervision in the hallways.

The standard objection to off-campus privileges is almost always attendance: administrators worry that freedom will translate to empty desks during fifth period. However, this assumption is contradicted by real data from schools just outside our district line. Fairmont, West Linn, and Cascade high schools all operate with an open campus for upperclassmen. According to their published attendance records, none of these three districts experienced an increase in tardiness or unexcused absences after implementing the policy. Students quickly learn to manage their time because they recognize that tardiness puts their privileges at risk. If three neighboring communities with similar demographics and driving conditions can manage open lunch without academic disruption, there is no reason to assume our student body is incapable of doing the same.

Furthermore, this change carries overwhelming student support and offers a structured way to practice independence. In an informal survey conducted across our school last month, 71 out of 80 students surveyed favored implementing open campus lunch for upperclassmen. Most students do not view this policy as an excuse to wander, but as an earned milestone. High school is intended to prepare students for the demands of adulthood, where time management is an essential skill rather than a luxury. An open campus offers a low-stakes environment to practice that balance: students must plan a meal, coordinate transportation, watch the clock, and return ready to learn. For administrators who still harbor reservations, the policy could easily be tied to academic and behavioral standing, turning off-campus lunch into an incentive for maintaining passing grades and regular attendance.

A closed campus may feel like the safest default, but it ignores the strain on our cafeteria and underestimates the maturity of upperclassmen. With our facilities over capacity and clear evidence from Fairmont, West Linn, and Cascade that attendance remains steady, the case for change is practical and timely. setup: A small dog grooming salon owner is writing a how-to for dog owners about preventing coat matting between grooming visits.

a.text:
If your dog has a double coat or a curly coat, the weeks between grooming visits are usually where the trouble starts. I see it all the time: the coat looks fine from the top, but once I part it, the tangles are already tightening near the skin. The good news is you can do a lot at home to keep small snarls from turning into mats, as long as you catch them early and avoid the mistake that makes them worse.

At home, brush before the bath, never after. I know that sounds backward, because a lot of people think bathing first will loosen everything up. That is the mistake I see constantly. Water can make a matted coat feel softer for a minute, but wet matted fur tightens as it dries and can turn into something like a felt pad. Once that happens, it is much harder to brush out safely, and sometimes it cannot be brushed out at all. So if the coat is tangled, skip the bath and work on brushing first.

Use a slicker brush, and use short line strokes, not circles. Short strokes let you work through the coat in a controlled way without pushing the tangle around or making the outside look smooth while the base stays tight. Circles can drag the hair and make the mat denser, especially close to the skin. You want to be gentle, but you also want to make sure you are actually getting into the coat where the mat is starting.

Work in sections, and start where mats usually begin first: behind the ears and under the front legs. Those spots get a lot of friction from movement, collars, harnesses, laying down, and everyday life. If you can keep those two areas open, you are already ahead of the game. After that, move through the coat in small sections instead of just brushing over the top. With curly coats, watch for little curls that are starting to bind together. With double coats, pay attention to the softer undercoat, because that is often where the mat grabs first.

If you can already feel a mat forming, do not go straight at it with a brush or comb. Work a little conditioner into it with your fingers first. Be gentle. Let the conditioner help the hairs slide apart instead of pulling against each other. A lot of times, you can ease the beginning of a mat open enough that brushing becomes much safer. If you jump right in with a dry brush, you can tighten it faster and make it more uncomfortable for your dog.

The biggest thing I want you to remember is that bathing a tangled dog first usually makes the problem worse, not better. It does not loosen the mats. It locks them in tighter. Between visits, your goal is not to make the coat perfect. Your goal is to keep it from tightening. A few short brushing sessions, starting behind the ears and under the front legs, can keep small tangles from becoming the kind of mats that need to be shaved out. And if you already feel something tight, firm, or close to the skin, do not keep fighting it at home. Bring it in, and we can help you get ahead of it before it becomes uncomfortable for your dog.

b.text:
If you run your hands through your dog’s coat, feel a tangle, and immediately think, “I’ll just throw them in the tub and wash it out,” I need you to step away from the faucet. 

I see this happen in the salon every single week, especially with our curly doodles and thick double-coated breeds. People think warm water and a good lather will soften up tangles, but water actually does the exact opposite. Think about what happens when you wash a wool sweater: the fibers shrink, knit together, and turn into a solid, impenetrable felt pad. That is exactly what happens to your dog's hair. Bathing a matted dog locks those knots in tighter, and once that happens, my clippers are usually the only safe option left. 

The golden rule at home is to always brush *before* the bath, never after. If water hits a knot, you’ve lost the battle. 

When you sit down to brush, throw out the idea of just casually sweeping over their back while you watch TV. That just fluffs the top layer while mats quietly build up right against the skin. Grab a slicker brush, and instead of moving in circles or long, sweeping arcs, use short, gentle line strokes. You want to part the hair with your free hand so you can see the pink of their skin, then brush down through that section, working your way up layer by layer. 

Don't just start randomly in the middle of their back, either. Work in small sections and go straight to the friction zones first, because that’s where mats always start. Check right behind the ears where their collar rubs, deep in the armpits under their front legs, and back around the groin and tail base. If you can keep those hidden friction areas clear, the rest of the body is easy.

Now, if you’re doing your routine check and you feel a mat that’s already formed, put the brush down. Raking through a tight knot with metal pins hurts, and it only takes one painful session for your dog to decide they hate being groomed. Instead, take a little bit of dog conditioner (or a dog-safe detangling spray) and work it directly into the knot with your bare fingers. Massage it in, gently teasing the hairs apart with your fingertips to break up the core of the mat. Only after you’ve worked it loose with your hands and given the hair some slickness should you take a metal comb or slicker brush to gently finish working it out, starting from the tips and moving toward the skin.

A few minutes of line brushing in the right spots a couple of times a week will save your dog from discomfort, save their coat length, and save you from the dreaded "we had to shave them" phone call at their next appointment. As always, if you run into a knot you can’t safely separate with your fingers, leave it alone and bring them in—we're always here to help tackle it before it gets out of hand.

setup: A retired Army staff sergeant is writing about coming home after his second deployment for readers of the veterans' writing workshop anthology.

a.text:
# The Cereal Aisle

I flew home from my second deployment in October. My wife met me at the airport with our daughter, who was six.

I had a picture of that girl taped inside my locker for a year. In the picture she was five and missing a front tooth. The one at the airport had both her teeth back and was taller than I remembered, and when I came walking up she got behind her mother's leg and held on to it and looked at me like she was trying to place me. My wife put her hand on the back of our daughter's head and said, "That's Daddy." She didn't come out from behind the leg right away. I knelt down and waited. It took her a minute. I don't blame her. A year is a long time when you're six. A year is most of what you can remember.

She came around eventually. But I think about that minute a lot.

A few days later my wife sent me to the store for milk and a couple other things. I got the milk fine. Then she'd written cereal on the list, and I went to the cereal aisle, and I stood there.

I want to explain this right. There were maybe forty kinds of cereal. Probably more. I stood in front of them and I could not pick one. It wasn't that I couldn't decide which one tasted best. It was that I couldn't make the machinery in my head do the thing it was supposed to do. Over there you eat what they give you and you're grateful and you don't think about it. You don't stand in front of forty choices with nobody shooting at you and nothing to do but pick. I stood there long enough that a stocker asked me if I needed help finding something. I said no. I stood there some more. I want to say it was twenty minutes. It was a while.

I finally grabbed the one with the toucan on it because my daughter had that when she was little, and I left.

At home the hardest part came at night. For a year I'd slept facing the door. You do that so you can see it. You do it without thinking after a while, your body just turns you that way. And we kept our bedroom door shut at home, always had, and I couldn't do it. I'd lie there with the door shut and it felt wrong, like something was going to come through it and I wouldn't know. So I started leaving it open. My wife asked why. I said I liked the air. That wasn't it. I turned so I could see the open door and the hallway, and that was the only way I could get to sleep for a long time.

It got a little better. The door thing took months. My daughter warmed up faster than I did, honestly. By Christmas she was climbing on me like I'd never left.

I still don't love the cereal aisle.

b.text:
The second time I came back from Iraq, we landed at Fort Hood around two in the morning, went through the standard paperwork and medical checks, and finally got released to the gym where the families were waiting. 

I saw my wife first. Then I looked down for my daughter. She was six, and in twelve months she had grown out of her sneakers and lost two front teeth. When I knelt down and dropped my kit bag, she stepped back and tucked herself entirely behind her mother’s right leg. She gripped the denim with both hands and peeked out with one eye like I was a stranger asking for directions in a parking lot. 

My wife touched the back of her head and said, "It’s Daddy, honey. Go on." 

It took her about thirty seconds of staring at the uniform and my face before she let go of the jeans and walked over to let me hug her. She was stiff at first, then she rested her chin on my collarbone. I didn't say anything because my throat was completely dry.

Two days later, my wife sent me to the grocery store down the road for milk, eggs, and a box of cereal. 

I got the milk and the eggs without an issue. Then I turned into the cereal aisle and stopped. Downrange, you had whatever was sitting in the metal bins at the DFAC—usually mini boxes of Corn Flakes, Raisin Bran, or whatever hadn't expired yet. In this aisle, the shelves went from the floor to above my head, running thirty yards down. There were at least forty different kinds of cereal, all in bright red, yellow, and blue cardboard. Five different types of Cheerios alone. 

I stood in the center of the aisle with both hands on the push-bar of the cart. People went around me with their carts, looking at me once and moving on. I knew I should just reach out, grab a box of Rice Krispies, and walk to the register, but my brain wouldn't send the signal to my arm. I stood there for twenty minutes just reading the names on the boxes over and over until my legs got tired. Finally, I grabbed a plain box of Shredded Wheat and went to the checkout. 

Night was the hardest part to adjust to. For a year on the COP, my cot was positioned so that my feet pointed directly at the plywood door of our hooch. If that door moved, I was awake and looking straight at it with my rifle within reach. 

Back in our house, the bed sat along the far wall. My wife liked to sleep with the bedroom door open so the hallway fan would pull air through and so she could hear our daughter if she got up for water in the night. 

The first week, I couldn't do it. Every time she fell asleep, I’d get up quietly and click the door shut, then lie on my side facing the frame in the dark, waiting for the knob to turn. Around 0300 she’d wake up hot and open it again. 

By the third week, we made a deal to leave it cracked a couple of inches. I still slept facing the opening, on top of the covers with my boots lined up right below the mattress, watching the strip of light from the nightlight in the hallway. It took about six months before I could roll over on my right side, turn my back to the open door, and close my eyes.

setup: A high school junior is writing an argumentative essay to her English teacher and classmates arguing for open campus lunch for juniors and seniors.

a.text:
**Open Campus Lunch: A Practical Privilege for Upperclassmen**

Every day, 340 students at our school file into a cafeteria with 220 seats. The math doesn't work, and everyone who has survived that lunch wave knows it. Students eat sitting on hallway floors, balanced on the edges of trash cans, or standing in line so long that by the time they get food, half the period is gone. The district could spend years and millions of dollars expanding the cafeteria, or it could try something far simpler: let juniors and seniors leave campus for lunch. Our school should adopt an open campus lunch policy for upperclassmen because it would immediately relieve overcrowding, it is what the student body overwhelmingly wants, and nearby districts have already proven it can work.

The overcrowding problem alone justifies the change. A cafeteria built for 220 people cannot comfortably hold 340, and the difference isn't abstract. That's 120 students per lunch wave without a seat, every single day. Beyond being uncomfortable, it's a genuine health concern. Students who spend twenty minutes in line and ten minutes hunting for somewhere to sit end up rushing through meals or skipping them entirely. Open campus lunch addresses this without a single construction dollar. Even if only a portion of juniors and seniors chose to leave, the students who stayed would actually have a place to eat.

Students themselves clearly support the idea. In a survey I conducted of 80 students at our school, 71 said they were in favor of open campus lunch for juniors and seniors. That's nearly nine out of ten. Admittedly, 80 responses isn't the entire student body, but it's a strong signal of where opinion sits. It also makes sense when you consider who this policy would affect. Juniors and seniors are sixteen to eighteen years old. Many of them drive, hold jobs, and manage their own schedules outside of school. Within two years, every one of them will be in college, trade school, or the workforce, where nobody assigns them a lunch table or watches the clock for them. Being trusted with one unsupervised hour is not a radical leap. It's reasonable practice for the independence they're about to have.

The most common objection is that students won't come back. Administrators worry about tardiness, kids skipping afternoon classes, and the school's responsibility if something happens off campus. These concerns are fair, but they're predictions, and predictions can be checked against evidence. Three nearby districts, Fairmont, West Linn, and Cascade, already allow open campus lunch for their upperclassmen. Their published statistics show no rise in tardiness since the policies were put in place. Three different communities had the same fears ours does, and the feared outcome simply didn't happen. On top of that, the policy can be designed to protect itself. Limit it to juniors and seniors, require students to sign out or show ID at the door, and revoke the privilege permanently for anyone who returns late. That structure punishes the individual rule-breaker instead of assuming every student will be one.

Right now, more than a hundred students eat lunch without a seat while a workable solution sits just outside the cafeteria doors. The students want it, the overcrowding demands it, and three neighboring districts have shown it succeeds without the problems critics predict. The administration should pilot open campus lunch for juniors and seniors next semester and judge it by the same attendance data that has vindicated it elsewhere. Upperclassmen are asking to be trusted with one hour a day. All the available evidence says they'll handle it.

b.text:
Every day during fourth period, a collective anxiety builds. When the bell rings, it is a mad dash to the cafeteria—not just out of hunger, but out of a survival instinct to secure a plastic chair. Our school's lunch period has become a daily exercise in overcrowding. To solve this logistical bottleneck and grant upperclassmen a step toward independence, our school should implement an open-campus lunch policy for juniors and seniors. This policy is not just a student wishlist item; it is a practical solution backed by spatial reality, strong student consensus, and the proven success of our neighboring districts.

The most immediate argument for an open campus is simple math. Our cafeteria is officially rated to seat 220 people. However, during our designated lunch wave, there are currently 340 students trying to eat, socialize, and decompress. This leaves over one hundred students displaced every single day. Teenagers are forced to eat sitting on hallway floors, crowded on stairwells, or crammed into classroom doorways. This is not only uncomfortable and noisy, but it also creates a safety hazard and a supervision nightmare for staff. By allowing juniors and seniors—the oldest, most responsible segment of this wave—the option to leave campus for lunch, we would immediately alleviate this pressure, bringing the cafeteria back down to a manageable, safe capacity.

Furthermore, there is an overwhelming demand for this change among the student body, reflecting a readiness for greater responsibility. In a survey I conducted of 80 students at our school, 71 were in favor of an open-campus policy. This represents nearly 89% of the surveyed population. While critics might dismiss this as teenagers simply wanting to escape school grounds, the reality is that juniors and seniors are at a transitional stage in their lives. We are preparing for college and the workforce, environments where we will be expected to manage our own time, logistics, and safety. Giving upperclassmen the agency to choose where they eat is a small, controlled way to foster that necessary maturity. 

The primary opposition to an open campus usually centers on reliability, with opponents worrying that students will not make it back in time for fifth period. Fortunately, we do not have to guess how this policy would play out in reality; we can look to our neighbors. Three nearby districts—Fairmont, West Linn, and Cascade—already allow open-campus lunches for their upperclassmen. According to their published district statistics, none of these schools experienced a rise in tardiness after implementing the policy. When students are trusted with a privilege, they respect it, knowing that irresponsible behavior will result in losing their off-campus access. 

Ultimately, transitioning to an open-campus lunch policy is a win-win scenario for both the administration and the student body. It resolves a physical capacity crisis in our cafeteria without requiring a single dollar of construction budget, matches the overwhelming desire of the student population, and carries zero statistical risk of increased tardiness. It is time for our school to trust its juniors and seniors, ease the lunchtime crowd, and open the doors.

setup: A third-year electrical apprentice is writing an argumentative essay for the union newsletter against a 15% cut to apprenticeship funding.

a.text:
# Don’t Cut a Program That Puts People to Work

The state’s proposed 15% cut to apprenticeship funding is a bad way to save money. It takes support away from a program that trains workers, raises wages, and gives people a way to support themselves and their families.

I’m a third-year electrical apprentice with the local IBEW. I’m learning this trade on the job and in the classroom. Apprenticeship is not just a class you take and hope leads somewhere. We work while we learn, and we build toward a skill and a wage we can live on.

Look at the results: 24 apprentices started in our cohort, and 21 finished and are now working as journeymen. That’s nearly 88% finishing and moving into skilled jobs. Those are real workers filling real needs.

Apprentices start at around $19 an hour, with pay reaching around $46 an hour as journeymen. At 40 hours a week for 52 weeks, that works out to about $39,500 a year at the start and $95,700 at the journeyman rate, before taxes and without overtime. Actual yearly earnings depend on hours worked, but the path forward is clear.

That kind of wage growth helps people get off assistance programs and pay their own bills. Instead of needing more public support, workers can contribute more in taxes and spend more at local businesses. That is a return on public money, not just an expense.

The cost comparison matters, too. The total public cost is about $14,000 per apprentice who finishes, compared with roughly $48,000 in average public subsidy per four-year college graduate who finishes. That puts apprenticeship at less than a third of the public cost.

This isn’t an argument against college. We need college graduates, too. But college is not the only path worth funding. The state should support a route that lets people earn while they learn and finish with skills employers need.

A 15% cut may look like savings on a budget sheet. But training still requires instructors, equipment, classroom space, and time. Cutting funding puts pressure on programs to take fewer apprentices, charge workers more, or stretch resources further. None of that helps build the skilled workforce our state needs.

Electrical work has to be done safely and correctly. You cannot replace solid training with a promise to figure it out later.

State legislators should reject this cut. Apprenticeship is doing what public workforce funding is supposed to do: helping people learn a trade, earn a decent living, and do work their communities depend on.

Don’t cut a program that is getting the job done.

b.text:
Don't Cut Apprenticeship Funding

The state wants to cut apprenticeship funding 15 percent. That is a bad idea. I am a third-year electrical apprentice with the IBEW. This program works and it costs the public a lot less than people think.

My class started with 24 apprentices. Twenty-one of us finished. All 21 are working journeyman jobs right now. That is not luck. That is how these programs run when they are funded.

We start at about $19 an hour. When we journey out we make around $46 an hour. People get off food stamps and other assistance fast because they can pay their own bills. We start paying taxes instead of collecting them.

The public cost for each apprentice who finishes is about $14,000. A four-year college graduate who finishes costs the public around $48,000 on average. We cost less, we work while we train, and we go straight into jobs that need doing.

Electricians are already in short supply. Cutting the money that trains the next ones will make that worse. Contractors need us. The grid needs us. New buildings need us. This is not some extra program. It is how we get skilled people on the job without loading them with debt.

Legislators, look at the numbers. Twenty-one out of 24 from my group are working and paying taxes. The cost per finisher is $14,000 versus $48,000 for a college grad. Do not cut this. Fund it. It pays for itself.

setup: A local sports columnist is writing an opinionated season-ending commentary for readers of the local paper's sports section.

a.text:
**They Had the Hammer. They Put It Down.**

Eight and two is a good season. I want to say that up front, because what follows is going to sound like a man who forgot it.

Dez Kowalski threw for 2,340 yards this fall, and nobody in the history of this program has done that. He earned every one of them. The kid played the last three weeks with a shoulder he wasn't talking about and kept putting the ball where it needed to be. Years from now his name is going to be on a board in that gym and it belongs there.

But we lost in the second round of the state playoffs to a team we beat by 20 in September, and I don't think we lost because they got better. I think we lost because we stopped doing the thing that was working.

Go back and look at the first half. We ran the ball, we ran it well, and we ran it right at them. They didn't have an answer. The line was getting a push on nearly every down and our backs were falling forward for four, five, six yards at a clip. That's how you build a lead against a team that's out for revenge — you make them tackle for two hours until they don't want to anymore.

Then halftime happened, and whatever was said in that locker room, the plan that came out of it was a different plan. Down three. Three points. And we came out throwing on first down, throwing on second down, and finding ourselves in third-and-long against a defense that finally got to sit back and rush the passer.

I understand the temptation. When you have the best quarterback in school history, every play call that isn't a pass feels like leaving money on the table. But a three-point deficit isn't an emergency. It's a field goal. It does not require you to abandon what got you there and start playing the other team's game.

That's what happened. We took the one thing they couldn't stop and set it aside voluntarily, and by the time the fourth quarter got tight we'd lost the rhythm up front and couldn't get it back. Kowalski ended up throwing into coverage that wouldn't have existed if the safeties still had to worry about the run. Nobody made him do that. The situation didn't demand it. It was a choice.

I've heard people this week blame the officiating, and I've heard people say the other team just wanted it more. I don't buy either one. The officiating was ordinary and the other team wanted it exactly as much as they did in Week 3. The difference was that in Week 3 we kept our foot on the gas, and in Round 2 we changed drivers at the half.

None of this makes it a bad year. The seniors leave with a record most classes here would trade for, and the juniors got a taste of what November football feels like. That matters. But the honest lesson from that game isn't about heart or toughness or wanting it. It's simpler and it's more fixable than that.

When something is working, keep doing it. Especially when you're only down three.

b.text:
The season ends not with a bang but with a head-scratcher. Our high school football team finished 8-2 and made a solid run to the second round of the state playoffs, only to fall to a squad they had dismantled by 20 points back in Week 3. Dez Kowalski put an exclamation point on his year with 2,340 passing yards—a school record that will stand for a while.

But records and regular-season wins don’t decide playoff games. What decided this one was the decision to abandon the run in the second half. The ground game was working. They were only down three. Yet the ball kept going in the air, the clock kept running against them, and a winnable contest slipped away. Stick with what’s moving the chains when you’re that close. That’s football 101, and it cost them a deeper run. 

Solid season, no question. Just a tough way to learn the lesson.

setup: A local sports columnist is writing an opinionated season-ending commentary for readers of the local paper's sports section.

a.text:
**One Play Call Haunts the Season**

Eight wins, two losses, and a school-record 2,340 passing yards for Dez Kowalski—by the numbers, this was a season to celebrate. But numbers don’t tell the whole story, and neither does the final score of last Friday’s playoff loss. The truth stings because it’s avoidable: we lost because we stopped doing what was working.

Up 20 points on that same opponent back in Week 3, we ran the ball down their throats. Last Friday, down just three in the second half, we abandoned the run. Four straight pass plays, three incompletions, a sack, and suddenly the momentum was gone. The defense, gassed from long drives earlier in the game, couldn’t hold up when we needed them most.

Football is a game of adjustments, sure, but sometimes the best adjustment is sticking with what got you there. We had them on their heels. Instead of pounding the rock, we put it all on Dez’s arm—and for the first time all season, it wasn’t enough. That’s not on him. It’s on the play-calling.

This team had heart, talent, and a shot at something special. But in the end, we outsmarted ourselves. And that’s the hardest loss to swallow.

b.text:
An 8-2 season and a school-record 2,340 yards from Dez Kowalski is a year most programs around here would take. It still ended with a second-round playoff loss to a team this bunch beat by 20 back in week three.

They were only down three at the half and the run was moving the chains. Then they abandoned it. Started slinging it like they were chasing two scores instead of one. That’s how you give a winnable game away. Stick with what’s working when you’re that close. The talent was there. The decision wasn’t.

setup: A solo SaaS founder is posting a thread to indie hackers and customers about a pricing mistake and the fix.

a.text:
1/ I raised prices 40% on every customer overnight. Lost 30 of 140 customers in a week. Here’s what I did wrong and what I changed.

2/ The mistake wasn’t wanting to charge more. It was doing it to everyone at once.

3/ No warning. No grandfathering. No real communication. Just a notification that their bill was going up 40%.

4/ For gym owners running on tight margins, that’s not a pricing update—it’s a betrayal. Some had been with Tallyup from the start.

5/ Within days, 30 customers churned. Not because the product stopped working, but because I broke trust.

6/ What I changed: existing customers stay on their current price. New customers see the higher price. No more overnight hikes for anyone already in.

7/ If I ever increase prices for existing customers again, I’ll give advance notice, explain the reasoning, and offer a yearly lock-in option.

8/ Pricing is a relationship decision. A 40% overnight increase cost me 30 of 140 customers in a week. That’s a trade I won’t make again.

9/ Tallyup is still here, still building. But if you’re thinking about a big price jump, don’t do it like I did.

b.text:
1/5
I raised Tallyup’s prices 40% on everyone overnight.

We lost 30 of our 140 customers in a week.

Tallyup helps gym owners track member retention. That irony isn’t lost on me.

Here’s the pricing mistake I made—and what I changed.

2/5
I treated two decisions as one:

• Should Tallyup cost more?
• Should every existing customer pay more immediately?

Even if the answer to the first was yes, that didn’t automatically justify the second.

3/5
I can’t neatly separate the impact of the higher price from the impact of changing it overnight.

That’s part of the mistake. I changed both at once.

“Customers won’t pay more” would be too convenient a lesson to take from this.

4/5
What I changed:

[Add the actual changes you made: the new pricing, who it applies to, how much notice customers get, or how you handled affected customers. Include only what happened.]

5/5
My takeaway isn’t “never raise prices.”

It’s that the rollout is part of the pricing decision—not an admin detail to figure out afterward.

Sharing the uncomfortable part of building in public, not just the launches.

setup: A wedding photographer is posting that couples who ditch rigid shot lists get better photos, using the rained-out Barrera wedding as an example.

a.text:
The best wedding photos never come from a checklist. 

After eight years of shooting full-time in the Texas Hill Country, I’ve seen my share of "must-have" shot lists. But here is an industry truth: the more a couple clings to a rigid Pinterest checklist, the more they miss out on the actual magic of their day. 

When you force a photographer to constantly look down at a piece of paper, they miss the fleeting, real-life moments happening right in front of them. 

Case in point: The Barrera wedding. 

Mother Nature had other plans for their outdoor ceremony, and the skies absolutely opened up. Instead of panicking because our timeline and "perfect" photo list were out the window, we adapted. We moved the entire celebration under the shelter of a giant pecan tree. 

Because the Barreras trusted the process—and ditched the rigid expectations—we captured some of the most raw, honest, and breathtaking images of my entire career. The rain, the intimacy of everyone crowding under the branches, the sheer joy of the unexpected—you can't plan that. And you certainly can't put it on a checklist. 

For the couples planning their big day: Hire vendors whose work you love, and then give them the creative freedom to do what they do best. The magic happens in the unplanned moments.

For my fellow wedding industry pros: How do you handle the "shot list" conversation with your clients?

b.text:
The couples who ditch the shot list usually end up with the best photos.

The Barrera wedding is a perfect example. It rained, we changed plans, and everything moved under a big pecan tree. No rigid timeline. No forcing moments. Just a beautiful, real celebration unfolding exactly as it needed to.

And honestly, that’s where the magic lives.

A shot list can be helpful for the essentials, but the best images rarely come from checking boxes. They come from presence, flexibility, and trusting the day to be what it is.

When couples let go of “perfect,” they make room for something better: genuine moments, real emotion, and photographs that actually feel like them.

If you’re planning a wedding, my best advice is this:
Have a plan.
Then leave space for the unexpected.

That’s usually where the best photos happen.

a.text:
When Dolores started with us 14 months ago, just hanging from the bar for a few seconds was a struggle.

setup: An in-house recruiter is posting a contrarian observation about candidates asking about the team’s last failed project in interviews to recruiters, hiring managers, and job seekers.

a.text:
Some of the best candidates I’ve met in roughly 200 interviews have asked a version of this:

“What was the last project here that didn’t work out?”

Not the biggest success. Not the five-year vision. The thing that went sideways.

In logistics, that can tell you more about a team than a polished answer about “fast-paced environments.”

Here’s how that conversation might go:

Candidate: “What was the last project that failed?”

Hiring manager: “We rolled out a new scheduling process, but had to pull it back.”

Candidate: “What did you miss?”

Hiring manager: “We didn’t get enough input from the people running the shifts.”

Candidate: “And did those people have more say in the next rollout?”

That follow-up is the part I notice.

They’re not just checking whether we make mistakes. Of course we do. They’re trying to understand whether anything changes afterward—and whether the people closest to the work get heard.

As an in-house recruiter, I want us to have an honest answer ready. Not a success story dressed up as a failure.

Candidates are making a decision too. They deserve to know what happens here when the plan doesn’t survive contact with the operation.

b.text:
Over the last nine years, I’ve sat through roughly ~200 interviews for logistics roles. The questions candidates ask almost always follow the same script: culture fit, growth paths, tech stack, team structure. Then there’s the group that shifts the entire dynamic.

They ask about our last failed project.

It never lands as gossip or doubt. It cuts straight to operational maturity. Here’s exactly how that conversation typically goes:

“I’d love to hear about the last major initiative that didn’t hit its targets. What broke first, and what changed after?”

We usually walk through a delayed vendor integration that stalled warehouse throughput for three weeks. The candidate listens, absorbs it, then follows up: “Where did the contingency plan assume reliability that reality overrode? And would you build that verification step into the next rollout?”

That’s it. No rehearsed answers. Just systems thinking.

In logistics, nothing runs perfectly on paper. Supply chains fracture, carrier capacity dips, and assumptions turn fast. Candidates who ask about failure aren’t hunting for red flags—they’re checking how we respond to them. They want to know if leadership audits mistakes or buries them. If the solution was a quick patch or a structural fix. If transparency actually survives when timelines slip.

Job seekers: lean into the hard questions. Hiring managers: answer honestly. Recruiters: watch who stays curious instead of cautious.

How many times have you asked—or been asked—about a recent miss?

We’re hiring our first support person at Ridgepoint.

The honest version: it’s not scaling. We’re losing time on product and sales, and some customers are waiting longer than we think they should.

So we’re bringing on a full-time support person to own the day-to-day.

What the job actually looks like:

You’re comfortable being practical, clear, and patient. You like fixing things. You’re okay with early-stage ambiguity, but you don’t need the company to hold your hand.

You’re fine with:

- A small team
- Fast-moving priorities
- Writing a lot
- Learning messy customer workflows
- Saying “I don’t know yet, I’ll find out” and then finding out

If this sounds like you, apply with a short note on why you’re interested and what kind of support work you’re looking for next.

If you’re a customer reading this: we’re doing this because we want support to be faster, more consistent, and less dependent on three founders constantly context-switching.

setup: A real estate agent is posting one specific observation about early block walks and happier buyers to LinkedIn buyers, agents, and lenders.

a.text:
Twelve years in, you stop guessing and start noticing patterns.

One that’s held up every time: the buyers who walk the neighborhood at 7 a.m. before we tour the house are the ones who still love the place two years later. Not because the house changes, but because they actually know what they’re buying into.

I learned that with the Pruitts. They were under contract on a little craftsman just off Sycamore Street, and the inspection was clean, the numbers worked, everything looked good on paper. But I’d watched enough buyers grow quiet six months after closing to know that paper isn’t the whole story. So I told them to grab coffee at the shop on the corner, walk the full length of Sycamore at 7 a.m. on a Tuesday, and then call me.

They did. They saw the retired guy three doors down who hoses off his driveway every morning and waves whether you wave back or not. They heard the school bus stop at the end of the block, which meant kids, which meant the Pruitts—who were expecting their first—wouldn’t be the only young family on the street. They realized the “quiet” street they’d driven through at 5 p.m. on a Saturday was actually alive in a way they liked at 7 a.m. on a weekday.

They closed three weeks later, and last I checked they were still happy. Not because the house was perfect, but because Sycamore Street felt like home before they ever walked through the front door.

I don’t have a statistic for this. I just know that when buyers fall in love with the context around the house, the house itself tends to stick.

b.text:
After 12 years of selling homes in Asheville, mostly to first-time buyers, I've noticed something I now tell every client: walk the neighborhood at 7am before we ever tour the house. Not the afternoon of the showing. Not a quick drive-by. Seven in the morning, on foot.

The buyers who do it end up happier with the house months later. Not because the house is different, but because they already know what their life there actually feels like before they fall in love with a kitchen.

The Pruitts taught me this. A few years back they were set on a house on Sycamore Street. Beautiful listing photos, right price, they were ready to write an offer sight unseen if I'd let them. I asked them to do the 7am walk first. They grumbled a little, but they went.

What they found: the street was quieter than they expected, a neighbor was out watering tomatoes and talked to them for twenty minutes, and there was a steady stream of people walking dogs toward a little trail entrance they didn't even know existed. They also noticed the morning sun hit the front porch directly, which mattered to Mrs. Pruitt more than any feature on the listing sheet, because she drinks her coffee outside every single day.

They bought the house. But here's the part that stuck with me: when I checked in a year later, the things they loved most were the things they discovered on that walk. The neighbor with the tomatoes. The trail. The porch coffee. The house was the container. The morning was the life.

I've also seen the walk save people. Buyers who discovered the charming street backed up to a commuter shortcut, or that the "quiet cul-de-sac" was where every delivery truck in the county turned around. Better to know at 7am on a Tuesday than at closing.

You can stage a house. You can't stage a morning.

setup: A solo indie game developer is writing a devlog recap for subscribers about his game's launch week sales, subreddit attention, review feedback, and upcoming 1.1 patch.

a.text:
**Week 1 numbers, a floaty feeling, and the next patch**

The game launched last week. I didn’t do anything fancy with the announcement, mostly because I spent the final stretch making sure things didn’t break on release. On launch day I posted in the subreddit I’d been around for a while, answered questions in the support email that hadn’t existed before, and checked my phone more than I should have.

First week sales: 412 copies.

That number feels enormous to me. For three years, the only version of this game people knew about was the version I made at 1:00 a.m., sometimes with terrible lighting and an art style that was not yet a thing anyone else needed to agree on. 412 people bought it, opened it, and gave the game some of their time. That’s not a failure by any measure, and it’s not a success story either. It’s just the first week.

For about six hours, the game hit the front page of a small subreddit. It wasn’t huge. It wasn’t Steam. It wasn’t a featured placement. But it was enough for the little counter on my developer dashboard to start moving in a way it never had before. I kept thinking, “Do not refresh again,” then refreshed again.

A few people left reviews, which was more than I expected. Some played it for a few minutes, some got much farther, and one review mentioned that the movement feels floaty.

They’re right.

It’s one of those things that becomes easy to miss after you’ve been living with the same game files for too long. You start to compensate unconsciously. You know where the collision is supposed to feel wrong. You know which jump is slightly too soft. You know which landing doesn’t have enough weight. Then someone describes it in one sentence, and it’s immediately obvious.

So the floaty movement is getting patched.

1.1 will focus on movement feel first. I’m tightening acceleration, adjusting air control, and making the landings read less like the character is drifting on top of the level and more like they have weight. I’ll probably also do a small pass on the early camera behavior while I’m in there, since those two things are harder to separate than they should be.

I’m not promising an exact date yet beyond “next month.” Solo developer, small patch scope, but I still have to test, package, and push things out without accidentally making other parts of the game worse. The release week taught me that much at least: every change becomes more noticeable when other people are already playing it.

The next few weeks are mostly going to be support, bug fixes, and the 1.1 movement patch. If you played and ran into something, I’m seeing it. If you haven’t played yet, the game is out. If you have, thanks for actually buying it during launch week and not waiting until I inevitably start saying things like “the next big patch” like I’m a one-man studio trying to sound like I have a release roadmap and a marketing department.

I do have a roadmap, but it’s more like: patch movement, make the game less floaty, keep fixing what breaks, then figure out what comes next.

b.text:
It’s been a week since launch. Honestly still feels surreal typing that.

412 copies sold in the first seven days. I know that’s not earth-shattering by any stretch, but for a solo project I’ve been chipping away at on nights and weekends for three years, it’s way more than I let myself hope for. A bunch of you grabbed it day one, and seeing usernames I recognize from the devlog pop up in the purchases was genuinely the best feeling.

Mid-week the game hit the front page of a small subreddit for about six hours. Nothing huge, but enough to give the Steam page a noticeable spike and bring in some really thoughtful early feedback. One post in particular stuck with me: a player said the movement feels “floaty.” I went back and replayed a few levels trying to see it from their perspective, and… yeah, they’re right. The air control has a bit too much hang time, and the deceleration isn’t snappy enough. Can’t un-feel it now. So I’m addressing that directly in patch 1.1, which I’m targeting for next month. I’m tightening up the horizontal drag, reducing the midair turn radius, and adding a tiny bit of downward pull on the jump apex so the character feels more planted without losing the sense of weight I originally wanted. I’ll post detailed patch notes when it’s closer.

Other things on the 1.1 list: fixing a rare softlock in the third area, some menu navigation polish (controller support was a little janky on certain screens), and a few audio balance tweaks people pointed out. Nothing massive, just cleanup.

After that, I want to take a real breath and finally play some games I’ve been ignoring for years. Then I’ll figure out what’s next—whether that’s a content update, porting to another platform, or starting the next thing. For now, just patching and catching up on sleep.

Thanks to everyone who’s played so far and sent bug reports, reviews, or just a nice message. It means a lot.
