setup: A bakery owner is writing a warm blog and newsletter post to regular customers explaining why wedding cake orders are ending.

a.text:
A little bakery update from us: we’ve decided to step away from custom wedding cakes.

This was not an easy decision. Wedding cakes have been part of our work for a long time, and it has been such an honor to be invited into so many celebrations. We’ve loved hearing your stories, talking through flavors, making sugar flowers at odd hours, and seeing photos of a cake surrounded by people you love.

But as a three-person bakery, we have had to take an honest look at where our time goes.

A single wedding cake often begins with a free consultation and tasting, followed by design conversations, ordering specialty ingredients, baking, filling, frosting, decorating, delivery planning, and all the little details in between. By the time it is finished, one order can take around fourteen hours of work outside of the baking we do for the shop every day.

This year, we also had three wedding orders cancel at the last minute. We understand that plans change, and we truly do not hold that against anyone. But those cancellations meant ingredients had already been purchased and time had already been set aside, and for a small business like ours, that is a hard loss to absorb.

Most importantly, taking on custom wedding work was beginning to pull us away from the pastry case, the morning breads, the birthday cakes, and the everyday treats that bring so many of you through our door. Those are the things that keep the lights on, pay our rent, and allow us to keep showing up at 4am to make this little bakery what it is.

So we are choosing to put our energy back into the daily bakery: the croissants still warm from the oven, the cookies you pick up after school, the cakes you bring to dinner, the loaf of bread that becomes tomorrow’s toast. We’ll continue making celebration cakes in our regular style when our schedule allows, but we will no longer be offering fully custom wedding cakes.

Thank you for understanding, and thank you for continuing to support us in all the ordinary, wonderful moments in between the big ones.

b.text:
I need to tell you all something, and I'd rather just say it straight than make some big announcement.

After a lot of thinking (and a few sleepless nights, if I'm being honest), we've decided to stop taking custom wedding cake orders.

This wasn't a snap decision. I love wedding cakes. I love sitting with couples and hearing how they met, I love sketching tiers on napkins, and there is nothing like seeing a cake set up in a venue with the light coming in and everyone milling around with champagne. Some of my favorite memories in this shop have come from wedding cakes.

But here's what I've had to be honest about. Each custom order eats up about fourteen hours of my time before I ever bake a single layer. Consultations, tastings, emails back and forth about flavors and design, sketches and revisions, logistics. Fourteen hours. And that's time I'm not spending on the case, on the sourdough, on the things that walk out the door every day and keep the lights on.

This year we had three last-minute cancellations. I don't say that to shame anyone, things happen, life falls apart sometimes. But the ingredients for a wedding cake are expensive, and when someone cancels two weeks out, that cost doesn't come back. Three times in one year was enough to make me sit down with the numbers and realize I was running part of this business at a loss while working harder than ever.

That's the heartbeat of this place. And every time I disappeared into a wedding cake, the case got thinner and the everyday stuff suffered. If you need a cake for a big gathering, talk to me and we'll figure something out from what we already do well. But the big custom orders are done.

setup: A fourth-generation soybean and corn farmer is writing a newsletter commentary on crop insurance costs and SB 214 for county readers and state legislators.

a.text:
This spring the rain wouldn't quit, and by the late May deadline I had only 60 percent of my soybean and corn acres in the ground. That alone is hard enough. Then came the USDA's 22 percent base-rate hike on prevented-planting coverage for our region. On my operation that single change is costing an extra $46,000 this year.

The acreage caps make it worse. Those caps hit a fourth-generation family farm like mine harder, proportionally, than the larger operations down the road that can absorb the same percentage hit across far more acres. The numbers don't lie: smaller family outfits are paying a steeper relative price for the same weather risk.

Senate Bill 214 would fix the acreage-cap problem. It deserves our full support. Call your legislators, show up at the next Farm Bureau meeting, and make sure they know the math that family farmers are living with right now.

b.text:
**A 22% Prevented Planting Hike Shouldn’t Penalize Family Farms**

USDA raised the prevented planting base rate in our region by 22% this year. On my fourth-generation soybean and corn operation, that increase added about $46,000 in extra cost.

Then came the rain.

By the late-May planting deadline, I had only 60% of my acres planted. The rest were too wet to touch. Prevented planting coverage exists for exactly this kind of spring, when the calendar runs out and the fields never dry. But a premium increase of this size makes that safety net more expensive at the very moment producers are most likely to need it.

The bigger problem is how the acreage cap works. Under the current structure, family operations like mine are hit harder proportionally than larger operations nearby. A bigger farm can absorb higher costs across more acres and more flexibility. A family operation takes the same hit on a smaller base, and the cap magnifies the damage. In a year when nearly half my intended acres couldn’t be planted, that isn’t just frustrating—it threatens the financial stability of the operation.

That is why SB 214 matters. It would fix the acreage cap so prevented planting coverage works more fairly for family farms. It would not eliminate bad weather, and it would not reverse this year’s rate increase. But it would make sure the program does not disproportionately squeeze mid-size and family operations when they need support most.

If you believe farm policy should keep family operations viable—not just protect the largest operations—please encourage our legislators to support SB 214.

setup: A small dog grooming salon owner is writing a how-to for dog owners about preventing coat matting between grooming visits.

a.text:
# Keeping Your Dog’s Coat Mat-Free Between Grooming Visits

The mistake I see most often is bathing a tangled dog and hoping the water will loosen everything up. Unfortunately, it usually does the opposite. Water, shampooing, and rubbing with a towel can tighten those tangles into a dense, felt-like mat that’s much harder to remove.

So before you run the bath, reach for the brush. This is especially important for curly coats and double coats, where tangles can hide underneath hair that looks perfectly tidy on top.

Start behind the ears and under the front legs. Those soft, friction-prone spots are often the first places mats develop. Then check around the collar or harness, the chest, the back legs, and the tail. You don’t have to tackle the whole dog in one long session. A few calm minutes at a time are better than a wrestling match.

Use a slicker brush and work in small sections. Part the coat so you can see where the hair meets the skin, then brush a thin layer at a time with short, gentle, straight strokes—not circles. Start at the ends of any tangles and gradually work closer to the skin. Keep the pressure light; slicker pins can irritate skin if you keep scraping the same spot.

This is called line brushing, and it helps you get beyond that fluffy top layer. On double-coated dogs, loose undercoat can collect underneath and start packing together. On curly dogs, the curls can wrap around each other and trap loose hair. Brushing only the surface misses both.

If you find a small tangle starting, pause before putting a brush or comb into it. Gently work a dog-safe detangling spray or leave-in conditioner through it with your fingers, following the product directions. Loosen the hairs carefully, then brush a little at a time without pulling on the skin. Conditioner can help with a loose tangle, but it won’t make a tight mat safe to brush out.

Once a section feels clear, check it with a metal comb, gently working through to the base of the coat. If it catches, don’t force it—that spot needs another look.

Only bathe once the coat is free of tangles. Brushing before the bath is essential, but it doesn’t mean you should never brush afterward: once the coat is properly dried, a gentle brush and comb check can catch any new tangles. Blot with the towel rather than rubbing vigorously.

If a mat feels tight against the skin, covers a large area, or makes your dog flinch, leave it for us. Please don’t cut it out with scissors; skin can be pulled up inside the mat where you can’t see it.

And if you’re unsure whether you’re reaching through the coat, ask us at your next visit. We’re happy to show you on your own dog—it’s much easier once you’ve seen and felt what you’re aiming for.

b.text:
Look, I get it. You bring your dog in looking great, and two weeks later there's tangle city happening and you're wondering what went wrong. The truth is, coats don't wait for the next groom. Especially with double-coated breeds like Goldens, huskies, or retrievers, and curly breeds like poodles and doodles, what you do at home between visits matters more than what I do in the tub.

So here's the thing, and I can't stress this enough: brush your dog before the bath, never after. The biggest mistake I see constantly is people bathing the dog first, thinking the water and shampoo will loosen the mats up. It does the opposite. Wet matted fur just turns into a felt pad. You ever put a wool sweater in the wash by accident and it comes out three sizes smaller and stiff? Same thing. Water and friction lock those tangles in tighter, and then you've got a mess that I have to shave out instead of brush out.

When you do brush, grab a slicker brush. Not a pin brush, not one of those rubber mitt things, a proper slicker. Use short line strokes, not circles. I know circling feels satisfying, but you're just spinning the hair around and creating twist mats at the base. Short line strokes, working down to the skin, lifting out and repeating.

Work in sections. Don't just swipe down the back and call it done. Start behind the ears and under the front legs, because that's where mats start first every single time. Friction points. Then move down the flanks, the haunches, the tail. If your dog has a curly coat, fluff dry as you go so you can see what you're actually dealing with. Wet curly hair hides knots.

If you already see a mat forming, don't go at it with a brush or comb right away. Work some conditioner into it with your fingers first. Just a dab, work it in, gently pull the hairs apart. You'd be surprised how many mats will release with a little patience and slip. Once you've loosened it, then you can carefully work through it with your slicker.

I'd rather you brush for ten minutes every few days than do an hour-long session once a week. Consistency keeps the undercoat from packing down and keeps the curls from clumping. And honestly, if you're staying on top of it, most dogs only need a solid brush-out once or twice a week. The doodles and the double-coated dogs with longer coats, maybe a little more.

a.text:
**Corlane SM6 Stand Mixer: 8-Month Review for Serious Bakers**

After eight months of near-daily use for my farmers market sourdough, the Corlane SM6 has earned its place in my kitchen—but it’s not for everyone.

**The Good:** This mixer laughs at heavy dough. A double batch of stiff bagel dough? No problem. The motor doesn’t flinch, even under prolonged kneading. The 6-quart bowl is deep enough for large batches, though the included dough hook falls short (literally—I swapped it for a third-party one that reaches the bottom). The tilt-head design is sturdy, and the attachments feel solid.

**The Annoying:** The bowl-lift lever squeaks like a haunted door hinge. A monthly dose of WD-40 keeps it quiet, but it’s an unnecessary chore. At $429, it’s also $80 pricier than the equivalent KitchenAid, which might make you pause if you’re not pushing its limits.

**Verdict:** Buy it if you knead heavy dough weekly. The power and durability justify the cost for serious bakers. Skip it if you’re mostly whipping up cake batter or cookies—the KitchenAid will do just fine for half the wear and tear.

b.text:
After 8 months of near-daily use, I can say the Corlane SM6 is a workhorse, but it is not the mixer I’d recommend to everyone.

I use mine almost every day for market sourdough, and the motor has been impressively steady. It handles a double batch of stiff bagel dough without stalling, which is exactly the kind of test that exposes a weak mixer fast. If your baking life involves heavy dough on a regular basis, this machine has real muscle.

That said, it is not perfect. The bowl-lift lever squeaks enough that I have to hit it with WD-40 about once a month, which is annoying on a mixer this expensive. The included dough hook is also too short for the deep bowl, so I had to buy a third-party hook to make it work properly. At $429, it costs about $80 more than the comparable KitchenAid, and that extra money should buy better fit and finish than this.

My verdict: buy the Corlane SM6 if you knead heavy dough every week and want a mixer that can take real abuse. Skip it if your main jobs are cookies, cake batter, or the occasional casual loaf. For that kind of baking, the extra cost and quirks are not worth it.

setup: A remote software engineer is writing a 6-month standing desk review for blog readers researching standing desks.

a.text:
I’ve been using the Jarvik L2 standing desk for 6 months now, and I have a pretty clear opinion on it: it is a good desk at the sale price I paid, and a bad deal at full price.

I bought it for $549. At that price, I think it’s worth considering. At $749, I would skip it.

The short version:
- Motor: quiet, fast, and good
- Stability: decent sitting, shaky at full height if you type aggressively
- Memory presets: useful, but mine drift by about 1 cm
- Cable tray: genuinely bad
- Value: strong at $549, weak at $749

## What I use it for

I’m a remote software engineer, so this desk gets used every day. It’s not a decorative piece in a showroom. It holds a monitor setup, laptop, keyboard, mouse, dock, and the usual mess of cables, chargers, and random desk clutter that accumulates when you work from home full time.

That matters, because a standing desk can sound great on paper and still annoy you in practice. After 6 months, the Jarvik L2 has proven to be mostly solid, with a few annoyances that are hard to ignore.

## The motor is the best part

The motor is quiet and fast. That’s the cleanest compliment I can give this desk.

When you raise or lower it, it moves smoothly and doesn’t sound like it’s fighting itself. It’s not silent, but it’s quiet enough that I don’t think about it. That matters more than people expect. A loud desk gets old fast, especially if you shift positions a lot during the day.

Speed is also genuinely good. I don’t feel like I’m waiting around for it to get where I want. If you switch between sitting and standing multiple times a day, this makes the desk feel more premium than it probably is.

## Stability is okay until it isn’t

At normal seated height, the Jarvik L2 is fine. Nothing dramatic, nothing annoying.

At standing height, the story changes. If I’m typing lightly, it’s acceptable. If I type hard, it wobbles. Not enough to make the desk unusable, but enough that I notice it every time I’m in a more focused coding session and hammer out a bunch of text quickly.

This is the part that separates “good enough” from actually good. A standing desk should feel planted when you’re using it the way most people actually use a desk. The L2 does not fully deliver there. It gets close, but not close enough to call it stable.

If your setup is light and you type gently, you may not care. If you use a heavy monitor arm or you’re a particularly aggressive typist, expect some movement at full height.

## The memory presets are useful, but not precise

The memory presets work, but mine drift by about 1 cm.

That sounds small, and it is small, but it’s also annoying because it defeats the point of presets being exact. You press a saved position expecting to land in the same spot every time, and instead you’re off just enough to notice.

It’s not a dealbreaker. It doesn’t ruin the desk. But it does make the product feel a little less polished than it should at this price. If a desk advertises presets, I expect them to be consistent. “Close enough” is not impressive.

## The cable tray is terrible

The cable tray is garbage.

I don’t say that lightly. I think a lot of desk accessories are mediocre and people exaggerate. This one is actually bad.

It feels like an afterthought. It’s awkward to work with, not especially well designed for real cable management, and just makes the whole setup more frustrating than it should be. I ended up not trusting it for anything important and would not buy the desk for the tray alone, obviously.

If you care about clean cable management, plan on solving that separately. Don’t assume the included tray will help much. It won’t.

## Build quality and day-to-day use

Overall build quality is somewhere in the middle: better than cheap junk, not premium enough to excuse the flaws.

The desk has been reliable over 6 months. No weird failures, no motor issues, no dramatic sagging, no electronic nonsense. In that sense, it does its job. But that’s also the problem: “does its job” is not the same as “great.”

There’s enough polish in the motor and enough basic functionality elsewhere that I don’t hate using it. But there are also enough little shortcomings that I wouldn’t describe it as a desk I love. It’s a practical purchase, not a satisfying one.

## Who should buy it

Buy the Jarvik L2 if:
- you can get it around $549
- you want a reasonably fast, quiet motor
- you care more about basic function than perfect finish
- you can tolerate some wobble at height

Skip it if:
- the price is $749 or higher
- you want rock-solid stability when standing
- you expect presets to be exact
- you want the included cable tray to be useful

## Final verdict

After 6 months, my take is simple: the Jarvik L2 is worth it at the $549 sale price, and not worth it at $749.

I’m glad I bought it at a discount. I would not pay full price for it. The quiet, fast motor is real value, but the wobble at standing height, the drifting presets, and the useless cable tray keep this from being an easy recommendation.

If you see it on sale, it’s a decent buy. If not, keep looking.

b.text:
# Jarvik L2 Standing Desk: 6-Month Review

Setup context: I'm a remote software engineer, dual 27" monitors, mechanical keyboard, 8+ hours a day on it. This is desk #3 over the past decade.

## The Motor

The best part of this desk. Quiet, fast, smooth. Reaches full standing height in about 10 seconds, doesn't grind or whine. My partner works nights in the same room and the beep on preset activation is the loudest thing about it. Compared to the Fully Jarvis I had before, it's noticeably quieter and a touch faster.

## The Wobble

At sitting height: rock solid. I can hammer on the keyboard and nothing moves.

At standing height (around 44"): the moment I type with any force, the whole desk shimmies. Not catastrophic, not enough to make my monitors visibly shake, but enough that I feel it in the keyboard and enough that hard typing gets annoying after an hour. For mouse work and reading code? Fine. For a coding sprint where I'm clacking away? I notice it. For people who do voice calls with a heavy mic arm at full height, I'd be more worried.

This is the single biggest compromise of the desk.

## The Memory Presets

Off by about 1cm after 6 months. Both of them. Doesn't matter how many times I recalibrate. It's a small drift, but if you're the type to set your perfect standing elbow height and forget about it, you'll be micro-adjusting every few weeks.

Not a dealbreaker, but a sign the height sensors are mid.

## The Cable Tray

Garbage. I want to be specific here because reviews gloss over this: the tray is too small to hold a standard power strip plus a single large power brick, the "cable management" is basically a single piece of thin Velcro that sags within a month, and there's no channel for the motor cable so it just hangs out the back looking sad. I ended up buying a $25 third-party tray from Amazon and that's the only reason the under-desk area isn't an eyesore.

For a desk at this price tier, this is embarrassing.

## What I Actually Think After 6 Months

I use the standing function daily. I hit the preset 4-5 times a day. The motor is genuinely good. The frame is fine if you're not a hard typist at full height. Everything else about the desk is average-to-bad.

The $549 sale price is honest value for what you get: a fast, quiet motor on a usable frame. At $749 full retail, you're paying for a name and a subpar cable tray.

**Verdict: Buy it at $549, skip it at $749, and budget an extra $30 for a real cable tray regardless.**

setup: A third-year electrical apprentice is writing an argumentative essay for the union newsletter against a 15% cut to apprenticeship funding.

a.text:
Say No to the 15% Cut

Three years ago, 24 of us started as electrical apprentices in this local. Today, 21 of us finished and are working journeyman jobs. We are not a theory. We are proof this program works.

We started at around $19 an hour. Now we top out around $46 an hour as journeymen. That kind of wage means we get off assistance programs fast and we start paying real taxes. That is good for us and good for the state.

Here is the number taxpayers and legislators need to see: the total public cost to train an apprentice who finishes is about $14,000. Compare that to about $48,000 in public money spent on the average four-year college graduate. We cost less than one-third, and we go straight into jobs that keep the lights on.

A 15% cut to apprenticeship funding breaks a system that already gives the state a great deal. If you cut the funding, you shrink the program. Fewer apprentices means fewer journeymen. That means more people stuck in low-wage jobs or staying on public assistance. It means less tax money coming in and fewer skilled workers to keep projects running. It is a bad deal.

We are electricians, not accountants, but the math is simple. Spend about $14,000 to train someone who earns $46 an hour, pays taxes, and works for decades. Or spend $48,000 on a four-year degree that does not guarantee any of that. The choice is obvious.

I am asking our union brothers and sisters to stand up, and I am asking state legislators to look hard at these numbers before they vote. Do not cut apprenticeship funding by 15%. Invest in it. It works.

b.text:
# A 15% Cut to Apprenticeship Funding Is a Bad Deal for Everyone

Let me lay this out plain. The state wants to cut apprenticeship funding by 15%. I'm a third-year electrical apprentice, and I'm here to tell you that's a mistake. Not because it hurts me personally, but because the numbers don't add up.

Here's what an apprenticeship actually does.

My cohort started with 24 people. Twenty-one of us made it through and are now working journeyman jobs or on our way there. That's not a fluke. That's what a real program with real funding looks like. Nobody handed us anything. We worked full days and went to class on top of it. But the structure was there, and the structure works.

Now let's talk money, because that's what this cut is really about.

An apprentice starts out around $19 an hour. By the time you top out as a journeyman, you're making around $46 an hour. That's not minimum wage. That's a wage you can raise a family on, buy a house on, pay taxes on. And here's the part the legislators should pay attention to: people get off state assistance programs fast when they're earning like that. We stop being a cost to the state and start being a source of revenue. We pay in instead of taking out.

Here's the number that matters most. The total public cost per apprentice who finishes is about $14,000. Compare that to the average public subsidy for a four-year college grad who finishes, which runs around $48,000. So for the price of one college grad, the state can put more than three journeymen to work.

Three skilled workers for the price of one. And these are workers the state actually needs. You can't outsource wiring a building. You can't ship a hospital's electrical system overseas. This work stays here.

So what does a 15% cut actually buy the state? A little bit of savings on paper. What does it cost? Fewer people in one of the cheapest, most effective job programs there is. More people stuck in low-wage work or on assistance. Fewer skilled tradespeople right when we're already short on them.

That's not saving money. That's stepping over dollars to pick up dimes.

I'm not an English professor. I'm an electrician. But I know a bad deal when I see one, and this is a bad deal. Apprenticeships take people with nothing but willingness to work and turn them into skilled, taxpaying professionals for about a third of what college costs the public. That's exactly the kind of thing the state should be putting more money into, not less.

To the legislators reading this: look at the numbers again before you vote. Twenty-one out of twenty-four. Fourteen thousand versus forty-eight. Nineteen dollars to forty-six an hour. Those numbers make the case better than I ever could.

Don't cut what's working.

*— A third-year IBEW electrical apprentice*

setup: A home baker is reviewing the Corlane SM6 mixer for blog readers deciding whether to buy it.

a.text:
# 8 Months with the Corlane SM6: An Honest Look from a Farmers Market Baker

I’ve had the Corlane SM6 on my counter for eight months now, and it hasn’t had an easy life. Prepping for my weekend sourdough drops means this machine gets put to work nearly every single day, often running back-to-back batches of high-hydration loaves and enriched doughs. 

If you’ve been eyeing this mixer and wondering if it justifies the price tag over the standard alternatives, here is the unvarnished reality.

---

### The Powerhouse: Motor Performance
The standout feature of the SM6 is, without question, the motor. 

Most consumer-grade mixers start groaning the second you load them with anything under 60% hydration. To test its limits, I threw a double batch of stiff, 54%-hydration bagel dough at it—a volume that would cause most tilt-head mixers to dance across the counter and overheat. The SM6 didn't stall, shudder, or click. The torque is consistent, the planetary action stays true under resistance, and the machine stays firmly planted on the counter. For raw kneading capability, it completely outclasses the competition in this size category.

---

### The Flaws: Cheap Trim and an Annoying Hook
That raw power comes with two frustrating oversights you need to know before buying:

1. **The Squeaky Lift Lever:** The bowl-lift mechanism has solid lockup, but the internal hinge started shrieking within three weeks. It requires a quick shot of WD-40 roughly once a month to keep it operating smoothly. It’s purely cosmetic/mechanical friction, but on a mixer at this price point, you shouldn't need a lubrication maintenance schedule just to raise the bowl.
2. **The Stock Dough Hook is Too Short:** The bowl is deep, but the factory spiral hook leaves too much clearance at the bottom. With smaller batches (under 800g of flour), the hook simply slaps the top of the dough instead of turning and kneading it against the base. I ended up spending an extra $28 on a third-party, extended spiral hook to make the machine fully functional for single-loaf bakes. 

---

### The Price Tag
The Corlane SM6 retails for **$429**. 

That puts it roughly **$80 higher** than the equivalent bowl-lift KitchenAid model. You are paying a premium almost entirely for the internal drivetrain and motor longevity, because the included attachments and lever finish certainly don't reflect that extra cash.

---

### The Verdict

**Buy it if:** You knead heavy, low-to-medium hydration doughs (sourdough, bagels, sandwich loaves, brioche) on a weekly basis. The motor reliability and torque under load are worth the extra $80 and the aftermarket hook purchase. It is a workhorse built for serious dough.

**Skip it if:** Your baking focuses primarily on cookies, layer cakes, meringues, and the occasional soft no-knead bread. You do not need the excess torque, and you will just be overpaying for a machine with an annoying lift lever and attachments poorly configured for smaller, lighter batters. Stick with a standard mixer instead.

b.text:
# Corlane SM6 Stand Mixer Review: Eight Months of Heavy Dough

I’ve used the Corlane SM6 almost daily for eight months, primarily to make sourdough for my weekend farmers market. It has mixed everything from high-hydration loaves to stiff bagel dough, and its greatest strength is clear: the motor is built for serious kneading.

The SM6 handles a double batch of stiff bagel dough without stalling, slowing down, or sounding strained. That matters more to me than extra attachments or a long list of speed settings. Heavy dough is where many home stand mixers struggle, but the Corlane keeps working through repeated batches without overheating or walking across the counter.

It isn’t flawless. The bowl-lift lever started squeaking, and I now give it a quick spray of WD-40 about once a month. That fixes the noise, but it’s an annoying maintenance chore on a $429 mixer.

The included dough hook is the bigger disappointment. It’s too short for the SM6’s deep bowl, so it doesn’t reach or work smaller amounts of dough effectively. I ended up buying a third-party hook that fits deeper into the bowl. The replacement improved kneading noticeably, but Corlane should include a properly sized hook at this price.

And the price is significant: the SM6 costs $429, about $80 more than the comparable KitchenAid. That premium is difficult to justify for cookies, cake batter, frosting, or occasional bread. A less expensive mixer can handle those jobs perfectly well and may offer a better selection of attachments.

## Verdict

**Buy the Corlane SM6 if you knead heavy dough every week.** Its strong, stall-free motor has earned its place in my near-daily market-baking routine, and I would buy it again for sourdough, bagels, and other demanding doughs.

**Skip it if you mostly make cookies and cakes.** You’ll be paying extra for power you won’t use while still dealing with a squeaky lift lever and an undersized dough hook.

a.text:
## One Week In: 412 Copies and a Movement Patch

I launched my game last week after about three years of working on it during nights and weekends.

The first week ended at 412 copies sold, which is more than I knew how to picture when I started making the game. It’s been surreal seeing people actually play something that spent so long existing mostly on my hard drive.

The game also hit the front page of a small subreddit for around six hours, which brought in a noticeable spike of traffic and a lot of new players. I’m still catching up on some of the comments and messages, but it’s been great seeing people talk about specific levels, mechanics, and weird little details I wasn’t sure anyone would notice.

The most consistent criticism so far has been about the movement. One review described it as feeling floaty, and honestly, they’re right. I’ve been playing it for so long that I had started compensating for it without really noticing, but watching new players move around made the problem much more obvious.

I’m working on a movement update for version 1.1, currently planned for next month. I’m adjusting the acceleration, deceleration, and jump timing to make the controls feel more responsive without changing the overall feel of the game too drastically. I’m still testing different versions, so I don’t want to promise exact changes yet.

For now, I’m going through feedback, fixing the smaller bugs that have come up, and working on the 1.1 patch. Thanks to everyone who bought the game, left a review, sent feedback, or shared it somewhere. The first week has been a lot to process, but I’m glad the game is finally out in the world.

b.text:
Well, it’s finally out. After three years of spending my nights and weekends staring at the editor, my first commercial project actually launched last week. It still feels a little surreal to see it out in the wild.

Here is a quick breakdown of how week one actually went. 

First off, the numbers: the game sold 412 copies in the first week. I also managed to hit the front page of a smaller gaming subreddit for about six hours, which definitely drove a good chunk of that traffic and visibility. For a first game built entirely in my spare time, seeing over four hundred real people pick it up is pretty incredible. Thank you to everyone here who grabbed a copy, played it, and supported the launch.

I've been reading through all the feedback, let's plays, and reviews since release day. One review in particular pointed out that the player movement feels a bit too floaty. Honestly? So, here is what is happening next. I'm already working on patch 1.1, which will be dropping next month. The main priority for this update is overhauling the movement to make it tighter and less floaty, alongside a handful of standard post-launch bug fixes and tweaks. 

That’s where things stand right now. I'm diving back into the code to get 1.1 ready. Thanks again for following along.

setup: A long-haul trucker is writing a short Roadstar DC4 dual dash cam review for other owner-operators on a trucking forum.

a.text:
Roadstar DC4 Dash Cam — 14 Months / 140k Miles

Been running this thing since I got the truck, so figured I owe a real review, not the star-rating fluff.

The good: it does its main job. Caught a four-wheeler doing a dumb lane change into my trailer, and having that footage got my insurance claim approved in 9 days instead of the usual 6-week runaround. That alone paid for the camera about ten times over. Front camera footage is solid day or night, road signs and plates readable, no complaints there.

The not-so-good: rear cam night footage turns to mush past 30 feet. Fine for seeing if someone's tailgating, useless if you need plate detail on something that happened further back. Also had the suction mount pop off twice during summer runs through the desert — heat just cooked the adhesive on it. Switched to the actual adhesive mount and haven't had an issue since, so if you're buying this thing, just skip the suction mount altogether and order the sticky one from the start.

App situation is a mess. It wants wifi to pull footage off the cam remotely, which sounds nice until you realize most truck stops either don't have wifi or it's too weak to move video files. I stopped messing with the app months ago and just pull the SD card straight into my laptop when I need something off it. Faster anyway.

Bottom line: for the price, it's a decent camera that's already proven its worth once when it mattered most. Just know the rear night vision has limits, swap the mount before the heat kills it for you, and don't bother with the app unless you're parked somewhere with real wifi. 140k miles in and it's still running, so durability's not an issue.

3.5/5 — would buy again, but I'm keeping an eye out for something with better rear night vision when this one finally dies.

b.text:
**Roadstar DC4 – 14 Months / ~140k Miles**

I’ve had the Roadstar DC4 mounted for 14 months while putting roughly 140k miles on this rig. Here’s the straight breakdown for any owner-ops considering it.

The headline reason I bought it paid off immediately. A driver rolled through my lane change and clipped my quarter panel. The front cam caught license plate, impact angle, and everything leading up to it. My insurer processed the claim in 9 days instead of the normal 6-week drag. That footage literally paid for the unit ten times over.

Night performance on the rear lens is the weak spot. Past roughly 30 feet, the footage turns noticeably grainy. Fine for daytime traffic, but don’t expect clean plate reads or yard maneuvering shots after dark.

Mounting tip: scrap the suction cup. It popped loose twice during peak summer heat. Switched to the included adhesive pad and it’s been dead quiet since.

Skip the app unless you plan to stay parked next to a strong hotspot. It requires active Wi-Fi to pull footage, which doesn’t exist at most truck stops. I just power down, yank the SD card, and dump clips straight to my laptop. Faster, zero drama.

Bottom line: Reliable crash documentation, handles high-mileage vibration fine, and forces the insurance company’s hand when you need it. Just use the adhesive mount, forget the app, and accept the rear lens isn’t built for deep-night visibility. Works for long-haul reality. Recommended.

setup: A family plumbing company owner is writing a blog post for Minneapolis homeowners about winterizing outdoor pipes.

a.text:
# How to Winterize Your Outdoor Spigots Before the Minneapolis Freeze

If you leave water sitting in your exterior sillcocks when the ground freezes solid in Hennepin County, that copper pipe will split open. You won’t notice it when it happens—you’ll notice it during the first spring thaw when water starts pouring into your finished basement or crawl space.

Here is the exact step-by-step process we tell our customers to follow every October. It takes ten minutes.

---

### Step 1: Disconnect all hoses, splitters, and timers immediately

If you only do one thing on this list, do this. 

Leaving a garden hose connected to an outside spigot is responsible for roughly 80% of the burst-pipe calls we run in January and February. Even if you have a modern "frost-free" spigot, leaving a hose attached traps water inside the barrel of the valve. The water cannot drain out. It freezes, expands, and splits the brass tube wide open inside your wall. 

Unscrew the hose, drain it, roll it up, and put it in the garage. Take off brass splitters and plastic timers, too.

### Step 2: Locate and close the interior shutoff valve

Head into your basement, utility room, or crawl space. Look at the wall roughly where the outdoor faucet sits outside, and follow that copper line inward. 

You’re looking for a shutoff valve. It will usually be either:
* **A round wheel handle (gate valve):** Turn it clockwise until it stops tight.
* **A lever handle (ball valve):** Turn it a quarter-turn so the handle sits perpendicular across the pipe.

### Step 3: Drain the trapped water (Don't skip the bleeder cap)

Turning off the interior valve only stops incoming water; you still have water sitting between the shutoff and the outside spigot. You need to get that water out.

1. **Go outside:** Turn the spigot handle all the way open. Let whatever water is inside run out. Leave this tap open all winter.
2. **Go back inside:** Grab a small bucket or a rag. On the side of your interior shutoff valve, you’ll usually see a tiny brass cap—that’s the bleeder port. Unscrew that cap with a pair of pliers. A cup or two of water will drain out into your bucket. 
3. Once it stops dripping, screw the tiny bleeder cap back on hand-tight.

If you don't open that bleeder cap, an airlock keeps the water trapped in the line, defeating the whole purpose of shutting off the valve.

### Step 4: Install a $3 foam faucet cover

Run down to your local hardware store and buy an insulated foam faucet cover—they usually cost less than five bucks. Hook the rubber loop over the spigot handle and slide the foam dome tight against the exterior siding. 

While this won't save an undrained pipe from twenty below zero, it blocks cold Minneapolis drafts from creeping directly through your foundation rim joist.

---

### What if you don't have an interior shutoff valve?

A lot of older homes in Minneapolis—especially in South Minneapolis, Northeast, and older parts of St. Paul—never had dedicated interior shutoff valves installed for the hose bibbs. Or, the old gate valve is corroded and won't turn without snapping.

If you can't find an interior shutoff, **give us a call.** We can get out to your house quickly, sweat in a reliable quarter-turn ball valve with a bleeder, or upgrade you to a true commercial frost-free hydrant before the hard freeze sets in. It costs far less to install a shutoff today than it does to remediate water damage in mid-winter.

b.text:
How to Winterize Your Outside Spigots

If you haven’t winterized your outdoor spigots yet, do it this weekend. This is the 20-minute job that prevents most of our January emergency calls.

The big mistake we see every cold snap in Minneapolis is hoses left connected. A hose traps water against the spigot and pipe. When that water freezes, it expands back into the wall and splits the pipe. That’s most of our January burst-pipe calls.

Here’s the order we do it on our own houses:

1. Shut off the interior valve. Find the shutoff for each outdoor spigot—usually in the basement or crawl space near where the pipe exits the house. Turn it all the way off. If you can’t find one, stop and call us.

2. Drain the spigot. Go outside, open the spigot all the way, and let the water run out. Leave it open for a minute so the line drains back.

3. Disconnect the hose. Unscrew every hose, drain it, and store it in the garage or shed. This is the step that saves the pipe.

4. Cover the spigot. Put on a $3 foam spigot cover. Pull the string tight so the wind doesn’t carry it away. That’s all you need.

Even if your spigot is “frost-free,” still follow these steps. A frost-free spigot can’t do its job if a hose is attached or the interior valve isn’t shut off.

If your house doesn’t have an interior shutoff valve, don’t guess. Call us and we’ll either install one or winterize the line properly. It’s a small job compared to a burst pipe in January.

setup: A small coffee shop owner is writing testimony to city council opposing a parking meter rate increase.

a.text:
**Testimony on the Proposed Downtown Parking Meter Rate Increase**

Members of the City Council,

My name is [Name] and I am the owner of [Shop Name], an independent coffee shop on Main Street. I am here today to ask the council to vote no on the proposed parking meter rate increase from fifty cents to one dollar and fifty cents per hour.

That is a 200% rate increase, and I want to share three specific pieces of evidence with you about what it will mean for downtown businesses.

**First, I have direct observational data.** In 2019, when a comparable parking rate increase was implemented in the neighboring downtown, I tracked my own register for six weeks. Foot traffic dropped 18%. That was not a seasonal dip and it was not a coincidence. It was a direct, measurable response to parking becoming more expensive at a magnitude similar to what you are considering tonight.

**Second, the proposed rate is not calibrated to how people actually use downtown businesses.** My customers average a 22-minute visit. The current one-hour minimum at fifty cents already covers their stay with time to spare. Under the proposed rate, that same 22-minute visit costs one dollar and fifty cents instead of fifty cents — a one-dollar increase per customer for the exact same transaction. This is not a marginal adjustment. It is a threefold increase in the cost of an ordinary visit to a Main Street business.

**Third, the city's own financial data undermines the premise of this proposal.** According to the city's own report, meter revenue currently covers approximately 4% of the downtown budget. Even in the most optimistic scenario, in which the new rate triples that figure with no reduction in demand — which the evidence I just cited tells us will not happen — meter revenue would still cover only about 12% of the budget. You would be asking downtown businesses and their customers to absorb a 200% rate hike to close a small fraction of a gap that this measure cannot realistically close on its own.

I want to be clear about what an 18% drop in foot traffic means in practice. It does not just mean fewer customers at my coffee shop. It means fewer customers at every business on Main Street — the bookstore, the diner, the boutique down the block. When a customer decides the meter is not worth it, they do not skip one stop. They skip the trip.

I am not here to tell the council how to balance its budget. I am here to tell you that this proposal, at this magnitude, will produce real and measurable harm to the small businesses that anchor this district, in exchange for a budgetary gain that even your own report shows is modest. The math does not justify it.

I respectfully urge the council to reject the proposed rate increase and to work with the downtown business community on solutions that do not place the entire burden on the customers and independent businesses who keep this district alive.

Thank you for your time.

---

Respectfully submitted,

[Name]
[Shop Name]
[Address]
[Phone / Email]

My name is [Your Name], and I have owned [Coffee Shop Name] on Main Street for [number] years. I am submitting this testimony in opposition to the proposed parking meter rate increase from 50 cents to $1.50 per hour.

I understand the city faces budget pressures, but I believe this rate increase will harm downtown businesses without meaningfully addressing the city's financial needs. I want to present three specific concerns based on data I have gathered and reviewed.

First, I have direct evidence of how parking rate increases affect foot traffic in similar markets. In 2019, the neighboring municipality implemented a comparable parking rate increase. I tracked my sales register data for six weeks before and after that increase. The result was an 18 percent decline in customer visits during that period. My customers are not commuters or all-day parkers—they are coffee drinkers. My data shows the average customer visit is 22 minutes. The current one-hour minimum already covers their parking needs with time to spare. A tripling of the hourly rate will discourage these short-visit customers from coming downtown at all.

Second, I want to address whether this increase actually solves the city's budget problem. Even if this rate increase generates additional revenue, the math is clear: parking meters are not and cannot be the solution to downtown funding gaps. We would be creating a genuine hardship for local businesses and their customers in exchange for addressing perhaps 4 or 5 percent of a much larger problem.

I urge the city council to explore alternative revenue sources that do not penalize people for shopping and dining downtown. Our small businesses depend on accessible, affordable parking to survive.

setup: A home baker is reviewing the Corlane SM6 mixer for blog readers deciding whether to buy it.

a.text:
# 8 Months with the Corlane SM6 Stand Mixer: A Market Baker's Honest Review

I’ve put the Corlane SM6 through absolute hell over the last eight months. Prepping for my weekend sourdough stall at the farmers market means this machine doesn't sit on my counter looking pretty—it runs almost daily, kneading dense, high-volume bread doughs back-to-back. 

If you're on the fence about dropping serious cash on this machine, here is my raw, long-term breakdown of how it actually performs in a heavy-baking kitchen.

### The Powerhouse Motor
The motor on the SM6 is an unyielding beast. Most consumer mixers start to smell like hot metal and strain the moment you feed them dense dough. Last month, I loaded this machine with a double batch of stiff bagel dough—the kind of low-hydration, stubborn mix that makes standard planetary mixers sound like a dying lawnmower. The Corlane didn't even drop RPMs. No stalling, no grinding gears, and no overheating. For pure torque and heavy-duty kneading capacity, it is unmatched in its class.

### The Annoyances
For all its brute strength, the SM6 has two glaring design flaws that drive me crazy:

1. **The Squeaky Lever:** The bowl-lift mechanism started screeching about three weeks after I unboxed it. I now have to hit the lever joint with a squirt of food-grade lubricant or WD-40 once a month just to keep it raising and lowering smoothly. 
2. **The Terrible Stock Dough Hook:** The included dough hook is simply too short for the deep mixing bowl. On your first mix, you'll notice a stubborn dead zone of unmixed dry flour trapped at the very bottom. I got so tired of stopping the machine to scrape it down that I bought a longer, third-party spiral dough hook online. That solved the issue completely, but you shouldn't have to buy aftermarket parts just to make a brand-new mixer function properly.

### Price & Value
At **$429**, the Corlane SM6 sits $80 higher than its equivalent KitchenAid competitor. Once you factor in the $20–$30 you’ll inevitably spend on a proper replacement dough hook, you're looking at a $450 total investment. 

### The Final Verdict

* **BUY IT** if you knead heavy sourdough, bagels, or stiff rye doughs on a weekly basis. The sheer strength of the motor justifies the higher price point and the minor annoyance of replacing the stock hook. It will survive workload demands that would burn out cheaper machines.
* **SKIP IT** if your baking routine leans heavily toward cookies, quick breads, sponge cakes, and lighter batters. You do not need this much torque for creamed butter and sugar, and the $80 premium is better spent elsewhere in your kitchen.

b.text:
# Corlane SM6, Eight Months In: What Nobody Tells You Before You Spend $429

I bought this mixer last spring, right after a bagel order nearly killed my old machine. Since then it's run almost every day — four to six market batches a week, plus whatever I'm testing midweek. That's enough hours on it to say something useful, so here it is.

## The motor is the reason to buy this thing

I'll start where it counts. A double batch of stiff bagel dough — the kind that comes out at maybe 55% hydration and looks more like modeling clay than dough — does not faze it. No stalling, no smell of hot motor, no slowing down in the last two minutes when the gluten really tightens up and lesser machines start begging. It just grinds through. I've done back-to-back doubles on a Saturday morning with no cooldown break and never had the machine complain.

If you've ever stood over a mixer with your hand on the switch, ready to shut it off before something expensive breaks, you know exactly what that's worth. I don't do that anymore. That's the whole review in one sentence, honestly.

## The bowl lift lever squeaks, and it will keep squeaking

Somewhere around month two, the bowl lift lever developed a squeak. Not a subtle one — an actual metallic shriek when I raise the bowl. A shot of WD40 on the pivot fixes it for about four weeks, then it comes back. So now it's a monthly chore, right alongside descaling the kettle.

Is it a dealbreaker? No. Is it annoying on a $429 machine? Yes. It reads like a lubrication or tolerance issue in the lift assembly, and I'd expect better at this price. Budget thirty seconds a month for it and move on.

## The included dough hook is too short. Buy a third-party one immediately.

This is my real complaint. The bowl is deep — which is great, it's part of why you can run a double batch — but the stock dough hook doesn't reach far enough down to work the bottom of it. You end up with a stubborn cuff of unincorporated flour and shaggy dough sitting under the hook, and you're scraping it up by hand halfway through every mix.

I put up with it for about six weeks before ordering an extended spiral hook from a third-party seller. Around $30. Problem completely solved, and the mixing got noticeably better on top of it — real gluten development without me intervening. Corlane should ship this hook in the box. They don't. Factor the $30 into your math and order it the same day you order the mixer, because you're going to want it.

## About that $80

The comparable KitchenAid is about $349. So you're paying $80 more, plus $30 for a hook that should have been included, which makes the real gap $110.

That $110 buys you a motor that doesn't flinch at heavy dough. That's it. That's the entire value proposition. It doesn't buy you better fit and finish, it doesn't buy you a quieter lift mechanism, and it doesn't buy you better accessories.

## The verdict

**Buy it if you knead heavy dough every week.** Bagels, bread, pizza, pretzels, anything stiff and anything in volume — this machine will outlast the KitchenAid doing that work, and $110 is cheap compared to replacing a burned-out motor in year two. For market bakers and serious bread people, it's the right call. I'd buy it again.

**Skip it if you're mostly making cookies, cakes, and batters.** You will never touch the top of this motor's capability, and you'll be paying $110 for headroom you don't use — while putting up with a squeaky lever and a hook you have to replace. Buy the KitchenAid, spend the difference on flour.

The line is genuinely that simple. Heavy dough weekly: yes. Everything else: no.

setup: A bakery owner is writing a warm blog and newsletter post to regular customers explaining why wedding cake orders are ending.

a.text:
I’ve been trying to figure out how to write this for a little while, mostly because I don’t want it to sound like a complaint, and I really don’t want it to sound like we’re closing a door on people we care about. But I also think it’s important to say things plainly when we make a change, especially with the people who support us every week.

So here it is: we’re not taking custom wedding cake orders anymore.

I know that might be disappointing to some of you, especially if you’ve been dreaming about what you’d want for your own day, or if you were hoping to ask us someday. Please know that this decision didn’t come from a place of frustration with weddings, or with celebrating love, or with the people who come to us during one of the biggest seasons of their lives. We have loved being part of those moments. But over time, we’ve had to face the fact that custom wedding cakes were becoming harder and harder for a bakery our size to carry without pulling us away from the things that keep us open.

We are a very small team. There are three of us, and most mornings I’m here baking by 4am, trying to get the case ready before the doors open. When we take on a custom wedding cake, it isn’t just the baking. There are emails back and forth, phone calls, design conversations, tastings, scheduling, revisions, pricing, and a lot of thinking that happens outside the kitchen. When I sat down and actually added it up, each custom wedding order was asking for around fourteen hours of consultation and tasting time before we ever got to the cake itself. That’s time we were giving freely, and it was becoming more than we could realistically absorb.

That part alone might have been manageable once in a while. But this year we also had three last-minute cancellations, and when that happens, it doesn’t just mean an empty date on the calendar. It means ingredients already bought, time already set aside, and plans already built around a cake that no longer needs to exist. I understand that life happens. Plans change. Families shift. Nobody cancels a wedding lightly. But for a shop like ours, those losses hit hard, and they made it clear that we needed to stop stretching ourselves into places we couldn’t afford to stretch anymore.

The hardest truth, and maybe the simplest one, is that the everyday case is what keeps this bakery alive. It’s the croissants, the loaf cakes, the cookies, the morning buns, the little birthday cakes, the treats people grab on the way to work, the things you pick up because you’re having people over and want to bring something nice. That’s what pays the rent. That’s what keeps our lights on and our oven warm and our little team able to show up every day. When wedding orders started taking more and more of our time, energy, and ingredients, we started feeling the strain in the daily work that actually sustains us.

I don’t say that to make anyone feel bad. I say it because I think small businesses sometimes try to make everything look effortless, and I don’t want to do that anymore. I want to be honest with you. If we keep saying yes to things that quietly drain us, we risk losing the part of the bakery that most of you know and love. And I don’t want that. I want to still be here, baking in the early morning, making the things that make this place feel like home.

There’s also something about the daily rhythm of the bakery that I’ve come to appreciate more and more. There’s a kind of quiet joy in making things that don’t require months of planning. A cake someone sees in the case and takes home that afternoon. A pastry that makes someone’s Tuesday a little better. A loaf of bread for dinner. Those things matter to me. They’re the heart of what we do.

If you’re getting married, or if you know someone who is, I hope you find a baker who can give your cake the time and attention it deserves. I hope your day is full of people who love you and details that feel like you. I hope you get a cake that makes you happy. I truly mean that. This isn’t us stepping away from celebration. It’s us choosing a shape of work that we can keep doing well, without burning out or losing the thing that makes this bakery ours.

And if you’ve ordered a wedding cake from us in the past, thank you. Thank you for trusting us with something so meaningful. Thank you for letting us be a small part of your story. That means more than you know.

For now, I’ll be here early in the mornings, doing what I always do: mixing, baking, trying to get everything ready before the first hello of the day. And I hope you’ll still stop by, say hi, and pick out something good from the case. That everyday rhythm is what keeps us going, and we’re grateful for every single person who is part of it.

b.text:
Okay, so this is one I've been putting off writing because I really have loved being a tiny, flour-dusted part of your weddings.

We’re not going to be taking custom wedding cakes anymore. At least not for a while, maybe not for a long while.

There are only three of us here, and most days I’m in at 4am to get the ovens going. I sat down last week and actually added up what a wedding cake takes, and between the emails and the consults and the tasting boxes I make up for free, it’s about 14 hours before I even turn the mixer on for the real cake. I love that part, I do, sitting with you and sketching and tasting frostings, but when there are only three of us it turns into a whole second full-time job.

And honestly this year was just hard. We had three weddings cancel pretty last-minute after we’d already bought and prepped everything for them. I get it completely, plans change and life happens, but as a little shop we just ate all of that cost and we don’t have any wiggle room to do that.

The biggest thing though is I noticed I was spending so much time in the back on wedding stuff that I wasn’t paying attention to the front case. And that case — the morning buns and the croissants and the chocolate chip cookies that you come in for on a Tuesday — that’s what actually pays our rent. That’s our day to day, and I want to be good at that again.

It’s been such an honor to do what we’ve done. Thank you if you trusted us with your wedding, really.

We’ll still be here at 7am with coffee and everything in the case, and we’re still doing little birthday cakes and everyday stuff. Just not the big custom wedding ones.

Come say hi this week, okay?

setup: A fourth-generation soybean and corn farmer is writing a newsletter commentary on crop insurance costs and SB 214 for county readers and state legislators.

a.text:
By the time the late May final planting date came and went, my planter had only touched 60 percent of our ground. The rest was sitting under standing water, rutted out by weeks of unrelenting rain. For a fourth-generation corn and soybean operation, taking prevented planting is never the goal—it’s the absolute last resort to keep the lights on. 

What made a brutal spring worse was the bill that followed. 

This year, the USDA raised the base premium rate on prevented planting coverage in our region by 22 percent. On our farm alone, that adjustment translates to roughly $46,000 in additional, unexpected costs. That is $46,000 paid out on ground that won't produce a single bushel to help offset the expense.

If that hike fell evenly across agriculture, it would still be a hard pill to swallow. But because of the way prevented planting acreage caps are calculated, it hits independent family farms far harder than the massive, multi-county operations down the road. 

Large corporate outfits running tens of thousands of acres have the scale and diversified footprint to absorb and dilute these rate spikes across multiple units. Family operations like mine—where our ground is concentrated in this county—don't have that luxury. Under the current cap formulas, when localized weather drowns out half a township, the family farmer pays a higher proportional penalty per acre than the mega-operation that can offset those drowned acres against dry ones two counties away. The math simply works against the smaller guy.

We are not asking for a handout. We pay our premiums and we take the risks. But the safety net should not punish family-scale agriculture for existing.

Senate Bill 214 directly addresses this flaw by restructuring the acreage cap calculations to ensure rate hikes and risk determinations are applied equitably, rather than landing heaviest on independent operators. It fixes an outdated formula and levels the playing field before another season gets washed out.

Our state lawmakers need to understand that policies designed in a vacuum have real dollar consequences in our fields. I urge every Farm Bureau member reading this to call your state senator and representative this week. Tell them what the 22 percent hike is costing your balance sheet, and tell them to vote "yes" on SB 214. We can’t control the rain in May, but we can fix the rules that govern the aftermath.

b.text:
Sixty percent. That was the final tally on my planter’s monitor when the late May final planting date came and went. Four out of every ten acres I farm sat empty, drowned out by six straight weeks of unrelenting rain. 

That loss hurts on its own, but the real blow arrived in the mail with the crop insurance statement. This year, the USDA hit our region with a 22 percent hike on the prevented planting base premium rate. On my operation alone, that rate jump amounts to roughly $46,000 in additional out-of-pocket premium costs—cash paid on ground that won't yield a single bushel of corn or beans to offset the expense.

A $46,000 hit might be absorbed as a rounding error by institutional outfits running tens of thousands of acres across three states. But on a fourth-generation family farm, it cuts right into our operating capital for next season. 

Worse still is how the current acreage cap framework interacts with this increase. The flat limits and tiers currently in place mean that once a family-sized operation hits certain acreage thresholds, the proportion of covered ground that bears the full brunt of these hikes spikes dramatically. The mega-operations down the road have the acreage volume and entity structuring to dilute those caps and absorb the hit. Family operations our size land squarely in the crosshairs: large enough to carry massive weather exposure, but not large enough to game the caps. We end up paying significantly more per eligible acre proportionally than the biggest operators in the county.

We cannot control the rain, but our lawmakers can control the rules that determine whether an independent farm survives it. 

Senate Bill 214 is designed to fix this specific failure. It recalibrates the acreage cap structure to reflect actual operational scale, ensuring that family farms are not paying a disproportionate penalty simply for being caught between small-scale exemptions and corporate-scale loopholes.

setup: A general contractor is writing a short X thread to contractors, homeowners, and architects about a hidden joist problem and the lesson learned.

a.text:
Pulled up the kitchen subfloor on the Maple Ave job yesterday and found two joists notched almost halfway through their depth. Someone ran a drain line through them 20+ years ago and just hogged out whatever they needed. Floor had a noticeable bounce right over it.

Notch that deep in the middle third of a joist is basically cutting its strength in half. You're allowed a notch, but there are rules about depth and location for a reason. Whoever did this either didn't know or didn't care.

Fix was sistering both joists full length and rerouting the drain properly. Added about $1,400 and a day and a half to the schedule the client wasn't planning on.

The lesson: that bounce in your floor is rarely "just how old houses feel." It's usually something structural someone hid behind finishes. Open it up before you tile over it, not after.

b.text:
1/
On the Maple Ave kitchen last month, we opened the ceiling to run new electrical and found the original 2x8 joists had been notched almost halfway through to clear a 3" PVC waste line. House is 1923, long span over the kitchen (~16'), and the drywall had been cracking along the seams for years. Previous owners just kept patching it.

2/
Joists were 2x8 spanning ~16' with that bad a notch midspan. Deflection was obvious — you could see the sag in the ceiling. Brought in an engineer ($650) who spec'd sistering two joists full length and adding a flush LVL under the worst one. Kept the ceiling flat and didn't require dropping the whole kitchen.

3/
Total hit: about $4,200 including the engineer, the LVL, and a day and a half of crew time. Added roughly a week to the schedule. Homeowners were good about it — I'd already flagged it in a change order before they ever saw the damage — but it's the kind of thing that eats your margin if you miss it.

4/
Lesson: on any older home with a long-span kitchen, I cut at least one access hole before I quote. Joist notches from previous plumbing or HVAC work are the rule, not the exception. Fifteen minutes with a flashlight beats a $4k surprise every time.

setup: A long-haul trucker is writing a short Roadstar DC4 dual dash cam review for other owner-operators on a trucking forum.

a.text:
**RoadStar DC4 Dash Cam – 14 Months, 140K Miles In**

Got this thing installed right when I bought my current rig. Front cam is solid – daytime footage is sharp enough to read plates clear as day, and it held up through everything from desert heat to mountain snow. No issues there.

The rear cam is where things get mixed. Daytime is fine. Nighttime? Anything past 30 feet starts getting grainy and you lose detail. Fine if you're documenting a close call, not fine if someone tags you from two car lengths back.

The accident test is the big one though. Some yahoo merged into my lane near Amarillo last spring. Hit the camera, pulled the footage, insurance had my claim approved in 9 days. Every other claim I've ever filed took 6 weeks minimum. That's the whole reason most of us run these things, and on that front it delivered.

Mounting was my only real complaint. The suction cup fell off twice in summer heat – once on I-10 in Arizona, once in a Walmart parking lot in Georgia. Switched to the adhesive mount and haven't had a problem since. If you run hot routes, skip the suction cup entirely.

The app needs WiFi to pull footage, which is pointless at 95% of truck stops. I just pull the SD card and dump it to my laptop. Not a dealbreaker, but they should fix that.

Bottom line: front cam is great, rear cam is decent but not great at night, and the insurance payoff alone justifies the price. If you're on the fence, get one. Just buy the adhesive mount upfront and skip the headache.

Rating: 4/5. Would buy again.

b.text:
**Roadstar DC4 dash cam — 14 months, ~140k miles**

Couple of you asked about this one, so here's where it stands after 14 months and about 140k miles on my current rig.

The important part first: it already paid for itself. Got hit in a lane change accident and the DC4 caught the whole thing clean. Insurance claim went through in 9 days instead of the usual 6 weeks. If you've ever sat around waiting on an adjuster, you know what that's worth. If you're on the fence about running a cam at all, that's the whole argument.

Now the gripes.

Rear cam night footage gets grainy past about 30 feet. Daytime is fine and the front cam does okay in the dark, but don't expect to read a plate off the rear at night unless a four-wheeler's right on your bumper.

The suction mount doesn't survive summer heat. Mine let go twice before I wised up and switched to the adhesive mount. Hasn't budged since. Skip the suction mount and go straight to adhesive.

The app needs wifi to pull footage, which makes it useless at most truck stops. I just pop the SD card and transfer straight to my laptop. Works fine, but know going in that the app is mostly an ornament.

Bottom line: it's held up through a year of vibration, heat, cold, and everything else we throw at these trucks, and the footage is good enough to settle a claim in 9 days. Mount it with the adhesive, ignore the app, and it's a solid buy.

There is a public forum on July 28 at the Grange Hall, and the USPS district manager is going to be there. I am asking everyone in Kettle Falls to show up. We need to pack the room and tell them face-to-face what closing this counter will actually do to our town.

setup: A solo SaaS founder is posting a thread to indie hackers and customers about a pricing mistake and the fix.

a.text:
1/ I raised prices 40% on every Tallyup customer overnight. Lost 30 of 140 in a week. Here's what happened and what I changed.

2/ Tallyup had been priced at the same number since launch. I was undercharging and everyone knew it, including me. So I pulled the trigger. Sent an email, updated the pricing page, done.

3/ The problem wasn't the increase. The problem was how I did it. No warning. No tiers. No grace period. Just "your price goes up next billing cycle." People don't love that.

4/ 30 customers cancelled in the first week. Some sent nice emails. Most just left. A few were gym owners who'd been with me since the beginning, which stung.

5/ What I changed:

- Grandfathered existing customers at old pricing for 6 months
- Added a middle tier instead of forcing everyone to the top
- Gave 30 days notice before any future changes
- Emailed the 30 who left and offered the old price to come back

6/ A few came back. Most didn't, and that's fair. The revenue still worked out because the new price is sustainable, but I burned trust I didn't need to burn.

7/ Lesson: raising prices is fine. Surprising people with it isn't. The 6 months of runway would've cost me less than losing 30 customers and whatever goodwill came with them. Building in public means owning the mistakes too. This one's mine.

b.text:
Here's a thread on the pricing mistake and what I changed 🧵

1/ Six months ago I raised Tallyup's prices 40% overnight. On everyone. No grandfathering, no warning emails, just flipped the switch on a Tuesday morning. Here's what happened: we lost 30 of our 140 customers in a week. ~21% churn, out of nowhere.

2/ The reasoning at the time felt solid. MRR was flat, I figured the product was underpriced, and I'd read enough "raise your prices" posts to think I was leaving money on the table. I was solving my boredom, not a real customer problem.

3/ What I missed: my customers are gym owners running small facilities. They don't have procurement budgets. A 40% jump in a line item they'd been paying for a year feels like a billing error before it feels like a value conversation. Most of the 30 who left didn't even email. Just canceled.

4/ First thing I changed: rolled back pricing for anyone who stayed. Sent a personal email, no template, explaining the jump was a mistake and their old price was locked in for 12 months. Kept 22 of the remaining 110 that way. The other 8 churned within the month anyway.

5/ Second change: any future price increase is on new customers only, for at least 6 months before existing customers see it. And existing customers get 30 days notice with a real explanation, not a Stripe receipt. Announcements > assumptions.

6/ Third change: I started charging new signups the new price and tracking conversion rate weekly instead of just MRR. Conversion dropped ~15% the first month, which told me the new price was probably 10-15% too high, not 40%. I'd been anchoring to the wrong number.

7/ What I'd tell other solo founders: your existing customers are your cheapest source of validated pricing. If you raise on them and a chunk leave instantly, the market just told you something your spreadsheet didn't. Listen to it before you keep raising.

8/ Tallyup today: ~115 customers, MRR is higher than it was at 140 because new signups come in at the new price, but the lesson wasn't "raise prices." It was "raise prices the way your customers can actually absorb them." Wild concept, I know.

(end 🧵)
