setup: A high-school senior is writing a personal essay for college admissions readers about working at her family's Vietnamese restaurant.

a.text:
The register died at 11:40 on a Saturday in October, right as the lunch line started bending toward the door. My mom tapped the screen twice, then harder, the way you pat a flashlight before you admit the batteries are gone. I did my own math: four tables waiting to pay, six people in line, one of me.

Under the counter we kept an old order pad with the carbon sheet still in it, left over from before my parents bought the system. Nobody remembered why we kept it. I grabbed it and a pen and went to work.

I've rung in the number 7 — grilled pork over vermicelli — more times than I've done just about anything else in my life, homework included. Three years of weekends will do that. So I didn't need the screen. I wrote tickets in abbreviations I made up on the spot, table number big in the corner, tax figured on my phone while the next person ordered. My mom read my handwriting through the pass without once asking what anything meant, which should tell you how long the two of us have been doing this. Around one, a man watched me total his check and said I was faster than the machine. I didn't tell him the machine never has to explain the difference between the fried rolls and the fresh ones.

By two the rush was done, my hand ached, and there were fifty-some tickets stabbed on the spindle by the fryer. The repair guy fixed the register that week. My mom kept the tickets until the books were done, and then I took a handful home for scratch paper. Which is how my AP Calculus homework ended up on the back of an order for two number 9s, no cilantro, extra lime.

Spring rolls are where we start every new hire, because it's the one job you can't mess up in a way that costs money — except the new kid kept doing exactly that. His rolls opened in the fryer one after another, and he stood there fishing out the wrappers like it was the oil's fault.

I showed him my grandma's fold. One pass through warm water, not a soak. Wrapper flat, filling low, bottom edge up and over, corners in, then roll. Tighter than you think — that's the whole secret, and it's the part nobody believes. My grandma taught me when I was eleven, standing on a milk crate so my hands cleared the counter. She didn't explain anything. She just undid my roll and did hers again until mine looked right.

"Tighter than you think," I told the new kid, and his next six held. My grandma fried up his early ones anyway and we ate them at staff meal, because nothing in that kitchen gets thrown out. She didn't comment on me teaching him. She nodded once, which from her is a speech.

We don't have a break room. We have a folding chair by the water heater that nobody wants, so on my twenty minutes I go to the walk-in. It's the quietest place in the building, and the cold keeps me awake. I prop the door with a #10 can, sit on a milk crate, and work problems on the backs of the October tickets. They still smell faintly like the fryer. Related rates is mostly ladders sliding down walls, which is not a situation that comes up much in a restaurant, where everything is bolted down. By the last problem my handwriting has gone shaky from the cold, same as a ticket at the end of a rush.

On Saturday the new kid opened the door and found me in there. He didn't say anything about the calculus. "Break's over," he said.

I had four problems left. I told him I'd finish them tomorrow, same crate, same can holding the door.

b.text:
On Saturdays the restaurant opens at eleven, but we get there at nine. My dad unlocks the back door and the first thing you smell is the fish sauce from the night before, and then the rice cooker starts and it smells like our house.

The register died on a Saturday in October. Not a slow reboot, not a frozen screen—dead, the little lights gone. My mom kept pressing the power button like it was a person she could wake up. So I got a pad of paper and started writing tickets by hand. Table four, two vermicelli bowls, one with extra pork, no peanuts. Table six wanted the pho with tendon, and I had to remember it wasn't on the paper receipt because there was no receipt, just my handwriting getting worse as it got busier. I did the math for everyone's change in my head. I got one order wrong all day, a spring roll count, and my dad only found out because I told him. The system came back around three. By then I didn't need it.

We hire people sometimes and they don't last. There's a lot to remember and the kitchen gets hot. In the spring we hired a guy named Danh who was maybe nineteen and he could cook but he couldn't fold a spring roll right. My grandma folds them a specific way, tight, so they don't come apart in the oil. She showed me when I was little and now I showed him. You lay the wrapper like a diamond, filling near the bottom, fold up once, fold the sides in, then roll and seal the edge with water. Danh's first ten fell apart. His eleventh held. I didn't tell my grandma I taught him because she likes to think only she can do it, and honestly she does it better, but his are fine now.

I do my homework in the walk-in cooler. This sounds worse than it is. The dining room is loud and there's nowhere to sit, but the cooler has a shelf at the right height and it's quiet in there with the boxes of vegetables and the sound of the fan. I did most of my calculus in the cooler this year. Related rates, integrals, all of it, sitting on a milk crate with my jacket on. My mom would open the door to grab lemongrass and see me and say don't stay too long, you'll get sick. I never got sick. I got a lot of problem sets done.

That's most of my Saturdays. I'll probably work them until I leave for school, and then my parents will figure something out, or they won't and it'll be harder for them, which I think about. I'm not going to pretend the restaurant taught me some big thing. It's just where I've been every weekend since tenth grade. I know how to run a register with no register. I know how my grandma folds a spring roll. I can do calculus at forty degrees. These are the things I know.

setup: A small coffee shop owner is writing testimony to city council opposing a parking meter rate increase.

a.text:
Members of the City Council,

My name is [Name], and I own a small independent coffee shop on Main Street. I am writing to oppose the proposed increase in downtown parking meter rates from 50 cents to $1.50 per hour.

This proposal would triple the hourly rate—a 200% increase—for customers who come downtown to shop, eat, and support local businesses. For a small business like mine, that increase matters. Customers do not experience parking costs as an isolated fee; they add it to the cost of every coffee, meal, or purchase they make downtown. Even a modest increase can influence whether someone chooses to visit Main Street, how long they stay, or whether they go somewhere with free parking instead.

I have firsthand evidence of how a similar increase affected downtown activity. In 2019, after the town next door raised its parking rates, I tracked my register and customer activity for six weeks. During that period, I observed an 18% drop in foot traffic. I recognize that this tracking does not prove that the parking increase alone caused every bit of that decline, but the timing and scale of the change are concerning. An 18% reduction in customers is significant for any small business operating on narrow margins.

The proposed increase also does not appear to match how long most of my customers actually visit. Their average visit is approximately 22 minutes. Under the current system, the one-hour minimum already covers that typical visit. Raising the rate from 50 cents to $1.50 would therefore triple the cost for customers whose parking needs have not changed. They would pay substantially more without receiving additional parking time or a meaningful improvement in their experience.

Most importantly, the city’s own report indicates that meter revenue covers only 4% of the downtown budget. That figure suggests this increase will not solve the city’s broader financial challenges. Even if the rate increase produces additional revenue, it will address only a very small portion of the downtown budget while placing a disproportionate burden on the local businesses and customers who rely on downtown activity.

I understand that the city must manage its budget and parking system responsibly. However, a policy that triples parking costs, risks reducing foot traffic by a measurable amount, and contributes to only 4% of the downtown budget deserves careful reconsideration. The city should evaluate alternatives that support revenue needs without making Main Street less accessible and less attractive to customers.

I respectfully ask the Council to reject the increase from 50 cents to $1.50 per hour, or at minimum to delay it and conduct a more complete analysis of its likely effect on downtown businesses, customer visits, and overall revenue. Our downtown businesses are part of the city’s economic foundation. Policies intended to strengthen downtown should not make it harder for customers to visit and for small businesses to remain open.

Thank you for considering my testimony.

b.text:
Dear Members of the City Council,

My name is [Name], and I own a small independent coffee shop on Main Street. I am writing in opposition to the proposed increase in downtown parking meter rates from 50 cents per hour to $1.50 per hour.

This proposal would triple the cost of parking downtown. For many people, that may sound like a small difference—an additional dollar—but for a downtown business district that depends on frequent, short visits, price changes like this affect customer behavior quickly.

I have seen this firsthand. In 2019, when a nearby town implemented a similar parking-rate increase, I tracked my own register and customer traffic for six weeks afterward. During that period, foot traffic dropped by 18 percent. An 18 percent decline is not an abstract concern for a small business. It means fewer coffees sold, fewer breakfast orders, fewer customers browsing neighboring stores, and less activity on the sidewalk throughout the day.

My customers do not generally occupy parking spaces for hours. Based on my own observations and customer patterns, the average visit to my shop is approximately 22 minutes. The current one-hour minimum already gives customers far more time than they typically need to park, order, meet someone briefly, or take a drink to go. Raising the hourly rate from 50 cents to $1.50 does not encourage better turnover for these customers; it simply triples the price they pay for a short visit.

For a customer stopping in for 22 minutes, the effective cost of parking would become $1.50 under the proposed minimum, rather than 50 cents today. That is a significant added cost alongside a cup of coffee or a small breakfast purchase. It gives customers one more reason to choose a drive-through, a shopping center with free parking, or a business outside downtown.

I also ask the Council to consider the city’s own financial analysis. According to the city report, meter revenue covers only 4 percent of the downtown budget. Even if meter revenue increased, this proposal would not solve the larger budget challenge. What it could do, however, is place a disproportionate burden on the independent businesses that make downtown worth visiting in the first place.

Downtown is not sustained by parking meters alone. It is sustained by repeat customers, employees, residents, visitors, and small business owners who depend on accessible and reasonably priced parking. A policy that results in fewer short visits risks reducing sales-tax activity, weakening storefronts, and making the district less competitive with areas where parking is free.

I respectfully urge the Council not to approve a tripling of meter rates from 50 cents to $1.50 per hour. The evidence from my own six-week tracking period after a similar increase in 2019—a drop of 18 percent in foot traffic—shows the potential effect on customer activity. With an average customer visit of only 22 minutes and meter revenue accounting for just 4 percent of the downtown budget, this increase asks too much of downtown customers and small businesses while doing too little to address the city’s financial needs.

Thank you for your consideration.

setup: A small HVAC company owner is writing a how-to for homeowners on bleeding air from hot water baseboard radiators before winter.

a.text:
1. **Turn off the boiler and circulator, and let the system cool.**  
   Turn the thermostats down, then shut off the heating system at its service switch. Don’t bleed baseboards while the boiler is hot or the circulator is running—hot water can cause serious burns.

2. **Find the bleeder valve on the first baseboard.**  
   Start with the unit closest to the boiler, then work outward through each heating loop. Look near the end of the baseboard for a small manual bleeder valve. You may need to remove an end cover to reach it.

   These steps are for **hot-water baseboards with individual bleeder valves**, not electric baseboard heaters. Some hot-water systems don’t have bleeders at each unit and must be purged at the boiler instead. If you can’t find a bleeder, don’t loosen a pipe fitting or open a drain or pressure-relief valve as a substitute.

3. **Put a cup under the valve.**  
   Keep a towel underneath, too. The first water out may be dirty, and it can still be warm. Keep your face and hands out of the discharge path.

4. **Open the bleeder slowly.**  
   Use a radiator key or a flathead screwdriver, depending on the valve. Turn it counterclockwise just enough to release air—usually only a small fraction of a turn. **Do not remove the screw.**

   You may hear hissing, followed by sputtering water. Leave the valve slightly open until water flows steadily with no hissing or air spurts. You don’t need to drain a cupful once the air is gone.

5. **Close it snugly, not forcefully.**  
   Turn the valve clockwise until the water stops. Overtightening can damage or crack the valve seat and leave you with a leak. Wipe the valve dry and check for drips.

6. **Repeat at every baseboard—including the basement loop.**  
   Work unit by unit, starting closest to the boiler and moving outward. Don’t bleed only the upstairs units and call it done. A basement loop can hold trapped air, too, and skipping it may leave part of the house cold. Check every loop rather than assuming the air is all upstairs—or all downstairs.

7. **Check system pressure, then test the heat.**  
   Bleeding releases some water and can lower system pressure. Before restarting, check the boiler gauge against the cold-fill pressure specified for your system. If pressure is low, no water comes out of a bleeder, or you’re unsure what the gauge should read, stop and call for service rather than adding water blindly.

   Restore power, turn up a thermostat, and let the system run. Check that each baseboard warms up and that the bleeders stay dry.

**Still have a cold baseboard?** A zone valve, circulator, low system pressure, or a loop that needs proper purging could be the problem. If air keeps returning or a valve won’t stop dripping, contact us to have the system checked.

b.text:
If your baseboards are gurgling or they're hot on one end and ice cold on the other, you've got air trapped in the loop. Here's how I bleed them in the field.

**What you need:** small cup or plastic container, an old towel, and a radiator key or flathead screwdriver.

**1. Shut the system down first.**
Hit the emergency switch for the boiler and turn off the circulator. You don't want the pump pushing more air around while you're bleeding, and you don't want to get hit with scalding water. Give it 10-15 minutes to cool down if it's been running.

**2. Find the bleeder valve.**
It's on the end of each baseboard unit, under the end cap. Little brass fitting with a flat or square head. That's it.

**3. Put your cup underneath it and have the towel ready.**
Even when you do it right, it'll spit a little.

**4. Open it slow.**
Quarter-turn with the key or flathead until you hear hissing. Don't crank it wide open. Let the air come out until the water runs in a steady stream with no sputtering or hissing.

**5. Close it snug.**
Snug, not Hercules tight. If you overtighten these you'll crack the valve seat and then you really have a leak. Just firm until the water stops.

**6. Go unit by unit, closest to the boiler and work out.**
Start with the baseboard closest to the boiler and work your way to the end of each loop. Do every unit, even if it feels hot.

The mistake I see that causes 90% of our "cold radiator" calls: people only bleed the upstairs units and skip the basement loop. The basement loop is usually where the air is actually sitting. If you skip it, you'll be right back where you started.

Once you're done, turn the boiler and circulator back on. Check the pressure gauge on the boiler - you should be around 12-15 psi cold. If a zone is still cold after you've bled everything, or you're not getting any water out of a bleeder, give us a call and we'll get you on the schedule.

setup: A local sports columnist is writing an opinionated season-ending commentary for readers of the local paper's sports section.

a.text:
The season ended Saturday in the second round of the state playoffs, but it should be remembered as much for what this team accomplished as for how it lost.

An 8-2 record is nothing to dismiss. Neither is a school-record 2,340 passing yards by Dez Kowalski, who gave this team a steady presence at quarterback all season. And yet, the playoff loss will sting because it felt avoidable.

This was a team the Tigers had already beaten by 20 points in Week 3. In the rematch, the offense found success running the football early. That was the formula working against a familiar opponent.

Then, in the second half, the run game largely disappeared.

That decision changed the game. The team was down only three points, not facing an insurmountable deficit. There was no need to panic or suddenly make the offense one-dimensional. The running game was producing, the defense was keeping the margin within reach, and the situation called for patience.

Instead, the offense leaned away from what had been working and put more pressure on Kowalski and the passing game. Kowalski has earned plenty of credit for his record-setting season, but asking one player to carry the offense late in a playoff game is not always the best answer—especially when the ground game is giving you something.

That is the frustrating part of this loss. It was not simply that the team ran into a better opponent. It was that the game seemed to be there for the taking, and the offense moved away from its best option before the deficit demanded it.

Still, one questionable second half should not erase an excellent season. An 8-2 record, a state playoff win and a new school passing record represent real progress and plenty of reasons for this program to be proud. Kowalski’s season will be remembered in the record book, and the seniors leave having raised expectations for everyone who follows.

But good teams learn from disappointing endings. This one should remind the coaches and players that playoff football is often about trusting the plan when the pressure rises. When the run is working and you are down three, stay with it.

That may be the lesson this team carries into next season—and the difference between a promising year and a deeper playoff run.

b.text:
On paper, an 8-2 finish and a trip to the second round of the state playoffs looks like a banner year. Add in Dez Kowalski putting his name at the top of the record books with a jaw-dropping 2,340 passing yards, and most folks in town are content to call this season a resounding success.

I’m not most folks, and if you listen to me on the radio every morning, you know I don't do fake sunshine. 

Friday night was a blown opportunity, plain and simple. Losing in the postseason is always bitter, but getting knocked out by a team you buried by 20 points back in Week 3? That stings. And what hurts worst of all is that we didn’t get beat—we gave it away.

Trailing by just three points coming out of halftime, the coaching staff inexplicably panicked. The running game was working. Our offensive line was setting the line of scrimmage two yards deep in their secondary and giving us manageable third downs. We had them right where we wanted them. 

Instead, the play-calling completely abandoned the ground attack. I get the temptation—Kowalski had a historic year, and it's easy to rely on a record-setting arm. But dialing up four straight passing plays on a third-quarter drive when you only need two yards to keep the chains moving isn't aggressive; it's bad math. Being down a field goal with 18 minutes left on the clock isn't a fire drill. 

This team had the talent to play deep into November. An 8-2 record is a fine achievement, and Kowalski’s 2,340 yards will stand for a long time. But let’s not pretend Friday was just bad luck or a bad bounce. The Panthers stopped doing what worked at the absolute worst time, and that’s why the pads are already packed away in the fieldhouse.

setup: A solo indie game developer is writing a devlog recap for subscribers about his game's launch week sales, subreddit attention, review feedback, and upcoming 1.1 patch.

a.text:
## One Week In: 412 Copies and a Movement Patch

I launched my game last week after about three years of working on it during nights and weekends.

The first week ended at 412 copies sold, which is more than I knew how to picture when I started making the game. It’s been surreal seeing people actually play something that spent so long existing mostly on my hard drive.

The game also hit the front page of a small subreddit for around six hours, which brought in a noticeable spike of traffic and a lot of new players. I’m still catching up on some of the comments and messages, but it’s been great seeing people talk about specific levels, mechanics, and weird little details I wasn’t sure anyone would notice.

The most consistent criticism so far has been about the movement. One review described it as feeling floaty, and honestly, they’re right. I’ve been playing it for so long that I had started compensating for it without really noticing, but watching new players move around made the problem much more obvious.

I’m working on a movement update for version 1.1, currently planned for next month. I’m adjusting the acceleration, deceleration, and jump timing to make the controls feel more responsive without changing the overall feel of the game too drastically. I’m still testing different versions, so I don’t want to promise exact changes yet.

For now, I’m going through feedback, fixing the smaller bugs that have come up, and working on the 1.1 patch. Thanks to everyone who bought the game, left a review, sent feedback, or shared it somewhere. The first week has been a lot to process, but I’m glad the game is finally out in the world.

b.text:
Launch Week

It's out. After three years of nights and weekends, v1.0 went live last week.

I don't really know how to start these things other than just saying the numbers, so: 412 copies sold in the first week.

That's not a lot by Steam standards, but it's about 400 more than I was honestly expecting. I kept refreshing the dashboard on day one like an idiot.

The weirdest part was Tuesday(?) when someone posted it to a small subreddit and it hit the front page of that sub for like 6 hours. Traffic just spiked out of nowhere. I sat there watching the wishlist graph go vertical and didn't know what to do with myself.

Got the first real negative-ish review too. Said the movement feels floaty. And... yeah, they're right. I tuned it on my machine for so long I just got used to it. I reread the review like five times and then opened the controller code.

So what's next:

I'm working on 1.1 now. Main thing is tightening up the movement — more gravity, less drift on the jump landing, better air control. Shooting to have that out next month.

Thanks for playing it / wishlisting it / reading these posts while I was still just posting broken screenshots. I'll put up the full 1.1 patch notes when it's closer.

setup: A home baker is reviewing the Corlane SM6 mixer for blog readers deciding whether to buy it.

a.text:
I’ve been pulling preorders for my farmers market stall for nearly two years, which means my kitchen sees serious daily and weekend traffic. The Corlane SM6 has lived on my counter for eight months, spinning almost every day. If you’re reading this with your credit card hovering, here’s exactly how it performed under real load.

Let’s start with the motor. I regularly run a double batch of stiff bagel dough through this machine, and it never bogs down or stalls. The torque is immediate and relentless. For anyone committed to frequent heavy dough, that raw pulling power is the entire reason to consider it. It doesn’t struggle, it doesn’t overheat, and it doesn’t ask you to slow the dial.

It isn’t flawless out of the box. The bowl lift lever develops a loud squeak within weeks of daily use. I’ve had to wipe it down and apply a thin strip of WD-40 to the pivot joints roughly once a month just to stop it from sounding like a rusted hinge. It’s a simple fix, but it’s recurring maintenance that shouldn’t be glossed over.

The stock dough hook is also a miss. The SM6’s bowl sits deeper than standard mixers, and the factory hook barely clears the bottom edge during a full knead. Dough gets trapped underneath instead of folding properly. I bought a third-party stainless hook specifically sized for deeper bowls, and the difference was night and day. Plan to spend another $25 to $30 there.

At $429, the SM6 costs $80 more than the equivalent KitchenAid. You’re not paying for flash or a massive accessory ecosystem. You’re paying for sustained heavy-lift durability and a motor that refuses to choke on stiff, low-hydration doughs.

Here’s the verdict: Buy it if you are actively kneading heavy bread or pretzel dough every single week. Skip it entirely if your baking routine lives in cookies, cakes, and whipped cream. That $80 premium will never pay for itself on light batters, and the squeaky lift lever will only grate on you faster when the mixer isn’t earning its keep. The SM6 is a dedicated, no-nonsense bread workhorse. Get it for the loaves, walk away from it for the dessert trays.

b.text:
**Corlane SM6 Stand Mixer: 8 Months of Almost-Daily Sourdough**

I’ve run the Corlane SM6 nearly every day for eight months, mostly for farmers market sourdough. It has also worked through double batches of stiff bagel dough, which is where this mixer really proves itself.

The motor is the highlight. A double batch of low-hydration bagel dough—heavy, stiff, and exactly the kind of thing that makes weaker mixers stall or overheat—kneads without stalling. The mixer doesn’t sound like it’s struggling, and the head stays stable. For weekly market production, the SM6 has been dependable in a way I didn’t fully expect at this price.

The downsides are specific and real. The bowl-lift lever squeaks, and I have to WD-40 it about once a month. That’s not difficult, but it’s annoying on a $429 mixer. The included dough hook is too short for the deep bowl, so it leaves unincorporated flour and dough at the bottom. I bought a third-party dough hook, which solves the problem but adds extra cost and means the out-of-box accessory isn’t quite right for bread dough. And at $429, the Corlane is $80 more than the equivalent KitchenAid bowl-lift model.

**Verdict:** For heavy dough bakers—sourdough, bagels, stiff whole-grain loaves—this is a buy. The motor is the reason to choose it. For cookie and cake bakers, skip it. You’ll pay more than the KitchenAid and inherit the squeak and hook issue without getting any real benefit. This is a bread mixer, not an all-purpose mixer.

setup: A local sports columnist is writing an opinionated season-ending commentary for readers of the local paper's sports section.

a.text:
**Season worth remembering, playoff loss worth questioning**

The final score is going to sit there for a while, and that’s the cruel part about playoff football. One week you’re still playing, the next you’re spending the whole winter wondering what happened.

What happened for our team shouldn’t be buried under the result. An 8-2 season is something to be proud of. This group played hard, played tough, and gave the town a fall worth talking about.

But I’m not going to pretend Friday night didn’t leave a bad taste.

This was a loss the team didn’t have to take. Not against this opponent. Not the way the game was set up. Not when they were only down three and still very much in control of their own fate.

They lost because they stopped doing what worked.

For long stretches, the run game was moving the chains and keeping the offense ahead of the sticks. It was physical, it was balanced, and it gave the team a chance to control tempo. Then, somewhere in the second half, the team got away from it. I still don’t understand why.

You don’t abandon your best weapon when the game tightens up. You lean on it. You make the other team adjust to you. Instead, the offense became one-dimensional, and that’s exactly what a good defense wants.

That’s what made the loss so frustrating. This wasn’t a case of being overmatched. This wasn’t a team getting punched in the mouth and never answering. They were right there. They had already beaten this same team by 20 back in Week 3. They knew they belonged.

And maybe that’s part of it. Sometimes the hardest thing in sports is to stay simple when the lights get brighter. You start pressing. You start searching for the big play instead of trusting the thing that got you there.

Still, this season was bigger than one bad stretch in one game.

Dez Kowalski set a school record with 2,340 passing yards. That’s not a small thing. That’s the kind of number people will be talking about around this program for years, and it should be celebrated. He made plays all season and gave this offense a real identity through the air.

But records don’t erase decision-making, and this loss still falls on the choices made when the game mattered most.

That said, I’m not about to tear down a group that won eight games and gave us a season worth caring about. These kids earned their heads held high. They earned the right to be proud of what they built.

They just also earned the right to know the truth.

They didn’t lose because the season caught up to them.  
They lost because they stopped trusting themselves when it mattered most.

b.text:
# We Had Them, and We Got Cute

An 8-2 season is a good season. Let's say that up front, because the next few hundred words aren't going to feel that way, and I don't want anybody thinking I've lost sight of what these kids accomplished.

But I've been doing this long enough to know the difference between a team that got beat and a team that beat itself. Friday night, in the second round of the state playoffs, we beat ourselves.

Here's what sticks in my throat. We beat that team by 20 back in Week 3. Twenty. And we didn't beat them by scheming them into oblivion — we beat them by lining up and running the ball down their throat. So you'll forgive me if I don't buy the idea that they were simply the better team this time around. They weren't. We just decided, somewhere around the middle of the third quarter, to stop doing the thing that was working.

Because it *was* working. We were moving the chains on the ground. We were down three — three! — and controlling the clock, keeping their offense on the sideline, wearing on a defense that didn't want any part of it. And then we got cute. We put it in the air, went three-and-out, put our defense back on the field, and the whole complexion of the game changed. You could feel it in the stands.

I understand the instinct. Dez Kowalski threw for 2,340 yards this year, a school record, and that's a genuinely special thing that this town should be proud of for a long time. When you've got an arm like that, the temptation is to let it fly, especially when the pressure's on. But football's a simple game more often than we make it. When something works, you keep doing it until they prove they can stop it. They never proved it. We just stopped asking.

That's the part that'll bother me all winter. Not that we lost — everybody loses eventually in a single-elimination bracket. It's that we had the answer in our hands, the same answer that worked in September, and we set it down.

Eight and two is a good season. It should have been better. And the reason it wasn't had nothing to do with the kids on that field and everything to do with a decision to abandon what got us there.

Get 'em next year. And when we do, let's remember what we're good at.

setup: A home baker is reviewing the Corlane SM6 mixer for blog readers deciding whether to buy it.

a.text:
Corlane SM6 Stand Mixer After 8 Months of Market Sourdough

I bought the Corlane SM6 last March because my old mixer started dying on 1,200-gram batches of stiff bagel dough. I bake almost every day for the Saturday market: two or three loads of sourdough, plus bagels twice a week. The SM6 has been on the counter the entire time.

The motor is the reason to consider this machine. A double batch of 65% hydration bagel dough (about 1.8 kg of very stiff stuff) never made it hesitate. No stalling, no overheating, no that-smell-of-hot-plastic. It just chewed through it on speed 2 for eight minutes. KitchenAid’s equivalent 5-quart bowl-lift would have been screaming by minute four. That extra torque is real.

Two problems showed up fast. The bowl-lift lever started squeaking after six weeks. I hit it with WD-40 once a month and it stays quiet for three weeks, then starts again. Annoying, not fatal. Worse: the stock dough hook is too short for the deep bowl. On a 900-gram loaf it barely reaches the bottom third of the dough. I ordered a third-party spiral hook ($28) and that fixed it. Corlane should have shipped the right length in the first place.

Price: $429. That’s $80 more than the KitchenAid Professional 5 Plus that most people would compare it to. You’re paying for the extra power and the bigger bowl. If you mostly mix cookie dough and cake batter, that extra money is wasted. Those jobs don’t need this motor.

If you knead heavy dough every week—sourdough, bagels, pizza, pretzels—buy it. The motor earns the extra $80. If that’s not you, skip it and get the KitchenAid. I wouldn’t own anything else at this point.

b.text:
**Corlane SM6 Stand Mixer Review: After 8 Months of Daily Sourdough Production**

I’ve been using the Corlane SM6 almost daily for eight months now, which means it is not sitting on my counter collecting dust. It is pulling heavy mix loads for weekend sourdough, bagels, and everything dough that I take to the farmers market. If you’re wondering whether it’s worth the money, here’s the honest picture from a home baker who actually puts it to work.

**The Good: The Motor Does Not Quit**

This is the main reason the mixer earns a recommendation. The SM6 handles a double batch of stiff bagel dough without stalling. That is not an exaggeration. I know exactly what heavy dough feels like when a mixer starts to struggle—the head shifting, the motor bogging down, the smell of stress. With the SM6, the dough comes together cleanly and the motor never seems close to giving up.

For sourdough, the mixer is strong enough to pull gluten quickly without heating the dough too aggressively. That matters when you are making dough at home that still needs to stay cool and manageable. For bread bakers, this is the mixer’s strongest point.

**The Bad: The Bowl Lift Lever Squeaks**

The mixer is not perfect. The bowl lift lever squeaks, and I have to lubricate it with WD-40 once a month to keep it quiet. It’s not a dealbreaker, but it is annoying. If I’m mixing early in the morning, that squeak is the one part of the routine I do not miss.

This is the kind of maintenance you shouldn’t have to do every month, but it’s easy enough to deal with. Still, it’s worth knowing before you buy.

**The Awkward Part: The Included Dough Hook Is Too Short**

The dough hook that comes with the SM6 is too short for the deep bowl. This is a real flaw because the hook is the one accessory most people expect to work properly with the mixer they just bought. Instead of mixing correctly, it does not reach or scrape the deep bowl the way it should.

I ended up buying a third-party dough hook, which fixed the problem. If you buy this mixer for bread or bagels, budget for the better hook. Do not let the stock hook discourage you from a machine that otherwise performs very well.

**The Price: More Than a Comparable KitchenAid**

The Corlane SM6 is $429, which is $80 more than the equivalent KitchenAid I would normally compare it to. That difference is noticeable. You need to understand that you are not buying this because it is the cheapest option. You are buying it for heavy dough performance.

For cookie bakers or cake bakers, that extra $80 is hard to justify. For a baker mixing double batches of stiff dough every week, the price is easier to defend.

**Final Verdict: Buy It If You Knead Heavy Dough Every Week. Skip It If You Mostly Bake Cookies and Cakes.**

The Corlane SM6 is a serious mixer for serious dough. If your baking involves sourdough, bagels, dense bread dough, or anything thick enough to make a weaker mixer stall, this one is worth buying. It earns its keep in my kitchen because I use it for work, not just convenience.

But if you mostly make cookies, cake batter, meringue, or light bread dough, you do not need this machine. You are paying for strength you probably won’t use. For that kind of baker, the SM6 is not a smart buy.

For me, the SM6 is a yes. It has the motor performance I need for market bread, even with the squeaky lift lever and the poor included hook. It is not flawless, but it is strong, reliable, and worth the upgrade if heavy dough is a regular part of your week.

setup: A wedding photographer is posting that couples who ditch rigid shot lists get better photos, using the rained-out Barrera wedding as an example.

a.text:
The Barreras had a shot list. Then it rained.

Not a light drizzle. The kind of Hill Country downpour that turns a ceremony lawn into a creek in twenty minutes. The list said first look by the arbor, family formals on the stone steps, portraits at golden hour in the field.

None of that happened.

What happened instead: we grabbed the whole party and moved everything under the big pecan tree on the property. Ceremony, family photos, the two of them, all of it. Wet grass, borrowed umbrellas, people packed in shoulder to shoulder because that was the only dry ground.

Those are some of the best photos I've made in eight years of doing this.

Here's the thing I've noticed over a lot of weddings. The couples who hand me a rigid list and want it checked off, line by line, end up with photos that look like everyone else's. Technically fine. Nice enough. Interchangeable.

The couples who tell me what matters to them and then let the day be the day? Those are the galleries people cry over.

It's not that planning is bad. I want to know your grandmother is flying in from Monterrey and it's a big deal she made it. I want to know the two of you met at a bar with a pecan tree out back, so the fact that we ended up under one wasn't lost on anybody.

But a shot list can't anticipate the moment your dad ducks under the umbrella with you and the two of you just stand there laughing at the rain. It can't schedule the way light looks coming through wet leaves. It can only tell you what you thought you'd want, months ago, on a sunny afternoon at your kitchen table.

So if you're interviewing photographers right now: ask them about the wedding that went sideways. Ask what they did. The list is the floor, not the ceiling.

And if it rains, find the biggest tree on the property.

b.text:
The couples who hand me a 40-item shot list are almost never the ones who end up with photos they cry over.

I say this with love, because I understand the impulse. You're spending real money, you've been on Pinterest for eight months, and a list feels like insurance. I get it.

But here's what a shot list actually does: it turns me into a task-completer instead of someone watching your day for the thing nobody planned.

The Barrera wedding is the example I come back to.

Outdoor ceremony, Hill Country, and the sky opened up about ninety minutes before go time. We lost the aisle, the arch placement, the golden hour spot I'd scouted twice. Everything moved under an old pecan tree on the property because it was the only cover big enough to hold everybody.

Nobody had a plan for that. There was no list item that said "bride laughing while her uncle holds a tablecloth over her head."

That's the photo they printed big.

What made it work wasn't my genius. It was that they'd told me early on they trusted me to read the day, and they hadn't handed me a checklist I'd feel obligated to chase while the actual moment was happening ten feet to my left.

So my honest advice, after eight years and a few hundred weddings:

Give your photographer the non-negotiables. The family combinations. The heirloom detail. Grandma, because grandma might not be here next year. Those matter and I want them written down.

Then stop. Leave the rest open.

The best frames from any wedding I've shot were not on a list. They couldn't have been. Nobody knew they were coming.

And to my vendor friends — you already know this. The rain plan weddings are the ones we talk about years later.

#weddingphotography #texashillcountry #weddingvendors

setup: A local sports columnist is writing an opinionated season-ending commentary for readers of the local paper's sports section.

a.text:
An 8-2 record looks good in the yearbook. It looks fine on a banner, and in twenty years, folks flipping through the trophy case will call this a great football team. 

They won’t be wrong. But if you were sitting in the bleachers Friday night, you know darn well this season shouldn’t be over.

Losing in the second round of the state playoffs stings no matter what. Losing to a ballclub you pushed around by 20 points back in September makes your stomach turn. And the worst part about Friday’s heartbreak isn't that our boys were outmatched. It’s that the sideline outsmarted itself.

Let’s stop dancing around it: they panicked, and they abandoned the run. 

Coming out of the locker room at halftime, you’re down 17-14. Three points. You have two full quarters of playoff football left to play. On the ground, the offensive line was getting push, churning out five yards a pop whenever we kept it between the tackles. The defense was tired, the temperature was dropping, and the road to the quarterfinals was paved right through the A-gap. 

Instead, the clipboard decided it was time to play hero ball. 

Don't misunderstand me—Dez Kowalski gave this town one of the greatest quarterback seasons we’ll ever see under center. Shattering the school record with 2,340 passing yards is something nobody can take away from that kid. He’s got an electric arm and ice in his veins. But falling in love with the stat sheet in November will get you beat. Forcing a teenager to drop back into obvious passing situations against a pinned-back pass rush—while your running backs stand in the backfield picking up blitzes—isn't playoff football. It’s self-sabotage. 

You don't throw your way out of a three-point hole in high school playoffs when the ground game is chewing up clock and moving the chains. You run it until they prove they can stop it, and Friday night, they never proved they could. We just stopped doing it.

Tip your cap to the seniors. It was a thrilling, record-setting autumn that gave this town plenty of Friday nights to be proud of. But when the dust settles and the staff sits down to watch that second-half tape, it’s going to be a tough pill to swallow. Because the only team that truly stopped this offense from making a deep state run was the one wearing our own headsets.

b.text:
It’s quiet around the fieldhouse this week, and honestly, it shouldn't be. An 8-2 season is something ninety percent of the programs in this state would trade their left arm for. But as I sat in the press box Friday night watching the clock tick down on our season in the second round of the state playoffs, I couldn't shake the feeling that we left food on the table.

First, let’s give credit where it’s absolutely due. This was a historic, explosive football team to watch. We got to witness senior quarterback Dez Kowalski rewrite the record books, spinning it for 2,340 yards this season. That’s a new school record, and it couldn’t happen to a harder-working kid. Dez gave this town everything he had, and his name is going to sit at the top of that leaderboard for a very long time.

But that’s what makes Friday’s exit so frustrating. We lost to a team we absolutely handled back in Week 3—a team we beat by 20 points on their own turf. 

So, what went wrong? 

We panicked. Plain and simple. 

Coming out of halftime, we were down by three. Just three points. That is a single field goal; it is not a crisis. Yet, we completely abandoned the run game. In the first half, our line was getting a push, and our backs were churning out four and five yards a carry. It was working. It was keeping their defense honest and keeping our defense rested. 

But in the third quarter, the play-calling went entirely one-dimensional. When you stop running the ball in a tight playoff game, you do two things: you make yourself predictable, and you put your star quarterback in a vice. Dez is great, but nobody can throw against a defense that knows a pass is coming on every single down. We had the physical advantage upfront, and we chose to stop using it. 

It’s a tough pill to swallow, especially for the seniors who don't get a next year. This 8-2 campaign was a massive success in the grand scheme of things, and these boys brought a lot of pride back to our community. But when we look back at how it ended, we’ll always know we had the keys to the quarterfinals—we just chose to throw them away.

Dear Hiring Manager,

setup: A retired rural mail carrier is writing a letter to the Kettle Falls Courier urging residents to oppose the post office counter closure at the July 28 forum.

a.text:
To the Editor,

I drove 38 miles on Route 4 every single day for 22 years before I retired last year, so I think I know Kettle Falls about as well as anybody. I am not much of a writer, but I cannot sit quiet while the Postal Service tries to shut down our counter service.

The Postal Service is telling folks our branch is losing $40,000 a year. What they leave out is why. A while back, they cut our counter hours to 8:00 a.m. to noon. If you close the doors during the exact hours working people need to drop off a package or buy stamps, naturally your business drops off too. They broke the service first, and now they are using the low traffic to prove nobody needs it. They pointed at a problem they made themselves.

This is not just an inconvenience. It hurts real people in this town. Take Mrs. Halloran up on Kettle Hill. She is in her eighties, lives by herself, and gets her heart medication delivered by mail. She counts on that counter service to buy money orders to pay her monthly bills. If they close our counter, she is expected to drive twenty minutes out to Fairview just to get basic business done. A lot of folks her age do not need to be driving on the highway like that, and plenty do not have a car at all.

There is a public forum coming up on July 28 at the Grange Hall, and the USPS district manager is supposed to be there. I am asking everybody in Kettle Falls to fill that room. We need to make sure the people making these decisions look us in the eye and hear what this post office actually means to our community.

Jim Miller  
Kettle Falls  
Retired Carrier, Route 4

b.text:
To the Editor:

I carried mail on Route 4 for 22 years. Thirty-eight miles a day, six days a week, until I retired last year. I am not a writer, but I know this town about as well as anybody, so I want to say something about the Postal Service closing our counter.

The district office says the Kettle Falls branch loses $40,000 a year. What they leave out is why. Two years ago they cut the counter hours from a full day down to 8 to noon. Anybody who works a job could not get there anymore. Of course the traffic dropped. Now they are pointing at the drop in traffic as the reason to shut the window for good. They made the problem and now they are using it as the excuse.

Here is what that means for real people. Mrs. Halloran up on Kettle Hill is in her eighties. She gets her heart medication through the mail and pays for it with money orders she buys at that counter. When it closes, the nearest window is Fairview, twenty minutes each way on the highway. She does not drive that road. I do not know what she is supposed to do, and I do not think the people making this decision have thought about her at all. There are more like her on every route out of this office. I delivered to them.

A post office counter is not a luxury in a town like ours. It is how people who do not have a computer or a car or a bank account do their business.

The Postal Service is holding a public forum on July 28 at the Grange Hall. The district manager will be there. If you care about this, show up. Bring your neighbors. Bring your parents. Fill the chairs. If the hall is empty, they will take that as permission. If it is full, they will have to explain themselves to our faces.

I will be there. I hope to see you.

[Name]
Retired carrier, Route 4
Kettle Falls

setup: A freelance wedding photographer is writing a blog post for couples about why to book a winter wedding.

a.text:
**I Didn't Expect to Like Winter Weddings. Now I Book Them On Purpose.**

I've been freelancing as a wedding photographer in this metro area for six years now. Same venues, same parks, same downtown blocks, just different couples. Which means I know exactly what a Saturday in June looks like: you can feel it before you even get out of the car.

For a long time I was a summer purist too. Then I shot 11 winter weddings in the last two years - November through February - and it kind of flipped for me.

Here’s why I actually like them now, honestly:

**1. Your money goes so much further and you feel it.**

This isn't just photographer pricing. My winter couples tell me their overall bookings - venue, catering, rentals - are running about 30% cheaper than what their friends paid for a June date at the same places. That changes the whole day. You’re not stressed about squeezing every penny out of a 6-hour rental. You can actually afford the extra hour of coverage, or the live band, or just... not be stressed.

**2. The light is better. I will die on this hill.**

Everyone thinks June = good light. Most of our Junes are flat, white, overcast at 2pm. It’s soft, sure, but it’s flat and you look a little washed out unless we work really hard.

In November, around 3pm, when the sun drops low and comes through the bare trees? It’s perfect. No leaves means the light just filters and stripes through the branches instead of getting blocked. It’s warm, directional, sculpted. It hits your face instead of just sitting on top of you. Some of my favorite portraits ever from the last two seasons were taken at 3:15pm in November in a park I’ve shot 40 times in the summer.

**3. We actually get to use the venue.**

In June, I pull into a venue I’ve shot a dozen times and I’m sharing the parking lot with 3 or 4 other vendors. There’s another ceremony flipping in the garden, another bride getting out of a limo, the coordinator is on a headset sprinting between two weddings. We’re timed to the minute because someone else needs the staircase at 4:30.

In winter, the lot is half empty. The venue staff isn’t fried. We get the good window in the bridal suite without curtains drawn against the heat. We can take an extra 10 minutes on portraits because no one is waiting to kick us out. It’s calmer, and it shows in the photos.

I get why couples default to June. I did too. But if you’re browsing dates right now and trying to decide when to book - if you like that low, golden light, want a day that feels less like an assembly line, and wouldn’t mind your total coming in about 30% lower - winter is worth a real look.

I’ve got a few winter weekends left for this year. If you’re thinking November, December, or January, send me a note and I’ll tell you which spots look best at 3pm.

b.text:
**Why I Actually Like Shooting Winter Weddings Now**

I used to default to peak season like everyone else. June through September felt like the “real” wedding months. Then the last two years happened, and I shot eleven winter weddings. That number surprised me when I tallied it. What surprised me more is that I started looking forward to them.

Here’s the unvarnished version of why.

First, the light. Around 3 p.m. in November, when the sun is low and the trees are bare, the light filters through in a way that is just better for portraits than the flat, even overcast you often get in June. It’s directional without being harsh. Faces look sculpted instead of washed out. Couples stand in a clearing or along a path and the background opens up instead of turning into a wall of green. I’ve had more “wait, that frame is actually perfect” moments in late afternoon winter light than I have in high summer. It’s not softer. It’s just more interesting.

Second, the logistics feel human again. In June I’m routinely pulling into a venue parking lot at the same time as three or four other vendors. Everyone’s rushing, spaces are tight, and the day already feels crowded before anyone has walked down the aisle. Winter is quieter. I can actually park, unload, and take a breath. The couple usually has more of the venue’s attention. Things move at a pace that lets me notice the small stuff—the way the light hits a ring, the quiet moment before guests arrive—instead of just surviving the schedule.

And yes, the money part is real. Winter dates typically run about 30% less for the couple. That isn’t a gimmick I invented; it’s just how demand works in this market. Same photographer, same level of coverage, same files and albums. The calendar simply has more room, so the pricing reflects it. For a lot of the couples I’ve worked with, that difference meant they could keep the photography they actually wanted instead of cutting elsewhere or settling.

I’m not going to tell you winter is magically more romantic or that every season is equally perfect. Some people want the full green-and-gold summer look and that’s completely valid. But if you’re looking at dates and feeling the pressure of peak season—or if the idea of softer light, fewer people in the parking lot, and a meaningful savings sounds appealing—winter is not the compromise I once assumed it was. I’ve shot eleven of them in two years. The work holds up. The days feel better. And the portraits… honestly, some of my favorites now have bare branches in them.

If you’re still deciding when to book, I’m happy to talk through what a winter timeline actually looks like for your venue and style. No pitch, just the practical side from someone who’s been there eleven times recently.

setup: A high school junior is writing an argumentative essay to her English teacher and classmates arguing for open campus lunch for juniors and seniors.

a.text:
Open campus lunch for juniors and seniors should be allowed at our school because it would reduce overcrowding, respect older students’ responsibility, and match what nearby districts are already doing successfully. Juniors and seniors are close to adulthood, and many of them are ready for the independence that comes with more freedom during the school day. A policy like this would not be reckless; it would be a practical change that benefits students and improves the lunch period for everyone.

The biggest reason to allow open campus lunch is that our cafeteria is already too crowded. The cafeteria seats only 220 students, but 340 students are in the lunch wave. That means more than 100 students do not have a real seat available at lunch. Instead of giving students enough space to eat comfortably, the school forces a large group to stand, squeeze together, or find awkward places to sit. Lunch is supposed to be a break in the day, but overcrowding turns it into a stressful and uncomfortable experience. If juniors and seniors were allowed off campus, the cafeteria would not have to serve as the only option for every student in that lunch period.

Another reason is that many students would use the privilege responsibly. I surveyed 80 students at our school, and 71 said they were in favor of open campus lunch. That is a strong majority. Students are not asking for something unreasonable; they are asking for a limited privilege for upperclassmen, who are generally older and more capable of managing their time. Juniors and seniors already handle harder classes, jobs, sports, and other responsibilities. If they can manage those commitments, they can manage a lunch break without being treated like younger students who need as much supervision. Open campus lunch would recognize that maturity.

Nearby districts have already shown that this policy can work. Fairmont, West Linn, and Cascade all allow open campus lunch for upperclassmen, and their published statistics show no rise in tardiness. That matters because one of the main concerns about open campus lunch is that students will come back late and disrupt the school day. However, those districts provide real evidence that this does not have to happen. If schools similar to ours can allow juniors and seniors to leave campus without increasing tardiness, then our school can do the same. We do not need to guess whether the policy works when other districts have already demonstrated it.

Some people may argue that open campus lunch could create safety problems or encourage students to leave and not come back on time. Those concerns are understandable, but they are also manageable. Juniors and seniors already earn more privileges than underclassmen in other parts of school life, and a lunch pass would simply be another privilege tied to age and responsibility. The school could require students to return on time and lose the privilege if they abuse it. That is a fair consequence and a better solution than keeping every student locked into an overcrowded cafeteria because of what a few might do.

Open campus lunch for juniors and seniors would improve lunch at our school in a realistic and responsible way. It would reduce overcrowding in a cafeteria that cannot fit the students assigned to it, give mature students a privilege they are ready for, and follow the example of nearby districts that have already made this work without increasing tardiness. This policy would not weaken the school; it would show trust in students who have earned it. For those reasons, our school should allow open campus lunch for juniors and seniors.

b.text:
Title: The Case for Open Campus Lunch: Trusting Upperclassmen and Solving the Cafeteria Crisis

Every day when the lunch bell rings, a wave of 340 students floods into a cafeteria built to hold only 220. The result is a daily scramble for seating, long lines, and a stressful environment that defeats the purpose of a midday break. While the administration has maintained a closed campus to keep students contained, this policy is no longer serving the school’s best interests. Our high school should implement an open campus lunch policy for juniors and seniors because it immediately alleviates severe cafeteria overcrowding, aligns with the proven success of neighboring districts, and reflects the clear desire of the student body.

The most immediate and practical argument for open campus lunch is simple math. Currently, our cafeteria has a hard capacity of 220 seats, yet our largest lunch wave consists of 340 students. This means that at any given moment, over a hundred students are left standing, sitting on the floor, or rushing through their meals just to give up their seat for someone else. By allowing juniors and seniors to leave campus for lunch, we can instantly reduce the lunch wave population to a manageable number. This does not just benefit the upperclassmen who get to leave; it drastically improves the daily experience for the freshmen and sophomores who remain, finally giving them the space to sit down and eat in peace. 

Beyond the physical logistics of the building, the primary administrative hesitation regarding open campus lunch is the fear of afternoon tardiness. However, we do not have to guess how students will handle this privilege; we can look at the districts right next door. Fairmont, West Linn, and Cascade all currently allow open campus lunch for their upperclassmen. These are similar schools with similar student demographics, and their published statistics show absolutely no rise in afternoon tardiness. The data proves that when juniors and seniors are trusted with the responsibility of managing their own time, they return to class on time. Treating our upperclassmen like they are incapable of making it back by the bell ignores the reality that students in neighboring towns are already doing it successfully every single day.

Furthermore, implementing this policy respects the overwhelming consensus of the students who are actually affected by it. In a recent survey of 80 students at our school, 71 expressed strong support for an open campus lunch. That is nearly a 90% approval rating. High school juniors and seniors are on the cusp of adulthood, preparing for college and the workforce, where they are expected to manage their own schedules and make responsible choices. Granting them this privilege acknowledges their maturity and gives them a voice in their own daily environment. 

Ultimately, keeping juniors and seniors trapped in an overcrowded cafeteria does not make them better students; it just makes them more stressed. By adopting an open campus lunch, the school can solve a severe logistical problem, follow the successful, data-backed precedents of Fairmont, West Linn, and Cascade, and reward responsible students with the autonomy they have earned. It is time to update our policies to reflect the reality of our building's capacity and the maturity of our upperclassmen.

setup: A small HVAC company owner is writing a how-to for homeowners on bleeding air from hot water baseboard radiators before winter.

a.text:
If your baseboard radiators are cold to the touch or making a loud clinking, gurgling sound when the heat kicks on, you have air trapped in your heating lines. Air blocks the hot water from circulating, leaving you with cold rooms. Getting that air out is a straightforward job you can do yourself in about 30 minutes. 

Here is exactly how to bleed your baseboard system to get the heat flowing again.

### Step 1: Shut off the system
Never try to bleed your radiators while the system is running. If the circulator pump is active, it will keep the air moving through the pipes, making it impossible to get it all out, and it might even suck more air into the system. Turn off your boiler at the thermostat or the main switch and wait about 10 to 15 minutes. This lets the water settle and ensures you won’t get sprayed with scalding hot water.

### Step 2: Map your route (and avoid the #1 mistake)
You need to bleed your radiators in a specific order: **start with the unit closest to your boiler and work your way outward.** 

This brings us to the mistake that causes about 80% of our cold-radiator service calls: **homeowners only bleeding the upstairs units.** People assume that because air rises, the blockage must be on the top floor. But in a closed residential loop, air often gets trapped in the basement or ground-floor lines, blocking the flow to the rest of the house. Even if your basement is unfinished and you don't care about heating it, you *must* bleed the basement loops first. If you skip them, you aren't fixing the problem.

### Step 3: Locate the bleeder valve
Go to your first baseboard unit. Look at the end caps of the metal cover—usually on the side where the copper pipe enters the unit. Pop the end cap off. Inside, you will see a small brass valve. It will have a small stem in the middle, either with a square head (which requires a radiator key, available for two dollars at any hardware store) or a slot for a flathead screwdriver.

### Step 4: Open the valve slowly
Position a small cup, bowl, or a thick rag directly underneath the valve spout. 

Insert your key or flathead screwdriver and turn it slowly counterclockwise—about a half-turn is usually enough. You will hear a hissing sound. That is the trapped air escaping. 

### Step 5: Wait for a steady stream
Keep your cup under the valve. You might get a mix of spitting air and dirty water. Keep the valve open until the hissing stops completely and you get a steady, solid stream of water with no air bubbles. 

### Step 6: Close it snug (Do NOT overtighten)
Once you have steady water, turn the valve clockwise to close it. 

**Pay attention here:** Only tighten it until it is snug. These valves are made of soft brass. If you crank down on them too hard, you will crack the valve seat. If that happens, it won't shut off, it will drip constantly, and you’ll have to call us to drain your system and solder in a brand-new valve. Snug is plenty.

### Step 7: Repeat the process
Move to the next closest radiator to the boiler and repeat the steps. Keep going until you have bled every single unit in the house, ending with the one furthest away from your boiler.

Once you’re finished, turn your boiler back on. Check your thermostat, let the system run for a few minutes, and feel the baseboards. They should be hot from end to end. If you still have cold spots after running through this sequence, or if you notice your boiler pressure gauge has dropped too low after bleeding, give us a call and we’ll come out to get your system balanced and pressurized properly.

b.text:
# How to Bleed Air Out of Your Baseboard Heating Before Winter

If your baseboards gurgle, or one room stays cold while the rest of the house heats fine, you've probably got air trapped in the system. Bleeding it out takes about 20 minutes and no special skills — here's how to do it right.

## What You'll Need

- A radiator key or a flathead screwdriver (depends on your valve type)
- A small cup or bowl
- An old towel, just in case

## Step 1: Shut Off the Circulator and Boiler

Before you touch anything, turn off the boiler and circulator pump. You don't want the pump pushing water around while you're trying to bleed a valve, and you don't want to be working with scalding water. Give the system a few minutes to settle.

## Step 2: Find the Bleeder Valve on Each Baseboard

Look at the end of each baseboard unit — usually behind the end cap, you'll find a small valve with either a square stem (that's what the key is for) or a slotted screw head. Every unit on the system should have one.

## Step 3: Cup Underneath and Open the Valve Slowly

Hold your cup under the valve and open it slowly. Don't crank it — a quarter to half turn is usually plenty. If there's air in the line, you'll hear it hiss out. Let it run until you get a steady stream of water with no sputtering or hissing. Steady water means the air is out of that section.

## Step 4: Close It Snug — Not Tight

Once the water runs steady, close the valve until it's snug and the drip stops. **Do not crank it down.** Overtightening cracks the valve seat, and then instead of a free 20-minute job, you've got a leaking valve and a service call.

## Step 5: Work Unit by Unit, Starting Closest to the Boiler

Start with the baseboard nearest the boiler and work your way outward through the loop. Air moves through the system, so bleeding in order gets it all out instead of chasing it around the house.

## The Mistake That Causes Most of Our Cold Radiator Calls

Here it is: **people bleed the upstairs units and skip the basement loop.**

We get called out every fall for "cold radiators," and more often than not, the homeowner already bled every baseboard on the main and second floors — but never touched the basement. That's usually exactly where the air is sitting. If your system has a basement zone or any baseboard down there, bleed those units too. Don't skip them because the basement doesn't need to be warm — trapped air down there affects the whole system.

## After You're Done

Turn the boiler and circulator back on and check your pressure gauge. Most residential systems should sit around 12–15 psi cold. If bleeding dropped your pressure below that, the system needs water added back — some setups have an automatic feed valve that handles this, others need it done manually.

If you're not sure how to add water, or you've bled everything (basement included) and you've still got cold spots, that's when it's worth having someone take a look. Could be a stuck zone valve, a failing circulator, or a bigger air problem that needs a power purge.

Give us a call and we'll get you sorted before the real cold hits.

setup: A real estate agent is posting one specific observation about early block walks and happier buyers to LinkedIn buyers, agents, and lenders.

a.text:
After 12 years in real estate, I’ve noticed that buyers who walk a neighborhood around 7 a.m. before a showing are often much happier with the house later.

The Pruitts did this before we toured a home on Sycamore Street. They wanted to know what the neighborhood felt like during an ordinary weekday—not just when the house was staged, the lights were on, and I was standing there with a key.

That morning walk gave them a better sense of the street’s rhythm: who was heading to work, how much traffic came through, where people walked their dogs, and whether they could picture starting their own day there. By the time we toured the house, they weren’t only evaluating the kitchen and bedrooms. They already understood what it might feel like to live there.

They bought the house, and later told me that walk was one of the reasons they felt so confident about the decision.

A showing tells you a lot about a property. An early walk tells you something about the life around it—and that’s usually harder to change.

b.text:
# The 7am Walk

Last month I had first-time buyers, the Pruitts, scheduled to tour a house on Sycamore Street. The night before, they couldn't sleep—nerves, excitement, all of it. So at 7am they drove over and just... walked the neighborhood.

When we did the official tour later, they already knew the street. They'd seen the retired couple watering their garden. They'd noticed the coffee shop two blocks down. They'd watched the school buses load up. They'd felt what it was actually like to live there, not just visit.

They made an offer that day. Closed three months later. Last week I got photos of them on the porch.

In 12 years, I've noticed the buyers who are happiest long-term are almost always the ones who've done this. They walk at different times. They sit in the driveway. They check out the commute during rush hour. They talk to neighbors. By the time they buy, the house isn't a transaction anymore—it's a place they already know.

If you're looking at houses: go back at 7am. Go back at 6pm. Go back on a Saturday. You'll know if it's right. You really will.
