setup: A general contractor is writing a short X thread to contractors, homeowners, and architects about a hidden joist problem and the lesson learned.

a.text:
Opened up the Maple Ave kitchen ceiling this morning to scope a new soffit run. Pulled a bead of plaster and saw joist #4 had a notch cut in it — big one, maybe 2 inches deep, bottom flange nearly gone. Probably from some cable install in the 90s. Nobody told the homeowner. Nobody told me. I found it because I had to go in.

Fix: sistered #4 with a full 2x10 LVL, glued and lag-screwed both sides. Two days for one guy instead of the half-day I had in the schedule. Materials about $60. Labor ate me about $480. Had to shift the backsplash guy to Thursday. All manageable, but it wasn't in the bid because you can't bid what you can't see until the drywall's off.

The lesson I keep having to relearn: your contingency isn't padding. On a 1923 rowhome where every previous contractor made a "quick fix" behind plaster, that 10% line item is the whole game. Not a surprise. Not an exception. The default assumption should be that something ugly is waiting behind the finish. Budget for the discovery, not just the planned scope.

Anyway. Maple Ave moves this afternoon. The homeowners got a $480 lesson about their own house, which is cheaper than the alternative. That's the job sometimes.

b.text:
1/ On the Maple Ave kitchen, we opened the ceiling over the sink and found two 2x8 floor joists cut midspan years ago to fit a drain. The floor still felt solid, but the cut was in the worst possible spot for load transfer.

2/ We temp-supported the floor, got an engineer’s note, sistered the damaged joists with LVL, and added hangers/blocking. Total cost to the client: about $2,600 and 2 extra days.

3/ Lesson: on older Pittsburgh houses, assume someone already made a mess behind the finish. Open early, price structural contingencies in writing, and don’t let a pipe route get solved with a saw.

setup: A solo indie game developer is writing a devlog recap for subscribers about his game's launch week sales, subreddit attention, review feedback, and upcoming 1.1 patch.

a.text:
# Week One

The game's out. Three years of nights and weekends, and now it's a thing people can buy, which still feels strange to type.

412 copies in the first seven days.

I've been staring at that number a lot. I don't have a good frame for it. It's not a breakout. It's also more than the zero I'd braced for at 3am on launch night when the store page went live and nothing happened for four hours. A few hundred of you follow this blog, so statistically some of those 412 are you, and I've been trying not to think too hard about what percentage of my sales are just people who felt bad for me. Either way: thanks. Genuinely.

Sales came in a spike on day one, dropped hard on day two, then flattened into a slow trickle of five to fifteen a day. Wishlist conversion was better than I expected. Refund rate is under 3%, which I'm choosing to read as a good sign.

The one thing that actually moved the needle was getting to the front page of a smallish subreddit — about 40k subscribers — where the post sat near the top for maybe six hours before sliding off. I watched the sales graph tick up in near real time, which was the most video-gamey experience I've had with my own video game. I didn't post it myself; someone else did, which I think is why it worked. I have not figured out how to replicate this and I suspect you can't.

A handful of reviews so far, mostly positive. One of them says the movement feels floaty.

They're right. I knew it before they said it. I've known it for probably a year and a half, and at some point "floaty" quietly became "the way the game feels" in my head because I'd stopped being able to tell the difference between a design decision and a thing I'd gotten used to. Reading someone else say it out loud in public was like getting caught. Not in a bad way. Just — oh, yeah, that.

So that's what 1.1 is. Targeting next month:

- **Movement overhaul.** Faster acceleration curve, shorter coyote time, actual snap on direction changes. Higher gravity on the descent so jumps have a shape instead of a drift. This will change how some of the mid-game platforming rooms play and I'll have to retune a few of them, which is most of why this is a month out and not a week.
- **A few soft-lock fixes** in the second area that two people have hit and reported. Embarrassing but easy.
- **Controller rebinding**, which I cut for launch and immediately regretted.
- **Options for the screen shake**, per about six separate requests.

I'm going to keep the old movement available behind a toggle for the first patch or two, mostly because I don't fully trust myself to not overcorrect.

Beyond that I don't know yet. There's a bigger content thing I've been sketching, and there's also the fact that I haven't had a free Saturday since 2022. Going to sit with both of those for a bit.

If you're playing it and something feels off, tell me. Turns out I need that more than I thought.

b.text:
# One Week In

I launched the game last Tuesday. 412 copies sold in the first week.

That's the headline. It still doesn't feel entirely real to type out.

The launch day was chaos in the best way—the game hit the front page of r/indiegames for about 6 hours, which sent a spike of traffic that made my hosting sweat a little. I kept refreshing Steam to see the numbers climb, which is probably not healthy but I couldn't stop myself. By end of day I'd made more money than I spent on the game's development. That's the part that actually feels surreal.

The reviews have been mostly positive. A lot of people loved the art direction and the puzzle design. A few people noted performance issues on older hardware that I'm already working on for the next patch. And yeah, one review said the movement feels floaty. They're right. I've been thinking about it since, and I know exactly what they mean—the character model isn't giving enough weight to the jump arc. I started prototyping a fix last week and it's already feeling better. That's going into 1.1 next month.

The player comments have been great to read. Some people are finding secrets I forgot I hid. Someone made fan art. Someone else said they played for five hours straight and lost track of time, which is honestly all I've ever wanted a game to do.

Right now I'm running through the bug reports, planning that movement patch, and trying not to work myself into the ground on updates. Three years of nights and weekends to get here. I'm going to try to actually sleep for a bit before I keep going.

Next devlog will be in two weeks when 1.1 is closer to done.

setup: A freelance wedding photographer is writing a blog post for couples about why to book a winter wedding.

a.text:
**Why I Actually Look Forward to Shooting Winter Weddings**

After six years behind the lens, mostly working within this metro area, I’ve heard the same assumption every single season: people treat winter weddings like the consolation prize. But here’s what actually happened in the back half of my career—in the last two years alone, I’ve shot eleven of them. Somewhere between November chill and January gray, my mindset shifted completely. Winter isn’t a placeholder anymore. It’s a different rhythm, and if you’re currently weighing your options on which month to lock in, here’s exactly what changes when you choose a cold-weather date.

**The pricing is real, not promotional.**  
Winter bookings run about thirty percent cheaper than peak-season rates. This isn’t a limited-time promo or a hidden fee waiver—it’s standard market adjustment. Thirty percent across a full photography package means you’re redirecting real capital toward other priorities: an upgraded menu, a better sound system, extra guest experiences, or simply a healthier financial buffer. I’m not saying you should pick a date solely for the discount, but if there’s a specific venue, caterer, or layout you’ve had your eye on that felt out of reach in August or September, winter pricing frequently makes it viable.

**The light behaves differently, and usually better.**  
I’ll be honest about the summer months we all romanticize: flat, overcast June skies kill contrast, flatten facial tones, and leave very little room for visual interest in outdoor portraits. Step into mid-November around three o’clock, and the equation flips. The sun sits lower, cuts cleaner angles, and passes straight through the canopy of deciduous trees still holding their last leaves or fully stripped to bare branches. Those limbs create natural frames, dappled shadows, and directional highlights that give portraits depth without artificial strobes. I’ve spent years learning to read that specific winter afternoon glow, and the images consistently deliver the quiet intimacy and striking clarity my clients ask for. It’s not softer because it’s colder; it’s stronger because it’s directional.

**Your timeline won’t be bottlenecked by vendor traffic.**  
In June, I’m routinely arriving at venues where the primary service road doubles as a loading zone for three or four other photography teams, videographers, rental companies, and floral designers all trying to unload simultaneously. Coordinated chaos sounds manageable until you’re watching your start time slip, your setup location shift twice, and your movement between ceremony space and cocktail hour dictated by who has the forklift first. Winter Saturdays are quiet. I pull into an open spot, load gear without navigating a convoy, move through doors without checking whose crew owns the hallway, and actually have breathing room to adjust lighting, reposition subjects, or step outside to catch a break in the clouds. That operational smoothness doesn’t just help me work faster—it keeps your day from feeling rushed or logistically cramped.

I’m not suggesting you abandon the long daylight hours or the garden-backdrop classic. If that’s your vision, pursue it. But if you’ve been hesitating to commit because you assumed winter just means shorter days and fewer options, reconsider. Eleven winter weddings in twenty-four months taught me to stop viewing these dates as secondary. They reward couples who prioritize intentional pacing, efficient vendor environments, and a light source that actually sculpts faces instead of washing them out. Plus, they respect your bottom line.

If you’ve already scoped a venue or started narrowing down months, drop me a note. Let’s look at your actual timeline, your must-have shots, and whether your ideal celebration lands better in the quiet grip of February than it does in the crowded stretch of June. Your date doesn’t have to follow the crowd to be the right one.

b.text:
# Why I Actually Like Shooting Winter Weddings

*Or: a confession from a photographer who spent years dreading them.*

For my first few years shooting weddings in this city, winter inquiries felt like a calendar problem. I said yes because January needed filling, not because I wanted the job. Somewhere along the way, that flipped. I've shot eleven winter weddings in the last two years, and they're now the bookings I look forward to most. Since a lot of couples asking me "when should we book?" are really asking "when is the best wedding," let me make the case for the season nobody plans for.

## The light. I'm serious about this one.

In November, around 3 p.m., the sun is already low. It comes in sideways through the bare branches, and those leafless trees break it into shafts and patterns that no lighting kit I own can replicate. There's direction to it. It gives a face shape.

Here's the part that might get me in trouble: that light is better for portraits than what we often get in June. Flat overcast June light is like a giant ceiling fixture — even, forgiving, and forgettable. Everyone is lit identically from every angle, which sounds kind and is actually the problem. Portraits need light with an angle and an opinion, and bare-tree light at 3 p.m. in November has both.

And because the sun sets early, your best-light portraits happen mid-afternoon — when your makeup is fresh and you've still got energy — instead of at 7:30 p.m., after you've been on your feet for eight hours and the schedule has already slipped twice.

## Nobody is fighting over your Saturday.

In June, I pull into a venue lot and there are regularly three or four other vendors there — another photographer's van, a videographer, a florist's delivery, all of us on overlapping timelines.

You feel that even if you never see the parking lot. It's why the getting-ready suite has a stranger's garment bag in it. It's why the coordinator is impossible to find, why the room flip starts while your grandmother is still sitting in it, why everyone is rushing. In January, the venue is yours. My timeline holds. The staff isn't stretched thin, so they're not rushing you either.

I know "the parking lot was roomy" sounds like a photographer convenience. It isn't. Calm is the thing I need most on a wedding day, and winter days have it.

## The part you already guessed: it's cheaper.

Winter bookings run about 30% cheaper for couples than peak-season dates. That's not a gimmick — it's how the industry prices the slow months, and it adds up fast. That difference is your videographer, or a real chunk of your venue, or the honeymoon.

But I want to be honest about the other side of it, because I've had couples seem almost apologetic about booking a discounted date: I'm not shooting eleven of these a year out of charity. The discount exists because demand is lower. I keep saying yes anyway because these have become my favorite weddings to shoot — the calm, the light, the day that actually runs on schedule. You're not getting a lesser wedding at a lower price. You're getting the same wedding at the time of year fewer people want it.

## Yes, it's cold. Plan for it, don't fear it.

I won't pretend otherwise. We plan around it: portraits in twenty-minute bursts with a warm room to retreat to, and a timeline that puts the outdoor portraits in that good light instead of after dark. And coat shots are not a compromise — a great coat is a better portrait prop than a shawl pretending it isn't freezing. The short day is a constraint, but it's the kind that makes the timeline better, not worse.

## If you're flexible on your date

Ask me about winter. After six years shooting in this area, I know exactly which spots near you hold that low November light at 3 p.m. — and my winter calendar has room in it.

setup: A small HVAC company owner is writing a how-to for homeowners on bleeding air from hot water baseboard radiators before winter.

a.text:
**How to Bleed Air from Baseboard Heating Before Winter**

Before the cold sets in, take a few minutes to bleed your baseboard heating system—it’s a simple task that can save you from uneven heating and costly service calls. Here’s how to do it right:

1. **Shut off the circulator/boiler** – Safety first. Turn off the system to prevent hot water from circulating while you work.

2. **Locate the bleeder valve** – Each baseboard unit has a small valve at one end, usually near the top. It may look like a tiny square or slotted screw.

3. **Prepare for water** – Place a cup or small container under the valve to catch any drips. Have a rag handy too.

4. **Open the valve slowly** – Use a bleeder key (or a flathead screwdriver if the valve is slotted) to turn the valve counterclockwise. You’ll hear a hissing sound as air escapes. Keep it open until water flows steadily with no air bubbles.

5. **Close the valve snugly** – Once water runs clear, tighten the valve just enough to stop the flow—don’t overtighten, or you could damage the valve seat.

6. **Work systematically** – Start with the baseboard unit closest to the boiler and move outward. **Don’t skip the basement loop**—this is where trapped air often hides, and ignoring it is the most common reason for cold radiators upstairs.

7. **Restart the system** – Once all units are bled, turn the boiler back on and check for even heat.

A little maintenance now means a warmer, more efficient home all winter. If you run into issues or prefer a pro to handle it, give us a call—we’re happy to help.

b.text:
# How to Bleed Air From Your Baseboard Radiators

Air gets trapped in your heating system every time the boiler cycles or water levels drop. When that air settles in your baseboard units, whole sections of the radiator stay cold while others heat up fine. The good news is bleeding them out takes maybe 20 minutes and costs you nothing.

## What You'll Need

- Flathead screwdriver or baseboard radiator key (the key works better and costs about $5)
- Small cup or container
- Towel or rag

## The Steps

**1. Turn off your boiler and circulator pump.** Let the system sit for a few minutes so the water settles.

**2. Locate the bleeder valve.** It's a small screw on the end cap of each baseboard unit, usually at the top. Most look like a tiny brass fitting.

**3. Start with the unit closest to your boiler.** This matters—you're working with gravity and water pressure, so starting nearest the source gets better results.

**4. Cup your hand underneath the valve.** You're about to release water, so catch it or put a small container there.

**5. Open the valve slowly.** Turn it counterclockwise a quarter-turn or less. You'll hear hissing—that's the air escaping. Keep it open until water flows out steady and the hissing stops completely. This usually takes 10-30 seconds per unit.

**6. Close it snug.** Turn clockwise until it's finger-tight. Don't crank it—the valve seat is brass and cracks easily if you overtighten.

**7. Move to the next baseboard unit.** Work your way through the house, always progressing outward from the boiler.

**8. Don't skip the basement.** This is where most homeowners mess up. Air rises, but heavy air and sediment settle in lower loops. If your upstairs radiators are hot and your basement units are still cold after bleeding them, you've found your problem.

**9. Turn the boiler and circulator back on.** Listen for normal cycling sounds. The system should quiet down after a minute or two.

## When to Call a Pro

If you've bled every unit including everything in the basement and you still have cold sections, you might have a circulation problem or a leak somewhere. That's when you want us out there to take a look.

setup: A retired Army staff sergeant is writing about coming home after his second deployment for readers of the veterans' writing workshop anthology.

a.text:
When I got back from my second deployment, I landed at the airport on a Tuesday. I had my A-bag slung over my shoulder and my uniform was stiff from thirty hours of travel. When I came off the terminal ramp, I saw my wife standing by the stairs. My daughter, Maya, was right next to her. She was six years old. I dropped my bag and walked toward them, but Maya didn't run out to meet me. She pulled back and hid behind her mother's leg, clutching the denim of Sarah’s jeans and peeking out with one eye. She didn't recognize me. To her, I was just a tall man in camouflage with a shaved head and a heavy voice she had only heard through a bad laptop speaker once a month. It took a while and a pack of gum from my pocket before she let me touch her shoulder.

A few days later, Sarah sent me to the store to get something for breakfast. I walked down the cereal aisle and stopped. I just stood there. There were forty different kinds of cereal stacked from the floor to the top shelf. Red boxes, blue boxes, boxes with cartoon characters, boxes with dried fruit. Down range, you ate whatever MRE was in the crate or you took the tray they handed you at the chow hall. You didn't make a choice, you just ate. I stood in front of those shelves for twenty minutes, looking at the options until my throat felt tight and my hands started to sweat. A woman pushing a cart asked if I was in line, and I couldn't answer her. I grabbed the first red box my hand touched and walked straight to the register.

The nights were the hardest part. For a year, I had slept in a CHU with my cot positioned so I was facing the door. If the handle moved or the light changed, I wanted to see it before anything else happened. 

At home, Sarah liked to leave our bedroom door cracked open a few inches so we could hear Maya if she woke up in the night. The first night back, I laid in the dark and felt like the room was spilling out into the hallway. Every instinct I had told me to get up, pull the door shut, and turn the bed around. I laid on my back for hours, looking at the thin strip of hallway light cutting across the carpet, trying to train my mind to leave it alone. 

It took months to get used to it. Some nights I still woke up in a sweat, stood up in the dark, and walked over to touch the wooden doorframe just to make sure where I was. Then I would leave it open and go back to bed.

b.text:
My daughter was six when I came home from my second deployment. At the airport, she stood behind her mother’s leg. I could see one eye and part of her forehead.

I had been thinking about seeing her for months. I figured she would run to me. I had pictured putting my bag down so I could catch her.

Instead, I put my bag down and stayed where I was.

“Hey, kiddo.”

She pulled back behind her mother. She didn’t recognize me at first. She knew I was coming home. Those turned out to be different things.

Her mother put a hand on her head and told her it was okay. I crouched down, which wasn’t comfortable after the flight, and asked her about the stuffed animal she was holding. She showed me its face without coming any closer.

People went around us with their suitcases. Somebody was holding flowers. I stayed down there and listened while she told me the animal’s name.

Eventually she stepped out. I didn’t reach for her right away.

On the walk to the car, she held her mother’s hand. I carried my bag and tried not to walk too fast.

A few days later, I went to the grocery store. We needed milk and some other things. I said I would get them. I wanted to do an ordinary job without anybody needing to help me.

I got through most of the list and stopped in the cereal aisle.

There must have been forty kinds. More, counting the different sizes. The same cereal came in a regular box, a family box, and a box big enough to feed a squad. There were versions with almonds, without almonds, with less sugar, with extra something.

I stood there for about twenty minutes.

I’d pick up a box and read it, then put it back. I wasn’t looking for anything special. I just couldn’t settle on one. Every time I thought I had, I saw another.

A woman said, “Excuse me,” and I moved my cart. Later she came through again from the other end. I was still there.

I had made decisions on deployment. Some had mattered a great deal. Now I couldn’t put cereal in a cart.

I finally took the kind I remembered eating before I left. At home, I put it in the cupboard and the milk in the refrigerator.

“What took so long?”

“Couldn’t find a few things.”

Nobody asked which things. I was glad of that.

At night, I slept facing the bedroom door. I had done it for a year, and I kept doing it after I got home. If I woke up turned the other way, I rolled back.

My wife liked the door open so we could hear our daughter. I wanted it shut. With it open, there was a stretch of hallway I couldn’t see from the bed.

The first few nights, I got up and closed it after my wife fell asleep. Then our daughter would need something, and my wife would get up, and the door would be open again.

We had a short argument about it one morning. We were both tired. I said I slept better with it closed. She said our daughter had been able to come in whenever she needed to for the whole year I was gone.

I didn’t have much to say to that.

I tried leaving it open a few inches. The latch would click when the air came on, so I opened it farther. I lay on my side and watched the doorway. Sometimes I got up to check the hall even though I knew what was in it: the bathroom, the linen closet, my daughter’s room.

During the day, she got used to me being around. She asked me to open things. She brought me papers from school and explained which ones I was supposed to keep. Sometimes she started telling her mother something, then remembered I was sitting there and told me too.

I learned which cereal she ate. It wasn’t the one I had bought.

One night I woke to her standing in the bedroom doorway. I lifted my head too fast, and she stopped.

“What’s wrong?” I asked.

“I need water.”

There was a cup in the bathroom, but I got up and went to the kitchen with her. She waited while I took a glass down. I filled it halfway so she wouldn’t spill it carrying it back.

She drank standing by the sink, both hands around the glass. Then she handed it to me.

I walked her back to bed. She climbed in and pulled the blanket up, and I moved a stuffed animal out from under her shoulder.

“Night, Dad,” she said.

I went back to our room. My wife shifted when I got in, then settled. I lay down facing the doorway. I could hear our daughter cough once down the hall.

The door stayed open.

1/7 Last Saturday night, 220 people showed up for Hendricks County Food Bridge's annual gala. I cried in the kitchen at 7:45 pm. Not sad tears. You'll understand in a sec. Thread on the evening, the disaster, and the $38,000 you all said yes to. 🧵

3/7 Two days before the event, our caterer called. "I'm in. I'm out. Can't make it work." 220 plates. 48 hours. I sat at my kitchen table in my work clothes and thought, well. We're serving cheese cubes and crackers at the Holiday Inn ballroom.

4/7 I called everyone I knew. Then I called Maggiore's. Full honest ask: "We are desperate. Can you feed 220 people Saturday?" They said yes. Full dinner. Baked chicken parmesan, the works. Delivered, plated, on time. Maggiore's, you saved our whole year. Thank you. Truly.

5/7 So. Saturday night. 220 neighbors in a room. The auction got loud. Someone's grandma won the fishing trip. A volunteer I've known for nine years grabbed my hand mid-speech and said "you good?" and I was. The room felt like a family reunion where everyone brought a plate.

6/7 Final number: $38,000 raised against a $30,000 goal. That's roughly 12,000 meals. That's the September problem not being a problem. Every dollar here is someone choosing to be in the room with us, which honestly matters more than the total.

7/7 So thank you. To everyone who bought a ticket, volunteered at the door, donated an auction item, or just shared the flyer. And Maggiore's specifically: you had no obligation, and you showed up like it was your own family's kitchen. That's the county we live in. Grateful beyond words. 🤍

setup: A high school girls' soccer and track coach is writing an op-ed urging turf funding for the girls' field.

a.text:
**Put Our Girls On Turf Too**

The last two seasons, my team has had nine games rained out or moved. Not delayed. Rained out or moved to another school's field because ours was underwater.

I coach girls soccer and track at the high school. I'm not a writer, I do it for the coaching stipend. But I'm tired of telling 16-year-olds we don't have a place to play because it rained yesterday.

Our field is the low grass field behind the school. It doesn't drain. After any real rain it's ankle-deep mud for three days. We practice in it, we slide all over it, and we try not to get hurt in it. We sprint around the swampy spots and we tell parents to bring boots to sit on the hill.

Last October one of my sophomores tore her ACL in a game. She wasn't hit. She was dribbling, stepped in a rut in our own field where the grass had washed out, and her knee went. She missed basketball season and she's missing this whole season. I coach track, too. I know what a bad surface looks like. That field is a bad surface.

This is a safety problem and it's a fairness problem.

The boys football field got turf in 2019. It's great. It drains, it's lined, they never lose a home game to weather. Our girls have been playing on a field that floods if you look at it wrong for six more years. If this were the football field, it would have been fixed a long time ago. Actually, it was.

I get it, turf isn't cheap. The board has a lot to pay for. But we are not asking for a stadium or lights or a press box. We are asking for a flat field that works when it rains. A field where we don't have to bus to the other team's school and call it a "home" game. A field where kids aren't worrying about what hole they're going to step in.

The school board votes on the facilities budget next week. Put turf for the girls soccer field in it.

Our girls deserve the same shot the boys have had since 2019 - to actually play their home games, on their home field, without getting hurt.

b.text:
The girls' soccer field at our high school is a hazard, plain and simple. 

Over the last two seasons, we’ve had nine games either rained out or moved to other facilities because our grass field floods the second it drizzles. You can’t play real soccer in a mud pit, and spending half the season rescheduling games teaches these kids that their time doesn't matter.

But the scheduling headaches are nothing compared to the safety risks. Last October, one of my players tore her ACL. She wasn’t tackled. She didn’t make a bad cut. She stepped in a deep rut near the 18-yard box and her knee gave out. She had surgery, missed her club season, and is still doing rehab. That injury was entirely preventable if she had been playing on a level, maintained surface. 

Meanwhile, the boys’ football field has had artificial turf since 2019. I’m glad they have it. Football is a brutal sport and they need a safe, reliable surface. But it is incredibly difficult to look my girls in the eye and explain why their safety is treated as secondary. They put in the same offseason work, they run the same conditioning, and they represent this school just as much as the boys do. 

The school board is finalizing next year’s facilities budget. Putting turf on the girls' soccer field isn't a luxury request. It is a basic requirement for player safety and fairness. 

I coach for the stipend and because I care about these kids, not because I want to be a writer. But I am tired of watching my players pay the physical and competitive price for a double standard. Fund the turf for the girls' field. Let them play on equal ground.

setup: A remote software engineer is writing a 6-month standing desk review for blog readers researching standing desks.

a.text:
**6-Month Review: Jarvik L2 Standing Desk**

**No affiliate links. No sponsorships. Just six months of daily use.**

I bought the Jarvik L2 about six months ago as my primary standing desk for remote software engineering work. If you’re researching this desk and want a straight answer: at $549, it’s worth buying. At $749, I’d look elsewhere.

The L2 is a solid mid-tier standing desk, but it has some quirks that matter when you’re using it eight to ten hours a day.

### The Good: Fast, Quiet Motor

The first thing you notice is the motor speed and noise. The Jarvik L2 lifts noticeably faster than a lot of comparable single-motor desks, and it’s quiet enough that I don’t feel self-conscious using it while on video calls.

For reference, I use it at a full-time remote engineering job with daily standups, pairing sessions, and client calls. The motor hum is there, but it’s not whiny, buzzy, or obnoxious. It’s a clean mechanical sound, not something that makes your guests on Zoom ask, “Is that a drill?”

That matters. If you’re in a quiet apartment or you’re on calls all day, a loud lift can become its own weird problem. The L2 doesn’t have that issue.

It also moves without jerking or hesitating under normal load. My setup is typical for software work: dual monitor arm, keyboard tray/stand, mouse, speakers, laptop, cables, and a few office accessories. The desk handles it fine.

### The Bad: It Wobbles at Full Height

This is the biggest downside.

When I raise the L2 to my maximum standing height, it wobbles when I type hard. Not dramatically, not in a way that feels unsafe, but in a way that becomes noticeable and mildly annoying. The problem is specific to height. Lower down, it’s stable enough. At full standing height, aggressive typing, clicking, or shifting pressure can create a subtle shake.

For some people, that may not matter. If you have a lighter typing style or don’t max out the height, it might be invisible. But for a developer who spends most of the day typing at a high-ish standing desk, it’s a real issue.

The wobble isn’t catastrophic, but it undercuts the premium feel. It’s also the kind of thing that doesn’t show up in a five-minute showroom test, but absolutely does after months of daily use.

I’ve learned to live with it, but I wouldn’t pretend it’s perfect. If you need full stability at maximum standing height, test the desk at the height you’ll actually use before buying. Do not rely on the manufacturer’s “it’s stable” claim alone.

### The Weird: Memory Presets Drift About a Centimeter

The Jarvik L2 has memory presets, which should be convenient. In practice, mine drift by roughly a centimeter over time.

I set “sit” and “stand” positions once, assuming I’d never touch them again. For a while, that worked. Then I started noticing that the stand preset no longer hit the exact height I wanted. Not by much. Maybe 5–10mm. I would have dismissed it as feeling if I hadn’t measured it.

It’s not enough to break the desk’s usefulness, but it is enough to break the promise of the feature.

If you’re the kind of person who obsessively cares about ergonomic precision—and honestly, some software engineers do—that one-centimeter drift can be annoying. You end up re-saving the preset more often than you should. It’s minor, but it’s a quality-of-life thing that shouldn’t happen on a desk at this price point.

At $549, it’s forgivable. At $749, it’s annoying.

### The Ugly: Cable Tray Is Garbage

The cable tray is, bluntly, garbage.

It looks like a reasonable add-on on paper. In reality, it’s fiddly, under-designed, and not worth the desk price. The mounting and routing system feels like an afterthought. It does not help organize cables in a meaningful way for a normal dual-monitor dev setup.

If you’re expecting it to clean up your desk, you’ll be disappointed. If you already have your own cable management solution, you can ignore it. If you’re counting on the Jarvik L2’s cable tray to do the job, don’t budget for that.

This is the part of the desk I most wish had been better executed.

### Build and Daily Experience

Overall build quality is good. The desktop feels solid, the frame is mostly sturdy, and the desk doesn’t look cheap once set up. Assembly was not glamorous, but it was manageable. The instructions are fine. The hardware is fine. Nothing is perfect, but nothing is a dealbreaker either.

The surface is easy enough to keep clean, which matters when you’re working from home all day. It doesn’t feel fragile under monitor arms or regular use. The frame is stable enough for sitting and lower standing positions, but not fully satisfying at max height.

For remote work, it does the job. I spend most of my day standing, and the fast motor encourages me to move between positions. That’s one of the real benefits of the desk: because raising and lowering is quiet and quick, I actually use it throughout the day.

That’s important. A standing desk is only valuable if you move. The L2 does not make movement feel like a chore.

### Who It’s For

I’d recommend the Jarvik L2 if:

- You want a fast, quiet motor.
- You spend most of your workday at a sitting-to-standing range.
- You value simplicity and don’t want a giant touchscreen or overly complicated control panel.
- You’re comfortable doing your own cable management.
- You caught it on sale.

I’d be cautious if:

- You need absolutely stable typing at your maximum standing height.
- You care about precise memory positions.
- You expect the included cable tray to solve your cable mess.
- You are comparing it at full MSRP.

### Verdict

**Worth it at $549. Not at $749.**

The Jarvik L2 is a good desk at a discounted price. It is not a great desk at the full price when you factor in the wobble at full height, the drifting presets, and the useless cable tray.

If you buy it on sale, you get a fast, quiet, capable standing desk with only minor annoyances. If you pay full price, those annoyances stop being minor. The price makes the difference.

For me, after six months of daily remote engineering use, it still earns its keep. But it earns it because I paid $549—not $749.

b.text:
Six months ago, I bought the Jarvik L2 standing desk to replace a static butcher-block setup in my home office. I work remotely as a software engineer, which means this desk gets used 45 to 50 hours a week, holding a 34-inch ultrawide, a vertical 27-inch secondary display, studio monitors, a laptop dock, and a heavy mechanical keyboard. 

I don’t use affiliate links, and I bought this with my own money. Here is the reality of living with the L2 after half a year of daily use.

### The Motor and Lifting Mechanism
The dual motors are genuinely good. They are whisper-quiet—more of a low-pitched hum than the whiny electric grind you get on sub-$400 Amazon specials—and they clear the travel range fast (roughly 1.5 inches per second under load). Transitions don't interrupt calls, and the anti-collision sensor is sensitive enough to stop before crushing an armrest without throwing false positives. From an electro-mechanical standpoint, the lifting columns perform well.

### The Annoyances: Wobble and Drift
Now for the trade-offs:

**1. High-extension wobble.** 
I’m 5'11". At my preferred standing height (around 43 inches), the desk is stable enough. But at full extension (48 inches), lateral rigidity falls apart. If you are a heavy typer—especially on tactile or clicky mechanical switches—your monitors will shake. It’s not going to dump a cup of coffee, but the micro-vibrations on mounted displays are noticeable and annoying when reading code. If you are over 6 feet tall, the structural stability at your standing height will be a compromise.

**2. Memory preset drift.** 
The handset looks sleek, but the firmware has a calibration retention problem. Over the course of three to four weeks, my standing preset drifts upward by about a centimeter. I only notice because my shoulder alignment starts feeling slightly off, and a quick check with a tape measure confirms the height readout is lying. Power cycling the controller and resetting the zero-point fixes it, but I shouldn't have to recalibrate my desk's digital brain once a month.

**3. The stock cable management tray is garbage.** 
Don’t factor the included cable tray into your buying decision. It’s stamped sheet metal that flexes under the weight of a single heavy-duty surge protector and a couple of power bricks. The mounting brackets also leave almost no clearance for bulky plugs. I threw it in the recycling bin within forty-eight hours and bolted a third-party wire basket underneath instead.

### The Verdict
The Jarvik L2 is a classic mid-tier product masquerading as high-end hardware. 

* **At its $749 MSRP:** Hard pass. At that tier, you should be looking at an Uplift V2 Commercial or a Deskhaus frame that offers real crossbar stability, better controller firmware, and usable wire management out of the box.
* **At the $549 sale price:** Buy it, with reservations. If you can snag it on sale, the smooth, quiet motor drive justifies the cost—provided you’re willing to spend an extra $40 on an aftermarket cable tray and don't mind a slight monitor wobble while typing at full extension.

setup: A first-year nursing student is writing a scholarship essay about her first ER rotation for scholarship committee readers.

a.text:
My first week in the ER didn't look anything like my textbooks. On my second day, I tried to draw blood from an older guy with diabetes. His veins were in bad shape. I missed the first time. Then the second. Then the third. He was getting pale and I was sweating through my scrubs. I had to step back, take a breath, and apologize. I asked him for one more try. I felt around, found a deep spot on his arm, and finally got the flash of blood in the tube on the fourth try. He patted my arm and told me I'd get it easier next time. It taught me that messing up in front of a patient is part of the job, and being honest about it is how you earn their trust.

The next day, I learned that nursing isn't always about needles and meds. A man came in with a deep cut on his leg that needed to be cleaned out. It was going to hurt, and his wife was stuck in traffic. He was scared and gripping the bed rails. My preceptor told me to just stay with him. So, I pulled up a stool and held his hand while the doctor scrubbed the wound. I just talked to him about his dog and squeezed his hand when he winced. It wasn't a medical procedure, but it was the most important thing I did that shift.

By the end of the week, the ER showed me its harder side. A patient's heart stopped in one of the bays. The room was packed, and my preceptor told me to step out and restock the gauze. I stood at the supply cart just outside the door. Through the heavy curtain, I could hear the sound of chest compressions and the team counting out loud. I packed the gauze, my hands shaking a little. I felt pretty useless in that moment, but I also realized that every single job in that room mattered. The team needed that gauze ready for when they got the patient back.

I am applying for this scholarship because I know I have a lot to learn, but I also know I am in the right place. The ER is loud, messy, and hard. But holding a scared patient's hand, pushing through a failed blood draw, and standing outside a curtain listening to a team fight for a life showed me what this job really is. I just want the chance to keep learning how to do it well.

b.text:
In the skills lab, the plastic arm never flinches. It has thick, blue rubber veins that never roll, never collapse, and never bleed when you mess up. 

My third day in the ER, I met a real arm. It belonged to an older man with diabetes who had been poked so many times over the last twenty years that his skin felt tough, like an old baseball glove. I prepped the site, anchored the vein, and slid the needle in. Nothing. I tried again on the other side. Nothing. By the third miss, my face was burning hot under my mask, my hands were shaking, and I was about ready to apologize and run out of the room to find my preceptor. 

The man just looked at me, let out a tired breath, and said, "Take a second, kid. Try one more time. I’ve got all day." I took a deep breath, backed out, found a tiny vein near his wrist, and went in slow. Dark red blood finally filled the tube. He gave me a small nod, and I taped a cotton ball over the puncture. That fourth stick taught me more about nursing than any textbook: when you fail, you don't get to run away and feel bad for yourself. You take a breath, adjust, and do the job right because the person in the bed needs you to.

The ER moves fast, and as a first-year student, most of my job was trying to stay out of the way while still being useful. On Thursday, an ambulance brought in a woman in cardiac arrest. The room exploded into motion—doctors, respiratory therapists, nurses shouting numbers and drawing meds. I froze in the doorway until a nurse shoved a box into my chest and said, "Go restock the gauze in cart three." 

I felt embarrassed, like I was being sent to sit at the kids' table. But as I stood outside the bay, stuffing packages of 4x4 gauze into the plastic bins, I could hear them through the curtain. "One, two, three, four, five..." counting out chest compressions. Steady and loud. I realized then that somebody has to make sure the gauze is there when the bleeding starts, and somebody has to make sure the suction tubes are ready. It wasn't glorious, but it mattered. Being a nurse isn't always about being the hero in the middle of the room; it’s about making sure the machine keeps running so the patient has a chance.

Later that same shift, a man came in with a nasty, infected laceration on his leg that needed a deep cleaning. The doctor said it was going to hurt. The man looked terrified. His wife was his rock, but she was stuck in bumper-to-bumper traffic on the interstate, thirty miles away. He had nobody with him. When the doctor picked up the scrub brush, the man reached out into the empty air, and I stepped in and put my hand in his. He squeezed down so hard my knuckles ground together. He didn't say a word, and neither did I. I just stood on my sore feet, leaned against the rail of the gurney, and let him squeeze until the doctor was finished. 

Before this rotation, I thought being a good nurse was mostly about knowing your lab values, your dosages, and your anatomy. Those things matter, of course. You can't help anyone if you don't know the science. But walking out of the ER at the end of that first week, my scrubs stained and my back aching, I realized the hard part is the human part. It’s staying calm when your hands are shaking, doing the grunt work without complaining, and standing still so a scared stranger doesn't have to hurt alone.

Nursing school is the hardest thing I have ever done, and paying for it on my own makes it even harder. Between tuition, gas to get to clinicals, and the hours I have to spend studying instead of working a full-time job, money is tight every single month. This scholarship would take off some of that financial weight so I can focus on passing my classes, sharpening my skills, and getting back onto the floor. I know I have a lot left to learn, but I also know I'm meant to be there, and I’m ready to put the work in.

setup: A solo indie game developer is writing a devlog recap for subscribers about his game's launch week sales, subreddit attention, review feedback, and upcoming 1.1 patch.

a.text:
# Week One: The Game Is Out

So it happened. After three years of nights and weekends, the game launched last Tuesday.

## The numbers

412 copies sold in the first week.

I don't have a great frame of reference for whether that's good or bad for a first release from a nobody with no marketing budget, but it's 412 more than zero, and honestly seeing the sales counter tick up that first day was surreal. I refreshed the dashboard way more than I'd like to admit.

## The reddit thing

Someone posted the game to a smaller subreddit and it hit the front page there for about six hours. That drove the biggest spike in wishlists and probably a decent chunk of the sales. I had nothing to do with it — I found out because my Steam traffic graph suddenly looked wrong. If you were part of that thread, thanks. That was a fun six hours.

## The floaty movement

One review said the movement feels floaty. My first instinct was to get defensive, and then I played my own game for twenty minutes and... yeah. They're right. It's floaty. I think I got so used to it over three years that I stopped noticing.

So that's getting fixed. I'm reworking the acceleration curves and adding a bit more weight to landings. It's already feeling better in my dev build.

## What's next

Patch 1.1 is coming next month. Main focus is the movement fix, plus a handful of smaller bugs people have reported (thank you to everyone who emailed or posted in the discussions — you've caught stuff I never would have).

After that ships, I'll figure out what comes next. For now I'm going to keep answering emails, keep fixing bugs, and maybe sleep a normal amount for the first time in a while.

Thanks for following along. More soon.

b.text:
**Week one**

It's out. It's been out for eight days now, which is long enough that I've stopped refreshing the sales page every twenty minutes and moved on to refreshing it every hour or so.

Here's where things stand.

412 copies sold in the first week. I don't have a great sense of whether that's good or bad relative to other first-time solo releases, and honestly I've stopped trying to figure it out. It's 412 people who paid money for something I made at my kitchen table over three years of evenings and Saturdays. That's the number. I keep looking at it.

On day two, someone posted it to a subreddit I'd never heard of — small, a few thousand people, very specific about the kind of games it likes. It sat on the front page there for about six hours. I watched the comment thread the whole time like it was a sporting event. Most of the sales spike came from that window, and then it tapered off the way everyone told me it would. I did not post it there myself. I don't know who did. If it was one of you, thanks.

Reviews are mostly positive so far, which I'm relieved about. A handful mention the writing, a couple mention the art, one person wrote three paragraphs about a puzzle in the second area and I've read it maybe a dozen times.

One review said the movement feels floaty. It's a mixed review, not a negative one, and the person was pretty fair about it. And they're right. I've known the movement was a little soft for a long time — I'd tuned it early on, got used to it, and after a certain point I just stopped noticing. Reading someone describe it fresh made me boot the game up and play the first area again, and yeah. It's floaty. Jump apex hangs too long, air control is too generous, landing doesn't have enough weight to it. I'd convinced myself it was a stylistic choice. It wasn't really. It was just the first thing that felt okay and then I built everything else on top of it.

So that's the main thing going into 1.1, which I'm aiming to have out next month:

- Retuning jump gravity and air control. Tighter fall, less drift. I'll probably keep a hair of the floatiness because the level geometry was built around it and I don't want to break every gap in the game, but it'll be noticeably firmer.
- Landing feedback — a small squash and a bit more sound on touchdown.
- Two crash bugs that got reported on launch day. Both are fixed on my end already; they'll ride along with the patch.
- The settings menu doesn't remember your resolution between sessions. It will.
- A few text fixes people caught.

I'll put a beta branch up in a couple of weeks for anyone who wants to try the new movement before it goes live, since I'd rather hear "this is worse now" from thirty people than from four hundred.

After 1.1 I genuinely don't know yet. There's a list of things I cut during development that I'd like to look at again, but I'm not going to promise any of it until I've had a few weeks to not be exhausted.

That's it. That's the week. Thanks to everyone who bought it, everyone who told a friend, and the person who wrote three paragraphs about the puzzle.

More when there's more.

setup: A small dog grooming salon owner is writing a how-to for dog owners about preventing coat matting between grooming visits.

a.text:
If there’s one thing I see almost every week on my grooming table, it’s a sweet pup whose owner tried to do the right thing at home, only to accidentally turn a tiny tangle into a major headache. The mistake I see constantly is people giving their dog a bath first, thinking the warm water and shampoo will help loosen up the mats. I totally understand the logic, but water actually does the exact opposite. Wetting matted fur—especially on curly doodley coats or thick double-coated breeds—acts just like wool in a hot wash. It shrinks, tightens, and turns that soft hair into a dense, felt pad that locks the knots in way tighter than they were before. Always, always brush thoroughly before a bath at home, never after. 

When you do sit down for a brushing session, the tool you want in your hand is a good slicker brush. The trick here is technique: use short, straight line strokes rather than rubbing the brush in circles. Moving in circles just twists the hair around itself and creates brand-new tangles. Think of it like a gentle "pat and pull" motion, lifting up a section of coat with one hand and brushing out the hair underneath it layer by layer so you’re actually reaching the skin, not just skimming the surface.

Don't try to tackle the whole dog at once. Work in small sections, and make a habit of starting in the sneaky trouble spots where mats always form first. Check right behind the ears where the skin is delicate, and tuck your fingers under the front legs into the armpits. Those high-friction areas gather tiny tangles long before you’ll ever notice them on the dog's back or sides.

If you’re working through a section and catch a mat that’s already starting to clump together, step away from the brush for a second. Ripping through a tight knot hurts your pup and makes them dread brush time. Instead, grab a little dab of dog conditioner—or even a leave-in coat spray—and work it straight into the knot using just your fingers. Gently massage it in and use your thumbs to wiggle the hair strands apart from the outside in. Once you’ve broken up the bulk of the knot with your hands, *then* you can bring in your brush or comb to finish smoothing it out. 

Taking five or ten minutes to work through these high-friction spots a couple of times a week keeps your dog comfortable and saves their coat. And remember, if a mat ever gets too tight or sits right against the skin, don't fight it—just let us know at your next visit and we’ll safely take care of it on the table.

b.text:
One of the biggest things I wish more dog owners knew is that if you’re trying to keep a coat from matting, the work starts before bath time, not after.

I see this all the time with double-coated dogs and curly-coated breeds: a pet comes in for grooming, the coat has a few tangles, and the owner has already tried bathing first thinking it would help loosen everything up. It usually does the opposite. Once that coat gets wet, especially if there are already knots starting, those tangles can tighten up and turn into a felt-like pad that’s much harder to work through.

At home, the best habit is to brush before the bath, never after. If the coat is already a little tangled, get those areas handled first while the hair is dry. A slicker brush works well for this, but the key is how you use it. Go in short, straight line strokes instead of scrubbing in circles. Circles tend to just mash the hair around and hide the problem instead of actually separating it.

It also helps to work in small sections so you’re not missing the spots that mat the fastest. Around here, I always tell people to start behind the ears and under the front legs, because that’s where mats usually show up first. Those spots rub a lot, and they can go from “a little fluffy” to “oh no” pretty quickly if they’re ignored.

If you already feel a mat starting, don’t go straight in with a brush or comb and try to force it apart. That usually just makes the dog uncomfortable and can tighten the knot more. Instead, use your fingers first and work a little conditioner into the area to help loosen it up before you start brushing.

The main thing is to catch tangles early and keep up with them between grooming visits. A few minutes of brushing in the right way can save your dog a lot of discomfort later, and it makes the next grooming appointment much easier too.

setup: A freelance wedding photographer is writing a blog post for couples about why to book a winter wedding.

a.text:
# Why I Actually Like Photographing Winter Weddings Now

After six years photographing weddings, mostly in the same metro area, I have opinions about seasons. And lately, winter has been moving up my list.

I’ve photographed 11 winter weddings in the last two years. That’s enough to say this isn’t me remembering one unusually lovely afternoon and building a whole argument around it. I genuinely like shooting them now—and not just because couples can save money.

Although, let’s start there.

## About 30% cheaper is worth talking about

Winter bookings run about 30% cheaper for the couple. The exact difference depends on your date and what you’re booking, but that’s a meaningful amount—not a tiny discount you’ll barely notice.

It might give you room for something you really want. It might simply mean spending less on your wedding. Both are perfectly good outcomes.

I wouldn’t tell you to choose a winter date solely for the savings if you’ve always wanted an outdoor ceremony in warm weather. But if you’re choosing a June Saturday because it feels like the default, winter deserves a proper look before you commit.

## I’ll take November light through bare trees

Here’s my very specific photography opinion: the light coming through bare trees around 3 p.m. in November is honestly better for portraits than flat, overcast June light.

Overcast summer light is easy to work with. It’s soft and fairly predictable. But easy isn’t always interesting.

That low November sun can give portraits direction and depth. Without a full canopy of leaves, light reaches places it doesn’t in summer. The branches make a quieter backdrop, and we can use the light coming between them rather than hunting for a gap in dense shade.

This is not a promise that your November wedding will come with sunshine. Weather remains weather. But winter light isn’t something I’m reluctantly making the best of. On the right afternoon, it’s the light I’d choose.

The catch is timing. If you want those portraits, we need to build the day around the available daylight. We can’t leave them until after a late-afternoon ceremony and expect June hours.

## Even the parking lot is less of a production

This isn’t the glamorous part of wedding photography, but it affects how a day feels.

In June, I’m often sharing the parking lot with three or four other vendors, all trying to get where they need to be. There’s equipment coming out of cars, people unloading, and everyone working against a clock.

At winter weddings, I’m not dealing with that same parking-lot pileup.

Does a quieter parking lot make your portraits better by itself? No. But fewer logistical bottlenecks help. Getting in, getting set up, and moving between parts of the day with less friction is genuinely pleasant. After six years, I appreciate that more than I expected to.

## Winter works best when we plan for winter

I like winter weddings. I don’t like pretending they’re summer weddings with different flowers.

There’s less daylight. It may be cold enough that a long outdoor portrait session stops being fun very quickly. We need an indoor option we actually like, not just somewhere to retreat if the weather gets unpleasant.

My approach is to plan the outdoor photographs deliberately: know where we’re going, use the best light we have, and avoid keeping you outside longer than necessary. Then let you get back to your people.

That’s also why I’d rather talk about your photography timeline before you lock in every detail of the day. A small change to the ceremony time can make a big difference to what’s possible.

## So, should you book a winter wedding?

If warm evenings and a late sunset are central to the wedding you want, probably not. There’s no need to talk yourself out of something you care about.

But if you’re flexible on the season, I’d seriously consider it. About 30% cheaper, the possibility of genuinely excellent portrait light, and less of the June logistical scrum are solid reasons.

Eleven winter weddings in two years have changed how I think about these dates. I’m not looking at them as the compromise option anymore.

If you’re weighing a winter date, get in touch before you set the ceremony time. Let’s look at the daylight as well as the calendar.

b.text:
## Why I’ve Genuinely Fallen for Winter Weddings

Six years ago, if you’d asked me when I wanted to shoot weddings, I would have said late spring through early fall without hesitating. Everyone does. Warm weather, long evenings, green trees, easy driving—on paper, it sounds like the dream.

And I still love a good summer wedding. But after shooting more off-season weddings over the last couple of years, I’ve realized something that surprised me:

I actually love winter weddings now.

Not in a “well, every season has its own beauty” sort of way. In a very practical, photographer-brain, I’m-honestly-having-more-fun way.

There are a few reasons for it.

### The light is better than people think

Couples often worry that winter means dark, gray, depressing photos. I get it. But winter light can be gorgeous in a way people don’t expect.

In November, especially around 3 p.m., the sun sits lower and the light comes through bare trees in this soft, directional way that I love for portraits. It’s not harsh. It’s not flat. It has shape. It has mood.

Honestly, I’ll take that over a flat overcast June day many times.

Summer light can be beautiful too, but it’s not automatically better. Bright midday sun can create hard shadows. Overcast summer days can look dull and washed out. Winter gives me something different to work with—more texture, more atmosphere, more dimension.

And bare trees? They’re not the disadvantage people think they are. They create natural framing, interesting lines, and a sense of place. They let light through in ways full summer foliage doesn’t. Some of my favorite portraits from the last couple of years were shot in conditions couples initially worried would be “too bleak.”

They weren’t bleak at all. They were striking.

### Winter weddings are calmer

This is the part nobody really talks about when they’re choosing a date.

In June, I might show up to a venue and realize I’m sharing the parking lot with three or four other vendors all shooting different events, or the space feels crowded, or the timeline is tight because everything is booked back-to-back.

Winter weddings often feel different.

There’s more breathing room. Fewer events competing for the same spaces. Less chaos. Sometimes venues are more flexible, timelines feel less rushed, and the whole day has a quieter rhythm.

That matters for photos.

When a day feels calmer, couples usually feel calmer. And when couples feel calmer, they photograph more like themselves. Less performance. Less stress. More real.

That’s always going to make better images.

### Your photos can feel more like yours

Winter weddings have a built-in sense of atmosphere.

Maybe it’s the earlier sunset, the candlelight, the layers, the texture of a coat or shawl, the moodiness of a dark sky behind a venue at dusk. Maybe it’s the fact that winter weddings often feel more intentional because the couple chose them for a reason, not just because it was the “default” wedding season.

Whatever it is, I’ve noticed that winter weddings often end up feeling more distinctive.

They don’t look like every other summer wedding at the same venue in the same golden hour slot. They have their own tone.

I like that.

### It can also be a smarter booking decision

This is the practical part.

Winter bookings often run about 30% cheaper for couples. That’s not a tiny difference. For a lot of couples, that’s the difference between affording the photographer they really want and feeling stretched too thin.

I’ve shot eleven winter weddings over the last two years, and I keep coming back to the same conclusion: couples considering an off-season date should seriously consider it.

Not because it’s cheaper—though it can be.

But because the day can feel more personal, the light can be surprisingly beautiful, and the experience can be calmer than the peak-season version.

If you’re trying to decide between a June date and a winter date, I wouldn’t automatically choose June just because that’s what everyone does.

Some of my favorite work has come from weddings couples planned outside the box.

And if you’re nervous about winter light? Don’t be.

That 3 p.m. November glow through bare branches might end up being one of the best parts of your gallery.

setup: A freelance wedding photographer is writing a blog post for couples about why to book a winter wedding.

a.text:
**Why I Actually Look Forward to Shooting Winter Weddings**

After six years behind the lens, mostly working within this metro area, I’ve heard the same assumption every single season: people treat winter weddings like the consolation prize. But here’s what actually happened in the back half of my career—in the last two years alone, I’ve shot eleven of them. Somewhere between November chill and January gray, my mindset shifted completely. Winter isn’t a placeholder anymore. It’s a different rhythm, and if you’re currently weighing your options on which month to lock in, here’s exactly what changes when you choose a cold-weather date.

**The pricing is real, not promotional.**  
Winter bookings run about thirty percent cheaper than peak-season rates. This isn’t a limited-time promo or a hidden fee waiver—it’s standard market adjustment. Thirty percent across a full photography package means you’re redirecting real capital toward other priorities: an upgraded menu, a better sound system, extra guest experiences, or simply a healthier financial buffer. I’m not saying you should pick a date solely for the discount, but if there’s a specific venue, caterer, or layout you’ve had your eye on that felt out of reach in August or September, winter pricing frequently makes it viable.

**The light behaves differently, and usually better.**  
I’ll be honest about the summer months we all romanticize: flat, overcast June skies kill contrast, flatten facial tones, and leave very little room for visual interest in outdoor portraits. Step into mid-November around three o’clock, and the equation flips. The sun sits lower, cuts cleaner angles, and passes straight through the canopy of deciduous trees still holding their last leaves or fully stripped to bare branches. Those limbs create natural frames, dappled shadows, and directional highlights that give portraits depth without artificial strobes. I’ve spent years learning to read that specific winter afternoon glow, and the images consistently deliver the quiet intimacy and striking clarity my clients ask for. It’s not softer because it’s colder; it’s stronger because it’s directional.

**Your timeline won’t be bottlenecked by vendor traffic.**  
In June, I’m routinely arriving at venues where the primary service road doubles as a loading zone for three or four other photography teams, videographers, rental companies, and floral designers all trying to unload simultaneously. Coordinated chaos sounds manageable until you’re watching your start time slip, your setup location shift twice, and your movement between ceremony space and cocktail hour dictated by who has the forklift first. Winter Saturdays are quiet. I pull into an open spot, load gear without navigating a convoy, move through doors without checking whose crew owns the hallway, and actually have breathing room to adjust lighting, reposition subjects, or step outside to catch a break in the clouds. That operational smoothness doesn’t just help me work faster—it keeps your day from feeling rushed or logistically cramped.

I’m not suggesting you abandon the long daylight hours or the garden-backdrop classic. If that’s your vision, pursue it. But if you’ve been hesitating to commit because you assumed winter just means shorter days and fewer options, reconsider. Eleven winter weddings in twenty-four months taught me to stop viewing these dates as secondary. They reward couples who prioritize intentional pacing, efficient vendor environments, and a light source that actually sculpts faces instead of washing them out. Plus, they respect your bottom line.

If you’ve already scoped a venue or started narrowing down months, drop me a note. Let’s look at your actual timeline, your must-have shots, and whether your ideal celebration lands better in the quiet grip of February than it does in the crowded stretch of June. Your date doesn’t have to follow the crowd to be the right one.

b.text:
# Why I Actually Like Shooting Winter Weddings Now

I’ll be honest: a few years ago, I thought winter weddings were mostly a trade-off. Couples chose them for the lower venue rates, accepted an earlier sunset, and hoped everyone stayed warm enough for photos.

After shooting 11 winter weddings over the last two years, I’ve changed my mind.

Winter weddings aren’t just a budget-friendly version of a summer wedding. They have some real advantages—especially for couples who care about photos and don’t want their wedding day to feel like they’re sharing a venue with half the city.

## The budget difference is real

In my area, winter bookings are often about 30% less expensive for couples than comparable spring or summer dates. That can mean a better venue for the same overall budget, more room for guest experience, or simply less pressure around every other decision.

That doesn’t automatically make winter the right choice for everyone. If you’re dreaming of an outdoor ceremony at 6:30 p.m. followed by a long golden-hour cocktail hour, June may still be your month. But if you’re flexible on timing, a winter date can free up a meaningful part of your budget without requiring you to compromise on the things that matter most.

## The light is better than people expect

Here’s the part I didn’t fully appreciate until I started shooting more winter weddings: the light can be incredible.

Around 3 p.m. in November, light moving through bare trees has a softness and direction that is genuinely beautiful for portraits. It’s warm, low, and dimensional. It gives photos shape. Faces look good, dresses catch the light, and even a simple patch of woods or an outdoor walkway can look intentional.

Compare that with a flat, overcast June afternoon—the kind of light that is technically easy but doesn’t always have much personality. Summer can absolutely be beautiful, but “summer” does not automatically mean “better photos.”

The key with winter is planning around the daylight. Portraits may need to happen before the ceremony, or we may build in a short window earlier in the afternoon. But when couples embrace that schedule instead of treating it like a limitation, the results are often some of my favorite images from the day.

## The venue feels like yours

In June, I’m often sharing a parking lot with three or four other vendors. There may be another wedding arriving as yours is getting ready, a florist unloading next to the catering team, and guests trying to figure out which event entrance is theirs.

Winter weddings tend to have more breathing room.

There are fewer overlapping events, fewer people competing for the best portrait locations, and less of that hectic wedding-industry traffic happening around you. It may sound like a small thing, but it changes the feeling of the day. You get more space. Your guests have an easier time arriving. We can take portraits without waiting for another wedding party to clear the staircase or the garden path.

That calm shows up in photos, too.

## Winter is not a backup plan

I’m not going to tell you every season photographs exactly the same. They don’t. Winter comes with earlier sunsets, colder temperatures, and a little more planning around weather.

But it also brings better availability, lower booking costs, quieter venues, and some of the most interesting portrait light I get all year.

If you’re deciding between a peak-season Saturday and a winter date, don’t assume the winter option is the compromise. It might be the date that gives you more room in your budget, more space at your venue, and photos with light you didn’t know you were looking for.

setup: A third-year electrical apprentice is writing an argumentative essay for the union newsletter against a 15% cut to apprenticeship funding.

a.text:
Don't Cut Apprenticeship Funding

I'm a third-year electrical apprentice with the local IBEW. I work hard every day learning this trade, and I'm writing because the state wants to cut apprenticeship funding by 15 percent. That is a bad idea. It hurts working people, wastes a proven program, and costs the public more in the long run.

My cohort started with 24 apprentices. Twenty-one of us finished and are working journeyman jobs right now. That is a strong completion rate. We start around $19 an hour and top out around $46 an hour as journeymen. Those wages get people off assistance programs fast. We pay taxes. We buy houses. We support our families without needing help from the state.

Look at the numbers. The total public cost per apprentice who finishes is about $14,000. Compare that to the average public subsidy of around $48,000 for a four-year college grad who finishes. Apprenticeships give better results for less money. We leave with a real skill, a license, and a job. We do not walk out with student debt and no clear path.

Cutting 15 percent will mean fewer training slots, fewer tools, fewer instructors, and fewer people like me getting a fair shot. That does not save the state money. It just pushes costs somewhere else—more people stuck in low-wage work or needing public help longer. Our program already works. Keep funding it.

Union members, talk to your legislators. Tell them this cut is shortsighted. State leaders, look at the facts. Twenty-one out of 24 finished. Good wages. Low public cost. Do not gut a program that builds skilled workers and strong communities.

b.text:
**Don't Cut What Actually Works**

Right now our state is looking at a 15% cut to apprenticeship funding. The people in charge need to think hard about what that money actually does before they touch it. Because once you look at the numbers, the case for cutting this program makes no sense at all.

Let me tell you what I see from where I stand.

I'm a third-year apprentice with our local. My cohort started out with 24 apprentices. Twenty-one of us finished the program and are working as journeymen right now. That's an 87% completion rate. Think about that the next time somebody tells you a "real" education is the only way to build a career.

Here's what the state puts into an apprentice like me who finishes the program: about $14,000 total. That covers classroom time, instructor pay, books, facility costs, the whole thing. Fourteen thousand dollars. That's it.

Now here is the comparison that should make any legislator sit up straight. The average public subsidy for a student who finishes a four-year college degree is around $48,000. That is more than three times what we get. And a lot of those college grads walk out the door with student loan debt on top of it.

So the state spends less on us and gets more back. How does cutting that math help anybody?

Here is the other part people don't talk about enough. Wages.

I started at $19 an hour as a first year. By the time I top out as a journeyman I will be at $46 an hour. That is not a made-up number, that is the scale. A guy like me is off food stamps, off Medicaid, off housing assistance, and paying real taxes into the system within a year or two of starting. Some of us had those benefits for a few months and never went back.

Every apprentice who finishes is a family that does not need help from the state anymore. Every apprentice who finishes is a new taxpayer. Cut the funding and you get fewer of those, not more.

The 15% cut sounds small when somebody says it out loud in a hearing room. It is not small. It is people who never get into this trade. It is families who stay on assistance longer. It is contractors who cannot find qualified workers. It is taxpayers who end up paying more down the road for college subsidies and social programs because we did not make the cheap option work.

Our legislators like to talk about return on investment. This is the best one they have got. Fourteen thousand dollars in, a skilled tradesperson out, paying taxes for the next thirty years, off public assistance in months.

I am asking every state senator and representative who reads this to vote against this cut. I am asking every union member to call their office and say the same thing. This program works. Don't break it.
