setup: A solo indie game developer is writing a devlog recap for subscribers about his game's launch week sales, subreddit attention, review feedback, and upcoming 1.1 patch.

a.text:
# Week One

It's been a week since launch, so here's what actually happened.

412 copies sold. That's the number as of this morning. I know some of you have asked directly, so there it is instead of me dancing around it.

The reddit thing was wild while it lasted. Someone posted a gif of the grapple hook mechanic on a small subreddit (maybe 40k members) and it sat on the front page for about six hours before getting buried under other stuff. Traffic to the Steam page spiked hard during that window, then dropped off just as fast when it fell off the page. I refreshed the analytics dashboard more times than I want to admit.

Reviews are trickling in slowly, which I expected. Six so far, mostly positive. One of them called out the movement feeling floaty, and honestly, they're right. I've known this for a while but kept telling myself it was fine, that momentum-based movement is supposed to feel a little loose. But going back and playing it fresh after not touching the code for two weeks, yeah. It's floaty in a way that isn't intentional, it's just under-tuned.

So that's going into 1.1. I'm targeting next month for the patch. The main changes:

- Tightening acceleration/deceleration curves on the player controller
- Adjusting air control values (this is probably 80% of the floaty feeling)
- Fixing a minor collision bug with moving platforms that two people mentioned in comments

I'm not going to pretend I have some grand roadmap beyond that right now. Right now it's just: fix what's broken, listen to what people are saying, keep going.

Thanks to everyone who bought a copy, left a review, or just told a friend about it. Three years of nights and weekends led to this week, and I'm still figuring out how to feel about that.

More soon.

b.text:
# Week One Launch Recap: 412 Copies and Floaty Movement

Well, it’s out. After three years of nights, weekends, and staring at code after my day job, my first game is officially live. 

I wanted to drop a quick update on how the first seven days went.

### The Numbers and the Reddit Spike
We sold 412 copies in week one. For a solo project with basically zero marketing budget outside of this devlog, I'm really happy with that. Seeing actual people buy and play something I built in my spare room is a weird feeling, but a good one.

The biggest traffic push happened on Thursday. A post I made hit the front page of a small niche subreddit and stayed there for about six hours. That single window accounted for a solid chunk of the week's sales and brought in a wave of fresh wishlists.

### The Feedback (And the Floaty Controls)
The reviews and community messages have been coming in, which has been great to read through. 

One review specifically called out the movement mechanics, saying the player character feels "a bit floaty." I booted up the build, played through a few levels with fresh eyes, and... yeah. Honestly, they’re completely right. When you’ve been testing your own jump physics for three years, you get used to the quirks, but stepping back, it definitely lacks weight.

### What’s Next
I'm not doing a post-mortem or pulling out some big philosophical lesson from launch week—I'm just getting back to work.

Right now, I’m working on Patch 1.1, which will drop next month. The main priority is tightening up the movement physics so it feels far more responsive, along with fixing a few ultra-wide display bugs that players reported over the weekend.

Thanks to everyone who bought a copy, left a review, or has been reading these posts over the last three years. 

More updates soon.

setup: A freelance wedding photographer is writing a blog post for couples about why to book a winter wedding.

a.text:
**Confessions of a Peak-Season Photographer: Why I Actually Want You to Book a Winter Wedding**

After six years of shooting weddings in this metro area, I know the drill. Everyone wants a Saturday in June or September. For a long time, I was right there with you, secretly dreading the dark, cold days of the off-season. But over the last two years, I’ve shot 11 winter weddings, and my perspective has completely shifted. 

If you’re currently staring at a calendar trying to decide when to book your date, here is the unfiltered, behind-the-lens truth about why I actually prefer winter weddings now—and why you should seriously consider one, too.

**Your budget goes a lot further.**
Let’s talk numbers first. Winter bookings run about 30% cheaper for the couple across the board. Venues know it’s the off-season, and they price accordingly. That 30% drop isn’t just a minor discount; it’s the difference between stressing over your catering minimum and effortlessly upgrading to the premium bar package you actually wanted. 

**The 3 PM lighting is unbeatable.**
As a photographer, light is everything. People assume summer guarantees great photos, but a flat, overcast June afternoon gives me dull, shadowless light that I have to work hard to make interesting. Compare that to a crisp November day. Around 3 PM, the sun sits low in the sky. When that late-afternoon light filters through the branches of bare trees, it creates a moody, dimensional backdrop for portraits that you simply cannot get in the middle of summer. It’s dramatic, it’s striking, and it makes my job incredibly easy.

**You actually get the venue to yourselves.**
In peak season, popular venues are booking machines. In June, I am routinely sharing the loading dock and parking lot with three or four other vendors from different weddings. You’re rushing through your timeline because the next couple’s florist is waiting to unload their truck, and the venue staff is exhausted from flipping the dining room. In the winter? The venue is yours. We have the space and the time to breathe, which means your photos look relaxed, not rushed.

I’m not going to give you a cheesy spiel about how "love is beautiful in every season." I’m just telling you that from a logistical, financial, and photographic standpoint, a winter wedding is a massive cheat code. 

If you’re on the fence about a November, January, or February date, take the leap. Head over to my contact page, and let’s get your winter date locked in.

b.text:
If you’d asked me a few years ago what kind of wedding I preferred to photograph, I probably would have said a classic summer Saturday without thinking twice.

That’s changed.

I actually like shooting winter weddings now, and not in the vague, “every season has its charm” kind of way. I mean it in the practical, real-world, I’ve-photographed-enough-weddings-to-know-what-works kind of way.

Over the last two years, I’ve shot 11 winter weddings. That’s enough to notice a pattern: winter weddings can be smarter, calmer, and honestly more photogenic than a lot of couples expect.

One of the first things couples usually notice is the budget. Winter bookings typically run about 30% cheaper for the couple than prime summer dates. That alone can make a big difference if you’re trying to stretch your wedding budget without cutting the things you care about most. For a lot of couples, that means hiring the photographer they really want, booking the venue they love, or just giving themselves a little more breathing room elsewhere.

But the savings aren’t the only reason I like them.

Let’s talk about light.

In November, around 3 p.m., when the leaves are gone and the trees are bare, the light can be surprisingly gorgeous for portraits. It’s softer, cleaner, and more interesting than the flat overcast light I end up working with far too often in June. People assume summer is automatically the best photo season because the weather is warmer and the days are longer, but warm doesn’t always mean better. For portraits, winter light can be incredibly flattering in a way that makes the whole gallery feel calm and polished.

There’s also something to be said for the atmosphere of the day itself. In June, especially in busy wedding areas, I’m often dealing with the reality of multiple vendors all using the same space at the same time. I’m not exaggerating when I say I’ve shared a parking lot with three or four other vendors in June. That means more congestion, more rushing, more waiting around, and more little logistical headaches that add up fast.

Winter weddings tend to move differently. There’s usually a little more breathing room. Less chaos. Fewer people competing for the same patch of space. As a photographer, that matters. It gives me more room to work, and it gives couples more room to actually enjoy the day instead of feeling like they’re being shuffled through it.

I don’t think winter weddings are automatically better than summer weddings, and I’m definitely not trying to convince every couple to get married in January. But if you’re open to a winter date, I think it’s worth considering seriously.

You may save money.

You may get better portrait light than you’d expect.

And you may avoid some of the summer wedding gridlock that makes even the simplest timeline feel crowded.

If you’re planning your wedding and wondering when to book, I’d say this: don’t rule out winter just because it’s not the “traditional” choice. Some of the best weddings I’ve photographed lately have happened when everyone else assumed the season was off-limits.

setup: An in-house recruiter is posting a contrarian observation about candidates asking about the team’s last failed project in interviews to recruiters, hiring managers, and job seekers.

a.text:
Over the last 9 years, I’ve sat in on roughly 200 final-round interviews for our logistics and ops roles. 

I’ve noticed a very specific pattern: the absolute best candidates always ask about our last failed project. 

They don’t ask about our "biggest weakness" or "areas for improvement." They ask about a concrete, operational failure. 

Here is what that conversation actually looks like in the room:

Candidate: "What’s a project your team bet big on recently that didn't work out, and how did leadership handle it?"

Hiring Manager: "We tried to roll out a new route-optimization software at our Midwest hub last Q3. It was a disaster. The drivers hated the interface, it actually slowed down dispatch times, and we had to pull the plug after six weeks."

Candidate: "That makes sense. How did you manage the fallout with the drivers who lost time on it, and what did you change in your vendor evaluation process for the next tool?"

That follow-up is where the magic happens. 

When a candidate asks about failure, it forces the hiring manager off the polished employer brand script. It immediately reveals how the company handles adversity, whether leadership throws people under the bus when things go sideways, and how they actually iterate. 

It also shows me the candidate isn't just looking for a paycheck. They are evaluating the gritty reality of the environment they are about to step into. 

Hiring managers: what happens in the room when a candidate asks you to unpack a recent failure?

b.text:
After sitting in on close to 200 interviews the last couple years, I've started listening for one question.

"What's the last project here that failed?"

Had a candidate for an Ops Supervisor role ask it just like that last month. No softening it.

I told him about our attempt to move one building to staggered start times last fall. Looked clean on the whiteboard. Fell apart in under two weeks because we didn't account for inbound detention from two of our biggest customers. Carriers started missing windows, OT blew up, leads were running freight themselves.

He didn't move on. He just said, "So who finally called it? And what did you keep from it?"

We spent the next ten minutes talking about that mess. I learned more about how he thinks, how he talks to drivers, and how he pushes back on a plan in those ten minutes than I do from any "tell me about a time" question I ask.

If you're interviewing right now, steal that question.

And hiring managers, what do you say when someone asks you that honestly?

# Why I Actually Like Shooting Winter Weddings

*Or: a confession from a photographer who spent years dreading them.*

For my first few years shooting weddings in this city, winter inquiries felt like a calendar problem. I said yes because January needed filling, not because I wanted the job. Somewhere along the way, that flipped. I've shot eleven winter weddings in the last two years, and they're now the bookings I look forward to most. Since a lot of couples asking me "when should we book?" are really asking "when is the best wedding," let me make the case for the season nobody plans for.

## The light. I'm serious about this one.

In November, around 3 p.m., the sun is already low. It comes in sideways through the bare branches, and those leafless trees break it into shafts and patterns that no lighting kit I own can replicate. There's direction to it. It gives a face shape.

Here's the part that might get me in trouble: that light is better for portraits than what we often get in June. Flat overcast June light is like a giant ceiling fixture — even, forgiving, and forgettable. Everyone is lit identically from every angle, which sounds kind and is actually the problem. Portraits need light with an angle and an opinion, and bare-tree light at 3 p.m. in November has both.

And because the sun sets early, your best-light portraits happen mid-afternoon — when your makeup is fresh and you've still got energy — instead of at 7:30 p.m., after you've been on your feet for eight hours and the schedule has already slipped twice.

## Nobody is fighting over your Saturday.

In June, I pull into a venue lot and there are regularly three or four other vendors there — another photographer's van, a videographer, a florist's delivery, all of us on overlapping timelines.

You feel that even if you never see the parking lot. It's why the getting-ready suite has a stranger's garment bag in it. It's why the coordinator is impossible to find, why the room flip starts while your grandmother is still sitting in it, why everyone is rushing. In January, the venue is yours. My timeline holds. The staff isn't stretched thin, so they're not rushing you either.

I know "the parking lot was roomy" sounds like a photographer convenience. It isn't. Calm is the thing I need most on a wedding day, and winter days have it.

## The part you already guessed: it's cheaper.

Winter bookings run about 30% cheaper for couples than peak-season dates. That's not a gimmick — it's how the industry prices the slow months, and it adds up fast. That difference is your videographer, or a real chunk of your venue, or the honeymoon.

But I want to be honest about the other side of it, because I've had couples seem almost apologetic about booking a discounted date: I'm not shooting eleven of these a year out of charity. The discount exists because demand is lower. I keep saying yes anyway because these have become my favorite weddings to shoot — the calm, the light, the day that actually runs on schedule. You're not getting a lesser wedding at a lower price. You're getting the same wedding at the time of year fewer people want it.

## Yes, it's cold. Plan for it, don't fear it.

I won't pretend otherwise. We plan around it: portraits in twenty-minute bursts with a warm room to retreat to, and a timeline that puts the outdoor portraits in that good light instead of after dark. And coat shots are not a compromise — a great coat is a better portrait prop than a shawl pretending it isn't freezing. The short day is a constraint, but it's the kind that makes the timeline better, not worse.

## If you're flexible on your date

Ask me about winter. After six years shooting in this area, I know exactly which spots near you hold that low November light at 3 p.m. — and my winter calendar has room in it.

setup: A real estate agent is writing a commentary on the local market for brokerage blog and local paper readers.

a.text:
**This Isn’t a Crash. It’s a Pricing Problem.**

If you’ve been watching the local market this spring, you may be feeling whiplash. Last year, homes in my zip code were flying off the market in about eight days. This spring, the median days on market has stretched to 34. Showings per listing have dropped by half. And yet, list prices are still up about 6% year over year.

To some people, that combination sounds confusing. To others, it sounds alarming. But after 10 years of selling homes in this suburb, here is my take, plainly: this is not a crash. This is a market where too many sellers are still pricing like it’s last spring.

Buyers are still out there. But they are more deliberate. They are comparing homes more carefully. They are noticing when a property has been sitting. And they are no longer willing to chase an overpriced listing just because inventory feels tight.

I see this up close. Right now, I personally represent three sellers whose homes have been on the market for more than 60 days, and all three are resisting a price reduction. Meanwhile, the data is telling us something very clear: the homes that are priced correctly from the start are still going under contract in under two weeks.

That is not a weak market. That is a market punishing unrealistic pricing.

There is a big difference between slowing down and falling apart. What we are seeing locally is not demand disappearing. It is buyers refusing to bail out sellers who missed the shift.

Last spring, sellers could get away with testing the market. You could price a little high, wait for the frenzy, and still end up fine. That strategy does not work the same way now. When showings drop sharply and days on market climb, buyers notice. The longer a home sits, the more likely it is to become “that house” instead of “the one.”

And yet, list prices are still up 6% year over year. That tells me we have not fully reset expectations yet. Some sellers are still anchoring to last year’s comps, last year’s bidding wars, or the price their neighbor got three months ago. But today’s buyers are not underwriting yesterday’s market.

The sellers winning right now are the ones who understand the pace has changed. They are pricing sharp from day one. They are respecting the fact that buyers now have more breathing room, more time to think, and more leverage to walk away. Those sellers are still getting showings, still getting offers, and still moving quickly.

So no, I do not believe this is a crash. I believe it is a correction in seller expectations.

If you are thinking about selling, the biggest mistake you can make right now is treating this market like a rerun of last year. The buyers are still here. But the days of pricing high “just to see” and waiting for the market to rescue you are over.

In this market, price is not a suggestion. It is the strategy.

b.text:
**The Market Isn’t Crashing. Sellers Are Just In Denial.**

After ten years selling real estate in this town, I’ve learned to spot the difference between a market crash and a reality check. Right now, what we’re watching in our neighborhoods isn't a crash. It’s a standoff.

Look at the numbers for our zip code. Last spring, the median home was on the market for eight days. This spring, that number jumped to 34 days. Showings per listing have dropped by half. By those metrics alone, you might think the sky is falling. 

Except it isn't. List prices in our area are actually up 6% year-over-year. 

How do you cut foot traffic in half, quadruple the time a house sits on the market, and still see higher asking prices? It’s simple: buyers have reached their financial limit, but sellers are still living in 2022.

Right now, I personally have three sellers with homes sitting past the 60-day mark. All three are stubbornly refusing to drop their price. They see that 6% appreciation stat and assume it applies automatically to their house, regardless of condition, interest rates, or what buyers are actually willing to pay per month. They remember when putting a "For Sale" sign in the yard meant five over-ask offers by Sunday evening. 

That market is gone. But the narrative that the market is "dead" is equally false.

Let’s be completely direct about what is happening: the market hasn't broken; it has simply stopped subsidizing bad pricing strategies. 

Buyers haven't vanished. They are still out there, mortgage pre-approvals in hand, but high interest rates have made them selective and cautious. They aren’t going to stretch their budgets for a home that is priced like it’s peak-frenzy season. 

The proof is in the closing data. When a home is priced correctly for today’s reality—not last year’s memories—it doesn't sit. Homes that are launched at an accurate, compelling price point are still going under contract in under two weeks. 

If a house in our suburb is sitting at 45, 60, or 90 days right now, it isn’t because the local economy collapsed or because buyers disappeared into thin air. It’s sitting because the seller is overcharging for the current climate. 

The market hasn't crashed. It just shifted gears, and it's time for sellers to catch up.

setup: A local sports columnist is writing an opinionated season-ending commentary for readers of the local paper's sports section.

a.text:
**They Ran It Right Up Until They Didn't**

I've had a week to sit with it, which is about six days longer than I usually need to figure out how I feel about a football game. And I still land in the same place.

We didn't get beat Friday night. We talked ourselves out of it.

Let's start where we should start: 8-2, a second-round playoff appearance, and a quarterback who threw for 2,340 yards, which is more than anybody has ever thrown for at this school. Dez Kowalski has been a joy to watch and a joy to have on the air — funny kid, honest kid, never once gave me a canned answer when a canned answer would've been easier. That record is his and nobody can take it. Twenty years from now somebody's going to look that number up and wonder who he was.

But I'm not writing a valentine this week. That's what the banquet's for.

Here's what happened. We were down three at halftime to a team we beat by twenty in Week 3 — same team, same personnel, no great mystery to them. And we had been running the ball down their throat. Not flashy, not pretty, just four and five yards a crack and a defense that was starting to stand up a half-second slower each time. Anybody in that stadium with a pulse could see it working.

Then we came out in the third quarter and threw it.

And threw it. And threw it.

I understand the instinct. You're behind, the clock feels like it's moving faster than it is, and you've got a record-setting arm standing back there. Throwing the ball feels like *doing something*. Handing it off on second-and-six feels like waiting.

But you weren't behind. You were down three. Three points is not a deficit, it's a rounding error. Three points is one drive that you were already perfectly capable of putting together the boring way. Down three with a run game that's grinding is the single best position a high school offense can be in, and we treated it like we were down seventeen with four minutes left.

What it did — and this is the part that actually cost us — is it let their defensive line stop thinking. When you're running it, those kids have to be honest. They have to read, they have to hold their gap, they have to worry. The second we went one-dimensional, they got to pin their ears back and come. Dez spent the entire second half getting hit, and he still nearly brought us back, which tells you everything about the kid and not much good about the plan.

I'm not calling for anybody's job. That's lazy radio and it's lazier column-writing, and frankly this staff has built something here that didn't exist six years ago. Eight and two doesn't happen by accident, and I've watched enough bad football in this town to know the difference.

But I do think there's a real lesson sitting there for next fall, and it's not complicated: trust what's working longer than feels comfortable. The run game is boring. It's supposed to be boring. Boring is the point. You don't abandon four yards a carry because four yards a carry doesn't feel dramatic enough for the playoffs.

We had the better team Friday. We'd already proven that in September. We just decided, somewhere in that locker room at halftime, to play a different game than the one we were winning.

Seniors, thank you. Genuinely. You gave this town a fall worth talking about, and I got to talk about it five mornings a week, which is a pretty good gig.

Everybody else — see you in August. Bring the running backs.

b.text:
Friday night was a tough pill to swallow. Finishing a high school football season 8-2 is a fantastic achievement by any local standard, but when that second loss sends you packing in Round 2 of the state playoffs, it stings. It burns even more when the team ending your season is the exact same squad you ran off the field by 20 points back in Week 3.

Look, nobody can take away what this offense accomplished this fall. Dez Kowalski was nothing short of electric under center. He threw for 2,340 yards this year, shattering the school record and giving us highlight-reel throws every single week. If you had told me in August that we’d have a 2,300-yard passer, I’d have printed state championship tickets right then and there. 

But Friday night proved that a shiny passing record doesn’t win a gritty November playoff game on its own. I’ll just say what everyone shivering in the bleachers was already thinking: we panicked. We completely abandoned the run game in the second half, and for the life of me, I can't figure out why. 

We were only down by three points. A single field goal. More importantly, the ground game was actually working. We were getting push up front, moving the chains, and controlling the tempo. Instead of sticking to the script and wearing out a defensive line we already proved we could bully, the play-calling suddenly turned into a frantic 7-on-7 drill. 

When you start dropping back on every down in a tight, one-possession game, you let the opposing defense pin their ears back and ignore the run entirely. That’s exactly what happened. The pass rush teed off, the drives stalled, and we watched a winnable playoff game slip right through our fingers. 

You don't reinvent the wheel when you're only trailing by three. It's a bitter end to an undeniably great season, and a harsh lesson in playoff football. Congratulations to Dez and the seniors on an unforgettable 8-2 run, but that second-half play sheet is going to keep this coaching staff awake until August.

setup: A parent of two middle-schoolers is writing an op-ed to local readers urging an 8:45am middle-school start time.

a.text:
Every weekday morning at 6:15, I stage the same battle. I walk into my kids’ rooms, flip on the lights, and try to coax two exhausted middle-schoolers out of bed. By the time they grab their backpacks and head out the door for the early bell, they’re practically sleepwalking.

If you have teenagers or pre-teens in Millbrook, you know this routine all too well. That is why I am strongly urging our school board to approve the proposal to move our middle and high school start times to 8:45 a.m. when they vote next month.

This isn’t about letting kids be lazy or indulging bad bedtime habits. It’s basic biology. The American Academy of Pediatrics has long recommended that middle and high schools start no earlier than 8:30 a.m. to align with adolescent sleep cycles. During puberty, biological rhythms shift, making it difficult for teens to fall asleep before 11:00 p.m. Expecting them to absorb algebra at 7:30 in the morning simply works against how their brains are wired.

We don’t have to guess whether a later start time works—we already have local proof. Look at the results from the pilot program at Lincoln Middle. When they shifted to a later schedule, attendance improved and first-period grades went up significantly. Teachers reported fewer heads on desks and more kids actually awake and ready to participate. 

I understand why some parents and community members are hesitant. Change is tricky, and the biggest concern I’ve heard around town is the bus schedule. But if you look closely at the district's proposal, this issue has already been thoroughly addressed. The plan re-tiers the existing bus routes, staggering elementary and secondary pickups so our current fleet can handle the change smoothly, without blowing up the budget or leaving families stranded.

Our kids only get one shot at these critical school years. Right now, we’re sending them into the classroom running on empty before the day even starts. 

When the board votes next month, let’s choose common sense, real data, and our children’s health. Please reach out to our school board members and tell them to vote "yes" on the 8:45 a.m. start time.

b.text:
Every morning, I watch my two middle-schoolers drag themselves out of bed in the dark, bleary-eyed and fumbling for cereal, and I think: *this can’t be right*. Their alarm clocks scream at 6:15, and we’re out the door before the sun has even thought about warming the pavement. I’m not a sleep scientist or a logistics expert—just a parent who’s read the school board’s proposal for an 8:45 start time and knows, deep in my bones, that it’s the right move for our kids.

The American Academy of Pediatrics has been clear for years: adolescents need 8 to 10 hours of sleep, and their natural sleep cycles shift later. Waking a teenager at 6 a.m. is like waking an adult at 4 a.m.—it works against biology, not with it. An 8:45 start isn’t an indulgence; it’s simply aligning school with what we know about growing brains.

But I don’t need a national study when we have proof here at home. Lincoln Middle’s pilot program shifted its first bell to 8:45, and the results were remarkable. Attendance rose, and first-period grades climbed. When I spoke with a teacher friend at Lincoln, she described a roomful of students who were actually *present*—not just physically, but mentally, ready to learn. That’s what every parent wants: kids who can focus on algebra, not on staying upright.

The main objection I hear is about bus schedules. I get it—changing start times feels like untangling Christmas lights. But the proposal on the table already re-tiers the routes. The transportation department has mapped it out, and it works without adding cost or leaving younger students waiting in the dark. We’re not being asked to choose between our middle-schoolers and the rest of the district; the plan is balanced and ready to go.

Next month, the school board will vote. I’m asking my neighbors to see this for what it is: a rare, evidence-backed chance to give our kids something as basic as enough sleep. Let’s stop fighting their biology and start giving them mornings that make sense. I’ll set a later alarm for that—happily.

setup: A bakery owner is writing a warm blog and newsletter post to regular customers explaining why wedding cake orders are ending.

a.text:
I should probably start this by saying that if you emailed me about a wedding cake in the last few months and I got back to you with a kind but vague “let me check our calendar,” I’m sorry for the slow dance. I knew the answer was probably no, but saying it out loud—or, well, typing it—took me longer than I expected.

We’re not taking custom wedding cake orders anymore. I want to tell you why, and I don’t want it to sound like one of those corporate policy memos, so bear with me while I just talk it through.

It’s four in the morning when I get here most days. The dark still feels different at four—thicker, quieter. I turn on the ovens, start the coffee, and by six we’re pulling the first scones and the regulars start filtering in. That’s the part I love. The rhythm of it. The woman who gets the same sourdough roll every Tuesday, the kid who presses his nose to the pastry case waiting for the chocolate croissants. That everyday case—the muffins, the loaves, the little birthday cakes you grab on the way home from work—is what keeps our lights on. It’s what pays the rent on this little shop.

Somewhere along the way, we started saying yes to wedding cakes. And don’t get me wrong, they were beautiful. There’s something about a three-tier cake that makes you feel like a real artist. But here’s the thing nobody tells you when you’re dreaming of buttercream flowers: before you even turn on the mixer, you’ve already given away about fourteen hours. Tastings, consultations, emails at midnight about whether the shade of blush is too peach, sketching, resketching, driving to venues, driving back. All of it unpaid. And for a shop our size—there’s three of us, and two of those hands are mine by four a.m.—that time has to come from somewhere. It was coming from the case. It was coming from sleep. It was coming from the bread that actually pays the bills.

Then this year, three couples cancelled last minute. Full stop, no deposit, no nothing. I’d already bought the specialty chocolate, the vanilla beans, the fondant, rented the stands. When you’re small, you can’t just absorb that. You also can’t get back the weeks of planning and the early mornings that went into a cake that never got made. I stood in the walk-in looking at ingredients for a wedding that wasn’t happening and I just... I couldn’t do it anymore. Not without letting down the part of this business that keeps us here.

I know some of you will be disappointed. Maybe you were saving up to ask us. I hate that. But I also know you come in because you trust that the sourdough will be ready at seven and the cinnamon rolls won’t sell out before eight. To keep that promise, I have to be here, fully, for the daily stuff. The stuff that smells like home when you walk through the door.

We’re still making cakes, of course. If you need something for a Saturday dinner or a small party, we’ll do our best. But the big, elaborate, months-in-the-making wedding cakes? That’s a chapter we’re closing. Not because we don’t love love—we do. But because we love this shop, and our regulars, and the quiet magic of an ordinary Tuesday morning too.

Thank you for understanding. See you tomorrow—I’ll have the coffee on.

b.text:
A little bakery update from us: we’ve decided to stop taking custom wedding cake orders.

This wasn’t an easy decision. We’ve loved being part of so many wedding days, and it means a lot when someone trusts our tiny team with such an important cake. But the truth is that each wedding order takes around 14 hours in consultations, tastings, planning, emails, and design work before we even get to the baking and decorating. With only three of us here, that’s a lot of time away from the ovens and the everyday work of keeping the bakery running.

We’ve also had three last-minute cancellations this year after ingredients had already been ordered or prepared. For a small shop, those costs are difficult to absorb.

Most importantly, custom wedding cakes have been pulling us away from the case—the morning buns, loaves, cookies, slices, and celebration cakes you come in for every week. That everyday case is the heart of the bakery, and quite honestly, it’s what pays the rent. We want to put our time and energy back into making it as good, full, and dependable as we can.

We’re so grateful to everyone who has invited our cakes into their celebrations. This change isn’t because we care any less about those moments. It’s because we need to take care of the little bakery that makes them possible in the first place.

Thank you, as always, for showing up, saying hello, and taking our baking home with you. We’ll see you at the case.

setup: A real estate agent is writing a commentary on the local market for brokerage blog and local paper readers.

a.text:
**Spring Market Reality Check: This Isn’t a Crash, It’s a Pacing Shift**

If you’ve walked through open houses or watched your own listing sit a little longer than expected this season, you’ve probably heard the rumor mill spinning: *“Is the market crashing?”* Let’s kill that headline before it takes root. Nothing broke. Buyers didn’t vanish. Inventory didn’t flood. What actually happened is much simpler: last spring’s frenzy is gone, and a lot of sellers haven’t caught up to the new pace.

In my zip alone, the median days on market jumped from eight days last spring to thirty-four this spring. Showings per listing dropped by half. Meanwhile, list prices are still tracking up six percent year over year. On paper, those numbers sound contradictory. In practice, they tell a very clear story: buyers are showing less because fewer homes meet their price expectations, and prices stay elevated because sellers who priced correctly are still commanding full demand.

I’m working with three sellers right now who have been on the market for sixty-plus days and flatly refuse to move their asking price. They’re waiting for bidding wars to return. They’re holding out for 2023. But holding onto peak-market pricing isn’t patience; it’s friction. And friction kills deals.

This isn’t a crash. It’s a correction in how homes move. When you price a property to yesterday’s desperation, you get today’s hesitation. Homes priced at actual market value—backed by comps, fresh, and willing to adjust when feedback says otherwise—are still going under contract in under fourteen days. I see them weekly. They go fast, they sell clean, and they close without months of carrying costs stacking up. Homes anchored to unrealistic highs? They linger. They stalemate. They eventually get marked down so deeply that sellers wonder why they waited at all.

Let’s be direct about what “pricing right” means now. It doesn’t mean undervaluing your home. It means pricing where the serious buyers are looking, knowing that a well-positioned home will draw competition within the first ten days, while a stretched price pushes buyers to the sidelines until interest cools further. In a slower pace environment, time is the enemy of net proceeds. Sixty extra days on market means another two mortgage payments, another round of HOA fees, another season of maintenance, and a neighborhood stigma that makes future offers harder to come by. Speed protects equity. Stubbornness erodes it.

For sellers reading this: trust the data over your feelings. Your agent’s comparative market analysis isn’t designed to lower your number; it’s designed to capture the strongest offer possible. If the showings aren’t there, the price is out of step. Adjust early. Adjust decisively.

For buyers: this market rewards accuracy, not guessing. Look for homes priced fairly from day one. Skip the ones that have sat past forty-five days expecting a surprise discount—the math rarely works out in your favor once a listing goes stale.

The Midwest market isn’t broken. It’s just telling us the truth about supply, demand, and buyer behavior. Price realistically, move decisively, and you’ll still win. Hold out for a boom that already passed, and you’ll pay for it in time, money, and stress. The game hasn’t changed. Only the rules have.

b.text:
**The Spring Market Reality Check: It’s Not a Crash, It’s a Price Tag Problem**

If you’ve driven around our neighborhoods lately, you’ve probably noticed something we haven't seen in a while: yard signs that are actually sticking around for more than a weekend. 

Last spring, selling a home in our ZIP code was a sprint. The median days on market was a breakneck 8 days. You put a sign in the yard on Thursday, went away for the weekend, and sorted through a dozen offers on Monday. 

This spring, the median days on market has climbed to 34 days. At the same time, the number of showings per listing has cut clean in half. 

Looking at those two stats, it’s easy to jump to the conclusion that the sky is falling. But here is the kicker: local list prices are still up 6% year-over-year. 

So, how do we reconcile fewer buyers through the door and longer wait times with prices that are still climbing? 

I’ll give you the honest answer, because I’m living it every day. Right now, I personally have three listings sitting at over 60 days on the market. The sellers are frustrated, and they are flatly refusing to drop their prices. They are holding out for the frenzy of 2021 and 2022, convinced that the perfect buyer is just around the corner.

But the reality is, that buyer isn't coming. Not at that price. 

There is a lot of talk in the national news about a housing crash, and plenty of pundits hedging their bets by saying "the market is complex and depends on many factors." 

I’ve been doing this in our community for ten years, and I’m here to tell you: it’s not that complex. We are not experiencing a crash. What we are experiencing is a massive disconnect between sellers who haven’t caught up to the new pace of the market, and buyers who are pushing back against high interest rates. 

The buyers are still out there. They are qualified, and they want to buy. But they are tired of being stretched to their absolute financial limits for homes that need work or are priced at the very top of the market. 

The proof is in the data. The homes in our neighborhoods that are priced correctly from day one—not priced where the seller *wishes* the market was, but where the market actually *is*—are still selling in under two weeks. 

If you are thinking of selling this spring, you don't need to panic, but you do need a reality check. The days of naming your price and waiting for a bidding war are over. If your home has been sitting for over a month, it’s not because the market is broken. It’s because your price is. 

Price it right, and it will sell. Price it for three years ago, and you'll be joining my sellers on day 61.

setup: A first-year nursing student is writing a scholarship essay about her first ER rotation for scholarship committee readers.

a.text:
During my first week in the ER, I held a stranger’s hand while his wound was cleaned. His wife was stuck in traffic. I could not make the cleaning hurt less or get her there any faster, but I could stay beside him. So I did.

Before that week, I thought mostly about the skills I needed to learn. I wanted to take blood pressure correctly, remember what I had studied, and not freeze when someone needed me. I knew being kind mattered, but I had not understood how much it could matter in one small moment. Holding his hand did not require a test or a checkoff. It required me to notice that he was alone.

Other moments made me feel much less useful.

During a code, I was sent to restock gauze. Behind the curtain, I could hear the team counting. I wanted to be able to help, but I was a first-year student with more to learn than I knew how to do. At that moment, helping meant getting supplies where they belonged and staying out of the team’s way.

It felt strange to do such an ordinary task while something so serious was happening a few feet away. But the supplies still needed to be there. That experience taught me that I cannot judge the value of a task by how important I feel while doing it. Sometimes my job will be small. It will still be my responsibility to do it well.

Then there was the patient with diabetes whose veins were difficult to access. I missed his blood draw three times before getting it on the fourth try. I was relieved when I finally got it, but I was also aware that every missed attempt had happened to him, not just to my confidence.

I have thought about that blood draw since. I want to become skilled, but I do not want to get so focused on completing a task that I lose sight of the person going through it. I need to learn when to keep trying, when to pause, and when to ask for help. Getting something done matters. So does how the patient is treated along the way.

I left my first week in the ER knowing more, but also knowing how much I still had to learn. I had seen how quickly a room could change and how much trust patients place in people they have just met.

This scholarship would help me continue my nursing education and build the skills to meet that trust. I want to become a nurse who can act when things are urgent, admit when I need help, and notice when someone needs a hand to hold. My first week did not make me that nurse yet. It gave me a clearer idea of who I am working to become.

b.text:
I thought my first ER clinical would be all fast moves and big emergencies. Instead, I learned that a lot of nursing happens in the small parts.

On my first day, I did not know where to stand. My shoes squeaked on the floor, and I kept holding my clipboard like it was there to protect me. A nurse asked if I wanted to help with a wound cleaning, and I said yes. The patient had cut his arm. His wife was supposed to be there, but she was stuck in traffic. He kept looking toward the door.

When the nurse got ready to clean the wound, he looked nervous. I asked if he wanted someone to stay with him. He nodded. When the cleaning started, he grabbed my hand. His grip was tight, and his fingers were cold. I did not say much. I just stood there and let him hold on. The nurse worked carefully and talked him through each step. When he squeezed harder, I stayed still. When he opened his eyes and looked at me, I told him he was doing good.

It felt like a small thing, but when his wife finally came in, his shoulders relaxed. He let go of my hand and said, “Thank you for not leaving.” I did not have a big medical skill for that moment. I just had to be there. But I learned that being there can still be part of care.

Later that week, I was helping where I could when a code started behind a curtain. Someone told me we needed more gauze, so I went to get it. My hands felt clumsy while I opened cabinets and counted packs. Through the curtain, I could hear voices counting. They sounded quick but calm. It reminded me that emergency care is not just chaos. It is people doing their jobs one step at a time.

I brought the gauze back and put it where I was told. Nobody cheered. There was no big moment for me. But I felt what it means to be part of a team. Sometimes your job is not the dramatic part. Sometimes your job is to make sure the next person has what they need.

The moment I keep thinking about the most was a blood draw. The patient had diabetes and bad veins. He already looked tired, and he had been poked enough for one day. A nurse asked if I wanted to try, and I said yes because I wanted to do it right.

The first try did not work. I apologized. He said it was okay. The second try did not work either. I could feel my face getting hot. I tried again and missed. I wanted to walk away. I thought maybe I was not cut out for this. But the patient looked at me and said, “Take your time.”

I took a breath and tried again. This time I went slower. I found a vein, held still, and watched the blood fill the tube. I felt relief more than pride. I was grateful he gave me another chance. After I finished, I thanked him for being patient with me. He said, “You’ll get better.” I know I will.

That week taught me that nursing is not only about what you can do with your hands. It is also about how you show up. I held a stranger’s hand while he was scared. I helped during a code by doing a small task. I missed a blood draw three times, then tried again with a patient who let me learn.

I am still new. I still do not know a lot. But I know I want to be the kind of nurse who stays calm, keeps trying, and treats people like people instead of tasks. My first week in the ER made me more sure about nursing, not because I felt perfect, but because I felt real. I want to keep learning, and I want to earn the trust patients gave me before I fully knew what I was doing.

setup: An in-house recruiter is posting a contrarian observation about candidates asking about the team’s last failed project in interviews to recruiters, hiring managers, and job seekers.

a.text:
Somewhere around interview 200 I started noticing a pattern I can't unsee now.

Almost every candidate asks some version of "what does success look like in this role?" Fine question. Safe question. I've heard it so many times I could answer it in my sleep, and honestly the answer is usually whatever the hiring manager wrote in the req.

The candidates I end up fighting for ask a different one: what's the last thing this team tried that didn't work?

Had it happen last month. Ops analyst role, second round with our director of transportation. Candidate asks him what the team's last real miss was. He tells her about a route optimization pilot we ran in the Southeast — good software, decent data, died about five months in because the dispatchers never trusted the output and kept overriding it by hand.

She didn't nod and move on. She asked whether the dispatchers were involved before the pilot or after it was chosen. (After.) She asked if anyone tracked which overrides actually saved money versus which were just habit. (No.) Then she said something like: so the tool wasn't really the problem, you had a trust problem and no way to prove either side was right.

My director sat back in his chair. That was the whole interview, right there. She'd figured out in four minutes what took us five months and a written-off license fee.

Here's why I think it works. Asking about a failure tells you what the team actually does when things go sideways — do they blame the vendor, blame the frontline, or look at their own process? You learn whether the org is honest. You learn what kind of resistance you'll be walking into. And you find out whether your future boss can talk about a loss without getting defensive, which is genuinely one of the most useful things you can know before you sign.

It's also the hardest question to fake your way through as an interviewer. "What's our culture like" gets you the poster on the wall. "What did we get wrong recently" gets you the truth.

Job seekers: ask it. Hiring managers: have a real answer ready. The vague ones are telling on themselves.

b.text:
Here's what I've noticed across my last 200 interviews: the best candidates always ask about our last failed project.

It's not about the failure itself—it's about the learning. When a candidate asks this, they're showing they care about growth, not the highlight reel.

One conversation that stuck with me:

I'd just finished asking about their experience with process improvements. Then the candidate leaned in and asked, "Can you tell me about a project that didn't go as planned? What happened, and what did you take away from it?"

I shared that we'd tried to launch a new route optimization tool and it flopped because we didn't account for the drivers' input early enough. The candidate didn't just nod—they responded, "I've seen that happen too. What would you change if you did it again?"

We ended up spending the next ten minutes discussing how to build in feedback loops from the start. By the end, I wasn't just impressed by their resume—I could see how they think: someone who learns from missteps instead of hiding them.

If you're prepping for interviews, consider asking about a failed project. It's a question that reveals both your curiosity and the company's culture of learning.

What's the most insightful question you've been asked in an interview?

setup: A wedding photographer is posting that couples who ditch rigid shot lists get better photos, using the rained-out Barrera wedding as an example.

a.text:
The couples who get my best photos are the ones who never sent me a shot list.

Eight years of weddings, and the pattern holds.

The Barrera wedding is the proof I point to.

They didn't give me a list. No spreadsheet of family formals, no Pinterest board, no must-have poses. Just: we trust you, photograph what happens.

Then it rained. An hour before the ceremony, everything already set up on the lawn, and the sky just opened.

We moved the whole wedding under a pecan tree at the edge of the property. Chairs squeezed in tight. Rain coming down past the branches while they said their vows. Every guest pressed close together under the canopy.

No shot list would have covered that. No shot list could have.

So I photographed the wedding they actually had, not the one they'd planned. Those are the photos they still talk about.

A shot list documents the day you imagined. Trust gets you the day that happened. The second one is always better.

To couples choosing a photographer: ask them how they handle a rained-out ceremony. The answer matters more than the portfolio.

b.text:
Over eight years shooting roughly 35 weddings a year here in the Texas Hill Country, I’ve learned something consistent: the couples who willingly set aside their detailed shot lists usually end up with the most powerful photos.

Shot lists are fantastic for keeping the day on track and making sure you don’t miss the cake cutting or the grand exit. But they’re pretty bad at capturing what actually happens. They can’t predict spontaneous laughter, an unexpected guest hug, or how the weather completely changes the mood of a venue.

Last month, we saw this play out perfectly during the Barrera wedding. We had a solid, printed timeline. Then, right before the ceremony, a heavy Texas downpour rolled in. Instead of stressing over missing checklist items, we made a quick call and moved everything under a sprawling old pecan tree. 

What unfolded in those next few hours wasn’t scheduled. It was the quiet conversations while waiting for the rain to ease, the intimate way families grouped together under the branches, and the soft, diffused light filtering through wet leaves. That unscripted moment didn’t just save the day—it became the emotional centerpiece of their gallery.

To the couples still drafting their photography checklists: keep the true must-haves, but leave room for flexibility. Trust your photographer to capture the day as it unfolds. And to my fellow vendors: when you build partnerships based on adaptability rather than rigid expectations, operations run smoother and results speak for themselves. You’ll still get your essentials. But you’ll also get the images that actually feel like your story.

How do you balance planning with spontaneity on event days? I’d love to hear how you and your teams navigate the unexpected.

setup: A wedding photographer is posting that couples who ditch rigid shot lists get better photos, using the rained-out Barrera wedding as an example.

a.text:
After 8 years shooting around 35 weddings a year, I’ve seen it enough to say it: couples who ditch the shot list always end up with the best photos.

Take the Barrera wedding. It was supposed to be outdoors, and then the rain came in hard. We moved everything under the big pecan tree and just went with it. There was no shot list to cling to, so nobody was stressed about what we were missing. The photos from under that tree feel like the actual day—not a checklist.

If you’re planning a wedding, my advice is simple: give your photographer a few must-haves, then let the rest unfold. The best images come from what actually happens, not what you planned to happen.

b.text:
The couples who hand me a 40-item shot list are almost never the ones who end up with photos they cry over.

I say this with love, because I understand the impulse. You're spending real money, you've been on Pinterest for eight months, and a list feels like insurance. I get it.

But here's what a shot list actually does: it turns me into a task-completer instead of someone watching your day for the thing nobody planned.

The Barrera wedding is the example I come back to.

Outdoor ceremony, Hill Country, and the sky opened up about ninety minutes before go time. We lost the aisle, the arch placement, the golden hour spot I'd scouted twice. Everything moved under an old pecan tree on the property because it was the only cover big enough to hold everybody.

Nobody had a plan for that. There was no list item that said "bride laughing while her uncle holds a tablecloth over her head."

That's the photo they printed big.

What made it work wasn't my genius. It was that they'd told me early on they trusted me to read the day, and they hadn't handed me a checklist I'd feel obligated to chase while the actual moment was happening ten feet to my left.

So my honest advice, after eight years and a few hundred weddings:

Give your photographer the non-negotiables. The family combinations. The heirloom detail. Grandma, because grandma might not be here next year. Those matter and I want them written down.

Then stop. Leave the rest open.

The best frames from any wedding I've shot were not on a list. They couldn't have been. Nobody knew they were coming.

And to my vendor friends — you already know this. The rain plan weddings are the ones we talk about years later.

#weddingphotography #texashillcountry #weddingvendors

setup: A remote software engineer is writing a 6-month standing desk review for blog readers researching standing desks.

a.text:
**Jarvik L2 Standing Desk: 6 Months of Daily Abuse**

I bought the Jarvik L2 six months ago during a sale for $549. I’m a remote software engineer, which means this desk sees 8–10 hours of use nearly every day, with a dual-monitor setup, a mechanical keyboard, and a laptop dock. I don’t do affiliate links and I don’t pull punches. Here’s what you actually need to know.

**The motor: genuinely good.**  
The L2’s dual-motor lift is fast — about 1.5 inches per second from my rough timing — and quiet enough that I can raise or lower it during a video call without anyone asking what that hum is. It’s smoother than the Uplift V2 I used at a previous job, and it doesn’t strain or slow down even with roughly 90 pounds of gear on top. Over six months, the motor hasn’t hiccuped once. That’s the best part of this desk.

**The wobble: real, but not a dealbreaker at the sale price.**  
At sitting height (28–30 inches), the L2 is rock solid. At standing height for me — 44 inches — it’s fine for normal typing and mousing. But if I type hard, which I do on a tactile mechanical keyboard, the whole desk shudders side-to-side. My monitors visibly shake. It’s not enough to make me nauseous, but it’s enough that I’ve learned to type lighter when standing or brace my forearms on the edge. If you’re a heavy typist or you hammer your mouse, you will notice this. At 46 inches, it’s worse. This is a two-leg desk with a crossbar, not a four-leg tank. Manage your expectations.

**Memory presets: they drift. About a centimeter.**  
The L2 has four programmable height presets. I set mine to 29.5” for sitting and 44” for standing. Within a week, both had drifted — sitting crept up to 30.1”, standing down to 43.9”. It’s not huge, but I can feel the difference in my elbow angle, and it means I’m recalibrating every two or three weeks. The control panel is easy enough to reset, but for a desk that markets “precision memory,” this is sloppy. If you’re picky about ergonomics, it’ll annoy you.

**The cable tray is garbage. Full stop.**  
Jarvik includes a flimsy metal cable tray that mounts under the desk. The mounting clips are thin plastic, and two of mine snapped within the first month just from the weight of a power strip and a few cables. The tray itself is too shallow to hold a standard surge protector without it sliding out when the desk moves. I ended up ripping it out and using adhesive cable channels and zip ties instead. Don’t factor the tray into your buying decision — it’s basically e-waste.

**Everything else.**  
The desktop surface (I got the 60” x 30” bamboo) has held up fine — no scratches, no warping, even with coffee spills. The frame is sturdy and the lift columns don’t creak. Assembly took me about 45 minutes solo, though the instructions are mediocre and the included hex wrench is soft metal that started stripping on the last bolt. The desk does have a slight front-to-back rock on carpet, but I fixed it with furniture pads.

**Verdict.**  
At $549, the Jarvik L2 is a genuinely good value. You get a fast, quiet motor, a decent-sized surface, and a desk that works reliably for daily standing use — as long as you can live with the wobble at full height and the drifting presets. I’d buy it again at that price.

At $749, the current full price, I would not. For that money, you’re within striking distance of a Uplift V2 or Fully Jarvis (when they run sales), both of which have better stability and more reliable memory. The L2’s flaws are tolerable when you’re saving $200. They’re not when you’re paying a premium.

**Bottom line:** Wait for a sale. If you see it under $600, grab it. If it’s $749, keep scrolling.

b.text:
# Jarvik L2 Standing Desk: 6 Months Later

I’ve been using the Jarvik L2 as my full-time remote-work desk for six months now. I bought it myself, no review unit, no affiliate links. This is the desk I use for coding, video calls, writing, and occasionally eating lunch over my keyboard like a degenerate.

Short version: the Jarvik L2 is a good desk with a few annoying flaws. At the $549 sale price, I’d buy it again. At $749, I’d keep shopping.

## What I Like

### The motor is quiet and fast

This is the L2’s best feature. The height adjustment is noticeably quicker than my old desk, and the motor noise is low enough that I can adjust it during a call without sounding like a blender next to the mic.

It goes up/down smoothly under normal load. I usually raise it after lunch, lower it when I’m done for the day, and it doesn’t hesitate. For a desk I move a few times a day, that matters.

### The memory presets are convenient

There are preset buttons, and in theory they’re great. I use them daily. I don’t want to hold the button and eyeball the height every time.

In practice, they mostly work — but not perfectly. More on that below.

## What I Don’t Like

### It wobbles at full height when I type hard

This is the big one.

At sitting height, the desk feels fine. At a lower standing height, it’s mostly fine. But at my full standing height, there is noticeable side-to-side and front-to-back movement if I’m typing aggressively.

I’m not talking about gently resting my hands on the desk. I mean when I’m writing code quickly, hitting keys with actual force, or moving the mouse around during a frustrating debugging session, the monitor shifts just enough to be annoying.

It doesn’t feel unsafe. It doesn’t feel like the desk is going to collapse. But it feels less stable than I want from a desk at this price.

If you are a light typist, you may not care. If you are a mechanical-keyboard person who types like they’re mad at the compiler, you will notice.

My workaround: I lowered my standing height by about an inch. It helped, but I shouldn’t have to compromise ergonomics because the frame gets nervous at full extension.

### The memory presets drift about a centimeter

The presets are close, but they’re not consistent.

I have my standing height saved, and most days the desk stops roughly where I expect. But over the past few months, I’ve noticed it drifts by about a centimeter. Sometimes it’s slightly high. Sometimes slightly low. It’s not enough to make the desk unusable, but it’s enough that I end up micro-adjusting after every preset move.

That defeats part of the point of having presets.

If Jarvik fixed this with a firmware update or better calibration, I’d upgrade my opinion. As it stands, the presets are useful but not reliable enough to fully trust.

### The cable tray is garbage

I hate the cable tray.

It feels like an afterthought. It doesn’t hold enough, it doesn’t route cables cleanly, and it makes cable management feel worse than if I’d just used velcro ties and a power strip.

For a desk marketed to people who presumably own more than one electronic device, this is a miss.

I ended up removing it and using my own cable management underneath the desktop. If you buy the L2, do yourself a favor and skip the included tray unless you enjoy disappointment.

## Build Quality

The frame itself feels solid enough. The finish is fine. The desktop is decent, though I’d still recommend getting a desk mat if you write or type hard.

The controls are simple. The handset isn’t fancy, but it works. I don’t need Bluetooth, RGB, or a smartphone app to make my desk go up and down. I need it to go to the right height and stay there. The L2 mostly does that, with caveats.

## Who Should Buy It

Buy it if:

- You can get it on sale around $549
- You want a quiet, fast motor
- You need a desk for mixed sitting/standing throughout the day
- You don’t type like you’re punishing the keyboard
- You plan to use your own cable management

Skip it or look elsewhere if:

- You’re paying $749
- You need maximum stability at full standing height
- You want memory presets that are actually precise
- You expect the included cable tray to be useful

## Verdict

The Jarvik L2 is a solid midrange standing desk with a great motor and a few irritating execution problems.

At $549, those flaws are easier to accept. You’re getting good performance for the money, especially if you catch it on sale.

At $749, the wobble and preset drift become harder to ignore. For that much, I expect better stability and more consistent height memory.

Final rating: 7/10 at $549. 5.5/10 at $749.

setup: A third-year electrical apprentice is writing an argumentative essay for the union newsletter against a 15% cut to apprenticeship funding.

a.text:
The state legislature is currently looking at a 15% cut to apprenticeship funding, and as a third-year electrical apprentice with this IBEW local, I can tell you exactly why that is a terrible idea. I am an electrician, not an English professor, so I am going to skip the fancy speeches and just look at the hard numbers. 

Let’s look at my own group. My apprenticeship cohort started with 24 people. Out of those, 21 finished the program. That is a massive success rate. Those 21 men and women aren't sitting at home looking for work. They are out in the field right now, working full-time journeyman jobs, paying taxes, and building this state's infrastructure. 

When we start out as apprentices, we make around $19 an hour. By the time we finish and become journeymen, we top out around $46 an hour. If the state wants to know the fastest way to get people off public assistance programs, this is it. You train them for a career that pays a wage they can actually live and raise a family on. Apprentices get off government assistance fast because we are put straight to work. Gutting the funding that makes this possible doesn't save the state money in the long run. It just keeps people broke.

But here is the math that really proves how backward this proposed cut is. The total public cost for an apprentice who finishes their training is about $14,000. Compare that to a traditional college student. The average public subsidy for a student who finishes a four-year degree is somewhere around $48,000. 

I don't have anything against people who go to college, but the state needs to explain why it wants to cut funding for a program that costs a third of the price and actually guarantees a high-paying job at the end of it. We are delivering a better return on the state's investment, hands down. 

To my brothers and sisters in the local, we need to make some noise. Call your state representatives and tell them to vote against this cut. And to the legislators reading this: do the math. Apprenticeships work. We are the ones wiring your hospitals, schools, and businesses. Do not pull the ladder up on the next group of apprentices trying to get to work. Keep our training fully funded.

b.text:
The state is proposing a fifteen percent cut to apprenticeship funding. On paper, that looks like a modest line-item adjustment. In practice, it means fewer open doors for people who want to learn a skilled trade and a heavier long-term hit to the state budget. I’m a third-year electrical apprentice with IBEW Local 1234. I don’t write speeches. I read blueprints, pull wire, and show up on time. And from where I’m standing, this cut makes no sense.

Let’s look at what actually happens when these programs get fully funded. My training cohort started with twenty-four apprentices. Twenty-one finished. Those are the same twenty-one now working journeyman jobs across the state. Three dropped out, mostly because of personal issues, not lack of ability. When you give people a clear path, a fair wage, and proper tools, most of them cross the finish line. Choke the funding, and you shrink the pipeline before it even starts filling up.

Here’s how quickly those programs pay for themselves. We start out making about nineteen dollars an hour. It’s entry-level, but it’s steady. Every six months, as we log hours and pass tests, our pay goes up. By the time we become journeymen, we’re making around forty-six dollars an hour. That income jump happens inside a four-year window. More importantly, we get off assistance programs fast. Food stamps, rental help, Medicaid—it all drops away quickly when you’re bringing home a solid paycheck. We stop being a cost to the state and start being taxpayers who buy houses, service cars, and pay sales tax.

Do the actual math on what this costs the public. The total public expense to train one apprentice who finishes is about fourteen thousand dollars. Compare that to the average forty-eight thousand dollars in public subsidies spent on a four-year college graduate who walks out with a degree. Both paths lead to careers. But one delivers a licensed, bonded, safety-trained trade worker ready to step onto a job site day one, for less than half the cost. If the goal is stretching taxpayer dollars, which program deserves protection?

A fifteen percent cut won’t magically balance the books. It’ll just push the problem forward. Fewer funded slots means fewer qualified electricians graduating each year. That leads to slower project timelines, higher bidding costs for contractors, and bigger headaches for developers and homeowners alike. It also means turning away kids and career-changers who want a real shot at the middle class without drowning in student debt. Trade work isn’t a consolation prize. It’s a tested route to financial stability, and it works when you let it work.

This isn’t about union turf. It’s about basic economics. We’re asking for enough support to keep the training sites stocked, the instructors paid, and the materials available. Fund the programs that already prove they deliver, and stop looking for savings that create bigger problems later. Keep apprenticeship funding intact. Scale it if you can, but don’t cut it. The math is simple, the outcomes are real, and the workers are ready to go.

It stung. Not just the revenue hit, but realizing I'd treated the people who took a chance on me like strangers.
Spent the week talking to as many as I could and just listening.

5/
What I changed:
- Immediately grandfathered every remaining customer at the old price
- New customers get the higher price
- Any future increase now comes with clear notice and an explanation of why
- I talk to customers before big pricing moves instead of deciding alone

6/
Biggest lesson for other indie founders:
Existing customers bought into a specific deal. Surprise overnight hikes feel like bait-and-switch even if the product is solid.
How you raise prices matters more than the percentage.

Still building in public. Smaller base, clearer rules going forward.
What pricing mistakes have you made?

b.text:
I made a massive pricing mistake with Tallyup recently.

I raised prices by 40% on everyone, overnight.

The result? We had 140 customers. Within a week, 30 of them cancelled.

Here is what went wrong, what I changed, and what I learned the hard way 🧵

2/ The logic in my head seemed sound:
• Tallyup drives clear ROI by helping gym owners track retention.
• I felt we were underpriced for the value we provided.

So instead of thinking it through, I flipped the switch and applied a 40% increase across the board. No warning. No transition period.

3/ Gym owners run on tight margins and trust. 

Springing a 40% jump overnight didn't feel like a normal software update to them—it felt like a breach of trust from a tool they relied on.

The cancellations started rolling in immediately. Losing 30 customers in 7 days was a brutal wake-up call.

4/ What I changed to fix it:

1. Swallowed my pride and reached out directly to every customer who cancelled to apologize.
2. Grandfathered all existing customers back to their original rate.
3. Kept the higher price point, but applied it strictly to new signups only.

5/ The takeaway for other indie founders:

Raising prices isn't the mistake. Most of us undercharge anyway.

The mistake was punishing the early adopters who took a chance on me when the product was barely functional. 

If you're going to raise prices, grandfather your early champions or give them plenty of warning. Don't pull the rug overnight.

a.text:
Hi team,

I wanted to give you an update on yesterday's outage.

**Status: Fixed.** Our service was down for about 40 minutes yesterday around 2 PM. We've identified the cause, rolled back the change, and everything is back to normal.

**What happened:**
During our routine deployment yesterday, we ran a database update that accidentally locked up a critical table in our database for much longer than expected. This made it impossible for customers to access the service. We caught it quickly, reversed the change, and service came back online.

**Why it happened:**
The database update was supposed to be a quick operation, but the way it was written caused it to hold a lock on that table for the full 40 minutes instead of releasing it immediately. We didn't catch this in testing because it depends on the exact size of our production database.

**What we're doing about it:**
Going forward, any database updates like this one will run during our scheduled maintenance windows (when we've already notified customers to expect potential disruptions) instead of during regular deployments. This gives us more control and means updates won't accidentally impact live customer traffic.

I know some of you fielded customer questions and concerns yesterday—thanks for handling those. If anyone has follow-up questions, I'm happy to discuss.

b.text:

To prevent this from happening again, database migrations will run separately during planned maintenance windows rather than as part of regular deployments. We’ll also add additional checks around migrations before they are applied.

setup: A first-year nursing student is writing a scholarship essay about her first ER rotation for scholarship committee readers.

a.text:
# My First Week in the ER

My hands were shaking the first time I put on gloves in the ER. I'd practiced skills in the lab a hundred times—blood draws, wound care, vital signs—but the lab never mentioned what you do when someone needs you to just be there.

Mr. Chen came in with a laceration on his forearm from a work accident. The wound needed cleaning, and his wife was stuck in traffic across town. He kept apologizing for being nervous, which made me want to cry a little. I pulled up a chair next to the stretcher and took his hand. I didn't do anything special—just held it while the nurse cleaned the wound. He squeezed my fingers pretty hard a couple times, but I didn't move. When his wife finally showed up, he thanked me like I'd saved his life. I'd just sat there.

That same shift, I was restocking the gauze station when I heard it. The code alarm. Then the counting, rapid and rhythmic, coming through the curtain behind me. *One, two, three, four...* The voices were calm but urgent in a way I'd never heard before. My hands kept moving—gauze, tape, saline—automatically, like I was on autopilot. But my brain was somewhere else, behind that curtain, understanding for the first time that everything we learn has a reason.

Then there was Marcus, the diabetic patient who had terrible veins. I missed the first stick. Missed the second. The third time, I felt him tense up, and I hated myself for it. But he told me to try again, that he believed I could do it. So I did. The fourth time, the needle went in clean, and I felt something shift inside me—not just relief, but something bigger. A kind of trust he gave me when he didn't have to.

I came home that first week exhausted and doubting everything. But I kept thinking about those moments. Not the ones where I knew what I was doing, but the ones where I just showed up and tried. Where showing up mattered as much as the skill.

I want to be a nurse because I've seen that it isn't about being perfect. It's about standing there when someone needs you to stand there. Holding a hand. Staying steady during chaos. Trying again when you've already failed. These are the things they can't teach you in a lab, but they're the things that matter most.

b.text:
My first week in the ER taught me more than any classroom could.

I came in nervous, trying to keep up and not get in the way. The ER moves fast. People are hurting, scared, tired, and sometimes all three at once. I knew that before I started, but it felt different once I was actually there. It is one thing to read about care. It is another to stand in a room and see what people need in real time.

One moment that stayed with me was when I helped with a wound cleaning for an older man. His wife was stuck in traffic and could not get there yet. He kept looking toward the door. He was trying to act calm, but I could tell he was worried. I stood beside him and held his hand while the nurse cleaned the wound. I did not do anything dramatic. I just stayed there. But I could see it helped. Sometimes people do not need a speech. Sometimes they just need someone to sit with them and not make them face it alone.

Another moment happened during a code. I was sent to restock gauze, and as I stood outside the room, I could hear the team counting through the curtain. It was organized, fast, and serious. Even though I was not in the room, I could feel how much everyone mattered in that moment. I learned that nursing is not just one person at the center. It is a team working together, each person doing their part. Even something as simple as bringing supplies back quickly can make a difference.

I also had a hard time with a blood draw on a diabetic patient who had very poor veins. I missed the first time. Then I missed again. And again. I felt awful. I did not want to give up, but I also did not want to keep poking him and making it worse. On the fourth try, I finally got it. I was relieved, but I also knew I had to be honest with myself. I was frustrated, and I was embarrassed, but I kept going. That patient was patient with me, and I will not forget that. It reminded me that learning takes time, and that skill comes with practice, patience, and respect for the person in front of you.

That first week showed me that nursing is not only about being right the first time. It is about staying calm, paying attention, and caring even when things are busy or hard. It is about being useful in the small moments and steady in the hard ones. I left that week more sure than ever that I want to do this work.

I am applying for this scholarship because I want to keep learning and keep growing into the kind of nurse my patients can count on. My first week in the ER did not just teach me skills. It showed me the kind of nurse I want to become: someone who shows up, stays steady, and treats every patient like they matter.
