setup: A real estate agent is writing a commentary on the local market for brokerage blog and local paper readers.

a.text:
# The Market Didn't Slow Down. Sellers Just Haven't Noticed Yet.

Let me tell you what's actually happening in our zip code this spring, because the headline numbers are getting read the wrong way.

Last spring, the median home here sold in 8 days. This spring, it's 34. That's a big jump, and I've watched sellers see that number and start bracing for a crash. Meanwhile, list prices are still up 6% year over year. Showings per listing, though, have dropped by half.

Put those three facts next to each other and you get the real story: buyers are still here, they're still paying strong prices, but they are no longer in a panic. They're not showing up to fifteen houses a weekend and firing off offers on twelve of them. They're being selective. And selective buyers move slower.

That's it. That's the whole shift. The market didn't fall apart. It just stopped rewarding lazy pricing.

Here's where I'll be honest, because I think honesty is more useful than hedging. I have three sellers right now who've been on the market 60-plus days and won't drop their price. Every one of them is pointing at that 6% number and saying, "The market's up, so my price is fine." But 6% is what *correctly priced* homes are commanding. It is not a coupon you get to staple onto an overpriced listing. A house that's been sitting for two months isn't proof the market is soft. It's proof the price is wrong.

Because the homes priced right? They're still going in under two weeks. I'm watching it happen. The 34-day median is being dragged up by the stubborn listings, the ones chasing last spring's frenzy. Strip those out and the well-priced homes are moving almost as fast as they did a year ago.

So no, I'm not going to tell you the market is "complex and depends on many factors." Here's my actual advice: price it to today, not to what your neighbor got in a bidding war fourteen months ago. Buyers have their footing back, and they can tell the difference between a home priced to sell and a home priced to sit. The ones priced to sell are still selling.

The frenzy is over. The market is fine. The only thing that's crashed is the seller's ability to name any number and get it.

If you're thinking about listing this year, that's not bad news. It just means the strategy changed. Let's price it right the first time and skip the 60 days of watching it sit.

b.text:
**It's Not a Crash. It's a Lag.**

Last spring, the median home in our zip code sold in 8 days. This spring, it's 34. If you only read that headline, you'd think the market fell off a cliff.

It didn't. I've been selling homes here for ten years, and I'll tell you plainly what's going on: the market caught its breath, and a lot of sellers haven't noticed yet.

Here's the part that seems to confuse people. List prices are still up 6% over last year. Showings per listing are down by half. Homes are sitting longer while asking prices keep climbing. That looks like a contradiction — until you realize what those numbers are actually measuring. Not value. Stubbornness.

Let's start with some honesty about the 8 days. That was never normal. That was a once-in-a-career frenzy — cheap money, panic buying, offers sight unseen. For most of my decade in this business, 30 to 40 days on market was an ordinary, healthy spring. What we're living through now isn't a collapse. It's a return to earth. The problem is that a lot of sellers got used to the stratosphere.

I have three sellers right now whose homes have been listed for more than 60 days. I've recommended a price adjustment to all three. All three have said no. These aren't unreasonable people, and they're not bad at math. Each of them watched a neighbor's house sell in a weekend with a stack of offers a couple of years ago, and that number is stuck in their heads like a song they can't turn off. I understand it. But the buyer pool from that era doesn't exist anymore — mortgage rates took care of that — and no amount of sitting will bring it back.

Here's what I tell them, and what I'll tell you: the market hasn't rejected your home. It has rejected your price. Those are two very different problems, and only one of them is fixable.

I know it's fixable because I watch it get fixed every week. Homes priced to *today* — not to last April, not to the neighbor's sale, not to what the seller needs to net for their next place — are still going under contract in under two weeks. Let me say that again, because it's the whole story: correctly priced homes in this zip code are selling in fourteen days or less, right now, in the same market where other homes sit for two months. Same streets. Same schools. Same buyers. Different price.

And "priced right" doesn't mean priced low. It means priced current. There's a real cost to learning this the hard way. A home that sits for 60 days and then cuts its price almost always sells for less than it would have if it had been priced honestly on day one. Buyers smell a stale listing the way you smell rain coming. The showing requests slow down, and the offers that do come in come in low. The market will wait you out. It has nothing better to do.

If you're a buyer reading this and waiting for the crash before you make your move — stop waiting. A crash requires panicked sellers, and what we have is the opposite: patient ones. What you have today that you didn't have two years ago is time and leverage. You can actually get an inspection. You can negotiate. You can sleep on a decision. That's worth more than the imaginary discount you're holding out for.

So no, I'm not worried about this market. I've worked through genuinely bad ones, and this isn't that. This is a normal market wearing a costume from a weird one. The sellers who take the costume off are selling in two weeks. The ones who don't are hosting open houses in month three.

The market moved. The only question is whether your price moved with it.

setup: A real estate agent is posting one specific observation about early block walks and happier buyers to LinkedIn buyers, agents, and lenders.

a.text:
After 12 years of selling houses in Asheville, almost all to first-time buyers, I've started asking people to do one slightly annoying thing before I'll show them a house they really like. Go walk that street at 7am by yourselves, get coffee, just loiter a little, and then we'll tour in the afternoon.

Last year Ben and Lauren Pruitt fell hard for the photos of a little 1920s bungalow on Sycamore Street, and I could tell they were already picturing furniture in the living room. They did the morning walk and called me from their car kind of laughing, because in twenty minutes they'd met an off-leash beagle named Biscuit, watched the middle-school bus stop fill up on the corner, and realized you could hear the morning backup on I-240 just faintly from the backyard.

We toured that afternoon and they still loved the house, sloped kitchen floor and sticky back door and all, but now they actually knew what mornings felt like there. They bought it last June, and when I stopped by with pumpkin bread in October they weren't talking about the paint colors at all, they were talking about Biscuit's owner bringing their trash cans up and the bus-stop parents they now know by name.

That's why I keep pushing the 7am walk. You're not really buying square footage, you're buying Tuesday mornings for the next five years.

b.text:
After 12 years of selling real estate here in Asheville, mostly working with first-time buyers, I’ve noticed a subtle pattern that has nothing to do with square footage, quartz countertops, or school ratings. 

The buyers who end up the happiest with their home long after the closing dust settles are almost always the ones who visited the neighborhood at 7:00 AM before we ever put in an offer.

A few years back, I was helping the Pruitts look for their first home. They found a property they were excited about on Sycamore Street, but before our scheduled afternoon walk-through, they decided to drive over early on a Tuesday morning just to sit on the curb with a cup of coffee. 

In thirty minutes, they learned things no MLS listing could ever tell them. They saw three different neighbors stop to chat while walking their dogs, noticed exactly where the morning sun hit the front porch, and confirmed that commuters weren't using Sycamore as a high-speed shortcut to avoid main road traffic. When we walked through the house later that day, they weren’t just evaluating room sizes—they already understood the rhythm of the block. Five years later, they still tell me it’s their favorite thing about living there.

An afternoon tour or a Sunday open house shows you a property at its polished best. A 7:00 AM walk shows you what your actual life will feel like on a random Tuesday. If you're house hunting right now, set an early alarm, grab a coffee, and go walk the street before you make a decision. It’s the single best test drive you can give a home.

setup: A bakery owner is writing a warm blog and newsletter post to regular customers explaining why wedding cake orders are ending.

a.text:
**On Wedding Cakes, and Why We're Saying Goodbye to Them**

I've been putting off writing this one for a few weeks, mostly because I kept thinking I'd find a way to say it that didn't feel like a letdown. I haven't found it yet, so I'm just going to say it: starting this fall, we're not taking custom wedding cake orders anymore. If you've already got a date on our books, nothing changes — we'll be there, and your cake will be exactly what we promised. But we're not booking anything new.

I want to tell you why, because you've been good to us and you deserve more than a line on the order page.

The short version is that wedding cakes were quietly eating the shop.

The longer version starts with the part nobody sees. A custom cake isn't really a baking job — it's a project. There's the first conversation, usually an hour, sometimes two, where we talk through what you're imagining. Then there's the tasting, which means baking four or five small cakes and three or four fillings on a day we're already baking everything else, and then sitting down for another ninety minutes to go through them. Then the follow-up emails about whether the buttercream can be a shade warmer. Then the second tasting, because your mother couldn't make the first one. Then the sketch, the revision to the sketch, the call about whether we can match the ribbon. Then the delivery logistics, which are their own small novel.

I finally sat down and added it up this spring, and it came to somewhere around fourteen hours per cake before I ever start the actual cake. Fourteen hours that aren't billed, because that's how the industry does it — the consult is free, the tasting is free, the eight rounds of emails are free. I don't blame anyone for that. It's just how it's always worked. But there are three of us here, and fourteen hours is most of a person's week.

Then there's the other thing, which is harder to talk about without sounding sour, so I'll just be plain about it. We had three cancellations this year inside of two weeks of the date. Weddings fall apart, and I genuinely mean it when I say I hope those folks are all right — I'm not telling you this to shame anybody. But by two weeks out, the flour and the butter and the good vanilla and the fruit are bought. The specialty order for the particular chocolate is in. The day is blocked off, which means we turned down other work to hold it. When it goes away, that all just sits there. Three times in one year is real money for a shop our size, and it's money that came out of a place where there isn't a lot of slack.

But honestly, if it were only those two things, we'd have figured out a way. Deposits, contracts, a consult fee, something. The real reason is the third one, and it's the one that took me longest to admit.

Every hour I spent on wedding cakes was an hour I wasn't spending on the case.

The case is what pays rent. It's the morning buns and the sourdough and the seeded rye and the cardamom knots that go by ten-thirty on a Saturday. It's the birthday sheet cakes and the pie orders in November. It's you, coming in on a Tuesday because you always come in on a Tuesday. That's the actual business. That's what's been here for six years. And I kept noticing that on the weeks with a wedding in them, the case got thinner, or the laminated stuff didn't get the attention it wanted, or I ran out of the rye and just didn't have it in me to fix it. I'd be in the back at 4am piping sugar flowers for eighty people I'd never met while the thing that actually feeds us got the leftovers of my attention.

That's backwards. It took me an embarrassingly long time to see that it was backwards.

So here's what we're doing instead. We're keeping celebration cakes — the eight and ten-inch rounds, the sheet cakes, the ones you order with a week's notice and pick up at the counter. We'll still write on them. We'll still do the flavors you like. We just won't be doing tiers, or sugar work, or delivery, or the whole long courtship that a wedding cake requires. And we're putting that reclaimed time straight back into the case, which is where I've wanted it for a while now.

If you're getting married and you were hoping we'd do it, I'm sorry, truly. Come talk to me anyway — I know most of the good people in town doing this work and I'll happily point you at whoever's right for what you want.

And thank you for reading a long one. See you Tuesday.

b.text:
It’s just past two in the afternoon, the ovens are finally cool, and I’m sitting at the back prep table with a cup of coffee that I’ve reheated twice, trying to put words to something we’ve been turning over in our heads for months. 

Starting next season, we are stepping away from custom wedding cakes. 

If you’ve followed us for a while, you know how much love we’ve poured into those tiers over the years. Getting to be a tiny, sweet part of someone’s biggest day is genuinely an honor, and saying that out loud makes this feel like a hard decision. But the truth is, when you peel back the romance of it, our kitchen is just three pairs of hands. 

Lately, the math and the hours just haven't been working. Between the initial emails, the sketches, the sit-down consultations, and the tasting boxes, each custom wedding order eats up roughly fourteen hours of work before we even crack an egg for the actual tier. For a big studio with an office manager, that’s just standard business. For the three of us, it means answering emails until midnight after being on our feet since 4 a.m. 

This year was also particularly tough on our margins. We had three different couples have to cancel at the eleventh hour. We completely understand that life happens, but in a shop this small, absorbing the cost of all those specialty ingredients and holds on our calendar leaves a mark that’s really hard to shake off. 

More than anything, though, we realized wedding cakes were pulling us away from the heart of this bakery: the front case. The morning scones, the flaky hand pies, the sourdough, the little six-inch birthday cakes you grab on a whim for a coworker—that’s what actually pays our rent every month. It’s also where we get to see your faces on an ordinary Tuesday. We were spending so much energy stressing over sugar flowers and dowel rods that we were running on fumes for the people who walk through our door every single day.

We’re not giving up on celebrations entirely. We’re still going to bake our standard menu cakes, and if you want to order a couple of rustic nine-inch rounds from our regular list for a backyard reception, we will happily box them up for you. But as far as the bespoke, multi-tiered, delivery-and-setup wedding circuit goes, we are hanging up our aprons. 

Thank you so much to every couple who trusted us with their reception over the years. We loved it, truly. But right now, we need to protect our sleep, our sanity, and the daily pastries that make this little shop what it is. 

I’m heading home to put my feet up for a few hours. I’ll see you at the counter tomorrow morning—there will be warm cinnamon buns waiting.

setup: A retired Army staff sergeant is writing about coming home after his second deployment for readers of the veterans' writing workshop anthology.

a.text:
# Coming Home

The cereal aisle got me before anything else did. I'd been stateside maybe three days. My wife sent me to the store for a few things, normal errands, and I stood in front of the cereal for twenty minutes. I'm not exaggerating. I looked at my phone to check the time when I got there and I looked again when a stock kid asked me if I needed help finding something.

Forty kinds of cereal. Maybe more. When I left there had been a lot too, I guess, but I never noticed. A year of eating whatever was in the bag or the tray, no choices at all, and now there were forty boxes and they all needed a decision from me. Honey Bunches or Raisin Bran or the one with the tiger or the one with the stupid leprechaun. I understood the words on the boxes. I understood what cereal was. I could not pick one. The kid with the apron was waiting for an answer and I said I was fine, just looking, and he went back to his carton and I stood there some more until I grabbed the blue box my wife always bought because it wasn't a decision if I already knew the answer.

The airport was two weeks before that. That's the order things actually happened, but the cereal is where my head went first, so that's where I started.

I came through the arrivals gate at Fort Carson and the whole families-waiting thing was happening, the signs and the flags and the kids on shoulders, and my wife was there with my daughter off to the side a little because she's smart enough to stay out of the crush. Maya was six. I'd been gone just over a year, and six-year-olds change in a year. I'd seen her on video calls the whole time, but the camera flattens you, makes you smaller and quieter than you are.

She knew who I was supposed to be. That's the part that mattered. She just didn't know me on sight anymore. I came around a family reunion-ing some specialist and she saw me and stopped walking and put her hand on her mom's leg and stepped halfway behind her and looked up at my wife's face to check whether this large man was safe. My wife said, "Maya, it's Daddy," and Maya kept looking at me like she was running the math and not quite finishing it. I got down on one knee, which is what I'd have done anyway because you get down to talk to a six-year-old, and I said, "Hey, bug," which was what I'd called her since she was two, and that did it. The voice. The word. She came the rest of the way around her mother's leg and hit me hard enough that I had to put a hand down on the floor.

I don't hold it against her. Why would I. She was six and I was a guy on a screen for a year. But I've thought about that half-second where she checked her mother's face more times than I've thought about most things that happened over there.

The door was the slow one. After the airport, after the cereal, that was what took the longest.

Over there you sleep facing the door. Nobody has to teach you this. You just start doing it. You sleep on the side of the bed closest to the door, or if there's no bed you position yourself so the door is in your line of sight, and you sleep light, and you sleep in pieces. My roommate and I had our bunks arranged so we were both angled at the door, and we never once discussed it.

So I came home and my wife sleeps with the door open. Always has. She says a closed door makes her feel like she's suffocating. Fine by me, before. When I got back, we left the door open like always and I could not make it work. I'd lie there staring down the hallway the open door created, every sound in the house sorted and cataloged, every settling of the house read as approaching footsteps. I'd wake up at three, four, five. I'd hear Maya get up to pee and track her the whole way there and back by ear.

I didn't want to make my wife sleep behind a shut door over my stuff, so for a while I just did the thing where you sleep badly and call it fine. She caught on, because wives catch on. She started leaving it open just a crack and we called that a compromise. It took months. What actually worked was this: one night Maya had a bad dream and came padding in at two in the morning, and I was awake anyway, and she climbed in between us, and at some point I realized I'd fallen asleep facing away from the door because I was facing her. I woke up at six with her foot in my kidney and the door wide open and the hallway just a hallway.

It's not that it stopped. I still sleep lighter than I did before. I still know where the door is. But most nights now I face the middle of the bed, which is to say I face my wife, which is to say I face the opposite of the door, and that's about all the sense I've managed to make of any of it.

The cereal, for the record, is still the blue box. Some decisions you only have to survive once.

b.text:
I came off the plane and went through the line with everybody else. They had a little area set up for families. I saw my wife first. She had our daughter with her. The girl was six.

I walked over. She looked at me and then she stepped behind her mom’s leg and held on. She didn’t come out right away. I said her name. I got down on one knee so I wasn’t standing over her. After a minute she came around, but she stayed close to her mom.

A few days later I went to the grocery store. We needed cereal. I walked down the aisle and stopped. There were rows of it. Boxes stacked high. Different colors, different names. I counted maybe forty kinds. I stood there looking at them. I couldn’t decide. I just stood there. A woman with a cart asked if I needed help finding something. I said no. I grabbed a box of the plain kind we used to get and put it in the cart.

At night I still slept facing the door. That’s how it was over there for a year. You kept the door in sight. Now I leave the bedroom door open because that’s what we do at home, but I catch myself turning toward it anyway. I have to turn back over. It takes a while some nights.

setup: You're everyone at the startup. Yesterday's 40-minute outage was caused by a bad database migration during deploy.

a.text:
Hi all,

Quick update on yesterday's outage: everything is fully back to normal and has been stable since about 2:45pm yesterday. No customer data was lost or affected.

**What happened**

Around 2pm yesterday, the app went down for about 40 minutes. The cause was part of a routine software update we were rolling out. One step of that update involved making a change to our database, and that change ended up locking a key part of the database for much longer than expected. While it was locked, the app couldn't read the information it needed, so customers saw errors or couldn't load anything.

Once we identified the problem, we rolled back the change, and things came back up right away.

**What we're changing**

Going forward, any database changes like this will no longer happen as part of a normal deploy. Instead, they'll run in a scheduled maintenance window, when we can plan for them, monitor closely, and avoid impacting customers during peak hours. This means a routine update can't accidentally take us down the way it did yesterday.

**For those of you who heard from customers**

Thanks for fielding those messages, and sorry for the scramble. If any customers are still asking, you can tell them: we had a roughly 40-minute outage yesterday afternoon caused by an internal database issue, it's fully resolved, no data was affected, and we've changed our process to prevent it from happening again.

setup: A high school junior is writing an argumentative essay to her English teacher and classmates arguing for open campus lunch for juniors and seniors.

a.text:
# The Case for Open Campus Lunch

Every day at 11:42, the bell rings and 340 juniors and seniors funnel into a cafeteria built to hold 220 people. Students eat standing up, balance trays on windowsills, or give up and sit on the hallway floor. This is not a hypothetical problem that might occur someday—it is happening right now, five days a week, to over a hundred students who simply have nowhere to sit. Our school should adopt an open campus lunch policy for juniors and seniors, allowing them to leave school grounds during the lunch period. The evidence from comparable schools, the overwhelming preference of our own student body, and the physical reality of our overcrowded cafeteria all point to the same conclusion: it's time.

The most immediate argument for open campus lunch is the simplest one: our cafeteria cannot physically hold the students assigned to it. A room with 220 seats is being asked to serve 340 people every single day. This isn't a minor inconvenience—it's a logistical failure that affects the basic dignity of the lunch experience. Students shouldn't have to treat finding a place to sit as a competitive sport. Allowing even a portion of upperclassmen to leave campus during lunch would immediately relieve this pressure, giving the students who remain enough space to actually sit down and eat.

Opponents of open campus lunch often raise a specific fear: that letting students leave will make them late coming back, disrupting the schedule for the rest of the day. This concern deserves to be taken seriously, but it does not hold up against the evidence available from schools that already do this. Fairmont, West Linn, and Cascade—three districts comparable to ours in size and structure—all currently allow open campus lunch for upperclassmen. Their published attendance data shows no measurable increase in tardiness following the start of fifth period. If the policy caused the disruption critics predict, we would expect to see it in the numbers from schools already running the experiment. We don't. The fear is understandable, but it is not supported by the facts.

Beyond the practical case, there is also the matter of what students themselves want. I surveyed 80 students at our school, and 71 of them—nearly 89%—said they were in favor of open campus lunch. This is not a narrow preference or a fringe opinion; it is close to a consensus among the people who would actually be affected by the policy. Administrators do not have to guess at what students want here. They have a clear, overwhelming answer, and it would be a mistake to ignore it simply because the current system is easier to maintain on paper.

Some may argue that convenience for students shouldn't outweigh the school's responsibility to supervise them during the day. That's a fair principle in the abstract, but it doesn't grapple with the reality that juniors and seniors are, in a matter of months, going to be living independently—driving to jobs, attending college classes, managing their own schedules entirely. Trusting them to walk to a restaurant and return in 45 minutes is not a radical leap of faith. It's a reasonable extension of the responsibility they're already expected to carry.

Open campus lunch is not a fringe idea or an untested gamble. It is a policy already working in nearby districts, one that our own students overwhelmingly support, and one that would solve a real, physical problem in our cafeteria that has no other easy fix. The evidence is not ambiguous. It's time our school caught up to it.

b.text:
Open Campus Lunch Is Overdue for Juniors and Seniors

Every day during B lunch, about 340 students try to eat in a cafeteria built for 220. Some of them sit on the floor by the vending machines. Some eat standing up in the hallway outside the gym, which is technically against the rules, though nobody enforces it because there is nowhere else to send them. A few just skip lunch and go to the library. This is the situation our school has chosen instead of a policy that three nearby districts already use without problems: letting juniors and seniors leave campus for lunch. Open campus lunch for upperclassmen would solve a real overcrowding problem, and the evidence from schools around us shows it can be done without hurting attendance or student safety.

The overcrowding is not an exaggeration or a matter of opinion. The cafeteria has 220 seats. The B lunch wave has 340 students. That means on any given day, roughly 120 students have no place to sit, and that number does not go down when it rains and the courtyard is closed. Juniors and seniors together make up close to half of that wave. If even a third of them left campus, the cafeteria would go from overcrowded to full, which is a very different thing. The school has spent years treating this as a scheduling puzzle, adding a third lunch period one year and then removing it when it cut into class time. Open campus is the only fix that does not require rebuilding the cafeteria or rearranging the master schedule.

The most common objection is that students who leave for lunch will come back late, or not at all. This is a fair concern, but it is also one we can actually check, because other districts have already run the experiment. Fairmont, West Linn, and Cascade all allow open campus lunch for upperclassmen, and all three publish attendance data. None of them show a rise in tardiness after adopting the policy. This matters because these are not distant schools in some other state with a different culture; they are districts a short drive away, drawing students from similar communities, dealing with the same traffic and the same fast food places. If open campus caused a wave of tardy students, it would show up in their numbers. It doesn't.

Students at our school also clearly want this. I surveyed 80 students across grade levels, and 71 said they were in favor of open campus lunch for juniors and seniors. That is almost 89 percent. I will be honest that 80 students is a small sample and I was not able to randomize it the way a real study would, so the exact percentage should be taken loosely. But the size of the gap is hard to dismiss. Even if the real number is closer to 75 percent, that is still a policy with overwhelming support from the people it would affect. Schools regularly ask for student input and then explain why it cannot be acted on. This is a case where the input points in one direction and the practical evidence points the same way.

Some will argue that open campus is a privilege upperclassmen have not earned, or that it creates a liability for the school if a student is hurt off campus. On the first point, the policy can easily be tied to standing. Fairmont, for example, revokes the privilege for students with excessive absences or discipline referrals, and our school could do the same. That turns open campus into an incentive rather than a giveaway. On the liability question, the three districts I mentioned all require a signed parent permission form, which shifts responsibility to families the same way a field trip form does. This is a solved problem, not a new one.

Our school does not need to be the first to try this. It needs to be the fourth. The overcrowding in the cafeteria is measurable and getting worse, students strongly support a change, and the districts closest to us have already shown that the main fear about open campus lunch does not come true. Juniors and seniors are a year or two from being trusted to manage their own time in college or at a job. Trusting them to eat lunch and come back on time is a reasonable place to start.

setup: A high school girls' soccer and track coach is writing an op-ed urging turf funding for the girls' field.

a.text:
**Our Girls Deserve a Field They Can Actually Play On**

Over the last two seasons, our girls’ soccer team has had nine games rained out or moved because our grass field floods.

Nine games. That means players, families, officials and opposing teams have made plans, only to have them canceled or relocated because the field cannot handle ordinary weather. It means lost home games, lost revenue and lost opportunities for our athletes to compete in front of their classmates and families.

It also means we are asking students to play on a surface that can become unsafe.

Last October, one of our players tore her ACL after stepping into a rut on the field. I am not going to pretend that a new surface eliminates every sports injury. It does not. Soccer is physical, and injuries happen. But we should not be putting our athletes on a field with ruts, standing water and uneven footing when we have the ability to provide something safer and more reliable.

The school board is considering next year’s facilities budget. Installing turf on the girls’ soccer field should be part of that budget.

This is not a request for luxury. It is a request for a basic athletic facility that works.

The boys’ football field received turf in 2019. That investment made sense. Football needed a dependable field, and the school made the decision to provide one. But girls’ soccer deserves the same consideration. Our athletes work just as hard. They practice in the same weather, represent the same school and compete under the same academic and athletic expectations.

This is also a fairness issue.

We should not have one group of athletes playing on a dependable, all-weather surface while another group is routinely displaced by rain. We should not tell girls that their games can be moved, shortened or canceled because their field is not a priority. If the school is willing to invest in facilities for one program, it should be willing to invest in facilities for another program with a demonstrated need.

The current field does not just create inconvenience. It affects the quality of the season. When games are moved, families have to rearrange work schedules and transportation. Opposing teams have to travel again. Coaches have to rebuild practice plans. Senior nights and other events become harder to schedule. Players lose the experience of playing at home, in front of their community.

And when a game is moved to another field, that field may not be ideal either. We end up scrambling for space instead of giving our athletes the stable, well-maintained facility they deserve.

A turf field would allow us to keep more games at home and make better use of the schedule. It would provide a more consistent playing surface and reduce the damage caused by wet conditions. It would give the school a facility that can serve students more reliably instead of sitting unusable after every heavy rain.

I understand that the district has competing needs. Facilities budgets are not unlimited, and every project has to be examined carefully. But fairness should be part of that examination. So should safety. So should whether students are actually able to use the facilities we already ask them to depend on.

Our girls are not asking for special treatment. They are asking for equal treatment.

They show up early. They stay late. They play through heat, cold and pressure. They represent this school with pride. The least we can do is give them a field that drains, holds up and does not turn a season into a series of weather-related cancellations.

The school board should put turf for the girls’ soccer field in next year’s facilities budget. It is the fair decision, the practical decision and the responsible decision.

b.text:
Every time it rains, we lose the girls’ soccer field.

Not because the girls don’t show up. Not because the team doesn’t have enough players. Not because the season is short. We lose it because the grass field floods, turns to mud, and becomes unplayable. Over the last two seasons, nine games have been rained out or moved because of it.

That is not a rare inconvenience. That is a pattern. And it is costing our girls real opportunities to play, compete, and finish their season on a field that is safe and usable.

Last October, one of my players tore her ACL stepping into a rut on that field. Anyone who coaches knows injuries happen in sports. But when a field is uneven, soft in some places and hard in others, and full of holes after rain, we are no longer talking about normal risk. We are talking about preventable danger.

That should matter to the school board. It should matter to parents. It should matter to anyone who believes our athletes deserve the same basic conditions we already gave the boys.

The boys football field got turf in 2019.

That is the plainest reason this should move forward: fairness. If the boys’ program deserves a safe, reliable playing surface, then the girls’ program does too. Our girls are not asking for something extra. They are asking for the same standard.

Turf would not solve every problem in girls’ athletics, but it would solve this one. It would keep more games on the schedule. It would reduce cancellations, make practice and competition more dependable, and give our athletes a field that can handle the weather we actually get here. It would also mean fewer dangerous holes, fewer muddy patches, and fewer excuses for why a team has to keep starting over.

And yes, it matters that this is girls’ soccer. When the boys’ field gets the investment and the girls’ field is left to flood, people notice. Our student-athletes notice. They know when they are being treated as an afterthought.

This is a facilities budget decision, but it is also a values decision. We can spend money on the field that serves half our athletes and say that is good enough, or we can do the right thing and make sure the girls have a field that is safe, usable, and equal.

I coach because I care about these kids, not because I enjoy writing letters and making budget arguments. I would much rather spend my time on the field than talking about turf. But after nine rainouts or moved games in two seasons, after an ACL injury tied to a rut in the grass, and after watching the boys already get the upgrade years ago, this should not be a hard call.

Give the girls turf.

setup: A general contractor is writing a short X thread to contractors, homeowners, and architects about a hidden joist problem and the lesson learned.

a.text:
1/ Opened up the ceiling on our Maple Ave kitchen remodel this week and found a classic Pittsburgh old-house surprise. Sometime in the 80s, somebody completely severed a floor joist just to run a PVC drain line. The bathroom floor upstairs was practically floating.

2/ We had to halt drywall prep, bring in the engineer to spec a fix, reroute the plumbing, and properly sister the joist. It cost the client about $1,200 out of pocket and set our schedule back two days. Never a fun phone call to make, but it had to be done.

3/ The lesson for homeowners: this is exactly why you need a 10-15% contingency budget. If a contractor tells you they know exactly what's behind an 80-year-old plaster ceiling before they open it, they're lying. You have to financially plan for the unknown.

4/ The lesson for guys newer to the trade: don't just cover this stuff back up because it's "not in the original scope." In residential remodeling, you touch it, you own it. Have the hard conversation with the client immediately, fix the structure, and sleep well at night.

b.text:
1/ Tore out the plaster ceiling on our Maple Ave kitchen and found it: two 2x10 joists cut almost clean through for a 3" PVC toilet drain from a 90s upstairs bath. Been hanging on for 30 years.

2/ Upstairs floor felt spongy. Homeowner thought that was just "old Pittsburgh house." It was those joists flexing every time that toilet flushed. We stopped and called our engineer.

3/ Fix was sister both joists + box header around the pipe per spec. $2,400 labor/material, $450 for the letter, 2.5 days lost. Covered as unforeseen conditions T&M. Not fun, but way cheaper than a collapse.

4/ 15 years doing remodels and lesson is the same: before you price a kitchen under a bath, look from below first. Stains, patches, fresh PVC in old wood = red flag. 10 mins with a flashlight saves you.

b.text:
We're hiring our first support person.

Here's the honest version: the three of us have been answering every ticket ourselves since we started. It worked for a while. It doesn't anymore. We need someone to take that over so we can stop doing it badly at 11pm.

**What the job actually is day to day:**

setup: An in-house recruiter is posting a contrarian observation about candidates asking about the team’s last failed project in interviews to recruiters, hiring managers, and job seekers.

a.text:
One question consistently changes the tone of an interview:

“What’s a project that didn’t go the way you hoped—and what happened after?”

I’ve probably had this come up in around 200 interviews. The strongest candidates don’t ask it to catch anyone out. They’re trying to understand how work actually happens when the plan meets reality.

In logistics, it might sound like this:

Candidate: “What’s a recent project that failed?”

Me: “We rolled out a new scheduling process at one site. The timeline was aggressive, training wasn’t consistent across shifts, and adoption stalled.”

Candidate: “What did the team do once you realized it wasn’t landing?”

Me: “We paused the wider rollout, brought in the site leads earlier, rebuilt the training, and restarted with a smaller pilot.”

Candidate: “If I joined, how much room would I have to raise a concern before a project gets that far?”

That last question tells me far more than “What does success look like in this role?”

It tells me they’re thinking about judgment, communication, accountability, and whether the company learns—or just moves on to the next initiative.

Job seekers: asking about failure isn’t negative. It’s one of the fastest ways to find out whether a company is honest about its operating reality.

Hiring managers: have a real answer ready. Candidates can tell when “our weakness is that we care too much” is doing the talking.

b.text:
Somewhere around interview 200 I started keeping a mental tally of who asks about our failures. Not "what's the culture like." Not "what does success look like in this role." Specifically: tell me about the last project that didn't work.

It's a small group. But almost everyone in it has been someone I fought to hire.

Here's roughly how it went with an ops analyst candidate last spring.

She asked: "What's the last thing this team tried that didn't land?"

I told her about a routing change we rolled out to three warehouses in Q4. We'd modeled it, it looked great on paper, and within two weeks the night shift leads were quietly reverting to the old process because the new one assumed dock availability that never existed after 9pm.

She didn't say "wow, that's a great learning opportunity." She asked who found out first, and how long it took to get back to leadership. I told her: the shift leads knew day two, leadership knew week three.

Then she said, "Okay, so the gap I'd actually be working in is between those two groups." That was it. She'd just described the hardest part of the job better than the job description did.

What that question does is skip the brochure. Anyone can tell you what they're proud of. How a team handles the thing that broke tells you what it's actually like to sit in the chair on a Tuesday.

If you're interviewing this month, ask it. And if you're the one answering and you can't think of a recent failure, that's worth sitting with too.

setup: A parent of two middle-schoolers is writing an op-ed to local readers urging an 8:45am middle-school start time.

a.text:
**Let Our Kids Sleep: Why 8:45 is the Right Call for Millbrook**

Every morning at 6:15 a.m., I fight the same losing battle: dragging my two middle-schoolers out of bed. They are exhausted, cranky, and running on fumes. I know I’m not the only parent in Millbrook living this daily struggle, which is why I’m writing to strongly support the school board’s proposal to push our start time to 8:45 a.m.

This isn’t just about letting kids sleep in; it’s about basic biology. The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends that adolescents get 8 to 10 hours of sleep, noting that their natural sleep cycles shift later during puberty. It's not a choice; it's chemistry. When we force them into classrooms before the sun is fully up, we are fighting their biology.

We don’t have to guess if a later start time works. We already have the data from right here in our backyard. When Lincoln Middle ran their pilot program last year, the results spoke for themselves. Chronic absenteeism dropped, and first-period grades went up across the board. Teachers noticed kids were actually engaged instead of staring blankly at their desks. Our kids aren’t lazy; they’re just sleep-deprived. When they actually get enough rest, they show up and they succeed.

I’ve heard the main argument against this change: the buses. Parents are worried about traffic, longer commutes, and scheduling nightmares. It's a valid concern for working parents. But if you actually read the board’s proposal, you’ll see they’ve already solved this. The plan includes a re-tiered bus schedule that staggers the routes efficiently. The transportation department has mapped it out, and the logistics simply work. We shouldn't let a solvable routing puzzle stand in the way of our children's health and academic success.

Next month, the school board will vote on this proposal. I urge the board members to look past the fear of change and look at the facts. And I urge my fellow parents to support this shift. Let’s give our kids the chance to wake up, eat a real breakfast, and actually be ready to learn. An 8:45 start time is a simple change that will make a massive difference for Millbrook’s students. Let’s vote yes.

b.text:
**Let Our Kids Sleep: Why I'm Backing the 8:45 Start Time**

Every weekday morning at my house looks the same: two groggy middle-schoolers shuffling to the bus stop in the dark, half-eaten toast in hand, while I wonder why we've decided this is normal. Next month, the school board has a chance to fix it, and I hope they take it.

The proposal to move middle and high school start times to 8:45 isn't a fad or a favor to lazy teenagers. The American Academy of Pediatrics has recommended for years that adolescents start school no earlier than 8:30, because their body clocks genuinely shift in the teen years. Telling a 13-year-old to just go to bed earlier is like telling the rest of us to fall asleep at 7 p.m. It doesn't work, and the sleep they lose shows up in the classroom.

We don't have to take the pediatricians' word for it. We can look one district over. When Lincoln Middle piloted a later start, attendance went up and first-period grades improved. That tracks with what any parent already knows: a kid who's awake learns better than a kid who's fighting to keep their eyes open through pre-algebra.

I know the biggest worry is the buses. I had the same concern until I actually read the proposal. It doesn't just push start times back and hope the transportation department figures it out. It re-tiers the routes, so elementary schools run on the earlier tier and secondary schools on the later one, using the same fleet of buses we have now. Younger kids, who genuinely are up with the sun, ride first. Teenagers ride later. Nobody has to buy new buses, and the plan lays out the routing in detail. It's worth reading before assuming it can't work.

Will it require adjustment? Sure. Some sports practices will shift. Some families will need to rework afternoon pickup. Change is inconvenient. But we ask our kids to do hard things every day, and I think the adults in this district can handle moving a schedule by an hour, especially when the payoff is healthier, more alert, better-performing students.

My two won't be in middle school forever, and honestly, this change may barely reach them. I'm writing anyway, because the kids coming up behind them deserve mornings that set them up to succeed instead of to struggle.

School board members: the research is clear, the pilot results are real, and the logistics are solved. Please vote yes on the 8:45 start time.

setup: A small coffee shop owner is writing testimony to city council opposing a parking meter rate increase.

a.text:
**Testimony Submitted to the City Council Regarding the Proposed Downtown Parking Meter Rate Increase**

Submitted by [Your Name], Owner, [Business Name], [Address], Main Street

Members of the Council,

Thank you for accepting written testimony. I own [Business Name] on Main Street. I want to speak against the proposal to raise downtown meter rates from $0.50 to $1.50 per hour, and I want to do it with numbers rather than adjectives, because I think the numbers are the strongest argument I have.

**First, the size of the increase.**

This is not an adjustment. It is a 200 percent increase — the rate triples in a single step. I have not seen any other downtown cost, including my own lease, move by that much at once. Whatever the merits of raising rates eventually, the magnitude here is the problem, and it is worth stating plainly at the top of the discussion.

**Second, what happened when a neighboring city did this.**

When [Neighboring Town] raised its downtown meter rate in 2019, I did not want to guess at the effect, so I tracked it. For six consecutive weeks after the change took effect, I logged daily transaction counts against the same six-week window from the prior year. Foot traffic came in 18 percent below the comparison period.

I want to be honest about what that figure is and is not. It is one operator's data from one commercial district, not a controlled study, and I cannot rule out every other variable in those six weeks. But it is real, it is measured, and it is more evidence than has been presented in support of this proposal. If this Council has data showing a downtown retail corridor absorbed a tripling of meter rates without a measurable traffic decline, I would genuinely like to see it before you vote. In its absence, 18 percent is the best available estimate of what we are being asked to accept.

For my shop, an 18 percent drop is not a rounding error. It is the difference between covering payroll and cutting a shift.

**Third, the increase is badly matched to how people actually use downtown parking.**

The average visit to my shop is 22 minutes. My customers come in, order, wait a few minutes, and leave. They are not occupying a space for an hour, and they are not the long-term parkers this policy is presumably aimed at.

But there is no 22-minute option at the meter. There is a one-hour minimum. So today, a customer buying a $4.50 coffee and pastry pays $0.50 to park — an 11 percent surcharge on their purchase, and an effective rate of about $1.36 per hour of parking they actually use. Under the proposal, that same customer pays $1.50 — a 33 percent surcharge on the same order, at an effective rate of roughly $4.09 for every hour of parking they actually consume.

That is the transaction my customers will be evaluating at the meter, and it is the number that decides whether they come to Main Street or to a shopping center with a free lot. The current 50-cent hour minimum already covers a 22-minute visit comfortably. The proposed rate does not make short visits more efficient; it just makes them three times as expensive.

**Fourth, and most importantly: this does not solve the problem it is being offered to solve.**

The city's own report states that meter revenue accounts for 4 percent of the downtown budget. Four percent. Even a perfectly executed tripling — assuming zero behavioral change, zero decline in occupancy, zero lost sales tax from businesses like mine — moves a line item that constitutes one twenty-fifth of downtown spending.

And it will not be a perfect tripling, because the 18 percent figure suggests fewer people will park downtown at all. The Council should ask staff a direct question before voting: what is the projected net revenue after accounting for reduced occupancy, and how does that net figure compare to the sales tax receipts generated by the foot traffic it displaces? I suspect that analysis has not been run. It should be, because a policy that risks 18 percent of Main Street's customer traffic to improve a 4 percent budget line is not a solution. It is a trade the city loses on both ends.

**What I am asking for.**

I am not asking that rates never change. I am asking for three things:

1. **Reject the $1.50 rate as proposed.** If an increase is necessary, phase it — to $0.75, hold for twelve months, and measure.
2. **Create a short-stay option.** A 15- or 30-minute rate, or a free first 20 minutes, would align meter policy with a 22-minute average visit and protect exactly the turnover a merchant district needs.
3. **Require a net revenue analysis before any vote,** including projected occupancy loss and downstream sales tax impact, measured against the 4 percent figure in the city's own report.

I have run my business on this street for years and I intend to keep doing it. I am asking the Council to make this decision with the numbers in front of it.

Respectfully submitted,

[Your Name]
Owner, [Business Name]
[Address] | [Phone] | [Email]

b.text:
Good evening, members of the council. My name is [Name], and I’m the owner of [Coffee Shop Name], the independent coffee shop on Main Street. I’m here to speak against the proposal to raise parking meter rates downtown from 50 cents to a dollar fifty an hour. I’m not going to lean on vague warnings—I’m going to give you the numbers, because I’ve lived them, tracked them, and I believe they make the stakes plain.

In 2019, the town right next to us put through a very similar meter hike—right around tripling the hourly rate. I have a good relationship with a shop owner there, and with his permission, I tracked his daily register data for the six weeks right after that change. What I found was an 18% drop in foot traffic. Not a slow decline over months—an immediate, sustained 18% loss of customers walking through the door. For a small coffee shop, that was the difference between a modest profit and a serious loss. We aren’t talking about a theoretical risk; we’ve already seen the experiment run a few miles away.

Now bring that closer to home. I clock my own customers’ visits. The average stay for someone grabbing a coffee and maybe sitting for a few minutes is 22 minutes. Under the current 50-cent-per-hour minimum, a customer drops two quarters and has plenty of time—they’re not rushed, they’re not bitter about paying for parking they didn’t use. But if you raise the meter to a dollar fifty, you’re forcing that same 22-minute customer to pay triple for a full hour they don’t need. For many of them, that’s the cost of the small coffee they just bought. They’ll feel it, and some of them will just stop coming downtown for what used to be a quick, easy ritual. You’ll be charging them 200% more for the same 22-minute errand, and in my business, that friction is real. I see it on faces when the sidewalk outside is empty.

Finally, I want to point to the city’s own numbers. Your own budget report shows that parking meter revenue currently covers just 4% of the downtown budget. Four percent. Tripling the rate might bump that slightly, but it won’t close any meaningful gap—it’s not going to fix roads, it’s not going to fund a new initiative. What it will do is bleed the very foot traffic that generates the sales tax, the business license fees, and the vibrancy that actually sustain our downtown. We are, right now, the shops and cafes that make Main Street a place people want to visit. An 18% drop in foot traffic, even if it’s only a fraction of that here, would wipe out far more in overall economic activity than this increase could ever return in meter coins.

I’m asking you, respectfully, to vote no. The data from next door, the 22-minute reality of my customers, and the 4% figure from your own report all tell the same story: this doesn’t solve a problem, but it will create one. Thank you for your time.

setup: A local sports columnist is writing an opinionated season-ending commentary for readers of the local paper's sports section.

a.text:
The sting of Friday night won’t fade because the season ended. It’ll linger because the season ended unnecessarily.

Yes, the team finished 8-2. Yes, Dez Kowalski set a school passing record with 2,340 yards. But none of that salves a second-round playoff loss to a team this group already beat by 20 in Week 3. That’s not just losing; that’s stepping on a rake you saw lying in the grass.

Here’s the brutally simple reason they’re clearing out lockers instead of preparing for a quarterfinal: They abandoned the run in the second half. The ground game was grinding, controlling the clock, moving the chains—and they were only down three. Then, as if a switch flipped, it vanished. Instead of leaning on what worked, the play-calling went airborne, as if the record books needed padding and not a playoff win. That’s not on the kids. That’s a decision from the sideline, and it was the wrong one.

Kowalski’s arm is a weapon, but it’s not the only one. Championships aren’t won by forgetting what got you there. This loss wasn’t about talent or effort; it was about a staff that outthought itself at the worst possible moment.

b.text:
The season ended sooner than anyone in this town expected, and it ended in the most frustrating way possible.

This was an 8-2 team that had already proven it could beat its second-round opponent. Back in Week 3, they beat that same team by 20 points. Friday night, with the score still within one possession and the Bulldogs down only three in the second half, the formula was right there.

Run the football.

It had been working. The line was getting movement, the backs were finding room, and the offense was keeping the game from turning into a track meet. Instead, they drifted away from it and put too much of the burden on the passing game.

That is not a criticism of Dez Kowalski, who had a remarkable season. His 2,340 passing yards are a school record, and he gave this team a chance every Friday night. But a record-setting quarterback does not mean every meaningful snap has to become a throw. The best offenses use what the game gives them. On Friday, the run game was giving them enough.

Playoff losses are rarely about one call or one series. But this one will stick because the Bulldogs did not need to reinvent themselves. They needed to stay patient, stay physical, and keep doing what was working.

Still, an 8-2 season deserves respect. Kowalski’s record is one that will stand in the school’s history, and this group gave the community plenty to cheer about. But that does not make the ending any easier to accept.

They were down three, not down three touchdowns. And they let the game get away from the part of their offense that could have kept them in it.

a.text:
**A 22% Hike, 60% of My Acres, and a Bill Worth Your Phone Call**

This year USDA raised the base rate on prevented planting coverage in our region by 22 percent. On my operation that works out to roughly $46,000 more than I paid last year for the same protection.

I'd have paid it grudgingly in a normal spring. This wasn't a normal spring. The rain started the second week of April and did not quit in any meaningful way until it was too late to matter. By the late May final planting date I had 60 percent of my acres in the ground. The other 40 percent sat there with standing water in the low spots and mud you couldn't drive a four-wheeler across, let alone a planter. Anybody farming west of the river knows exactly what I'm describing because you were looking at the same thing out your own kitchen window.

So the year I actually needed prevented planting coverage is the year the premium jumped by nearly a quarter. That's the first thing I want people to sit with.

Here's the second thing, and it's the reason I'm writing.

The rate hike doesn't land evenly. The way the acreage caps are structured, the full increase applies across every acre on an operation my size. Once an operation crosses the cap threshold, the effective cost per acre starts coming down. The result is that the two large operations that farm on either side of me, both good neighbors, both running several times my acreage, are seeing a smaller percentage increase in their total premium cost than I am. Same county. Same rain. Same deadline. Same 40 percent left unplanted. Different bill.

I ran the numbers with my crop insurance agent, who I trust and who didn't argue with me. On a per-acre basis I'm paying meaningfully more for the same coverage than the operations next door. Not because I'm a worse risk. Because I'm smaller.

I don't begrudge the bigger outfits. They didn't write the rules. But a program that's supposed to help farmers stay in business through a bad spring shouldn't be quietly structured so that the fourth-generation operation on 1,200 acres carries a heavier share than the one on 6,000. That's backward, and I don't think it's what anybody intended when the caps were drawn up.

SB 214 would fix the acreage cap. It adjusts how the threshold applies so the premium increase falls proportionally instead of piling onto the operations least able to absorb it. It doesn't take anything away from the larger farms. It doesn't touch the coverage itself. It just corrects the math so that a 22 percent hike is a 22 percent hike for everybody, not 22 for some and less for others.

The bill has been sitting in committee since February. I'm told it's stalled less from opposition than from nobody making much noise about it. That part we can do something about.

If you farm in this county and you had ground you couldn't plant this spring, you already know what I'm talking about. If you didn't have that problem this year, you will eventually, and the cap will be waiting for you when you do.

Call your state senator. Call your representative. Their numbers are on the back page of this newsletter. Tell them you farm here, tell them how many acres you got planted by the deadline, and tell them you want SB 214 out of committee and onto the floor. You don't need to be eloquent. You need to be one more voice they can't ignore.

I'll be at the county meeting on the 14th. If you want to compare premium statements, bring yours. I'll have mine.

b.text:
When the late May planting deadline hit, four out of every ten acres on my place were still too wet to touch. Between the relentless rain and standing water, my family managed to get just 60 percent of our corn and soybeans in the ground. 

Filing prevented planting is never the plan, but it’s the safety net we pay for to keep the lights on after a disastrous spring. This year, however, that safety net came with a staggering price tag. The USDA quietly raised the prevented planting base rate in our region by 22 percent. On my operation alone, that policy shift translates to roughly $46,000 in additional out-of-pocket costs. 

In a year where margins were already razor-thin, taking a $46,000 hit just for the privilege of insuring ground we couldn't plant is a heavy blow. But what makes this hike particularly galling is the way the current acreage caps are structured. 

Because the cap system scales the way it does, medium-sized family operations like mine absorb a far higher proportional cost than the massive, multi-thousand-acre corporate entities down the road. The mega-operations have the sheer volume to dilute the impact of these cap thresholds, while family-run farms get squeezed on both ends: we take the full brunt of the percentage hike on our unplanted ground, and we lack the total acreage volume to offset the penalty. It’s a formula that punishes the very farms that form the backbone of this county. My great-grandfather didn't build this farm to be wiped out by administrative arithmetic, and neither did yours.

We can't control the rain, but we can fix the policy. 

Senate Bill 214 was introduced specifically to correct this acreage cap distortion and protect family operations from taking a disproportionate hit when disaster strikes. It adjusts the cap math so that medium-scale farms aren't penalized simply for existing in a mid-tier acreage bracket. 

If we want four- and five-generation farms to survive in this state, our policy needs to reflect reality on the ground. Call your state legislators this week. Tell them what the 22 percent hike is costing your farm, and tell them to vote yes on SB 214.

setup: A fourth-generation soybean and corn farmer is writing a newsletter commentary on crop insurance costs and SB 214 for county readers and state legislators.

a.text:
By the time the late May final planting date came and went, my planter had only touched 60 percent of our ground. The rest was sitting under standing water, rutted out by weeks of unrelenting rain. For a fourth-generation corn and soybean operation, taking prevented planting is never the goal—it’s the absolute last resort to keep the lights on. 

What made a brutal spring worse was the bill that followed. 

This year, the USDA raised the base premium rate on prevented planting coverage in our region by 22 percent. On our farm alone, that adjustment translates to roughly $46,000 in additional, unexpected costs. That is $46,000 paid out on ground that won't produce a single bushel to help offset the expense.

If that hike fell evenly across agriculture, it would still be a hard pill to swallow. But because of the way prevented planting acreage caps are calculated, it hits independent family farms far harder than the massive, multi-county operations down the road. 

Large corporate outfits running tens of thousands of acres have the scale and diversified footprint to absorb and dilute these rate spikes across multiple units. Family operations like mine—where our ground is concentrated in this county—don't have that luxury. Under the current cap formulas, when localized weather drowns out half a township, the family farmer pays a higher proportional penalty per acre than the mega-operation that can offset those drowned acres against dry ones two counties away. The math simply works against the smaller guy.

We are not asking for a handout. We pay our premiums and we take the risks. But the safety net should not punish family-scale agriculture for existing.

Senate Bill 214 directly addresses this flaw by restructuring the acreage cap calculations to ensure rate hikes and risk determinations are applied equitably, rather than landing heaviest on independent operators. It fixes an outdated formula and levels the playing field before another season gets washed out.

Our state lawmakers need to understand that policies designed in a vacuum have real dollar consequences in our fields. I urge every Farm Bureau member reading this to call your state senator and representative this week. Tell them what the 22 percent hike is costing your balance sheet, and tell them to vote "yes" on SB 214. We can’t control the rain in May, but we can fix the rules that govern the aftermath.

b.text:
**When the Cap Doesn’t Fit**

This spring, I planted 60% of my acres. The other 40% sat underwater. It wasn’t a management decision—it just kept raining, and the late May final planting date came and went. Like a lot of you, I turned to prevented planting coverage, the safety net we pay for precisely because years like this happen.

Then the premium bill arrived. USDA raised the base rate for prevented planting in our region by 22% this year. For my operation, a fourth-generation corn and soybean farm, that increase alone adds $46,000 to my insurance cost. Forty-six thousand dollars. That’s a hard number to swallow after losing nearly half my planting window.

But the premium hike isn’t the whole story. What makes it truly lopsided is the acreage cap baked into the prevented planting program. That cap doesn’t scale with the size of your operation—it’s a fixed number of eligible acres per crop. On my farm, the cap already covers a big slice of my total ground before a single seed goes in. So a 22% rate hike on those capped acres cuts deep, eating into a much larger share of my potential revenue than it does for the 5,000-acre operation down the road. They might hit the same cap, but for them it’s a fraction of their total acres; for family-scale farms like mine, it’s a direct hit to our ability to keep the doors open.

The math is simple: a one-size-fits-all cap punishes smaller farms disproportionately, year after year, and a premium spike like this rubs salt in the wound. We need an acreage cap that reflects the reality of family farm scale, not just the averages for giant operations.

There’s a fix on the table. Senate Bill 214 restructures the prevented planting acreage cap so it’s proportional to actual farm size. That means your premium costs would align with your real exposure, not an arbitrary cutoff that treats a half-section farm the same as a 10,000-acre conglomerate. SB 214 gives family operations a fair shake, and it’s the kind of common-sense adjustment our state legislators can get behind.

Please take five minutes to call or email your state senator and representative. Tell them you’re a farmer, that the 22% prevented planting hike just cost your neighbor $46,000 on a rain-wrecked spring, and that SB 214 is the right tool to stop the cap from capping us out of business. If enough of us speak up, we can make sure the safety net actually catches the farms that need it most—ours.

setup: A family plumbing company owner is writing a blog post for Minneapolis homeowners about winterizing outdoor pipes.

a.text:
# How to Winterize Your Outdoor Spigots (Advice from a Minneapolis Plumber)

Every January, a big share of our burst-pipe calls trace back to the same thing: an outdoor spigot that didn't get winterized. The whole job takes about ten minutes and costs three bucks. Here's exactly how to do it.

Do this by mid-October. Around here the first hard freeze can hit early, and it only takes one cold night to split a pipe.

## 1. Disconnect your hoses

Start here, because everything else depends on it. Unscrew every hose, splitter, and timer from every outdoor faucet. Drain the hoses, coil them, and put them in the garage or shed — they'll last longer anyway.

This matters even if you have a frost-free spigot. A frost-free only works if water can drain out of it. A connected hose traps water inside, and then it's no better than the old-style faucet.

## 2. Shut the interior valve

Go down to the basement and find where the pipe runs from the spigot through the wall. There should be a shutoff valve on that line, usually within a few feet of where it exits the house. Turn it clockwise until it stops.

One valve per spigot — if you have faucets on multiple sides of the house, each one has its own shutoff.

## 3. Drain the spigot

Go back outside and open the spigot. Let it run until the water stops — that's the water trapped between the shutoff and the faucet, and it's the water that would otherwise freeze.

If your interior valve has a little bleeder cap on the side, open that too (hold a cup under it). It lets air into the line so it drains completely.

Leave the outdoor spigot in the open position all winter. If any water is left in there, it has somewhere to go when it expands.

## 4. Put on a foam cover

The hard foam faucet covers are about $3 at any hardware store. It slips over the spigot and cinches tight against the siding. It's cheap insurance against wind chill hitting the pipe where it comes through the wall.

## The mistake that causes most of our January burst-pipe calls

Leaving the hose connected. That's it — that's the big one.

Here's what happens. The hose traps water in the spigot, and because the hose is still on, most people never shut the interior valve either. So you've got a pressurized line, full of water, sitting against an exterior wall. January rolls around, we get a real cold snap — the minus-twenty kind Minneapolis does every year — and that water freezes, expands, and splits the pipe. Often it splits *inside* the wall, where you can't see it.

Then you've got water pouring into your wall cavity or basement, and a ten-minute job just became an emergency call, a plumbing repair, and drywall work.

Take the hoses off. It's the single most important step on this list.

## Don't have an interior shutoff?

A lot of older Minneapolis homes don't — the spigot line runs straight out through the wall with no way to isolate it. If that's your setup, don't try to get through winter with just a foam cover and good intentions.

Give us a call at [phone number]. We can install an interior shutoff valve, or swap the spigot for a frost-free sillcock that drains itself every time you turn it off. Either one is a quick, inexpensive job — and it's a whole lot cheaper than the burst-pipe version of the same visit.

b.text:
# How to Winterize Your Outside Spigots (Minneapolis Homeowners)

If you have an outdoor spigot on the side or back of your house, it needs to be winterized before the first deep freeze. In Minneapolis, that usually means sometime in November.

Here’s the quick version.

## What You Need

- A pair of pliers or your hands, if the hose is not stuck
- A bucket or towel, just in case a little water drips out
- A $3 foam spigot cover

## Step 1: Shut the Interior Valve

Most Minneapolis outdoor spigots are fed by a pipe that runs through the house. Look for a shut-off valve inside near the spigot’s location. It may be in a basement ceiling, utility room, garage, bathroom, or closet.

Turn the valve to stop water from getting to the outside spigot. If the valve is a lever, turn it until it lines up across the pipe. If it’s a round handle, turn it clockwise until it’s snug. Don’t force it.

## Step 2: Drain the Spigot

Once the interior valve is off, go outside and open the spigot. Let it drain. You may see a small amount of water come out, then stop. Leave it open until you’re sure the line is empty.

After it drains, turn the spigot off again.

## Step 3: Disconnect Hoses

Take off every garden hose left attached to the spigot. Pull the nozzle down so water in the hose drains out. If the hose is stiff or frozen, thaw it gently — don’t yank it and risk breaking the spigot.

## Step 4: Put On a Foam Cover

Slide a $3 foam spigot cover over the spigot and secure it in place. This isn’t magic, and it doesn’t turn the spigot into a heated pipe. It helps block cold wind from getting directly into the fitting. It’s just one layer of protection.

## The Big Mistake Homeowners Make

Leaving the hose connected.

That is one of the main reasons we get January burst-pipe calls. A hose left attached traps water inside the spigot. Even after you shut the valve, water can stay in the exposed pipe and hose. When it freezes, it expands, and something can split.

The hose is the problem. If you leave it on, you’ve basically given the winter a place to freeze the water.

## If You Don’t Have an Interior Shutoff

Some older Minneapolis homes have spigots that don’t have an obvious interior shut-off valve. If you can’t find one, or you’re not sure which one controls the outside pipe, don’t guess.

That’s the point where it makes sense to call us.

We can find the valve, label it properly, and make sure you can shut down the outside lines quickly before the next cold snap. It’s a lot cheaper to do it now than to chase water in the basement after one pipe gives way.

setup: A solo indie game developer is writing a devlog recap for subscribers about his game's launch week sales, subreddit attention, review feedback, and upcoming 1.1 patch.

a.text:
Well, it’s finally out. After three years of nights and weekends, I launched my first commercial game last week. It feels incredibly weird to actually have it out in the wild.

For the numbers nerds out there, we sold 412 copies in the first seven days. I’m really happy with that for a debut. We also caught a nice little wave of traffic when the game hit the front page of a smaller subreddit, though the spike only lasted for about six hours before dropping off. Still, it definitely helped push the algorithm at the right time.

As for the feedback, I’ve been reading through all the reviews. Most of it has been great, but one reviewer pointed out that the movement feels "floaty." And honestly? They’re completely right. I spent so long staring at the same project that I just got used to it and lost my perspective. 

So, that’s the main focus for the 1.1 patch. I’m tightening up the controls, adjusting the acceleration curves, and making the character actually feel grounded. Expect that update to roll out sometime next month.

For now, I'm going to take a few days to just sleep and catch up on my backlog before diving back into the engine. Thanks to everyone who bought the game, played it, and left a review. I'll see you all when 1.1 is ready.

b.text:
# One Week In

I launched the game last Tuesday. 412 copies sold in the first week.

That's the headline. It still doesn't feel entirely real to type out.

The launch day was chaos in the best way—the game hit the front page of r/indiegames for about 6 hours, which sent a spike of traffic that made my hosting sweat a little. I kept refreshing Steam to see the numbers climb, which is probably not healthy but I couldn't stop myself. By end of day I'd made more money than I spent on the game's development. That's the part that actually feels surreal.

The reviews have been mostly positive. A lot of people loved the art direction and the puzzle design. A few people noted performance issues on older hardware that I'm already working on for the next patch. And yeah, one review said the movement feels floaty. They're right. I've been thinking about it since, and I know exactly what they mean—the character model isn't giving enough weight to the jump arc. I started prototyping a fix last week and it's already feeling better. That's going into 1.1 next month.

The player comments have been great to read. Some people are finding secrets I forgot I hid. Someone made fan art. Someone else said they played for five hours straight and lost track of time, which is honestly all I've ever wanted a game to do.

Right now I'm running through the bug reports, planning that movement patch, and trying not to work myself into the ground on updates. Three years of nights and weekends to get here. I'm going to try to actually sleep for a bit before I keep going.

Next devlog will be in two weeks when 1.1 is closer to done.
