setup: A first-year nursing student is writing a scholarship essay about her first ER rotation for scholarship committee readers.

a.text:
# What I Learned My First Week

I didn't cry during my first code. I want to be honest about that because I spent the whole drive home that night feeling guilty about it, like something was wrong with me. I thought I'd be the student who tears up, who has to step out. I wasn't.

What happened was this: a patient came in and things went bad fast, and my preceptor looked at me and said, "Go restock the gauze in Bay 3." So I did. I walked down the hall and pulled open the drawers and started counting out packages, and through the curtain I could hear them calling it out. One. Two. Three. Four. The counting didn't stop. I stood there with gauze in my hands and listened and didn't cry. I just stood there. I think I was useful in the way they needed me to be useful, which was small and out of the way. I'm still figuring out whether that's enough.

---

The hand thing happened on day two. A guy came in with a gash on his forearm, pretty deep, needed cleaning and stitching. His wife was on her way but stuck in traffic on I-95, and he was sitting on the table waiting and he looked scared. Not the kind of scared where you say it out loud. The kind where your foot won't stop moving and you keep looking at the door like maybe she'll walk through it.

The nurse got everything set up and told him the cleaning part was going to hurt, and he nodded, and I could see his hand was shaking where he had it resting on the rail. So I just reached over and held it. I didn't ask first. I probably should have, but I didn't. I just took his hand and he held on. He held on hard.

The nurse flushed the wound and he squeezed my hand and I said, "You're good, you're good," even though I had no idea if he was good or not. I said it anyway. His wife got there about twenty minutes later, and when she came through the curtain he let go of my hand and reached for hers, and that was that. I went and helped another patient take off their shoes.

What I keep thinking about is that I didn't do anything that required a license. I didn't do anything they'll test me on at the end of the semester. But he needed someone to hold his hand right then, and his wife wasn't there yet, and I was. That's the part of nursing I'm most sure about, even though I can't really explain it in clinical terms.

---

The blood draw is the one that kept me up at night.

Diabetic guy, mid-fifties, rough veins from years of sticks. My preceptor said, "You try," and I thought, okay, I've practiced on the dummy, I've practiced on my classmates. I can do this.

First try: I went in and got nothing. Flash of blood, then nothing. He didn't flinch. I pulled out and said I was sorry.

Second try: I adjusted, went a little lower, and missed again. He said, "It's alright, honey." That made it worse.

Third try: I couldn't find the vein at all. It rolled on me and I froze with the needle in and my preceptor said, easy, "Pull back, try again." I pulled back and there was nothing. I wanted to disappear. My face was hot and I could feel sweat on the back of my neck and this man was sitting there being patient with me when I was the one who was supposed to be patient with him.

My preceptor asked if I wanted her to take over. And I did want that. I wanted to say yes and step back and let someone who knew what they were doing finish it. But I also knew that if I stepped back right then, I'd keep stepping back every time something got hard.

So I said, "Can I try one more time?"

He said, "Go ahead." Still calm. Still not making me feel stupid.

Fourth try: I went in slow, felt the vein, and the flash came and stayed. I held my breath and got the tube on and the blood started filling and I almost laughed. I didn't laugh. But I wanted to. I got the tubes filled, put pressure on the site, and labeled everything. My hands were shaking the whole time. He said, "See? You got it."

I said thank you and walked out to the hallway and leaned against the wall for a second.

---

Here's what I know after one week: I'm not good at this yet. I'm not supposed to be. I'm a first-year student and I missed a vein three times and I stood in a hallway holding gauze while someone's heart stopped and I didn't know what to do with my face. I held a stranger's hand because I didn't know what else to do, and it turned out that was the right thing, but I didn't know that when I did it.

What I'm asking for is help getting through the next two years so I can become someone who does know. Someone who finds the vein on the first try, or at least doesn't panic on the third. Someone who knows where to stand during a code and what to do with her hands besides hold gauze. And someone who still holds a patient's hand when they need it, even after she doesn't have to anymore, even after there are more important things she could be doing.

I want to be the nurse who does both. I think that's worth the work. I'm asking for help to do it.

b.text:
I walked into the ER on my first clinical day with my stomach in knots. I had the book knowledge, the mannequin practice, the very clean, very quiet skills lab. None of it prepared me for the noise.

The first thing I remember clearly is a man in his sixties with a deep gash on his forearm. The doctor numbed him up and started cleaning, and the man’s face went tight. His wife had been on her way for forty minutes, stuck in traffic, and you could see he was trying to be tough. I didn’t know what else to do, so I asked if he wanted me to hold his hand. He looked surprised, then nodded. I stood there while the wound was flushed and stitched, his grip strong, and I didn’t say much. When his wife finally rushed in, she took my place and he smiled at me. That was it. I didn’t dress the wound or calculate a drip rate. I just showed up. I think that matters, too.

The second day, something happened that I wasn’t supposed to see. A code blue came in, a man who’d crashed his bike. The room filled up fast with staff, all moving in a kind of controlled rush. My instructor told me to go restock the gauze carts in the hallway. It was busy work, the kind of task that makes you feel invisible. But the curtain was thin. I heard someone call out “starting compressions,” and then the counting started. Steady, one after another. I could hear the rhythm of it, the pause for breaths, and under that the beeping of machines. I just kept pulling packages of gauze, loading the drawers, and listening. Nobody needed me in that room. I was too new. But standing outside that curtain, I understood that nursing isn’t only about being the hands on the chest. Sometimes it’s about making sure everything else is ready. That moment taught me what teamwork really means. I was a tiny part of something big, and I felt it.

The third thing I remember is the blood draw. A diabetic patient with veins that rolled and hid. I stuck him once, twice, three times, and missed every one. My face burned. My preceptor, a nurse named Ellen, just watched and waited. The patient, a man named Rafael, was patient too. He had the kind of tired look that comes from years of needles. I was about to apologize and step away, but Ellen said quietly, “Try one more time.” So I did. I felt the vein before I saw it, a faint little give under my fingers. The fourth try, the flash of blood in the chamber. I capped it and looked up, and Rafael gave me a small nod. Ellen didn’t clap, just said, “Good. Now label it.” I learned more about nursing in that five minutes than I had in a month of lectures. Persistence. Trust. The fact that patients are willing to give you a chance even when you’re learning.

I’m still a first-year student. I have a thousand skills yet to learn. But after that first week in the ER, I know I’m where I’m supposed to be. Nursing isn’t all about the big saves. It’s the small stuff—a hand to hold, a stocked cart, a fourth try. This scholarship would help me keep showing up, keep learning, and keep getting better at the small stuff that honestly doesn’t feel small at all.

setup: A small coffee shop owner is writing testimony to city council opposing a parking meter rate increase.

a.text:
To the Members of the City Council,

My name is Sarah Mitchell, and I own Daily Grind, a small independent coffee shop at 214 Main Street. I am submitting this essay as testimony for the public record regarding the proposal to raise the downtown parking meter rate from 50 cents to a dollar fifty an hour. I respectfully ask you to vote against this increase.

I want to speak to you not with predictions, but with numbers I have actually tracked.

In 2019, the town of Millerton, twenty minutes from here, raised their downtown meters by a similar amount. At the time I was managing a shop there before opening my own here. After the increase took effect, I tracked my own register and transaction counts for the following 6 weeks. In those 6 weeks, my foot traffic dropped 18%. It was not a slow season or a weather issue. It was an immediate, measurable decline right after the meters went up. People who used to stop in for a quick coffee while running errands decided it wasn't worth feeding the meter. I have seen what a hike like this does to a block like ours, and I logged that 18% drop myself.

I have also tracked what my customers actually do here on Main Street. On average, a customer visit in my shop lasts 22 minutes. They come in, order, wait for their drink, maybe sit for a few minutes, and go. The current structure, with a 50 cent one-hour minimum, already covers them fine. They pay 50 cents to stay 22 minutes. Under your proposal, that same 22-minute visit would cost them a dollar fifty. You are not charging them for more time. You are tripling the cost of the time they already use. It is a 200% increase for the same cup of coffee.

I have read the city's own Downtown Parking and Revenue Report from last quarter. According to your own numbers, all meter revenue combined currently covers only 4% of the downtown operating budget. Even if you triple the rate, you are not closing a budget gap. You are putting the burden of that 4% squarely on the short-term customers that every small shop on Main Street depends on. For an extra fraction of that 4%, you are risking the kind of 18% loss in traffic I have already watched happen once.

I have built my business on regulars, but also on the person who has a spare 22 minutes and decides to stop because it's easy and affordable to do so. If a quick stop downtown costs a dollar fifty before they even buy anything, many of them simply won't.

Please keep the meter rate at 50 cents an hour.

Thank you for your time and for your service to our downtown.

Sarah Mitchell
Owner, Daily Grind Coffee
214 Main Street

b.text:
# Testimony Regarding Proposed Parking Meter Rate Increase

**Submitted to the City Council for the Public Record**

Members of the City Council,

My name is [Name], and I own [Coffee Shop Name] on Main Street. I have operated my shop downtown for [number] years, and I am submitting this testimony in opposition to the proposed increase in parking meter rates from 50 cents per hour to $1.50 per hour — a 200 percent increase.

I am not here to speak in generalities. I want to give you three specific numbers and explain what each one means for my business and for this downtown.

**First: an 18 percent drop in foot traffic.** In 2019, when [neighboring town] raised its meter rates by a comparable margin, I paid close attention because I knew the same proposal could eventually come to us. For six weeks following their increase, I tracked my own register data against the same six-week period before the hike, and I spoke with business owners there who were doing the same. The foot traffic decline I documented was 18 percent. That is not a rounding error. For a small shop like mine, an 18 percent drop in customers is the difference between making payroll comfortably and lying awake at night. Margins in independent coffee are thin. I cannot absorb a decline of that size, and neither can most of my neighbors on this street.

**Second: my customers average a 22-minute visit.** I know this because I watch it every day — a customer parks, comes in, orders, sits or takes it to go, and leaves. The current one-hour minimum on the meters already more than covers the typical visit to my shop. In other words, the existing rate structure is not underpricing the parking my customers actually use. Tripling the hourly rate does not make my customers pay their fair share; it makes them pay triple for time they never use. A customer who runs downtown for a coffee will now pay $1.50 for 22 minutes of parking. At some point, the math tells them to go to the drive-through on the highway instead, where parking is free. And once that habit forms, it does not come back.

**Third: 4 percent.** According to the city's own report, meter revenue covers only 4 percent of the downtown budget. I want to sit with that number for a moment, because it is the heart of this issue. Even if this rate increase performed perfectly — even if not a single driver changed their behavior and revenue tripled — we would be talking about moving from 4 percent to roughly 12 percent of the downtown budget. That is not a solution to the city's budget challenges. But if the increase drives away foot traffic the way I watched it do in 2019, the city loses more than it gains: reduced sales tax receipts, struggling storefronts, and eventually vacancies. You would be trading a small, uncertain revenue gain for a real risk to the tax base that downtown businesses generate.

I want to be clear that I understand the city needs revenue, and I do not envy the decisions this council has to make. I am not asking you to do nothing. I am asking you not to solve a budget problem worth far more than 4 percent by putting a 200 percent increase on the backs of the customers who keep Main Street alive.

If the council believes parking rates must rise, I would ask you to consider alternatives: a smaller, phased increase; a free first 30 minutes to protect quick-visit customers like mine; or a genuine study of the projected impact on downtown sales tax revenue before this vote, not after.

I built my business on this street because I believed in this downtown. I still do. I am asking you to weigh the numbers I have given you — an 18 percent drop in foot traffic, a 22-minute average visit, and a 4 percent contribution to the budget — and conclude, as I have, that this proposal costs downtown more than it earns the city.

Thank you for your time and for entering this testimony into the record.

Respectfully submitted,

[Name]
Owner, [Coffee Shop Name]
[Address], Main Street

setup: A first-year nursing student is writing a scholarship essay about her first ER rotation for scholarship committee readers.

a.text:
I didn’t expect to learn so much in one week. My first clinical rotation in the emergency department moved faster than I could keep up. People came in needing help in ways I couldn’t predict, and I had to figure out how to stay focused without freezing. By the time Friday rolled around, I realized nursing isn’t just about following steps. It’s about showing up when people are scared, in pain, or just really tired. It started with a few quiet moments that stayed with me long after my shoes came off.

One afternoon, I helped clean a deep cut on an older man’s forearm. The nurse handled the irrigation and packing, but his wife was supposed to be there and got stuck in traffic. When it was time to position him, he glanced at me and asked if I could hold his hand. I pulled a chair closer. His grip was tight. I didn’t have a way to numb the sting or make the bleeding stop faster, so I just kept my hand firm under his and matched his breathing when he clenched his teeth. I stayed still until the bandage was secure. He let go slowly and said, “Appreciate you.” It wasn’t complicated, but it taught me that sometimes your whole job is just to be steady for someone else.

Later that same week, I was sent to the utility room to restock gauze while a code happened behind a curtain down the hall. I heard the monitor flatline before I heard them start talking. Then came the counting. “Twenty-four… twenty-five…” I stood there folding sterile packages, wishing I could pull the curtain back and assist, but I knew I wasn’t trained for that yet. You can’t guess your way through a code. I kept working, listening to the rhythm of their voices, feeling how heavy the air got in the hallway when they called it. I took a minute to reset my mind, wiped down the counter, and waited for my next assignment. That moment made it clear how much happens beyond my reach right now, and how hard I’ll have to push myself to earn the chance to step inside that circle.

The hardest lesson came from a diabetic patient whose veins had been damaged from years of draws. I tried three times. Three missed sticks. Each time, blood welled and then disappeared. My cheeks burned. I apologized every time, knowing I was adding stress to someone who was already having a rough day. He didn’t snap. He just rubbed his arm and muttered, “Fourth time’s the charm, right?” I relaxed my shoulders, checked the angle, and went slower. On the fourth attempt, the vein caught. I finished the draw quickly, applied pressure, and labeled the tubes. He gave me a short nod. No grand speech, just a quiet sign that I hadn’t walked away. Failure doesn’t usually look dramatic in nursing. It just looks like keeping your hands steady when you want to put them down.

Those three moments shaped more than my technical skills. They showed me what kind of nurse I’m trying to become. Someone who doesn’t run when things get loud, who understands that presence and persistence matter just as much as procedures, and who treats mistakes as practice instead of proof that she should quit. This scholarship would take a real weight off my shoulders as I finish my coursework and move into higher-level rotations. I’m not walking onto campus pretending I already know how to save lives. I’m just trying to show up, learn from every error, and build the kind of steady, dependable care that patients can count on. If you’re looking for someone willing to do the hard work, listen closely, and keep improving, that’s exactly what I’m ready to do. Thank you for your time and for supporting students who are just getting started.

b.text:
# What I Learned in Room 6

I didn't expect the first person I helped to be a stranger whose name I'd forget by the end of the shift, but whose hand I'd remember for a long time.

He was maybe seventy, in for a leg wound that needed cleaning before it got stitched up. His wife was supposed to be there, but traffic had her stuck somewhere on the interstate, and he kept looking at the door like she might walk through it if he waited long enough. The nurse doing the cleaning told him it was going to sting. He nodded, and then he looked at me, standing there in my student scrubs not doing much of anything, and he just said, "Would you mind?"

I didn't know what he meant until I did. I took his hand. He squeezed it hard when the solution hit the wound, and he apologized for squeezing so hard, and I told him not to worry about it. We didn't talk about anything important. I think I asked him about his dog. But I stood there and let him hold onto me because his wife couldn't be there to do it, and that was the job in that moment. Nobody taught me that in a lecture hall.

Not everything that week made me feel useful. During a code, somebody told me to go restock gauze, which felt like being sent to the kids' table while the adults handled things. I went. I stood in the supply room and counted gauze packs and listened to someone on the other side of the curtain counting compressions instead. One, two, three, four. I didn't see what happened in that room. I just heard the numbers and the quiet after them. I still think about that quiet. I didn't do anything heroic that day. I stocked gauze. But I learned that the job isn't always about being in the room. Sometimes it's about doing the small thing so the people who need to be in there can be.

Then there was the blood draw that humbled me completely. The patient was a diabetic guy, older, with veins that rolled and hid and generally did not want to be found. I missed the first stick. I missed the second. By the third, I was sweating more than he was, and I apologized so many times he started laughing at me instead of getting mad, which I think was his way of being kind about it. He told me his veins had been giving nurses trouble for twenty years, so I shouldn't take it personally. On the fourth try, I found it. I actually said "there it is" out loud like an idiot, and he said "there it is" right back at me, like we'd done something together instead of me just finally doing my job. Small win. But I felt it in my chest for the rest of the shift.

None of these moments were dramatic in the way I thought the ER would be dramatic. Nobody yelled "clear." Nobody coded and came back in some big cinematic way in front of me. What I got instead was a hand to hold, a hallway full of counting I couldn't see the end of, and a vein that took four tries to find. But I think that's the actual job. It's not always the big save. It's showing up for the parts that are small and slow and a little embarrassing, and doing them anyway, because someone needs you to.

I came into that week wondering if I could handle the big emergencies. I left it realizing the real question is whether I can handle the quiet, unglamorous moments in between them, the ones where nobody's watching and nothing photographs well, but somebody still needs your hand, or your gauze, or just you not giving up on the fourth try. I think I can. I want the chance to keep finding out.

setup: A remote software engineer is writing a 6-month standing desk review for blog readers researching standing desks.

a.text:
# Jarvik L2 Standing Desk: My Six-Month Review

After six months with the Jarvik L2, my verdict is simple: **worth buying at $549. Not worth $749.**

The motor is quiet and fast. The desk also wobbles at full height when I type hard, the memory presets drift by about a centimeter, and the cable tray is garbage. At the sale price, I can live with those compromises. At full price, I shouldn’t have to.

## The motor is the best part

As a remote software engineer, I want changing desk height to be an interruption I barely notice—not a small mechanical event in the middle of my workday.

The L2 gets this right. The motor is quiet, and the movement is fast enough that I don’t find myself waiting impatiently for it to finish. That matters more than it sounds. A standing desk needs to make switching positions easy, or it becomes an expensive desk you leave at one height.

If the rest of the L2 were as good as the motor, this would be a much shorter review.

## It wobbles at full height

At full height, hard typing makes the desk wobble. Not touching it deliberately to see whether I can provoke movement. Typing.

That distinction matters. I’m not interested in whether a desk stays perfectly still while someone gently rests a laptop on it for a product photo. I’m interested in what happens while I’m working.

The L2 isn’t as stable as I want it to be at its tallest setting. If you type lightly or don’t need to raise it all the way, this may matter less to you. If you’re a forceful typist and expect a rock-solid surface at full extension, consider this a warning.

A quiet motor is nice. A desk that moves under your hands is harder to ignore.

## The memory presets are close, not exact

The memory presets drift by about a centimeter.

That’s not a catastrophic difference, but it defeats some of the point of saving a height. I want to press a button and get back to the position I chose—not approximately that position, followed by a small correction.

This is a minor annoyance individually and a more irritating one over time. Presets are supposed to remove fiddling. These don’t quite manage it.

## The cable tray is garbage

Cable management should not feel like an afterthought on a desk whose defining feature is moving up and down.

The included tray is the weakest part of the package. I would not count it as a reason to buy the L2, and I would plan on a different cable-management solution rather than assuming the supplied tray has you covered.

That’s especially annoying at $749. An included accessory doesn’t become a meaningful feature just because it appears on the spec sheet.

## $549 versus $749 changes the recommendation

At **$549**, the L2’s trade-offs make sense to me. The motor handles the main job well, and the flaws are ones I can tolerate—though the full-height wobble deserves serious consideration before you buy.

At **$749**, I’d pass. That’s another $200 without fixing the instability, making the presets more consistent, or improving the cable tray. For that price, I want fewer excuses attached to something I use for work.

**My recommendation: buy it on sale if you can live with the full-height wobble and plan to sort out cable management yourself. Skip it at full price.**

Six months in, I like the motor more than I like the desk. At $549, that’s enough. At $749, it isn’t.

*No affiliate links.*

b.text:
I bought the Jarvik L2 six months ago because I needed a desk that could keep up with 8-hour coding days, dual monitors, a laptop stand, and a mechanical keyboard that I absolutely hammer on. Here’s what I think after daily use, no sugarcoating.

The motor is fast and quiet—shockingly so. Transitions take about 10 seconds, and the sound is a low hum that doesn’t travel through walls. That matters to me because I often switch positions at 6 a.m. while my partner sleeps. Zero complaints here. It also lifts my roughly 80 pounds of gear without any hesitation, no lag or grinding.

But the stability at full standing height is a problem. At my preferred 43.5 inches, the desk wobbles when I type with any force. Not just a tiny shiver—the monitors visibly tremble. I use a tactile-switch keyboard and bottom out hard, and the bounce is distracting enough that I sometimes drop the desk an inch or two just to settle it. If you type like a butterfly, maybe you won’t notice. For me, this is the desk’s biggest flaw.

The memory presets are a nice idea, but they drift. I set four heights, and every couple of weeks my standing preset has crept up about a centimeter—I’ll hit the button and end up uncomfortably high. It’s easy to fix (just re-save it), but a memory function that doesn’t remember is just a mislabeled button.

The included cable tray is garbage. It’s a shallow metal trough held on by flimsy plastic clips. I tried to fit a surge protector, monitor cables, and a USB hub in it; the clips popped off within a month. Now it hangs at an angle, cables spilling everywhere. It’s barely usable, and I’ll be buying a proper under-desk tray. A complete afterthought.

Everything else is fine. The laminate top has survived coffee spills and hadn’t scratched yet. The frame feels solid, and the dual motors run smoothly. But these don’t redeem the wobble at full height or the useless add-ons.

I paid $549 on sale. For that price, I can tolerate the wobble, the finicky presets, and a cable tray that’s basically landfill. But at the regular $749? Absolutely not. That puts it in direct competition with desks like the Fully Jarvis or Uplift V2, both of which I’ve used in offices and are noticeably more stable. At $549, it’s a decent deal for a fast, quiet desk that mostly gets the job done. Pay a dollar more, and you’re being overcharged.

setup: A wedding photographer is posting that couples who ditch rigid shot lists get better photos, using the rained-out Barrera wedding as an example.

a.text:
Here's a post for you:

---

The couples who ditch the shot list always end up with the best photos.

I learned this years ago, but it hit differently during the Barrera wedding. Rain forced us to scrap the plan entirely—the ceremony moved under an old pecan tree, the timeline went out the window, and the "must-haves" became irrelevant.

What happened instead? Magic. Unplanned moments between family members sheltering together. The groom helping his bride over muddy ground. Light filtering through those pecan branches in ways no shot list could predict.

The couples I work with who hold their vision lightly—who trust the day to unfold—walk away with images that feel alive and true. Not because I'm capturing what they planned. Because I'm capturing what's actually happening.

Your shot list is a safety net, not a destination. The real photos live in the moments between the boxes you wanted checked.

---

b.text:
After 8 years and hundreds of weddings, I've noticed a pattern: the couples who hand me a shot list and then let go of it get better photos than the ones who stick to it minute by minute.

Case in point: the Barrera wedding.

Rain moved in about an hour before the ceremony. The outdoor setup they'd planned for months was suddenly underwater. We ended up moving everything under this massive old pecan tree on the property, no arch, no draping, no aisle runner in place, just the tree and everyone crowded in under it.

It wasn't the plan. It wasn't on any shot list. And it produced some of the best images I've shot all year.

Here's what I think is actually happening: a shot list is a security blanket. It's couples trying to control an outcome months in advance because the whole process feels overwhelming. Totally understandable. But weddings don't run on schedules, they run on weather, on emotions, on 80 people in one place at one time. The second something doesn't go as planned, a rigid list becomes a source of stress instead of a source of comfort.

The couples who do best are the ones who tell me what matters to them (grandma's ring, dad's reaction, the first look) and then let me handle the rest. That trust is what lets me actually see what's happening in front of me instead of checking boxes.

The Barrera's didn't get the wedding they planned. They got a better one. And they got photos they'll be looking at for the next 50 years.

If you're planning a wedding right now: bring me your must-haves, then let the day do what it's going to do. That's usually where the best photos are hiding.

setup: A real estate agent is posting one specific observation about early block walks and happier buyers to LinkedIn buyers, agents, and lenders.

a.text:
After 12 years in real estate, I’ve noticed something that consistently helps buyers feel better about a home long after closing: they walk the neighborhood before we tour the house.

The Pruitts did this on Sycamore Street. They met me there at 7 a.m., before we went inside. They walked the block, paid attention to how the street felt in the morning, and got a sense of the neighbors, traffic, parking, and daily rhythm.

By the time we toured the house, they weren’t just asking, “Can we make this kitchen work?” They were asking whether they could picture their life there.

They ultimately bought the home, and when I checked in later, they told me that early-morning walk had been one of the best parts of the process. They already knew what the neighborhood felt like before they fell in love with the house.

A home is more than its walls. If you’re considering a property, visit the neighborhood at a time when you’d normally be there—before work, after school, or on a weekend morning. It may tell you more than a perfectly staged showing ever could.

b.text:
In my 12 years selling real estate here in Asheville, I’ve noticed a very specific pattern among first-time buyers. The ones who end up the happiest in their homes years down the road almost always do the exact same thing before we ever write an offer: they walk the neighborhood at 7:00 AM on a weekday. 

I always think about the Pruitts when I share this advice. A few years ago, they were eyeing a great little bungalow on Sycamore Street. On paper, it was exactly what they wanted, but as first-time buyers, they were naturally anxious about making the leap. I told them to go grab some coffee and walk the street early on a Tuesday morning before work. 

When we talked later that afternoon, their hesitation was completely gone. During their morning walk, they didn't just look at property lines or siding; they watched the neighborhood actually wake up. They saw a group of kids walking together to the bus stop at the corner, chatted with a neighbor who was out walking his dog, and realized the commuter traffic they were worried about from the nearby main road was completely buffered by the mature trees. They bought the house and still absolutely love it today.

A Sunday afternoon tour is basically a house and a neighborhood putting on its best behavior. But 7:00 AM on a Tuesday is real life. That’s when you find out if the local school traffic backs up right across your driveway, if there are actually other young families around, or if the daily rhythm of the street just naturally fits how you want to live. 

If you're looking to buy a home this year, don't just rely on the perfectly staged afternoon tours. Set your alarm, get a cup of coffee, and go see what your actual Tuesday morning is going to look like.

setup: A remote software engineer is writing a 6-month standing desk review for blog readers researching standing desks.

a.text:
# Jarvik L2 Standing Desk: 6 Months Later

I’ve been using the Jarvik L2 as my full-time remote-work desk for six months now. I bought it myself, no review unit, no affiliate links. This is the desk I use for coding, video calls, writing, and occasionally eating lunch over my keyboard like a degenerate.

Short version: the Jarvik L2 is a good desk with a few annoying flaws. At the $549 sale price, I’d buy it again. At $749, I’d keep shopping.

## What I Like

### The motor is quiet and fast

This is the L2’s best feature. The height adjustment is noticeably quicker than my old desk, and the motor noise is low enough that I can adjust it during a call without sounding like a blender next to the mic.

It goes up/down smoothly under normal load. I usually raise it after lunch, lower it when I’m done for the day, and it doesn’t hesitate. For a desk I move a few times a day, that matters.

### The memory presets are convenient

There are preset buttons, and in theory they’re great. I use them daily. I don’t want to hold the button and eyeball the height every time.

In practice, they mostly work — but not perfectly. More on that below.

## What I Don’t Like

### It wobbles at full height when I type hard

This is the big one.

At sitting height, the desk feels fine. At a lower standing height, it’s mostly fine. But at my full standing height, there is noticeable side-to-side and front-to-back movement if I’m typing aggressively.

I’m not talking about gently resting my hands on the desk. I mean when I’m writing code quickly, hitting keys with actual force, or moving the mouse around during a frustrating debugging session, the monitor shifts just enough to be annoying.

It doesn’t feel unsafe. It doesn’t feel like the desk is going to collapse. But it feels less stable than I want from a desk at this price.

If you are a light typist, you may not care. If you are a mechanical-keyboard person who types like they’re mad at the compiler, you will notice.

My workaround: I lowered my standing height by about an inch. It helped, but I shouldn’t have to compromise ergonomics because the frame gets nervous at full extension.

### The memory presets drift about a centimeter

The presets are close, but they’re not consistent.

I have my standing height saved, and most days the desk stops roughly where I expect. But over the past few months, I’ve noticed it drifts by about a centimeter. Sometimes it’s slightly high. Sometimes slightly low. It’s not enough to make the desk unusable, but it’s enough that I end up micro-adjusting after every preset move.

That defeats part of the point of having presets.

If Jarvik fixed this with a firmware update or better calibration, I’d upgrade my opinion. As it stands, the presets are useful but not reliable enough to fully trust.

### The cable tray is garbage

I hate the cable tray.

It feels like an afterthought. It doesn’t hold enough, it doesn’t route cables cleanly, and it makes cable management feel worse than if I’d just used velcro ties and a power strip.

For a desk marketed to people who presumably own more than one electronic device, this is a miss.

I ended up removing it and using my own cable management underneath the desktop. If you buy the L2, do yourself a favor and skip the included tray unless you enjoy disappointment.

## Build Quality

The frame itself feels solid enough. The finish is fine. The desktop is decent, though I’d still recommend getting a desk mat if you write or type hard.

The controls are simple. The handset isn’t fancy, but it works. I don’t need Bluetooth, RGB, or a smartphone app to make my desk go up and down. I need it to go to the right height and stay there. The L2 mostly does that, with caveats.

## Who Should Buy It

Buy it if:

- You can get it on sale around $549
- You want a quiet, fast motor
- You need a desk for mixed sitting/standing throughout the day
- You don’t type like you’re punishing the keyboard
- You plan to use your own cable management

Skip it or look elsewhere if:

- You’re paying $749
- You need maximum stability at full standing height
- You want memory presets that are actually precise
- You expect the included cable tray to be useful

## Verdict

The Jarvik L2 is a solid midrange standing desk with a great motor and a few irritating execution problems.

At $549, those flaws are easier to accept. You’re getting good performance for the money, especially if you catch it on sale.

At $749, the wobble and preset drift become harder to ignore. For that much, I expect better stability and more consistent height memory.

Final rating: 7/10 at $549. 5.5/10 at $749.

b.text:
Jarvik L2 Standing Desk: 6 Months Later

I bought the Jarvik L2 six months ago for $549. I'm a remote software engineer, so this thing gets 9-10 hours of use a day, five days a week, switching between sitting and standing 3-4 times daily. No sponsorship, no affiliate links, just my own money and my own back pain.

**The motor is actually good.**

This is the best part of the L2. Dual motor, goes from my sit height of 73cm to my stand height of 109cm in about 12 seconds. It's quiet enough that I've moved it mid-Zoom call and no one noticed. Just a low hum, no grinding, no jerk at the start/stop. After six months of daily moves, it hasn't slowed down or gotten louder. Jarvik got this right.

**It wobbles at full height.**

I'm 5'6" and stand at 109cm. If I'm typing normally, it's fine. If I'm typing hard — like actually hammering out code in a hurry — there's noticeable side-to-side wobble. My 27" monitor on a single arm visibly shakes. It's not going to tip, but it's distracting. Below 100cm it's rock solid. Above 105cm, don't expect to do any precision work without some shake. For a desk that advertises a 125cm max height, that's weak.

**The memory presets don't hold.**

It has 4 presets, which I liked. I set 1 to 73cm and 2 to 109cm. After a week or two, 2 was stopping at 108cm. Recalibrated. A month later, it was at 107.8cm. It's drifted about a cm every time. Not the end of the world, but annoying when you paid for presets so you don't have to look at the display. I now just hold the up button and watch the numbers. The controller is basically dumb up/down after six months.

**The cable tray is garbage.**

Thin, sharp-edged metal basket that mounts under the back. My power strip doesn't fit in it flat. My dock barely fits. After two weeks, cables were sagging out the back anyway because there are no real retention clips and the included velcro straps are a joke. I replaced it with a $25 aftermarket tray from Amazon and haven't thought about it since. Factor that into your cost. Jarvik should just not include theirs.

**Verdict**

At $549 on sale, keep it. The frame and motor performance for the price is solid if you work under 110cm and can live with resetting your presets and trashing the cable tray.

At $749 full price, absolutely not. The wobble and preset drift at that price are unacceptable when you're in Uplift / FlexiSpot E7 territory. Wait for the sale or buy something else.

setup: A high-school senior is writing a personal essay for college admissions readers about working at her family's Vietnamese restaurant.

a.text:
I'm in the kitchen Monday to Friday for school, and then on the weekends, I'm at the restaurant. My family owns a Vietnamese place in a strip mall off Route 12. My parents run it, my grandma cooks, and I do whatever needs doing: wash dishes, refill the Sriracha bottles, bus tables, take orders. I've been doing this since sophomore year, every Saturday and Sunday, from 11 a.m. to 9 p.m. I get paid, but it's not about the money.

There was a Saturday when the register system died. I don't know why. It just went blank in the middle of the lunch rush. My mom looked at me, and I looked at the line of people waiting, and she said, "Paper." So I grabbed a notepad from the counter and started writing tickets by hand. No one seems to think about what happens when the computer stops. I didn't either, until that day. I wrote fast. I had to remember the prices from memory because the menu was on the screen. I shorthand everything: pho-12, spring rolls-6, vermicelli-14. The kitchen had to read my handwriting. It was messy, but they got it. We served everyone. No one waited too long, I think. At the end of the night, my hand was sore, and we totaled up the receipts and the numbers were off by a little, but close enough.

Sometimes I teach new hires how to fold the spring rolls. That's my grandma's method. You lay the wrapper flat, put the filling in the middle, fold up the bottom, fold in the sides, then roll it tight. It seems simple, but if you don't crimp the edges right, they stick together or fall apart when you fry them. People don't know that. They think it's just rolling. I show them. I watch their hands. Sometimes they get frustrated. I tell them, "It's like folding a letter you don't want to send." That's what my grandma told me. I don't know what that means exactly, but it helps hold the fold. I don't know if she meant it or if she just said it.

On my breaks, I do homework in the walk-in cooler. It's cold in there, obviously, but it's quiet. I can hear the fridge humming and sometimes the sound of the kitchen yelling from outside. I pull out my calc book and do problems. It's weird to be doing derivatives while the smell of lemongrass and fish sauce is on my clothes. But it's fine. It's my break. I sit on a crate or sometimes I lean against the shelves where they keep the egg rolls. I don't have much time, so I do the problems fast. If I get one wrong, I don't care that much. I just move on to the next one. It's not like school where there's time to think about it. I'm on a break. I'll be back on the floor in fifteen minutes.

Most Saturdays, I'm there from 11 a.m. to 9 p.m. I don't think about it as a job exactly, even though I am paid for it. It's just what I do. I put on my apron, I cash out customers, I refill the water, I wipe the tables. My hands smell like fish sauce by the end of the day, and no matter how many times I wash them, the smell stays. I like it. It's my family's smell, I guess. I don't know what else to call it.

b.text:
The milk crates in our walk-in cooler are stacked three high next to the five-gallon buckets of fish sauce. That is where I sit on my fifteen-minute breaks on Saturdays. It stays thirty-eight degrees in there, which is cold enough to see my breath, but it is the only room in the building where nobody is yelling an order or dropping a wire basket into boiling oil. 

I wear my apron over my jacket and prop my calculus binder against a cardboard case of cabbage. Limits and derivatives make more sense when your teeth are slightly chattering; the cold keeps me from nodding off after four hours on my feet. If I stay in past minute twelve, my fingers get too stiff to hold the mechanical pencil, so I pack up, shove the binder back into my tote bag, and push open the heavy metal door.

I’ve worked weekends at my family’s restaurant since sophomore year. I take orders, bus tables, chop scallions, and run the floor depending on who called out sick. Last fall, my dad hired a high school junior named Tyler who had never touched rice paper before. The first few spring rolls he tried to make looked like wet paper towels stuffed with shredded pork. 

"Watch," I told him, wiping down a section of the stainless steel prep table. 

You dip the rice paper in warm water for two seconds, not three. If it feels soft when you pull it out of the bowl, it’s already ruined—it will tear the second the vermicelli hits it. You lay it flat, stack the lettuce, mint, and noodles across the bottom third, and lay three shrimp pink-side down near the top so they show through the translucent wrapper once it’s closed. Then the fold: pull the bottom edge up tight, tuck both sides in like an envelope, and roll forward with the flats of your palms, never your fingertips. 

My grandma showed me that fold when I was nine. She didn’t speak much English, and Tyler didn’t speak any Vietnamese, but the motion doesn't need translation. You don’t squeeze; you just guide it. By his third tray, Tyler was turning out rolls tight enough to be sliced on a bias without the filling spilling onto the cutting board.

That kind of routine keeps the restaurant moving, but things still fall apart. A few months ago, right at the peak of the 6:30 dinner rush on a rainy Saturday, the touchscreen POS terminal let out a long beep, flickered, and went entirely black. There were forty people seated in the dining room, three tables waiting at the door, and four delivery drivers pacing by the counter. 

My dad tapped the screen twice with his knuckle, looked over at me, and said, "Paper."

I grabbed a legal pad from under the counter, tore the sheets into quarters, and dug three pens out of my apron pocket. For the next two and a half hours, I did the math by hand. Table 4 wanted two bowls of phở tái, one extra broth, no cilantro. Table 8 wanted three broken rice plates with pork chops, well done. I had to keep the menu prices straight, calculate the 8.25% sales tax in the margins, and translate each ticket into the kitchen’s shorthand before sliding it onto the order wheel. "PT-X-NC" for Table 4. "Com Tam Suon" for Table 8. 

My handwriting started out neat and ended up looking like a seismograph readout, but the kitchen never stopped firing bowls, and the wrong food never went to the wrong table. When we finally flipped the door sign to "Closed" at nine, my thumb was dented from the ballpoint pen, and the back of my neck burned from looking down. 

My friends ask me why I don't quit and find an easier job where I don't go home smelling like star anise and dish soap. But on Sunday nights, after the dining room chairs are flipped onto the tables and my dad turns off the neon "Open" sign, there is a half-hour where the restaurant is completely silent. My mom counts down the cash drawer, my dad sweeps the entryway, and I run the wide mop across the red floor tiles, working my way toward the back exit. 

Tomorrow morning is AP Chemistry at 7:45. I lean the mop against the sink, pack my backpack, and sit down at the front booth to finish my lab report while the floor dries.

setup: A long-haul trucker is writing a short Roadstar DC4 dual dash cam review for other owner-operators on a trucking forum.

a.text:
**RoadStar DC4 Dash Cam — 14 Months / ~140,000 Miles**

I’ve had the RoadStar DC4 in my truck for about 14 months now and put roughly 140k miles on it. For the money, it’s been worth having.

Main reason: it caught a lane-change accident that involved me, and the footage got my insurance claim approved in 9 days instead of the usual 6-week headache. That alone paid for the camera several times over.

Front camera footage is solid in daylight and decent at night. Rear camera is usable, but don’t expect miracles after dark. Anything past about 30 feet starts getting pretty grainy. It’ll show what happened close behind the truck, but it’s not going to read a plate from way back at night.

One thing to skip: the suction mount. Mine fell off twice during summer heat, which is not what you want when you’re rolling down the interstate. I switched to the adhesive mount and haven’t had an issue since.

The app is my biggest complaint. You need Wi-Fi to pull footage through it, which is pretty useless when you’re parked at most truck stops with weak or overloaded service. I quit messing with the app and just pull the SD card when I need video. Faster and less aggravating.

Bottom line: not perfect, rear night footage could be better, and the app is more trouble than it’s worth. But it’s reliable, records what matters, and already saved me a pile of time with insurance. I’d buy it again, just use the adhesive mount from day one.

b.text:
**Roadstar DC4 Dash Cam — 14-Month Review**

I’ve had the Roadstar DC4 in my truck for 14 months and around 140,000 miles. Overall, it’s been worth having, mainly because it already paid for itself.

The biggest plus: it caught a lane-change accident on video, and the footage helped get my insurance claim approved in nine days instead of the usual six weeks. That alone makes this camera worthwhile for an owner-operator.

The front footage has been reliable, but the rear camera gets grainy past about 30 feet, especially at night. It’s still useful for showing what happened, but don’t expect perfect detail at longer distances.

The suction mount also isn’t great in summer heat. Mine fell off twice before I switched to the adhesive mount. Since then, it’s stayed put.

The app is another weak spot. You need Wi-Fi to pull footage, which is pretty useless at most truck stops. I usually just remove the SD card and copy the clips directly. It’s faster and less frustrating.

After 14 months and 140,000 miles, I’d recommend the DC4, especially for the insurance protection. Just use the adhesive mount from the start, and plan on pulling the SD card instead of relying on the app.

setup: A fourth-generation soybean and corn farmer is writing a newsletter commentary on crop insurance costs and SB 214 for county readers and state legislators.

a.text:
**Paying 22 Percent More for Less Coverage**

USDA raised the base prevented planting premium rate 22 percent in our region this year. I can tell you exactly what that looks like on a real farm, because this spring I got only 60 percent of my corn and bean acres in the ground before the late-May deadline. It would not stop raining. The other 40 percent sat too wet to work, week after week, until the calendar made the decision for me.

The rate increase will cost my operation about $46,000 this year.

For anyone who doesn't carry crop insurance, prevented planting coverage is the part of the policy that applies when weather keeps you out of the field entirely. You pay the premium every year, wet or dry. Most years it's money out the door and you're glad to lose it, because losing it means you got a crop in. This was the other kind of year — the kind the coverage exists for.

Here's where a rate hike turns into something worse. Prevented planting payments are subject to acreage caps. When 40 percent of your farm can't be planted, the cap means a share of your actual, documented loss simply isn't covered — even though you paid the higher premium on every acre you insure. And the cap doesn't scale with the size of the operation. On a farm the size of mine, the unplanted ground is a large share of the whole business, so the uncovered share is a serious hit. A few miles from here are operations running several times my acreage. The same cap touches a much smaller fraction of theirs. The bigger you are, the easier it is to absorb. The smaller you are, the more it defines your year.

So the math on my place this spring is this: a 22 percent premium increase on coverage that then declined to cover a large part of the acres the weather took from me. More money for less protection. A family farm pays the same rate as everyone else and gets less out of it, acre for acre, than the big operation down the road.

There's a fix sitting in the state legislature right now. SB 214 would correct the acreage cap so family operations aren't penalized for being family-sized. It doesn't raise anyone's rates and it doesn't ask for a new program. It makes the coverage a farmer pays for apply to the acres that farmer actually farms. That's it.

I'm asking everyone reading this to do two things. First, call your state senator and your state representative and tell them to support SB 214. Second, get your neighbors to do the same. If you've farmed more than a few years, you've had a spring like this one or you will. This bill is about you whether you filed a claim this year or not.

My family has farmed this ground for four generations. We've paid into crop insurance every one of those years without complaint, because that's the deal: you pay in the good years so the bad ones don't end you. A 22 percent rate hike stacked on top of

b.text:
# The Prevented Planting Hike Is Hitting the Wrong Farms

Sixty percent. That's how many of my acres I got in the ground by the late May deadline this spring. The rest sat under water, because it wouldn't stop raining long enough to run a planter across the field. Anybody who farmed this county this year knows exactly what I'm talking about.

So I did what the crop insurance program is designed for—I filed prevented planting on the acres I couldn't get to. And that's when the second problem showed up.

USDA raised the base prevented planting rate in our region by 22% this year. On paper, a premium increase sounds like something that just nicks you a little at the margins. In practice, on my operation, that 22% adds up to about $46,000 out of pocket this year. Not for coverage I chose to expand. Not for new ground. Just the same acres, same program, more money.

Here's the part that ought to bother every family operation in this county: the way the acreage caps are written, the increase doesn't land evenly. The cap structure means the extra cost falls harder, proportionally, on operations my size than it does on the bigger outfits down the road. A farm running several times my acreage absorbs the hike as a smaller slice of its overall cost. For a fourth-generation family place trying to stay in the black through a wet spring, $46,000 is the difference between a workable year and a bad one.

That's backwards. A safety net program shouldn't be structured so that the smaller you are, the more it costs you per acre to use it.

There's a fix on the table. **SB 214** would correct the acreage cap so the burden is spread fairly instead of concentrated on family-scale operations. It doesn't gut the program or ask for anything we're not entitled to. It just stops penalizing the farms least able to eat a $46,000 surprise.

If you farm in this county, this affects you—maybe not this year, but the first wet spring that comes along, it will. I'd ask you to call your state legislator and tell them to support SB 214. And if you see them at a county event before then, tell them in person. They need to hear it from the people writing these checks.

We can't do anything about the rain. We can do something about a rule that makes a hard year harder for the wrong farms.

Hi team,

**Current Status:** All systems are fully operational, healthy, and stable. 

I want to share a quick update on what happened during yesterday’s 40-minute outage around 2:00 PM, especially for those of you who were fielding customer questions and concerns.

**What Happened**
During a routine software deploy yesterday afternoon, we ran a database update (a "migration") that was meant to reorganize how some data is stored. Instead of applying instantly as expected, the update locked up a core database table, which prevented the app from reading or writing data and caused the platform to become unresponsive for roughly 40 minutes.

**How It Was Resolved**
Once we identified the lockup, the engineering team rolled back the deployment to the previous working version, which unlocked the database and restored full service to customers.

**What We’re Changing**
To make sure this doesn’t happen again:
* **Maintenance Windows:** Moving forward, any database updates that carry a risk of locking tables will only be run during scheduled, off-peak maintenance windows rather than during regular daytime deploys.
* **Testing:** We are adding additional staging tests to measure database lock times before changes go anywhere near production.

Thank you to everyone who stepped up to manage customer communication while we were working through the fix. If anyone needs specific context for follow-ups with customers, or if you have any questions, please feel free to reach out to me directly.

setup: A home baker is reviewing the Corlane SM6 mixer for blog readers deciding whether to buy it.

a.text:
**Corlane SM6 Stand Mixer Review: 8 Months of Heavy Dough**

It’s been eight months since I unboxed the Corlane SM6 stand mixer, and it has seen the inside of my kitchen almost every single day. Between prepping my weekend farmers market sourdough orders and testing recipes for the blog, this machine has been put through the wringer. Here is my honest, unvarnished take on whether it deserves a spot on your counter.

Let’s start with the motor, because that’s what really matters when you’re baking at volume. The Corlane SM6 is an absolute workhorse. I regularly throw massive, high-hydration sourdough batches at it, but the real test was a double batch of stiff, low-hydration bagel dough. The motor didn't even flinch. There was zero stalling, no overheating, and no struggling walk across the counter. It powered through the stiffest doughs I could throw at it with total ease.

But it’s not a perfect machine. The bowl lift lever has an annoying squeak that develops after a few weeks of heavy use. I’ve resigned myself to giving it a quick blast of WD-40 once a month to keep it quiet and smooth. More frustrating is the included dough hook. For some reason, Corlane designed a beautifully deep bowl but paired it with a dough hook that is too short to reach the bottom effectively. I ended up having to buy a third-party hook just to get a proper knead on my standard batches.

Then there is the price. At $429, the Corlane SM6 is exactly $80 more than the equivalent KitchenAid model. That is a premium you need to justify. 

Here is my final, definitive verdict: Buy the Corlane SM6 if you knead heavy dough every week. If you are baking market-level volumes of sourdough, bagels, or stiff pizza dough, the superior motor torque easily justifies the $80 premium over the KitchenAid, and the deep bowl is fantastic for large batches. Skip it entirely if you are mostly doing cookies and cake batter. If you are primarily mixing butter and sugar, the KitchenAid is cheaper, the attachments fit perfectly out of the box, and you simply do not need this level of heavy-duty motor power.

b.text:
# Eight Months with the Corlane SM6: The Honest Baker’s Verdict

I bought the Corlane SM6 eight months ago to take the strain off my wrists during Friday prep for the weekend farmers market. Since then, it has run five to six days a week, churning through country batards, enriched sandwich loaves, and stiff bagel dough. 

If you bake sourdough for a crowd—or you’re just sick of your current machine groaning under the weight of a high-hydration rye—you’ve probably seen the SM6 pop up in your feeds. 

Here is what it’s actually like to live with, flaws and all.

---

### The Power: An Absolute Workhorse

Let’s get straight to the reason you’d buy this machine: the motor. 

Most consumer stand mixers claim to handle bread dough, but what they really mean is a single loaf of soft sandwich bread. The true test in my kitchen is a double batch of 56% hydration bagel dough. It’s stiff, it’s dense, and it has sent lesser mixers dancing across my countertop smelling like burning wire. 

The SM6 doesn’t care. It muscles through a double batch without a single stutter, stall, or speed dip. The direct-drive system stays planted on the counter, runs surprisingly cool through a 12-minute knead, and develops gluten evenly without shaking itself to pieces. If your primary frustration with mixers is lack of torque, the SM6 solves that completely.

---

### The Frustrations: Squeaks and a Flawed Hook

For all its motor strength, the SM6 has two glaring mechanical annoyances you need to know about before handing over your card.

1. **The Bowl-Lift Lever Needs Babysitting:** About two months in, the lift mechanism developed a high-pitched, metallic shriek every time I raised or lowered the bowl. There is clearly tight metal-on-metal friction inside the track. I have to hit it with a shot of food-safe lubricant or standard WD-40 roughly once a month to keep it moving smoothly. At this price point, a squeaky lever feels cheap.
2. **The Included Dough Hook is Too Short:** I don't know who designed the accessories, but they didn’t test them in their own machine. The stock spiral hook stops about an inch and a half too high from the base of the deep-well bowl. If you’re running smaller batches (under 800 grams of flour), the hook simply spins above the ingredients, leaving an unmixed pool of dry flour and water at the bottom. I got fed up with stopping to scrape down the bottom by hand and bought an extended aftermarket hook three weeks in. Factor that extra purchase into your budget.

---

### The Cost: $429

The Corlane SM6 retails for **$429**. 

That puts it roughly **$80 higher** than the standard equivalent KitchenAid bowl-lift model. You are paying a premium for a smaller brand, and you’re doing so while accepting a squeaky lever and an accessory you’ll likely replace. 

---

### The Verdict

I am not going to give you an “it depends on what you value” cop-out. The line here is very clear.

* **Buy it** if you bake heavy, low-hydration, or large-batch doughs every single week. The motor power blows standard consumer mixers out of the water, and it will not burn out on your bread days. It is built to work, and for a serious bread baker, that alone makes it worth the $429 and the minor headaches.
* **Skip it** if your regular routine is cookies, sheet cakes, brioche, and the occasional holiday loaf. You don't need this kind of raw torque for creaming butter and sugar, and you will be annoyed by the deep bowl clearance, the extra $80 cost, and the monthly maintenance. Save your money and buy a standard tilt-head KitchenAid instead.

setup: A local sports columnist is writing an opinionated season-ending commentary for readers of the local paper's sports section.

a.text:
**They Didn't Get Beat. They Beat Themselves.**

Let's get the hard part out of the way: Friday night's loss stings more because it didn't have to happen.

Nobody should be embarrassed by an 8-2 season, and I'm not here to tell you the boys don't deserve a hand. They do. But I've watched every snap of this team since August, and I'm not going to sit here and pretend that second half was anything other than a coaching failure.

We beat that team by 20 in Week 3. Twenty. And we did it the same way we won most of our games this year — by running the ball down their throats until they quit wanting to tackle. Friday night, the ground game was working again. We were moving the chains, controlling the clock, and we walked into halftime down three points. Three. That's a field goal. That's nothing.

Then, for reasons I still can't explain, we came out throwing on nearly every down like we were trailing by three touchdowns. The run game didn't stop working. We stopped using it. Their defensive line got to pin their ears back and rush the passer all night, our drives got shorter, their offense got the ball back over and over, and by the fourth quarter the game was gone. That's not the kids' fault. Kids run the plays they're given.

None of this is a knock on Dez Kowalski, who was asked to carry too much and nearly did it anyway. His 2,340 passing yards this season broke the school record, and it's a record that'll stand a while. He's the best quarterback this town has seen in a generation, and Friday night he was throwing into coverage everybody in the stadium knew was coming.

So here's my hope for next year: that the staff trusts what got them to 8-2 in the first place. This program is close. The talent's there, the record proves it, and the loss proves the margin between a good season and a great one is sometimes just one halftime decision.

Congratulations on a fine season, boys. Now go get the next one — and run the dang ball.

b.text:
End of Season Doesn't Feel Like an Ending

The bus pulled back into the lot Saturday night and most of these kids already know what I'm about to say, because their coaches have been telling them the same thing all fall. But somebody ought to say it in print.

That second-round loss to Westbrook wasn't a loss. It was a choice.

You don't lose a playoff game 21-17 to a team you beat 34-14 in your own house back in September because you're the worse football team. You're not. You go 8-2, you handle your business, and you walk into a rematch with a team that has every reason to be scared of you. You were up on them in the third quarter. The run game was chewing them up. Your offensive line was winning the line of scrimmage on every snap.

And then you threw it.

I don't know if it was panic, or whether somebody on the sideline decided the game needed to be in Dez's hands. I get it. Dez Kowalski just set a school record throwing for 2,340 yards, and he's the best player to wear that jersey in maybe a decade. You want your best guy with the ball.

But your best guy didn't need the ball. Your running backs did. They were getting four, five yards a carry against a front seven that could not stop them, and you were only down three points when you decided the running game wasn't good enough anymore. That's not coaching. That's not trusting what works.

Westbrook's secondary is fine. It's not 2,340-yards-against fine, and Dez was going to get his regardless. But when you take the thing that's winning away from yourself and put the game on one kid's arm, you're asking a 17-year-old to do something the scoreboard didn't require. He didn't fail you. The gameplan did.

And here's the part that should sting most. Dez will be back. Most of that offensive line will be back. The defense that kept you in it all year doesn't lose much. This wasn't the end of a window. It was a door you walked away from when you didn't have to.

The seniors who played their last game Saturday, I wish I could tell them it doesn't matter. It does matter. That's why it hurts.

But for everybody else still wearing that jersey in August, the loss to Westbrook isn't a lesson in how football can break your heart. It's a lesson in not abandoning what works when you're scared it won't be enough.

Eight and two is a good year. Next year can be better. But only if the coaches — and the kids — are willing to trust the run when the run is there.

That's not a knock on Dez. That's just football.

a.text:
# Corlane SM6 Stand Mixer: 8 Months In

I bake sourdough for the farmers market every weekend, which means this mixer doesn't get a gentle life. Here's what actually happens when you put it to work daily instead of pulling it out twice a year for birthday cake.

**The good:** The motor is the real story here. I regularly run double batches of stiff bagel dough through it — the kind of dough that makes cheaper mixers whine and stall — and the SM6 just keeps turning. No burning smell, no motor lag, no babysitting it to make sure it doesn't overheat. For someone kneading heavy, low-hydration dough multiple times a week, this is the whole reason to buy this machine.

**The annoying:** The bowl lift lever has developed a squeak that I now have to WD40 about once a month. It's not a dealbreaker, just an unglamorous maintenance chore nobody mentions in the marketing copy. More frustrating: the dough hook that ships with it is too short to properly reach the bottom of the deep bowl. I ended up buying a third-party hook to get real contact with the dough. That's an extra cost and an extra Amazon order you shouldn't have to make on a $429 machine.

**The price problem:** Speaking of $429 — that's about $80 more than the equivalent KitchenAid. You're paying a premium for that motor.

**Verdict:** Buy this if you knead heavy dough every week. If you're making sourdough, bagels, pizza dough, or anything stiff on a regular basis, the motor alone justifies the price difference, and you'll make back the cost of a third-party hook in saved frustration within a month. Skip it if you're mostly making cookies, cake batter, or the occasional loaf of banana bread — you're paying $80 extra for horsepower you'll never actually use, and you'll be stuck with the same finicky lever and undersized hook without ever needing the thing that makes this mixer worth owning.

b.text:
After eight months of using the Corlane SM6 stand mixer almost every single day to prep sourdough for my weekend farmers market stand, I finally have a definitive answer on whether it’s worth the price tag. 

Let’s start with the motor, because that is where this machine truly shines. If you bake bread, you know the ultimate stress test is a stiff bagel dough. The Corlane handles a double batch of bagel dough without a single stutter, stall, or terrifying gear-grinding noise. It just churns through it like a champion. For heavy, low-hydration doughs and massive batches of market prep, the raw power is undeniably impressive.

But it is not a perfect machine, and for $429—which is $80 more than the equivalent bowl-lift KitchenAid—the flaws are genuinely irritating. 

First, the hardware is a bit finicky. A few months in, the bowl lift lever developed a terrible squeak. I now have to hit the mechanism with WD-40 about once a month just to keep it operating smoothly. 

The much bigger issue, however, is the dough hook. The stock hook that comes in the box is inexplicably short for how deep the bowl is. It clears the bottom by far too much, leaving a thick layer of unmixed flour and water sitting in the base of the bowl. I ended up having to buy a third-party dough hook just to make the machine usable for my daily bread prep. When you are already paying a premium over the standard KitchenAid, having to immediately buy aftermarket parts to fix a glaring design flaw is a tough pill to swallow.

**The Verdict**

Buy the Corlane SM6 if you are kneading heavy bread doughs every single week. The motor easily outpaces the competition and will save you from burning out a lesser machine. 

Skip it if you are mostly whipping up cookies, cake batters, or the occasional single loaf of bread. Between the squeaky lever, the poorly designed stock dough hook, and the $429 price tag, it is absolutely not worth the extra $80 over a KitchenAid for casual or sweet baking. Save your money.

setup: A family plumbing company owner is writing a blog post for Minneapolis homeowners about winterizing outdoor pipes.

a.text:
# How to Winterize Your Outside Spigots (And Avoid a January Burst Pipe)

Freezing temps in Minneapolis don't give you much room for error when it comes to outdoor plumbing. If water sits inside your outdoor faucet or the supply line behind it, it will freeze, expand, and split the pipe inside your wall. You won’t even know it happened until you turn the water back on in the spring—or worse, during a mid-winter thaw when it floods your basement.

Here is the exact four-step process to winterize your outdoor spigots before the hard freeze hits.

---

### Step 1: Disconnect All Garden Hoses Immediately
Do this today. If you take only one thing away from this post, make it this: **never leave a hose connected to an outdoor spigot over the winter.** 

Even if you have a modern "frost-free" sillcock, leaving a hose attached prevents the water inside the faucet body from draining out. The trapped water freezes right at the exterior wall, splits the brass tube, and causes a massive leak inside your home. Easily 80% of the burst-pipe calls our family takes in January and February happen because someone forgot to disconnect a hose.

Disconnect the hose, drain it, roll it up, and store it away. Remove any splitters, timers, or quick-connect adapters, too.

---

### Step 2: Locate and Shut Off the Indoor Valve
Head down to your basement, utility room, or crawlspace. Look for the water line heading directly toward the outside wall where your outdoor spigot is located. 

On that line, you should find a shutoff valve (either a round wheel-handle gate valve or a straight lever-handle ball valve). 

* Turn a **round wheel-handle** clockwise until it stops completely.
* Turn a **lever-handle** a quarter-turn until it is perpendicular (across) the pipe.

---

### Step 3: Drain the Residual Water Out of the Line
Shutting the indoor valve stops new water from entering, but there is still water trapped between the valve and the outside wall. You need to drain it.

1. Go outside and open the outdoor spigot all the way. Let whatever water is inside drain out. Leave the spigot in the **open** position all winter.
2. Go back inside to your shutoff valve with a small bucket or towel. Most indoor shutoff valves have a tiny brass "bleeder cap" on the side of the valve body. Unscrew that cap slowly. 
3. Let the trapped water drain into your bucket. 
4. Once the water stops dripping, screw the bleeder cap back on tightly.

---

### Step 4: Add a $3 Foam Faucet Cover
Go to your local hardware store and grab an insulated styrofoam faucet cover. They cost about $3 to $5 and hook right onto the spigot handle, pulling tight against your siding with a rubber gasket. 

While draining the line is the main defense, these covers add an extra barrier against biting Minneapolis wind chills, protecting the fixture itself from extreme cold drafts.

---

### Can’t Find an Indoor Shutoff Valve?
A lot of older homes in Minneapolis—especially in neighborhoods like South Minneapolis, Northeast, or Saint Paul—either don't have indoor shutoffs for the outside lines, or the old gate valves are seized shut and won't turn.

If you don't have a dedicated indoor shutoff, or if your valve is leaking when you try to turn it, don't force it. Give our team a call. We can install a reliable, modern ball valve and a proper frost-free sillcock so you never have to worry about a frozen pipe wrecking your basement.

b.text:
# How to Winterize Your Outdoor Spigots (Before the Freeze)

Frozen outdoor spigots are one of the easiest problems to prevent and one of the most expensive to fix. Here's what you need to do, and it'll take you maybe 15 minutes.

## The Four Steps

**1. Shut off the interior valve**

Find the shutoff valve inside your house that controls water to that outdoor spigot. Usually it's in the basement, laundry room, or crawl space—look for a valve on the line running to the wall where your spigot is. Turn it clockwise until it stops. Don't force it.

**2. Drain the spigot**

Go outside and turn the handle on fully. Water should come out if there's any left in the line. Let it run for a few seconds, then turn it off.

**3. Disconnect your hoses**

This is the big one. I'm going to be direct: leaving hoses connected to your spigots is why we get slammed with burst-pipe calls in January. Water gets trapped in the hose, freezes, expands back into the line, and cracks the pipe inside your wall. Disconnect every hose, drain them out, and store them.

**4. Add a foam cover**

Pick up a foam spigot cover at any hardware store (around $3). Slip it over the spigot. It's not fancy, but it works.

## What If You Don't Have an Interior Shutoff?

Some older Minneapolis homes don't have interior shutoffs for outdoor lines. If that's you, call us. We can add one—it's a quick job and it's worth it for the peace of mind. It's also worth it so you're not the one calling us in January with a frozen pipe in the wall.

That's it. Do this before the first hard freeze and you won't have this problem.
