setup: A third-year electrical apprentice is writing an argumentative essay for the union newsletter against a 15% cut to apprenticeship funding.

a.text:
Don't Cut Apprenticeship Funding

I'm a third-year electrical apprentice with the IBEW. I'm writing this because the state wants to cut apprenticeship funding by 15%. That is a bad idea and it will hurt working people.

Look at my own cohort. We started with 24 apprentices. 21 of us finished. All 21 are working journeyman jobs right now. That's 21 good paychecks, 21 taxpayers, 21 people not sitting on the sidelines.

Here's why this program works. You start earning right away. Apprentices start around $19 an hour. When you top out as a journeyman you're around $46 an hour. That means people get off assistance programs fast. You're working, you're paying taxes, you're supporting a family. You're not stuck with debt.

And it's cheap for what you get back. The total public cost per apprentice who finishes is about $14,000. Compare that to a four-year college grad. The average public subsidy per four-year grad who finishes is something like $48,000. So we cost less than a third and we all have jobs waiting.

If the state cuts 15%, what happens? Fewer spots. Bigger classes. Less hands-on training. Older equipment. More guys dropping out because they don't get the help they need. We already have a waitlist of people who want in. This cut will shut the door on them.

Legislators say they want to save money and create jobs. Cutting this program does the opposite. You save a little now and you lose a lot later. You lose electricians, you lose taxpayers, and contractors have to turn down work because they can't find hands.

I'm asking my union brothers and sisters to speak up. And I'm asking any legislator reading this to come out to the training center and see where your money goes. It works.

Don't cut what works.

b.text:
# Keep the Funding, Keep the Pipeline

I'm a third-year electrical apprentice with the local IBEW, and I'm writing this because the state is talking about cutting apprenticeship funding by 15%. That's a bad idea, and I want to explain why using numbers that actually mean something.

My cohort started with 24 apprentices. 21 of us finished, and every one of us is working journeyman jobs right now. That's not a feel-good story. That's a success rate, and it's real. We didn't drop out because we got bored or because the program wasn't worth our time. We stuck with it because the path was clear: put in the work, learn the trade, come out making a living wage.

Apprentices in our program start around $19 an hour. By the time you top out as a journeyman, you're making around $46 an hour. That means within a few years, people who might have been on food stamps or other assistance are off it. Not because someone gave them a pep talk, but because they learned a skill that pays. I've watched guys in my cohort go from barely getting by to buying homes and supporting families. That happens because the training is funded and the jobs are there.

Now look at the cost side. The total public cost per apprentice who finishes our program is about $14,000. Compare that to roughly $48,000 in average public subsidy per four-year college graduate who finishes. I'm not knocking college. Some jobs need a degree, and that's fine. But if the state is looking at where it gets return on its money, apprenticeship programs are a better deal by a long shot. We produce working tradespeople at less than a third of the public cost, and those tradespeople start paying taxes and spending in their communities right away.

A 15% cut doesn't sound huge until you think about what it actually does. It means fewer apprentices accepted. It means less classroom instruction time. It means tools and materials that are already stretched thin get stretched thinner. When my cohort went through, we had what we needed. If you cut 15% off the budget, the next cohort won't. You can't train electricians on hopes and good intentions. You need funded seats, funded instructors, and funded materials.

Here's what I want the legislators reading this to understand: apprenticeship funding isn't a handout. It's an investment that pays back fast. Every apprentice who finishes becomes a taxpayer, a consumer, and a skilled worker the state needs. Every apprentice who doesn't get a seat because of budget cuts is someone who stays underemployed or on assistance longer. The math on that is simple, and it doesn't require a fancy economic study to figure out.

My cohort is proof this works. 21 out of 24 finished. We're working. We're paying taxes. We're not drawing on public assistance. And the state got all of us trained for $14,000 each. Find me a better deal than that anywhere in the budget.

Keep the funding where it is. Better yet, increase it. The trades are short on people, and the people are ready to do the work. All we need is the state to not pull the rug out from under the programs that get us there.

setup: A freelance wedding photographer is writing a blog post for couples about why to book a winter wedding.

a.text:
If you’d asked me a few years ago what kind of wedding I preferred to photograph, I probably would have said a classic summer Saturday without thinking twice.

That’s changed.

I actually like shooting winter weddings now, and not in the vague, “every season has its charm” kind of way. I mean it in the practical, real-world, I’ve-photographed-enough-weddings-to-know-what-works kind of way.

Over the last two years, I’ve shot 11 winter weddings. That’s enough to notice a pattern: winter weddings can be smarter, calmer, and honestly more photogenic than a lot of couples expect.

One of the first things couples usually notice is the budget. Winter bookings typically run about 30% cheaper for the couple than prime summer dates. That alone can make a big difference if you’re trying to stretch your wedding budget without cutting the things you care about most. For a lot of couples, that means hiring the photographer they really want, booking the venue they love, or just giving themselves a little more breathing room elsewhere.

But the savings aren’t the only reason I like them.

Let’s talk about light.

In November, around 3 p.m., when the leaves are gone and the trees are bare, the light can be surprisingly gorgeous for portraits. It’s softer, cleaner, and more interesting than the flat overcast light I end up working with far too often in June. People assume summer is automatically the best photo season because the weather is warmer and the days are longer, but warm doesn’t always mean better. For portraits, winter light can be incredibly flattering in a way that makes the whole gallery feel calm and polished.

There’s also something to be said for the atmosphere of the day itself. In June, especially in busy wedding areas, I’m often dealing with the reality of multiple vendors all using the same space at the same time. I’m not exaggerating when I say I’ve shared a parking lot with three or four other vendors in June. That means more congestion, more rushing, more waiting around, and more little logistical headaches that add up fast.

Winter weddings tend to move differently. There’s usually a little more breathing room. Less chaos. Fewer people competing for the same patch of space. As a photographer, that matters. It gives me more room to work, and it gives couples more room to actually enjoy the day instead of feeling like they’re being shuffled through it.

I don’t think winter weddings are automatically better than summer weddings, and I’m definitely not trying to convince every couple to get married in January. But if you’re open to a winter date, I think it’s worth considering seriously.

You may save money.

You may get better portrait light than you’d expect.

And you may avoid some of the summer wedding gridlock that makes even the simplest timeline feel crowded.

If you’re planning your wedding and wondering when to book, I’d say this: don’t rule out winter just because it’s not the “traditional” choice. Some of the best weddings I’ve photographed lately have happened when everyone else assumed the season was off-limits.

b.text:
Why I Actually Like Shooting Winter Weddings Now

After six years shooting weddings almost entirely in the same metro area, I didn't expect to become a winter wedding person. I did. Actively.

I've shot 11 of them in the last two years, and I now tell couples who are flexible on dates to seriously consider it. Not because "weddings are beautiful year-round" — because winter gives you specific advantages you don't get in June.

First, the practical one: my winter bookings run about 30% cheaper for the couple. Same coverage, same albums, same me running around fixing your veil. It's just off-season, so I price it that way. If budget is part of why you're debating dates, that difference is real.

Second, the light. Everyone assumes summer = better photos. It's not. Give me the light through bare trees around 3pm in November over flat overcast June light any day. In June here, we get that bright white-gray sky that washes everything out at noon and then we’re racing the harsh evening sun. In November, the leaves are gone so the light actually comes through the branches instead of getting blocked, and by 3pm it's low, warm, and directional. It sculpts faces instead of flattening them. Some of my favorite portraits from the last two years were taken in 20 minutes in a park in November while everyone stayed warm in coats between shots.

Third, the day itself is calmer. In June, I pull up to a venue and I'm sharing the parking lot with 3 or 4 other vendors — another wedding flipping out of the ceremony space, a corporate event loading in, a DJ double-parked behind the caterer. We're all negotiating for the same patch of shade at the same golden hour. In winter, it's usually just us. Your venue team isn't exhausted from their third wedding that weekend. We get the good getting-ready room, not the overflow one. We can take our time and actually use the whole space for photos without waiting for another party to clear out.

Winter weddings aren't for everyone. It gets dark early, you need a coat plan, and you have to embrace it. But if you want better light for portraits, a less hectic venue, and a date that costs you about 30% less on photography — winter is worth a look.

If you're deciding between seasons, tell me what you're picturing and I'll tell you honestly what that date would look like to shoot.

setup: A remote software engineer is writing a 6-month standing desk review for blog readers researching standing desks.

a.text:
**6-Month Review: The Jarvik L2 Standing Desk**

I bought the Jarvik L2 in February - 60x30, laminate top, black frame - with my own money. No affiliate links here, nothing to sell you.

I'm a remote software engineer. This desk gets 9-10 hours a day, 5 days a week, dual 27" monitors on an arm, MacBook, heavy mechanical keyboard.

After 6 months of actual use:

**The motor is legitimately good.**

It's fast and quiet. Jarvik claims 1.4"/sec and that's about right - it goes from my sitting height (28.5") to standing (44.5") in ~11 seconds. And it's quiet enough that I can adjust it mid-Zoom call without muting. My old Flexispot sounded like a forklift. This one is just a low hum.

**It wobbles at full height.**

I'm 5'10" and I stand at 44.5 inches. At that height, if I'm really hammering on the keyboard or leaning to grab something, there is noticeable side-to-side wobble. The monitor shake is visible. At sitting height it's rock solid. At 40" it's fine. At full max height (47") it's borderline unusable for me if I'm typing hard. If you're over 6' and plan to stand tall all day, this is not the frame you want.

**The memory presets drift.**

I have preset 1 at 72cm and preset 2 at 113cm. After 2-3 weeks, preset 1 will stop at 71cm or 73cm. It's consistently off by about a centimeter. Not the end of the world, but annoying when you expect it to hit your exact ergonomic position every time. I've had to recalibrate it twice in 6 months by holding down+up until it resets.

**The cable tray is garbage.**

Throw it away. It's thin, stamped metal, too shallow to hold a power strip plus cables, and the included wood screws stripped out of the pre-drilled holes on day one. I replaced it with a $35 under-desk tray from Amazon that holds everything. For a company selling a $700+ desk, this tray is insulting.

**Verdict:**

At the $549 sale price I paid, it's a good desk. The motor alone makes it better than anything else in that price range.

At $749 full price? Absolutely not. For that money, buy a Uplift V2 or Fully Jarvis frame and get a more stable frame and presets that actually stay put.

If you can get it on sale and you're under 6 feet and don't mind fixing the cable management yourself, it's worth it. If you see it at $749, close the tab.

b.text:
# Jarvik L2 Standing Desk: My 6-Month Review

I’ve used the Jarvik L2 as my primary desk for six months, working from home as a software engineer. It gets raised and lowered multiple times a day, carries a dual-monitor setup, and has survived the usual mess of cables, chargers, notebooks, and too many coffee cups.

The short version: **it’s a good desk at the $549 sale price and a bad deal at $749.** The motor is fast and genuinely quiet, the frame feels solid at normal sitting and standing heights, and the controls are straightforward. But the wobble at full height is real, the memory presets aren’t perfectly reliable, and the included cable tray is bad enough that I stopped using it.

## What I like

### The motor is quiet and fast

This is the L2’s best feature. The motor is much quieter than I expected from a desk in this price range. It makes a low mechanical hum rather than a loud whine or grinding noise, and it doesn’t sound like it is struggling under a normal work setup.

More importantly, it moves quickly. I don’t have to stand there waiting for the desk to crawl from sitting height to standing height. That sounds minor, but it matters when you actually change positions several times a day. A desk that takes forever to move ends up staying in one position because using it feels annoying. The Jarvik L2 is fast enough that I use the standing function without thinking about it.

### It feels stable at the heights most people will use

At sitting height, it is completely fine. No complaints.

At my usual standing height, it is also stable enough for normal work: typing, using a mouse, adjusting monitors, writing in a notebook, and leaning lightly on the desk. It does not feel flimsy or cheap. The frame has enough weight and stiffness that it feels like a real piece of office furniture rather than one of those lightweight standing-desk frames with a tabletop thrown on top.

For regular day-to-day use, I have been happy with it.

## What I don’t like

### It wobbles at full height

The L2 is not rock-solid when raised all the way up. If I type hard, especially when I am in an aggressively caffeinated coding sprint, I can see some movement in the monitors. The desktop itself has a noticeable front-to-back wobble at maximum height.

To be clear: it does not shake constantly, and it has never felt unsafe. It is not collapsing, sliding, or doing anything dramatic. But it is there, and if you are tall enough to use this desk near its upper limit—or if you type heavily—you will notice it.

This is the sort of issue that reviews often dismiss with “all standing desks wobble.” That is technically true, but not especially helpful. The question is whether the wobble is annoying. For me, at normal standing height, no. At full height, yes.

If you need a desk that stays absolutely steady at its maximum extension, spend more money. The Jarvik L2 is not that desk.

### The memory presets drift

The memory presets are convenient, but they are not precise enough to trust blindly.

Over time, I noticed that a preset can land roughly a centimeter off from where I originally set it. That does not sound like much, and for some people it won’t matter. But desk height is one of those things where a centimeter can be noticeable, especially if you have your monitor arms, chair height, and keyboard angle dialed in.

I now treat the presets as approximate positions rather than exact ones. They get me close, then I make a small adjustment.

That is not a dealbreaker, but it is sloppy. A memory preset should return to the same height consistently. Six months in, I should not have to second-guess whether my standing preset is going to be slightly too low today.

### The cable tray is garbage

The included cable tray is the weakest part of the package by far.

It is awkward, undersized, and not designed around how people actually set up desks in 2026. Once you have a power strip, monitor power supplies, charging cables, and the various thick cables from a real workstation, it becomes cramped fast. Access is annoying, routing is annoying, and the result still looks messy.

I tried to make it work. I gave it more effort than it deserved. Eventually, I replaced it with a better under-desk cable-management solution.

If Jarvik removed the tray entirely and lowered the price by $20, I would consider that an improvement. If you buy this desk, assume you will want a separate cable tray or cable-management basket.

## Who should buy it

Buy the Jarvik L2 if:

- You can get it around **$549**
- You want a fast, quiet electric standing desk
- You work at standard sitting and standing heights
- You do not need perfectly precise memory settings
- You are willing to handle cable management yourself

Skip it if:

- You are paying **$749**
- You are tall and expect to use the desk at maximum height regularly
- You are extremely sensitive to desk wobble
- You want presets that are consistently exact
- You expect the included cable tray to solve your setup

## Verdict

At **$549**, the Jarvik L2 is worth buying. The motor is excellent, the desk is pleasant to use every day, and the compromises are reasonable for the price.

At **$749**, I would pass. The full-height wobble, drifting presets, and terrible cable tray are easier to tolerate when the desk is discounted. At full price, they feel like corners that should not have been cut.

It is a solid midrange standing desk, not a premium one. Buy it on sale, replace the cable tray immediately, and do not expect maximum-height stability to rival more expensive desks.

setup: A small dog grooming salon owner is writing a how-to for dog owners about preventing coat matting between grooming visits.

a.text:
I can usually tell the second a dog walks into my shop whether he's just been bathed at home or actually brushed out.

With our curly kids like doodles and poodles, and our thick double-coated pups like huskies and shepherds and goldens, that bath-first instinct gets people in trouble. I get why you do it — you think warm water is going to loosen everything up. It does the exact opposite. Wet matted fur just locks down and turns into a felt pad. Once that happens, I can't brush it out without hurting your dog, and half the time we end up having to shave it.

Always brush before the bath at home, never after. If the coat is dry and brushed clean first, then the bath is great. If it's tangled, the bath will set those tangles in tighter.

When you brush, grab a slicker brush and think short and gentle, not big circles. Circles just wind the hair around and make more knots. I do little line strokes, lift a small section up with one hand and brush down a little bit at a time.

Start where the mats always start first, behind the ears and right under the front legs in the armpits. That's the spot everyone misses. If you do those first and then work outward in sections, you'll catch 90% of it.

And if you already feel a little mat starting to form, don't go straight at it with the brush or comb. Put a dab of conditioner right on it and just work it in with your fingers first until those fibers start to slip apart. Then you can ease through it with the brush.

b.text:
If you have a doodle, a golden, or really any double-coated or curly-haired pup, you already know the struggle of keeping their fur tangle-free between our grooming appointments. The absolute biggest mistake I see well-meaning owners make is throwing their dog in the tub first, thinking the warm water and shampoo will help loosen up any tangles. Please don't do this! Water actually tightens mats up. If you bathe a matted dog, that wet fur shrinks and locks together, basically turning into a solid felt pad that I’ll eventually have to shave off. Bathing first locks them in tighter, so you always want to brush before the bath at home, never after.

When you’re doing your brush-out, grab a good slicker brush and use short, straight line strokes rather than scrubbing in circles. Line brushing is much gentler on their skin and actually gets down to the undercoat instead of just polishing the top layer. Work in small sections, and always start behind the ears and under the front legs. Those are the high-friction areas where mats love to hide and form first, so it's best to tackle them right away. 

If you’re working through the coat and feel a mat starting to form, put the brush down for a second. Grab some dog conditioner and work it directly into the tangle with your fingers. Gently massage it and try to pull the hair apart with your hands before you ever touch it with a brush or comb. The slip from the conditioner saves the hair and saves your dog from the pain of having a brush ripped through a tight knot. Taking just a few extra minutes to do a proper brush-out before bath time makes a world of difference for your pup's comfort, and it keeps their coat looking beautiful until I see you at the salon next!

setup: A small dog grooming salon owner is writing a how-to for dog owners about preventing coat matting between grooming visits.

a.text:
Between grooming visits, the biggest thing I see with double coated and curly breeds is mats that could have been caught early if the brushing happened at the right time. And here's the part most people get backwards: you brush before the bath, never after. Once that coat gets wet, any tangles you missed turn into a felt pad that's ten times harder to get out. So if you're doing an at-home bath, get the brush out first and make sure the coat is completely dry and tangle-free before water touches it.

When you do brush, use a slicker brush and keep your strokes short and straight—no circles. Circles just push the hair around and tighten any knots that are already forming. Work in sections, and don't skip the spots where mats love to start: behind the ears and under the front legs. Those areas rub and trap moisture, so they mat up first even if the rest of the coat looks fine. If you feel a mat starting while you're brushing, stop right there. Don't dig at it with the brush or a comb. Work a little conditioner into the mat with your fingers, let it sit for a minute, then gently tease it apart with your fingers or a wide-tooth comb. That conditioner gives the hair some slip so you're not just yanking and making it worse.

And please, don't bathe the dog first thinking the water will loosen things up. It does the opposite—wet matted fur shrinks and locks in tight, and then you're stuck with a solid clump that usually has to be shaved out. So remember: dry brush first, short strokes, behind the ears and under the front legs, conditioner on any mat before you touch it with a tool. That'll keep your dog comfortable between visits and make your next appointment a whole lot easier on both of us.

b.text:
If you have a doodle, a poodle, a husky, or anything with that thick double coat at home, you know how fast it can go from fluffy to tangled. It doesn't take much — a rainy walk, a harness rubbing, just sleeping curled up funny.

The biggest thing I wish I could tell everyone before they try to fix it at home is brush before you ever get them wet. Never after. I see it in the salon constantly — someone gives their dog a nice bath first thinking it will loosen everything up, and it does the exact opposite. It locks them in tighter. Wet matted fur doesn't loosen, it just turns into a felt pad and then I have to shave it out, which none of us want.

When you do brush, grab a slicker brush and forget the big circle scrubbing motion. You want short, little line strokes, almost like you're pulling the hair away in layers. And don't just go over the top. You have to work in sections. Lift the coat and get underneath. I always tell people to start behind the ears and right under the front legs in the armpit area, because that's where mats start first every single time. If you can keep those spots clear, you're winning most of the battle.

If you do feel a little clump starting to form, don't go straight at it with the brush or a comb. Put a little dab of conditioner — the regular dog conditioner you use for bath time is fine — right on it and work it in with your fingers only. Let it sit and soften and gently start to pull the hairs apart with your fingers first. Once it feels looser, then you can go in with the brush.

A quick brush like that a few times a week before bath day will save you, save your dog, and save me having to do a big shave-down when you come in.

setup: A small HVAC company owner is writing a how-to for homeowners on bleeding air from hot water baseboard radiators before winter.

a.text:
Shut off the circulator pump or boiler before you open any valves. If the system is running when you crack a bleeder, you’ll force air down the line instead of out of it, and you’ll probably get sprayed. Give the boiler ten minutes to settle and the pressure to flatten out.

Start with the baseboard unit closest to the boiler and work your way outward, one by one. Each unit has a bleeder valve on one end—usually a small brass fitting with a square nut or a slotted stem. Slide a cup, small bowl, or heavy rag underneath before you touch it.

Open the valve slowly with a bleeder key or a flathead screwdriver. You’ll hear hissing first. That’s the air leaving. Keep it cracked until the stream of water runs steady and quiet, with no sputtering or bubbles. Depending on how much air is trapped, this can take thirty seconds or several minutes.

Once the flow is solid, close the valve snug, but do not reef on it. These brass seats crack easily, and an overtightened bleeder will drip or weep all winter. Finger-tight plus a quarter turn is usually enough.

Repeat this at every unit in the house. The mistake that generates most of our cold-radiator calls is homeowners bleeding only the upstairs baseboards and skipping the basement loop. The air that collects at the top of the system usually got pushed there from below. If you skip the basement, you’ll be bleeding the upstairs again in a week.

When you finish the last unit, check the boiler pressure gauge. Bleeding drops the system pressure, so you may need to add water through the fill valve to get back to the manufacturer’s recommended range—usually 12 to 15 psi for a one- or two-story home. If you’re unsure how to add water or the pressure won’t hold, shut the boiler down and give us a call.

b.text:
Grab a small cup, a rag, and either a radiator key or a small flathead screwdriver. 

Here is how to bleed your hydronic baseboard system properly:

### 1. Shut off the boiler and circulator pump
Turn your thermostat all the way down or hit the emergency shutoff switch for the boiler. You need the circulator pump completely off before you touch a valve. If the pump is running while you bleed the lines, it will push air bubbles right past the open valve or suck more air into the system. Let the pipes settle for about 10 to 15 minutes.

### 2. Start closest to the boiler (Do not skip the basement)
The single biggest mistake we see on service calls is homeowners going straight to the second floor, bleeding those units, and calling it a day. 

Air moves with water flow before it settles. More often than not, the air pocket causing your heating issue is actually sitting down in the basement loop or on the first floor. Start at the baseboard unit closest to the boiler—typically in the basement or ground floor—and work your way outward and upward from there.

### 3. Locate the bleeder valve
Pop the end caps off the metal baseboard cover. Look for a small brass valve pointing up or slightly outward off the copper pipe elbow. It will have a small slotted screw in the center or a square peg for a radiator key.

### 4. Open the valve slowly
Hold your cup directly under the valve spout and keep a rag in your other hand. Slowly turn the screw counter-clockwise—usually a quarter to a half turn is plenty. 

You’ll hear a hissing sound as trapped air escapes. It might sputter with a mix of air and dirty water. Keep the valve open until that hissing stops and you get a steady, solid stream of water with no bubbles. 

### 5. Close it snug (Do not overtighten)
Turn the screw clockwise to close the valve until the water stops. 

**Watch your torque here.** These are small brass fittings. Turn it until it's snug and dry, but do not crank down on it with all your strength. Over-tightening will crack the valve seat, turning a simple five-minute maintenance job into an active leak that requires draining the whole zone to replace.

### 6. Work through the rest of the house
Move to the next unit along the loop, working through the ground floor before moving to the upper levels. 

Once every baseboard has been bled and wiped dry, switch the boiler and thermostat back on. Check your boiler’s pressure gauge—most residential systems run between 12 and 15 PSI when warm. If the pressure drops too low after bleeding or a room stays stone-cold, you likely have an autofill valve issue or a larger air lock in the main run that needs to be purged from the manifold.

setup: A high school girls' soccer and track coach is writing an op-ed urging turf funding for the girls' field.

a.text:
Over the last two seasons, my varsity girls’ soccer team has had nine games rained out, delayed, or relocated to an opponent's field because our grass doesn't drain. 

Nine times, parents rearranged their work shifts for nothing. Nine times, visiting teams sat on idling buses waiting for a call. And nine times, I had to walk into a locker room of teenagers who did everything right—trained all summer, kept their grades up, showed up ready to compete—and tell them they couldn’t play on their own home field because three hours of rain turned the pitch into a retention pond.

Worse than the schedule disruptions is the safety hazard. Last October, one of my starting midfielders stepped into a mud-covered rut near the sideline. Her foot stuck, her body twisted, and her ACL went. Her season was over in a split second, followed by surgery and nine months of painful physical therapy. It didn’t happen because of a hard tackle or a freak collision. It happened because the district expected teenage girls to sprint at full speed on uneven, waterlogged dirt. 

Next month, the school board will vote on the upcoming facilities budget. Turf for the girls' soccer field needs to be approved. Period. 

I know what the pushback will be. Someone will clear their throat and bring up the cost. But nobody seemed to worry about the price tag back in 2019, when the board found the money to put down a brand-new turf field for the boys’ football program. 

Five years later, the boys play every single scheduled game, rain or shine, on a smooth, modern, reliable surface. Meanwhile, the girls are still out back, sharing space with the geese, waiting for the mud to dry, or being packed onto a bus on two hours' notice to forfeit our home-field advantage. 

I don't coach to make a political statement, and I certainly don't do it for the writing credits. I do it because I care about these kids, and I get a small stipend at the end of the term to make sure they are coached properly and kept safe. Right now, the district isn't holding up its end of that deal. 

The board needs to look at the budget, remember what year they put turf on the football field, and do what should have been done five years ago. Fund the turf. Let the girls play.

b.text:
**Put Our Girls On Turf Too**

The last two seasons, my team has had nine games rained out or moved. Not delayed. Rained out or moved to another school's field because ours was underwater.

I coach girls soccer and track at the high school. I'm not a writer, I do it for the coaching stipend. But I'm tired of telling 16-year-olds we don't have a place to play because it rained yesterday.

Our field is the low grass field behind the school. It doesn't drain. After any real rain it's ankle-deep mud for three days. We practice in it, we slide all over it, and we try not to get hurt in it. We sprint around the swampy spots and we tell parents to bring boots to sit on the hill.

Last October one of my sophomores tore her ACL in a game. She wasn't hit. She was dribbling, stepped in a rut in our own field where the grass had washed out, and her knee went. She missed basketball season and she's missing this whole season. I coach track, too. I know what a bad surface looks like. That field is a bad surface.

This is a safety problem and it's a fairness problem.

The boys football field got turf in 2019. It's great. It drains, it's lined, they never lose a home game to weather. Our girls have been playing on a field that floods if you look at it wrong for six more years. If this were the football field, it would have been fixed a long time ago. Actually, it was.

I get it, turf isn't cheap. The board has a lot to pay for. But we are not asking for a stadium or lights or a press box. We are asking for a flat field that works when it rains. A field where we don't have to bus to the other team's school and call it a "home" game. A field where kids aren't worrying about what hole they're going to step in.

The school board votes on the facilities budget next week. Put turf for the girls soccer field in it.

Our girls deserve the same shot the boys have had since 2019 - to actually play their home games, on their home field, without getting hurt.

setup: A long-haul trucker is writing a short Roadstar DC4 dual dash cam review for other owner-operators on a trucking forum.

a.text:
Roadstar DC4 after 14 months / 140k miles

Ran this cam hard for 14 months and about 140k miles. Overall it’s held up, but there’s some stuff you should know before buying.

The rear cam is the weak link at night. Anything past 30 feet gets grainy enough that you’re not reading plates or fine details. Daytime rear footage is fine, front cam is solid day and night. If you’re mostly running daytime or just want basic coverage, it’s workable. If you need clean night rear footage, look elsewhere.

The one time it mattered, it paid for itself. Caught a lane change accident on camera where the other driver tried to say I drifted into him. Sent the clip to insurance and the claim got approved in 9 days instead of the usual 6 weeks. That alone makes me keep it in the truck.

Mounting: the suction mount fell off twice in summer heat, both times while parked. Switched to the adhesive mount and haven’t had an issue since. If you buy this, throw the suction mount in the glove box and go straight to adhesive.

The app is basically useless on the road. It needs wifi to pull footage, and most truck stops don’t have wifi worth using. I just pull the SD card and plug it into my laptop. Faster and no app headaches.

For the price, it’s decent. Not perfect, but the front footage is good and it saved me a long insurance fight. If you can live with the rear cam limits and don’t care about the app, it’s worth a look.

b.text:
**Roadstar DC4 Dash Cam - 14 Months / 140k Mile Review**

Been running the Roadstar DC4 in my current rig for 14 months and about 140,000 miles. Here’s the straight dope for anyone looking at picking one up.

The biggest plus: It pays for itself. It caught a four-wheeler making a blind lane change right in front of me. Sent the clip to my insurance, and my claim was approved in 9 days instead of the usual 6-week BS. 

The drawbacks:
- Rear night vision: Gets pretty grainy past 30 feet. It's fine for seeing if someone is riding your bumper, but don't expect to read plates in the dark.
- The mount: The suction cup fell off the glass twice in the dead of summer. Switched to the adhesive mount and it's been rock solid. Do yourself a favor and just use the adhesive right out of the box.
- The app: It needs Wi-Fi to pull footage to your phone, which is completely useless at most truck stops. I just pull the SD card and use a reader on my laptop.

Bottom line: It’s a solid, no-frills workhorse that did exactly what it needed to do when it counted. Just ditch the suction cup and ignore the app.

setup: An in-house recruiter is posting a contrarian observation about candidates asking about the team’s last failed project in interviews to recruiters, hiring managers, and job seekers.

a.text:
I’ve done close to 200 interviews over 9 years, all in-house for a logistics company乃and there’s one question I only hear from the best candidates:

“What project failed recently, and what did the team learn from it?”

Not “tell me about the culture.”
Not “what does success look like in this role.”
They ask about the failure. Specifically the recent one.

Most candidates want to know how the company wins.
The strongest ones want to know how the company loses—and what happens after.

Here’s how that conversation usually goes with a candidate I end up fighting for:

Them: “What’s a project that didn’t go as planned in the last year?”

Me: “We rolled out a new routing tool last spring. Adoption was rough. Drivers hated it, dispatchers bypassed it, and we basically ran dual systems for three months.”

Them: “What did leadership do when they realized it wasn’t working?”

Me: “We pulled the rollout back, put a few dispatchers in the room with the vendor, and rebuilt the workflow around how they actually operate—not how we assumed they would.”

Them: “So the original timeline slipped. Did that impact how you plan rollouts now?”

And that’s the moment I know. They’re not just vetting the company. They’re trying to understand how problems get solved here, who gets blamed, and whether people are allowed to speak up after things go sideways.

Most candidates interview to survive the process. The best ones interview to understand how your team actually functions when it’s not a highlight reel.

b.text:
I've done ~200 interviews for ops and dispatch roles in the last two years.

The candidates I still think about a week later almost always do the same thing at the end. They ask me about a project that failed here.

Not "what's the culture like." They want to know what happens here when things go sideways.

Had this happen last month. Final round for a Site Supervisor role in Louisville.

He goes: "Can you tell me about the last big thing that didn't work out at your site?"

I told him: "We tried to flip Louisville to 6-day receiving last Q3 to get ahead of peak. Looked great on a spreadsheet. We didn't staff for it right, burned out our two best leads, OT blew up, and service actually got worse. We killed it after four weeks and went back to five."

He didn't miss a beat. He said: "How did you guys talk about it with the floor team after you rolled it back?"

That follow-up is the whole ballgame.

He wasn't looking for gossip. He was trying to figure out if we blame people or fix the plan. If he'd get cover when he inevitably makes a bad call, too.

I was honest with him about it. He took the offer.

Curious for other hiring managers - is there a failure story you're actually willing to share in interviews?

setup: A first-year nursing student is writing a scholarship essay about her first ER rotation for scholarship committee readers.

a.text:
Before my first clinical rotation in the emergency room, most of my nursing education lived inside textbooks and plastic mannequins. In a simulation lab, everything is controlled. The lights are steady, the fake skin doesn't bleed real blood, and nobody is crying. My first week in the ER changed all of that completely. It showed me what nursing actually demands: patience, grit, and the willingness to stay steady when someone else is falling apart.

One of my first patients was an older man with a severe, dirty leg wound that needed to be cleaned out. His wife was his main support, but she was stuck in bumper-to-bumper traffic on the highway trying to get to the hospital. He was visibly terrified, gripping the sides of the gurney with white knuckles. My preceptor had to focus on irrigating and debriding the tissue, which was painful and messy. I didn't have the clinical skills to do the cleaning yet, so I stepped up to the head of the bed, introduced myself, and offered him my hand. He grabbed it immediately and didn't let go for twenty minutes. He squeezed so hard my fingers went numb, but having someone there kept him grounded until his wife finally walked through the door. That was my first real lesson: sometimes the most important tool you have isn’t a syringe or a stethoscope, but just standing there so someone doesn’t have to hurt alone.

Later that same week, a Code Blue was called for a patient in cardiac arrest. As a first-year student, you want to jump in and do something heroic, but the reality is you have to know your limits so you don’t get in the way of the team saving a life. The charge nurse looked at me and told me to restock the supply cart outside the room with 4x4 gauze and saline flushes. While the doctors and senior nurses worked, I stood by the supply shelves with an armful of supplies, listening to the rhythmic counting of chest compressions through the blue curtain—one, two, three, four. It was heavy, and it was loud, but it taught me that there are no small jobs in a hospital. Keeping the room stocked so the next nurse could grab what they needed without looking was my part in that fight.

The moment that tested me the most came near the end of the week. I had to draw blood on a diabetic patient who had spent years getting poked and prodded. His veins were scarred down, fragile, and almost impossible to see. On my first attempt, I missed. I apologized, adjusted, and tried a second spot, but the vein rolled. My palms started sweating. On the third try, I missed again. I felt terrible, embarrassed, and ready to walk out of the room to find my instructor so I wouldn't cause the man any more discomfort. But the patient looked at me, saw how nervous I was, and said, "Take a breath. You’re learning. Try the side of my left wrist." I took a slow breath, anchored the vein the way I’d practiced on the rubber arm in lab, and on the fourth try, I saw the flash of dark red blood fill the chamber. Getting that draw taught me that mistakes and misses happen, but you can’t let panic take over. You have to reset, listen, and keep going until you get it right.

I did not go into nursing because I thought it would be clean or easy. I chose it because I want to do work that matters to people on the hardest days of their lives. Balancing tuition, books, and the long hours required for clinicals is tough, and this scholarship would take a huge weight off my shoulders financially. It would allow me to keep my focus entirely on my studies and my clinical training, so I can graduate, pass my boards, and become the kind of nurse who is reliable, skilled, and ready for whatever walks through the hospital doors.

b.text:
I went into my first clinical thinking I would feel like a nurse. Instead I felt like a kid wearing scrubs that were too big, trying not to get in anyone’s way.

By Monday afternoon I was already lost in the ER supply closet when a nurse poked her head in and said a man in room four needed someone to hold his hand. His wife was stuck across town in traffic, and they were cleaning gravel out of a road rash that ran from his shoulder to his elbow. I followed her back and stood on the side where his wife would have been. The nurse warned him it was going to hurt. He gripped my hand before she even started. He didn’t say much, just squeezed hard when the saline hit, and I squeezed back. That was the whole thing. I didn’t do any actual nursing. But he didn’t let go until his wife ran through the door twenty minutes later, and I realized that sometimes being there is the job.

The next day a code got called in the bay next to where I was shadowing. My preceptor told me to step out and restock the gauze cart. I was glad to have something to do with my hands, but standing in the hallway I could hear them through the curtain. Someone counted compressions. One and two and three and four. Over and over. I kept counting in my head even after I stopped hearing them. I had never been that close to it before. I didn’t see the patient, but I understood why the ER runs through supplies so fast, and why nobody walks in that room unless they have to.

Then there was the blood draw on Thursday. Diabetic patient, older guy, veins like cooked spaghetti. I missed the first stick. I missed the second. By the third I was sweating through my shirt and apologizing every time he flinched. He just said, “You’re learning, it’s alright.” I didn’t believe him. I almost asked my preceptor to take over, but she stood back and said, “Try the other arm. You’ve got it.” The fourth stick went in. I saw the flash of blood and almost cried. He said, “There you go,” like he knew it would happen all along. I taped the tubing down and cleaned up and realized I had spent more time with him than I would have if I’d gotten it on the first try. That’s not an excuse for missing three times. But it taught me that nursing isn’t about doing everything perfect right away. It’s about not walking away when you’re embarrassed.

That week stripped away a lot of what I thought nursing was. I didn’t save anyone’s life. I didn’t know enough to be useful in a code. I stuck a guy four times and probably hurt his feelings. But I also held a stranger’s hand so he wasn’t alone, and I stayed in the hallway while someone fought to come back, and I kept trying on that blood draw until I got it because the patient let me. I learned that ER nursing is mostly showing up, paying attention, and not quitting when you feel stupid.

I’m a first-year student, so I still have a lot to learn. But after that first week, I know I want to keep going. I want to get good enough that I can be in the room during the code instead of outside it. I want to hit the vein on the first try. Most of all, I want to be the kind of nurse who stays late enough to hold someone’s hand until their family gets there. This scholarship would help me stay in school and get there faster. I’m ready to put in the work.

setup: A wedding photographer is posting that couples who ditch rigid shot lists get better photos, using the rained-out Barrera wedding as an example.

a.text:
After 8 years and hundreds of weddings, I've noticed a pattern: the couples who hand me a shot list and then let go of it get better photos than the ones who stick to it minute by minute.

Case in point: the Barrera wedding.

Rain moved in about an hour before the ceremony. The outdoor setup they'd planned for months was suddenly underwater. We ended up moving everything under this massive old pecan tree on the property, no arch, no draping, no aisle runner in place, just the tree and everyone crowded in under it.

It wasn't the plan. It wasn't on any shot list. And it produced some of the best images I've shot all year.

Here's what I think is actually happening: a shot list is a security blanket. It's couples trying to control an outcome months in advance because the whole process feels overwhelming. Totally understandable. But weddings don't run on schedules, they run on weather, on emotions, on 80 people in one place at one time. The second something doesn't go as planned, a rigid list becomes a source of stress instead of a source of comfort.

The couples who do best are the ones who tell me what matters to them (grandma's ring, dad's reaction, the first look) and then let me handle the rest. That trust is what lets me actually see what's happening in front of me instead of checking boxes.

The Barrera's didn't get the wedding they planned. They got a better one. And they got photos they'll be looking at for the next 50 years.

If you're planning a wedding right now: bring me your must-haves, then let the day do what it's going to do. That's usually where the best photos are hiding.

b.text:
The couples who ditch the shot list always seem to end up with the best photos.

Not because shot lists are bad. They are helpful. But a wedding day is alive, and the best images usually happen when you trust the moment more than the checklist.

At the Barrera wedding, rain took over the day. We moved everything under the pecan tree, set the original plan aside, and stopped trying to force what we thought the day was supposed to look like.

What we got instead was one of the most honest, joyful galleries I have delivered.

Crowded under branches.
Laughing through the weather.
Completely real.

After eight years of photographing weddings full time, I have learned this: my job is not just to check off poses. It is to notice what is happening, protect your time, and make space for the moments you will actually remember.

If you are planning a wedding, bring your must-have family photos. Bring your vendor list. Then give yourself permission to let the rest unfold.

Sometimes the backup plan becomes the best part.

setup: A parent of two middle-schoolers is writing an op-ed to local readers urging an 8:45am middle-school start time.

a.text:
To the Editor:

Every weekday morning in my house starts the same way: a chorus of alarms, heavy sighs, and me trying to coax two exhausted middle schoolers out of bed. If your household is anything like mine, you know the struggle is real. Our kids are chronically sleep-deprived, which is why I’m writing to urge our community—and our school board—to support the proposed 8:45 a.m. start time.

This isn't just about making our mornings a little less chaotic. It’s a matter of basic health. The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends that middle and high schools start no earlier than 8:30 a.m. Science tells us that during puberty, children’s sleep cycles naturally shift later. They aren't just being lazy; their brains physically resist falling asleep early. Expecting them to absorb pre-algebra at 7:45 a.m. is fighting a losing battle against biology. 

We already have proof right here in Millbrook that a later start works. Just look at the results from the pilot program at Lincoln Middle. When Lincoln pushed its start time back, the school saw a noticeable rise in attendance, and first-period grades went up. When we give kids just a little more sleep, they show up, and they actually learn. 

I know some parents are worried about how this change will affect transportation. Change is hard, and logistics are always a puzzle. But if you read the school board’s proposal closely, you’ll see they have already addressed this. The plan includes a smart re-tiering of our bus routes. By shifting the windows for elementary, middle, and high schools, the district can handle the new schedule using the fleet we already have, without costing taxpayers extra money. It’s a practical, well-thought-out solution.

Our school board votes on this proposal next month. As parents, we want to give our kids every tool possible to succeed. Let’s support a policy that prioritizes their mental health, safety, and academic success. Please join me in contacting the school board to voice your support for the 8:45 a.m. start time. It’s time to let our kids get the sleep they need.

b.text:
**Let Our Kids Sleep. The Numbers Say We Should.**

Every school morning at 6:20, I stand in my daughter's doorway and say her name three times before she moves. She is thirteen. She is not lazy. She is doing exactly what her body is built to do at that age, which is sleep.

That's why I'm asking the school board to approve the 8:45 start time when it votes next month.

I'm not a doctor, but the doctors have been clear on this. The American Academy of Pediatrics says middle and high schools should start no earlier than 8:30, because teenagers' internal clocks genuinely shift later during puberty. They physically cannot fall asleep at 9:30 the way a second-grader can. Ask them to be at their desks by 7:40 and you are guaranteeing they show up short on sleep. The AAP ties that chronic shortfall to worse grades, more depression, more car accidents among teen drivers, and more sick days. That's not a parenting opinion. That's the pediatricians.

We don't have to take it on faith, either. Lincoln Middle ran this as a pilot, and the results are in the proposal for anyone to read. Attendance went up. First-period grades went up. The kids who used to sleep through pre-algebra started actually doing pre-algebra. When a change works in our own district, with our own kids and our own teachers, I don't know what more evidence we're waiting for.

I know the objection. I've heard it at soccer practice and in the pickup line: "It'll wreck the buses." I had the same worry, so I read the transportation section twice. The proposal doesn't add buses. It re-tiers the routes, so elementary runs first and middle school runs second, instead of the other way around. Same fleet, same drivers, same number of trips. It's a schedule change, not a budget request. If someone has read that section and found a hole in it, I'd like to hear it, but "the buses" isn't an argument on its own anymore.

Will it be an adjustment? Sure. Some families will need to rethink before-school care. Practices may shift. I'm willing to do that, because the alternative is what we're doing now, which is asking twelve- and thirteen-year-olds to fight biology every single morning and then wondering why they're irritable, distracted, and falling behind.

We tell our kids that when the evidence changes, you change your mind. Here's a chance for the grownups to model it.

Vote yes on 8:45.

setup: A long-haul trucker is writing a short Roadstar DC4 dual dash cam review for other owner-operators on a trucking forum.

a.text:
**Roadstar DC4 Dash Cam – 14 months / ~140k miles in. Honest rundown.**

Hey folks. Figured I'd put my 2 cents in since I've been running the Roadstar DC4 for about 14 months now, 140k miles on the odometer with it, front and rear cams. Not writing a manual, just stuff I wish someone had told me before I ordered it.

The big one. The thing that justifies the price tag no matter what else you think about this cam: it caught a lane-change accident on I-20 outside Shreveport. Some idiot merged into my trailer, full contact, no contact zone. Rear cam had the whole thing. Filed the claim with the footage attached, adjuster approved it in 9 days. Nine. Last time I had a claim without video I sat on it for 6 weeks waiting for "further review." That alone paid for this thing four times over, easy. You know how it goes.

Now the stuff that ain't great.

Rear cam at night past about 30 feet gets real grainy. If you're trying to ID a plate on a truck in a rest area parking lot, forget it. For the road footage, the brake lights ahead, the general "what happened" of a night collision, it's fine. It's a dash cam, not a night-vision scope. Just know going in.

Suction mount is garbage. I'm not kidding. Fell off twice in July in Texas, both times I'm pulling in and I'm like "that's a weird thud sound." Switched to the adhesive mount after the second one and haven't had a problem since. Don't even try the suction thing in summer if you're running anywhere south of Nebraska.

App pulls footage over wifi. Just... just don't count on it. Most truck stops the wifi's locked behind a paywall, password changes every 20 minutes, or it's barely got a bar to begin with. I've stopped trying to pull clips from my phone. Just pop the SD card into the laptop at the end of the week. Took me three months to stop fighting the app and do it the dumb simple way.

Bottom line: camera's solid, the insurance-saving factor is real, the mounts and app need to go in the trash. Keep it, swap the mount, ignore the software.

Happy to answer questions if y'all got any. Back to the road, I'm 40 miles behind schedule.

— T.

b.text:
**Roadstar DC4 — 14 months, ~140k miles**

Bought this thing figuring it'd die by month six. It didn't, so here's the honest rundown.

**What earned it a permanent spot on my windshield:**

Guy changed lanes into me outside Amarillo. Front cam got the whole thing clean — his mirror, his signal that never came on, all of it. Sent the clip to my insurance and had the claim approved in 9 days. Nine. Last time I went through a claim without footage it took six weeks of phone calls and them squinting at my word against his. That alone paid for the camera about forty times over.

**Where it falls short:**

Rear cam night footage goes to mush past about 30 feet. Close-in stuff at the dock or somebody riding my bumper, fine. But if you're hoping to read a plate on a car that clipped you and kept going in the dark, you'll be disappointed. Daytime it's sharp enough.

The suction mount is garbage in summer. Fell off twice — once in Phoenix in July, once in Vegas. Both times it landed on the dash still recording, so no damage, but I'm not gambling on it. Switched to the adhesive mount and it hasn't budged since. If you buy this, just start with the adhesive mount and skip the aggravation.

The app is the other gripe. It needs WiFi to pull footage off the camera, and truck stop WiFi is a joke on a good day. I quit fighting it. Now I just pop the SD card and read it on my laptop, which is faster anyway. If the app being useless is a deal-breaker for you, look elsewhere — but I don't know many guys who are pulling clips off their dash cam in the sleeper for fun.

**Bottom line:** Front cam is solid and that's the one that matters for claims. Rear cam is a nighttime weak spot. Buy the adhesive mount, ignore the app, keep a spare SD card in the console. Held up through 140k miles of heat, cold, and washboard road without a hiccup, and it got me paid. Good enough.

setup: A high school junior is writing an argumentative essay to her English teacher and classmates arguing for open campus lunch for juniors and seniors.

a.text:
Let Juniors and Seniors Leave for Lunch

Every day at 11:42, our lunch wave turns into a scramble for chairs. People end up sitting on the floor in the hallway or standing around trash cans trying to eat because there is nowhere else to go. Our school should allow open campus lunch for juniors and seniors. It would fix a real space problem, it has already worked in schools near us, and students are clearly ready for it.

The most immediate reason is space. Our cafeteria only seats 220 people, but there are 340 students assigned to that lunch wave. That math does not work. When more than a hundred students do not have a seat, lunch is not really a break. It is loud, crowded, and stressful, and custodians and lunch supervisors have to deal with the overflow. Letting juniors and seniors who want to leave go off campus would take pressure off the cafeteria for everyone, including freshmen and sophomores who would stay.

The other thing is that we know this policy can work because nearby schools are already doing it. Fairmont, West Linn, and Cascade all allow open campus lunch for upperclassmen. According to their published attendance stats, none of them have seen a rise in tardiness since they started it. That matters because the biggest worry adults have about open lunch is that students will not get back in time for fifth period. In these three districts, they do get back. There is no reason to assume our school would be different.

Some teachers and parents might still argue that only some juniors and seniors are responsible enough to handle leaving campus. But at this point most of us are driving to school, holding part-time jobs, and applying to college. Going out for lunch and getting back on time is a pretty basic level of responsibility. I surveyed 80 students at our school and 71 said they were in favor of open campus lunch. That shows students actually want this privilege and understand what comes with it.

Open campus for juniors and seniors is not about getting out of school. It is about trusting upperclassmen with a normal choice and solving an overcrowding problem at the same time. The cafeteria cannot fit us, other schools have proven it does not cause tardiness issues, and students support it. It is time for our school to make the change.

b.text:
# Open Campus Lunch for Juniors and Seniors

At our school, 340 students share a lunch wave in a cafeteria that seats only 220. That leaves 120 students without a cafeteria seat if everyone tries to eat there at once. Lunch should be a chance to eat and take a break, not a daily struggle to find space. Allowing juniors and seniors to leave campus during lunch would give students more choices while helping address this overcrowding. Our school should adopt an open campus lunch policy for upperclassmen, with clear expectations for returning on time.

The strongest reason for this change is the cafeteria’s limited capacity. The school assigns 340 students to the same lunch wave but cannot seat all of them in the cafeteria. An open campus policy would allow some juniors and seniors to eat elsewhere, reducing the number of students competing for the available seats. It would not guarantee that overcrowding disappears, since we do not yet know how many students would leave each day. Still, giving upperclassmen that option is a practical way to ease the pressure on a space that is already too small for the group assigned to it. Students who choose to stay would benefit as well.

Student opinion also supports considering a change. In a survey I conducted of 80 students at our school, 71 favored open campus lunch—nearly 89 percent of those surveyed. That result does not prove that every student supports the policy, and popularity alone is not enough to make a school rule worthwhile. However, it shows substantial interest among the students who responded. A policy meant to improve students’ lunch experience should take their views seriously, especially when those views align with a clear problem such as overcrowding.

One reasonable objection is that students who leave campus might return late and disrupt afternoon classes. However, nearby districts offer evidence that open campus lunch does not necessarily cause that problem. Fairmont, West Linn, and Cascade already allow it, and their published statistics show no rise in tardiness. Their results do not guarantee that our school would have exactly the same experience, but they weaken the argument that allowing students to leave will inevitably lead to more late arrivals. Rather than rejecting the idea based on that prediction, our school should examine how those districts manage the policy.

Our school could also address concerns by introducing open campus lunch as a trial for juniors and seniors. Students would still be responsible for arriving at their next class on time, and repeated late returns could result in losing the privilege. During the trial, administrators could track afternoon tardiness and cafeteria use to see whether the policy is working. This would give the school evidence from its own students instead of forcing it to make a permanent decision based only on expectations.

Open campus lunch would not solve every problem in the school day, but it offers a reasonable response to an overcrowded cafeteria. The survey shows strong student interest, and the experience of nearby districts suggests that the policy can work without increasing tardiness. With clear rules and a trial period, our school can give juniors and seniors greater independence while holding them accountable. Students should have the opportunity to show that they can handle that responsibility.

setup: A third-year electrical apprentice is writing an argumentative essay for the union newsletter against a 15% cut to apprenticeship funding.

a.text:
# Don't Cut the Ladder Out From Under Us

I'm a third-year apprentice with our local. I want to tell you why the state's proposed 15% cut to apprenticeship funding is a bad idea, using real numbers from my own cohort.

We started with 24 apprentices. Twenty-one finished. That's an 87% completion rate. Those 21 people are now working journeyman electricians, earning around $46 an hour. We started at about $19 an hour as first-years — enough to get by, not enough to get comfortable. But that number climbs fast, year over year, as we learn the trade and take on more responsibility. By the time you're a journeyman, you're not just off government assistance, you're paying good money back into the system through taxes.

Here's the number that should matter most to legislators looking to save money: the total public cost per apprentice who finishes our program runs about $14,000. Compare that to a four-year college degree, where the average public subsidy per graduate who finishes is around $48,000. That's not a small gap. That's more than three times the cost, for a program where a good chunk of students don't even finish and end up with debt and no degree to show for it.

Our program doesn't work that way. If you finish, you have a skill. You have a job waiting. You're not sending out a hundred resumes hoping someone calls back. The work is here, the pay is real, and the path is clear from day one.

Cutting apprenticeship funding by 15% doesn't save the state money in any real sense — it just shifts costs somewhere else. Fewer apprentices trained means fewer skilled electricians in five years, which means higher costs for every construction project, every repair, every new build that needs qualified people to do the work safely and correctly. It also means fewer working-class kids get a shot at a stable, well-paying career without taking on a mountain of student debt.

We're not asking for a handout. We're asking the state to keep funding something that already works, that already proves itself in the numbers. Twenty-one out of 24. $14,000 versus $48,000. Off assistance and into the middle class in four years. That's not a program that needs cutting. That's a program that needs protecting.

If you're reading this and you're one of our state legislators, I'd invite you to come see an apprenticeship class in session. Come see what your investment actually looks like on the ground. It looks like people learning a trade, showing up on time, and building a future for themselves and their families — at a fraction of the cost of a lot of other programs the state funds without blinking.

Don't cut the ladder out from under the next generation of tradespeople. We're proof it works.

b.text:
**Why the 15% Apprenticeship Cut Is Bad Math for the State**

My name's in the back of the newsletter with my job classification, but you probably know me already if you've walked a job site in this county. I'm a third-year inside wireman. Day three of my first week on a commercial job, my foreman handed me a stack of blueprints for a parking garage lighting retrofit and said, "Read it. Figure it out. I'll check your work." Twenty-one months later I'm pulling 600-amp feeders and roughing in a hospital wing. That education cost you $14,000.

Let me be specific about that number, because the legislature's fiscal note just says "program costs" and stops there, like it's all the same bucket of money. Twenty-one of my cohort finished. Started with 24. Three dropped. That's an 87.5% completion rate, and the state paid, all-in, about fourteen grand per head across the whole program. Tuition, instructor salaries, tool subsidies, the works. Fourteen thousand dollars, and at the end of it there's a journeyman wiring a hospital.

Now look at the other side of the ledger. The average public subsidy for a four-year college grad who actually finishes—which, by the way, is closer to two-thirds, not 87%—is about $48,000. Forty-eight. The apprenticeship program finishes people at a higher rate for a third of the cost. That's not me spinning a chart. That's the comptroller's own per-pupil numbers. You are not saving money by cutting the cheaper, better-finishing program. You are just spending more later.

Because what happens in year four, when a kid finishes college at twenty-three with $32,000 in debt and a degree in something that doesn't pay the rent? He's on SNAP. He's living with his parents. His parents are tapping a 401(k). That's a public cost too, it just shows up in a different budget line where nobody's watching.

I've been at $19 an hour in this program. I'm headed toward $46 by year five, and that's before overtime, before the pension contribution, before health and welfare. But even at nineteen—nineteen!—I stopped being a number on an assistance roll about three months in. By year two I was pulling more than my buddy who graduated with a general business degree from the state school and "is still figuring out his thing." He's still figuring it out. I've been paying income tax into the same state that's now proposing to take 15% of the funding that made me a taxpayer instead of a line item.

I don't need you to feel sorry for us. I don't need a ribbon-cutting or a plaque on the training center wall. What I need is for somebody in the building to do the actual subtraction before this cut goes through. You will trim a program that graduates 87% of its people in five years at $14k per head. You will do nothing about the program that graduates 66% of its people in four to six years at $48k per head. You will make the cheaper, faster, working-class option harder to get into, and you will not touch the expensive, slower one, because that's the one your donors went to.

I'm not asking for a handout. I'm asking you to leave the ladder where it is. Twenty-four of us walked in three years ago. Twenty-one of us are on the payroll now. The three who left, at least they left with skills and a reason to try a different trade. Nobody on this program is sitting in a living room collecting a check while they "find themselves." We're up on a scissor lift at six a.m. running EMT conduit in February, and we did not sign up so you could balance a budget by making the next kid's ladder shorter.

Fifteen percent. That's classroom nights we cut. That's instructor positions we cut. That's the tool subsidy we cut that keeps a nineteen-year-old from walking off after two months because he can't afford a set of Klein pliers and a voltage tester and the program is supposed to help him get those, not watch him fail for want of $200 in hand tools.

I'm three years in. I've got the work. I'll finish what I started no matter what. But the next cohort, the one that walks in next fall—they'll hear the program got slashed, and two or three of them will sign up for something else. Something that costs the state $48,000 apiece and has a worse finish rate. And that's on you.

Vote your conscience if you want. But do the math first. Fourteen versus forty-eight. Eighty-seven percent versus sixty-six. Five years versus six. We are the cheaper, faster, more honest answer to "how do you make a state with more people working and fewer people on assistance." Cutting us is not fiscally responsible. It's just picking the program that doesn't have anybody in the gallery to push back.

We're in the gallery. We're just on a different schedule.

setup: A retired rural mail carrier is writing a letter to the Kettle Falls Courier urging residents to oppose the post office counter closure at the July 28 forum.

a.text:
**Don’t Close Our Post Office Counter**

To the Editor:

I drove Route 4 for 22 years before retiring last year. That was 38 miles a day, and I got to know this town and the people who live outside it.

USPS says our branch loses $40,000 a year. But they already cut the counter hours from 8 a.m. to noon. Of course traffic dropped. Many working people cannot get there before noon. Now USPS is pointing to a problem it helped create as a reason to close the counter altogether.

This is not just about convenience. Mrs. Halloran up on Kettle Hill is in her 80s and gets her heart medicine by mail. She does not drive, and she cannot simply make a 20-minute trip to Fairview when she needs a money order or help with a postal problem. There are plenty of other people around here in the same position.

A small-town post office is a service, not a business that should be judged only by what happens at the counter. Once we lose it, we will not get it back.

Please come to the public forum on July 28 at the Grange Hall and speak up. The district manager needs to hear from the people who actually live here.

—A retired Route 4 carrier

b.text:

setup: A long-haul trucker is writing a short Roadstar DC4 dual dash cam review for other owner-operators on a trucking forum.

a.text:
**Roadstar DC4 Dash Cam — 14 months / 140k miles**

Figured I'd put some real miles on this thing before writing it up. Here's where I landed.

**The good:**

It earned its keep back in the spring. Four-wheeler cut across my lane, clipped me, and of course told his insurance I drifted into him. Front cam footage said otherwise. Claim approved in 9 days. My last claim without footage took 6 weeks. That alone paid for the camera several times over, so if you're running without one, that's the whole argument right there.

Daytime footage front and rear is solid. Plates are readable, no complaints.

**The bad:**

Rear cam night footage gets grainy past about 30 feet. Close stuff is fine, but if someone's tailing you at a distance in the dark, don't count on reading a plate. Front cam handles night better.

The suction mount is junk in the heat. Fell off my windshield twice last summer, once while I was rolling. Switched to the adhesive mount and it hasn't budged since. Just skip the suction mount and go adhesive from day one.

**The annoying:**

The app needs wifi to pull footage. Sounds fine until you realize truck stop wifi is garbage or nonexistent half the time. I gave up on the app and just pull the SD card and stick it in my laptop. Works fine, just know going in that the app is basically useless on the road.

**Bottom line:**

Not perfect, but after 140k miles it's still recording every day and it already saved me a claim fight. Buy the adhesive mount with it, keep a spare SD card, and don't expect miracles from the rear cam at night. Would I buy it again? Yeah.

Questions, drop em below.

b.text:
**Roadstar DC4 Dash Cam – 14 Months / 140k Miles Review**

Been running the Roadstar DC4 for 14 months and about 140,000 miles. Here’s the quick and dirty for you guys.

**The Save:** It pays for itself when it matters. A few months back, it caught a four-wheeler swapping lanes right into my trailer. Sent the footage to insurance, and my claim was approved in 9 days instead of the usual 6-week headache. That alone makes the camera worth every penny.

**The Mount:** The factory suction cup is garbage. It fell off twice during the summer heat. I swapped it to the adhesive mount and haven't had an issue since. If you buy this, just throw the suction cup in the trash right away.

**The App:** Useless. It requires Wi-Fi to pull footage, which is a joke at most truck stops where the internet is barely dial-up. Save yourself the frustration and just pull the SD card directly into your laptop.

**Video Quality:** Front camera is solid day and night. The rear camera is fine during the day, but at night, the footage gets pretty grainy past 30 feet. It's good enough to show what happened, but don't expect to read plates if someone is riding way back in the dark.

**Bottom Line:** It's a solid, no-BS camera that will protect your livelihood when someone else screws up. Just plan on using the adhesive mount and skipping the app entirely.

setup: A high-school biology teacher is writing a cover letter to a customer success hiring manager at the edtech company.

a.text:
Dear Hiring Manager,

For two years, your platform was the backbone of my biology classroom. I didn’t just use it—I depended on it. I built my lesson flow around it, trained 30 new students on it every semester, and became the go-to person on my campus when colleagues hit a snag. As the campus admin, I troubleshooted everything from login chaos to grade-sync panic, often while a lab was mid-explosion and a parent was on hold.

That experience is exactly why I’m stepping out of the classroom and into customer success.

Eight years of teaching taught me what no onboarding script can: how to read a room, simplify the complex, and keep my cool when someone is frustrated. I’ve handled angry parents, skeptical administrators, and teenagers who forgot their passwords five minutes after I reset them. I’ve translated “the mitochondria is the powerhouse of the cell” into a hundred different explanations until it clicked. That’s the core of customer success—meeting people where they are and getting them to value the tool in front of them.

I already know your product from the inside. I know what teachers love, what makes them want to throw their laptops, and what they actually need when they say “it’s not working.” I can speak their language because I’ve been them. And I can speak yours because I’ve already been your user, your advocate, and your unpaid support rep.

I’m ready to help other teachers feel the same relief I did when your software finally made my job easier. Let’s talk about how I can bring that teacher perspective to your customer success team.

Best,
[Your Name]

b.text:
For two years, I served as the campus admin for your product while teaching high school biology. I onboarded 30 new students every semester, trained reluctant colleagues across the department, and became the go-to person for troubleshooting SSO issues and calming frustrated users before first period.

Teaching is customer success with higher stakes. I turned skeptical freshmen into daily active users, retained nearly all of them through May, and de-escalated "angry parent" calls with the same calm, jargon-free approach I used to explain feature updates to our IT director. When a student—or a teacher—was stuck, I didn't just fix the problem; I redesigned the workflow so it wouldn't happen again.

After eight years in the classroom, I'm leaving to scale that impact. I know firsthand where your platform saves teachers time and where new users get overwhelmed, because I lived it. I want to put that frontline knowledge to work helping your districts succeed.

I'd welcome the chance to discuss how my experience as a power user and educator can help your team drive deeper adoption and reduce churn.
