Watching you single-handedly steer our used book fair this past week was something else. You weren’t just present; you were everywhere: before the first bell, when you’d already be hauling heavy boxes in from your car, and again long after the last bus pulled away, stacking tables and sorting the final donations. When I’d poke my head in, you were recruiting another parent on the spot, calmly making sure every shift was covered, and somehow keeping the whole thing humming with a smile.

Because of that tireless, behind-the-scenes work, we raised more than double what the fair brought in last year. That’s not just a number on a spreadsheet—it’s the entire classroom library fund for this year. It means I’ll be able to put fresh, diverse books into my students’ hands all year long, the kind that turn reluctant readers into kids who argue over who gets to borrow *Dear Martin* first. You made that possible, Renata. You didn’t just run a fundraiser; you planted hundreds of reading moments that haven’t even happened yet. Thank you, deeply and truly, for all of it.

setup: A local sports columnist is writing an opinionated season-ending commentary for readers of the local paper's sports section.

a.text:
**COLUMN: Abandoning the ground game cost us a deeper playoff run**

It’s tough to swallow a season ending the way ours did on Friday night. Going 8-2 is a banner year for this program, and nobody is taking that away from these kids. But losing in the second round of the state playoffs to a team we beat by 20 points back in Week 3 leaves a bad taste in your mouth. 

We didn’t lose because we were out-athleted. We lost because of a baffling second-half game plan.

Let’s look at the facts. At halftime, we were down by just three points. More importantly, our run game was dictating the tempo. We were moving the chains, controlling the clock, and keeping their defense on their heels. Then the third quarter started, and for some reason, the coaching staff decided to put the ball entirely in Dez Kowalski’s hands.

Don't get me wrong, Dez is a phenomenal talent. He threw for 2,340 yards this season, shattering the school record, and he’s got the arm to make any throw on the field. But you don’t abandon a working ground game just to chase highlight-reel passes, especially when you’re only trailing by a single field goal. 

By going pass-heavy in the second half, we became one-dimensional. We let their defensive line pin their ears back and hunt our quarterback. We gave up the clock, we gave up the physical advantage we’d established in the first half, and ultimately, we gave up the game. 

You have to play to your strengths, and on Friday, our strength was right between the tackles. Next year’s squad will need to remember that when the lights are brightest, you don't get cute. You just line up and run it down their throats.

b.text:
When the Better Team Loses

Let's get this out of the way first: this was a good season. Eight wins. A school record for Dez Kowalski, who threw for 2,340 yards this year and made Friday nights a lot more fun to watch. That's real, and it shouldn't get buried under how the year ended.

But I'm not going to sit here and write a nice, tidy season wrap-up like the scoreboard in the second round didn't happen, because it did, and it's still bugging me a week later.

Here's the thing that gets me: this team lost to an opponent they beat by 20 points back in Week 3. Same team. Same coaching staff. And down by three in the second half — three points, in a game they were controlling on the ground — the offense stopped running the ball.

Not because it wasn't working. It was working. That's what makes it maddening instead of just disappointing. When the run game is moving the chains and you're down a single score, you don't need to get cute. You don't need to prove anything. You need to keep doing the thing that's working until they stop it. Instead, the offense drifted away from it, started leaning on the pass in obvious passing situations, and let a defense that had spent a whole half chasing tailbacks suddenly pin its ears back and tee off on Kowalski.

I get the instinct. When you fall behind, the coach's brain screams "we need points fast," and the pass looks like the quicker route there. But three points isn't a two-score deficit. Three points is one good drive. One good, patient, run-it-until-they-stop-it drive. This team had exactly that drive in its bag all night and put it away in favor of hope.

That's not a talent problem. It's not a Kowalski problem — the kid deserved better play-calling support in that stretch, not less of it. It's a discipline problem, and discipline problems are the kind you can actually fix.

So no, I'm not writing the "great year, on to next season" column, at least not only that one. This team was good enough to still be playing right now. They didn't lose to a better team. They lost to a version of a team they'd already beaten, and they helped them do it by walking away from what was working.

Next year's team will have the tools to be even better. Here's hoping somebody in that coaches' booth remembers this game the next time it's a one-score contest and the run is humming. Trust it. Ride it. Make the other team prove they can stop it before you decide to stop doing it yourself.

setup: A freelance wedding photographer is writing a blog post for couples about why to book a winter wedding.

a.text:
**Why I Actually Like Shooting Winter Weddings Now**

I used to think winter weddings were the off-season compromise. After six years in this metro area and 11 winter weddings in the last two years, I’ve changed my mind for reasons that are more specific than “every season is beautiful.”

The first reason is money, and I’ll be blunt: winter bookings run about 30% cheaper for you. That’s not because the photos are worse or vendors are phoning it in. It’s because demand drops. Venues have open Saturdays, caterers have openings, and photographers like me have calendar gaps we’d rather fill with a wedding than leave empty. You can often get the higher package, the second shooter, or the venue you actually wanted for the same budget that would have bought you a peak-season baseline. I’ve watched couples do exactly that.

But I didn’t come around just because it’s cheaper. I came around because the images can be better.

The light through bare trees around 3 p.m. in November is honestly better for portraits than flat overcast June light. I know that sounds like a hot take, but I’ve shot both. In June, I’m often dealing with a flat white sky or harsh overhead sun that makes people squint and turns every tree into the same green background. In November, the sun sits lower. It comes through bare branches at an angle, and it gives you warm, directional light that’s much easier to work with for portraits. The trees themselves become part of the composition—branches instead of a green wall. Some of my favorite portraits from the last two years were taken in the middle of a mostly empty park at 3:15 p.m., no sweating, no squinting, no waiting for another group to clear the frame.

That brings me to the part nobody puts in a brochure: in winter, I am not sharing the parking lot with three or four other vendors like I am in June. That matters more than it should. In peak season, popular venues get stacked with multiple events. You’re waiting for the loading zone, waiting for the elevator, waiting for the staircase while another photographer works the same shot. It eats into your timeline and adds background noise to what should be a calm day. In winter, it’s usually just us, the venue staff, and your people. The day moves differently. I can actually take my time with details instead of looking over my shoulder for the next vendor’s arrival.

Yes, winter has a shorter light window, and yes, it can be cold. We plan for that. We do portraits in a 20-minute block when the light is right, keep coats nearby, and have an indoor backup. After 11 winter weddings, I’ve found that constraint usually makes the day feel more intentional, not less.

If you’re trying to stretch your budget or you just want a wedding day that doesn’t feel like a crowded peak-season Saturday, ask me about winter dates. I have the availability, I have the experience, and now I actually have a preference.

b.text:
# Why I Actually Like Shooting Winter Weddings Now

For the first few of my six years shooting weddings, I treated November through February as the off-season. The calendar wound down in October, I caught up on editing, and I waited for May to fill back up. That's just how it worked.

Then I shot eleven winter weddings across the last two years, and somewhere in the middle of that stretch, I changed my mind. I don't just tolerate winter weddings anymore. Given the choice, I'd take one over a June Saturday. Here's why.

**The light is better. That's not a typo.**

Around 3pm in November, the sun is already low, and it comes through the bare trees at this long, slanting angle that wraps around people beautifully. It's directional, it's warm, it gives faces shape. Compare that to a flat overcast June afternoon, where the sky turns into one giant gray ceiling and the light comes from everywhere and nowhere at once. That's honestly the hardest light I shoot in all year.

There's also a scheduling bonus nobody mentions: in June, the best light of the day shows up around 8:30pm, when you're sitting down to dinner. In November, it shows up at 3pm — right when we're actually outside doing portraits. The good light clocks in when we do.

**It costs you less.**

Winter bookings run about 30% cheaper for the couple. Venues drop their rates in the off-peak months, and a lot of vendors do the same. Same room, same cake, same photographer — meaningfully less money. If you're deciding between dates and the budget matters, that gap is real, not theoretical.

**We're not sharing.**

On a June Saturday at a popular venue, I'm sharing the parking lot with three or four other vendors from the events booked alongside yours, and we're all rotating through the same two good portrait spots like a receiving line. In winter, the place is yours. No waiting for another wedding's cocktail hour to clear out of the courtyard. The staff is relaxed, the timeline breathes, and the whole day feels less like airport security and more like, well, a wedding.

**The honest fine print.**

It's cold. You'll want a coat you don't mind being photographed in, and we'll do portraits in shorter blocks so nobody's shivering through the good stuff. The early sunset also means the timeline has to be built around the light — you can't wing a winter day the way you can wing a long June one. I plan that out with every winter couple, but it's worth knowing before you book the date, not after.

**If you're still picking a date:**

Everyone will tell you to aim for June. I used to be one of them. Eleven winter weddings later, I'm converted

setup: A high school junior is writing an argumentative essay to her English teacher and classmates arguing for open campus lunch for juniors and seniors.

a.text:
Every day at the sound of the bell, a logistical nightmare unfolds in our school. A wave of students rushes toward the cafeteria, competing for limited space in a room that was never designed to hold them all at once. The solution to this daily chaos is simple, yet it is often dismissed due to unfounded administrative fears: allowing off-campus lunch. By implementing an open campus lunch policy for juniors and seniors, our administration can solve the immediate physical problem of cafeteria overcrowding, honor the clear preference of the student body, and align our school with the highly successful policies of neighboring districts. 

The most pressing reason to allow open campus lunch is a matter of basic mathematics and facility limits. Currently, our cafeteria is designed to seat a maximum of 220 people. However, during the upperclassmen lunch wave, 340 students are assigned to this space. That leaves 120 students without a seat, forcing them to sit on the floor, crowd into the hallways, or wander the building. Lunch is supposed to be a necessary mental break in the middle of a rigorous academic day; instead, it has become a stressful, overcrowded environment. Allowing juniors and seniors to leave campus would instantly relieve this bottleneck, providing adequate space for the underclassmen and those upperclassmen who choose to stay behind.

Beyond the logistical necessity, an open campus policy is something the student body actively desires and is ready to handle. I recently conducted a survey of 80 students at our school regarding off-campus lunch. Out of those polled, 71 students were firmly in favor of the policy. While student preference alone does not dictate school rules, this overwhelming majority highlights a collective desire for greater independence. Juniors and seniors are already driving to school, holding down part-time jobs, and preparing for college. Trusting them to manage their own lunch period is a natural step in treating them like the young adults they are.

The traditional counterargument against open campus lunch is the fear that students will abuse the privilege and return late to their afternoon classes. However, regional data proves this fear is entirely unfounded. We do not have to guess how this policy will play out because three nearby districts—Fairmont, West Linn, and Cascade—have already implemented it. According to their published district statistics, none of these schools experienced a rise in tardiness after allowing upperclassmen to leave campus for lunch. These districts recognized a simple truth: when students are granted a meaningful privilege, they are highly motivated to follow the rules in order to keep it. Our students are just as capable of managing their time and acting responsibly as the students at Fairmont, West Linn, and Cascade. 

An open campus lunch for juniors and seniors is not just a frivolous student demand; it is a practical, immediate solution to a glaring infrastructural problem. By simply opening the doors at lunchtime, the school can instantly resolve a 120-seat deficit in our cafeteria, acknowledge the readiness of the student body, and follow the proven, data-backed models of neighboring districts. It is time for our school to trust its upperclassmen and adopt a policy that makes logical sense for everyone.

b.text:
**The Case for Open Campus Lunch**

Every day at 11:40, three hundred and forty students file into a cafeteria built to seat two hundred and twenty. Some grab tables. Some eat standing against the wall or sit on the floor near the vending machines. This is not a hypothetical problem or a matter of student preference—it is a basic math problem our school faces every single lunch period. Granting open campus lunch privileges to juniors and seniors would relieve this overcrowding, and the evidence from neighboring districts shows it can be done without the disciplinary problems administrators fear.

The most immediate argument for open campus lunch is the state of our cafeteria itself. With 340 students assigned to a lunch wave and only 220 seats, the room is over capacity by more than fifty percent. That gap doesn't just mean discomfort; it means longer lines, more crowding at the doors, and students eating in hallways where food isn't supposed to be. If even a fraction of upperclassmen left campus for lunch, the students who remain—including all freshmen and sophomores—would have a cafeteria that actually functions as designed. Open campus lunch is often framed as a privilege for older students, but in our case it would directly benefit the younger students who stay behind.

Critics of open campus policies usually raise the same concern: students who leave for lunch will come back late, or not at all. This is a reasonable worry, but it is also a testable one, and nearby schools have already run the experiment. Fairmont, West Linn, and Cascade—three districts within driving distance of ours—all allow open campus lunch for upperclassmen, and their published statistics show no rise in tardiness after the policies took effect. These aren't distant schools in different circumstances; they are our neighbors, with similar schedules and similar students. If tardiness didn't spike there, there is no clear reason to assume it would spike here. A cautious administration could even follow their lead by starting with seniors only, or by making the privilege contingent on attendance records, as some of these districts do.

Finally, this is a change students actually want. In a survey I conducted of 80 students at our school, 71 said they were in favor of open campus lunch for juniors and seniors—nearly ninety percent. A survey of 80 students is not the whole school, but a margin that lopsided suggests broad support rather than a vocal minority. Student buy-in matters here, because a privilege students value is a privilege they will work to keep. If the policy comes with clear conditions—return on time, maintain grades, keep the privilege—students have every incentive to follow the rules, because they were the ones asking for the policy in the first place.

Some will still argue that lunch supervision exists for student safety, and that the school is responsible for us during the day. But juniors and seniors are sixteen to eighteen years old. Many of us drive to school, hold jobs, and are trusted to manage our own schedules everywhere except the lunchroom. A policy that treats a seventeen-year-old with a part-time job and a driver's license as incapable of buying a sandwich and returning in forty minutes is out of step with the responsibility we're expected to show in every other part of our lives.

Open campus lunch for juniors and seniors would ease a genuine overcrowding problem, and the experience of Fairmont, West Linn, and Cascade shows that the most common objection—tardiness—doesn't hold up in practice. The students support it, the neighboring districts have proven it workable, and the cafeteria numbers make the current situation unsustainable. Our school shouldn't wait until the crowding gets worse to consider a solution that is already working a few miles away.

setup: A remote software engineer is writing a 6-month standing desk review for blog readers researching standing desks.

a.text:
# Jarvik L2 Standing Desk: 6-Month Review

**TL;DR:** Good motor, mediocre stability at height, sloppy presets, embarrassing cable management. Worth $549. Not worth $749. Buy it on sale or buy something else.

I bought the L2 in [month], paid the $549 sale price with my own money, and have used it 8+ hours a day, five days a week, ever since. No affiliate links in this post — nobody makes money if you buy this thing, including me. My setup: two 27" monitors on a gas-spring arm, mechanical keyboard, and a standing height of about 42.5". I switch positions 4–6 times a day, so the motor and presets have had a real workout — somewhere north of 700 cycles at this point.

## The motor is the best part of this desk

Genuinely. Sit-to-stand takes about 17 seconds under full load, it's smooth, and it's quiet enough that I've adjusted it mid-meeting with my mic unmuted and nobody noticed. There's a low hum, not a whine, and no grinding or hesitation at the top of travel. After 700+ cycles it sounds identical to day one.

This is the thing cheap desks get wrong — my previous budget frame started stuttering under two monitors within a year. The L2's motor has given me zero problems and I expect that to continue.

## Stability: fine sitting, wobbly standing

At sitting height, it's a rock. No complaints.

At my standing height (42.5"), there's front-to-back wobble when I type hard — and I type hard, because mechanical keyboard, because programmer. The monitors on my desk-mounted arm visibly sway for a second or two after I really get going. It's not alarming, nothing's going to fall, but it's noticeable and it's the kind of thing that bugs you more in month six than month one.

Two things made it better: torquing every frame bolt again after the first month (they settle), and moving my monitor arm's clamp closer to a leg. If you type gently or use a laptop, you may never notice. If you hammer a keyboard like you're mad at it, you will.

## The memory presets drift

There are four presets. Great. Except they drift by about a centimeter. I'll hit preset 2, the display says 42.5", and I can feel it's wrong — measure it, and it's at 41.6" or 43.1". It's not consistent in which direction it misses, which honestly offends me more. A centimeter doesn't sound like much until your elbows are slightly wrong for three hours.

I've done the factory recalibration (hold the down button, let it bottom out) three times. It helps for a week or two, then the drift creeps back. My fix is dumb but effective: I use the presets to get close, then nudge with the manual buttons and watch the readout. It works, but "the memory buttons get you within a centimeter" is a sad sentence to write about a desk that costs this much.

## The cable tray is garbage

I don't use that word lightly. It's a shallow stamped-metal trough that attaches to the underside of the desktop with four short screws into particle board. Here's what happened, in order:

1. I loaded it with one surge protector and the usual cable bundle. It sagged in the middle within a week.
2. The rear two screws loosened themselves from the desk's vibration. I re-seated them. One stripped the hole.
3. It's too shallow to close over a standard surge protector anyway, so the lid has been off since month one.

I ripped it out in month three, mounted a $15 under-desk cable raceway from [generic], and my cable situation is now better than the desk deserves. Budget for that. Plan on throwing the included tray directly in the trash and saving yourself the intermediate steps.

## Smaller stuff

- **The desktop** is laminate over particle board and it's fine. Edges haven't chipped, it wipes clean, and my monitor arm clamp hasn't dented it. Not premium, not a problem.
- **The controller** display is bright enough to read in a dark room, which also means it's bright enough to annoy you in a dark room. No way to dim it. I put a strip of electrical tape over half of it.
- **Assembly** took me about 50 minutes alone. Instructions were clear, hardware was labeled, nothing was missing. Genuinely good experience.
- **Anti-collision** works. It stopped on my chair arm once and reversed. Tested it deliberately a second time because I didn't trust it. It passed.

## The verdict

At **$549**, this desk is a good deal. The motor alone justifies it — quiet, fast, and proven over six months of daily abuse — and the flaws are livable if you know about them going in. Recalibrate occasionally, re-torque your bolts, replace the cable tray immediately, and you've got a desk that does its job.

At **$749**, it's overpriced. At that number you're in range of frames with better lateral stability and controllers that remember where 42.5 inches actually is. The wobble and the preset drift are forgivable at $549. They are insults at $749.

Jarvik runs sales constantly — I've seen it at $549 three separate times since I bought mine. So the advice is simple: if you want this desk, set a price alert and wait. Do not pay full price. Full price is for people who don't read reviews, and you just read 800 words about a cable tray.

b.text:
# Jarvik L2 Standing Desk: 6 Months Later (The Honest Review)

I bought this desk in August at $549 during a Labor Day sale. Six months of daily remote work means I've actually lived with this thing—not just unboxed it for Instagram. Here's what holds up and what doesn't.

## What Works

**The motor is genuinely quiet.** I'm not exaggerating. When colleagues video call me, they can't hear the desk moving. The Flexispot E8 I tested two years ago sounded like an angry robot. This isn't that. It's noticeably better than competitors in this price range.

**Speed is solid.** Desktop to standing takes about 8 seconds. That's fast enough that I actually use it instead of leaving the desk in one position all day. The 3-inch travel time between my preset heights feels snappy.

**The desktop itself is fine.** 48×30 inches of bamboo. No flex, no cheap particle board vibes. It's genuinely sturdier than I expected at this price point.

## What Doesn't

**The wobble at full height is real.** When I'm standing and typing aggressively—which I do—the desktop vibrates noticeably. It's not unsafe. But it's annoying. Sit down and it disappears. The moment you're vertical and tapping hard on the keyboard, you notice it. This is the thing I think about most.

**Memory presets drift about a centimeter.** I have four preset heights programmed. After two weeks, they've shifted. Not drastically. But enough that I manually nudge the desk up or down when I hit a preset. It's not a dealbreaker, but it's a QA problem. More expensive desks (looking at Uplift and Flexispot's pricier models) don't do this.

**The cable tray is genuinely bad.** It's shallow, the clips don't grip well, and cables slip. I ended up velcroing everything in place. For a desk at this price, I get that they cut corners somewhere, but this is where they made their cuts too visible.

## The Verdict

**At $549? Buy it.** The motor quality, speed, and wobble-under-duress offset each other into "worth the money." That's about $100 cheaper than the Flexispot E7 and it's the better desk for remote workers who actually use standing features multiple times daily.

**At $749 full price? Pass.** That price point puts you in dangerous territory where the Uplift V2 is only $200 more. You're also close to mid-tier Flexispot desks that don't have preset drift. The memory preset issue alone makes the price-to-reliability ratio worse the higher you go.

**Who should buy:** Remote workers who sit 4+ hours a day and will actually alternate positions. People who type aggressively (the wobble might bother you less if you're lighter-handed). Anyone whose cable situation is already a disaster (you'll manage the tray's limitations).

**Who should skip it:** Anyone needing silent operation at standing height while working. Anyone who sets presets once and expects them to hold steady for months. People who need a cable management solution that doesn't require additional purchases.

The Jarvik L2 is a desk that makes you aware of what you're not paying for. That's not always a criticism.

setup: A small HVAC company owner is writing a how-to for homeowners on bleeding air from hot water baseboard radiators before winter.

a.text:
# How to Bleed Air Out of Your Baseboard Heating Before Winter

If your baseboards gurgle, or one room stays cold while the rest of the house heats fine, you've probably got air trapped in the system. Bleeding it out takes about 20 minutes and no special skills — here's how to do it right.

## What You'll Need

- A radiator key or a flathead screwdriver (depends on your valve type)
- A small cup or bowl
- An old towel, just in case

## Step 1: Shut Off the Circulator and Boiler

Before you touch anything, turn off the boiler and circulator pump. You don't want the pump pushing water around while you're trying to bleed a valve, and you don't want to be working with scalding water. Give the system a few minutes to settle.

## Step 2: Find the Bleeder Valve on Each Baseboard

Look at the end of each baseboard unit — usually behind the end cap, you'll find a small valve with either a square stem (that's what the key is for) or a slotted screw head. Every unit on the system should have one.

## Step 3: Cup Underneath and Open the Valve Slowly

Hold your cup under the valve and open it slowly. Don't crank it — a quarter to half turn is usually plenty. If there's air in the line, you'll hear it hiss out. Let it run until you get a steady stream of water with no sputtering or hissing. Steady water means the air is out of that section.

## Step 4: Close It Snug — Not Tight

Once the water runs steady, close the valve until it's snug and the drip stops. **Do not crank it down.** Overtightening cracks the valve seat, and then instead of a free 20-minute job, you've got a leaking valve and a service call.

## Step 5: Work Unit by Unit, Starting Closest to the Boiler

Start with the baseboard nearest the boiler and work your way outward through the loop. Air moves through the system, so bleeding in order gets it all out instead of chasing it around the house.

## The Mistake That Causes Most of Our Cold Radiator Calls

Here it is: **people bleed the upstairs units and skip the basement loop.**

We get called out every fall for "cold radiators," and more often than not, the homeowner already bled every baseboard on the main and second floors — but never touched the basement. That's usually exactly where the air is sitting. If your system has a basement zone or any baseboard down there, bleed those units too. Don't skip them because the basement doesn't need to be warm — trapped air down there affects the whole system.

## After You're Done

Turn the boiler and circulator back on and check your pressure gauge. Most residential systems should sit around 12–15 psi cold. If bleeding dropped your pressure below that, the system needs water added back — some setups have an automatic feed valve that handles this, others need it done manually.

If you're not sure how to add water, or you've bled everything (basement included) and you've still got cold spots, that's when it's worth having someone take a look. Could be a stuck zone valve, a failing circulator, or a bigger air problem that needs a power purge.

Give us a call and we'll get you sorted before the real cold hits.

b.text:
# How to Bleed Air Out of Your Baseboard Heating

Air trapped in your baseboard loops is the number one reason we get "my radiator's cold" calls this time of year. The good news is you can usually fix it yourself in an afternoon. Here's how we do it.

## 1. Shut Down the System First

Turn off the boiler and the circulator pump before you touch anything. You want the water still, not moving. If the system's running while you bleed, you'll fight against the circulator and never get a clean result. Give it a few minutes to settle.

## 2. Find the Bleeder Valve

Look at the end cap of each baseboard unit. The bleeder valve is a small fitting, usually round with a square nub or a slot for a flathead. Some take a special bleeder key (they're a couple bucks at any hardware store), others open with a screwdriver.

## 3. Cup Underneath It

Hold a cup or rag under the valve before you open it. Water is going to come out, and it can be dirty. Protect the floor and the wall behind it.

## 4. Open It Slow

Crack the valve open slowly with your key or flathead. You'll hear air hissing out first — that's exactly what you're after. Keep it open until the hissing stops and water runs out in a steady stream with no sputtering. That steady flow tells you the air is gone from that unit.

## 5. Close It Snug — Don't Crank On It

Once the water's running clean, close the valve. Snug is enough. If you muscle it down hard, you can crack the valve seat, and now you've got a leak on top of a cold radiator. Firm, not forced.

## 6. Work Unit by Unit, Boiler to Farthest

Start with the unit closest to the boiler and work your way out to the farthest one. Doing it in order pushes the air through the system the right direction instead of trapping it.

## The Mistake That Causes Most of Our Cold Radiator Calls

People bleed all the upstairs units, feel good about it, and skip the basement loop entirely. That basement loop is almost always where the air actually is. If your upstairs is fine but a room stays cold, or if you did all the visible units and still have a problem, get down to the basement and bleed that loop too. Nine times out of ten, that's the fix.

---

Once you've bled everything, turn the boiler and circulator back on, let it run, and check your pressure gauge — you may need to top off the water. If units are still cold after all this, or if you can't find a bleeder valve on a unit, give us a call and we'll come take a look.

setup: A small coffee shop owner is writing testimony to city council opposing a parking meter rate increase.

a.text:
Members of the City Council,

I am writing to you today as the owner of a small, independent coffee shop on Main Street to formally express my opposition to the proposed parking meter rate increase. Tripling the downtown parking rate from $0.50 to $1.50 an hour is not a minor administrative adjustment; it is a direct threat to the economic viability of our downtown corridor, and the data clearly demonstrates why this proposal is a mistake.

My opposition is not based on vague anxieties about what might happen to local commerce; it is rooted in hard numbers and historical precedent. In 2019, when the next town over implemented a similar parking rate hike, I carefully tracked my own register data to see how it affected consumer behavior. Over a six-week period following their increase, foot traffic dropped by exactly 18%. When the cost to simply park a car becomes a barrier, consumers do not adapt to the new rates; they simply go elsewhere, specifically to suburban drive-thrus and strip malls where parking is entirely free. Main Street cannot afford to artificially suppress our daily foot traffic by nearly a fifth.

Furthermore, the nature of downtown commerce makes this flat hourly increase disproportionately punitive to quick-service businesses. I closely monitor consumer habits at my shop, and the average customer visit lasts exactly 22 minutes. Under the current structure, a customer paying the $0.50 minimum for an hour is already paying for more time than they use. They accept this as a reasonable baseline cost for downtown access. However, forcing a customer to pay $1.50 just to run in and grab a coffee for 22 minutes fundamentally alters the cost of their daily routine. It turns a quick, convenient stop into an overpriced hassle. 

Finally, we must look at the actual financial benefit to the city, which the data shows is negligible. According to the city’s own financial report, parking meter revenue currently covers only 4% of the downtown budget. This proposed increase is not a silver bullet for our municipal deficits. Attempting to squeeze more money out of a revenue stream that accounts for just 4% of the budget does not actually solve any of the city's financial problems, but it absolutely will choke the daily foot traffic that independent businesses rely on to survive. 

We are being asked to risk an 18% drop in customers to marginally inflate a budget line item that is functionally insignificant to the city's overall financial health. The math simply does not justify the damage this will do to the small businesses that give Main Street its character and economic heartbeat. I urge the council to look at these specific numbers, recognize the minimal civic gain compared to the severe local impact, and vote against the parking meter rate increase.

b.text:
SUBMITTED TESTIMONY IN OPPOSITION TO PROPOSED DOWNTOWN PARKING METER RATE INCREASE

TO: City Council Members and the Public Record
FROM: Owner, Independent Coffee Shop, Main Street

Members of the City Council, 

I am submitting this testimony to formally oppose the proposed increase in downtown parking meter rates from 50 cents to $1.50 per hour. While I understand the city's desire to optimize revenue and manage parking turnover, this specific proposal relies on assumptions that do not align with the operational realities of our local small business economy. I urge the council to reject this hike based on the following data.

The primary justification for raising meter rates is typically to encourage parking turnover. However, this logic fails when applied to my business and many others on Main Street. I have tracked my customer data extensively, and my patrons average a 22-minute visit. The current one-hour parking minimum already provides more than enough time for them to park, order, enjoy their coffee, and leave. Tripling the cost of parking will not turn over these spots any faster; it will simply penalize the customers who are already utilizing the current time limits efficiently. The infrastructure is already working as intended for the actual duration of a downtown retail visit.

Furthermore, we do not have to guess at the economic impact of this price increase; we have recent, localized data. In 2019, the neighboring town implemented a similar rate hike. Anticipating the potential impact, I tracked my own register data daily for six weeks following their increase. The result was a documented 18% drop in foot traffic. That is not a marginal fluctuation; it is a severe contraction in customer volume that directly threatens the profit margins of independent businesses. A 200% price increase on our own meters will undoubtedly replicate this 18% loss in downtown foot traffic, pulling revenue directly out of our local economy.

Finally, the financial benefit to the city does not justify the economic damage to the downtown corridor. According to the city’s own report, parking meter revenue currently covers only 4% of the downtown budget. Tripling the rate will not suddenly transform meters into the financial backbone of our city infrastructure, especially when factoring in the likely decrease in overall parking volume as drivers avoid the downtown area entirely due to the cost. This policy is not solving a structural budget deficit; it is extracting a marginal revenue gain at the direct expense of Main Street's vitality.

I urge the council to look at the hard numbers: a 22-minute average customer visit, a documented 18% drop in foot traffic from a neighboring town's identical policy, and a mere 4% contribution to the downtown budget. Please vote no on the proposed increase from 50 cents to $1.50 an hour and work with local business owners to find solutions that support, rather than penalize, our downtown economy.

setup: A real estate agent is writing a commentary on the local market for brokerage blog and local paper readers.

a.text:
The market has changed. A lot.

If you’ve been watching headlines and waiting for a dramatic crash, this is not that. What we’re seeing in our part of the Midwest is something much more ordinary, and honestly, more fixable: sellers are still pricing to last spring, while buyers are moving at this spring’s speed.

Here’s what the numbers are telling us in plain English. In my zip code, the median days on market has jumped from 8 days last spring to 34 days this spring. That’s a big shift. At the same time, list prices are still up 6% year over year. On paper, that sounds like a strong market. In practice, showings per listing have dropped by half.

That mismatch is the story.

A home can be beautifully updated, in a great neighborhood, and still sit if it’s priced like we’re in the frenzy of 2021 or early 2024. Buyers are not chasing the market the way they were. They’re selective. They’re comparing more homes. They’re taking their time. And they are absolutely willing to move quickly for the right house — but only when the price makes sense.

I have three sellers right now who have been on the market more than 60 days and still don’t want to adjust. I get it. Nobody likes hearing that the number they hoped for isn’t the number the market is supporting. But the market does not negotiate with our feelings. It responds to value, condition, and price. If a home is sitting, the market is telling you something. Ignoring that signal doesn’t make the message go away.

What’s frustrating is that some sellers are treating a slower sale as a sign that buyers are “broken” or that the market is weak. That’s not what this is. The buyers are there. They’re just no longer willing to overpay for homes that are priced ahead of the curve.

And that’s the part sellers need to catch up to.

The homes that are priced right are still moving. In fact, the well-priced homes are still selling in under two weeks. That’s the real market right now. Not the stale listing that sits for two months. Not the overpriced home that gets a handful of showings and no offers. The homes that are aligned with today’s pace are selling, because buyers recognize value when they see it.

So if you’re thinking about selling, here’s my blunt advice: don’t ask what your neighbor got at the peak of last spring. Ask what buyers are actually paying now. If you want a quick sale, price it to win attention immediately. If you want to test the market, be prepared for silence. There isn’t much middle ground anymore.

This isn’t a crash. It’s a reset. And the sellers who understand that are the ones who are going to come out ahead.

b.text:
# The Market Didn't Crash. It Just Stopped Sprinting.

Last spring, the median days on market in our zip code was 8. Eight days. You'd list a house on Thursday, hold showings through the weekend, and be reviewing offers Monday morning, usually more than one.

This spring? Thirty-four days.

If you're a seller, that number probably feels alarming. And if you've been reading national headlines full of words like "correction" and "cooling," you might be bracing for the worst. So let me give you my honest read after ten years working this market, because I think most of the anxiety out there is aimed at the wrong problem.

This is not a crash. List prices in our area are still up 6% year over year. Nobody's underwater. Nobody's giving houses away. What has changed is the pace, and the mistake I see every week is sellers who haven't adjusted to it.

Here's the number that tells the real story: showings per listing have dropped by half. Buyers are still out there, but they're fewer, they're pickier, and they're no longer in a panic. Two years ago, a buyer who hesitated lost the house. Today, a buyer who hesitates loses nothing, because the house is still sitting there next weekend. The frenzy is gone, and with it went the seller's ability to name a number and dare someone to pay it.

I'll be blunt about what I'm seeing in my own book of business. I currently have three sellers who have been on the market for more than 60 days and are refusing to adjust their price. All three homes are nice homes. All three were priced for the market we had, not the market we have. And every week they sit, they get a little more stale, and the eventual conversation gets a little harder. I say this with genuine sympathy — I understand that a price cut feels like admitting the house is worth less than you believed. But the market doesn't care what any of us believed in March of last year.

Meanwhile — and this is the part that should give sellers real hope — the listings that are priced right are still selling in under two weeks. Not two months. Two weeks. Often with competing offers. The demand hasn't vanished; it's just gotten smarter. Buyers will still move fast for a home that's priced to its actual comps. What they won't do anymore is overpay to end a bidding war, because there is no bidding war.

So here's my actual advice, and I'll skip the usual "every situation is different" throat-clearing:

**If you're selling:** Price it right the first time. Not "leave room to negotiate." Not "we can always come down later." The first two weeks on market are when your buyers are paying attention, and an ambitious price wastes them. A well-priced home in this market still commands a fast, strong sale. An overpriced one commands 60 days of silence followed by a lowball.

**If you're buying:** This is the most breathing room you've had in years. You can sleep on a decision. You can negotiate an inspection. Use it — but don't wait for a collapse that the numbers simply don't support. Prices are still rising, just politely instead of violently.

The 8-day market was never normal. It was an anomaly, and I'd argue an unhealthy one. What we have now is a functioning market where preparation and pricing matter again. For the agents and sellers willing to work with reality instead of nostalgia, that's not bad news at all.

It's just news that requires listening.

setup: A freelance wedding photographer is writing a blog post for couples about why to book a winter wedding.

a.text:
# Why I Actually Love Shooting Winter Weddings Now

I'll be honest — for the first few years of my career, I didn't push winter dates. They weren't the most popular, and I was busy enough from May through October that I didn't need to. But in the last two years I've shot 11 winter weddings, and somewhere along the way I became a genuine convert.

If you're still deciding when to book your date, here's what I want you to know.

## You're paying about 30% less

This is just a fact. My winter package pricing runs roughly 30% below peak season, and most vendors in this area work the same way. Venues drop their minimums. Caterers are more flexible on Friday or Sunday dates. That's not because winter weddings are lesser — it's supply and demand. If your budget is tight, a January or February Saturday can feel more like a June Friday in terms of what you can afford.

## The light is actually better

People assume overcast June skies are great for photography. Soft light, no harsh shadows — sounds ideal. But flat overcast light is just that: flat. There's no direction, no depth, no warmth.

Around 3pm in November, when the sun sits low and comes through bare branches at an angle, you get directional light that's actually gorgeous for portraits. It wraps around faces. It catches in hair. It does things that a gray June sky physically cannot do because the sun is too high and the canopy is too dense. I'll take bare trees and low winter sun over flat overcast every time.

## I'm not fighting three other vendors for parking

In June, I show up to a venue and there are two other photographers, a videographer, and a limo driver all trying to load in through the same entrance. I'm sharing the getting-ready room with a makeup artist and a florist. I'm waiting for the other couple's portrait session to finish before I can use the good spot on the grounds.

In winter, I'm usually the only wedding at the venue that day. I can work at a real pace. I can take the time I want with portraits without feeling like I'm holding up someone else's timeline. It makes for a calmer day, and calmer days make for better photos.

## What you should actually consider

Winter weddings aren't right for every couple. If your vision is outdoor cocktails or a late-night exit under string lights at 9pm, that's a June wedding and you should book June. I'm not trying to talk anyone out of what they actually want.

But if you're flexible on season and you're weighing options, don't write off winter because you assume the photos will be worse or the day will feel lesser. In my experience, neither of those things is true — and your budget might thank you for it.

If you're considering a winter date, [get in touch] and I'll walk you through what's worked well at venues around the area.

b.text:
**Why I Actually Like Shooting Winter Weddings Now**

I’ve been shooting weddings around here for six years, and if you had told me at the beginning that I’d grow to genuinely love winter weddings, I probably would have laughed. I used to think the season was a compromise: too dark, too cold, too many things that could go wrong.

Then I shot 11 winter weddings in the last two years. That changed my mind.

Not because I suddenly became sentimental about cold feet and bare trees. I’m still not going to pretend every winter wedding is some cozy, fairytale event. Some couples hate the cold, some families can’t travel in icy weather, and not every venue works for a season where the sun disappears before your guests are comfortable.

But for the right couple, winter is not just a sensible backup plan. It can actually make the day better.

One obvious reason couples consider it is money. Winter bookings run about 30% cheaper for the couple than peak-season dates. That number matters if you are trying to protect budget for a venue, flowers, a photographer you love, or an actual wedding night instead of a mortgage payment.

But the pricing is not the only reason I like shooting them now.

The light is part of it.

In June, I often get that flat, overcast afternoon light that is technically “usable” but honestly kind of boring for portraits. It’s soft, sure, but it doesn’t do much. It doesn’t create shape, depth, or drama. Sometimes it makes every portrait look like it was shot on the same gray Monday.

Winter light is different.

Around 3 p.m. in November, when the sun is already low, it cuts through the bare branches in a way that feels specific to that season. It gives portraits something summer portraits often lack: contrast, warmth against cool shadow, and a real sense of place. You can stand in front of a leafless tree and suddenly the photograph has edges, texture, and mood. I’ve learned to chase that light instead of avoiding it.

Another reason winter feels better: logistics.

In June, I often show up to a venue and share the parking lot with three or four other vendors doing the same thing. That’s fine in theory, but in practice it means everyone is loading in at once, everyone is fighting for the same small space, and the whole day starts a little compressed.

Winter weddings usually breathe more. There are fewer other events on site. I have room to unload. I can walk the space. I can plan my shots without constantly stepping over someone else’s gear. For couples, that can make the day feel calmer. For me, it means I can be more present instead of spending the morning managing chaos.

That doesn’t mean winter weddings are easier. They are not.

You still need a plan for cold hands. You need a timeline that does not pretend sunset is at 8:30 p.m. You need to account for guests who may need coats, blankets, or a bar area that doesn’t turn them into ice sculptures during cocktail hour. If you are the couple who wants a bare-shoulder gown in a garden at golden hour, a winter date might fight you.

But if you are open to a day that feels a little quieter, a little sharper, and a little less crowded, winter can be a very smart choice.

I think a lot of couples make the mistake of assuming winter weddings should feel like a toned-down version of summer. They don’t. The best winter weddings are not pretending to be something they are not. They use the season. They lean into the early darkness, the bare landscape, the heavier fabrics, the candles, the low light, the intimacy of staying inside longer.

And for me as the photographer, those conditions often produce stronger images than the generic “pretty outdoor wedding” summer can deliver. There is more range. More texture. More reason for a photo to feel like it happened in that exact moment.

So if you’re deciding when to book, don’t just ask, “Can we have a wedding in winter?”

Ask if a winter wedding actually fits the day you want.

Do you care more about a specific date, a budget, a venue, or the type of light you like in photos? Are you excited about the atmosphere of a cold-weather celebration? Can you live with shorter daylight and maybe jackets over outfits during portraits? If the answer is yes, winter is not just the “cheaper” option. For a lot of couples, it is simply the better option.

I shot enough of them recently to know that for sure.

setup: A high-school senior is writing a personal essay for college admissions readers about working at her family's Vietnamese restaurant.

a.text:
I've worked every weekend at my family's restaurant since sophomore year. Saturdays I open with my dad at 10. Sundays I close with my mom. That's just how it is.

Our place is small. Eight tables, a counter, and a kitchen my parents can cross in three steps. We do pho, banh mi, spring rolls. Most of our customers are regulars. I take orders, pack takeout, wipe tables, wash dishes when the busser calls out, which is a lot.

One Saturday in March the register system died right in the middle of lunch. The screen froze and then went black. My dad kept unplugging it and plugging it back in. My mom was at the front trying to tell people it would just be a minute. The line kept getting longer.

I grabbed the pad we use for phone orders and started writing tickets by hand. Table number, what they wanted, drink. I ran them back to the kitchen and then added everything up with the calculator on my phone plus tax. My handwriting is bad when I'm rushing. My dad kept yelling, "What does this say?" I kept yelling back. We did the whole lunch like that. My hand was cramped by 2 p.m. Nobody walked out. One guy even tipped extra because he felt bad for us.

I usually make spring rolls in the back when it gets slow. My grandma taught me her fold when I was fourteen. You put down less filling than you think, fold the bottom up, tuck the sides in tight, then roll. You dab a little water at the end to seal it. If you don't roll it tight enough it falls apart when you fry it.

Last month my parents hired a new girl, Mai, who's a junior at my school. My mom told me to show her the rolls. I kept redoing hers at first because they were loose. Then I just stood next to her and did it slow so she could copy me. Tuck, roll, seal. She got it after like ten tries. Hers still look a little fat compared to my grandma's, but they hold.

On breaks I do homework in the walk-in cooler. It's the only place where it's quiet and no one will ask me for something. I bring my calc binder and sit on an upside-down milk crate. It's freezing, so I keep my hoodie back there on top of the boxes. Five minutes at a time, usually. I'll do two derivative problems, then my mom opens the door and says table six needs water, and I go back out.

Saturdays we get home around nine and my clothes smell like fry oil. I shower and finish whatever homework I didn't do in the cooler. Then Sunday we go back and do it again.

b.text:
The Saturday the register died, it was 5:40 and there were nine tables seated. My dad hit the screen a few times like that would help, then looked at me. I found a pad of guest checks in the drawer under the phone, the kind with carbon paper that nobody had used since before I was born, and started writing.

I know the menu. That's not the hard part. The hard part is that my dad in the kitchen reads tickets in a specific way—he wants the table number top left, drinks on their own line, modifications in the margin with an arrow. The printer did all that. I did it wrong for the first three tables and he sent two of them back out to me without saying anything. By the fourth I had it. Bún bò Huế, no tripe. Pho tái, extra onion. Arrow. I wrote until my hand cramped and then I wrote with my hand cramped. We did 61 tickets that night. I know because I counted them at close, stacked next to the register that still wasn't working, and my mom said we'd figure it out Monday. We got a new system in November. I still have the carbon copies in a shoebox. I don't really know why.

The spring roll thing is something my grandmother taught me when I was maybe nine, standing on a milk crate. You wet the rice paper for less time than you think—it keeps softening after you take it out—and you lay the lettuce down first so the shrimp shows through when you roll it. Tight enough that it holds, loose enough that it doesn't tear. You can't really explain the tightness. You have to feel it fail a few times.

Last spring we hired a girl named Destiny who was sixteen and had never made one. I showed her the water, the lettuce, the shrimp side down. Her first six rolls split. Her seventh didn't, and she held it up, and I realized I'd been holding my breath the same way my grandmother probably had with me. My grandmother doesn't work the line anymore. Her hands hurt. But the fold is still hers, and now it's Destiny's too, and Destiny doesn't know that or care, which is fine. The rolls are good. That's the point of the fold.

On breaks I do homework in the walk-in cooler. This started because the office has no door and the dining room is loud and the walk-in is thirty-eight degrees and completely silent. I sit on an upturned bucket between the cases of bean sprouts and the tubs of broth we make Thursday for Saturday. I did most of AP Calc in there. Related rates, chain rule, a lot of integration by parts. I'd get fifteen minutes, sometimes twenty, and the cold made me work fast. My mom would open the door and see me with my hoodie up and a pencil and say nothing, just check the dates on the broth and leave.

I got a 5 on the exam. I don't think the cooler had anything to do with that. But when I picture doing calculus, I picture the sound the compressor makes when it kicks on, and the light that's slightly green, and my breath.

I've worked every Saturday and Sunday since the fall of sophomore year. It's not a sacrifice and I don't want it read as one. It's what my family does and I'm in my family. My friends have jobs at Target and the frozen yogurt place and I have this. I know how to spot a table that's about to ask for the check. I know that the guy who comes in Sundays at noon wants his egg rolls before his pho, not with it. I know my dad's ticket format so well I could write it in the dark.

I'm applying to study accounting. My parents didn't ask me to and I'm not doing it for the restaurant, though I'll probably do the books someday because someone will have to. I just like when things add up at the end of the night. Sixty-one tickets. Seven rolls before one held. Twenty minutes in the cold, and a problem set done.

setup: A fourth-generation soybean and corn farmer is writing a newsletter commentary on crop insurance costs and SB 214 for county readers and state legislators.

a.text:
# When the Rain Won't Stop and the Bill Keeps Climbing

By late May this year, I had 60% of my acres in the ground. The other 40% sat under standing water, waiting on a break in the weather that never came before the final planting deadline passed. Any of you who farmed through this spring know exactly what that felt like — watching the calendar and the radar at the same time, doing math you didn't want to do.

What I didn't expect was to get hit twice. Once by the weather, and once by USDA.

This year, USDA raised the base rate on prevented planting premiums by 22% in our region. For my operation, that increase alone comes out to roughly $46,000 in additional cost — not for a payout, not for coverage I'm glad to have, but simply for the privilege of insuring against a risk that just became a reality on my own farm. That's $46,000 that isn't going toward equipment, inputs for next season, or the note at the bank. It's gone, and it's gone because of a rate change, not because of anything I did differently.

Here's the part that ought to concern every family operation reading this: the way the acreage caps are structured, this increase doesn't land evenly. Operations like mine — mid-sized, family-run, without the acreage base to spread the cap across — absorb a proportionally larger hit than the bigger operations down the road. Two farms can have the same percentage of prevented planting acres, and the smaller family operation pays a heavier premium burden per acre because of how the cap is written into the formula. That's not a market outcome. That's a policy design flaw.

I want to be clear about what this means in practice. A 22% base rate increase sounds like a modest technical adjustment when you read it in a USDA bulletin. It is not modest when you're the one writing the check, and it is especially not modest when the structure of the cap means family farms shoulder more of it, acre for acre, than the larger operations that have more acreage to absorb the same percentage increase.

This is exactly the problem SB 214 is written to address. The bill would fix the acreage cap calculation so that prevented planting coverage costs scale fairly regardless of operation size — closing the gap that currently penalizes smaller and mid-sized farms for the same weather risk everyone in the region is exposed to. It doesn't ask for special treatment. It asks for the cap to work the way most of us assumed it already did: proportionally, not punitively.

I'd encourage every member of this bureau to read SB 214, talk to your neighbors about it, and reach out to your state legislators before the session moves further along. Numbers like $46,000 aren't abstract to those of us who've already paid them this year. They're the difference between a hard year and an unrecoverable one. If we want family operations to still be here for a fifth and sixth generation, the policy has to reflect that math — not work against it.

b.text:
# Prevented Planting Premium: A Reminder That Family Farms Need Fair Policy

This spring, my fields stayed underwater through late May. By the time the soil dried enough to plant, I'd crossed the prevented planting deadline. I ended up getting only 60% of my usual acreage in the ground.

That's the reality of farming in our region some years. What's less inevitable is the policy that followed.

The USDA raised prevented planting insurance premiums by 22% in our area this year. For my operation, that's roughly $46,000 in additional costs annually. I'm paying more to insure against the same weather risk I've always faced.

But here's what really stings: the way the acreage cap is structured, operations like mine—family farms running four, five, maybe six thousand acres—get hit proportionally harder than the larger operations nearby. A 22% increase on capped acreage means I eat a bigger percentage loss than neighbors farming 20,000 acres or more. We're all paying more, but the formula punishes scale differently depending on where you fall.

This isn't about complaining. It's about asking our state legislators to act. Senate Bill 214 addresses exactly this problem by fixing how the acreage cap works. It's straightforward policy that would level an uneven playing field.

Family farming operations deserve insurance structures that don't inadvertently force consolidation. I'd ask everyone reading this to contact your legislators about SB 214. Tell them family farms matter—not just as nostalgia, but as the businesses they still are.

setup: A high school girls' soccer and track coach is writing an op-ed urging turf funding for the girls' field.

a.text:
# Girls' Soccer Deserves the Same Investment as Football

Our girls' soccer field floods. Again and again, we lose games to rain that wouldn't cancel anything on the boys' football field—which has had artificial turf since 2019.

Last season alone, we rescheduled or cancelled nine games because the grass turned to mud. Our athletes showed up ready to play. The field wasn't. This season we've already had two more postponements, and we're only halfway through.

But cancelled games aren't even the worst part. Last October, one of my seniors stepped into a rut in that waterlogged grass and tore her ACL. She missed the rest of her final season. A turf field wouldn't have prevented every injury, but it would have prevented that one.

Our school board installed artificial turf on the football field five years ago. I'm not arguing against that investment—football is important. But girls' soccer is important too. We have the same number of athletes. We play just as hard. We deserve a field that doesn't become a swamp every time it rains.

This isn't complicated. The boys got a modern facility. The girls are still playing on mud. When you're deciding next year's budget, I'd ask you this: Why?

Install turf on the girls' soccer field. Our athletes have waited long enough.

b.text:
**Give the girls a field they can actually play on**

Last October, one of my players tore her ACL stepping into a rut on the girls’ soccer field.

It wasn’t a bad tackle. It wasn’t one of those collisions coaches always worry about. It was the field itself. The ground was soft, the grass was torn up, and a spot that should have been routine became a season-ending injury.

That’s the part people miss when we talk about a flooded field or a beat-up lawn. It’s not just an inconvenience. It’s a safety issue.

Over the last two seasons, we’ve had nine games rained out or moved because the field floods. Nine. That means nine times our players got dressed, packed their bags, warmed up, and then found out they couldn’t play where they were supposed to. It means missed minutes, missed chances, and another schedule scramble that sends a pretty clear message: your sport can wait.

It also means we keep pretending a field that can’t hold up to normal weather is good enough for girls.

The school board will vote soon on next year’s facilities budget. That vote is a chance to fix this by funding turf for the girls’ soccer field.

This is not a luxury request. It’s a basic fairness issue.

The boys’ football field got turf in 2019. Since then, football has had a reliable surface that can take heavy use, recover quickly from rain, and give those athletes a consistent place to compete. I’m not asking for the girls to have more than the boys. I’m asking why they are still playing on a grass field that turns into mud and gets games canceled while the boys’ field has already been upgraded.

If we believe in equal opportunity, that has to show up in the budget. It can’t just be something we say at booster meetings or put on banners.

I coach for a stipend. I’m not doing this because I want a writing career or because I enjoy sending emails to parents about another schedule change. I’m doing this because these kids show up. They run track, they lift, they do the work, they ride the buses, and they represent our school. They deserve a field that lets them play safely.

Turf would reduce cancellations. It would give our teams a surface they can actually use after rain instead of waiting days for a field to dry out. It would lower the risk of injuries caused by ruts, bare patches, and unstable ground. And it would tell our female athletes that their season matters just as much as anyone else’s.

We can keep pretending this is just about grass. But it isn’t. It’s about what we decide is acceptable.

A field that floods repeatedly is not acceptable. A field that injures players is not acceptable. And a district that upgraded one field years ago while leaving the girls’ field behind should know better now.

To the school board: put the turf in the budget. Give the girls a field they can play on.

setup: A long-haul trucker is writing a short Roadstar DC4 dual dash cam review for other owner-operators on a trucking forum.

a.text:
Hey drivers, giving a quick 14-month, 140,000-mile update on the Roadstar DC4 dash cam I’ve been running in my rig. 

Bottom line up front: it pays for itself. I had a four-wheeler clip me on a bad lane change a while back and the DC4 caught the whole thing dead to rights. I sent the video to my insurance and had the claim approved in 9 days flat instead of the usual 6-week runaround. It's worth the price of admission right there.

That said, it’s not perfect. A few things to watch out for if you buy one:

First, the rear camera night footage gets pretty grainy once you look past 30 feet. You can still see what's happening, but don't expect perfect clarity in the dark. 

Second, ditch the suction cup mount right out of the box. Mine gave out and dropped the camera twice pulling through summer heat. I swapped to the adhesive mount and it hasn't budged since.

Finally, the companion app is basically useless. It needs a Wi-Fi connection to download footage to your phone. We all know how dead truck stop Wi-Fi is, so trying to pull a clip over the air is a massive headache. Save your time, skip the app entirely, and just pop the SD card straight into your laptop when you need to pull a video.

Overall? It does its main job: protecting your CDL and your wallet. Solid piece of kit for the money. Stay safe out there.

b.text:
**Roadstar DC4 Dash Cam – 14-Month / 140k-Mile Review**

Put about 140,000 miles on the Roadstar DC4 over the last 14 months running cross-country. Figured I’d drop a quick write-up for anyone looking to upgrade their cab setup.

**The Good:**
It already paid for itself. Had a four-wheeler try to slide into my lane and clip my steer tire, then tried telling the trooper I ran him off the road. Handed the footage over, and my insurance claim was fully approved in 9 days instead of the usual 6-week headache. Front video quality is sharp day and night, license plates show up clear, and the unit hasn't frozen up once despite constant cab vibration.

**The Bad:**
* **The Mount:** Toss the suction cup straight into the trash. It dropped off my windshield twice during the heat of July. Swapped to the included 3M adhesive mount and haven't had an issue since.
* **Rear Cam:** Fine during the day, but night footage gets real grainy past about 30 feet. It’ll prove positioning if somebody rear-ends you, but don't expect to read a plate number at distance in the dark.
* **The App:** Total waste of time. It requires a solid Wi-Fi connection to pull footage to your phone, which is useless when you’re parked in the back row of a packed truck stop with zero signal. Save yourself the blood pressure spike and just keep a cheap USB-C/Lightning SD card reader in your glovebox. Pull the card, plug it into your phone or tablet, done.

**Bottom Line:**
It’s got quirks, but it turns on every time I key the ignition, survives rough roads, and kept an at-fault accident off my record. Good enough for me. Worth a look if you need reliable coverage without spending four figures.

setup: A general contractor is writing a short X thread to contractors, homeowners, and architects about a hidden joist problem and the lesson learned.

a.text:
1/ Maple Ave kitchen, day 2 of demo. Pulled the soffit over the old cabinets and found two 2x10 joists notched deep into the bottom edge — old drain run from sometime in the 80s. One had maybe 4 inches of wood left doing the work of 9-1/4. Dead center over where the new island goes.

2/ Didn't touch it until the engineer looked. Letter, permit amendment, then sistered both full span with new 2x10s, solid bearing each end. $2,900 all in and four days lost — three of those waiting on paperwork, not carpentry.

3/ The part that gets glossed over: those joists hadn't sagged in 40 years. The old kitchen got lucky. New plan puts a loaded stone island right over that bay. If that soffit hadn't come down, nobody finds this until it's a much bigger conversation.

4/ The lesson: you don't pay for what you can see. You pay for what the last guy hid and left for whoever opened it next. Every old kitchen is holding something back. Contractors: keep concealed-conditions language in the contract and mean it. Homeowners: a bid that accounts for it isn't padding. It's experience.

b.text:
1/ Opened the kitchen ceiling on the Maple Ave job Tuesday. Previous remodel — not ours, looked mid-2000s — ran a 3" drain line through the middle of three 2x10 joists. Not drilled. Notched from the bottom, about 4" deep, then "fixed" with a scrap of plywood screwed to one side.

2/ That's basically a hinge. Bottom of a joist is where the tension is. Floor above had a soft spot the homeowner mentioned in passing and figured was just old house stuff.

3/ Fix was flitch plates on the three joists, new steel to carry the run, and rerouting the drain into the bay where it belonged. $4,800 and eight days added to the schedule. Engineer's letter was another $650. Homeowner covered it, but nobody enjoys that conversation.

4/ Real lesson isn't "don't notch joists," everybody knows that. It's that I priced this kitchen off a walkthrough and a basement look. I didn't cut an inspection hole in the ceiling because the finish was clean and I didn't want to open something I'd have to patch. Two hundred bucks of exploratory demo would've put this in the original number instead of a change order. I open ceilings now on anything pre-1990 with a bath above.

setup: A high school girls' soccer and track coach is writing an op-ed urging turf funding for the girls' field.

a.text:
Last October, one of my players stepped in a hidden rut on our grass soccer field and tore her ACL. Her season was over in a second, and she spent her junior year in physical therapy instead of on the field. That injury didn't happen because of a bad tackle or a lack of conditioning. It happened because our school’s field is a safety hazard. 

I don't coach soccer and track to write opinion pieces for the newspaper. I coach because I care about these kids, and right now, our school district is failing them. 

Over the last two seasons, we have had nine games either rained out or moved to opponent's schools because our grass field floods at the first sign of rain. Nine games. That means parents driving an hour away on short notice on a Tuesday night because our "home" field is a swamp. It means our athletes losing their home-field advantage and playing on patched-together schedules. We spend more time checking weather radar and moving goals to avoid mud pits than we do actually practicing. 

This is not a matter of the district lacking the funds to fix the problem; it is a matter of where those funds are being directed. In 2019, the school board approved and installed a brand-new turf field for the boys’ football team. I am glad they did. Those athletes deserve a safe, high-quality place to play. But so do our girls. 

Right now, we have a clear double standard. The boys play and practice on a pristine, all-weather surface, while the girls are left navigating ankle-breaking divots and standing water. It is a matter of basic fairness. 

Next week, the school board will vote on the facilities budget for the coming year. Funding turf for the girls' soccer field needs to be approved. This isn't a luxury request or a wishlist item. It is a safety issue, a scheduling issue, and an equity issue. 

The board has a chance to correct this imbalance next week. Let’s give these girls the same respect, and the same safe playing surface, that we gave the boys five years ago. Approve the turf.

b.text:
Nine games in two years. That’s how many times my girls’ soccer team has had a game rained out, postponed, or moved to an away field because ours turned into a swamp. This isn’t a minor inconvenience—it’s a pattern. And last October, it cost us more than a schedule shuffle. One of my starting defenders planted her foot in a deep rut that had been hidden by standing water the day before, heard a pop, and tore her ACL. That surgery, that recovery, that lost season—it all traces back to a grass field that can’t handle a hard rain.

I’m not a writer. I’m a coach. I do this for a small stipend because I care about the kids. So I’ll say it plainly: Our girls’ soccer field is dangerous and unfair. The boys’ football field got turf back in 2019. It drains perfectly, plays fast, and doesn’t chew up ankles when the weather turns. Meanwhile, my team dodges puddles and ankle-breakers every spring. We’ve had girls slide into a tackle and come up with mud in their mouths because the ground can’t take another step. We’ve had goal kicks that stop dead in a pool. The conditions are messing with our development—and our safety.

The numbers don’t lie. Over the past two seasons, nine games lost or relocated because of flooding. That’s nine fewer chances for these athletes to compete, to be scouted, to learn how to win and lose on their home soil. The football team hasn’t missed a single home game due to field conditions since their turf went in. They get a reliable, consistent surface. We get a lottery.

I’ve heard the argument: Grass is softer, cheaper to maintain. But our grass isn’t soft in October—it’s sodden and rutted. And the “cheaper” math ignores the cost of rescheduling buses, officials, and staff when we lose a home game. It ignores the cost of a knee surgery and months of PT. It ignores the simple message we send when we pour money into the boys’ Friday night lights while the girls’ soccer team is an afterthought.

The school board votes next month on the facilities budget. I’m asking them—and this community—to look at the facts, not the gender of the athletes who use the field. Turf for the girls’ soccer field isn’t a luxury. It’s a safety fix, an equity fix, and a long-overdue investment. We don’t need a new grandstand or a fancy press box. We need a surface that doesn’t flood, doesn’t rut, and doesn’t send my players to the emergency room.

One field. Two years. Nine lost games and one torn ACL. That should be enough. Fix the field. Fund the turf. It’s that simple.
