setup: A high-school senior is writing a personal essay for college admissions readers about working at her family's Vietnamese restaurant.

a.text:
The Square register froze at 5:15 PM on a Saturday in November. That is exactly when the dinner rush starts. My dad hit the screen a few times, unplugged it, and looked at me. I didn't say anything, just grabbed a stack of green paper order pads and a handful of pens from the back office.

For the next three hours, I hand-wrote every ticket. You have to write fast when the line is out the door, which means my handwriting turned into a messy scrawl. I had to memorize the table numbers and run the physical slips back to the kitchen window, shouting modifications over the exhaust fans. Table four, no cilantro on the pho. Table nine, extra peanut sauce. By 8:00 PM, my right hand was cramping and my fingers were stained with ink and grease, but the tickets kept moving and the kitchen didn't stall.

When the rush finally broke around 9:00, I took my break. The only quiet place in the restaurant is the walk-in cooler. I put on my heavy gray hoodie, sat on an overturned milk crate next to the bulk rice bags, and pulled out my AP Calculus worksheet. The cooler smells like raw pork, star anise, and damp cardboard. The compressor fan is loud, but it drowns out the clatter of plates and the Vietnamese pop music my mom plays in the dining room. I worked through optimization problems while my breath fogged in the cold, stopping every few minutes to rub my hands together so my pen wouldn't slip.

On Sunday afternoons, before we open, I usually help with prep. Last month, we hired a new line cook named David. My mom asked me to show him how to make the fresh spring rolls. It sounds easy, but my grandma has a very specific way of folding them that we still use. I stood next to him at the stainless steel prep table and demonstrated. You lay the rice paper flat, put the vermicelli and shrimp in the lower third, and fold the bottom up tight. Then you fold in the left and right sides before rolling the rest of the way. If you don't fold the sides in first, the ends stay open and the filling falls out when you dip it. David’s first few rolls looked like swollen cigars. I unrolled them and showed him how to keep the tension even. By his twentieth roll, he had the muscle memory down.

I work every Friday night, Saturday, and Sunday. I usually smell like fryer oil and fish sauce when I get home, and I have to wash my hair twice before Monday morning. It’s just the schedule. I know how to run the floor, how to prep the line, and how to study in a 35-degree room. Next weekend, I’ll be back at the host stand, waiting for the doors to open.

b.text:
My weekends have been the same since tenth grade. I work at my family's restaurant. It's called Pho An, it's on Main Street, and it has twelve tables. 

My mom works the front, my dad works the wok in the back, and my grandma comes in the mornings to make cha gio. I started out just bussing tables and running food. Now I do whatever needs doing.

There was a Saturday in October when the register died right in the middle of dinner rush. We use Toast and the screen just froze. My dad tapped it a few times and then unplugged it and plugged it back in and it was still frozen. My mom was on hold with support. The dining room was full and people were lining up to order takeout.

We have these little white paper pads we use for phone orders. I grabbed a stack of them. My mom said to just write everything down. So I did. I wrote the table number and every item and if they wanted no cilantro or extra chili oil. My handwriting is messy when I hurry. I had to shout the tickets to the kitchen because my dad couldn't see my writing from far away. "Two number 14 extra noodles! One tofu no fish sauce!" At the end I had to add up every check by hand and count change from the cash drawer. I gave one lady ten dollars too much and had to run outside to catch her in the parking lot. We figured it out. We didn't lose any orders.

During the week I have AP calc fourth period. Usually on weekends I bring the homework with me because I have a break between lunch and dinner. There isn't anywhere quiet to sit. The dining room has music and customers and my mom asking me to refill waters. So I sit in the walk-in cooler. Not for long, maybe ten minutes. I sit on the upside-down milk crate next to the tubs of pickled carrots. It's freezing and smells like cilantro and raw beef. My hands are dry from washing dishes and the paper gets a little damp. I'm doing derivatives and my breath makes a little cloud. Someone always opens the door to get more noodles and says, "Are you doing homework in here again?" My mom knocks if my break is too long.

Last month we hired a new girl, Elena, from my school. She had never rolled a spring roll before. My grandma tried to show her but she doesn't really explain in English, she just does it and expects you to watch. My grandma's way is specific. You lay the wrapper down, you put the pork and shrimp and noodles not too high up, you fold the bottom up, you tuck both sides in tight, then you roll it tight tight and seal the edge with water. If you don't tuck it tight it falls apart in the fryer.

Elena kept rolling them loose or with too much filling. They were fat and kept bursting open. I showed her next to my grandma, the way my grandma showed me. I did it slow and then she copied me. Her third one was better. My grandma stood behind us and nodded and fixed one of mine that wasn't perfect. She always fixes mine too. Elena is good at it now. She can do a tray by herself when we're busy.

On Sunday nights after we close, my dad turns the big sign off and we count the tips at a table in the back. My hair smells like oil. My mom gives me a container of rice and leftover chicken and I do the rest of my calc homework at the kitchen table when I get home.

setup: A real estate agent is posting one specific observation about early block walks and happier buyers to LinkedIn buyers, agents, and lenders.

a.text:
After twelve years of selling real estate in Asheville, mostly to first-time buyers, I’ve developed a handful of quiet rules. My favorite one to share is simple: if you’re serious about putting in an offer, walk the street at 7:00 on a weekday morning first.

Everyone falls in love with a house on a sunny Saturday afternoon. The light hits the hardwoods, the neighborhood feels peaceful, and nobody is rushing anywhere. But you don’t live your life in Saturday afternoons. You live it on Tuesday mornings.

A few years back, I was working with the Pruitts on a 1940s cottage off Sycamore Street. On paper, it checked every box. Beautiful screened porch, fenced yard for their dog, and an easy drive into town. During our second walkthrough on a Friday afternoon, they were ready to write an offer right there on the kitchen counter. 

I asked them to hold off and meet me at the corner of Sycamore at 7:15 the following Tuesday with travel mugs of coffee. 

When you walk a neighborhood while it’s waking up, the real personality comes out. On Sycamore, it wasn't bad news, but it was real clarity. We discovered that the street was a quiet cut-through for commuters dodging the traffic light two blocks over, meaning backing out of that blind driveway was going to require patience every single day. We also realized the ridge to the east blocked the early morning sun, so the frost lingered on the front steps long after the rest of the block thawed. 

At the same time, we ran into an older neighbor walking her beagle who stopped to introduce herself, pointed out which neighbor was the carpenter who helped everyone with storm damage, and told us the school bus stopped right at the corner. 

The Pruitts still wrote the offer, and they still bought the house. But they bought it without any illusions. They knew to re-gravel the parking pad so they could turn their cars around instead of backing into traffic, and they knew what their commute would actually look like before they unpacked a single box. 

They are still there, and whenever I run into them at the grocery store, they always mention that morning walk. 

Inspection reports can tell you if the roof has five years left, but they can't tell you how a street feels when the alarm goes off. If you’re touring homes right now, set your alarm early and walk the block. It prevents a lot of surprises.

b.text:
I've been selling houses in Asheville for 12 years, mostly to first-time buyers. One thing I keep noticing: the ones who walk the neighborhood at 7am before we even go inside tend to end up a lot happier with the house later.

The Pruitts on Sycamore Street are the ones I think about.

They liked the house but kept circling back to the street. The listing photos made it look busier than they wanted. I told them to go walk it at 7 the next morning, before our showing.

They showed up already smiling. Said it was quiet except for birds and a few people walking dogs. You could smell coffee from the place around the corner. They wrote the offer that afternoon.

They still send me pictures of their porch at sunrise. It's not complicated. You just get a better sense of what living there actually feels like.

b.text:
I made a massive pricing mistake with Tallyup.

I raised our prices by 40% on everyone overnight.

In just one week, I lost 30 of our 140 customers.

Here is what went wrong, why it blew up, and what I changed: 🧵

1/ The background:

Every advice thread for indie SaaS founders says the same thing: "Charge more."

As a solo founder building Tallyup (a retention tool for gym owners), I knew the value was there. So I decided it was time to adjust our pricing up by 40%.

2/ The mistake wasn't the price increase itself—it was how I rolled it out.

- I applied the 40% hike to existing users overnight.
- I gave zero advance notice.
- I didn't grandfather the early users who supported the product from day one.

3/ The fallout was fast.

In 7 days, 30 out of our 140 customers canceled. 

In a close-knit niche like gym owners, trust matters. Forcing a sudden 40% jump on existing users broke that trust, and the cancellations poured in.

4/ What I changed to fix it:

- Reverted the price hike for all impacted existing users and reached out directly to explain.
- Grandfathered existing accounts at their original rate.
- Applied the new 40% higher pricing ONLY to new sign-ups moving forward.

5/ Lessons learned the hard way:

- Protect your early supporters. Grandfather existing users when making big leaps.
- Test new pricing on new traffic, not your existing base.
- If you ever do change rates for current customers, give plenty of advance notice and clear reasoning.

Building in public means sharing the bad decisions alongside the wins. Hopefully, this saves another solo founder from making the same mistake.

2/ The reasoning at the time felt solid. MRR was flat, I figured the product was underpriced, and I'd read enough "raise your prices" posts to think I was leaving money on the table. I was solving my boredom, not a real customer problem.

3/ What I missed: my customers are gym owners running small facilities. They don't have procurement budgets. A 40% jump in a line item they'd been paying for a year feels like a billing error before it feels like a value conversation. Most of the 30 who left didn't even email. Just canceled.

4/ First thing I changed: rolled back pricing for anyone who stayed. Sent a personal email, no template, explaining the jump was a mistake and their old price was locked in for 12 months. Kept 22 of the remaining 110 that way. The other 8 churned within the month anyway.

5/ Second change: any future price increase is on new customers only, for at least 6 months before existing customers see it. And existing customers get 30 days notice with a real explanation, not a Stripe receipt. Announcements > assumptions.

6/ Third change: I started charging new signups the new price and tracking conversion rate weekly instead of just MRR. Conversion dropped ~15% the first month, which told me the new price was probably 10-15% too high, not 40%. I'd been anchoring to the wrong number.

7/ What I'd tell other solo founders: your existing customers are your cheapest source of validated pricing. If you raise on them and a chunk leave instantly, the market just told you something your spreadsheet didn't. Listen to it before you keep raising.

8/ Tallyup today: ~115 customers, MRR is higher than it was at 140 because new signups come in at the new price, but the lesson wasn't "raise prices." It was "raise prices the way your customers can actually absorb them." Wild concept, I know.

(end 🧵)

b.text:
1/ I made a pricing mistake at Tallyup.

I raised prices 40% on everyone overnight.

Within a week, we lost 30 of our 140 customers.

Here’s what happened, and what I changed:

2/ The mistake wasn’t just the increase.

It was the surprise.

Customers had signed up under one expectation, then woke up to a different one.

No warning. No transition. No chance to ask questions.

3/ When you raise prices on existing customers without context, it can feel like a broken promise.

Especially with gym owners. Retention is personal to them, and Tallyup is supposed to help with that.

4/ What I changed:

- No more overnight pricing decisions
- Separate new customers from existing customers
- Give advance notice
- Explain the reason before the change
- Make it easy for customers to reach out and talk

5/ The lesson: pricing is not just a spreadsheet decision.

It’s trust, timing, and communication.

A price change can be reasonable and still be delivered badly.

6/ I’m building Tallyup in public, and this is part of it.

I’d rather share the mistake than pretend we got everything right.

If you’re thinking about raising prices, don’t surprise the people who already believed in you.

setup: A small HVAC company owner is writing a how-to for homeowners on bleeding air from hot water baseboard radiators before winter.

a.text:
If one end of your baseboard is hot and the other is cold, you have air trapped in the line. Bleeding the system is a straightforward weekend fix, but it has to be done right to actually clear the loops. 

Here is the step-by-step process we use in the field:

**1. Shut off the boiler and circulator pump**
Before you touch a single valve, kill the power to the boiler so the circulator pump stops running. You do not want the pump kicking on while you have a valve open, and you want to avoid getting sprayed with scalding water. Give the system a few minutes to settle down.

**2. Locate the bleeder valve**
Pop the end cover off your baseboard unit and look down at the pipe. You are looking for a small brass or galvanized valve with a slot or hex head on top. It will usually be at the opposite end from where the pipe enters the baseboard. 

**3. Grab a cup and position it**
Hold a small cup or bowl directly underneath the bleeder valve. A little water always dribbles out before the air starts, and you want to keep it off your hardwood or carpet.

**4. Open the valve slowly**
Use a baseboard bleeder key or a small flathead screwdriver to turn the valve counterclockwise. Open it slowly. You will hear a distinct hissing sound—that is the trapped air escaping. 

**5. Wait for a steady stream of water**
Keep the valve open until the hissing completely stops and you get a solid, steady stream of water without any sputtering or air spitting. Once the water is flowing smoothly, the air is out of that unit. 

**6. Close it snug, but don't crank on it**
Turn the valve clockwise to close it. Tighten it until it is snug, but do not overtighten it. If you crank down on it with a screwdriver, you will crack the internal valve seat. A cracked seat means a slow, continuous leak that will rust out your baseboard and require a service call to replace.

**7. Work unit by unit, closest to the boiler first**
Move to the next baseboard and repeat the process. Always start with the unit physically closest to the boiler and work your way out to the farthest one. This pushes the air through the system in the right direction.

**Don't skip the basement loop**
The mistake that causes most of our cold radiator service calls is people bleeding all the upstairs units and completely skipping the basement loop. Nine times out of ten, the air is actually trapped down in the basement. If you only bleed the upper floors, the air will just keep migrating back up into the system. Always bleed the lowest level in the house first, then work your way up. 

If you've bled every baseboard in the house—including the basement—and you are still getting cold spots, you likely have a larger system pressure issue or a failing circulator pump. Give us a call and we'll get your heat back up and running.

b.text:
If your baseboards are cold, you likely have air trapped in the lines blocking the hot water from circulating. You can fix this yourself in about fifteen minutes with a cup and a flathead screwdriver or radiator key. 

**1. Shut off the boiler and circulator.** Don't try to do this while the system is running. Shut the power off at the emergency switch so the water settles and the pump isn't pushing more air through the lines.

**2. Start at the unit closest to the boiler.** You need to go unit by unit, starting at the boiler and working your way out to the end of the line. The mistake that causes most of our "cold radiator" service calls is when people only bleed the upstairs bedrooms and entirely skip the basement loop. Don't skip the basement—that is usually where the air actually is.

**3. Find the bleeder valve.** Pull the cover off the end of your baseboard unit. You'll see a small brass valve on the pipe with a slotted screw head or a square fitting for a radiator key. 

**4. Open the valve slowly.** Hold your cup right underneath the valve. Turn the screw or key counter-clockwise just a little bit until you hear air hissing out. 

**5. Wait for a steady stream of water.** Let it hiss and spit until the air is gone. Once the water flows out into your cup in a solid, steady stream with no sputtering or hissing, the air is cleared from that unit.

**6. Close it snug, but don't overtighten.** Turn the valve clockwise until the water stops. Make it tight enough to seal, but do not crank down on it hard. If you overtighten it, you will crack the valve seat and you'll be calling me to come out and solder in a replacement.

Work your way through every baseboard in the house. Once you're done, flip the boiler back on and let it run. The heat should distribute evenly now, but if you still have dead spots after bleeding the entire system, you might be dealing with a stuck zone valve or a failing circulator pump. Give us a call and we'll come get it sorted out.

setup: A family plumbing company owner is writing a blog post for Minneapolis homeowners about winterizing outdoor pipes.

a.text:
# How to Winterize Your Outside Spigots in Minneapolis

If your outside spigots are not winterized, a hard freeze can crack the pipe inside your wall and cause a mess that is much more expensive than a few minutes of prevention.

Here is the simple process we recommend to Minneapolis homeowners.

## 1. Disconnect all hoses

This is the big one. Leaving a garden hose connected to your outside spigot is one of the most common causes of winter plumbing emergencies we see in January.

Even if you have a “frost-free” spigot, the hose still needs to come off. A connected hose traps water in the spigot and pipe, which can freeze, expand, and burst.

Remove all hoses, drain them, and store them where they will not crack or be tripped over in the garage or shed.

## 2. Shut off the interior valve

Most outside spigots have a shutoff valve inside the house. It is usually in the basement, crawlspace, utility room, or mechanical room near where the pipe goes outside.

Turn the valve clockwise until it stops. If it is a lever-style valve, turn it so it is perpendicular to the pipe.

If you cannot find the shutoff, or if your home does not have one, call us. We can help you locate it, add one, or advise on the best fix before freezing weather hits.

## 3. Drain the outside spigot

After the interior valve is closed, go back outside and open the spigot. Let it run until it stops. Leave the spigot open for the winter.

This gives any remaining water a place to expand if it freezes, instead of putting pressure on the pipe.

If the spigot has a drain cap or bleeder cap near the interior shutoff, open that too to help drain the line.

## 4. Add a $3 foam spigot cover

Once the spigot is off and drained, put a foam outdoor faucet cover over it. They are cheap, easy to install, and worth every penny.

Just slip it over the spigot and secure it. If it is damaged, replace it. A cracked cover is better than nothing, but a snug one works best.

## The mistake we see the most

The most common mistake is simply leaving the hose connected.

A lot of homeowners assume the spigot will be fine because it is outside, or because it worked all summer. But once temperatures drop, trapped water can freeze inside the pipe. When that happens, the pipe can split behind the wall, under the floor, or in the rim joist.

That is where many of our January burst-pipe calls come from.

## When to call us

Call us if:

- You do not have an interior shutoff for your outside spigot
- You cannot find the shutoff valve
- The valve is stuck, leaking, or hard to turn
- The outside spigot drips after you shut it off
- You want a freeze-proof outdoor faucet installed
- You already suspect a pipe froze or burst

For Minneapolis homeowners, the best time to winterize outside spigots is before the first real hard freeze. It only takes a few minutes, and it can save you from a costly repair later.

b.text:
How to Winterize Your Outside Spigots in Minneapolis

Find the shutoff valve inside the house. It’s usually in the basement or crawlspace on the pipe that feeds that outdoor faucet. Turn it off.

Go outside, open the spigot, and let it drain completely. Leave it open.

Disconnect every hose. This is the one that matters. A connected hose traps water in the pipe. That water freezes, the pipe splits, and you have a flood. Most of the burst-pipe calls we get in January started with a hose somebody forgot.

Slap a $3 foam faucet cover over the spigot. Done.

If you cannot find an interior shutoff, or you’re not sure which valve it is, call us. We’ll shut it down and drain it the right way so you don’t find out the hard way in January.

setup: A remote software engineer is writing a 6-month standing desk review for blog readers researching standing desks.

a.text:
**6-Month Review: The Jarvik L2 Standing Desk**

I bought the Jarvik L2 in February - 60x30, laminate top, black frame - with my own money. No affiliate links here, nothing to sell you.

I'm a remote software engineer. This desk gets 9-10 hours a day, 5 days a week, dual 27" monitors on an arm, MacBook, heavy mechanical keyboard.

After 6 months of actual use:

**The motor is legitimately good.**

It's fast and quiet. Jarvik claims 1.4"/sec and that's about right - it goes from my sitting height (28.5") to standing (44.5") in ~11 seconds. And it's quiet enough that I can adjust it mid-Zoom call without muting. My old Flexispot sounded like a forklift. This one is just a low hum.

**It wobbles at full height.**

I'm 5'10" and I stand at 44.5 inches. At that height, if I'm really hammering on the keyboard or leaning to grab something, there is noticeable side-to-side wobble. The monitor shake is visible. At sitting height it's rock solid. At 40" it's fine. At full max height (47") it's borderline unusable for me if I'm typing hard. If you're over 6' and plan to stand tall all day, this is not the frame you want.

**The memory presets drift.**

I have preset 1 at 72cm and preset 2 at 113cm. After 2-3 weeks, preset 1 will stop at 71cm or 73cm. It's consistently off by about a centimeter. Not the end of the world, but annoying when you expect it to hit your exact ergonomic position every time. I've had to recalibrate it twice in 6 months by holding down+up until it resets.

**The cable tray is garbage.**

Throw it away. It's thin, stamped metal, too shallow to hold a power strip plus cables, and the included wood screws stripped out of the pre-drilled holes on day one. I replaced it with a $35 under-desk tray from Amazon that holds everything. For a company selling a $700+ desk, this tray is insulting.

**Verdict:**

At the $549 sale price I paid, it's a good desk. The motor alone makes it better than anything else in that price range.

At $749 full price? Absolutely not. For that money, buy a Uplift V2 or Fully Jarvis frame and get a more stable frame and presets that actually stay put.

If you can get it on sale and you're under 6 feet and don't mind fixing the cable management yourself, it's worth it. If you see it at $749, close the tab.

b.text:
# Jarvis L2 Standing Desk: My 6-Month Review

I’ve used the Jarvik L2 as my primary work desk for six months, working remotely as a software engineer. It has gone through daily height changes, long typing sessions, video calls, and the general abuse of a desk that is actually used—not just photographed in a minimalist office.

My verdict is straightforward: **buy it at the $549 sale price. Do not buy it at $749.** At the lower price, it’s a good, practical standing desk with a quiet and fast motor. At the regular price, the wobble and terrible cable tray are harder to excuse.

## The motor is the best part

The Jarvik L2’s motor has been consistently quiet and quick. Height adjustments don’t interrupt calls, and I can move from sitting to standing without waiting around or listening to a loud mechanical whine.

After six months, the motor still sounds and feels the same as it did when I installed the desk. There’s no grinding, hesitation, or noticeable slowdown. For a desk I adjust multiple times a day, that reliability matters more to me than having a long list of extra features.

## It wobbles at full height

The desk is stable enough at sitting height and at moderate standing heights. The problem appears when I raise it near its maximum height.

If I type aggressively—especially during a fast coding session—the monitor and desk surface wobble. It isn’t unusable, but it is noticeable and irritating. Light typing is fine. Resting my forearms on the desk is fine. Hard, rapid typing makes the desk move.

This is not a dealbreaker for me because I don’t spend the entire day at maximum height. However, if you’re tall, plan to keep the desk fully raised, or are particularly sensitive to monitor movement, you should take this seriously. The L2 is not rock-solid at full height.

## The memory presets drift

The memory presets are convenient, but they aren’t perfectly consistent. After six months, the saved positions can drift by roughly a centimeter.

That’s enough to notice if you’re trying to switch between a carefully tuned sitting height and standing height. I don’t have to recalibrate constantly, but I do occasionally find myself adjusting the desk manually after using a preset.

A one-centimeter difference isn’t catastrophic, but it undermines the point of having presets. I expected better repeatability.

## The cable tray is garbage

The included cable tray is the weakest part of the desk.

It doesn’t provide a clean or flexible way to manage cables, and it feels like an afterthought rather than a properly designed component. Once you add a monitor, laptop charger, peripherals, and a power strip, the tray becomes difficult to use effectively. Cables still hang awkwardly or require your own clips and ties to keep organized.

I ended up treating the tray as optional and using separate cable-management hardware. If clean cable routing matters to you, budget for a replacement or plan to improvise. I would not choose this desk because of its cable-management setup.

## Six-month durability

So far, the frame and lifting mechanism have held up well. There are no obvious signs of mechanical degradation, and the motor remains as quiet and fast as it was on day one.

The desk’s shortcomings are mostly design and stability issues rather than failures. It works every day, but it is not as polished as the price suggests when sold for $749.

## Final verdict

**At $549: worth buying.** The Jarvik L2 gives me a quiet, fast motor and a generally good sit-stand experience. The wobble at full height is manageable, the preset drift is annoying but minor, and the cable tray can be replaced or ignored.

**At $749: not worth it.** At that price, I expect better stability at maximum height, more accurate memory presets, and a cable tray that does its job. The L2 is a solid midrange desk, not a premium one.

If you can get it for **$549 or around that price**, I’d recommend it. If the price is **$749**, I’d keep shopping.

setup: A retired Army staff sergeant is writing about coming home after his second deployment for readers of the veterans' writing workshop anthology.

a.text:
# Coming Home

The cereal aisle got me before anything else did. I'd been stateside maybe three days. My wife sent me to the store for a few things, normal errands, and I stood in front of the cereal for twenty minutes. I'm not exaggerating. I looked at my phone to check the time when I got there and I looked again when a stock kid asked me if I needed help finding something.

Forty kinds of cereal. Maybe more. When I left there had been a lot too, I guess, but I never noticed. A year of eating whatever was in the bag or the tray, no choices at all, and now there were forty boxes and they all needed a decision from me. Honey Bunches or Raisin Bran or the one with the tiger or the one with the stupid leprechaun. I understood the words on the boxes. I understood what cereal was. I could not pick one. The kid with the apron was waiting for an answer and I said I was fine, just looking, and he went back to his carton and I stood there some more until I grabbed the blue box my wife always bought because it wasn't a decision if I already knew the answer.

The airport was two weeks before that. That's the order things actually happened, but the cereal is where my head went first, so that's where I started.

I came through the arrivals gate at Fort Carson and the whole families-waiting thing was happening, the signs and the flags and the kids on shoulders, and my wife was there with my daughter off to the side a little because she's smart enough to stay out of the crush. Maya was six. I'd been gone just over a year, and six-year-olds change in a year. I'd seen her on video calls the whole time, but the camera flattens you, makes you smaller and quieter than you are.

She knew who I was supposed to be. That's the part that mattered. She just didn't know me on sight anymore. I came around a family reunion-ing some specialist and she saw me and stopped walking and put her hand on her mom's leg and stepped halfway behind her and looked up at my wife's face to check whether this large man was safe. My wife said, "Maya, it's Daddy," and Maya kept looking at me like she was running the math and not quite finishing it. I got down on one knee, which is what I'd have done anyway because you get down to talk to a six-year-old, and I said, "Hey, bug," which was what I'd called her since she was two, and that did it. The voice. The word. She came the rest of the way around her mother's leg and hit me hard enough that I had to put a hand down on the floor.

I don't hold it against her. Why would I. She was six and I was a guy on a screen for a year. But I've thought about that half-second where she checked her mother's face more times than I've thought about most things that happened over there.

The door was the slow one. After the airport, after the cereal, that was what took the longest.

Over there you sleep facing the door. Nobody has to teach you this. You just start doing it. You sleep on the side of the bed closest to the door, or if there's no bed you position yourself so the door is in your line of sight, and you sleep light, and you sleep in pieces. My roommate and I had our bunks arranged so we were both angled at the door, and we never once discussed it.

So I came home and my wife sleeps with the door open. Always has. She says a closed door makes her feel like she's suffocating. Fine by me, before. When I got back, we left the door open like always and I could not make it work. I'd lie there staring down the hallway the open door created, every sound in the house sorted and cataloged, every settling of the house read as approaching footsteps. I'd wake up at three, four, five. I'd hear Maya get up to pee and track her the whole way there and back by ear.

I didn't want to make my wife sleep behind a shut door over my stuff, so for a while I just did the thing where you sleep badly and call it fine. She caught on, because wives catch on. She started leaving it open just a crack and we called that a compromise. It took months. What actually worked was this: one night Maya had a bad dream and came padding in at two in the morning, and I was awake anyway, and she climbed in between us, and at some point I realized I'd fallen asleep facing away from the door because I was facing her. I woke up at six with her foot in my kidney and the door wide open and the hallway just a hallway.

It's not that it stopped. I still sleep lighter than I did before. I still know where the door is. But most nights now I face the middle of the bed, which is to say I face my wife, which is to say I face the opposite of the door, and that's about all the sense I've managed to make of any of it.

The cereal, for the record, is still the blue box. Some decisions you only have to survive once.

b.text:
I stepped off the plane at Fort Benning with my duffel over one shoulder and the smell of jet fuel still in my nose. The terminal was loud in a way the desert never was. Kids running. Somebody’s grandpa in a veterans cap shaking hands. Balloons. I scanned the crowd and found my wife, Lisa, standing near the escalator with our daughter half-hidden behind her leg. Kayla was six. I’d left when she was five. She stared at me like I was a stranger who’d walked through the wrong door. I knelt down, said her name, and she pushed her face into Lisa’s jeans. Lisa touched her hair, coaxed her forward, but Kayla wouldn’t budge. I remember thinking, well, this is how it starts.

The drive home felt like somebody else’s life. Strip malls, billboards, the same pothole on the off-ramp still not fixed. Lisa talked about the new fridge, how Kayla had started first grade, how the neighbor’s dog kept digging up the flower beds. I nodded. The words didn’t stick. Everything was too bright, too full.

A few days later I went to the grocery store by myself because I needed something to do. Lisa gave me a short list: milk, bread, cereal. I stood in the cereal aisle for almost twenty minutes. When I’d left, there were maybe five or six kinds that I recognized. Now the whole damn aisle was nothing but colors and cartoon characters and promises in bold letters. Forty kinds of flakes and clusters and oats. I picked up a box, read the ingredients, put it back. Picked up another. Same thing. I couldn’t make the decision. A woman with a baby in the cart reached past me, grabbed a box without looking, and moved on. I just stood there like a man who’d forgotten how to buy breakfast.

At night, the house was too quiet and not quiet enough. I’d been sleeping facing the door for a year, one hand near the edge of the mattress, listening. Even in the barracks back on base, I slept like that. The door had to be in my line of sight. At home, Lisa wanted the bedroom door open so she could hear if Kayla called out. The first few weeks, I couldn’t do it. I’d get up after she fell asleep and close it. Then I’d lie there staring at the crack underneath for any shadow, any sign. After a while, I started leaving it open an inch. Then a little more. One night I didn’t close it at all. I woke up at three, saw the dark hallway, and my heart didn’t kick. I rolled over and faced the window instead.

Kayla started warming up after the first month. She’d bring me a book and sit beside me on the couch without touching. Then one day she crawled right into my lap while I was tying my boots. She didn’t say anything, just sat there. I tied my laces slow.

Nothing I brought back fits quite right. Not the uniform in the closet, not the habits, not the quiet. But I go to the store now and buy whatever cereal is on sale. And sometimes Kayla leaves her bedroom door open a crack, and I can hear her breathing when I walk down the hall. It’s enough.

setup: A parent of two middle-schoolers is writing an op-ed to local readers urging an 8:45am middle-school start time.

a.text:
**Let Our Kids Sleep: Why I'm Supporting the 8:45 Start Time**

I've watched my two middle-schoolers drag themselves out of bed at 6:15 for years now, and I'm done pretending it's normal. It's not. It's exhausting for them and for us, and it turns out there's real science behind why.

The American Academy of Pediatrics has been saying for years that middle and high schoolers shouldn't start school before 8:30. Their bodies are wired differently during adolescence — melatonin kicks in later at night, which means teens biologically can't fall asleep early even when we send them to bed at a reasonable hour. Asking them to be alert for a 7:30 first period is basically asking them to function on a permanent case of jet lag.

I know this isn't just theoretical, either. We already have proof it works right here in our district. When Lincoln Middle piloted the later start time last year, attendance went up and first-period grades improved. Not "stayed the same" — improved. That's not a fluke; that's tired kids finally getting enough sleep to actually learn.

I understand the biggest objection I keep hearing at school board meetings is about buses — that shifting start times will throw the whole transportation schedule into chaos. I get it; nobody wants a repeat of some logistical nightmare. But if you actually read the proposal (I have, several times), the district has already worked this out. Bus routes are being re-tiered so elementary schools shift earlier while middle and high schools shift later. It's not adding buses or costs — it's resequencing the same routes we already have. This isn't a hand-wavy "we'll figure it out later" plan. The tiering is right there in black and white.

I'm not a policy expert. I'm a parent who has watched my kids struggle through first period looking like zombies, and who has seen an actual pilot program in our own district prove that a later start helps. This isn't a radical experiment — it's catching up to what the research already tells us and what our own data already showed.

The school board votes on this next month. I hope they look at Lincoln's results, look at the transportation plan that's already built to handle this, and give the rest of our kids the same chance to succeed that Lincoln students already got.

*— A Millbrook parent, tired of watching tired kids*

b.text:
**A Later Start Time is the Right Choice for Millbrook’s Middle Schoolers**

As a parent of two middle schoolers in Millbrook, I’ve spent years watching my kids struggle to wake up for the 7:30 a.m. bell. Like many of you, I’ve seen the yawns at the breakfast table, the rushed mornings, and the way their energy flags by first period. That’s why I’m relieved the school board is finally considering an 8:45 a.m. start time—and why I hope the community will support it.

The science is clear: middle schoolers need more sleep. The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends that schools start no earlier than 8:30 a.m. to align with adolescents’ natural sleep cycles. When kids don’t get enough rest, it affects everything—mood, focus, even their immune systems. Chronic sleep deprivation isn’t just about being tired; it’s linked to higher rates of anxiety, depression, and lower academic performance. Our current start time isn’t just inconvenient—it’s working against our kids’ well-being.

We don’t have to guess what a later start would look like. Lincoln Middle School’s pilot program last year showed real results: attendance improved, and first-period grades went up. Teachers reported students were more alert and engaged. That’s not a coincidence—it’s what happens when we listen to the research and give kids the rest they need to thrive.

I know some parents worry about logistics, especially bus schedules. But the proposal already addresses this by re-tiering routes, so elementary and high school start times would shift slightly to accommodate the change. It’s not perfect, but it’s a workable solution—and one that prioritizes the age group that needs it most. Middle schoolers are at a critical stage, juggling harder coursework, social pressures, and physical changes. They deserve a schedule that sets them up for success, not one that leaves them exhausted before the day even begins.

Change is always hard, and I don’t take lightly the adjustments this will require for families. But when I think about the difference an extra hour of sleep could make for my kids—for all our kids—I believe it’s worth it. Let’s give them the best chance to learn, grow, and start their days with energy, not exhaustion. The school board votes next month, and I hope they’ll do the right thing for Millbrook’s students.

setup: A small coffee shop owner is writing testimony to city council opposing a parking meter rate increase.

a.text:
To Members of the City Council,

My name is [Your Name], and I am the owner and operator of an independent coffee shop on Main Street. I am submitting this testimony for the official record to express my strong opposition to the proposed parking meter rate increase from $0.50 to $1.50 per hour in our downtown district. 

A tripling of parking rates is not a minor adjustment; it is a 200% tax on downtown foot traffic. While municipal budgets face ongoing pressures, penalizing the customers who support local brick-and-mortar storefronts will generate negligible public revenue while inflicting measurable harm on our daily operations.

My business relies on quick, convenience-driven transactions. Our internal point-of-sale data shows that our average customer visit lasts exactly 22 minutes. Under the current structure, the 50-cent one-hour minimum already covers these visits with a reasonable buffer. When a customer stops in to buy a $4.50 latte or a quick bag of roasted beans, adding a mandatory $1.50 parking fee inflates the cost of that short trip by 33%. For routine daily purchases, that friction drives consumers away from downtown corridors and toward strip malls and regional chains with free surface parking.

This concern is not theoretical. We have direct historical precedent for how this policy plays out in our local market. In 2019, when our neighboring municipality implemented a nearly identical rate increase, I tracked our register and transaction counts over a six-week period. During those six weeks, foot traffic dropped by 18%. For an independent business operating on narrow margins, an 18% decline in transaction volume wipes out profitability entirely. 

Furthermore, this proposal fails even on its own terms as a fiscal solution. According to the city’s own downtown financial report, meter revenue accounts for just 4% of the total downtown operational budget. Tripling this rate will not solve the city's structural budget constraints, but it will disproportionately burden the small retail, service, and dining establishments that form the economic foundation of Main Street. We are risking the stability of the 96% of the commercial ecosystem to adjust a line item that represents only 4% of city downtown funding.

Thriving downtowns require accessibility. Increasing parking rates by 200% creates a direct barrier between local residents and the small businesses they want to support. I respectfully urge the council to vote against this proposed increase and instead explore revenue and transit solutions that do not penalize our local commercial base.

Sincerely,

[Your Name]  
Owner, [Coffee Shop Name]  
Main Street

b.text:
**Submitted Testimony — Proposed Downtown Parking Meter Rate Increase**

Dear Members of the City Council,

My name is [Name], and I own [shop name], a small independent coffee shop on Main Street. I'm writing to ask you to vote against the proposal to raise downtown meter rates from 50 cents to $1.50 an hour.

That is not a modest adjustment. It is a tripling — a 200% increase — and it will land squarely on the people who keep downtown running: customers making short, small, everyday stops.

Start with my customers. The average visit to my shop is 22 minutes. A coffee, maybe a bag of beans, a quick hello. Under the current rate, 50 cents buys the hour, and the hour covers that visit comfortably — cheap enough that nobody thinks twice about stopping in. At $1.50, that same 22-minute errand costs three times as much before my customer has spent a single dollar with me. For a regular who stops in five mornings a week, parking goes from $2.50 a week to $7.50 — an extra $260 a year for the exact same cup of coffee. People won't experience that as parking policy. They'll experience it as a reason to go somewhere else.

And they will go somewhere else. I know, because I've measured it.

In 2019, when [neighboring town] raised its meter rates, I tracked my own register for six weeks after the change and compared it against the weeks just before. Foot traffic dropped 18%. I'm not an economist — I'm a shopkeeper with six weeks of actual transactions, counted at my own till. An independent shop does not absorb an 18% drop in foot traffic and carry on as usual. Numbers like that are the difference between a business that anchors a block and a vacant storefront that doesn't.

Now weigh that against what this increase would actually accomplish. According to the city's own report, meter revenue covers just 4% of the downtown budget. Even if every meter stayed occupied exactly as often as it does today — which my data says it won't — tripling the rate moves that figure to roughly 12%. If usage falls anywhere near the 18% I measured, you're under 10%. So the proposal on the table is this: impose a 200% price increase on the customers of every small business downtown, in exchange for a single-digit dent in the budget. That doesn't solve anything. It shifts a cost onto the people least able to absorb it, in service of a gap the city's own numbers say this cannot close.

Downtown's real product isn't parking. It's the ease of parking for pocket change, running in for 22 minutes, and leaving feeling like the trip was simple. Triple the friction and people will get their coffee at a drive-through with a free lot — and once a habit moves, it rarely comes back.

Vote no on this increase. If the council believes downtown needs more revenue, there are fairer places to find it than a 22-minute errand. I can tell you from 18% worth of experience how this one ends.

Thank you for the opportunity to submit this for the record.

Respectfully,
[Name]
[Shop name], Main Street

setup: A parent of two middle-schoolers is writing an op-ed to local readers urging an 8:45am middle-school start time.

a.text:
As a parent of two middle-schoolers here in Millbrook, my mornings usually involve dragging two very grumpy kids out of bed before the sun is even fully up. It is a daily battle that leaves all of us exhausted before the day has even begun. That is why I am strongly urging our community and the school board to support the proposed 8:45 a.m. start time for our middle and high schools when they vote next month.

I’m not a medical expert or a policy analyst, just a parent who wants the best for my kids. But I did sit down and read the board’s proposal closely, and the facts just make sense. The American Academy of Pediatrics has been telling us for years that middle and high schools shouldn't start before 8:30 a.m. Adolescent biology naturally shifts, making it physically harder for them to fall asleep early and wake up early. By starting school at 7:30 or 8:00 a.m., we are fighting their basic biology, and our kids' learning is paying the price.

We don’t even have to look outside our own district to see that a later start time works. The recent pilot program over at Lincoln Middle School gave us hard, local proof. During the pilot, both daily attendance and first-period grades went up. It turns out that when kids actually get the sleep they need, they show up to school ready to learn instead of dozing off on their desks. 

I know the biggest worry I’ve heard around town is about the buses. People are understandably asking, “How are we going to manage the bus schedules without spending a fortune or creating a traffic nightmare?” If you look at the actual text of the proposal, the district has already solved this. The plan re-tiers the elementary and secondary routes, meaning we can use the same number of buses and drivers we already have. The logistics are already mapped out for us, so we don't have to choose between a functioning bus system and well-rested students.

Change is always a little bumpy at first, but our kids' health and education are worth the adjustment. Moving the start time to 8:45 a.m. is a practical, proven step that will make a massive difference in our children's daily lives. I hope the school board makes the right choice next month and votes "yes" on this proposal. I know my family’s mornings—and my kids' report cards—will be much better for it.

b.text:
# Why I'm Supporting the 8:45 Start Time

Like most parents of middle-schoolers, I've watched my kids drag themselves out of bed at 6:15 a.m. for the past two years. They're not lazy. They're not staying up too late scrolling on their phones (though yes, that happens sometimes). They're adolescents, and their bodies are doing exactly what adolescent bodies do.

The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends that middle and high schools start no earlier than 8:30 a.m. They didn't pick that number out of thin air. Research shows that puberty shifts kids' internal clocks, making it nearly impossible for them to fall asleep before 11 p.m. — and meaning that a 7:30 first bell has them waking up at the lowest point of their sleep cycle.

I've read the school board's proposal closely, and I know some people are concerned about the bus schedule. That was my first question too. But the proposal already addresses this directly: it re-tiers the bus routes so that elementary runs shift earlier and middle school routes move later. No new buses. No new drivers. No new cost. Just a reordering of who gets picked up when.

If you want proof this works, look at what happened at Lincoln Middle School. After their pilot program pushed start times later, attendance went up. First-period grades went up. Not test scores three years down the road — immediate, measurable improvements in the class that currently suffers most from sleepy teenagers.

I understand change is inconvenient. Families have built their lives around the current schedule. But the current schedule was built around adult work hours and bus logistics, not around what we know about how kids actually learn. We now have that information. We have a pediatricians' organization telling us our adolescents need more sleep. We have a local pilot showing real results. We have a proposal that solves the transportation problem without spending a dime.

My kids will be in high school before long, and this change may not fully benefit them. But the kids coming up behind them — the fifth graders who will be middle-schoolers next fall — deserve a schedule that gives them a fighting chance.

The school board votes next month. I hope they'll look at the evidence, look at the proposal, and do right by our kids.

*Millbrook parent of two*

setup: A remote software engineer is writing a 6-month standing desk review for blog readers researching standing desks.

a.text:
# Jarvik L2 Standing Desk: The Six-Month Review

I bought the Jarvik L2 in March at the $549 sale price. It's been my only desk since. I work from it roughly nine hours a day, five days a week, and I've moved it between sitting and standing at least four times per day the whole time. That's somewhere north of 500 height changes. Here's what I actually think.

**The short version:** Good motor, mediocre frame, bad accessories. Buy it on sale. Don't buy it at list.

---

## Setup

Took me about 50 minutes alone, with a drill. The instructions are pictograms only, which is fine because there aren't many steps, but the frame ships in two halves and you need to get the crossbar length right before you attach the desktop or you'll be flipping a 60-lb desk over twice. I did this. Learn from me.

The 60x30 bamboo top I got is flat, the edges are finished cleanly, and the pre-drilled holes actually lined up with the frame. That's not a given at this price. No complaints on the top.

## The Motor (Good)

This is the best thing about the desk. Dual motors, and they're genuinely quiet — I've taken calls while raising it and nobody has asked what the noise was. It goes from my sitting height (28.5") to standing (43") in about seven seconds. Jarvik claims 1.6"/second and I'd say that's honest.

It doesn't hesitate on the way up, doesn't shudder on the way down, and it hasn't gotten louder over six months. I have roughly 40 pounds on it (two 27" monitors on an arm, a laptop, a mechanical keyboard, a mic boom) and it has never strained.

If you're upgrading from a single-motor budget desk that sounds like a garbage disposal, this alone will feel like a huge jump.

## The Wobble (Not Good)

At sitting height, the L2 is rock solid. At full standing height, it is not.

I type hard — I use a heavy tactile board and I bottom out — and at 43" the monitors visibly sway. Not a little. Enough that I stopped noticing it after a month only because I got used to it, which is not the same as it going away. Side-to-side is the worst axis. Front-to-back is acceptable. If I lean my forearms on the desk and shift my weight, the whole thing moves with me.

I tightened every bolt at the two-month mark. It helped for about a week. I added a crossbar brace from a different brand that mostly fit — it helped more, but I shouldn't have to buy a part to make a $549 desk stable.

If you're tall (I'm 5'9" and my standing height is 43") and you type aggressively or use a monitor arm, you will notice this every single day. If you're shorter or you type like a normal person, you may not care. But go in knowing the frame is the weak point.

## Memory Presets (Slightly Annoying)

Four presets on a controller that sits under the front edge. Setting them is easy: hold the button, done. They work.

They also drift. Over about two weeks, my standing preset creeps roughly a centimeter — always down, never up. I've reset it four times now. It's not a big deal in isolation, but the whole point of a preset is that you don't have to think about it, and I do think about it, because I'll notice my elbows are slightly wrong and check and yep, it's dropped again. Jarvik support told me to recalibrate by lowering it all the way to the bottom and holding down for five seconds. I did. It drifted again. It's a firmware thing or a sensor thing, and either way they haven't fixed it.

The controller also has no lockout, so if you have a cat or a toddler, know that.

## The Cable Tray (Garbage)

I'm not going to be polite about this. The included cable tray is a stamped piece of thin steel with two flanges that hook over the rear crossbar, and it is bad in every way a cable tray can be bad.

It's too shallow to hold a standard power strip flat. It's too narrow to hold more than about four cables without them spilling out the sides. The hooks are loose enough that it rattles when the desk moves — which, on a desk that sells itself on quiet, is a genuinely stupid design outcome. Mine now has a folded piece of cardboard wedged under one hook to stop the noise.

The top edges aren't rolled, so they're sharp enough to scrape your knuckles when you're routing cables blind from the front. I did this twice before I got smart.

Rip it off, throw it in your parts bin, and spend $20 on a mesh under-desk tray from anywhere. Jarvik should not be shipping this.

## Miscellaneous

- **Feet:** Adjustable leveling feet, good range, they've stayed level on my slightly uneven floor.
- **Anti-collision:** Works. I've tested it against my chair arm twice by accident. It stops and backs off about an inch.
- **Finish:** The black powder coat on the legs has two small chips where I bumped them with the vacuum. Cosmetic, but it chipped easier than I'd expect.
- **Warranty:** 7 years on the frame, 5 on the electronics. Haven't had to use it.
- **Support:** Responded in one business day both times. Polite, not especially useful.

## Verdict

At **$549**, this is a good buy. The motor is better than anything else I've seen at this price, the top is solid, the presets and anti-collision work well enough, and the flaws are things you can live with or fix for under $50 (tray) or ignore (preset drift). The wobble is real, but every desk under $700 wobbles at full height to some degree, and this one is in the acceptable-for-the-money range.

At **$749**, no. At that price you're within striking distance of frames with real cross-bracing and controllers that hold a preset, and you'd be paying full price for a cable tray you'll throw away on day one. The L2 is a $550 desk that happens to have a $750 sticker most of the year. Wait for the sale. It comes around every few months.

Would I buy it again at $549? Yes. Would I recommend it to a friend who's tall and types hard? Yes, with a warning and a link to a crossbar brace.

*No affiliate links, no sponsorship, I paid for this desk myself and Jarvik has no idea this post exists.*

b.text:
Six months in. I’m a remote software engineer, I stand about 40 percent of my workday, and I’ve run the Jarvik L2 through daily height changes since March. I paid $549 during a spring sale. It’s currently listed at $749. Here is exactly what that money gets you.

The motor is the best part of the desk. It’s fast—roughly 1.5 inches per second—and the hum is low enough that it never triggers my microphone’s noise gate on Zoom calls. I shift between sitting and standing multiple times a day, and the transition is quick enough that I actually do it instead of making excuses. At sitting height, the thing feels like a fixed desk.

But max it out and the wobble shows up. At full standing height—roughly 48 inches with my monitor arm attached—hard typing sends a visible shimmy through my 27-inch display. Not a gentle sway; a rhythmic shake that’s distracting when I’m pounding out code or angry Slack messages. If you type lightly or don’t need the desk at absolute max extension, it’s manageable. I’m 5’9” and I need every inch, so I live with it.

The memory presets are technically broken. Over six months, they’ve drifted about a centimeter from where I originally set them. My “sit” position now sits slightly too low; my “stand” position sits slightly too high. It’s only a centimeter, but it’s a centimeter I have to fix manually every single time. That defeats the purpose of one-touch presets.

The included cable tray is garbage. It’s a shallow mesh basket that flexes under the weight of a standard power brick and mounts so close to the desktop that thick cables get pinched. I removed it after three weeks and spent $30 on a proper under-desk tray. Treat the bundled tray like packing material: throw it away.

At $549, the Jarvik L2 is a steal. You get a fast, quiet dual-motor frame and a surface stable enough for most work, provided you accept the top-end wobble. At $749, it’s a bad deal. That price puts you in range of fully stable four-leg competitors and desks that don’t suffer from preset drift or insult you with a mesh cable hammock.

Verdict: Buy it on sale. Ignore the tray. Know that you’ll be adjusting the presets manually. And don’t expect rock-solid stability if you’re a heavy typer at full height.

setup: A general contractor is writing a short X thread to contractors, homeowners, and architects about a hidden joist problem and the lesson learned.

a.text:
**Tweet 1:**
Maple Ave kitchen demo yesterday. Pulled up the subfloor and found the rim joist was completely rotted—not just surface, but punky all the way through. House was built in '78, no issues visible from below. This is why we open walls.

**Tweet 2:**
Called in a structural engineer to be safe. Turns out water had been wicking up from the foundation for years, probably from poor grading on that side of the house. The joist needed full replacement—$3,200 in materials and labor we didn't bid.

**Tweet 3:**
The lesson: if a kitchen is over the rim joist and you're doing demo, budget time for inspection. A $200 engineer call saves you from eating $3K+ in repairs. Also, always check grading around foundations during the estimate walk.

b.text:
1/ Opened up the ceiling on the Maple Ave kitchen Tuesday. Three floor joists under the upstairs bath notched more than halfway through for the original drain line. Somebody did it in the 60s, somebody else ran a new PVC stack through the same notch in the 90s and never fixed it. Floor above had a quarter inch of sag we'd all been calling "old house."

2/ Not in the scope. Not in the estimate. Homeowner didn't know, previous inspector didn't catch it because you can't see it through drywall. Nobody did anything wrong this decade, we just found it.

3/ Fix was sistering three full-length 2x10s, temporary shoring, rerouting the drain so it didn't cut through anything, and one visit from a structural engineer to sign off. About $4,100 all in and two extra days. Homeowner paid it. Not thrilled, but understood.

4/ Lesson isn't "old houses have surprises," everybody knows that. It's that I now line-item a demo contingency on every job over 50 years old and I walk the client through exactly what it covers before we sign. Not a vague 10%. A real number tied to real possibilities. The awkward conversation is a lot easier at the kitchen table than standing under an open ceiling.

b.text:
Nadine,

You're right to be upset, and I want to give you the full picture rather than a vague reassurance.

Yesterday afternoon a woman came to the door to pick up Mia. My substitute helper, Corrine, didn't recognize her and didn't release Mia. She had Mia stay inside with her, stepped away, and called you to confirm before anything else happened. When you said you didn't know the name, that was the end of it — the woman was told she couldn't take Mia and she left. Mia stayed with Corrine until you arrived. It turned out to be a mix-up on the other family's end; the woman was there for a different child and gave the wrong name at the door.

So the safeguard did hold. But I'm not going to pretend that's good enough. That situation should never have gotten to the point where a phone call to you was the thing standing between Mia and a stranger. Corrine had the approved pickup list — she should have checked it the moment someone she didn't recognize showed up, before Mia was anywhere near the door. She went with her gut instead of the list. Her gut was right, and I'm grateful for that, but I don't run a daycare on gut instinct.

Here's what's changing, effective immediately:

Photo ID at the door for every pickup, every time, including people I know well. No ID, no release, no exceptions. I'd rather annoy every parent I have than leave any room for judgment calls.

Corrine does not work another shift here until she and I have gone through pickup procedure in person, start to finish, with the list in her hand. Same goes for any sub I bring in going forward — pickup protocol gets walked through before they're ever alone with the kids, not handed to them on a sheet of paper.

I'm also asking each of you to review and update your approved pickup list this week so I know it's current, and I'll be re-confirming it every few months instead of only at enrollment.

I'm sorry you got that phone call. I know exactly what went through your head when you heard a name you didn't recognize, and I'm sorry I put you there. If you want to talk through this on the phone or in person, I'm happy to — just tell me when works and I'll make the time.

setup: A freelance wedding photographer is writing a blog post for couples about why to book a winter wedding.

a.text:
**Why I’ve Fallen for Winter Weddings (And Why You Might Too)**

I’ll be honest—six years ago, I wasn’t exactly *thrilled* when a couple asked me to shoot their January wedding. Cold fingers, slippery sidewalks, the sun setting before cocktail hour… what was there to love? But after shooting 11 winter weddings in the last two years, I’ve officially changed my tune. Here’s why:

**1. The Light is *Chef’s Kiss***
That soft, golden glow you get in June? It’s nice, but it’s also *everywhere*—and often drowned out by thick cloud cover. Winter light, though? Around 3 PM in November or December, the sun hangs low, filtering through bare branches like a natural diffuser. The result? Portraits with depth, warmth, and a moodiness that flat summer light just can’t match.

**2. Fewer Crowds, More Focus**
In June, I’m sharing the venue parking lot with three other photographers, a videographer, and a florist’s van. Winter weddings? It’s just me, the couple, and maybe a rogue squirrel. Fewer distractions mean I can actually *see* the details—the way the candlelight flickers on your dress, the steam rising from your coffee during golden hour, the quiet moments that get lost in the chaos of peak season.

**3. Your Budget Goes Further**
Winter weddings run about 30% cheaper on average. That’s not just a rumor—it’s a fact. Venues, caterers, even some vendors (ahem) offer off-season rates. That extra cash could mean an extra hour of coverage, a second shooter, or even just breathing room in your budget for the things that matter most.

**4. The Coziness Factor**
There’s something magical about a winter wedding. The crackle of a fireplace, the way your breath hangs in the air during a first-look moment, the glow of string lights against a dark sky. Summer weddings are vibrant, but winter weddings? They’re *intimate*. And intimacy is what makes for photos that feel like *you*.

So if you’re on the fence about a winter wedding, let me be the one to say: don’t write it off. The light is better, the crowds are smaller, and the memories? Just as unforgettable. (And yes, I *will* bring hand warmers.)

b.text:
I used to be a strictly May-through-October wedding photographer. When a couple asked about a January date, I’d smile politely and steer them toward “peak season.” That changed a couple of years ago almost by accident—a friend-of-a-friend needed a last-minute Saturday in early December, and I said yes mostly to help her out. I showed up braced for gray misery. I left that wedding buzzing. Since then, I’ve shot eleven winter weddings, and here’s the honest truth: I not only don’t mind winter anymore—I actually look forward to it.

Most couples don’t realize that winter dates almost always run about 30% less than a comparable Saturday in June. That’s real money—money that can go toward a dress upgrade, an extra hour of coverage, a live painter, or just padding the honeymoon fund. I’ve watched couples book a Friday evening in February and end up with the same full-day experience their friends had in peak season, without the compromises they expected. The pricing difference isn’t some marketing gimmick; it’s supply and demand, and winter couples are the ones who benefit.

Then there’s the light. If you’ve ever stood for portraits under a blazing flat June overcast that turns every face into a gray smudge, you know it’s not always the dream people sell you. In November and December, the sun sits lower all afternoon, and once the leaves drop, those bare trees turn into a huge softbox. Around 3 p.m., the light cuts through the branches and wraps around a couple in a way that’s honestly easier to work with than the blown-out high-noon haze I wrestle with in summer. I have frames from a November ceremony where the light looks like it was rigged by a Hollywood crew—and it was just an oak tree behind a church on a 42-degree day.

I also breathe differently now. In June, I might share a venue parking lot with three or four other wedding vendors—and I don’t mean friendly hellos. I mean dueling timelines, trolley drivers circling the block, and a quiet moment for the couple constantly interrupted by someone else’s sparkler exit. This past January, I pulled into a snowy lot and was the only photographer there. The coordinator had time to chat. The groom’s dad actually helped me carry my bag. The couple didn’t feel like they were on a wedding conveyor belt. It felt, for all of us, like a Saturday that happened to be theirs alone.

I don’t say any of this to knock summer weddings—I still love them. But after eleven winter dates in the last two years, I’ve stopped treating the off-season like a second choice. The money goes further, the portraits have a moodiness I can’t fake in July, and the pace is gentler for everyone involved. If you’re on the fence about a February or March date, I’m the photographer who will tell you it’s not a compromise. It might just be the best-kept secret in wedding planning.

setup: A remote software engineer is writing a 6-month standing desk review for blog readers researching standing desks.

a.text:
**6-Month Review: Jarvik L2 Standing Desk – The Good, The Wobbly, and The Overpriced**

Six months in, the Jarvik L2 is a mixed bag—one that’s worth your money only if you catch it on sale. Here’s the unfiltered breakdown.

### **The Good: Quiet, Fast, and (Mostly) Sturdy**
The dual-motor lift is impressively quiet—quieter than my old Uplift V2, and that’s saying something. It glides up and down at a brisk pace (about 1.5 inches per second), which matters when you’re switching positions 10 times a day. The steel frame feels solid at mid-height, and the desktop (I went with the 60" bamboo) is thick enough to resist sagging, even with two monitors and a laptop dock.

### **The Bad: Wobble, Drift, and a Cable Tray That Hates You**
- **Wobble at Full Height:** If you’re a heavy typist (or just aggressive with your keystrokes), the desk wobbles noticeably at its max height (47"). It’s not a dealbreaker, but it’s annoying when you’re trying to focus. Jarvik’s crossbar helps, but it’s not a miracle worker—this is still a two-leg desk, not a four-leg tank.
- **Memory Presets Drift:** The presets are convenient, but they’re not precise. Over time, they’ve drifted about a centimeter from where I originally set them. Not a huge issue, but if you’re OCD about exact heights, you’ll be recalibrating often.
- **Cable Tray is Useless:** The included cable tray is flimsy, poorly designed, and barely holds anything. I replaced it with a third-party under-desk basket within a month. Jarvik could’ve saved everyone the hassle by just not including it.

### **The Verdict: Worth It at $549, Not at $749**
At its sale price ($549 for the 60" model), the L2 is a solid buy—especially if you prioritize speed and noise over rock-solid stability. But at the regular $749? Hard pass. For that price, you could get a Uplift V2 with better stability, a sturdier cable management system, and a longer warranty.

**Final Rating: 7/10** (8/10 on sale, 6/10 at full price)
If you’re okay with minor wobble and can live with tweaking presets, it’s a good desk. But don’t pay full price for it.

b.text:
Jarvik L2 After Six Months

I paid $549 for the Jarvik L2 last winter and have used it every workday since. Dual 27-inch monitors, mechanical keyboard, the usual remote-engineer setup. I switch heights 8–12 times a day.

The motor is the best part of this desk. It is quiet enough that I raise it during standup calls and nobody comments. Full travel from 28" to 46" takes about 14 seconds. No grinding, no hesitation. Dual motors, advertised 220 lb capacity; my setup is well under that and it never strains.

Stability is the problem. Sitting height is fine. At standing height—my usual 44–46"—the desktop wobbles when I type hard. Not a little flex. A visible shimmy that travels into the monitors. It is worse with both screens mounted on a dual-arm. I can live with it, but I notice it every time I hammer out a block of code. If you type lightly or keep the desk lower, you may not care. I type like I mean it.

The four memory presets work until they don’t. They drift roughly a centimeter over a few weeks. I end up tapping the up/down buttons to correct. Recalibrating is simple but I shouldn’t have to do it. For someone who switches all day, this is a real annoyance.

The included cable tray is junk. Thin plastic, two flimsy clips, sags under a laptop brick and a USB hub. I ripped it off in week two and replaced it with a $22 metal tray from Amazon. The grommets are fine. The tray is not.

Desktop is a 1.2" laminate. No warping, no peeling after six months. Edges are decent. Assembly took 45 minutes with one other person; the instructions were adequate. Crossbar is solid. The wobble is in the legs/columns at extension, not the frame joints.

I would buy it again at $549. I would not pay $749. At full price you can get better stability from several competitors. The motor and speed are excellent. The height drift and the cheap tray are not. Wait for the sale.

Hi Gloria and Paul,

When we opened up the wall behind the sink and range yesterday, my electrician Dave found the original 1962 aluminum wiring running through the kitchen. That's what stopped us early. setup: You're Nadine Alvarado, emailing the daycare owner after a near-miss pickup mistake involving Mia and asking what happened and what changes are being made.

a.text:
Hi Nadine,

Thank you for emailing me, and I completely understand why that call yesterday was terrifying. You should never get a call about someone you don't know trying to pick up Mia.

Here is what happened — I want to be straight with you about it. I had a substitute helper covering the afternoon pickup while I was with the little ones. Someone came to the door asking for Mia who was not on your approved pickup list. My sub didn't recognize her. She did not release Mia — she kept Mia inside with me and called you from the door to check first, which is why you got that call and why Mia never left our supervision.

She did the right thing by calling and not releasing her, but you are absolutely right to be upset — it should never have even gotten to a phone call. That person should have been stopped at the door and checked against the list and ID right away.

This is what I'm doing starting today:

I'm adding a hard ID check at the door. No one gets in past the entry without showing photo ID that matches the approved pickup list exactly. I'm moving that list to a clipboard right at the door so it's not in the binder in the back anymore.

And my sub will not work again until we sit down and retrain on pickup. She won't be alone for pickup until I'm 100% confident in it. That's on me for not making that process clearer for her.

Mia was safe and with me the whole time yesterday, but I know that's not enough — you need to feel safe leaving her here. I am so sorry this happened.

Can we go over your pickup list together when you have a minute? If you want to add or remove anyone, or if you want to come a few minutes early this week and watch how we do pickup now, please do. I'm here all day and you can call or text me anytime.

Thank you for trusting me with Mia, and for telling me how scary that was for you.

b.text:
Nadine,

I'm sorry. I know how that call must have landed, and you deserve a straight account of what happened.

Yesterday afternoon a man came to the door saying he was there to pick up Mia. I wasn't in the room at that moment. Lisa, the substitute who was covering for me, didn't recognize him, checked Mia's file, saw his name wasn't on your approved list, and called you before letting him anywhere near the door with her. Mia never left the room. Once you said no, he was turned away. That's the whole sequence.

Lisa did the right thing in the end, and I'm glad she trusted her gut. But I'm not going to pretend the process worked, because it didn't. She should have been checking the list against an ID the second he said Mia's name, not after he'd already stated he was there for her and she'd started to think about it. The fact that it got far enough for you to receive that call is on me. The pickup list and the "if in doubt, don't" rule are things I've drilled into my regular staff for years, and I didn't drill them hard enough into someone who was here for one day.

Here's what's changing:

Starting today, anyone picking up any child shows a photo ID at the door before they come inside, no exceptions, including me being told "oh, that's so-and-so's grandpa." I know the regular parents by face, and I'll still be asking. It takes ten seconds and it means nobody has to rely on recognizing someone.

Lisa won't be working here again until I've gone through the full pickup procedure with her in person and she's walked through it with me watching. If I'm not confident, she doesn't come back.

I'm also going back through every child's file this week to make sure the approved lists are current and easy to find, so nobody is flipping through papers while a stranger is standing at the door.

I don't have an answer yet for who this man was or why he had Mia's name. If you have any idea, I'd like to know, and if you don't, I'd like to know that too, because it changes how worried I am about it.

Please call me if you want to talk this through. I'd rather have the hard conversation than have you wondering.

Karen
