setup: A parent of two middle-schoolers is writing an op-ed to local readers urging an 8:45am middle-school start time.

a.text:
**Our Kids Aren't Lazy. They're Tired.**

Every school morning at my house starts the same way: me flipping on the light at 6:15, my seventh grader burrowing under the covers like I'm the enemy. I used to think this was just a phase, or too much screen time. Then I read the research behind the school board's 8:45 start time proposal, and I realized my kids aren't being difficult. Their biology is.

The American Academy of Pediatrics has recommended for years that middle and high schools start no earlier than 8:30 a.m. The reason is straightforward: during puberty, teenagers' internal clocks shift. Their brains release melatonin later at night, which means they can't simply "go to bed earlier" — their bodies won't cooperate. Teens need eight to ten hours of sleep, and expecting a 13-year-old to be sharp in a 7:50 a.m. class is asking them to fight their own brain chemistry.

If that sounds too theoretical, look at what happened when Lincoln Middle tried it. After moving to a later start, attendance improved and first-period grades went up. Not because the teachers changed or the classes got easier — because the kids were actually awake enough to learn. That's the whole ballgame, isn't it?

Now, the objection I keep hearing at the grocery store and on Facebook: the buses. It's a fair question. Millbrook's buses run multiple routes every morning, and shifting one school's schedule affects the whole system. But the proposal before the board already answers this. It re-tiers the routes and staggers start times so the same buses can still cover the elementary, middle, and high school runs. This isn't a case of waving away logistics — the logistics are written into the plan. We should be debating the merits, not a problem that's already been solved on paper.

I won't pretend change is painless. Some families, mine included, will have to rework morning routines and childcare. But we make hard adjustments all the time when the evidence says our kids will be better off. This is one of those times.

The board votes next month. My two middle-schoolers will be asleep when I leave for work either way. I'd just rather they be asleep because it's 7:30 — not because they were up half the night fighting a schedule designed for adults instead of for them.

I urge the board to vote yes on 8:45.

*—[Name] is a Millbrook parent of two middle-schoolers.*

b.text:
Later Start Times Give Our Kids What They Need

As a parent of two middle-schoolers in Millbrook, I live the same morning routine as a lot of families here. The alarm rings too early. My kids are groggy, slow to eat, slow to talk. I pack lunches while they're still rubbing their eyes. They're not refusing to get up out of stubbornness. Their sleep patterns have changed, and the current start time leaves them short on rest no matter how hard we try to enforce bedtime.

I support the proposal to start school at 8:45.

The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends that middle and high schools start no earlier than 8:30 a.m. so adolescents can get 8.5 to 9.5 hours of sleep. That's not a suggestion from a wellness blog. It's from the doctors who study kids' health. Puberty delays their sleep cycle. They can't just go to bed earlier and make it work. An 8:45 start would finally line up with what their bodies actually need.

Lincoln Middle School already ran a pilot with later starts. Attendance went up. First-period grades went up. Those results should carry weight. When students aren't exhausted, they come to class more often and they perform better in the period that used to be wasted because half the room was still asleep. Those attendance and grade improvements mean kids are more present and more able to take in what's being taught. That's a direct benefit we can see in a school not far from here.

People raise the bus schedule as the reason we can't do this. I understand the concern—changing routes isn't simple. But the proposal already re-tiers the routes. The transportation plan is included. They're not leaving that for later. The objection has been answered in the document itself.

For me this is personal. I watch my two kids fight through mornings that don't have to be this hard. We all want them to do well. Giving them more sleep is one of the most straightforward ways to help. The pediatricians recommend it, Lincoln demonstrated the gains, and the buses have been accounted for.

The school board votes next month. I hope they approve the 8:45 start. Our middle-schoolers aren't asking for special treatment. They're asking for a schedule that lets them show up ready to learn. Next month's vote is our chance to get this right for the kids who are in these buildings right now.

setup: A small HVAC company owner is writing a how-to for homeowners on bleeding air from hot water baseboard radiators before winter.

a.text:
If your baseboard heaters are knocking, clanking, or staying lukewarm while the boiler runs, air is trapped inside the lines. Water can't flow through an air pocket, which leaves you with a cold room. 

Bleeding the air out is a simple job you can do yourself in about 20 minutes before you crank the heat up for the season. Here is the exact order and method to do it right.

### Step 1: Kill the power to the system
Before touching a valve, turn off your boiler and the circulator pump at the emergency switch. Never bleed a system while the pump is running. A running pump can actually pull more air into the lines, and you run the risk of pumping hot water or air pockets right past your bleeder valves. Let the system settle and cool down for a few minutes so you don't burn yourself.

### Step 2: Start at the basement loop (Do not skip this)
The single biggest mistake that triggers cold-radiator service calls to our shop is people bleeding only the upstairs units. Air rises, so logic tells you it’s all on the top floor—but in hydronic systems, air pockets frequently get locked into the lowest loops first. If you leave air in the basement baseboards, it will eventually push up into the rest of the house. 

Always bleed unit by unit, starting with the baseboard closest to the boiler (usually in the basement) and working your way out and up through the house.

### Step 3: Find the bleeder valve
Pop off the end caps on the metal baseboard housing. You are looking for a small metal valve soldered into the pipe at the end of the finned tube. It will have a tiny discharge nozzle on the side and either a square stem (which takes a radiator key) or a slotted top (which takes a small flathead screwdriver).

### Step 4: Catch the water and open slowly
Hold a small cup or rag directly beneath the valve spout. Insert your key or flathead screwdriver and turn the valve counterclockwise very slowly—usually just a quarter to a half turn is all it takes. 

You’ll hear a sharp hissing sound as trapped air escapes. Hold steady. 

### Step 5: Wait for a solid stream and close snug
Keep the valve open until the hissing stops completely and a steady, unbroken stream of water spurts into your cup. 

As soon as you get solid water, turn the valve clockwise to close it. **Tighten it until it’s snug, but do not crank down on it.** These valves are soft brass. If you overtighten them, you’ll crack the internal valve seat, turn a small bleed job into a dripping leak, and end up having to call us to drain the whole system and sweat on a new valve.

### Step 6: Repeat down the line
Move to the next baseboard unit along the zone, working away from the boiler, and repeat the process. Once you’ve hit every unit—basement included—head back to the boiler, check your system pressure gauge (a standard residential system usually sits around 12 to 15 PSI cold), turn the power switch back on, and let the pump circulate.

b.text:
# How to Bleed Air Out of Baseboard Heating Before Winter

1. **Shut off the boiler and circulator first.**  
   Turn off power to both. If the system has been running, give it a few minutes to cool so you’re not opening a hot valve.

2. **Start at the baseboard unit closest to the boiler.**  
   Find the small bleeder valve on the end of the baseboard enclosure. It’s usually a tiny slotted or square-headed screw. Put a small cup or rag underneath it to catch water.

3. **Open the valve slowly.**  
   Use a bleeder key or a flathead screwdriver and turn it counterclockwise about a quarter turn. You’ll hear hissing as air escapes. Keep the cup under the valve. When the hissing stops and the water comes out in a steady stream with no air bubbles, it’s bled.

4. **Close it snug, but do not overtighten.**  
   Turn the valve clockwise until it stops, then give it just a light seat. Overtightening cracks or distorts the valve seat, which means a leak and a bigger repair.

5. **Move to the next unit and work outward from the boiler.**  
   Bleed every baseboard loop, including basement runs. The mistake behind most of our cold-radiator calls is skipping the basement loop. Air usually settles there, so that loop often needs bleeding even if the basement itself feels warm.

6. **Turn the boiler and circulator back on.**  
   Check the pressure gauge and top up to the normal cold fill range if needed. Then walk the system and feel along each baseboard to confirm even heat.

If a loop still stays cold after every unit is bled, stop and call us. That usually points to a circulator, zone valve, or pressure problem, not just air.

setup: A high school junior is writing an argumentative essay to her English teacher and classmates arguing for open campus lunch for juniors and seniors.

a.text:
**Open Campus Lunch Would Benefit Upperclassmen**

Our school should allow juniors and seniors to leave campus during lunch. Right now, the cafeteria is overcrowded, many students feel restricted by the current policy, and nearby districts have already shown that an open campus lunch does not have to create attendance or tardiness problems. Giving upperclassmen this option would make lunch more manageable for the school while also treating older students with the responsibility they have earned.

The most immediate reason to allow open campus lunch is that our cafeteria does not have enough space for everyone who needs to use it. During one lunch wave, 340 students are expected to fit into a cafeteria that seats only 220 people. That means about 120 students do not have a seat available at the same time. As a result, students may have to stand, sit in crowded areas, rush through lunch, or find somewhere else to eat. Lunch is supposed to be a break in the school day, but overcrowding turns it into another stressful part of the schedule. Allowing juniors and seniors to leave campus would reduce the number of students in the cafeteria and give those who remain more space.

Students also support the idea. In a survey of 80 students at our school, 71 said they were in favor of open campus lunch for juniors and seniors. Although students should not make every school policy decision, their opinions matter when the policy affects their daily experience. The survey shows that this is not just an idea supported by a few students who want more freedom. Most of the students asked believed that upperclassmen should have the opportunity to leave campus during lunch. Since juniors and seniors are closer to adulthood and often have more experience balancing school responsibilities, they should be trusted with that choice.

Some people may worry that an open campus policy would lead to more tardiness after lunch. However, nearby schools provide evidence that this concern is not inevitable. Fairmont, West Linn, and Cascade already allow open campus lunch, and their published statistics show no rise in tardiness. These districts demonstrate that students can leave campus, eat elsewhere, and still return to class on time. Our school could also set clear expectations, such as requiring students who are repeatedly late to lose their open campus privilege. This would hold students accountable without taking the opportunity away from everyone.

Open campus lunch would not mean that students are being ignored or given unlimited freedom. It would be a practical solution to a real space problem and a reasonable privilege for upperclassmen. With overcrowding in the cafeteria, strong student support, and successful examples from nearby districts, our school has good reasons to allow juniors and seniors to leave campus during lunch.

b.text:
Opening the Doors: The Case for Upperclassmen Open Campus Lunch

Every day during fourth period, the bell rings and a frantic footrace begins. The destination is not an exciting assembly or an early dismissal, but the cafeteria—a space designed to secure a seat before the room reaches a breaking point. For juniors and seniors balancing advanced coursework, jobs, and extracurriculars, the thirty-minute lunch block should offer a genuine break in the day. Instead, it is spent navigating long lines and congested tables. Implementing an open campus lunch policy for upperclassmen is not merely a request for more freedom; it is a practical solution to our school’s severe space constraints, backed by overwhelming student support and successful precedents in our neighboring districts.

The most immediate argument for open campus lunch is simple mathematics: our school does not have enough room to seat its students. Our cafeteria has an official seating capacity of 220 people, yet our current lunch wave forces roughly 340 students into the room at the exact same time. That leaves over one hundred students every day balancing trays on their laps in the hallway, sitting on the radiator covers, or standing near the garbage cans just to eat. By allowing juniors and seniors to leave campus for lunch, the school would naturally cut the cafeteria population down to a manageable number. This would immediately eliminate overcrowded hallways, shorten food lines, and create a safer, calmer environment for underclassmen who remain on campus. 

The primary administrative hesitation toward open campus lunch is usually the fear that students will return late or skip their afternoon classes. However, regional data shows this fear is unfounded. Three nearby districts—Fairmont, West Linn, and Cascade—already permit open campus lunch for their upperclassmen. According to published attendance statistics from all three districts, none of them experienced a measurable rise in afternoon tardiness after implementing the policy. When students are granted a privilege that they value, they actively protect it by watching the clock and returning on time. High school juniors and seniors are on the verge of entering college or the workforce, where time management is an essential expectation. Letting them practice that responsibility in a controlled, daily setting actually reinforces good habits rather than breaking them.

Furthermore, this change aligns directly with what the student body wants and is ready for. In an informal survey conducted across our junior and senior classes, 71 out of 80 respondents—nearly 89 percent—expressed strong support for an open campus policy. Most students indicated they would use the time simply to grab food closer to home, run quick errands, or eat in a quieter environment where they can decompress. To address any lingering safety concerns, the school could easily implement basic guardrails, such as requiring parental permission forms and establishing minimum GPA or attendance benchmarks to maintain off-campus eligibility. 

Our current closed-campus model forces hundreds of students into an inadequate space while ignoring the proven success of neighboring schools. Allowing juniors and seniors to leave for lunch would instantly solve our cafeteria overcrowding, give students the opportunity to practice real-world accountability, and treat upperclassmen like the young adults they are. It is time for our administration to follow the evidence, trust its students, and open the doors.

setup: A first-year nursing student is writing a scholarship essay about her first ER rotation for scholarship committee readers.

a.text:
**The Fourth Try**

The first useful thing I did in the ER was hold a stranger's hand.

He was getting a deep cut on his arm cleaned out, and it hurt. His wife was stuck in traffic, and he kept looking at the door like he could make her appear. All the nurses were busy, so my preceptor nodded at me, and I stepped up next to the gurney and let him take my hand. He squeezed hard enough that my fingers went numb. I talked to him about nothing — the traffic, the rain, whether he'd eaten — because that was all I had. When his wife finally came through the door, he thanked me like I had done something big. All I did was stand there. But I stood there, and I think it mattered to him.

Not everything that week felt that clear. On my third day, a code got called one curtain over from where I was working. I wanted to help. What I was told to do was go restock the gauze. So I stood at the supply cart with my arms full of gauze packs and listened through the curtain while they counted compressions. One, two, three, four. Over and over. Somebody called out numbers I didn't understand yet. I felt about two inches tall, like a kid who got sent out of the room.

It took me a few days to see it differently. Every drawer

b.text:
My first week in the ER was not what I expected. I knew it would be busy, but I did not understand how many different kinds of hard could fit into one shift. There were alarms, people calling for supplies, families asking questions, and nurses moving quickly from one room to another. I was nervous the whole first day. I wanted to help, but I was also afraid of getting in the way.

One of the first moments that stayed with me happened during a wound cleaning. The patient was a man who had gotten hurt at work. The nurse was cleaning a deep cut, and he was trying hard not to react, but I could see that he was scared. His wife was supposed to be there, but she was stuck in traffic and had not made it yet. The nurse asked if I could stay by his side.

I held his hand while they cleaned the wound. I did not know what to say at first. I just told him that his wife was on her way and that he was doing a good job. He squeezed my hand every time it hurt. I remember thinking that I had not done anything medical in that moment. I did not place an IV or give medication. But I was still helping. He did not have to be alone while something painful was happening to him. That taught me that nursing is not only about skills. Sometimes it is about being the person who stays.

Later that week, there was a code in the ER. I was not part of the team in the room. I was sent to restock gauze and other supplies nearby. At first, I felt disappointed. I wanted to see what was happening and learn from it. Then I heard the team counting through the curtain. Their voices were steady and loud over everything else in the department.

I stood there with gauze in my hands and listened. It made the situation feel real in a way that class had not. I understood that emergencies do not pause because someone is new or because someone feels ready. Everyone had a job, even if that job seemed small. The team needed supplies ready. They needed the room to keep moving. I learned that being useful does not always mean being at the center of the action. It means doing what needs to be done well, especially when things are stressful.

Another day, I was trying to draw blood from a patient with diabetes and very difficult veins. I missed the first time. Then I missed again. By the third try, I felt terrible. The patient was kind, but I knew he was tired of being poked. I was embarrassed and frustrated with myself. My instructor talked me through it and reminded me to slow down, take a breath, and look again instead of rushing because I was nervous.

On the fourth try, I got it.

I felt relieved, but I also felt humbled. I did not walk away thinking I had mastered blood draws. I walked away knowing that I still have a lot to learn. That patient gave me more patience than I probably deserved that day. I thanked him, and I meant it. He reminded me that every skill I practice is happening to a real person, not just a practice arm in lab.

My first week in the ER showed me that nursing will ask a lot from me. It will ask me to stay calm when I feel nervous, to keep learning when I make mistakes, and to care for people during some of the worst moments of their lives. I know I am only at the beginning of my education. I will miss things, ask questions, and need help. But that week made me even more sure that nursing is where I belong.

I want to become the kind of nurse who can be steady in a crisis, honest when I need to learn, and kind when someone feels scared. Sometimes that may mean holding a stranger’s hand. Sometimes it may mean restocking gauze. Sometimes it may mean trying again after I miss. My first week in the ER taught me that all of those moments matter.

setup: A high school junior is writing an argumentative essay to her English teacher and classmates arguing for open campus lunch for juniors and seniors.

a.text:
# Room to Breathe: Why Our School Should Allow Open Campus Lunch for Juniors and Seniors

Every day at 11:40, three hundred and forty students funnel into a cafeteria built to seat two hundred and twenty. The math does not work, and everyone who has ever eaten lunch sitting on the floor outside the gym already knows it. Our school should adopt an open campus lunch policy for juniors and seniors — a policy that would let upperclassmen leave school grounds during their lunch period. This is not a request for a privilege so much as a practical solution to a problem the school has not otherwise addressed, and the experience of nearby districts suggests the risks administrators worry about do not actually materialize.

The most immediate argument for open campus is that our current lunch arrangement is physically overcrowded. With 340 students assigned to a lunch wave and only 220 seats available, more than a third of the students in that wave have nowhere to sit down. The overflow spills into hallways and stairwells, which creates exactly the kind of congestion and supervision headache that administrators say they want to avoid. Letting juniors and seniors leave would reduce the number of bodies in that room without requiring the school to build anything, hire anyone, or restructure the master schedule. It is the cheapest fix available.

The strongest evidence that open campus can work here is that it already works nearby. Fairmont, West Linn, and Cascade all allow open campus lunch for upperclassmen, and none of their published attendance data shows an increase in tardiness to fifth period since the policies were adopted. This matters because tardiness is the objection administrators raise first. The concern is reasonable in the abstract — students who leave might not come back on time — but three neighboring districts have effectively run the experiment for us, and the numbers did not move. If open campus reliably produced late students, it would be visible in the data of the districts closest to us, and it is not.

Student support for the policy is also overwhelming. In a survey I conducted of eighty students at our school, seventy-one said they were in favor of open campus lunch for juniors and seniors. That is nearly nine out of ten. A survey of eighty students is not a district-wide referendum, and I administered it myself rather than through the school, so it should be read as a strong indication rather than proof. Still, when a proposal has that level of buy-in from the people it affects, it is worth taking seriously — especially since a policy students actually want is a policy students are more likely to follow.

Critics will argue that open campus creates safety and liability problems, and this concern deserves a real answer rather than a dismissal. Students driving off campus and returning in a hurry is a genuine risk. But the same students already drive to school in the morning and away from it in the afternoon, and the school does not treat those trips as unacceptable dangers. Districts that allow open campus manage the risk with straightforward measures: parent permission forms, revocation of the privilege for students who abuse it, and grade and attendance requirements for eligibility. Fairmont, West Linn, and Cascade have not abandoned their policies, which suggests the risk is manageable at the scale of a normal high school.

Open campus lunch is not a radical idea. It is a policy that three districts in our area already use, that our own students strongly support, and that would relieve a seating shortage the school currently has no plan to solve. Juniors and seniors are, by definition, a year or two from managing their own schedules entirely. Giving them thirty minutes of that responsibility now — with clear conditions and consequences — is a reasonable step, and it would mean that a third of the students in my lunch wave finally get to sit in a chair.

b.text:
**Open Campus Lunch for Juniors and Seniors**

Our school’s lunch period is a logistical disaster. Every day, 340 students pour into a cafeteria built to hold 220, turning what should be a break into a cramped, stressful scramble for space. The solution is straightforward: our school should allow open campus lunch for juniors and seniors. Opening campus to upperclassmen would relieve dangerous overcrowding, follows a model already proven safe in comparable districts, and honors the clear preference of the student body.

The overcrowding is not a matter of opinion; it is a math problem. With only 220 seats for 340 students in the lunch wave, more than one hundred kids are left without a place to eat. They fill hallway floors, stairwells, and benches meant for passing traffic, creating congestion and a mess that staff must constantly manage. The issue is not the cafeteria food itself; it is basic capacity. Allowing juniors and seniors—students old enough to drive and hold jobs—to leave campus for lunch would immediately reduce that pressure. Those who remain, mostly freshmen and sophomores, would finally have room to sit down and eat like human beings.

The most common objection is that open campus lunch invites tardiness and truancy. But schools near us have already tested that fear and found it empty. Fairmont, West Linn, and Cascade all allow open campus lunch, and their published statistics show no rise in tardiness since adopting the policy. These districts share similar demographics, geography, and community values with our own. If their upperclassmen can leave campus and return to class on time, it is unreasonable to assume ours would do any worse. The data is right there; we should trust it rather than treat a responsible policy as a reckless gamble.

Beyond the numbers, students themselves are asking for this change. In a survey of eighty students at our school, seventy-one said they support open campus lunch for juniors and seniors. That is nearly 89 percent. This is not a fringe demand. Juniors and seniors are already entrusted with far greater responsibility, from driving themselves to school to representing the school in athletics and activities. Treating them as incapable of walking to a nearby restaurant and returning on time contradicts the maturity we expect from them in every other context.

Our school faces a capacity crisis that punishes everyone in the lunch wave. We have evidence from three neighboring districts that open campus lunch works without disciplinary downside. And we have a student population overwhelmingly in favor of the change. Opening campus lunch to juniors and seniors is not a risky experiment; it is a practical, proven solution. We should adopt it now.

setup: A solo indie game developer is writing a devlog recap for subscribers about his game's launch week sales, subreddit attention, review feedback, and upcoming 1.1 patch.

a.text:
**Devlog Update: Launch Week Numbers & What’s Next**

Well, it’s finally out. After three years of chipping away at this on nights and weekends, the game actually released last week. 

Here is a quick look at how week one went:

* **Copies sold:** 412. For a first commercial release with essentially zero marketing budget outside of this devlog and some social posts, I'm really happy with that. Seeing stranger's names pop up on the leaderboards has been surreal.
* **Visibility:** The biggest traffic spike happened mid-week when a gameplay clip hit the front page of a small subreddit for about six hours. It drove a solid chunk of day-two sales before it got buried, but it was cool to watch the real-time analytics spike while it lasted.

As for the feedback, it's been mostly positive, but there was one piece of criticism that stood out. A reviewer pointed out that the character movement feels floaty. 

Honestly, they’re completely right. When you spend three years playtesting your own physics, you compensate for the quirks automatically, but seeing fresh players struggle with precision made it immediately obvious. 

So, that's what I'm working on. Patch 1.1 is scheduled for next month. The main priority is overhauling the movement mechanics—tightening the deceleration, making the jumps snappier, and adding more weight to landings. I’ll also be squashing a handful of minor UI bugs that were reported over the weekend.

Thanks to everyone here who picked up a copy, left a review, or just followed along with the devlog while this was being built. 

Back to the code. More updates soon.

b.text:
# Week One

It's been a week since launch, so here's what actually happened.

412 copies sold. That's the number as of this morning. I know some of you have asked directly, so there it is instead of me dancing around it.

The reddit thing was wild while it lasted. Someone posted a gif of the grapple hook mechanic on a small subreddit (maybe 40k members) and it sat on the front page for about six hours before getting buried under other stuff. Traffic to the Steam page spiked hard during that window, then dropped off just as fast when it fell off the page. I refreshed the analytics dashboard more times than I want to admit.

Reviews are trickling in slowly, which I expected. Six so far, mostly positive. One of them called out the movement feeling floaty, and honestly, they're right. I've known this for a while but kept telling myself it was fine, that momentum-based movement is supposed to feel a little loose. But going back and playing it fresh after not touching the code for two weeks, yeah. It's floaty in a way that isn't intentional, it's just under-tuned.

So that's going into 1.1. I'm targeting next month for the patch. The main changes:

- Tightening acceleration/deceleration curves on the player controller
- Adjusting air control values (this is probably 80% of the floaty feeling)
- Fixing a minor collision bug with moving platforms that two people mentioned in comments

I'm not going to pretend I have some grand roadmap beyond that right now. Right now it's just: fix what's broken, listen to what people are saying, keep going.

Thanks to everyone who bought a copy, left a review, or just told a friend about it. Three years of nights and weekends led to this week, and I'm still figuring out how to feel about that.

More soon.

setup: A small HVAC company owner is writing a how-to for homeowners on bleeding air from hot water baseboard radiators before winter.

a.text:
If your baseboards are gurgling or they're hot on one end and ice cold on the other, you've got air trapped in the loop. Here's how I bleed them in the field.

**What you need:** small cup or plastic container, an old towel, and a radiator key or flathead screwdriver.

**1. Shut the system down first.**
Hit the emergency switch for the boiler and turn off the circulator. You don't want the pump pushing more air around while you're bleeding, and you don't want to get hit with scalding water. Give it 10-15 minutes to cool down if it's been running.

**2. Find the bleeder valve.**
It's on the end of each baseboard unit, under the end cap. Little brass fitting with a flat or square head. That's it.

**3. Put your cup underneath it and have the towel ready.**
Even when you do it right, it'll spit a little.

**4. Open it slow.**
Quarter-turn with the key or flathead until you hear hissing. Don't crank it wide open. Let the air come out until the water runs in a steady stream with no sputtering or hissing.

**5. Close it snug.**
Snug, not Hercules tight. If you overtighten these you'll crack the valve seat and then you really have a leak. Just firm until the water stops.

**6. Go unit by unit, closest to the boiler and work out.**
Start with the baseboard closest to the boiler and work your way to the end of each loop. Do every unit, even if it feels hot.

The mistake I see that causes 90% of our "cold radiator" calls: people only bleed the upstairs units and skip the basement loop. The basement loop is usually where the air is actually sitting. If you skip it, you'll be right back where you started.

Once you're done, turn the boiler and circulator back on. Check the pressure gauge on the boiler - you should be around 12-15 psi cold. If a zone is still cold after you've bled everything, or you're not getting any water out of a bleeder, give us a call and we'll get you on the schedule.

b.text:
# How to Bleed Air Out of Your Baseboard Heating Before Winter

If a baseboard runs cold along part of its length, or a whole zone barely warms up while the rest of the house is fine, you've got air in the line. Air pockets block water flow, and bleeding them out is a twenty-minute job you can do with a screwdriver. Here's the process, start to finish.

## What You'll Need

- A flathead screwdriver or a bleeder key (a couple bucks at any hardware store)
- A cup and a towel
- Twenty minutes

## Step 1: Shut the Boiler Off First

Flip the boiler off at its switch and let the circulator come to a stop. You want the system still while you bleed it — moving water carries air pockets past the bleeders instead of letting them collect where you can actually get at them. It also keeps hot water from coming at you under pressure if the boiler's been running.

## Step 2: Find the Bleeder Valve

Each baseboard unit has a small bleeder valve at one end, right where the finned pipe meets the end of the unit. Sometimes it's tucked behind the end cover — pop the cover off if you have to. Most valves open with a flathead screwdriver; some take a bleeder key.

## Step 3: Put a Cup Under It

Water comes out when you open the valve. Cup underneath, towel beside it.

## Step 4: Open It Slow

Open the valve about a quarter turn, slowly. You'll hear hissing — that's the air escaping. Keep it open until water runs out in a steady stream with no sputtering and no hiss. Sputtering means there's still air in that run; steady water means the unit's clear.

## Step 5: Close It Snug — and Stop

Snug the valve closed and leave it there. Do not crank on it. Overtightening cracks the valve seat, and a cracked seat means a slow drip behind your baseboard cover that you won't find until it's stained the wall. A firm snug is all it takes.

## Step 6: Work From the Boiler Outward

Go unit by unit, starting with the baseboard closest to the boiler and working your way out to the farthest loop. Bleed every unit, including the ones that seem to be heating fine.

## The Mistake That Causes Most of Our Cold Radiator Calls

When we get called out for a baseboard that won't heat, the story is almost always the same: the homeowner bled all the upstairs units, called it done, and skipped the basement loop entirely. The basement loop is usually where the air is actually sitting. You can bleed the whole first floor, get clear water out of every valve, and still have an air-bound system — because the pocket doing the damage never got a bleeder opened on it. If you only bleed one loop, make it the basement.

## When You're Done

Flip the boiler back on, let it run a full cycle, and put your hand along each baseboard. They should heat evenly end to end. If you've bled every unit — basement included — and a loop still runs cold, the problem is past what a bleeder valve can fix: low system pressure, a weak circulator, or a stuck zone valve. That's when to give us a call, and we'd rather come out now than after the first cold night.

setup: A small dog grooming salon owner is writing a how-to for dog owners about preventing coat matting between grooming visits.

a.text:
# Brush First, Bathe Second: Keeping Mats Out Between Grooming Visits

If you've got a doodle, a poodle, a golden, a husky — really any dog whose coat seems to be plotting against you between visits — this one's for you. Matting is the number one thing I see walk back through my door, and most of it is preventable with about ten minutes of brushing a few times a week. It's worth the effort, too, because mats aren't just ugly. They pull on the skin, hide problems underneath, and are genuinely uncomfortable for your dog.

Let me start with the mistake I see more than any other, because everything else hinges on it: bathing the dog first, thinking the water and shampoo will loosen the mats. It does the exact opposite. A wet mat, worked over with soap and a towel and then hit with the dryer, tightens and knits itself together — that's literally how felt gets made, wet fiber plus agitation. Once a mat has been through a bath, it isn't a tangle anymore. It's a felt pad welded to your dog's skin, and no brush on earth is getting through it. So the rule in your house should be: brush first, bathe second, never the other way around, and never on a damp dog. If there are mats in the coat, it doesn't get a bath until they're out.

When you do brush, use a slicker brush — the kind with the fine bent wire pins — and make short, straight line strokes. Not circles. Scrubbing in little circles feels productive, but all it does is swirl the hair around and encourage the very knots you're trying to prevent. Short lines, small strokes, all the way down to the skin. On a double-coated dog, the top layer can look smooth and perfect while the dead undercoat is packing itself down against the skin underneath, so part the hair, brush a line at a time, then move up an inch and do the next line. On a curly coat — your doodles and poodles — brushing only the surface is worse than useless, because it smooths the top and hides the matting forming beneath it. You have to feel the brush reach the skin.

Work in sections rather than running the brush over the whole dog at once, and always start behind the ears and under the front legs. Those are the spots mats show up first — friction from collars, harness straps, ears flapping around. Hit those areas every single time and you'll catch most mats while they're still small.

And if you do find a mat already forming, put the brush down. Work a little conditioner into it with your fingers first — really get it in there, gently pull the mat apart, give it a minute — before you ever touch it with a brush or comb. A dry mat fights you. A conditioned mat gives.

That's the whole system: brush before the bath, slicker with short line strokes, ears and armpits first, conditioner before the brush. If you run into a mat you can't work out, don't keep picking at it — you'll make the skin sore and teach your dog that brushing is something to dread. And please, no scissors at home. Bring them in instead. If we catch it early, we can almost always save the coat.

b.text:
If you have a Doodle, a Poodle, a Golden, or any dog with a thick, double or curly coat, you’ve probably felt that dreaded sinking feeling when your fingers hit a solid lump of tangled hair. Coat maintenance at home can feel like an uphill battle, especially in the weeks between your appointments with us, but a few small technique tweaks will completely change your routine.

First, let’s talk about the single biggest mistake I see pet parents make. A lot of folks notice their dog looking a little scruffy or tangled, so they pop them right into the bathtub thinking the warm water and shampoo will loosen everything up. Please, do not do this. Water does not untangle hair—it acts like a shrink-wrap machine on loose knots, binding them together into a dense, solid felt pad that even professional equipment can't gently save. You must *always* thoroughly brush and comb your dog out before the bath, never after. 

When you sit down to brush, throw out the idea of just running the brush over the top of their coat in big, circular sweeps. Surface brushing makes the outside look fluffy while the hair right against the skin is turning into dreadlocks. Grab a slicker brush and use short, straight "line" strokes. Part the hair with one hand so you can see the skin, and use gentle, short downward strokes with the other, working your way through the coat in small sections from the skin outward. 

I always recommend starting with the trouble zones where friction is highest. Mats almost always start behind the ears (from scratching and petting) and under the front legs in the armpit area (from walking and harnesses). Tackle those spots first while your dog is still patient, parting the fur and working through layer by layer. 

If you do find a knot that's already starting to clump together, step away from the brush for a second. Raking a brush directly over a tight mat just pulls the skin and hurts the dog, which makes them hate grooming time. Instead, take a small dab of dog-safe leave-in conditioner or detangler and work it deep into the knot using only your fingers. Gently wiggle and massage the hair apart with your fingertips to break up the core of the tangle. Once it’s softened and loosened with your hands, *then* you can gently tease it out with the edge of a slicker brush or the wide teeth of a metal comb.

Spending five to ten minutes doing this a couple of times a week will keep your pup comfortable, happy, and tangle-free until I see them next on the grooming table. And as always, if you're struggling with a specific spot, leave it alone so you don't hurt the skin, and let me know at drop-off—I'm always happy to show you the line-brushing motion in person!

setup: A family plumbing company owner is writing a blog post for Minneapolis homeowners about winterizing outdoor pipes.

a.text:
## How to Winterize Your Outside Spigots

If you’ve got outdoor spigots on your Minneapolis home, winterizing them is one of the easiest ways to avoid a burst pipe call in January.

The big mistake we see most often is leaving a hose connected. That traps water in the line, and when temperatures drop, that water freezes, expands, and can split the pipe or the spigot. Most of our January burst-pipe calls start with a hose left on outside.

Here’s how to do it right.

### 1. Shut off the interior valve
Most homes have a shutoff valve for exterior spigots inside the house, usually in the basement, utility room, or near the main water line. Turn that valve off before the first hard freeze.

If you do not have an interior shutoff for your outside spigot, call us. We can help you figure out what you’ve got and whether it needs to be updated.

### 2. Drain the spigot
After the interior valve is off, go outside and open the spigot so any water left in the line can drain out. Leave it open long enough for the water to stop running.

If there’s a drain cap or bleed point on the inside shutoff, use that too if your setup has one.

### 3. Disconnect every hose
This is the step a lot of people skip. Disconnect garden hoses, sprinklers, splitters, and hose timers from the spigot.

Even one hose left attached can hold water in the line and keep the spigot from draining properly.

### 4. Put on a foam cover
A basic foam spigot cover costs about $3 and gives you a little extra protection against wind and cold. It’s not a substitute for shutting off and draining the line, but it’s a good final step.

### Quick checklist
- Shut off the interior valve
- Open the outside spigot and drain it
- Disconnect all hoses and attachments
- Install a foam cover

That’s it. A few minutes now can save you from a frozen pipe, water damage, and an expensive repair later.

If you don’t have an interior shutoff for your outside spigots, or you’re not sure whether your setup is winterized correctly, give us a call. We’d be happy to take a look before the cold really sets in.

b.text:
# How to Winterize Outside Spigots in Minneapolis

The most important step is simple: **disconnect every garden hose from your outside spigots.**

Leaving a hose connected traps water inside the faucet and pipe. When that water freezes, it expands and can split the pipe—often inside the wall, where you won’t notice the damage until it thaws. This is behind many of the burst-pipe calls we get around Minneapolis every January.

Here’s how to properly winterize your outdoor faucets.

## 1. Disconnect All Hoses and Attachments

Remove garden hoses, splitters, timers, spray nozzles, and other attachments from every outside spigot.

Don’t just turn off the faucet and leave the hose attached. Even a frost-free spigot can freeze if a hose prevents it from draining.

After disconnecting the hose:

- Drain it completely.
- Coil it without sharp bends.
- Store it in a garage, basement, or shed.
- Remove any Y-connectors, quick-connect fittings, or timers from the spigot.

This is the easiest step, and it prevents a large share of frozen outdoor pipe problems.

## 2. Shut Off the Interior Valve

Find the interior shutoff valve that supplies the outside spigot. In Minneapolis homes, it may be located in the basement, utility room, crawlspace, or near the point where the pipe exits the foundation.

Turn the valve clockwise until it is fully closed. If you have a lever-style ball valve, turn the handle one-quarter turn so it is perpendicular to the pipe.

Don’t force a valve that is stuck or badly corroded. Older shutoffs can break or begin leaking when disturbed.

## 3. Drain the Outside Spigot

Once the interior valve is closed, go outside and open the spigot. Let the remaining water drain out.

Some interior shutoff valves have a small drain cap or bleeder screw on the side. If yours does, place a bucket underneath it and carefully open the cap to drain water trapped between the shutoff and the outdoor faucet. Close the cap when you’re finished.

If water continues flowing instead of slowing to a stop, the interior shutoff may not be closing completely. That should be repaired before hard-freezing temperatures arrive.

## 4. Install a Foam Faucet Cover

Place an insulated foam cover over the outside spigot. These usually cost around **$3** at a hardware or home-improvement store.

Hook the cover onto the faucet, pull it snug against the wall, and make sure there aren’t large gaps around the edges. The cover provides an extra layer of protection from cold air and wind.

A foam cover helps, but it does not replace shutting off and draining the pipe. Simply covering a water-filled spigot is not enough during a Minneapolis cold snap.

## What If You Have a Frost-Free Spigot?

Frost-free spigots are designed so the actual shutoff point sits farther inside the house, where temperatures are warmer. They still need to drain properly.

That means you must disconnect the hose and every other attachment. If a hose is left connected, water can remain trapped inside the faucet body and freeze. A frost-free faucet can also fail if it was installed without the proper downward slope.

If you’re unsure what type of outdoor faucet you have, winterize it using the steps above or have a plumber inspect it.

## Don’t Have an Interior Shutoff?

Some homes don’t have a dedicated interior shutoff for each outside faucet. Others have old valves that no longer work or are hidden behind finished walls.

If you can’t find a shutoff, or your valve leaks or won’t close, call us. We can inspect the line and install or replace an accessible interior shutoff so the outdoor spigot can be properly drained each fall.

## Quick Outdoor Spigot Winterizing Checklist

Before temperatures drop, make sure you have:

- Disconnected every hose and attachment
- Closed the interior shutoff valve
- Opened and drained the outside spigot
- Drained the line through the bleeder cap, if present
- Installed a $3 insulated foam faucet cover
- Checked for dripping, damaged, or stuck valves

A few minutes of work can prevent a split pipe, water damage, and an emergency plumbing call in the middle of a Minneapolis winter. If you don’t have an interior shutoff or aren’t sure your outdoor plumbing is protected, contact our family plumbing company for help.

setup: A high-school senior is writing a personal essay for college admissions readers about working at her family's Vietnamese restaurant.

a.text:
The walk-in cooler stays at thirty-eight degrees. On Saturday afternoons, after the lunch rush clears out, I take a fifteen-minute break on an overturned pickle bucket next to the crates of green onions. I keep my winter coat hanging on a hook by the meat slicer specifically for this. It’s the only place in the building quiet enough to concentrate, so I sit there with my knees pulled up, working through derivatives on scrap paper, the cold ink barely flowing from my pen until my fingers go numb and it’s time to prep for dinner.

I’ve worked weekends at my parents' restaurant, Phở Bình, since the first week of tenth grade. Most of what I know about efficiency I learned between the dish pit and the six-burner range. 

Last fall, we hired Tommy, a sophomore from my school, to help with prep. His first Saturday, he tore four rice papers in a row trying to roll *gỏi cuốn*. The wrappers are fragile; you dip them in warm water for two seconds, no longer, and let them soften on the cutting board while you lay down the shrimp, pork, and mint. 

"Don't pull so hard," I told him, showing him how my grandmother does it. "Tuck the sides in first like an envelope, then roll forward with your palms, not your fingertips. If there’s air inside, they fall apart when people bite them." 

We made eighty of them side by side. By the fiftieth, he stopped tearing the wrappers. By five o'clock, the metal tray in the cold well was full, covered with damp paper towels so they wouldn't dry out under the heat lamps.

Dinner service usually runs on muscle memory, but two months ago, right at six-thirty on a rainy Saturday, the entire point-of-sale system went black. The kitchen printer stopped feeding, the screen wouldn't reboot, and we had forty people seated with eight more waiting by the door. 

My mom started apologizing to Table 3, but apologies don't get noodles into bowls. I found three pads of carbon-copy guest checks in the dry storage closet, handed one to my sister, and kept two for myself. I took orders by hand, writing the table numbers in the top right corner and using our kitchen shorthand: *T* for tái, *G* for gầu, *B* for bún. I walked the tickets straight back to my dad on the line, calling out the bowl sizes and whether people wanted extra cilantro. 

For two hours, nobody sat down. My dad ladled broth, my mom dropped noodles into boiling water, and I ran food, cleared tables, and added up bills in my head, calculating the 8.25% sales tax on the back of the receipts before running credit cards through the manual dial-up terminal we usually keep under the counter for emergencies. 

When the rush finally died down around nine, the linoleum behind the line was slick with broth, my apron was soaked through, and the trash can was full of yellow duplicate slips. The system didn't come back on until Monday morning, but every table got their food, and the register drawer balanced within three dollars when we counted out the cash.

We swept the floor, bleached the cutting boards, and turned off the neon open sign. I took off my apron, got my backpack from the office, and checked my phone. It was almost ten. I still had forty pages of US History to read before Sunday morning prep, but my dad handed me a quart container of broth to take home, still hot enough to burn through the plastic.

b.text:
The register died on a Saturday in March, which is the worst day for anything to die. My dad hit the power strip twice and said a word in Vietnamese I'm not supposed to know. The screen stayed black. There were eleven tables seated and four more on the sidewalk looking at their phones.

I got the pad of green order tickets we keep in the drawer under the soy sauce, the ones nobody has used since before I was born, and I started writing. Pho tai, no onion. Bun cha gio, extra fish sauce on the side. Table six wanted their check split three ways and I did the math on the back of the ticket with a pen that kept skipping. I don't know how many I wrote. My handwriting got worse and worse until the last ones looked like a doctor's. My mom read every one of them anyway. She has been reading my dad's handwriting for twenty-six years, so mine wasn't a problem.

We didn't lose a single order. We were forty minutes behind by seven o'clock and a man at table two told me he'd waited longer at the DMV, which I think he meant nicely.

---

We hired a guy named Marcus in the fall. Nineteen, worked at a car wash before. My grandma was supposed to teach him the spring rolls but her hands were bad that month, so she sat on the milk crate by the prep table and pointed and I did the showing.

The fold is not hard. That's the thing people don't believe. You wet the wrapper but not too much, you put the filling in a line a little below the middle, you fold the bottom up, then the two sides in, then you roll it tight and you don't stop rolling once you start. Marcus's first ten came out like little pillows. Too loose. They'd blow open in the oil.

My grandma said something and I told him, tighter, and he said tighter how, and I couldn't explain it in English or in Vietnamese, so I put my hands over his hands and we rolled one together. It came out fine. He did the next four hundred that day and by the end they were all fine. He still works there. He's faster than me now.

---

There's a shelf in the walk-in cooler above the cases of Coke where nobody puts anything, and that's where I do calc.

It's thirty-eight degrees. My break is fifteen minutes and I take it at 3:40, after lunch and before the dinner people. I bring my notebook and a pencil because pens get weird in the cold. I sit on an upturned bucket with my back against the beer boxes.

It's loud out there. Order up, the fan hood, my uncle's phone playing a game show at full volume, somebody's kid. In the cooler it's just the compressor kicking on and off. I can hear my own pencil. I've done most of a semester of related rates in there with my coat on over my apron, and once I fell asleep for six minutes and my mom found me and said I was going to get pneumonia and be useless.

I got a 94 on that unit test. I don't think the cooler had anything to do with it. It's just quiet, and it's the only door in that building that locks from the inside.

---

setup: A small dog grooming salon owner is writing a how-to for dog owners about preventing coat matting between grooming visits.

a.text:
I see it all the time with double-coated and curly dogs—those beautiful coats that look so soft until you try to run a brush through them a couple weeks after their last appointment and hit a wall of mats. Between visits is when most of the trouble starts, and the biggest mistake I watch people make is jumping straight into a bath thinking warm water and shampoo will loosen everything up. It does the opposite. Once that fur gets wet, any little tangle turns into a dense felt pad that is ten times harder to get out. You end up with a dog that needs a full shave-down when a little dry brushing could have saved the coat.

So brush first, always, while the dog is completely dry. Grab a slicker brush and work in short line strokes—think gentle little lines, not big circles that just push the hair around and create more knots. Start in the spots where mats love to form first: right behind the ears and under the front legs. Those areas rub and collect moisture, so if you keep them clear, the rest of the coat usually stays manageable. Section the dog as you go so you can actually see what you’re doing instead of just skimming the surface.

If you already feel a mat starting to form, stop before you even pick up the brush. Work a little conditioner into it with your fingers, really massage it in, and let it sit for a minute. That softens the tangle so the brush or comb can slip through without ripping. Once it’s loosened, then you can carefully work it out. Trying to force a dry mat with a comb is how you end up with broken hair and a sore dog.

A few minutes of this a couple times a week keeps most coats from turning into a project between appointments. Your dog stays more comfortable, and when they come in for their next groom we can focus on the fun stuff instead of digging out weeks of mats.

b.text:
**Why your dog keeps coming in matted (and what to do at home)**

Most of the dogs I see with mats didn't get that way because anyone was neglecting them. They got that way because somebody did the exact thing that seems like it should help, and it made everything worse. So before I get into brushing, I want to talk about the bath.

Please don't bathe a matted dog. I know the logic. The coat's dirty and tangled, water and shampoo loosen things up, you'll deal with the knots after. That's how it works with our hair. It is not how it works with a doodle or a Golden or an Aussie. When a mat gets wet, the hairs swell and grip each other, and as it dries it shrinks down into something closer to felt than fur. What was a loose tangle I could have brushed out in a few minutes is now a solid pad against the skin, and the only kind option is to clip it off. If I've ever had to shave your dog shorter than you wanted, this is almost always why.

So the order is brush first, then bath. Always. If you find something you can't get through, leave the bath for another day or call me. I'd much rather you bring in a dry, tangled dog than a clean one that's been felted.

Now the brushing itself. For double coats and curly coats you want a slicker brush, the one with the flat head and all the fine bent wires. Not the soft bristle brush, not the rubber curry. Those feel nice to the dog and do nothing underneath. The slicker is what actually gets down into the layer where mats start.

The way you move it matters more than people think. You want short, straight strokes, a couple of inches at a time, always in the direction the hair grows. Line up a stroke, brush, move over, brush again. What you don't want is scrubbing in circles or dragging the brush in one long pull from neck to tail. Circles twist the hair around itself and start new tangles. Long pulls skate over the top and miss everything close to the skin. Think of it like you're combing through a little section at a time and checking that the brush is reaching skin before you move on.

Work in sections, and start where the trouble starts. On almost every dog that's behind the ears and under the front legs, in that armpit area where the collar and the harness rub. Those two spots mat before anywhere else, so if you only have five minutes, spend them there. After that go to the chest, the back legs and rear, the belly, the base of the tail. The back is usually the least of your worries even though it's the part that gets petted the most.

If you run your fingers through and feel a clump starting to form, stop. Don't go at it with the brush yet. Get a little leave-in conditioner or detangling spray and work it into that spot with your fingers. Actually massage it in and start gently pulling the hair apart with your fingertips. A lot of small mats will loosen up this way before a brush ever touches them. Once you can feel the individual hairs moving again, then you go in with the slicker, from the outside edge of the tangle toward the center, in those same short strokes. If it's tight against the skin and won't budge with your fingers, that's the point where you leave it for me. Pulling harder just hurts the dog and teaches them to hate the brush.

A few minutes every other day beats an hour on Sunday. The coat never gets a chance to lock up, the dog gets used to it, and you'll actually notice the small stuff before it turns into the big stuff. And when you bring them in, tell me where you've been finding tangles. It helps me know what's going on with the coat and whether the harness or the collar might need adjusting.

If you're not sure you've got the right brush, bring it to your next appointment and I'll take a look. Happy to show you the stroke on your own dog too, that's easier than reading about it.

setup: A retired rural mail carrier is writing a letter to the Kettle Falls Courier urging residents to oppose the post office counter closure at the July 28 forum.

a.text:
To the Editor,

Most folks around here know me from Route 4. I drove those 38 miles six days a week for 22 years before retiring last year, so I have a pretty fair idea of how this town works and what people need. 

The Postal Service says our counter service in Kettle Falls is losing $40,000 a year. What they leave out is that they cut our window hours down to four hours a morning—8 a.m. to noon—a few years back. When you cut the hours in half, cut the staff, and make it hard for working people to get in the door, of course customer traffic is going to drop off. It doesn't take an accountant to see they’re pointing at a problem they made themselves to justify shutting the counter for good.

This isn’t just numbers on a balance sheet. Think about folks like Mrs. Halloran up on Kettle Hill. She’s in her eighties, lives alone, and gets her heart medication through the mail. She doesn't use the internet, and she doesn't drive anymore. If she needs to send a package, buy stamps, or get a money order to pay her electric bill, she can’t just hop in a car and make the twenty-minute drive over to Fairview. There are dozens of people on my old route in the exact same boat.

The USPS district manager is coming to town for a public forum on Tuesday, July 28, at the Grange Hall. If you care about keeping our town whole, you need to show up and fill those seats. They need to look us in the eye and hear why Kettle Falls still needs a real post office.

Don Mason
Kettle Falls

b.text:
To the Editor:

I'm not a writer, so I'll keep this plain.

I drove Route 4 here in Kettle Falls for 22 years, 38 miles a day, and retired last year. I know this town and I know the folks on my route.

The Postal Service says our branch loses $40,000 a year and that's why they want to close the counter. But they don't tell you they already cut our window down to 8 to noon. Of course traffic dropped after that. Folks who work can't get in during those hours. They're pointing at a problem they made themselves.

Take Mrs. Halloran up on Kettle Hill. She's in her 80s, gets her heart meds by mail, and counts on that counter for stamps and money orders. She can't drive twenty minutes to Fairview to get a money order once our counter closes. There's a lot of folks like her that I used to deliver to.

If you care about keeping it, show up to the forum on July 28 at the Grange Hall. Let the district manager hear it in person.

Retired Rural Carrier, Route 4
Kettle Falls

setup: You're everyone at the startup. Yesterday's 40-minute outage was caused by a bad database migration during deploy.

a.text:
Hi everyone,

First, the most important update: our systems are fully stable, and all services have been running normally since yesterday afternoon. 

As you know, we experienced a 40-minute outage yesterday starting around 2:00 PM. I want to apologize to the team for the disruption, especially to those of you who had to field urgent messages and complaints from our customers while we were down. 

Here is a quick, non-technical breakdown of what happened and how we are making sure it doesn't happen again:

**What happened:**
During a routine software update, we ran a "database migration" (a command that updates how our database is structured). This particular update locked one of our main data tables for much longer than expected. Because the table was locked, the rest of the application couldn't talk to the database, which caused the site to go down. Once we identified the bottleneck, we rolled back the update to restore service. 

**How we are preventing this going forward:**
While we test our updates thoroughly, database behavior can be unpredictable under live traffic. Going forward, we are changing our process: any database migrations that carry a risk of locking tables will no longer be run during our regular daytime deployments. Instead, we will schedule them during designated off-peak maintenance windows to ensure zero impact on our users. 

Thank you all for your patience and for helping us manage the situation yesterday. If you need any specific details or language to share with customers who reached out, please let me know and I'll be happy to help.

b.text:
Hi team,

The outage from yesterday is fully resolved. Our service was down for about 40 minutes starting around 2pm, and it’s been running normally since we rolled back the change yesterday afternoon.

**What happened:** A routine deploy included a database update that took far longer than expected. While it was running, it blocked access to the data our product needs, which caused the downtime.

**What we did:** We identified the issue, rolled back the update, and restored service.

**What’s changing:** Going forward, we’ll run any database changes in a dedicated maintenance window rather than during a normal deploy. This lets us watch them closely and stop or fix issues before they affect customers.

I know some of you had to deal with frustrated customers during those 40 minutes—sorry for the headache. If you have any questions, just reply here or grab me.

setup: A small HVAC company owner is writing a how-to for homeowners on bleeding air from hot water baseboard radiators before winter.

a.text:
Shut the circulator and the boiler off first. Do not bleed with the pump running.

Start at the baseboard closest to the boiler and work outward, unit by unit. Each one has a small bleeder valve on the end. Hold a cup or rag underneath, then crack it open slowly with a radiator key or flathead. Air hisses out first. Keep it open until you get a steady stream of water with no more sputtering. Close it snug. Do not overtighten or you will crack the valve seat.

Do every unit, including the basement loop. Skipping the basement is the mistake behind most of our cold radiator calls. That is usually where the air is sitting.

Turn the system back on when you are finished.

b.text:
Shut off the circulator pump or boiler before you open any valves. If the system is running when you crack a bleeder, you’ll force air down the line instead of out of it, and you’ll probably get sprayed. Give the boiler ten minutes to settle and the pressure to flatten out.

Start with the baseboard unit closest to the boiler and work your way outward, one by one. Each unit has a bleeder valve on one end—usually a small brass fitting with a square nut or a slotted stem. Slide a cup, small bowl, or heavy rag underneath before you touch it.

Open the valve slowly with a bleeder key or a flathead screwdriver. You’ll hear hissing first. That’s the air leaving. Keep it cracked until the stream of water runs steady and quiet, with no sputtering or bubbles. Depending on how much air is trapped, this can take thirty seconds or several minutes.

Once the flow is solid, close the valve snug, but do not reef on it. These brass seats crack easily, and an overtightened bleeder will drip or weep all winter. Finger-tight plus a quarter turn is usually enough.

Repeat this at every unit in the house. The mistake that generates most of our cold-radiator calls is homeowners bleeding only the upstairs baseboards and skipping the basement loop. The air that collects at the top of the system usually got pushed there from below. If you skip the basement, you’ll be bleeding the upstairs again in a week.

When you finish the last unit, check the boiler pressure gauge. Bleeding drops the system pressure, so you may need to add water through the fill valve to get back to the manufacturer’s recommended range—usually 12 to 15 psi for a one- or two-story home. If you’re unsure how to add water or the pressure won’t hold, shut the boiler down and give us a call.

setup: A high-school senior is writing a personal essay for college admissions readers about working at her family's Vietnamese restaurant.

a.text:
I work weekends at my family's Vietnamese restaurant. Every Saturday and Sunday since sophomore year.

The register died one Saturday during lunch. Line out the door, dining room full. I grabbed a pad and a pen and started writing tickets. Table 12, two pho dac biet, one bun, extra herbs. I'd write it, tear the sheet, pass it through the window. Kitchen yelled when they couldn't read my writing. We went through the whole pad. My hand hurt by the time my dad got the system working again around three.

We hired someone new last month. I showed him how my grandma folds the spring rolls. Lay the rice paper down, filling in a straight line, fold the sides in first so nothing spills, then roll it. Tight enough it holds, not so tight it splits. He kept making them loose in the middle. I did a few more while he watched, then let him try again.

Breaks I take my calc book into the walk-in. Sit on a box of sprouts, do the problems. Fan noise, cold air. Fingers stiff after a while. When the break's over I put the book away and go back out.

That's the weekends.

b.text:
I have worked every weekend at my family's Vietnamese restaurant since sophomore year. Saturdays start early and run late.

One Saturday the register system died right in the middle of lunch. Screens went black. People kept walking in. I grabbed the old paper pads we keep in the drawer and wrote every ticket by hand. Table 4, two orders of pho with rare steak, one no onions, spring rolls, extra chili. I tore them off and stuck them on the wheel. The cooks asked me to rewrite a couple that got smudged. My hand cramped by dinner, but we filled every order that way.

I show new hires how to fold the spring rolls the way my grandma does it. Rice paper flat, filling in a thin line, bottom edge up first, sides tucked in tight so no air pockets form, then roll it closed and wet the last edge to seal. Loose ones fall apart in the fryer. The last kid I trained kept leaving them soft. I made a few next to him, slow, then watched him try until his looked right.

Breaks are short. Calculus needs quiet, so I take my book into the walk-in cooler. I sit on a milk crate in my jacket and work the problems while the compressor hums. Cold air keeps the numbers clear. When time is up I put the book back in my bag and step out to the floor again.

setup: A remote software engineer is writing a 6-month standing desk review for blog readers researching standing desks.

a.text:
# Jarvik L2 Standing Desk: 6-Month Review

I’ve been coding at the Jarvik L2 for exactly six months. I don’t use affiliate links, so this is just my unfiltered, practical take. If you’re researching standing desks, here is what you actually need to know before you pull the trigger.

### The Motor: Fast and Quiet
The motor is objectively the best part of this desk. Moving from my seated height (28.5") to my standing height (43") takes about 8 seconds and sounds like a low, muffled hum. You can easily take a Zoom call while it transitions without the person on the other end asking what the background noise is. It’s snappy and doesn't jerk the monitors when it stops. 

### The Wobble: A Problem at Max Height
Here is the physics problem. At its maximum height (around 48"), the L2 wobbles. If you are a light typist, you won't notice. I type hard on a heavy mechanical keyboard when I'm deep in a debugging session, and at max height, my dual 27" monitors shake enough to be visually distracting. The lateral sway is noticeable. I ended up lowering my standing preset by two inches just to mitigate the wobble, which means I'm not actually using the desk at its advertised maximum height. 

### Memory Presets: They Drift
The memory presets do not stop at the exact millimeter every time. Over a few weeks of daily use, the stopping point drifts by about a centimeter. It doesn't sound like much on paper, but when your forearms are resting on the desk, a 1cm shift is the difference between comfortable ergonomics and shoulder strain by 3 PM. I find myself manually micro-adjusting the height via the up/down arrows every Friday to reset my baseline. 

### The Cable Tray: Garbage
Do not factor the included cable management tray into your purchasing decision. It is garbage. It’s made of flimsy stamped metal, the screw holes didn't perfectly align with the pre-drilled holes in my desktop, and the tray physically sags if you put a heavy UPS or a large monitor power brick in it. Throw it in the recycling bin and buy a $15 under-desk mesh cable net. 

### The Verdict
The Jarvik L2 retails for $749, but I caught it on sale for $549. 

At **$749**, it is overpriced. You are paying a premium for a desk that wobbles when fully extended and requires you to babysit the memory presets. At that price point, there are more stable dual-motor options on the market.

At **$549**, it’s a highly utilitarian piece of hardware with a fantastic motor. If you can wait for a holiday sale, buy it for $549, and budget an extra $20 for a third-party cable management solution, it’s absolutely worth it. Pay full MSRP and you'll regret it.

b.text:
**6-Month Review: Jarvik L2 Standing Desk**

I bought the Jarvik L2 standing desk exactly six months ago. As a remote software engineer, I am stationed at this desk for 8 to 10 hours a day. I don’t do sponsored content, and there are zero affiliate links in this post. If you are researching this desk, here is exactly how it holds up to real, daily use. 

**The Good: The Motor**
The dual-motor system on the L2 is genuinely excellent. It is remarkably quiet—I routinely adjust it from sitting to standing during Zoom standups without muting my mic, and nobody hears a thing. It’s also incredibly fast. It clears the distance to my standing height in about five seconds and doesn't struggle or groan, even when lifting a dual 27-inch monitor setup, a heavy duty mount, my MacBook, and a pair of studio monitors. 

**The Annoying: Wobble and Drift**
The desk has two specific engineering flaws that you need to know about. 

First is the stability at height. When I am seated (around 29 inches), the desk is a rock. However, when I raise it to my standing height (42 inches) and type hard, the desk wobbles. I use a mechanical keyboard with heavy tactile switches, and my aggressive typing translates straight into lateral monitor jiggle. It’s not going to collapse, but if you are an aggressive coder, the screen shake will annoy you.

Second, the electronics have a bizarre quirk: the memory presets drift. Over a few months of use, my saved "standing" preset slowly creeps off target by about a centimeter. I end up having to manually dial it back in and re-save the preset every eight weeks. It feels like a lazy firmware issue that shouldn't exist on a modern desk.

**The Garbage: The Cable Tray**
Do not factor the included cable management into your buying decision. The tray Jarvik includes is absolute garbage. It’s a rigid, awkwardly designed piece of flimsy metal that doesn't hinge down for easy access. It barely has the clearance to hold a standard surge protector, let alone chunky monitor power bricks or a laptop charger. I threw it out in week two and drilled in a $25 third-party wire basket. Assume you will need to do the same.

**The Verdict: Buy the Sale, Skip the MSRP**
Jarvik lists the L2 at an MSRP of $749, but they constantly run sales dropping it to $549.
