setup: A retired rural mail carrier is writing a letter to the Kettle Falls Courier urging residents to oppose the post office counter closure at the July 28 forum.

a.text:
To the Editor:

I drove Route 4 out of the Kettle Falls post office for 22 years. Thirty-eight miles, six days a week, in mud season and in January. I retired last year. I am not a writer, so I will say this plainly.

The Postal Service wants to close our counter service. The reason they give is that the branch loses about $40,000 a year. I would like people to think about where that number comes from.

A few years back they cut the window hours from a full day down to eight to noon. Anybody who has ever run a business could tell you what happens next. Folks who work days can't get in. Folks who used to mail a package on their lunch hour go to Fairview instead, or they order a label online, or they just quit bothering. Traffic dropped. Of course it dropped. Then the receipts dropped with it.

So now they hold up the low numbers as proof the counter isn't needed. That is pointing at a problem they made themselves. It is like cutting a man's hours to half time and then firing him for not getting enough done.

I want to say something about what the counter actually does, because a report in an office somewhere does not show it.

Mrs. Halloran lives up on Kettle Hill. She is in her eighties. Her heart medication comes by mail, and it has come by mail for years, and I carried it up that hill more times than I could count. She does not drive to Fairview. Twenty minutes each way on that road is not a small thing when you are her age and the weather turns. When she needs a money order — and she does, she pays some bills that way, the way a lot of older people around here still do — she walks into our post office and a person she knows helps her. There is no website that replaces that. There is no cluster box that replaces that.

She is not the only one. There are dozens of people on that route in the same position, and most of them will not write a letter to the paper about it.

The district manager is coming to the public forum on July 28 at the Grange Hall. I am asking people to show up. Not to yell at anybody — the folks who work in our office are our neighbors and this is not their doing. Just show up, so the man from the district can see the room is full and can hear it from people who live here.

Numbers on a page are easy to close. A room full of your customers is harder.

Please come.

— [Name], Kettle Falls
Retired rural carrier, Route 4

b.text:
To the Editor:

I drove Route 4 for 22 years before I retired last year. Thirty-eight miles every day through this town and the hills around it. I know the people on that route, and I know what the post office means here.

Now they’re talking about closing the counter service at our Kettle Falls office. The USPS says the branch loses $40,000 a year. That number only showed up after they cut the hours from 8 a.m. down to noon. Of course the traffic dropped. Fewer hours, fewer customers. They’re pointing at a problem they made themselves.

Take Mrs. Halloran up on Kettle Hill. She’s in her eighties and gets her heart medicine by mail. Once the counter is gone she can’t just drive twenty minutes over to Fairview every time she needs a money order. A lot of folks in this town are in the same boat.

There’s a public forum on July 28 at the Grange Hall. The district manager will be there. Show up. Let them hear from the people who actually use this office.

I don’t write much, but this one matters.

A retired carrier,
Route 4

setup: An in-house recruiter is posting a contrarian observation about candidates asking about the team’s last failed project in interviews to recruiters, hiring managers, and job seekers.

a.text:
After interviewing over 200 people throughout my career, I’ve noticed a distinct pattern. 

The absolute best candidates—the ones who end up being the highest performers and the most resilient teammates—almost always ask some version of the same uncomfortable question. 

Usually, it comes at the end of the interview when I ask, "What questions do you have for me?"

Instead of the standard queries about culture or day-to-day duties, they ask: 

"What was your team’s last major failed project, and how did people react to it?"

Here is how that conversation usually goes:

Candidate: "I know every company has setbacks. What’s the last project on your team that completely fell apart, and why?"

Me: "Honestly, we tried to roll out a new routing software update last year. It was supposed to save our dispatchers two hours a day, but the integration failed, we lost real-time tracking for six hours, and we had to roll the whole thing back."

Candidate: "And what happened next? How did the leadership team handle the mistake, and what did the post-mortem look like?"

That second question is where the magic happens. 

They aren’t asking to catch me in a gotcha moment. They are trying to figure out if we have psychological safety. They want to know if we point fingers when things go sideways, or if we actually run blameless post-mortems and pivot. 

Top talent doesn't expect your company to be perfect. They just want to make sure you aren't pretending to be. 

If you are a job seeker, try asking this in your next interview. You’ll learn more about a company’s true culture in two minutes than you will in two weeks of reading reviews online. 

And if you are a hiring manager, don’t sugarcoat your answer. If you pretend you’ve never failed, the best candidates will see right through it.

b.text:
~200 interviews in, I've noticed one question that separates the best candidates from everyone else. It's not about growth, culture, or "what does success look like."

It's: "Tell me about your last failed project."

The strongest people I interview don't ask whether we fail. They assume we do. They want to know what happens next.

One example from a few months back. Ops manager candidate, interview going fine, nothing remarkable. Their turn to ask questions:

"Tell me about the last project here that actually failed. Not a setback. A failure."

Our ops director paused, then told them about a WMS cutover we botched a couple years ago. Three weeks of wrecked pick rates, a couple of accounts that walked, some very uncomfortable retrospectives. Didn't sugarcoat any of it.

Then the candidate asked the follow-up that told me everything:

"Are the people who ran it still here? And did anything structurally change?"

That's not a gotcha. That's due diligence. They were mapping how failure moves through this company — does it get owned and fixed, or buried along with whoever touched it?

We hired them. A few months in they killed one of our internal projects that wasn't working. Early, cleanly, no drama. I think about that a lot.

If you're interviewing somewhere: this question costs you nothing and reveals almost everything about how a company treats people when things go wrong.

If you're hiring: notice who asks it. In my experience, the people who ask about your failures have survived a few of their own.

a.text:
**RoadStar DC4 Dash Cam – 14 Months & 140K Miles In**

Been running the RoadStar DC4 for over a year now, and it’s mostly held up to the abuse. The front cam is solid—day or night, footage is clear enough to make out license plates at highway speeds. The rear cam? Not so much. Night footage gets grainy past 30 feet, but it’s still better than nothing.

Biggest win? Caught a four-wheeler sideswiping me during a lane change. Insurance had the claim approved in nine days instead of the usual six weeks. Worth every penny for that alone.

The suction mount is garbage in summer heat—fell off twice before I swapped it for the adhesive mount. Stick with the adhesive; it hasn’t budged since.

The app’s a joke. Needs Wi-Fi to pull footage, which is useless at most truck stops. I just pop the SD card and transfer files to my phone. Not ideal, but it works.

Battery life’s decent—no issues even in extreme temps. Build quality’s solid, no random shutdowns or overheating.

Bottom line: If you need a no-frills dash cam that’ll hold up to long-haul abuse, this one’s a solid pick. Just skip the suction mount and don’t expect miracles from the rear cam at night.

b.text:
**Quick Review: Roadstar DC4 (140k Miles / 14 Months)**

Figured I’d drop a quick, no-BS review on the Roadstar DC4 after running it for 14 months and about 140,000 miles across the lower 48. 

**The Good:**
This thing has already paid for itself ten times over. Had a four-wheeler try to merge into my steer tire on I-80. The front camera caught the entire lane change clear as day. Handed the video to the adjuster, and the claim was approved in 9 days instead of the usual 6-week finger-pointing match. Front video quality in daylight and standard night driving is crisp.

**The Annoying:**
* **The Mount:** Toss the suction cup in the trash right out of the box. It melted off my windshield twice during summer runs through the southwest. Swapped over to the semi-permanent adhesive mount and it hasn't budged an inch since.
* **The App:** Total waste of time on the road. It forces you onto a Wi-Fi connection to download clips, which is completely useless sitting in a truck stop parking lot. Don't bother fighting it—just keep a $10 USB card reader in your glove box and pull the micro SD card directly.

**The Rear Cam:**
It’s decent for backing and close-quarters daytime, but night footage gets real grainy past 30 feet. It’ll prove whether someone rear-ended you, but don't expect to read a license plate at a distance in the pitch black.

**Bottom Line:**
It’s got a few quirks, but it works when it counts. If you buy one, stick it on with the adhesive pad, manage your footage via the SD card, and let it do its job. Worth the money just for the insurance protection.

b.text:
We're hiring our first support person at Ridgepoint. Here's the honest reason: there are three of us, and right now we all answer every ticket ourselves. It worked at 20 customers. At the number we're at now it means one of us is context-switching out of product work five times a morning, and some tickets sit longer than a dispatcher with a truck waiting should have to wait.

So here's what the job actually is, day to day.

Our customers are small trucking dispatchers. Usually one or two people scheduling loads for a handful of drivers. They message us when something's in the way of getting a truck moving: a load won't drop onto the board, a driver's available hours aren't matching what they expect, a spreadsheet import came in wrong, they need to add a new shipper and don't know where. Mornings are the busiest because that's when they're lining up the day.

Most of it is figuring out what someone actually needs, walking them through it, and doing it fast enough that they can get back to work. Some of it is spotting that the thing they're describing is a bug, reproducing it, and writing it up clearly enough that one of us can fix it without asking you ten questions. setup: A general contractor is writing a short X thread to contractors, homeowners, and architects about a hidden joist problem and the lesson learned.

a.text:
1/4  
Maple Ave kitchen job taught me a good one this week: the floor looked fine from below, but once we opened it up, I found a joist issue hiding under the old subfloor.

2/4  
One joist had a bad notch near a bearing point and a couple others had been drilled way too generously by a previous crew. Nothing dramatic enough to notice day-to-day, but enough to matter once cabinets, tile, and a busy kitchen go back on top.

3/4  
Fix was straightforward but not cheap: sistered the damaged framing, added blocking, and reworked a small section of the floor system before we moved forward. Cost the job about $1,400 in labor and materials, plus the delay to get it right.

4/4  
Lesson: in remodels, the expensive part usually isn’t the repair itself — it’s the stuff you have to undo because someone assumed the framing was “probably fine.” If you’re opening walls or floors, check the structure early and budget for what’s actually there, not what the plans hope is there.

b.text:
**Tweet 1:**
Maple Ave kitchen demo yesterday. Pulled up the subfloor and found the rim joist was completely rotted—not just surface, but punky all the way through. House was built in '78, no issues visible from below. This is why we open walls.

**Tweet 2:**
Called in a structural engineer to be safe. Turns out water had been wicking up from the foundation for years, probably from poor grading on that side of the house. The joist needed full replacement—$3,200 in materials and labor we didn't bid.

**Tweet 3:**
The lesson: if a kitchen is over the rim joist and you're doing demo, budget time for inspection. A $200 engineer call saves you from eating $3K+ in repairs. Also, always check grading around foundations during the estimate walk.

setup: An in-house recruiter is posting a contrarian observation about candidates asking about the team’s last failed project in interviews to recruiters, hiring managers, and job seekers.

a.text:
After ~200 interviews over 9 years as an in-house recruiter in logistics, I’ve noticed one question that reliably separates the candidates I remember from those I don’t:

“What’s the last project here that didn’t go as planned?”

Most candidates ask about success stories—the big wins, the growth numbers. This one flips the script.

I had a candidate ask this recently. I told them about a warehouse automation pilot we launched two years ago that ended up delaying shipments for a week. The candidate didn’t flinch. They asked, “Why did it fail? What would you do differently? And how did the team react internally?”

We talked for 10 minutes about root causes, leadership response, and how the team rebuilt trust with customers. The candidate shared a similar story from their own experience—how they handled a tech rollout that broke a key process.

That conversation told me three things: they understand that every company has failures, they care about how an organization learns, and they have the maturity to talk openly about mistakes. It’s a low-key test for psychological safety and growth mindset.

To job seekers: skip the generic “what’s the culture like?” and ask about a real mess the team worked through. You’ll learn more about the company—and the interviewer will learn more about you.

#recruiting #interviews #logistics #hiring #careeradvice

b.text:
After roughly 200 interviews for our logistics teams, one specific moment consistently separates strong candidates from the ones we end up fighting to hire.

It happens at the end of the call, right when I ask, "What questions do you have for me?"

The candidates who usually get the offer don't ask about company culture perks or ideal start dates right away. They ask about our last failed project.

Here’s how that conversation usually goes:

Candidate: "What’s the biggest operational project that fell apart here recently?"

Me: "We tried rolling out a new route-optimization tool to three regional hubs last year. The software wasn't ready for our edge cases, drivers hated the interface, and on-time deliveries dipped for two straight weeks."

Candidate: "How did leadership react to that dip? Did they blame the hubs, or did they pivot?"

Me: "We pulled the tool from two hubs, kept it in one to debug, and put two fleet supervisors in the daily product feedback calls until it actually worked."

Candidate: "Good. That tells me failure isn't swept under the rug here, and field feedback actually influences tech decisions. That’s what I needed to know."

Average candidates want to know what success looks like on day one. Top candidates want to know what happens when things go wrong on day thirty. 

When a candidate asks about your worst moments, they aren't trying to catch you in a trap. They're checking for psychological safety, accountability, and how your teams handle pressure.

If you’re interviewing soon—on either side of the desk—don't just talk about the wins. Ask about the mess. You’ll learn more about a company in those five minutes than in the rest of the interview combined.

setup: A fourth-generation soybean and corn farmer is writing a newsletter commentary on crop insurance costs and SB 214 for county readers and state legislators.

a.text:
**A 22% Premium Hike Is a Real Cost to Family Farms**

This spring, I was able to get only about 60 percent of my acres planted before the late-May deadline. It simply would not stop raining.

That left prevented planting coverage as the only practical option on a significant share of our ground. But this year, USDA raised the base prevented planting premium rate in our region by 22 percent. For my operation, that increase means roughly $46,000 in additional crop-insurance cost this year alone.

That is not a small adjustment. It is money that would otherwise go toward seed, fertilizer, machinery repairs, land payments, payroll, or keeping more working capital available for the next season.

The increase is especially hard on family operations because of the way the acreage caps are structured. Once those caps apply, farms like mine can end up paying a much higher share of the cost than larger operations with more acres spread across their business. The weather does not distinguish between a family farm and a larger operation, but the current premium structure can.

Prevented planting coverage is not a windfall. It is a risk-management tool for the years when conditions make planting impossible. This year, many of us faced exactly that situation: fields too wet to plant, deadlines approaching, and no realistic way to make up the lost time.

State legislators have an opportunity to address the inequity in this system through SB 214. The bill would fix the acreage-cap issue that disproportionately burdens family-sized farms when prevented planting coverage is needed most.

I encourage Farm Bureau members and rural residents to contact their state senator and representative and ask them to support SB 214. A fairer acreage-cap structure will not change the weather, but it can make sure family farms are not carrying an unfair share of the cost when the rain will not let up.

b.text:
**A 22% Hike, 60% of My Acres, and a Bill Worth Your Phone Call**

This year USDA raised the base rate on prevented planting coverage in our region by 22 percent. On my operation that works out to roughly $46,000 more than I paid last year for the same protection.

I'd have paid it grudgingly in a normal spring. This wasn't a normal spring. The rain started the second week of April and did not quit in any meaningful way until it was too late to matter. By the late May final planting date I had 60 percent of my acres in the ground. The other 40 percent sat there with standing water in the low spots and mud you couldn't drive a four-wheeler across, let alone a planter. Anybody farming west of the river knows exactly what I'm describing because you were looking at the same thing out your own kitchen window.

So the year I actually needed prevented planting coverage is the year the premium jumped by nearly a quarter. That's the first thing I want people to sit with.

Here's the second thing, and it's the reason I'm writing.

The rate hike doesn't land evenly. The way the acreage caps are structured, the full increase applies across every acre on an operation my size. Once an operation crosses the cap threshold, the effective cost per acre starts coming down. The result is that the two large operations that farm on either side of me, both good neighbors, both running several times my acreage, are seeing a smaller percentage increase in their total premium cost than I am. Same county. Same rain. Same deadline. Same 40 percent left unplanted. Different bill.

I ran the numbers with my crop insurance agent, who I trust and who didn't argue with me. On a per-acre basis I'm paying meaningfully more for the same coverage than the operations next door. Not because I'm a worse risk. Because I'm smaller.

I don't begrudge the bigger outfits. They didn't write the rules. But a program that's supposed to help farmers stay in business through a bad spring shouldn't be quietly structured so that the fourth-generation operation on 1,200 acres carries a heavier share than the one on 6,000. That's backward, and I don't think it's what anybody intended when the caps were drawn up.

SB 214 would fix the acreage cap. It adjusts how the threshold applies so the premium increase falls proportionally instead of piling onto the operations least able to absorb it. It doesn't take anything away from the larger farms. It doesn't touch the coverage itself. It just corrects the math so that a 22 percent hike is a 22 percent hike for everybody, not 22 for some and less for others.

The bill has been sitting in committee since February. I'm told it's stalled less from opposition than from nobody making much noise about it. That part we can do something about.

If you farm in this county and you had ground you couldn't plant this spring, you already know what I'm talking about. If you didn't have that problem this year, you will eventually, and the cap will be waiting for you when you do.

Call your state senator. Call your representative. Their numbers are on the back page of this newsletter. Tell them you farm here, tell them how many acres you got planted by the deadline, and tell them you want SB 214 out of committee and onto the floor. You don't need to be eloquent. You need to be one more voice they can't ignore.

I'll be at the county meeting on the 14th. If you want to compare premium statements, bring yours. I'll have mine.

setup: A bakery owner is writing a warm blog and newsletter post to regular customers explaining why wedding cake orders are ending.

a.text:
**A little news about wedding cakes**

If you've been coming in for a while, you've probably seen a tiered cake or two go out our back door on a Saturday morning, wrapped in a box that's taller than the person carrying it. We've done a lot of those over the years, and we loved almost every one of them. So I want to tell you directly, before you hear it secondhand, that we've decided to stop taking custom wedding orders.

I've been going back and forth on how to say this for a couple of weeks, mostly because I don't want it to sound like a complaint. It isn't one. We're a three-person shop, and I just want to be honest with you about what the math looks like from our side of the counter.

A wedding cake isn't really a cake, it's a project. There's the first meeting, and then the tasting, and then the follow-up email about whether the ribbon should be sage or eucalyptus (there is a difference, I've learned), and then usually another meeting, and then the sketches, and then the delivery. When I actually sat down and added it up this winter, each order was taking something like fourteen hours of time we weren't charging for before a single egg got cracked. Fourteen hours, for us, is most of a workweek for one person. And I want to be clear, none of the couples did anything wrong. That's just what it takes to do it well, and I didn't want to start doing it badly.

The harder part, and the part that finally tipped it, is that we had three weddings cancel on us this year with only days to spare. Life happens, I truly understand that. But by the time we hear, the butter's been bought, the fruit's been ordered, sometimes the layers are already baked and cooling. Three times this year we ate all of that. For a shop our size, that's not a shrug, that's a real dent, and I found myself lying awake doing arithmetic instead of sleeping before a four a.m. start.

And while all of that was going on, the thing that actually keeps our lights on, the everyday case, the croissants and the rye and the seeded loaf you buy on Thursdays, was getting less of us than it deserved. There were mornings I was piping sugar flowers while the bread was proofing, and I'd catch myself thinking, this isn't what we're here for. You are what we're here for. The person who comes in at seven for a coffee and a morning bun and tells us about their kid's soccer game. That's the bakery I wanted to run when we opened, and I've been letting it get crowded out.

So that's the decision. If you've already booked with us for this year, please don't panic, we're honoring every one of those and we'll do them right. And if you're getting married and just want something beautiful for a small gathering, come talk to us anyway. We'll still happily make a lovely cake from what we already do well, we just won't be doing the consultations and the sketches and the custom designs anymore. There are some truly wonderful cake people in town who do that and only that, and I'm glad to point you their way.

Thank you for being the kind of customers who make a shop like this possible at all. I'll see you at the counter, probably with flour on my face.

b.text:
If you’ve been following along here for a while, you know we try to keep this bakery as personal and hands-on as we can. That’s one of the best parts of being a small shop: I get to know so many of you by name, I get to bake the things you come in for every week, and I get to spend my days making the treats that end up at your tables for birthdays, coffee breaks, Tuesday afternoons, and all the ordinary little celebrations that make up real life.

That’s also why I want to share a change with you directly, in plain language.

We’re no longer taking custom wedding cake orders.

That isn’t an easy thing to write, because I know wedding cakes can be deeply meaningful, and I’m honored every time someone even thinks of us for something that important. But the truth is that custom wedding cakes have become too much for our tiny bakery to carry well.

A single wedding cake order takes an enormous amount of time. Between the back-and-forth emails, consultation time, tastings, planning, design work, and all the coordination that comes with making something that has to be exactly right, each one eats up about 14 hours of time that pulls me away from the bakery floor and away from the bread, pastries, cakes, and cookies you actually see in the case every day.

And because we’re small, that time matters a lot.

This year alone, we had three last-minute cancellations. When that happens, we’re left with ingredient costs we can’t recover, plus all the time that already went into planning and preparation. For a larger business, that might be easier to absorb. For a three-person bakery, it’s a real strain.

More than anything, I’ve had to be honest with myself about where our energy needs to go. The everyday case is what keeps this bakery going. It’s what pays rent, covers payroll, and keeps the lights on. It’s also what most of you come in for, week after week. That’s the heart of the business, and I need to protect that.

So this isn’t us saying no to weddings. It’s us saying yes to the part of the bakery that’s sustainable, steady, and true to what we do best.

We’ll still be here with cakes for smaller celebrations, special desserts, and all the things that make a gathering feel complete. And if you’re planning a wedding, I truly wish you all the sweetness in the world as you find the right fit for your day.

Thank you, as always, for supporting this little bakery and for understanding the realities behind what it takes to keep it running. I’m so grateful for every one of you who shows up for us, and I want to keep showing up for you in the ways we can do well.

setup: A small HVAC company owner is writing a how-to for homeowners on bleeding air from hot water baseboard radiators before winter.

a.text:
## How to Bleed Air Out of Baseboard Heating

1. **Turn off the boiler and circulator pump.**  
   Shut the system down and let it cool for a few minutes before opening any bleeder valves. You do not want hot water spraying out while the circulator is running.

2. **Find the bleeder valve on each baseboard unit.**  
   Most baseboard radiators have a small bleeder valve at one end, usually near the top. It may have a square fitting for a radiator key or a slotted screw that takes a flathead screwdriver.

3. **Put a cup or small container under the valve.**  
   Have a rag handy too. Even when there is only air in the line, water will follow it once the air is released.

4. **Open the bleeder valve slowly.**  
   Turn the valve just enough to let air escape. You should hear hissing or sputtering if air is trapped in that section of baseboard.

5. **Wait for a steady stream of water.**  
   Keep the valve open until the hissing stops and water comes out in a smooth, steady stream without spitting air.

6. **Close the valve snugly.**  
   Tighten it only until it stops dripping. Do not overtighten it—too much force can damage or crack the valve seat and turn a simple maintenance job into a leak.

7. **Move from unit to unit, starting near the boiler.**  
   Bleed the baseboards closest to the boiler first, then work your way farther out through the house. This helps push trapped air through the system instead of leaving it stuck in another loop.

8. **Do not skip the basement loop.**  
   One of the most common reasons we get calls for cold radiators is that homeowners bleed only the upstairs baseboards. The basement loop is often where the air is actually trapped, especially if it runs lower than the rest of the system.

9. **Turn the boiler and circulator back on.**  
   Once every unit has been bled, restart the system and let it heat up. Check that each baseboard is warming evenly and that none of the bleeder valves are dripping.

If a baseboard still stays cold after bleeding, the problem may be low boiler pressure, a stuck zone valve, a circulator issue, or a blockage in the loop.

b.text:
**How to Bleed Air Out of Baseboard Heat Before Winter**

Half the "my radiators are cold" calls we run in October end up being trapped air, and it's a fifteen-minute job you can do yourself with a towel and a screwdriver. Here's how we do it.

**What you need**

- A radiator key or a flathead screwdriver (depends on your bleeder valve)
- A cup or small container
- A rag or towel for drips

**Step 1: Shut off the system**

Turn off the boiler and the circulator pump. Don't skip this. If the pump is running while you open a bleeder, it'll push air around the loop instead of letting it collect where you can get at it. Give the system a few minutes to settle before you start.

**Step 2: Find the bleeder valve**

Look at the ends of each baseboard unit, usually behind the end cap or just inside it. You're looking for a small brass fitting with either a square stem (needs the key) or a slotted screw (flathead works). Some units have them at one end only, some at both. Check both.

**Step 3: Start closest to the boiler**

Go to the unit nearest the boiler first and work outward along the loop. Air travels with the water, so you're clearing it in the direction it moves. Bleeding in random order means you'll be chasing the same pocket of air around the house.

**Step 4: Open it slow**

Hold your cup underneath and crack the valve open slowly. You'll hear hissing first. That's the air. Keep it open until the hissing stops and you get a steady stream of water with no sputtering. A trickle with bubbles means you're not done. Steady water, no noise, you're done.

**Step 5: Close it snug, not tight**

Turn the valve closed until it stops leaking. That's it. People crank these down like a lug nut and crack the valve seat, and now instead of a cold radiator you've got a drip and a service call. Snug is enough.

**Step 6: Repeat on every unit**

Every one. Which brings me to the part most people get wrong.

**The mistake that causes most of our cold radiator calls**

Homeowners bleed the upstairs units because that's where they notice the cold. Then they stop. But the air is almost never up there. It collects in the basement loop, the runs of baseboard or pipe down near the boiler that nobody looks at. You bleed the second floor, feel good about it, and the same air works its way back up in a week.

If you have baseboard in the basement, or a loop that runs through an unfinished area, bleed those too. In a lot of houses that's where the air actually lives, and it's the one spot people never think to check.

**After you're done**

Turn the boiler and circulator back on. Check the pressure gauge on the boiler. If it's low (most residential systems run around 12 to 15 psi cold), the fill valve should bring it back up, but if it doesn't, or if you keep getting air after bleeding a few times, that's a different problem. Could be the auto-fill, could be the expansion tank, could be a small leak somewhere pulling air in.

That's the point where it's worth having us take a look. But bleeding the system is the first thing we'd do anyway, so you might as well do it yourself and save the trip.

setup: A home baker is reviewing the Corlane SM6 mixer for blog readers deciding whether to buy it.

a.text:
# Review: Corlane SM6 Stand Mixer After 8 Months

I've been running the Corlane SM6 for eight months now, pushing it through near-daily sourdough production for my weekend farmers market stand. Here's where I've landed on it.

## The Good

The motor is the whole reason to buy this mixer, and it delivers. I run double batches of stiff bagel dough through it regularly—around 68% hydration, four pounds of flour—and the thing doesn't stall or strain. My old mixer would labor and smell hot halfway through that kind of load. The Corlane pushes through it like it's nothing.

Bowl capacity is generous. I can fit a full kilo of sourdough starter, flour, and water for my Saturday market prep without it climbing out of the bowl.

## The Annoying

The bowl lift lever squeaks. Not occasionally—consistently. I've been hitting it with WD-40 about once a month, which takes thirty seconds, but it's the kind of thing that shouldn't be necessary on a mixer at this price point. It's a small thing until you're loading dough at 6 AM and the squeak wakes up the dog.

The bigger issue is the stock dough hook. It's too short for the depth of the bowl, which means it leaves a chunk of dough sitting untouched at the bottom. I ended up buying a third-party hook off Amazon for $24 that actually reaches properly. The stock hook works fine for cake batter and lighter stuff, but for bread dough it's a real problem. The fact that I had to spend extra to make the mixer functional for its primary purpose is irritating.

## Price

At $429, it's $80 more than the comparable KitchenAid model. That gap stings a little, especially when you factor in the replacement hook. So you're really at about $450 all in.

## The Verdict

If you're kneading heavy bread dough every week—sourdough, bagels, pretzels, anything dense and stiff—buy it. The motor alone justifies the price, and you will not find this kind of power in a residential mixer without going to commercial equipment at twice the cost.

If you're mostly making cookies, cake batter, whipping cream, and the occasional soft loaf, skip it. You're paying for muscle you won't use, and the bowl and hook quirks will bother you more than the motor will benefit you.

I don't regret the purchase. It has changed how much I can produce for the market without babysitting the machine. But go in knowing you'll need a different dough hook and a can of WD-40.

b.text:
# Corlane SM6 Stand Mixer: 8 Months of Market Sourdough Later

I bought the Corlane SM6 in February because my old mixer died mid-batch two weeks before market season and I was hand-kneading twelve loaves' worth of dough on my counter at 5 a.m. I've now run it almost every day for eight months, mostly on high-hydration sourdough, plus a weekly double batch of bagels, which is the stiffest dough I make. Here's where I've landed.

## The motor is the whole reason to buy this

A double batch of bagel dough is roughly 2.2 kg of very low-hydration dough. It is the test that killed my last mixer and made my sister's KitchenAid smell like a hot electrical outlet. The SM6 has never stalled on it. Not once. It doesn't slow down, doesn't walk across the counter, doesn't get more than warm to the touch on the housing. I can run it on speed 2 for eight straight minutes and it sounds the same at minute eight as it did at minute one.

Same story with sourdough, which is easier on the motor but harder on patience because I do long mixes for gluten development. Fifteen minutes of continuous kneading on a 2 kg batch, four or five times a week, for eight months. Nothing has burned, stripped, or loosened. If you knead heavy dough on a real schedule, this is the part that matters, and it delivers.

## The bowl-lift lever squeaks, and it will keep squeaking

Around month two, the lever that raises and lowers the bowl started squeaking. Not a subtle squeak, a full metal-on-metal complaint every time I move it. A shot of WD-40 on the pivot fixes it completely for about a month, then it comes back. I've done this six times now.

It's not a functional problem. The lift still locks in firmly and the bowl doesn't drop under load. But on a $429 machine I shouldn't be maintaining a lubrication schedule for a lever, and it's the kind of thing that would drive me up the wall if I used this in a quiet kitchen instead of one with a radio going.

## The included dough hook is wrong for the bowl

This one actually annoys me. The SM6 has a deep bowl, which is great for capacity, but the dough hook that comes in the box doesn't reach far enough down. With a smaller batch, say a single loaf, the hook spins above a layer of flour and dough that just sits on the bottom. I had to stop and scrape every couple of minutes, which defeats the point of a mixer.

I ended up buying a third-party spiral hook, about $30, that's roughly an inch longer and actually reaches the bottom. With that hook, the machine is excellent. Without it, I'd call small-batch kneading unreliable. Budget for the replacement hook as part of the purchase price. Corlane should be shipping the right one.

## Price

$429. The equivalent bowl-lift KitchenAid is $349, so you're paying about $80 more, plus the $30 for a hook that works, so call it $110 more all in. That's real money.

## Verdict

**Buy it if you knead heavy dough every week.** Bagels, high-volume sourdough, anything stiff or over 1.5 kg at a time. The motor is genuinely a class above what I've used at this price, and after eight months of daily abuse there's no sign of it wearing down. The squeaky lever and the too-short hook are irritating, but they're irritating in a machine that does the hard job better than anything else I've owned. I'd buy it again tomorrow.

**Skip it if you're mostly doing cookies, cake batter, whipped cream, and the occasional loaf of bread.** None of that comes close to stressing the motor, so you're paying $110 extra for headroom you'll never use, and you'll still get the squeak and the bad hook. Get the KitchenAid and put the difference toward a good scale or a Dutch oven.

That's it. It's a dough machine. If you're a dough person, it's worth the money. If you're not, it isn't.

setup: A first-year nursing student is writing a scholarship essay about her first ER rotation for scholarship committee readers.

a.text:
My first week in the ER was last month. It was my first real clinical rotation. I thought I knew what it would be like from class, but it was nothing like that.

The first day, there was a man who came in with a big cut on his forearm from work. He needed it cleaned out before they could stitch it. That part stings really bad and he knew it. His wife was trying to get there but she was stuck in traffic on the highway. He kept checking his phone. The nurse who was showing me asked if I could stay with him and hold his hand. That was it. That was my whole job.

So I did. I held his hand while they poured the stuff over the cut. He squeezed hard. Really hard. He didn't yell, he just stared at the ceiling and squeezed my hand. I kept talking to him about nothing, about how traffic was probably bad because of construction. After, he said thank you like I had done something big. I hadn't. But it felt like maybe in the ER, just being the person who stays matters.

On Wednesday I had the opposite happen. Around lunch everything got fast. A code was called and they pulled the curtain around the bed two beds down from where I was. One of the nurses looked at me and said, "Can you go restock the gauze in supply? Now." So I did. I ran to the supply room and started counting boxes of gauze while on the other side of the curtain they were doing CPR. I could hear them counting out loud. "One and two and three and four..." and someone saying "keep going."

I just stood there shoving gauze onto a shelf and listening. I felt so useless. I wanted to be on the other side of the curtain helping, but I wasn't ready and I would have just been in the way. My instructor told me later that restocking is part of it too, that if they need gauze and it's not there, that's a problem. I get that now. Not every job in the ER looks important, but it all has to get done.

On Friday I had to do a blood draw on a guy in his sixties. He was diabetic and he told me right away his veins are always hard to find. He was right. I missed the first time. I said sorry. I tried a different spot and missed again. By the third try I could feel my face getting red and my hands were shaking a little. I kept saying sorry. He just said "it's okay, you take your time, honey."

On the fourth try I got it. I saw the blood come into the tube and I almost wanted to cry from relief. He smiled at me and said "see, you got it." He was nicer to me than I was expecting anyone to be after I poked him three times.

That whole week I learned that nursing isn't what I thought it was from the textbook. I thought it would be all skills and knowing the right answers. Some of it is, but a lot of it is just being there when someone is scared, or doing the small task that needs doing, or saying sorry and trying again when you mess up.

I am in my first year of nursing school and I have a lot left to learn. I work part-time to pay for school and this scholarship would really help me stay focused on clinical and my classes. I want to keep learning how to be the person who stays, who restocks the gauze, and who keeps trying until she gets it right.

b.text:
First Week in the ER

My first week in the ER, I learned that nursing is not about knowing everything. It is about showing up.

On my second day, a man came in with a deep cut on his arm. His wife was stuck in traffic, so he was alone. The doctor had to clean the wound, and the man was in a lot of pain. He reached out and grabbed my hand. I did not know what to say, so I just stood there and let him hold on. When his wife finally walked in, he let go and thanked me. I had not given him medicine or done a procedure. But I had stayed. That mattered.

A few days later, a code was called. I was too new to help, so a nurse told me to restock gauze. I stood outside the curtain with the boxes and heard them counting compressions. One, two, three, four. I kept counting gauze packs. It felt strange to do something so small while they worked to save someone. But then I realized the room needed gauze too. Even the small jobs have a place in a big emergency.

The hardest moment came with a diabetic man who had bad veins. I was supposed to draw blood. I missed three times. My hands were shaking, and I wanted to go get someone else. But the man looked at me and said, "Take your time. I know you are learning." On the fourth try, I got it. I almost cried. He just nodded. He did not complain or ask for another nurse. He gave me a chance to learn.

Before that week, I thought nursing was about being fast and knowing everything. Now I think it is about staying calm when things are not calm. It is about holding a hand, counting gauze, and trying again.

I am applying for this scholarship because I want to keep learning. I work part-time, and school and clinicals take most of my time. I do not want to cut back on clinical hours because that is where I learn the most. Every shift teaches me something I cannot get from a lecture.

My first week in the ER was not dramatic. I did not save a life. But I saw what saving looks like up close. It looks like a hand held, a small task done, and a fourth try. I want to be part of that for a long time.

setup: A real estate agent is writing a commentary on the local market for brokerage blog and local paper readers.

a.text:
**The Pace Has Changed. Sellers Who Ignore It Will Sit.**

Last spring in our zip, the median home sat eight days before going under contract. This spring? Thirty-four. Showings per listing have been cut in half. List prices are still up six percent year over year. And right now I have three sellers who have watched their homes sit past sixty days and still refuse to lower the price.

This is not a crash. It’s a reality check that too many sellers refuse to take.

Buyers are still out there. They have not vanished. What has vanished is the panic that made them ignore price, condition, and competition. They look at more houses. They negotiate harder. They walk away when the number feels wrong. The market has simply returned to a normal pace after years of frenzy, and a lot of sellers are still pricing as if 2021 never ended.

I see it every week. Homes priced to the current market—right price, right condition, clean presentation—still go under contract in under two weeks. Homes priced to last year’s fantasy sit. Then they sit longer. Then the seller digs in, convinced the market will come back to them. It will not. Every extra week on the market becomes a louder signal that the price is wrong, and buyers know it.

The data is not subtle. Days on market tripled. Showings halved. Prices still edged higher because the well-priced inventory continues to move and set the comps. The gap between those two realities is where stubborn sellers are living right now, and it is costing them.

If you are thinking of listing, price to today’s buyer, not yesterday’s memory. If you already have a house sitting, stop waiting for the market to “catch up.” It already has. You are the one who has not. Adjust the price, fix what needs fixing, and get it done. The agents who tell you otherwise are either protecting your feelings or protecting their own pipeline. Neither helps you sell.

This market is not broken. It is simply no longer willing to overpay for denial.

b.text:
**The Market Isn’t Crashing—It’s Just Moving at a New Speed**

Last spring, homes in our zip code were flying off the market in eight days. This spring? The median is 34 days. List prices are still up 6% year over year, but showings per listing have dropped by half. And right now, I’ve got three sellers sitting on 60+ day listings, refusing to budge on price.

Here’s the truth: This isn’t a crash. It’s a correction in pace, and the sellers who haven’t adjusted yet are the ones stuck in limbo.

The market shifted—interest rates climbed, buyer urgency cooled, and suddenly, the days of instant offers and bidding wars feel like a distant memory. But homes priced right? They’re still selling in under two weeks. The difference now isn’t demand; it’s realism.

Sellers, take note: The market isn’t broken. It’s just no longer handing out participation trophies. Price it sharp, and it’ll move. Wait too long to catch up, and you’ll be the one explaining to your neighbors why your listing’s collecting dust.

This isn’t doom and gloom—it’s the new rhythm. Adapt or get left behind.

setup: A high school girls' soccer and track coach is writing an op-ed urging turf funding for the girls' field.

a.text:
# The Girls' Soccer Field Needs Turf. Here's Why That's Not Optional.

I've coached girls' soccer and track at this school for years, and I'm not going to pretend I love writing op-eds. I do this for the stipend and because I care about these kids. But I'm asking the school board — and this town — to fix something that's gone unfixed for too long: our girls' soccer field floods, it's dangerous, and it's been treated like a lower priority than the boys' football field for six years running.

Let's start with the numbers, because they're not close. Over the last two seasons, we've had nine games rained out or relocated because our grass field can't drain. Not postponed by a day — cancelled, or moved to a field forty minutes away, cutting into study time, sleep, and family schedules for forty-plus girls and their parents. Meanwhile, our opponents with turf fields play through the same weather without blinking.

Then there's what happened last October. One of my players planted her foot in a rut — the kind that forms when a grass field takes on water all season and never fully recovers — and tore her ACL. She's out for a full year. Surgery, months of rehab, a season and a half of her high school career gone, because the ground she was playing on wasn't safe. That's not bad luck. That's a facilities problem with a name and a face attached to it now.

Here's the part that makes this personal for me, and for a lot of parents who've already called and emailed the board: the football field got turf in 2019. It drains fine. It doesn't grow ruts. Nobody's tearing an ACL stepping in a divot out there. I'm not saying football doesn't deserve a good field — it does. I'm saying our girls deserve the same standard, and they've been waiting six years for it.

I know turf isn't cheap. I know budgets are tight and there are a dozen good uses for every dollar. But I'd ask the board to weigh that cost against what we're already paying: rescheduled games, lost practice time, a kid's knee, and a message to forty girls that their season matters less than the boys' does. That message gets sent whether we mean it or not, every time it rains and only one team's field is playable.

This isn't a want. It's overdue. I hope the board votes like it.

b.text:
Nine girls’ soccer games have been rained out or moved in the last two seasons because our grass field floods. The boys’ football field got turf in 2019.

The school board is about to vote on next year’s facilities budget. It’s time to put turf on the girls’ soccer field—with the drainage and maintenance plan needed to make it work.

I coach girls’ soccer and track at our public high school. I’m not asking for a showpiece. I’m asking for a field we can count on using.

When a game gets moved, families have to rearrange rides and work schedules. When it gets canceled, players lose a chance to compete after putting in the work to prepare. Coaches can adjust. So can kids. But nine games in two seasons is not an occasional inconvenience. It is a facilities problem.

Last October, one of my players tore her ACL stepping in a rut on our field. I’m not going to claim that turf prevents ACL injuries. It doesn’t, and the board should look carefully at the safety, heat and maintenance requirements of any surface it considers. But we cannot talk about the drawbacks of replacing this field while ignoring the condition of the field our girls use now.

Keeping what we have is also a decision. Our players live with that decision every season.

Then there is the fairness question.

The district invested in turf for boys’ football in 2019. I’m glad those athletes have it. This is not an argument for taking anything away from them. It is an argument for giving girls’ soccer the same serious attention when its field repeatedly fails.

Our girls practice, compete and represent this school. They deserve more than being told to make do with a flooded field while another program has had turf for years.

I know facilities money is limited. Classrooms need repairs. Other teams have needs. A responsible board has to weigh all of that. It also has to account for the full cost of turf, including upkeep and eventual replacement—not just installation.

So get solid bids. Require proper drainage. Ask hard questions about player safety and long-term costs. Then fund the project instead of pushing it into another budget year.

I expect my players to show up prepared and take care of their responsibilities. They should be able to expect the district to take care of its responsibilities, too.

They have put in the work. Give them a field that does.

a.text:
**A Note About Wedding Cakes**

Some of the best things I've ever pulled out of these ovens have been wedding cakes. I've loved every part of it — the tastings, the sketches, the shaky hands on the drive over hoping the tiers hold, the look on someone's face when it turns out to be exactly what she'd been picturing since she was twelve. So this isn't a decision I made lightly, and I wanted you to hear it from me before the grapevine gets there first: we're not taking custom wedding cake orders anymore.

Here's what a wedding cake actually looks like from our side. It's not one bake — it's months. The emails back and forth while a couple settles on a vision. The tasting afternoon, where we set out half a dozen flavors and talk sugar flowers versus fresh, lemon versus chocolate, what his grandmother will and won't eat. The sketches, the test tiers, the sourcing, the scheduling around three people who were already up baking at four in the morning. All told it runs us about fourteen hours per order before we've cracked a single egg for the real thing, and none of those hours are ones anybody pays for. That's just how this corner of the business works. It worked fine when we were trying to grow. It stopped working when I ran out of room in the day.

Then there was this year. We had three cancellations come in close to the date — no hard feelings, truly, life happens and I'd never hold it against anyone — but each time we'd already bought the ingredients, and in a shop our size, that money comes straight out of somewhere else.

Mostly, though, it comes down to something simpler. The everyday case is what pays our rent. Not the big once-a-year orders — the Tuesday croissants, the Saturday loaves, the birthday cake somebody grabs on the way home from work. That's you, probably, if you're reading this. And every time a wedding cake took over a week, the case got a little thinner, the mornings got a little earlier, and the thing that actually keeps our lights on got the leftovers of our attention. I don't want to run a shop where anything gets the leftovers.

If you're getting married — congratulations, truly. I still want to hear all about it. Come by and tell me everything, and let me put something in a box that'll be right at home at the after-party. The case will be full, and it will have our whole hearts in it.

Thank you to every couple who let us be part of your day. It was an honor, every single time. And thank you, everyone who comes in on the regular, for being the reason we get to keep doing this at all. See you at the counter.

b.text:
Hey friends,

I wanted to share something that’s been on my mind for a while, because you’re the ones who keep showing up for us every week and I figure you deserve to hear it straight from me.

We’re stepping away from custom wedding cakes.

I know that might land a little heavy for a few of you who’ve been dreaming about one of our cakes for your day, and I want you to know how much it means that you’d even think of us for something that important. Truly. We’ve loved every single wedding cake we’ve made—the late-night sketching, the tasting plates we put together after the morning bake, the pure joy of watching a couple’s face when they try the first bite. But after this year especially, it’s become clear that continuing isn’t fair to the bakery, to the three of us, or honestly to the everyday customers who keep the lights on.

Here’s the real talk: each custom wedding order ends up taking about fourteen hours of free time—consults, sketches, multiple tastings, endless back-and-forth emails—before we even start baking. That’s time when one of us isn’t at the bench or helping with the morning rush. On top of that, we had three last-minute cancellations this year alone. We’d already bought the ingredients, blocked the days, and then… nothing. That cost lands square on a tiny shop like ours. And the biggest piece is that every hour spent on a wedding cake is an hour pulled away from the case you all actually come in for—the croissants, the cookies, the bread that pays the rent and keeps us open for you at 7 a.m. when you need your coffee and something warm.

I bake starting at 4 most mornings, and the blog (and everything else) gets written in whatever scraps of time are left. We’re three people. We love this work with our whole hearts, but we also have to protect the part of it that sustains us so we can keep doing it for years. Focusing on the everyday case—the things you grab on your way to work or for Sunday breakfast—is what lets us stay independent and keep showing up for this neighborhood.

So for now, no more custom wedding cakes. We’ll still have beautiful cakes in the case every day, and if you’re looking for something special for a smaller celebration, come talk to us. We just can’t take on the full custom wedding route anymore.

Thank you for understanding, for supporting us through all the early mornings and flour-dusted days, and for being the reason we get to keep baking at all. See you soon for a croissant—or three.

With love and a little butter on my sleeves,
[Your Name]

setup: A solo SaaS founder is posting a thread to indie hackers and customers about a pricing mistake and the fix.

a.text:
I raised prices 40% overnight. On everyone. Same day.

Lost 30 of 140 customers in a week.

Here's what I did wrong and what I changed 🧵

---

The logic seemed sound at the time:

Tallyup was underpriced. Support load was growing. I needed more revenue per customer to keep this sustainable as a solo founder.

So I bumped everyone 40% and figured the value justified it.

---

Mistake #1: I applied it to existing customers.

These were people who signed up at a price they agreed to. Changing the deal on them overnight felt like a betrayal, and honestly, it was.

New pricing should've been for new customers.

---

Mistake #2: No warning.

I didn't email anyone ahead of time. They found out when the charge hit or when they logged in.

No heads up. No "here's why." Just a bigger number.

---

Mistake #3: No grandfathering.

The people who believed in Tallyup early, when it was rough, got hit the same as everyone else.

Loyalty should've meant something. I gave it nothing.

---

What I changed:

1. Grandfathered every remaining existing customer back to their old price. Permanently.

2. New pricing only applies to new signups going forward.

3. Emailed everyone I lost with an apology and the old rate if they wanted back.

---

The result so far:

Some of the 30 came back. Not all. That's fair, I broke trust and trust doesn't fully reset with one email.

Revenue is lower than my spreadsheet fantasy. But the base I have now actually trusts me.

---

If you're thinking about raising prices:

- Grandfather existing customers
- New price for new people
- Communicate before you charge

Cheaper to learn this from my thread than from your own churn.

Ask me anything below 👇

b.text:
**1/** Two weeks ago I raised prices 40% on every Tallyup customer. Overnight. No warning.

I lost 30 of 140 customers in a week.

Here's what happened and what I'd do differently. 🧵

**2/** The logic felt airtight at the time.

I'd shipped a lot. Support was eating my week. I was underpriced compared to everyone I benchmarked against. Every pricing post I'd ever read said "just raise your prices."

So I did. Flipped the switch on a Tuesday night.

**3/** What I actually did wrong wasn't the 40%.

It was that I did it to existing customers, with no notice, with no explanation, and with nothing new in their hands that day.

I gave people a bill increase and called it a price change. Those are different things.

**4/** The cancellations weren't angry, which was worse.

Most were some version of "no hard feelings, this just isn't in the budget at that number." A few said they would have stayed if I'd asked first.

Gym owners run on thin margins. I knew that. I priced like I didn't.

**5/** The other thing I underestimated: existing customers didn't buy the current product.

They bought the thing I was selling when they signed up, at the price I promised. Changing both sides of that deal unilaterally broke something I couldn't fix with a discount code afterward.

**6/** What I changed:

New pricing applies to new signups only. Everyone who was here before the change is back on what they were paying, and I told them so directly.

**7/** For future increases:

— 60 days notice, sent by me, not a system email
— ships alongside something they asked for
— existing customers get a grandfathered tier, permanently
— I ask a handful of customers first instead of benchmarking against strangers

**8/** The part I'm still sitting with:

I wasn't underpriced for my market. I was underpriced for the market I wished I was in. Those are very different problems and raising prices only solves one of them.

**9/** Reaching out to the 30 this week. Some will come back, some won't, and that's fair.

Posting this because "raise your prices" is advice I took without the second half of the sentence. The second half is *how*.

setup: An in-house recruiter is posting a contrarian observation about candidates asking about the team’s last failed project in interviews to recruiters, hiring managers, and job seekers.

a.text:
Here’s your post:

---

I’ve interviewed close to 200 people in the last few years, and the best candidates always ask some version of: *"What’s a project or initiative your team tried that didn’t work out—and what did you learn from it?"*

It’s not about digging for gossip. It’s about seeing if the company actually reflects, adapts, and values transparency. The ones who ask it are usually the ones who’ve been burned before, who know that growth comes from failure, not just wins.

Here’s how a real conversation went last month:

**Me:** *"Tell me about a time you had to pivot when something wasn’t working."*
**Candidate:** *"We built a tool that was supposed to cut onboarding time in half, but it ended up creating more friction. We scrapped it after three months and went back to the drawing board. What’s something your team tried that didn’t stick?"*

**Me:** *"We rolled out a new scheduling system last year that was supposed to reduce overtime. Turns out, it just shifted the burden to different teams. We’re still tweaking it, but now we involve frontline managers earlier in the process."*

**Candidate:** *"That’s rough. How did the team react when you had to pull back?"*

That’s it. No grandstanding, no performative humility—just two people acknowledging that work is messy and improvement is a moving target. Those are the hires who last.

What’s a question you’ve asked (or been asked) in an interview that actually revealed something useful?

b.text:
In about 200 interviews, I’ve noticed a pattern: the strongest candidates almost always ask about our last failed project.

Not to be “difficult.”
Not to catch anyone out.

They ask because they understand that failure tells you more about a team than a polished success story ever will.

One version of that conversation usually goes like this:

Candidate: “Can you tell me about a project that didn’t go as planned, and what you learned from it?”

Me: “Sure. We rolled out a process change in our logistics ops team that looked good on paper, but we underestimated how much it would disrupt the handoff between recruiting, onboarding, and site operations. The idea was right. The sequencing wasn’t.”

Candidate: “What was the part you missed?”

Me: “We focused on speed and didn’t pressure-test the people side of the change early enough. We had the plan, but not enough buy-in from the teams who had to live with it.”

Candidate: “And what changed after that?”

Me: “We brought those teams in earlier, simplified the rollout, and gave managers more room to adapt it locally. The next version took longer to launch, but it worked better.”

That’s the kind of question that stands out to me.

Because the best candidates aren’t just evaluating the role.
They’re evaluating how a company thinks when things go wrong.

setup: A solo SaaS founder is posting a thread to indie hackers and customers about a pricing mistake and the fix.

a.text:
I made a pricing mistake with Tallyup.
  
Raised prices 40% overnight. Lost 30 of our 140 customers in a week.

Here’s what happened and what I changed. 🧵

1/ I thought we were underpriced. Competitors charged more, and I felt our value justified the jump. So I bumped every plan by 40% and sent a “new pricing” email. No warning. No grandfathering. Just an update.

2/ Within 24 hours, cancellations started rolling in. A few angry DMs. Then more. By the end of the week, 30 customers had left. That’s 30 people who trusted a tiny indie tool, and I blindsided them.

3/ I panicked. This is a bootstrapped SaaS; every customer counts. The immediate fix: I reverted the price for every existing customer and told them their rate was now locked indefinitely. I apologized publicly and privately.

4/ What I changed permanently:
  
– New customers now see the higher price, but with a clear 30-day notice promise if it ever changes.  
– Existing customers are grandfathered for life. No exceptions.  
– Any future price tweaks will be tested with a small subset first, never blanket overnight.

5/ The lesson: pricing isn’t just about value. It’s about trust. I broke trust by moving fast and not thinking about the humans on the other side. A 40% hike with no warning is a great way to burn relationships you spent years building.

Now I treat pricing like a conversation, not a surprise.

b.text:
1/ i made a pricing mistake with Tallyup that i want to walk through honestly.

a few months ago i raised prices 40% on every existing customer, overnight, no warning.

lost 30 of my 140 customers in a week.

here's what happened and what i changed.

2/ the reasoning at the time felt solid: we were underpriced, new customers were paying more than legacy ones, and i wanted to close that gap fast.

so i just... did it. one email, effective immediately, applied to everyone regardless of how long they'd been a customer.

3/ the mistake wasn't raising prices. it was raising them the same way for everyone, with zero notice, and zero acknowledgment that loyalty should count for something.

longtime customers who'd been paying on time for a year got treated exactly like someone who signed up last month.

4/ the churn wasn't evenly spread either. it was disproportionately the customers who'd been around the longest — the ones who felt the increase as a breach of trust, not just a price change.

that's the part that stung. i lost the people i most needed to keep.

5/ what i changed:

grandfathered existing customers at their old price for a fixed period (instead of forever, but with real notice this time)

gave 60 days notice for any future price changes

separated "new customer pricing" from "existing customer pricing" as a permanent policy, not an afterthought

6/ the lesson: pricing changes are a trust event, not just a revenue lever. how you communicate it matters as much as the number itself.

30 customers in a week taught me that faster than any amount of thinking about it in advance would have.

7/ still building Tallyup solo, still sharing the numbers as they come. if you're thinking about a price increase, happy to talk through it before you hit send on that email.

setup: A small dog grooming salon owner is writing a how-to for dog owners about preventing coat matting between grooming visits.

a.text:
I see this all the time—people trying so hard to keep their dog’s coat nice between appointments, but making one simple mistake that actually makes things ten times worse. They’ll bathe the dog first because they think water will loosen tangles. Here’s the problem: wet matted fur doesn’t loosen, it tightens into a solid felt pad, almost like wool that’s been shocked. And if your dog has a double coat or those tight curls, that felt locks in right against the skin. So the first rule, and I really can’t say it enough, is brush before the bath, never after.

If your pup is already dirty and you’re planning a quick home bath, you still need to work through the coat dry. Grab a slicker brush—not a pin brush, a slicker with fine bent wires—and use short line strokes, not circles. Lifting and flicking tiny sections at a time. The trick is to go in the direction the hair naturally falls and never just scrub over the surface. For double coats, that means gently parting the hair so you’re reaching the dense undercoat, not just slicking down the top. For curly breeds, those short strokes tease apart curls without stretching them into a bigger snarl.

Always start behind the ears and deep in the armpits. I know that sounds weird, but mats almost always set up shop there first because those spots get the most friction when the dog moves, sleeps, or wears a collar. Work in sections, lifting the ear, feeling for even a tiny rough patch, then moving down the neck and chest. Only when those hot spots are completely free do you move to the legs, belly, and tail. If you find a spot that’s already starting to mat up and feel solid, put the brush down. Take a dab of conditioner—nothing fancy, even the one you use on your own hair works—and work it into the mat with your fingers. Gently. You’re trying to add slip so the fibers can slide apart, not force them. Once it feels softer, you can go back with the slicker in those same short strokes, but honestly, if it’s stubborn, just leave it for me. Working it dry with a tool will only tighten it more and hurt your dog.

That whole “bath first” instinct people have is exactly backward. Water and shampoo swell the hair shaft and help those tangles cinch up like a knot. I’ve had to shave down double-coated dogs that were bathed at home without a single brush stroke first because the undercoat matted into a solid pelt. So remember: dry brush, short strokes, start behind ears and underarms, use conditioner on mats before you brush, and only then go for the bath. It’ll keep your dog comfortable and save both of us a lot of heartache at the next grooming visit.

b.text:
I want to talk to you about something I see almost every day at the salon, and it's honestly one of the easiest things to fix at home if you know what you're doing. Matting. Specifically, the kind that shows up between grooms and becomes my problem when you drop your dog off.

Here's what's actually happening. You give your dog a bath at home — I get it, they rolled in something, or you wanted them fresh for the weekend. You think a clean dog is a happy dog. So you lather them up, rinse, towel dry, maybe blow dry, and then you notice the coat feels a little tangly. By the time they get to me, what was a small tangle has turned into a solid mat the size of my palm behind the ear, and now we're either doing a demat session at extra charge or the coat has to come off.

When you wet a matted or even slightly tangled coat without brushing it out first, the water swells each hair and everything pulls tighter. As it dries, it sets into place. You've essentially felted the wool — and that's literally what matted fur is, just hair that's been felted together. So the bath you thought was going to loosen things up actually locked them in tighter. This is the single most common mistake I see, and I see it constantly. Please brush first, then bathe. Even if the coat looks fine to you, run a metal comb through it. If the comb snags anywhere, work through that spot before any water touches the dog.

For double coats and curly coats especially — your Goldens, your Berners, your Huskies, your Doodles, your Bichons — you want a slicker brush. The kind with the fine wire pins on a flat paddle. Here's how I want you to use it, because most people use it wrong. You're going to take short, gentle strokes in one direction. Think of it like painting a fence, not buffing a car. Long fluid motions through the coat, going the direction the hair grows. Do not go in circles. Circling wraps the hair around itself and creates exactly the mats you're trying to prevent. Short line strokes. Always.

And do it in sections, not by trying to do the whole dog in one pass. Start behind the ears, then under the front legs, then the armpits, then the belly, then the back legs, then the tail. Behind the ears and under the front legs are where mats start ninety percent of the time. If your dog has a mat somewhere, it's almost always in one of those two spots. Make those areas part of your weekly routine and you'll cut your mat problems in half overnight.

Now, what if you already see a mat forming? A small one, maybe the size of a dime or a quarter? Don't grab the brush and go at it. You're going to tear through the coat, hurt the dog, and probably make the mat worse. Put a little bit of conditioner directly on the mat — leave-in works great, even a tiny bit of regular conditioner is fine. Work it into the mat with your fingers. Gently. You're trying to lubricate the hairs so they can slide apart. Give it a minute. Then, and only then, try to work through it with your fingers or a wide-tooth comb. Still no brush on a formed mat until you've gotten most of it apart yourself.

If you do all of this — dry brush before any bath, short line strokes with a slicker in the direction of growth, work your sections starting behind the ears and under the front legs, and use conditioner on anything that's already starting to tangle — your dog won't be the one coming in needing a full shave-down. They'll be more comfortable between visits, your appointments will be quicker and cheaper, and your dog will look better longer. Everyone wins.

The couples who ditch the shot list always seem to end up with the best photos.

Not because shot lists are bad. They are helpful. But a wedding day is alive, and the best images usually happen when you trust the moment more than the checklist.

At the Barrera wedding, rain took over the day. We moved everything under the pecan tree, set the original plan aside, and stopped trying to force what we thought the day was supposed to look like.

What we got instead was one of the most honest, joyful galleries I have delivered.

Crowded under branches.
Laughing through the weather.
Completely real.

After eight years of photographing weddings full time, I have learned this: my job is not just to check off poses. It is to notice what is happening, protect your time, and make space for the moments you will actually remember.

If you are planning a wedding, bring your must-have family photos. Bring your vendor list. Then give yourself permission to let the rest unfold.

Sometimes the backup plan becomes the best part.

setup: A high school girls' soccer and track coach is writing an op-ed urging turf funding for the girls' field.

a.text:
**Nine Games. One Knee. Still No Turf.**

In the last two seasons, my girls' soccer team has had nine home games rained out or moved because our field floods. Nine. When it rains, that field doesn't drain — it holds water like a bathtub, and it stays soft and rutted for days after.

Last October, one of my players planted her foot in one of those ruts and tore her ACL. She lost the rest of her season and has been rehabbing ever since. Call it a fluke if you want. I watched it happen. It wasn't a fluke. It's what happens when you ask teenage athletes to compete on a field that floods every fall and never gets fixed.

Now here's the part that's harder to explain to my players: the football field got artificial turf in 2019. Same campus. Same weather. The boys play rain or shine on a surface that's flat, drained, and safe. The girls get a field that wipes out their schedule every October.

I want to be clear — I'm not against the football field having turf. Good for them. I'm asking a simple question: why did that project get done and this one didn't? If the board has an answer, I'd like to hear it out loud, at a public meeting. If the answer is "we'll get to it," we've been getting to it since 2019.

There's also a federal word for a district that installs turf for the boys and leaves the girls on a flooding field. It's called Title IX. I'd rather not lead with that word. I'd rather the board just put the money in the budget.

I already know the objection: it's expensive. It is. But rescheduling nine games isn't free. Sending my girls on the road for games that were supposed to be at home isn't free. And nobody has put a price on a sixteen-year-old's knee.

This isn't only a soccer problem, either. I coach track in the spring, and my runners train on that same field all season, dodging the same ruts. When it's flooded, we practice wherever we can find space. The seniors on this team don't get their home games back. They don't get a second senior night.

The board votes on next year's facilities budget soon. Put the girls' field in it. Fund it fully. Don't commission another study — this field has been studied plenty. It's also been under water plenty.

Nine games. One knee. And a boys' field that got fixed five years ago. My girls aren't asking for anything the boys don't already have. They're asking for the same field. The board can give it to them with one vote.

*[Name] is the girls' soccer and track coach at [High School].*

b.text:
Our soccer field flooded nine times in the last two seasons. Nine games rained out or moved. That’s not bad luck. That’s a field that can’t handle rain.

Last October one of my players tore her ACL stepping in a rut the water left behind. She’s a junior. That injury doesn’t just cost a season.

The boys’ football field has had turf since 2019. It doesn’t flood. Ours does. The girls play on the leftover grass.

This is safety and it is fairness. The school board votes on next year’s facilities budget. Put turf on the girls’ soccer field.
