setup: A co-founder is posting a LinkedIn hiring announcement for a first customer support hire to potential applicants and customers.

a.text:
We’re hiring our first support person at Ridgepoint. Not because we planned to—because the three of us handling every ticket ourselves is no longer sustainable.

Here’s what the job actually looks like day to day:

You’ll be the first line for small trucking dispatchers who use our tool to schedule loads and keep their business running. When something’s buggy or confusing, they’ll message you. Some are patient, some are losing money and stressed. Some barely use email. Your job is to figure out what’s really wrong, walk them through a fix if you can, or tag the right founder before the issue snowballs. Fast.

You’ll spend hours in our support queue, writing answers, updating our (very bare) help docs, and spotting patterns so we can push out real fixes. You’ll also be the internal voice of our users, telling the three of us plainly what’s broken, what’s poorly designed, and what dispatchers *actually* need—not what we assumed.

We’re a three-person team. That means you’ll sit close to the people who built the product (literally or via Slack). There’s no scripted playbook because we haven’t had time to make one. You’ll help build it. You’ll learn the product inside out because you’ll be the one explaining it every day.

This isn’t a “culture first” post. It’s a decent, honest job where you’ll get yelled at occasionally, solve a lot of puzzles, and directly affect whether we make it or not. Pay is real, equity is on the table, and you’ll have a ton of ownership.

If reading this gave you a weird sense of “that actually sounds like my kind of chaos,” DM me or check the link in the comments. Tag someone who’d thrive here.

b.text:
For the last 18 months, the three of us at Ridgepoint have been splitting customer support between writing code, selling, and keeping the lights on. It’s not working anymore. We’re hiring our first support person.

Ridgepoint is a small SaaS company that helps small trucking dispatchers schedule loads. Our users are dispatchers at 5- to 20-truck fleets. They’re busy, they’re not always software people, and when something breaks—or they just can’t figure out the schedule view—they need help fast.

Here’s what you’d actually do day to day:

- **Own the support queue.** You’ll be the first person to see most tickets and the last person to resolve them. We don’t have a support playbook yet. You’ll write it.
- **Answer emails and take calls.** Our users are dispatchers with a driver waiting on a load assignment. You need to be calm, fast, and actually useful.
- **Troubleshoot bugs.** Sometimes it’s user error, sometimes it’s a real bug. You’ll reproduce it, gather details, and either fix it (if it’s data/setup) or hand it to us with enough context that we can patch it in hours, not days.
- **Train new customers.** We don’t have a formal academy yet. You’ll walk dispatchers through the product over Zoom, improvising based on how they actually run their board.
- **Tell us what’s broken.** You’ll be the voice of the customer in our Slack. If three people hit the same confusion this week, you’ll flag it so we can fix the UI instead of answering the same question forever.

This is not a role where you escalate everything and clock out. We’re three people. You’ll be the fourth. You’ll work directly with the founders, and you’ll have a lot of autonomy. But you’ll also have to figure things out without a 50-person support org behind you.

If you’re good at explaining software to non-technical people, you can stay cool when a customer is frustrated, and you want to join a tiny team where your work is visible immediately, send me a DM or drop a comment.

We’re moving fast on this because, frankly, our ticket backlog is embarrassing.

setup: A family plumbing company owner is writing a blog post for Minneapolis homeowners about winterizing outdoor pipes.

a.text:
# How to Winterize Outside Spigots in Minneapolis

Winterizing your outside spigots helps prevent frozen pipes, water damage, and emergency plumbing repairs. In Minneapolis, outdoor faucets can freeze quickly when temperatures drop, especially if water is trapped in the spigot or the pipe behind it.

Follow these steps before the first hard freeze.

## 1. Shut off the interior water valve

Find the interior shutoff valve that controls your outdoor spigot. It is usually located in the basement, utility room, crawl space, or near where the pipe passes through the foundation wall.

Turn the valve clockwise until it is closed. If your home has more than one outdoor faucet, check for a separate shutoff valve for each one.

If you cannot find an interior shutoff valve, call a Minneapolis plumber for help. Some homes do not have a dedicated valve, and forcing or incorrectly closing the wrong valve can create additional problems.

## 2. Disconnect the garden hose

Remove every hose, splitter, timer, nozzle, and other attachment from the outdoor spigot.

This is the most important step—and the mistake we see most often. Leaving a hose connected can trap water inside the faucet and the pipe. When that water freezes, it expands and can crack the spigot or the water line inside your wall.

A connected hose is responsible for many of the burst-pipe calls we receive in January.

Store the hose indoors or in a protected garage space after draining it.

## 3. Open the outside spigot

Once the interior shutoff valve is closed, open the outdoor faucet completely. Let any remaining water drain out.

Leave the spigot open through the winter. This gives trapped water a place to expand if it freezes and helps relieve pressure in the pipe.

If your shutoff valve has a small bleeder cap or drain screw, place a bucket underneath and open it carefully to drain water from the section of pipe between the valve and the outside faucet. Close the bleeder cap after the line has drained, but leave the outdoor spigot open.

## 4. Install a foam faucet cover

After the spigot has drained, install an inexpensive foam faucet cover. These covers typically cost around $3 and are available at most hardware stores.

To install one:

1. Place the cover over the outdoor spigot.
2. Secure it according to the manufacturer’s instructions.
3. Make sure it fits snugly against the wall.

A foam cover adds insulation and helps protect the faucet from cold air. It does not replace shutting off and draining the water line.

## What if you have a frost-free spigot?

Frost-free or freeze-resistant outdoor faucets are designed to drain when they are shut off. However, they still require the hose and attachments to be removed. A hose can prevent the faucet from draining properly and may cause the pipe to freeze.

If a frost-free spigot leaks, does not drain, or continues running after you shut it off, have it inspected by a plumber.

## What to do if you cannot find the shutoff valve

Do not assume the outdoor faucet is safe just because it has a foam cover. If you do not have an interior shutoff valve—or cannot locate it—contact a professional plumber before freezing weather arrives.

A plumber can help identify the correct valve and determine whether the outdoor water line needs to be drained or repaired.

For Minneapolis homeowners, the basic winterization checklist is simple:

- Shut off the interior valve.
- Disconnect all hoses and attachments.
- Open and drain the outside spigot.
- Install a foam faucet cover.
- Call a plumber if there is no interior shutoff valve.

Taking a few minutes to winterize your outdoor spigots can help prevent a burst pipe and costly water damage during a Minneapolis winter.

b.text:
# How to Winterize Outside Spigots in Minneapolis

Outdoor spigots can freeze and burst when Minneapolis temperatures drop below zero. The good news: winterizing them usually takes less than 10 minutes per spigot.

The most important thing is to disconnect every garden hose. Leaving a hose connected is one of the biggest causes of frozen outdoor faucet and burst-pipe calls we get in January.

## 1. Disconnect Every Hose, Sprayer, and Timer

Remove garden hoses, splitters, spray nozzles, timers, and anything else attached to the outdoor faucet.

Even if the faucet is turned off, water can stay trapped inside a connected hose. When that water freezes, it expands backward into the spigot and the pipe inside your wall.

After disconnecting the hose:

- Drain it completely
- Coil it up
- Store it in a garage, shed, or basement if possible

Don’t leave a “short hose” or sprinkler attachment connected either. It only takes a small amount of trapped water to create a problem.

## 2. Find and Shut Off the Interior Water Valve

Many Minneapolis homes have an indoor shutoff valve for each outdoor spigot. It may be located:

- In the basement ceiling near the exterior wall
- Near your water meter or utility room
- Under a sink in an older addition
- In a crawlspace or mechanical room

Turn the valve clockwise to shut off water going to the outdoor faucet.

Not every house has separate shutoffs, especially in older homes. If you cannot find one, don’t force random valves. You do not want to accidentally shut off water to part of the house.

## 3. Drain the Outdoor Spigot

Once the interior shutoff valve is off, go outside and open the spigot fully.

Let it run until the water stops. This drains the water left in the pipe between the interior shutoff and the outdoor faucet.

Leave the outside spigot open for the winter after it has drained. That gives any remaining moisture room to expand instead of building pressure inside the pipe.

Some interior shutoff valves have a small drain cap or bleeder screw near the valve. If yours does, place a small cup or towel underneath it and open it briefly to drain any water on the house side of the valve. Close it again when it stops dripping.

## 4. Install a Foam Spigot Cover

A basic foam faucet cover costs around $3 to $5 at most hardware stores. It is inexpensive extra protection, especially on older homes or exposed walls.

To install it:

1. Make sure the spigot is drained and left open.
2. Place the foam cover over the faucet.
3. Tighten the strap or drawstring so it fits snugly against the siding.

A foam cover is not a substitute for shutting off and draining the line. It helps, but it cannot protect a faucet with water trapped inside it during a Minneapolis cold snap.

## What If You Have a Frost-Free Spigot?

Many newer homes have frost-free outdoor faucets. These have a longer valve stem that shuts the water off farther inside the heated part of the house.

They are more freeze-resistant, but hoses still need to be disconnected. A frost-free spigot can still freeze if a hose is left attached because water cannot drain out properly.

If you are not sure whether your home has frost-free faucets, winterize them the same way: remove hoses, shut off the indoor valve if one is available, and drain the outdoor faucet.

## Signs an Outdoor Pipe May Have Frozen or Burst

Check your outdoor faucets in spring before using them regularly. Call a plumber if you notice:

- Little or no water coming from the spigot
- Water leaking inside the basement or wall when the outdoor faucet is turned on
- Damp drywall, stains, or a musty smell near an exterior wall
- A cracked spigot or visible damage around the faucet

A frozen outdoor pipe often does not start leaking until temperatures warm up and the water is turned back on.

## Don’t Have an Interior Shutoff Valve?

If your outdoor spigot does not have an interior shutoff, it is worth having one installed. A dedicated shutoff makes winterizing easier and gives you better protection during Minneapolis winters.

Our family plumbing company can help locate your outdoor water lines, install shutoff valves, replace aging spigots, and repair frozen or burst pipes.

setup: A real estate agent is posting one specific observation about early block walks and happier buyers to LinkedIn buyers, agents, and lenders.

a.text:
After 12 years helping mostly first-time buyers find homes in Asheville, I’ve noticed something that keeps showing up: the buyers who walk the neighborhood at 7 a.m. before we tour almost always end up happier with the house later.

I think about the Pruitts and the place on Sycamore Street. They had found a bungalow that looked right on paper—good light, solid bones, price that worked. But before we even scheduled the showing, they drove over early one morning and walked the block. At 7 a.m. they saw the school bus stop at the corner, watched the couple two doors down watering their garden, heard how quiet the street stayed before the day started, and ended up talking for a few minutes with a neighbor walking his dog. By the time we stepped inside later that day, they already knew what mornings would feel like there. They put in an offer that week. When I checked in months later, they told me that early walk was the reason they still felt settled. They hadn’t just bought a house—they had already met the neighborhood.

The floor plan and the photos matter, of course. But the life that happens outside the front door at 7 a.m. is what people actually live with every day.

b.text:
After 12 years selling homes in Asheville, mostly to first-time buyers, I've started asking people to do one thing that feels a little annoying at first.

If they love a house online, I ask them to walk the neighborhood at 7am before we tour it.

The buyers who do it almost always end up happier later, even if they don't buy that house. You just learn different things at 7am.

The Pruitts are why I keep asking.

Last spring they were stuck on a little 1920s bungalow on Sycamore Street in West Asheville. It checked all their boxes online, and they wanted to see it that Saturday. I told them I would book it, but could they do me a favor and walk Sycamore and the two streets over at 7am first, before we went inside?

They texted me from the sidewalk on Tuesday morning. The woman next door was already out watering her garden and stopped to chat and ask if they were thinking of moving in. The guy across the street was loading his kid and a cello into a Subaru for early orchestra practice. And two old black Labs from three doors down dragged their owner straight over to say hello.

We walked the house at 9am. They still loved it, but now they weren't just buying the house, they knew what Tuesday on Sycamore actually felt like.

They closed in May. I ran into Maya at the River Arts farmers market last week and she said those same Labs still come to say hi every morning when she's making coffee.

You can learn a lot about a house at 2pm on a Saturday. You learn a lot more about whether you want to live there at 7am on a Tuesday.

setup: A first-year nursing student is writing a scholarship essay about her first ER rotation for scholarship committee readers.

a.text:
# My First Week in the ER

I thought my first week in the emergency room would be about big moments. Saving somebody. Doing something that mattered. What I learned is that most of it is smaller than that, and somehow harder.

On my second day, a man came in with a deep cut on his forearm. His wife was on her way but stuck in traffic, and I could tell he was scared even though he was trying not to show it. The nurse asked me to stay with him while she cleaned and dressed the wound. I didn't have anything useful to do with my hands, so I just held his. He gripped it tight the whole time. When it was over he thanked me like I had done something, but all I did was stand there. I've been thinking about that ever since. Sometimes a person just doesn't want to be alone with something scary. That's the whole job, some days.

Later that week there was a code. I wasn't allowed anywhere near it, which was the right call. A nurse handed me a list and sent me to restock gauze. So there I was, counting out packages in a supply room, and through the curtain I could hear them counting too. Compressions. Somebody calling out numbers. I stood there stocking shelves while a few feet away people were fighting to keep somebody alive. It didn't feel heroic. It felt like being small. But I understood, standing there, that a room full of people doing their small parts right is what makes the big part possible. The gauze has to be there. Somebody has to make sure it is.

The thing that humbled me most was a blood draw. A man with diabetes and bad veins. I missed the first stick. Then the second. Then the third. I could feel my face going red, and I kept apologizing, and he finally said, "You're okay, honey. Take your time." A patient comforting me while I poked him. On the fourth try I got it. I don't think I'll ever forget how patient he was with a nervous student who kept hurting him. He didn't have to be. He chose to be.

I don't have this all figured out. I'm a first-year student who misses veins and restocks gauze and holds hands because I'm not sure what else to do yet. But that first week showed me this is where I belong. Not because I'm good at it yet, but because I want to get good at it, for people like that man in the traffic and the man with the bad veins.

This scholarship would help me keep going. I promise I won't waste it.

b.text:
First Week in the ER

I didn't expect my first clinical rotation to teach me as much as it did. I thought I would mostly watch. I did watch, but I also held a stranger's hand, restocked a supply closet while someone down the hall might have been dying, and stuck a needle in the same man's arm four times trying to get blood. I learned more in that one week than in a whole semester of lectures.

The first day I was assigned to follow a nurse named Trish. She was fast and kind and did not seem nervous about anything, which made me feel better about being very nervous about everything. By midmorning she had me bringing patients water and blankets, which I thought was too simple to matter, until I watched a man drink a cup of water I had handed him and close his eyes like he had been waiting for it all morning.

The moment I keep coming back to happened that same morning. An older man came in with a deep cut on his forearm that needed cleaning and packing. His wife was on her way, but she was stuck in traffic on the interstate. He was in pain and trying to stay still and I could see his hands shaking. Trish asked him if he wanted someone to hold his hand and he looked at me, this total stranger, and said okay. I sat next to him and held his hand while the nurse cleaned out the wound. He squeezed tighter than I expected when it hurt the worst. His wife made it about forty minutes later, and by then my own hand was cramping up. He thanked her on the way in, and his wife grabbed my other hand and just cried for a second. I didn't say anything. I didn't know what to say. I just stood there.

Two days later I was in the back supply room, counting gauze and restocking gloves, when the alarm went off. A code. The curtain was pulled shut where they were working on the patient, but I could hear them counting. One, two, three, four. Compressions. Someone called out meds. The rhythm of it was steady and loud, and I remember standing there thinking how everyone in that room knew exactly what to do except me, and I was three feet away sorting 4x4s by size. I finished restocking the cart. I didn't know what else to do. That night I went home and read my BLS chapter twice.

The last thing I want to tell you about is a man I'll call Mr. D. He came in for high blood sugar and needed blood drawn. The veins in his arms were hard and scarred from years of diabetes and probably a lot of sticks before mine. My instructor let me try. I missed the first time. I missed the second. I missed the third. By the fourth try my hands were sweating and I could feel him staring at the ceiling, trying to be patient. I got it on the fourth. He said "thank you, sweetheart" when I labeled the tube, and I had to walk out of the room before I cried, not because I was upset, but because he had been so kind to me even after I had hurt him three times.

I don't think I went into nursing because I wanted to hold hands or start IVs. I think I went in because I wanted to be useful to people on the worst day of their life, or at least a hard one. That week showed me the job is mostly small things. A cup of water. A hand to hold. Counting to four over and over. Trying four times instead of giving up. I want to keep learning how to do the small things well, and I want to keep showing up on the hard days, even the ones where I feel like I'm just restocking gauze in the next room.

setup: A retired Army staff sergeant is writing about coming home after his second deployment for readers of the veterans' writing workshop anthology.

a.text:
My second tour ended on a Tuesday in October. 

When we got to the terminal, I saw Sarah first. She was waving, wearing a yellow sweater I’d never seen before. Lily was right next to her. Lily was six then, and she’d grown three inches since the deployment ceremony. When I got closer, dropped my green duffel, and knelt down, Lily took a step back. She got right behind Sarah’s leg, wrapping her arms around her mother’s jeans, looking at me like I was a stranger. She didn’t recognize me. A year is a long time when you’re six. I had to sit there on the linoleum floor and talk to her in my quiet voice for a few minutes before she would even let me hold her hand. 

Two days later, Sarah sent me to the grocery store. She wanted me to get out of the house, and she needed a few things. The list was simple: milk, bread, and cereal for Lily. 

I got the milk and the bread with no issue. Then I hit the cereal aisle. I stood there for twenty minutes. I know it was twenty minutes because I kept looking at my watch. There were forty different kinds of cereal. Blue boxes, red boxes, cartoon characters, store brand, name brand, organic bran, sugar-coated loops. Downrange, you eat what they put in the metal trays at the DFAC, or you tear open an MRE packet. You don’t think about it. I stood in the middle of that aisle, people pushing their carts past me, and I couldn't make my hand reach out and grab a box. My chest felt tight, like I was trying to solve a problem that had no correct answer. I ended up grabbing a box of plain Cheerios because the box was yellow and easy to see, and I went straight to the registers. 

Nights were different, too. In Iraq, I slept on a cot, facing the plywood door of our CHU. You always sleep facing the entry point, with your boots close. 

At home, our bed faced the windows, away from the door. Sarah liked to keep the bedroom door cracked an inch or two so she could hear Lily if she woke up in the night. The first week, I couldn't close my eyes with that door open. Every time I did, the hallway felt like an unsecured perimeter. I’d get up in the middle of the night, click the door shut, and lie back down. But then Sarah would wake up, notice the door was closed, and worry about Lily. 

So I had to learn to leave it open. I spent a lot of nights lying on my back, staring at the sliver of yellow light coming from the hallway bathroom, waiting for my body to believe that the front door downstairs was locked and there was nobody coming through.

b.text:
I went back to the deployment zone in August of '19 and came home September '20. Twelve months. I didn't get a whole lot to say about what happened over there. The workshop instructor, Maury, said we don't have to write about the war, just about the home part, and I said fine, and then I sat in my kitchen for three days with a legal pad and wrote nothing. What I finally put down is this.

My wife picked me up at the airport. That's where the whole home thing starts, at the baggage claim, which is stupid, but there it is. I'm waiting for my ruck and the duffel and I hear my daughter's voice from across the carpeted floor. "Mommy, who's that guy."

She's six now. When I left she was five and I had about four more weeks in her before I went. She hid behind Karen's leg. Not peeking. Full body behind. Both hands on Karen's knee like I was going to come grab her or something.

I knelt down. I didn't run, I didn't say hey baby, I knelt down on that ugly beige carpet in my BDUs and I said, "It's your dad." She came around slow. Touched my hand like she was making sure I was there. Karen stood there with her arms at her sides and I could tell she'd been crying in the truck on the way in and I pretended not to notice.

We got to the car. She sat in her booster in the back and kept watching me in the little mirror for about four miles. By then she was talking, telling me about some kid at her school named Devon who did something with a worm. I just said mm-hm the whole way. I couldn't make my face do anything else.

---

Two weeks later I went to Kroger on a Saturday morning. Karen had a headache. She said get cereal for the girl, she likes the one with the chocolate pieces, whatever's in the box. Fine. Easy. I walk down the aisle and it's forty-two kinds of cereal. Forty-two. Maybe more. There were like six kinds before I left, or maybe it was eight. I don't know. Now there's honey-nut-something, and a kind that's just a big round O, and a kind that says "protein" on the front, and a kind shaped like a dinosaur, and a kid's name on another one I've never heard of.

I stood there with the cart. Twenty minutes. I kept checking the box like maybe I'd get it wrong, like she'd open the milk and look at me and say no. There was a woman next to me with a toddler and she grabbed a box and moved on and I was still there. I grabbed three different boxes and put them back. I ended up getting the chocolate one. Karen said it was fine, said the girl wouldn't notice anyway. I said yeah. I stood in the kitchen after that for a while with the milk in my hand just looking at the refrigerator door.

---

The sleeping thing took longer. I didn't want to write this down because it sounds dumb, but here it is. I slept facing the door for a year over there. You get used to it. You get used to the door being the open side, the side where something would come in. When I came home I kept sleeping facing the bedroom door. Door closed. Karen tried to leave it open. I closed it. I'd close it in my sleep without knowing.

She stopped trying in November. Just let me. I slept facing that closed wood and I slept okay and for a while I thought it wasn't going to change, I was going to be forty-three and closing a door every night before I lay down.

It changed because she changed. My daughter. I don't know. February, maybe March. Karen left the door open one night and I woke up and noticed and just left it. Didn't get up and close it. The next night I did it myself before bed. Open. And then I slept facing the window. Which is the opposite of the door. I don't know when I decided that. It was just not the door anymore.

Karen walked past the open door once and looked in and saw me facing the window and she didn't say anything. I think she almost said something. But she didn't. Just walked on.

The cereal box is on the counter now. Dinosaur shape. The girl likes them. I just grab whatever box I pick up off the shelf and I don't look at the others. Twenty minutes is over. I don't know why it's over, it just is. She's seven. The kid Devon thing has been replaced by some other kid doing some other thing, and I say mm-hm, and I say wow, and I say is that right, and it comes out like words I know, and the apartment isn't a deployment anymore. It's just Tuesday.

setup: A high-school senior is writing a personal essay for college admissions readers about working at her family's Vietnamese restaurant.

a.text:
Every Saturday at 4:30 p.m., the front door of my family’s restaurant locks from the inside until five. I have spent almost every weekend since my sophomore year behind that counter, wearing an apron that smells like star anise and floor cleaner. 

Last November, on a rainy Saturday during the dinner rush, the POS system crashed. The screens froze blue, went black, and stayed that way. Table 4 needed a split bill, Table 12 was waiting on a takeout order for eight, and the line at the door stretched past the host stand. My dad stared at the main terminal, hit the power button twice, and looked at me. 

I grabbed a pad of green guest checks from the supply closet and a black ballpoint pen. For the next three hours, I hand-wrote every ticket. I used our family’s shorthand: *P1* for Phở Tái, *B1* for Bún Thịt Nướng, *A2* extra peanut sauce. My handwriting started neat and degraded into quick slashes as the kitchen wheel filled up. I calculated 6.25% sales tax on paper napkins. My wrist cramped, but the food went out, the orders were right, and the kitchen never stopped moving.

Training new hires usually falls to me because I speak English fast enough to explain the seating chart and Vietnamese fast enough to translate my grandma’s notes from the prep station. In September, we hired a junior from my school named Marcus. His first week, I had to teach him how to wrap gỏi cuốn. 

Grandma’s rule is exact: the rice paper has to be damp, not soaked, or it tears when you pull it tight. I laid a round sheet flat on the stainless steel, set down the lettuce, mint, pork, and vermicelli, then placed two halved shrimp pink-side down so they would show through the translucent skin. 

"Pull the bottom flap over, tuck it tight under the filling, fold the sides, then roll," I showed him. 

His first four burst, rice noodles spilling out onto the prep table. I didn't take the wrapper from him. I just ran another sheet through the warm water dish, placed it in front of him, and put my hands over his to show him how much tension the paper could hold before it gave out. By eight o'clock, his rolls looked almost like mine, which looked almost like Grandma’s.

When the dinner rush dies down around 8:30, I take my break. The kitchen gets hot from the broth pots that simmer for twelve hours straight, so I take my AP Calculus homework into the walk-in cooler. 

I sit on an overturned milk crate between the tubs of hoisin sauce and the stacked crates of Thai basil. The air inside is thirty-six degrees and smells like cold ginger. I pull my knees up, rest my notebook on my thighs, and work through derivatives. My breath fogs up the margins. Sometimes the ink from my gel pen slows down on the damp paper, but it is the quietest ten minutes of my week.

I don’t have a grand lesson about how working weekends made me a better person. It is mostly just work. It is sore feet, loud vent hoods, wet dish towels, and making sure the register balances down to the penny at the end of the night. But I know how to keep a dining room moving when the technology fails, I know how to teach someone a skill without taking the paper out of their hands, and I can clear a problem set while my knuckles are cold. At ten o'clock, I turn off the neon open sign, wipe down the glass, and go home.

b.text:
I haven’t had a free weekend since I was fifteen. While my friends are at football games or sleeping in, I’m at my family’s Vietnamese restaurant. Saturday and Sunday mean twelve-hour shifts. The air always smells like star anise, fried garlic, and industrial floor cleaner. 

There are days when things go smoothly, and there are days like the second Saturday in October. Right at 12:30, the middle of the lunch rush, the entire register system crashed. The screens froze, then went completely black. A line was backing up to the door. My dad tapped the main monitor, looked at me, and shrugged. 

I grabbed a stack of paper order pads from the back office and a handful of cheap pens. For the next three hours, I hand-wrote every ticket. *Number 14, no cilantro. Number 32, sub pork for chicken, allergy to peanuts.* I became the restaurant's entire routing system, running tickets back to the kitchen, shouting translations over the hiss of the fryers, and calculating totals in my head with the state tax added on. By three o'clock, my hand was cramping so badly I could barely grip the pen, but we hadn't dropped a single order.

When the rush dies down in the late afternoon, things get quiet. That’s usually when I train the new hires. Last month, we brought on a college student named Leo, and I was in charge of teaching him prep work. We stood at the stainless steel tables in the back, and I showed him my grandma’s spring roll fold. There’s a specific way to do it. You have to tuck the lettuce and vermicelli tight, but leave enough slack in the rice paper so it doesn’t tear when you roll it forward. Then you place the shrimp exactly in the last fold so the pink shows through the translucent wrapper. 

Leo kept ripping the paper. He was trying to force it. I stopped him, put my hands next to his, and showed him how to use the heels of his palms to apply pressure while his fingers guided the roll. We stood there for an hour, practicing until his rolls looked exactly like my grandma’s. 

Around four o'clock, I get a thirty-minute break. I usually spend it in the walk-in cooler. It’s the only place in the building where nobody can ask me for extra hoisin sauce or a refill on their diet soda. I drag a milk crate over to a fifty-pound sack of cabbages, sit down, and do my calculus homework. The hum of the heavy refrigeration unit drowns out the noise of the dining room. The air is forty degrees, which makes my fingers stiff, but the cold keeps me awake enough to figure out derivatives. 

When my shift finally ends at ten at night, my shoes are sticky with spilled soda and my back aches. I wipe down the front counters, turn off the neon Open sign, and lock the door. Monday morning is always just around the corner. I’ll be sitting in first period, turning in the math worksheet that smells faintly of beef broth, and by Friday afternoon, I’ll be putting my apron right back on.

setup: A real estate agent is writing a commentary on the local market for brokerage blog and local paper readers.

a.text:
## The Market Isn’t Crashing. Sellers Are Simply Behind It.

Last spring, the median home in my ZIP code spent just eight days on the market. This spring, that figure has climbed to 34 days. Showings per listing have fallen by roughly half.

Those numbers sound dramatic—and they are. But they do not mean our local housing market is crashing.

They mean the pace has changed, and too many sellers are still pricing their homes for last year’s market.

List prices remain about 6% higher than they were a year ago. That tells me seller expectations have continued rising even as buyer activity has cooled. Buyers today have more time, more choices and less willingness to overlook an inflated price. They are not disappearing; they are becoming selective.

I see this disconnect firsthand. I currently have three sellers whose homes have been on the market for more than 60 days, and all three are resisting a price adjustment. They remember hearing about multiple offers, bidding wars and homes selling over asking price in a weekend. Understandably, they want that outcome for themselves.

But the market does not care what a seller wants, what a neighbor received last year or how much money an owner put into the kitchen. Buyers compare a home with what is available today. If the value is not there, they move on.

The clearest evidence is what happens to homes that are priced correctly: They are still selling, often in less than two weeks.

That is not a crash. A crashing market does not consistently reward well-priced, well-prepared homes with quick sales. What we have is a market that has shifted from automatic urgency to price sensitivity.

For several years, sellers could start high and assume the market would catch up. That strategy is now risky. The first two weeks of a listing are when buyer attention is strongest. If a home enters the market overpriced, serious buyers may skip it, while everyone else watches and waits for a reduction. By the time the seller finally adjusts, the listing has accumulated days on market and buyers begin wondering what is wrong with it.

Often, nothing is wrong with the house. The original price was wrong.

Sellers also need to stop treating a price reduction as a defeat. If a home has been listed for 30, 45 or 60 days with limited showings and no serious offers, the market has already delivered its verdict. Refusing to respond does not protect the home’s value. It simply extends the listing and may ultimately result in a lower sale price than a realistic starting price would have produced.

My advice to sellers right now is direct: Price for the market you are entering, not the market you remember.

Look closely at recent sales, but pay equal attention to the active listings competing for the same buyers. Prepare the home properly. Address obvious condition issues. Make access for showings easy. Most importantly, take the first two weeks seriously.

Buyers should not mistake longer market times for a collapse, either. The best homes are still moving quickly, and waiting for a dramatic drop in prices could mean missing the right property. What buyers have gained is not unlimited leverage but breathing room—the opportunity to compare homes, inspect carefully and negotiate without the frenzy of last spring.

Our local market has slowed. It has not fallen apart.

The sellers succeeding this spring are the ones who understand that distinction. They are not chasing last year’s peak or testing an aspirational price. They are meeting today’s buyers where they are—and they are still getting sold.

b.text:
**Stop Calling It a Crash: The Real Story Behind Our Local Housing Shift**

I’ve been selling homes in this suburb for ten years. I’ve seen the wild frenzies, the steady climbs, and the occasional dips. Lately, I’ve been hearing a lot of nervous chatter from both buyers and sellers about the current state of our local real estate market. People are throwing around the word "crash." 

Let’s cut through the noise. The market isn't a complex puzzle right now, and it doesn't depend on a dozen shifting macroeconomic factors. The reality is incredibly simple: this isn't a crash. It’s a seller reality check.

Let’s look at the actual numbers in our zip code. Last spring, the median days on market was eight. This spring, it’s 34. Furthermore, showings per listing have dropped by half. If you only look at those data points, you’d think the bottom was falling out. But here is the crucial stat the doom-scrollers are ignoring: list prices are still up 6% year over year. 

Prices aren't plummeting. What has changed is the pace, and the vast majority of sellers simply haven't caught up to it. We are dealing with a massive disconnect between what sellers think their home is worth and the actual behavior of today's buyers. 

Right now, I personally have three sellers whose homes have been sitting on the market for over 60 days. All three are flat-out refusing to drop their price. They are clinging to the "list it high and wait for a bidding war" mentality of two years ago. They aren't victims of a bad market; they are victims of their own stubbornness. They want 2021 prices in a 2024 market, and they are willing to let their listings grow stale to get it. 

Those stubborn sellers are exactly why our median days on market has jumped to 34. The average is being heavily skewed by overpriced inventory that is just sitting and rotting. 

Here is the unvarnished truth: if you price your home correctly for today's reality, it is still selling in under two weeks. The buyers are absolutely still out there, and they are still buying. They just aren't tolerating overpriced ego-trips anymore. They are doing their research, they know what the comps are, and they are only making moves on homes that are priced accurately from day one.

The local housing market hasn't broken. The buyers are behaving perfectly rationally. It’s the sellers who need to wake up and catch up.

setup: A local sports columnist is writing an opinionated season-ending commentary for readers of the local paper's sports section.

a.text:
**8-2 And Out - That's The Frustrating Part**

Well, that's it. Friday night in the cold closed the book on this Wolves season, 8-2 with a second-round exit to a team we beat by 20 back in week 3.

It stings because it shouldn't have ended there. This was a good team. A really good team. Dez Kowalski throwing for 2,340 yards and setting the school record tells you that much. Those kids have a lot to be proud of.

But I'm not going to just recap the record and pat everyone on the back. You heard me say it Monday on the air and I'll say it here - we coached ourselves out of that game.

We were down three points to start the second half. Three points. That's nothing. And the run game was working. We were gashing them between the tackles all night.

Then we just stopped. 

We came out in the third quarter and decided we needed to throw our way back into it. Five straight pass plays on that opening drive, all incomplete or short. You can't tell me that's playing to your strengths when you're only down a field goal.

I get it. You have a kid like Dez who just rewrote the record book, you want to put the ball in his hands. But Friday night wasn't the night for it. They couldn't stop the run, and we got away from what was actually moving the chains because the scoreboard made us panic.

A three-point deficit in the third quarter is not a reason to abandon your identity. That's playoff football. You stay patient.

This team was good enough to play next week. 8-2, wins over teams that pushed them, a quarterback who made history. They deserved better than a one-and-done in November against a team they already handled.

Tough loss. Tougher way to lose. I'll talk more about it on the show tomorrow morning at 8.

b.text:
An 8-2 season deserves applause. It doesn’t mean the ending is above criticism.

The second-round state playoff loss will sting because this was a team they had beaten by 20 back in Week 3. That earlier result didn’t guarantee anything in the rematch. But it makes the question harder to shake: Was this a game they had to lose?

My answer is no. And the biggest reason is what happened to the running game in the second half.

It was working. They were down only three points. Yet they moved away from it as though the deficit demanded an entirely different offense.

Three points is a reason to stay patient, not abandon something the defense hasn’t stopped. Keep taking the yards. Make the opponent prove it can handle the run before deciding to do that job for it.

That isn’t a knock on Dez Kowalski. His 2,340 passing yards set a school record, an accomplishment that deserves to stand on its own—not get buried beneath the disappointment of the final game. He gave this offense a weapon few teams in school history have had.

But having a record-setting quarterback doesn’t make every situation a passing situation. A productive ground game helps a quarterback. Going back to it would not have been a vote of no confidence in Kowalski. It would have been a vote for what was working.

It’s easy to second-guess after a loss, and no play call comes with a guarantee. Staying with the run might not have changed the result. Still, the criticism here isn’t simply that the chosen approach failed. It’s that the score and the success on the ground offered little reason to leave that approach behind.

The players earned those eight wins. Kowalski earned his place in the record book. Neither should be diminished by one painful night.

But celebrating a good season doesn’t require pretending its final chapter was handled well. This team had a working running game and a three-point deficit. It needed patience more than a change of plans.

setup: A first-year nursing student is writing a scholarship essay about her first ER rotation for scholarship committee readers.

a.text:
I thought my first week in the ER would teach me how to do things. It mostly taught me how to stand there.

The first man whose hand I held was named Walter. He was seventy-one and he'd caught his forearm on a piece of sheet metal in his garage. The wound wasn't the worst thing I saw that week, but it was long, and it needed a lot of cleaning, and the nurse working on it was thorough in a way that took time. Walter kept looking toward the doorway. His wife was on the highway somewhere, stuck behind an accident, which he said out loud about four times like saying it would move traffic.

I wasn't doing anything. I was a first-year student with a name badge and no skills yet. So I asked if he wanted me to sit with him, and he said yes so fast it surprised me.

He took my hand. Not gently. He held it like a man holding a railing. His grip went tight when the saline hit the deep part and loosened when it didn't, and I just sat there and let him squeeze and told him his wife was probably three exits away. I made that up. I had no idea where she was. But it was the only useful thing I had, so I gave it to him.

She got there twenty minutes later. He let go of my hand and took hers and didn't say anything to me, and that was fine. That was the whole point.

Later that week, a code came in. I heard it before I saw anything — the overhead page, and then the sound of six people moving fast in a small space. A nurse turned to me and said, "Gauze. Supply room. Go."

I want to be honest about how that felt. I felt useless. I felt like I was being moved out of the way, which I was. I walked to the supply room and stood in front of the shelves and picked out four-by-fours, and on the way back I had to pass the curtain, and I could hear them counting compressions. One, two, three, four. Somebody's voice steady on top of it, calling out the rhythm.

I stopped walking. I don't know for how long. Probably four seconds. It felt like a lot longer.

Then I brought the gauze where it needed to go, and I restocked the rest of the shelf, because that was my job and somebody had to do it. Later I found out the patient didn't make it. I went home that night and sat in my car in the driveway for a while before I went inside.

Here's what I keep coming back to about that. Somebody had to restock the gauze. Not that day — the next day, the next patient. The shelf being full is why the nurse's hand finds it without looking. I didn't save anybody. But I understood for the first time that a hospital is a hundred small jobs stacked on top of each other, and the person doing the smallest one still has to do it right.

The blood draw was the hardest part of the week, and it wasn't even close.

The patient was a man in his fifties, diabetic, in for something unrelated. His veins were rough — scarred up from years of sticks, rolling, deep. My preceptor said I could try. She stood next to me the whole time.

I missed. I missed again. I missed a third time.

By the third one my hands were shaking and my face was hot and I was about two seconds from asking her to just take over. I apologized so many times he finally said, "You're gonna have to stop that, it's making me nervous." Which made us both laugh, a little, which helped more than anything anybody said to me that whole week.

My preceptor didn't take the needle. She said, "Feel again. Don't look for it, feel for it." So I put my fingers on his arm and closed my eyes for a second like an idiot, and I found something soft and springy near his wrist that I'd skipped over three times because it didn't look like anything.

Fourth stick. Flash of red in the hub. He said, "There you go," like he'd been rooting for me, and I think he actually had been.

I've thought about why that one stuck with me. It's not because I finally got it. It's because he let me try four times. He was tired, he'd been poked by better nurses than me his whole adult life, and he still put his arm out. People do that. They hand you their body and their bad day and they let you learn on them, and most of them never get thanked for it.

I don't have a big statement about what kind of nurse I'm going to be. I've had one week. But I know I want to be the person who sits down when there's nothing else to do, who keeps the shelf full for the next person, who feels for the vein instead of just looking at it.

This scholarship would help me keep going. I'm working part-time and the schedule is tight and the program is not going to get easier. But I'd like to be there for week two, and week fifty, and however many after that.

I'd like to get good at this. I think I could.

b.text:
**What I Learned in the ER**

Before my first clinical rotation, I thought I knew what nursing was. I had passed my classes. I could label a diagram of the heart. I knew what to do on a test. Then I spent a week in the emergency room, and I found out how much I didn't know.

On my second day, a man came in with a deep cut on his arm from a work accident. The nurse had to clean it out, and it was going to hurt. His wife was stuck in traffic and kept calling him, upset that she couldn't get there. He was trying to sound calm on the phone, but his free hand was shaking. When the cleaning started, I didn't have a real job to do. I was a student. So I held his hand. He squeezed hard enough that my fingers went white, and he apologized, and I told him not to. We didn't talk much. He just needed someone there until his wife could be. I always figured nursing was about the skills — the needles, the medications, the machines. That day the most useful thing I did was stand still and let a stranger hold on to me.

Later that week there was a code. A patient's heart stopped, and the room filled up fast with people who knew exactly what they were doing. I did not know what I was doing, and a nurse told me to go restock gauze in the supply room. At first I felt useless, like I was being sent out of the way. And I was — but restocking still needed to happen, and I was the person who could do it. Through the curtain I could hear them counting compressions out loud, steady and even, like a heartbeat the team was making with their own voices. I stacked gauze and listened and understood something: everyone in that department had a job, and every job mattered, even mine. Someday I'll be the one counting. Right now I'm the one making sure the shelf isn't empty when somebody reaches for it.

The hardest lesson came from a blood draw. The patient was a man with diabetes, and his veins were hard to find. I missed. He told me it was fine, try again. I missed a second time. Then a third. I wanted to hand the needle to someone else and disappear. My face was hot and my hands didn't feel like mine. He looked at me and said, "You'll get it. I've had worse." The nurse supervising me could have taken over, but she talked me through it instead. On the fourth try, I got it. The flash of blood in that tube was the best thing I saw all week. What stayed with me wasn't the success, though. It was that he trusted me after I had already failed him three times. Patients give students that kind of grace all the time, and I don't ever want to take it for granted.

I went into that week thinking the goal was to look competent. I came out understanding that the goal is to be useful, honest, and present, and that competence comes from staying in the room when it's uncomfortable — during the pain, the missed sticks, the moments when the most you can offer is your hand.

I'm a first-year student. I have a lot left to learn, and I know it. But that week in the ER showed me I'm in the right place, doing work I want to spend my life getting better at. This scholarship would help me keep showing up — to class, to clinicals, to the patients who are willing to let a student learn on them. I owe them my best effort. I intend to give it.

setup: A long-haul trucker is writing a short Roadstar DC4 dual dash cam review for other owner-operators on a trucking forum.

a.text:
**Roadstar DC4 Dash Cam – 14 Month / 140k Mile Review**

Put about 140,000 miles on the Roadstar DC4 over the last 14 months in my rig. Figure that’s enough road time and cab vibration to give an honest take for anybody looking at one.

Here’s the straight truth on it:

**The Good**
* **Saved my bacon on an insurance claim.** A four-wheeler chopped my front bumper taking a sloppy lane change. Cam caught the whole thing clear as day. Insurance had the claim approved in 9 days flat instead of the usual 6-week fight. It paid for itself right there.

**The Annoying (And How to Fix It)**
* **Ditch the suction mount.** The suction cup dropped off the windshield twice last summer when the cab got hot. Don't bother with it. Use the adhesive mount right out of the box and save yourself the headache. Hasn't moved an inch since.
* **Forget the phone app.** The app makes you connect to Wi-Fi to pull footage off the camera, which is completely useless at most truck stops. Don't waste your time fighting the app—just pull the SD card and slide it into a reader or laptop. It’s ten times faster anyway.
* **Rear camera night vision is mediocre.** Daytime rear footage is solid, but at night it gets grainy real quick past 30 feet. It’ll still prove if somebody rear-ended you, but you won't be reading license plates at a distance in the dark.

**Bottom Line**
It isn't perfect, but it’s tough, it runs constantly without freezing up, and the front video quality is sharp enough to protect your CDL when someone else screws up. Mount it with the tape, pull the card manually, and it’ll do the job. Worth the money for an owner-operator.

b.text:
**Roadstar DC4 dash cam – 14 months / ~140k miles**

Figured I'd put up my notes since a few guys asked.

**The good**
Front cam is solid. Day footage is clear enough to read plates a couple lanes over. Back in the spring a four-wheeler cut across my nose on I-40 and clipped my bumper, then tried to say I merged into him. Pulled the card, sent the clip to my adjuster, claim approved in 9 days. Usually that's a 6 week fight. That one clip paid for the camera ten times over.

**The not so good**
Rear cam is the weak spot. Daytime it's fine, but at night anything past about 30 feet turns to grainy mush. You'll see there's a car back there, you won't read a plate. If your main concern is getting rear-ended at night, look at something else or plan on a separate rear unit.

**Mounting**
The suction mount is junk for a truck. Fell off the windshield twice last summer, both times sitting in a lot in the heat. Second time it landed on the dash and I figured I'd find it in pieces. Switched to the adhesive mount that comes in the box and it hasn't budged since. Skip the suction cup, just go adhesive from day one.

**The app**
It needs wifi to pull footage off the camera. Most truck stops the wifi is either dead or so slow you'll give up. I stopped bothering. I keep a card reader in the cab and just pull the SD card and drop it on my laptop. Takes two minutes. Don't buy this expecting the app to do anything useful for you on the road.

**Bottom line**
Front camera does its job and it already saved me on a claim. Rear camera is average at best, mount and app are both annoyances you can work around. Would I buy it again? Yeah, probably, but I'd order the adhesive mount ready to go and I'd never open the app.

If you've got a rear cam with decent night footage let me know, that's the one thing I'd swap out.

setup: A bakery owner is writing a warm blog and newsletter post to regular customers explaining why wedding cake orders are ending.

a.text:
**A Change to Our Wedding Cake Orders**

Hi friends,

I've been putting off writing this one, mostly because I know some of you have been part of the wedding cakes we've made over the years, and those cakes carry a lot of good memories for me. But here it is: we've decided to stop taking custom wedding cake orders.

I want to explain why, because you all have been so good to us and you deserve more than a quiet line disappearing from the website.

When someone orders a wedding cake, the cake itself is honestly the easy part. It's everything around it that adds up. Between the consultations, the tastings, the sketches, the emails back and forth about ribbon colors and sugar flowers, each wedding order takes about fourteen hours of time that never shows up on an invoice. There are three of us here. Fourteen hours is a lot of hours when you're also the person mixing the morning croissant dough at 4am.

And this year we had three weddings cancel at the last minute. I understand that life happens, truly, and I don't hold it against anyone. But by the time a cancellation comes in, we've usually already bought the butter, the eggs, the fondant, sometimes cleared a whole day's production schedule to make room. Three times over, that's real money for a shop our size, and it stung.

The biggest reason, though, is simpler than either of those. Every hour we spent on wedding cakes was an hour we weren't spending on the everyday case. The sourdough, the morning buns, the cookies your kids press their noses against the glass to look at. That case is the heart of this place. It's what keeps the lights on, and honestly, it's what I love most. When wedding season got busy, I could feel the everyday stuff getting less of me, and that never sat right.

So we're choosing the case. We're choosing being here, rested enough to be cheerful when you come in, with the shelves full of the things you actually stop by for.

If you're planning a wedding, we can still be part of your day in smaller ways. We're happy to do sheet cakes, dessert tables, big boxes of pastries for a brunch reception, that kind of thing. Just no more tiered custom cakes with all the trimmings. And if you need a recommendation, ask me, there are some wonderful cake artists around here who do that work full-time and do it beautifully.

Thank you for understanding, and thank you, as always, for keeping this little place going. Come see us. The morning buns come out around 7.

With love (and flour on everything),

your baker

b.text:
I’m writing this at the little corner table by the back door, still dusting flour off my forearms while the afternoon sourdough cools. It’s quiet in the shop right now, which is usually the only time I get to sit down and talk to you all like this.

I wanted to share an update about a change we’re making around here, and because so many of you have been with us since day one, I wanted to just tell you straight from the heart.

Starting next month, we are no longer going to be taking on custom wedding cakes.

This wasn’t an easy decision. We’ve had the absolute joy of being a small part of so many incredible love stories in this town, and seeing photos of you all cutting into a cake we built with our own hands will always be special to me. But over the last year, it’s become really clear that custom wedding work just doesn’t fit the reality of our tiny shop anymore.

Right now, it’s just three of us back in the kitchen. To do a custom wedding cake the right way—the way you deserve—it easily takes about 14 hours of behind-the-scenes work before we even turn the ovens on for the big day. That’s emails back and forth, sketching designs, organizing private tastings, and prepping specialty ingredients. When you’re a crew of three starting at 4:00 in the morning, fourteen hours is a massive piece of our week. 

On top of the time, this past year brought us three separate last-minute wedding cancellations. In a small kitchen on tight margins, having hundreds of dollars in high-end butter, vanilla, and specialty ingredients suddenly go to waste hurts a lot. 

Most of all, we realized that pouring all our energy into two or three big weekend events was pulling us away from the heart of this bakery: the morning case. The sourdough loaves, the flaky croissants, the afternoon cookies, and the simple birthday cakes you pick up on a Tuesday—that’s what actually pays our rent, and that’s what feeds our neighborhood every single day. We want to put all our love, focus, and energy right back into making sure that display case is packed full of the best bakes we can possibly make for you.

We’ll still have our classic layer cakes available to order through the regular menu if you’re hosting a smaller, casual gathering and just want something delicious on the table. But the multi-tiered, custom-designed wedding orders are taking a bow.

Thank you, as always, for understanding and for letting us grow and adapt so we can keep our doors open and our ovens running for a long time to come. I’m going to go wipe down the bench now, but I’ll see you tomorrow morning for coffee and pastries.

setup: A small coffee shop owner is writing testimony to city council opposing a parking meter rate increase.

a.text:
**Testimony on the Proposed Downtown Parking Meter Rate Increase**

*Submitted by [Your Name], owner of [Business Name], Main Street*

Council members,

I own a small independent coffee shop on Main Street, and I want to make my case against this proposal with numbers rather than general worries — because I have the numbers.

The proposal would raise downtown meter rates from 50 cents an hour to $1.50 an hour. Let's call it what it is: a 200 percent increase. A tripling of the cost of parking in front of the businesses that employ your residents, pay your taxes, and give people a reason to come downtown at all.

I've watched this exact policy play out before, and I measured it. Back in 2019, the town next door passed a nearly identical hike. I tracked my own register for the six weeks after it took effect, and foot traffic there dropped 18 percent. That is not anecdote — that is register data, six weeks, 18 percent fewer customers coming through the door. An 18 percent drop isn't absorbed by a small shop's margin. For a lot of us, it *is* the margin.

Now consider who actually parks at our meters. My point-of-sale data shows my average customer visit runs 22 minutes. Under the current rate — 50 cents an hour with an hour minimum — that visit is already fully covered. My customers pay for an hour and routinely leave time on the meter. The spaces in front of my shop already turn over faster than an hour. So this increase doesn't change how long anyone stays, and it doesn't solve a turnover problem that doesn't exist. All it does is charge the same 22-minute customer a dollar more — three times what they paid last month for the identical trip. That extra dollar lands on top of a small-ticket purchase, and it is precisely the kind of thing that makes someone decide to stay home and brew their own.

Then there is the number the city itself published: meter revenue covers 4 percent of the downtown budget. Even if this increase performed perfectly — triple the rate, same number of cars — you would move that figure from 4 percent to 12 percent. And the 2019 data says it will not perform perfectly: knock 18 percent off the paid hours and you land near 10 percent. That means this proposal shrinks the shortfall from 96 percent to roughly 90 percent. That is the entire payoff, and it is purchased by taking an 18 percent bite out of every storefront on this street.

I understand the budget pressures are real, and I understand the council needs revenue. But this particular lever is too small to matter to the budget and too heavy not to matter to us. If parking revenue is 4 percent of the problem, then parking was never going to be the solution — and the city's own report effectively says so.

I'm asking the council to vote this down, or at minimum to table it until staff can show the arithmetic in public: projected paid hours, assumed visit lengths, expected traffic effects. I'll gladly bring my register data to that conversation. It's six weeks long, it's from 2019, and it says 18 percent.

Thank you.

[Your Name]
Owner, [Business Name], Main Street

b.text:
Good evening, Mayor and Council Members.

My name is [Your Name], and I am the owner of a small independent coffee shop on Main Street. I am here tonight to speak in opposition to the proposed increase in downtown parking meter rates from 50 cents an hour to $1.50 an hour.

I want to be clear from the start: this is not an abstract concern for me, and it is not just a general worry that “higher parking fees might hurt businesses.” I have looked at the numbers, I have seen what happens when similar changes are made, and I believe this proposal will have a measurable negative impact on downtown businesses without meaningfully solving the city’s budget problem.

First, the practical issue: my customers do not stay long. Based on my own observation and sales tracking, the average visit to my shop is 22 minutes. That means the current meter rate of 50 cents an hour already covers the typical length of time someone needs to park, come in, buy a coffee, and leave. In other words, the current system is already proportionate to how downtown customers actually use parking. Raising the rate to $1.50 an hour does not address a parking shortage or a turnover problem. It simply makes a short visit more expensive.

Second, I have direct evidence of what a similar rate increase can do to customer traffic. In 2019, when a nearby town implemented a comparable parking meter hike, I tracked my own register for six weeks afterward. During that period, foot traffic dropped by 18%. That is not a guess or a fear; it is the result I recorded in my own business after a similar policy change in a neighboring downtown. An 18% decline in foot traffic is significant for any small business, but especially for independent shops like mine that operate on narrow margins. When nearly one in five customers stops coming downtown as often, the effects are immediate: fewer sales, fewer impulse purchases, and less money staying in the local economy.

Third, I want to address the city’s stated reason for this increase. According to the city’s own report, meter revenue currently covers only 4% of the downtown budget. That means 96% of downtown funding comes from somewhere else. Increasing parking meters from 50 cents to $1.50 an hour is not a serious solution to the city’s budget needs if the existing revenue stream is only a small fraction of the overall budget. It may generate some additional dollars, but it will not come close to solving the downtown funding issue the way the proposal suggests. A policy that places a bigger burden on visitors and customers while covering only 4% of the budget to begin with is not a meaningful fix. It shifts costs onto the people who shop, dine, and spend time downtown without addressing the underlying financial challenge.

I understand that cities need revenue, and I understand that downtown maintenance and services cost money. But this particular proposal asks small businesses and their customers to absorb a substantial increase for a very limited return. My experience tells me that an 18% drop in foot traffic is a real and likely consequence. My customer data tells me that the current hour-long minimum is already enough for the average 22-minute visit. And the city’s own report tells us that meter revenue is only 4% of the downtown budget, so this change is not solving the problem it claims to solve.

For those reasons, I respectfully urge you to reject the proposed increase from 50 cents to $1.50 an hour.

Thank you for your time and for your consideration.

setup: A family plumbing company owner is writing a blog post for Minneapolis homeowners about winterizing outdoor pipes.

a.text:
# How to Winterize Your Outside Spigots in Minneapolis

If you want to avoid a burst pipe and a flooded basement this year, you need to winterize your outdoor faucets. Here is exactly how to do it.

**The Biggest Mistake Homeowners Make**
Before we get to the steps, let’s talk about the number one mistake we see. Almost all of our January emergency calls for burst pipes happen because a garden hose was left connected to the spigot. A connected hose traps water inside the faucet. When that water freezes, it expands and cracks the pipe right inside your wall. 

Here is how to properly winterize your outside spigots:

**1. Disconnect All Hoses**
Unscrew every garden hose, splitter, or timer from your outdoor faucets. Drain them and put them away for the season. 

**2. Shut the Interior Valve**
Go inside—usually down in the basement or crawlspace—and locate the water shutoff valve that supplies your outside spigot. Turn it completely off. 

**3. Drain the Spigot**
Go back outside and turn the spigot handle to the "on" position. This lets the trapped water drain out. Leave the handle open all winter. *(Note: If your interior shutoff valve has a small bleed cap, open that too and let any remaining water drain into a bucket).*

**4. Install a $3 Foam Cover**
Head to your local hardware store and pick up a foam spigot cover. They cost about three bucks and take ten seconds to strap on. It provides a great extra layer of insulation against brutal Minneapolis wind chills.

**Don't Have an Interior Shutoff Valve?**
Many older Minneapolis homes were built without interior shutoff valves for the outdoor faucets. If you can't find a valve to turn off inside your house, your pipes are at a much higher risk of freezing. 

Give our shop a call. We can install an interior shutoff valve for you, or upgrade your exterior spigot to a frost-free sillcock so you don't have to stress about it when the temperatures drop.

b.text:
# How to Winterize Your Outdoor Spigots Before Minneapolis Winter Hits

Most burst pipes we get called out for in January could have been prevented in October. Here's the whole job, start to finish, in about ten minutes per faucet.

## What You'll Need

- An indoor shutoff valve (more on this below)
- A pair of pliers, optional
- A foam faucet cover ($3 at any hardware store in the Twin Cities)
- A rag

## Step 1: Find and Shut Off the Interior Valve

Your outdoor spigot has a shutoff valve somewhere inside the house, usually on the same wall the faucet is mounted on. Look in the basement, crawl space, or utility room. It's often a small round handle, a lever, or a knob within a few feet of where the pipe exits the wall.

Turn it all the way off. Then go outside and open the spigot and let it drain. Leave the spigot open for the winter — that gives the remaining water somewhere to expand into if it freezes.

## Step 2: Disconnect Everything from the Spigot

Hoses. Splitters. Timers. Quick-connects. Y-valves. Take it all off.

This is the step that matters most, and it's where most people skip. More details below.

## Step 3: Drain and Store the Hose

Coil it up, dump any water out of it, and store it inside the garage or shed. A frozen water hose is a ruined water hose, but that's the cheap part of the problem.

## Step 4: Put the Foam Cover On

The $3 styrofoam dome with the rubber gasket. Push it firmly over the spigot until it seals tight. That's it.

The cover doesn't add heat. It blocks cold air from getting into the wall opening and onto the pipe behind it. In a Minneapolis winter, that matters.

---

## The Mistake That Bursts Most Faucets

**Leaving a hose connected.**

It doesn't matter if the hose is drained. It doesn't matter if it's one of those fancy frost-free hydrants. If there's a hose, a timer, or anything else attached to the end of the spigot, water can't fully drain out of the pipe. A small amount of water sits against the back of the valve all winter.

When it hits -15°F in February, that water freezes and expands. The pipe splits. You don't know it yet because the split is on the interior side of the wall. Then you turn the spigot on in April, water sprays into the basement, and now you're calling us at 7 a.m. on a Saturday.

The foam cover only works if the spigot can fully drain. A connected hose traps water. Hose off, cover on — that's the whole game.

---

## What If You Don't Have an Interior Shutoff?

Some older Minneapolis homes, especially bungalows in neighborhoods like Standish, Howe, and parts of Northeast, were built with the outdoor spigot on a direct line off the main with no interior valve. You can't shut it off from inside.

If that's your house, you've got two real options:

1. **Have us install a shutoff valve.** It's usually a 1-2 hour job, and it turns a recurring problem into a non-problem every winter.
2. **Call us to winterize the line professionally** by blowing it out or draining it from the main.

Don't try to "just wrap it really well" with towels and duct tape. We've seen the result. It doesn't work when it's -20°F.

---

## When to Do This

Before the first hard freeze. In Minneapolis, that's usually mid-to-late October. Doing it on a 50° Saturday in early November is fine. Doing it after the first night below 28°F is gambling.

---

**Need a shutoff valve installed, or want us to walk your exterior plumbing before winter? Call [Company Name] at [phone]. We do these calls all over Minneapolis, St. Paul, and the surrounding suburbs, and most jobs are same-week.**

— [Your name], owner

a.text:
1/ I made a pricing mistake at Tallyup.

I raised prices 40% for everyone overnight.

Within a week, we lost 30 of 140 customers.

2/ The mistake wasn’t raising prices.

We needed to charge more to keep building a sustainable product.

The mistake was treating existing customers the same as new customers — with no warning, no context, and no choice.

3/ For a gym owner, Tallyup is another operating expense.

A sudden increase doesn’t feel like “we’re improving the product.”

It feels like: “this tool I rely on just got more expensive without asking.”

That’s on me.

4/ What I changed:

- Existing customers are grandfathered or moved gradually
- Price changes get communicated before they happen
- New pricing applies to new customers first
- I explain what’s changing and why

5/ The lesson:

Pricing is not just a number on a checkout page.

It’s a trust decision.

Especially when you’re a small SaaS asking customers to bet on you long-term.

6/ I still believe Tallyup should be priced sustainably.

But I won’t make another “overnight” decision that asks customers to absorb the cost of my learning curve.

b.text:
1/
I raised Tallyup's prices 40% overnight. Every customer, no exceptions.

A week later, 30 of my 140 customers were gone.

What I got wrong, and what I changed:

2/
The backstory: like every indie hacker, I'd absorbed the advice.

"You're undercharging."
"Just charge more."
"Raising prices is the highest-leverage move in SaaS."

So one day I did. Every customer. Same day. Bigger number on the next invoice.

3/
No grandfathering.
No heads-up.
No "here's why."

Just a charge 40% higher than what they signed up for.

That was the whole mistake — but it took losing 30 customers to see it.

4/
The cancellations started almost immediately.

30 out of 140, gone in seven days.

And these aren't faceless accounts. Gym owners run small businesses. They notice every line item, and they'd taken a chance on a solo founder's tool.

5/
Here's the thing: the price probably wasn't the problem.

New customers might have paid it without blinking.

The problem was changing the deal on people who had already said yes. A price hike with no warning doesn't feel like strategy. It feels like a broken promise.

6/
What I changed:

→ Existing customers keep their original price
→ New pricing applies to new signups only
→ Any future increase gets announced well in advance, with a reason and a way to push back

The deal you sign is the deal you keep.

7/
I also emailed every customer who cancelled and offered their old price back.

Most didn't take me up on it.

Trust is fast to spend and slow to earn back. I knew that in the abstract. Now I know it for real.

8/
The "just charge more" advice isn't wrong. It's incomplete.

Charge more for new customers, fine. But your existing customers already made a deal with you. Honor it — or at least warn them before you change it.

9/
Rebuilding now, one gym at a time.

If you've raised prices on existing customers as a founder — how did you handle it? Genuinely asking.

setup: A wedding photographer is posting that couples who ditch rigid shot lists get better photos, using the rained-out Barrera wedding as an example.

a.text:
The couples who ditch the exhaustive shot list almost always end up with the best photos.

Not because planning is bad. Planning is essential.

But on a wedding day, the moments that matter most rarely happen because they were written down in column C of a spreadsheet.

At the Barrera wedding, rain changed everything. We moved the plan, the people, and the ceremony setup under a pecan tree—and suddenly the day became less about executing a perfect timeline and more about being present in it.

That’s where the photographs lived:

The quick glances while everyone adjusted to the weather.  
The laughter when the plan changed.  
The family and friends gathering close beneath the branches.  
The feeling of “this isn’t what we expected, but it’s still ours.”

I’ll always make time for the important family combinations, meaningful heirlooms, and the people you absolutely need photographed. Give me those priorities.

But you don’t need to direct every image.

The best wedding photography comes from a couple trusting their photographer enough to notice what’s unfolding—not just what’s on the list.

b.text:
Over eight years and nearly 300 weddings in the Texas Hill Country, I’ve noticed a consistent pattern: 

The couples with the shortest shot lists almost always get the best galleries.

Take the Barrera wedding. We had a clear plan mapped out, but Texas weather had other ideas. Right before the ceremony, a sudden downpour swept in and completely washed out their original outdoor setup. 

Instead of stressing over a rigid, multi-page checklist of must-have poses, they took a breath, embraced the chaos, and pivoted. We moved the entire ceremony under a massive pecan tree to wait out the storm.

Because they weren’t mentally checking off Pinterest poses, they were fully present. When the rain let up and the light broke through the wet leaves, we didn’t stage anything. We simply documented the genuine relief, the muddy boots, the unscripted laughs, and the raw emotion of the moment. 

Shot lists serve a purpose for family formals to keep logistics efficient. But for the rest of the wedding day, an overly detailed shot list turns a live event into a photoshoot where everyone is performing instead of experiencing.

To the couples currently planning: Do the heavy lifting beforehand. Hire a creative team you trust completely. 

Then, when the day arrives, put the list away and just live it. The best photos will follow.
