setup: A local sports columnist is writing an opinionated season-ending commentary for readers of the local paper's sports section.

a.text:
**They Had It in Hand. Then They Let It Slip Away.**

Eight wins. A school-record quarterback. A playoff run that ended in Round 2.

And yet, if you watched the last few minutes of Saturday night, you probably didn’t leave with the feeling you watched a team that got beaten up. You probably left with the feeling you watched a team beat itself.

The loss stings for the obvious reason. This is the same opponent the team had already beaten by twenty yards, maybe more depending on which stat sheet you trust, in Week 3. In basketball, sometimes you say teams match up differently. In football, when you’ve already won a game like that, and then you’re down only three in the second half of the rematch, the answer usually isn’t to throw the playbook at the wall and start looking for heroics.

That’s where my head is at with this one.

This team didn’t lose because it wasn’t good enough. It lost because it stopped trusting what had been working. The run game was there. It was moving the ball, it was controlling the clock, and it was giving the defense a break. Then, with the game still on the line, that identity started to disappear. Suddenly it felt less like execution and more like hope. Hope is not a game plan in the second half of a one-score playoff game.

Now, none of that takes away from Dez Kowalski’s season. Two thousand, three hundred and forty yards is a school record, and it didn’t happen by accident. He carried the offense for stretches, made throws under pressure, and kept this thing alive more times than anyone in these parts should remember. But here’s the uncomfortable part: a school-record season from your quarterback doesn’t erase a lost playoff game if the rest of the team was taken out of it. Sometimes the best answer is the boring one. And the boring one Saturday night was the run game.

Eight and two is a good season. Nobody should act like it isn’t. You don’t get to pretend playoff losses are just another Tuesday in a small town like ours. People cared. That matters. But if we’re being honest—and this column should be honest—the disappointment isn’t that this team got exposed. It’s that it got close, had something solid in its hands, and then let the game drift away because it forgot what made it good in the first place.

That’s what makes this one ache.

Not that they lost.

That they only lost by three.

b.text:
**A Great Season, A Coaching Mistake, and an Early Winter**

An 8-2 record looks great framed on the wall at the diner. It’ll read nicely in the spring sports banquet program, too. But let’s not sugarcoat Friday night: the boys should still be playing football this week. 

Losing in the second round of the state playoffs is tough enough. Losing to a team you ran off their own field by 20 points back in September makes it a bitter pill that's going to stick in this town's throat all winter. 

Before we get to the autopsy, credit where it’s due: Dez Kowalski put together the finest season under center this town has ever seen. Setting the school single-season record with 2,340 passing yards is a massive achievement, and Kowalski played with heart and grit from August two-a-days all the way through Friday night. He earned every bit of that record. 

But relying exclusively on Dez’s right arm in the second half is precisely why the season is over.

Coming out of the locker room down just three points, the game plan inexplicably went into panic mode. The ground game was chewing up five yards a pop in the first half and keeping the defense honest, yet the coaching staff put it in mothballs the minute the third quarter kicked off. You don't abandon the run when you're within one field goal. When you become one-dimensional against a playoff defense out for revenge, you’re playing right into their hands. They pinned their ears back, brought pressure, and dared us to beat them with an empty backfield. We couldn't.

It’s easy to look at an 8-2 finish and call it a total success, and these kids have plenty to be proud of. But championships aren't won by getting cute with the playbook when a fistfight is required. Friday night was a winnable game that got away because we stopped doing what got us there.

a.text:
1/4
We just opened up the ceiling on our Maple Ave kitchen remodel (1910 Pittsburgh home). 

What we found: a previous "pro" had notched out 90% of a main load-bearing floor joist to run a 3-inch plumbing drain. It was literally hanging by a 1-inch splinter of old-growth pine.

2/4
To fix it safely:
- Had an engineer spec the repair.
- Slowly jacked the sag out of the joist to avoid cracking the bathroom tile directly upstairs.
- Sistered it with an LVL and rerouted the drain line.

Total cost: $3,200 and 3 days added to the schedule.

3/4
The lesson for homeowners:
This is why a 10-15% contingency fund isn't optional on old homes. If we hadn’t opened this ceiling, that floor would have eventually failed under the weight of the new kitchen island. Always budget for what you can’t see.

4/4
The lesson for contractors & architects:
Never write a contract that guarantees a flat price for structural work before drywall comes down. Build an "exploratory demolition" clause into your contracts. It protects your margins and sets honest expectations from day one.

b.text:
1/4  
Maple Ave kitchen job taught me a good one this week: the floor looked fine from below, but once we opened it up, I found a joist issue hiding under the old subfloor.

2/4  
One joist had a bad notch near a bearing point and a couple others had been drilled way too generously by a previous crew. Nothing dramatic enough to notice day-to-day, but enough to matter once cabinets, tile, and a busy kitchen go back on top.

3/4  
Fix was straightforward but not cheap: sistered the damaged framing, added blocking, and reworked a small section of the floor system before we moved forward. Cost the job about $1,400 in labor and materials, plus the delay to get it right.

4/4  
Lesson: in remodels, the expensive part usually isn’t the repair itself — it’s the stuff you have to undo because someone assumed the framing was “probably fine.” If you’re opening walls or floors, check the structure early and budget for what’s actually there, not what the plans hope is there.

setup: An in-house recruiter is posting a contrarian observation about candidates asking about the team’s last failed project in interviews to recruiters, hiring managers, and job seekers.

a.text:
After 200+ interviews, the best signal I've found isn't in how candidates answer questions. It's in what they ask.

The strong ones ask about a project that failed.

Not "what's the biggest challenge on the team" — that question gets a rehearsed answer every time. I mean specifically asking about something that went wrong, recently, and what happened after.

Had this exchange a few months back, hiring for a logistics coordinator role:

Candidate: "Can you tell me about a project or initiative here that didn't go the way you planned?"

Me: We rolled out a new routing system last year that was supposed to cut delivery times. It didn't account for driver familiarity with regions, so efficiency actually dropped for the first six weeks.

Candidate: "What did the team do once you realized it wasn't working?"

Me: We rolled back the auto-assignment piece and let dispatchers override it manually while we retrained the model on actual driver patterns.

Candidate: "Who made the call to roll it back, and how long did that take?"

That last question told me more than anything on her resume. She wasn't asking to catch us out. She was trying to understand how decisions get made when something breaks — how fast, by whom, with what appetite for admitting it isn't working.

That's the thing about failure questions. Anyone can ask about wins and get a polished story back. Asking about failure forces the interviewer to be honest in real time, and how they handle that moment tells the candidate exactly what kind of place they're walking into.

I've started expecting this question from anyone who's done real diligence. When I don't get it, I don't hold it against them. But when I do, I pay attention to what they do with the answer.

b.text:
After roughly 200 interviews, the candidates who stick with me aren't the ones who nail the "tell me about a failure" question.

They're the ones who ask me about ours.

Last week a senior ops candidate did it mid-interview. We'd covered their background, some scenario work on carrier disruptions, the usual. Then they said:

"What's a project your team tried that didn't land the way you hoped—and what changed because of it?"

I told them about a routing optimization pilot we ran two years ago. We pushed hard on a new algorithm for multi-stop freight, sunk months into it, then watched on-time performance dip in three regions because we underweighted driver feedback and real-world dock constraints. We killed it, rebuilt the intake process with more frontline input, and the next version actually stuck.

They didn't rush to say "I'd never make that mistake." They asked what the team learned about decision speed vs. validation, and how we now decide when to pull the plug. That five-minute exchange told me more about how they think than any behavioral story.

If you're interviewing, try asking about the last thing that didn't work. If you're hiring, notice who does.

setup: A home baker is reviewing the Corlane SM6 mixer for blog readers deciding whether to buy it.

a.text:
**Eight Months with the Corlane SM6: Is This $429 Mixer Worth It for Bread Bakers?**

If you’ve bought a loaf of sourdough from my table at the farmers market recently, you’ve eaten bread that started its life in the Corlane SM6. 

I’ve put this mixer through near-daily abuse for the last eight months, pushing it to its absolute limits with heavy, high-hydration market prep. Now that the honeymoon phase is long gone, I’m ready to give you my honest, unfiltered review of whether this machine deserves a spot on your kitchen counter.

### The Powerhouse Motor
Let’s start with the absolute best thing about the Corlane SM6: the motor. If you bake bread, you know the dread of watching your mixer head shake violently while the motor groans under the weight of a heavy dough. 

To test its limits, I threw a double batch of stiff, low-hydration bagel dough at it. Most residential mixers would stall or smell like burning electrical wires within three minutes. The SM6 didn't even flinch. It kneaded that dense dough to perfect gluten development without a single stutter or stall. If you need raw, relentless power, this machine has it.

### The Annoyances (The Squeak and the Hook)
As much as I love the motor, the machine isn't perfect, and there are two major quirks you should know about before buying.

First, the bowl lift lever. After about a month of heavy use, it started emitting a high-pitched, metallic squeak every time I raised or lowered the bowl. My solution? I have to hit the mechanism with a squirt of WD-40 about once a month to keep it quiet. It’s an easy fix, but for a premium appliance, you shouldn't have to keep garage lubricants in your pantry.

Second, the included dough hook is a major design oversight. It is simply too short for the deep, narrow mixing bowl. On smaller batches, the hook spins right over the top of the ingredients, leaving dry flour pooled at the bottom of the bowl. I got so frustrated that I ended up buying a longer, aftermarket spiral hook from a third-party seller. It solved the problem completely, but it’s annoying to have to buy extra gear right out of the box.

### The Price Tag
The Corlane SM6 retails for $429. For comparison, that is about $80 more than the equivalent, similarly sized KitchenAid model. 

### The Verdict
I'm not going to give you a fuzzy "it depends on your needs" answer. Here is the bottom line:

**Buy it** if you are a serious bread baker who kneads heavy, stiff doughs every single week. The sheer power of the motor and its ability to handle dense doughs without burning out easily justifies the $429 price tag and the minor annoyances of a squeaky lever and a short hook.

**Skip it** if your baking consists mostly of cookies, birthday cakes, and occasional holiday pies. If you are mixing batters and soft doughs, you don't need this level of horsepower. Save yourself the $80 premium, avoid the squeaky lever maintenance, and buy a standard KitchenAid instead.

b.text:
**Corlane SM6 Stand Mixer: 8-Month Review**

Eight months ago, I unboxed the Corlane SM6 to replace the hand mixer I’d been beating to death with weekend market sourdough. Since then, it’s run nearly every day—sometimes twice a day—and it’s become the workhorse I was hoping for, with a few caveats that matter.

The motor is the real story. I mix double batches of stiff bagel dough, the kind that makes lesser machines smell like burning plastic and stall out mid-knead. The SM6 doesn’t blink. It powers through 75% hydration sourdough and shaggy rye without slowing down or heating up. If you’re buying this for heavy dough, the guts are absolutely there.

But Corlane cut corners on the details. The bowl lift lever squeaks like a rusty gate, and I’ve had to hit it with WD-40 every month to keep it from grinding. Worse, the included dough hook is too short for the deep bowl, leaving a dry ring of flour at the bottom every single mix. I ditched it after two weeks and bought a third-party spiral hook that actually reaches the base. Factor that extra $25 into your total cost.

Speaking of cost: the SM6 is $429, which is $80 more than the equivalent KitchenAid Artisan. You’re paying that premium for torque, not polish.

Here is the actual verdict. If you knead heavy dough weekly—sourdough, bagels, pizza, babka—buy this mixer. The motor justifies the price and the minor annoyances. But if you are mostly creaming butter for cookies and whipping cake batter, skip it. You will spend extra money on power you will never use, and you will still be oiling that squeaky lever for no good reason.

setup: A high-school senior is writing a personal essay for college admissions readers about working at her family's Vietnamese restaurant.

a.text:
The register died on a Saturday in October, right at the start of the dinner rush. It made a sound like a fan slowing down and then the screen went gray. My dad hit the side of it twice, which is his solution for most machines, and then looked at me.

We had maybe forty tickets that night. I wrote every one by hand on the pad we usually use for phone orders, and I learned fast that my handwriting is worse than I thought. The cooks couldn't read my 4s. Bún bò Huế became "BBH" by ticket six. A man at table nine wanted his phở with no onions, extra basil, broth on the side, and I wrote it all out and underlined "SIDE" three times because I knew if it came out wrong he would tell me about it, politely, at length. It came out right. My mom did the math for the checks in her head faster than I could on my phone calculator, which she did not let me forget for several weeks.

Nobody thanked me at the end of the night. My dad just said the register guy was coming Tuesday and handed me a container of leftover chả giò, which in our family is roughly the same thing.

The chả giò is my grandma's recipe, and the fold is hers too. Last spring we hired a new girl, Emily, and I had to teach her. There's a way to do it wrong that looks right. The roll holds together on the tray and then splits in the fryer, and you can't tell which ones will split until they do. My grandma taught me by doing it slowly one time and then watching me do it wrong about thirty times, saying "tighter" in Vietnamese, which was most of what she ever said to me in the kitchen. With Emily I heard myself say "tighter" in English and then I couldn't explain what tighter meant, exactly, so I just did it slowly one time and watched her do it wrong. Around her twentieth roll something changed in her hands. I couldn't have told you what. But I saw it, the same way my grandma must have seen it in mine.

On slow nights I take my break in the walk-in cooler. This sounds like a punishment but it's the quietest place in the building and there's an upturned bucket that works as a chair. I did most of my calculus homework junior year in there, next to the tubs of pickled daikon, wearing my jacket over my apron. Related rates, optimization, a lot of limits. It's 38 degrees in the walk-in, which is good for staying awake and bad for pencil grip. My friends did their homework at desks, in rooms that were room temperature. I don't think my derivatives were any worse than theirs. Sometimes my dad would open the door looking for lemongrass and see me hunched over a problem set and just take the lemongrass and leave, because by then this was normal.

I've worked every weekend since sophomore year. I don't want to make it sound harder than it was. Plenty of it is boring — refilling sriracha bottles, rolling silverware into napkins until my hands do it without me. But I know things now that I didn't plan on knowing. I can read a table before I get to it. I can tell from the sound of the fryer whether something's wrong. I know that "tighter" is a real instruction even when you can't define it, and that some things get taught by standing next to someone long enough.

When I leave for college, my parents will hire someone for my shifts. The restaurant will run fine without me. But the fold will still be my grandma's, and I'll still know it, wherever I am, whatever else my hands are doing.

b.text:
The first sign was the receipt printer making a noise like it was chewing paper. Then the screen froze, blinked once, and went black.

It was 12:15 on a Saturday, and the restaurant was already full. Every table had at least one bowl of pho or plate of broken rice. The kitchen tickets were hanging on the rail, but the new ones stopped coming. My mom tapped the screen a few times, then looked at me.

I grabbed a stack of order pads and a handful of pens.

For the next three hours, I wrote every ticket by hand. Table number, dish, modifications, no onions, extra broth, one order rare, one order well done. I used different colors so the kitchen would not mix up appetizers and entrees. Red for drinks, blue for food. When I ran out of red, I used pencil and underlined twice.

The kitchen did not slow down. If anything, it got louder because nobody trusted the system anymore. My dad called out orders from the pass. My aunt asked if table six got their egg rolls. Someone said table twelve had been waiting twenty minutes, but table twelve had just ordered. I kept the pad in front of me and wrote everything down before I moved.

At one point, a server handed me a ticket with coffee stains all over it. I could still read the table number, but not the drinks. I went to the table and asked the customers to repeat the order. They were patient, which surprised me. Usually people get annoyed when something goes wrong in a restaurant. Maybe they could tell we were trying.

By the time the repair guy came, my hand hurt. I had filled six order pads. The register came back on, printed a long list of errors, and then started working like nothing had happened. I kept the last page of my order pad. It had a smear of fish sauce on the corner.

When things calm down, I usually help prep. My favorite job is spring rolls, but only if nobody rushes me. My grandma taught me the fold when I was little. She did not explain it much. She just put a rice paper wrapper on the damp towel, added shrimp, pork, herbs, and noodles, then folded the sides in tight and rolled it once. The trick was not to overfill it and not to tear it.

Last month we hired a new girl named Lan. She was fast, but her spring rolls kept splitting. She kept putting too much lettuce near the edge. I showed her how to leave room at the sides and tuck the filling down before rolling.

“Like this,” I said. “Don’t be nice to it.”

She laughed and tried again. The next one looked better. The one after that looked almost like my grandma’s.

My grandma does not work full shifts anymore, but she still comes in and checks everything. She picked up one of Lan’s rolls and turned it over in her hand. She did not say anything for a second. Then she said, “Okay.”

That was enough.

During slow stretches, I do homework. The best place is the walk-in cooler. It is quiet, and nobody asks me to refill sauces or wipe down tables. I sit on a milk crate with my backpack and my calculator. The fan blows cold air behind the shelves of basil, cilantro, and sliced onions. Sometimes my nose runs. Sometimes my fingers get stiff. But I can focus.

Calc is hardest in there. Not because of the cold, but because if I lose track of one step, I have to start over. I keep my notebook on my knees and write small so I can fit more work on one page. Last week I was doing derivatives while someone behind me stacked boxes of frozen shrimp. He asked if I was studying chemistry. I said no, but then I had to explain what a derivative sort of is, and by the time I finished, my problem was all wrong.

I do not always finish homework before my shift ends. Sometimes I have to take it home, and sometimes I fall asleep with the notebook open on my bed. But I like knowing where everything is: the order pads, the spring roll wrappers, the calculator, the stack of clean towels by the sink.

On weekends, the restaurant smells like garlic and star anise. My shoes get sticky. My shirt smells like broth even after I wash it. I know which table wobbles, which fan squeaks, which customer asks for extra limes without asking nicely.

When the last customers leave, I stack chairs, sweep under the tables, and count the register drawer. My dad turns off the hood fan, and the room gets suddenly quiet. I take the trash out back, lock the side door, and check it twice.

Then I get in the car and ride home.

setup: A fourth-generation soybean and corn farmer is writing a newsletter commentary on crop insurance costs and SB 214 for county readers and state legislators.

a.text:
**Forty Percent Unplanted. Forty-Six Thousand Dollars More.**

By the late-May planting deadline, I had planted just 60% of my acres. The rain wouldn’t let up. Meanwhile, USDA’s 22% increase in the prevented planting base rate in our region is costing my operation about $46,000 extra this year.

That’s $46,000 more in expense in a spring when I couldn’t get 40% of my ground planted on time.

I’m a fourth-generation soybean and corn farmer. I understand that paying for protection is part of doing business. I don’t expect crop insurance to eliminate every loss, and I don’t expect anyone to guarantee me a profitable year. But I do expect the rules to treat farms fairly.

Right now, the acreage caps don’t meet that test. Because of how those caps work, this increase hits family operations like mine harder proportionally than the bigger operations nearby. The problem isn’t that my neighbors farm more acres. The problem is a policy structure that puts an uneven burden on the acres we each farm.

That distinction matters. This shouldn’t become an argument between smaller and larger farmers. We all need a dependable safety net when weather keeps us out of the field. The question is whether the rules distribute the cost fairly.

SB 214 would fix the acreage cap. It wouldn’t stop the rain or recover the planting days we lost. But it would address a part of this burden that lawmakers can actually change.

I’m asking fellow Farm Bureau members to support SB 214 and contact their state legislators. Tell them what the acreage cap means for your operation. Ask them to support the bill and help move it forward.

On our farm, $46,000 isn’t an abstract policy number. It competes with seed, equipment repairs, debt payments and the money we need to put another crop in the ground.

We can’t legislate a dry planting window. We can fix an acreage cap that makes a wet spring even more expensive for family farms.

b.text:
**What the 22 Percent Actually Cost Me**

USDA raised the prevented planting base rate 22 percent in our region this year. On my operation — about 3,000 acres of corn and beans — that came to roughly $46,000 in additional premium. Not $46,000 in lost yield, not $46,000 in equipment. Forty-six thousand dollars in extra premium on a policy I bought before I knew what kind of spring we were going to have.

Then I got the spring we had. Thirteen inches of rain between the second week of April and the May 25 final plant date for corn, which is close to double our thirty-year normal for that window. I got 1,800 acres in the ground. Twelve hundred acres I did not, and no amount of standing at the edge of the field looking at it was going to change that. I know I'm not alone; I've had the same conversation with half the people reading this.

So I paid 22 percent more for coverage in the exact year I needed to use it. That's how insurance works some years, and I'm not going to complain about paying a premium and then filing a claim. That's the deal.

The acreage cap is a different story. That one isn't bad luck. That one is written down on purpose.

Here's how it works, and I'd encourage anybody who hasn't looked closely to pull out their policy and check me on this. The eligible acreage under the enhanced coverage is capped per covered entity — 500 acres, flat, regardless of the size of the operation behind it. I farm as one entity. My grandfather set it up that way, my dad kept it that way, and I never had a reason to change it. So of my 1,200 prevented planting acres, 500 are eligible. Forty-two percent.

An operation nine miles from me farms somewhere north of 11,000 acres. It's a good outfit and I have nothing bad to say about how they treat their ground or their neighbors. But that operation is structured across four entities, which means it carries 2,000 acres of eligible cap. Their prevented planting acres this spring came in lower than mine proportionally — they're spread across three counties and didn't catch the same rain — and every acre they claimed fell under the cap with room to spare.

Same rule. Same rain event. One of us gets covered on 42 percent of the problem and the other gets covered on all of it. The difference isn't farming practice or risk management or how well anybody keeps their tile up. The difference is how many LLCs the operation is divided into.

I want to be careful here, because this argument gets made badly sometimes. I'm not asking anybody to punish scale. Scale isn't a moral failing and consolidation isn't going to be fixed by a crop insurance rule. What I'm saying is narrower than that: a flat per-entity cap is functionally a discount for operations with the size and the accounting to split themselves up, and a penalty for the ones that never had a reason to. It rewards a paperwork decision. That's it. And when you stack a 22 percent rate increase on top of a cap structure that already tilts against mid-size family operations, you get a year like this one, where the premium hike lands on everybody and the coverage lands unevenly.

The obvious response is that I should restructure. Maybe I will. But I'd point out that the cost of restructuring — legal, accounting, redoing every lease and loan document — is itself a fixed cost that's easier for a bigger operation to absorb. So even the fix favors the same people the rule already favors.

**SB 214**

SB 214 would replace the flat per-entity cap with a percentage-of-insured-acres cap that applies to the operation as a whole, however it's organized. Under that structure, my 1,200 acres and the 11,000-acre outfit's acres get treated on the same proportional basis. Nobody loses coverage they'd otherwise have. As I read the fiscal note, the change comes close to a wash for the state — it redistributes eligibility rather than expanding it.

That's the whole bill. It is not ambitious. It does not solve the rate increase, which is a federal question and a longer fight. It corrects one line of arithmetic that is currently producing an outcome I don't think anybody sat down and intended.

The Senate ag committee is expected to take it up this session. Two things worth doing:

setup: A fourth-generation soybean and corn farmer is writing a newsletter commentary on crop insurance costs and SB 214 for county readers and state legislators.

a.text:
**When the Rain Won't Stop, and the Bill Keeps Growing**

The USDA raised the prevented planting base rate 22% this year in our region. That's not a typo—twenty-two percent, in a single year. For me, that translated to roughly $46,000 in additional costs I didn't budget for and can't control.

This spring, it wouldn't stop raining. I'm not looking for sympathy—every farmer in this county knows what I'm talking about. But the facts are the facts: I could only get 60% of my acres planted before the late May deadline. That left 40% of my operation hitting the prevented planting program, and the premium hike hit right alongside it.

Here's what makes this worse for families like mine. The acreage caps don't scale with the size of your operation. On a 450-acre farm, losing a chunk of plantable acres pushes you up against that cap fast. When you're running 2,400 acres, you've got more room to absorb the hit proportionally. The way the system is structured, the smaller family farms carry a heavier burden percentage-wise. That's not a fair system. That's a system that's slowly squeezing us out.

There's a fix on the table: SB 214. It would revise the acreage cap so the program actually serves the family operations it's supposed to protect—not just the operations big enough to work around the rules.

I'm not asking for a handout. I'm asking for the rules to be fair. A 22% rate hike with no cap adjustment is a penalty on doing the right thing: trying to keep land in production, trying to keep this farm in the family, trying to be responsible stewards of the soil.

If you're reading this, whether you're a fellow farmer or someone in the statehouse who's never set foot in a field after rain, I'd ask you to look at the numbers. Forty-six thousand dollars is not a rounding error for an operation like mine. It's the difference between making ends meet and falling behind.

Support SB 214. The math doesn't lie, and neither does the mud.

b.text:
A 22% increase in the base rate for prevented planting premiums. That is the number the USDA handed us this year for our region. For my operation, that 22% hike translates to $46,000 in extra premiums out of pocket. 

When the rains wouldn't stop this spring, I was only able to get 60% of my corn and soybean acres in the ground before the late May deadline. Prevented planting coverage is supposed to be the safety net for exactly this scenario, but the cost to maintain that net has suddenly skyrocketed. 

The immediate sticker shock of the $46,000 is bad enough, but the deeper issue is how this hike interacts with current acreage caps. Because of how those caps are structured, this premium increase hits family operations like mine much harder proportionally than the larger operations nearby. The caps limit the total eligible acreage for bigger farms, which dilutes their effective rate increase across their total footprint. Meanwhile, mid-sized family farms shoulder the full, concentrated brunt of the 22% hike on our eligible acres. It is a structural flaw that disproportionately penalizes the operations that form the backbone of our local ag economy.

We need a legislative fix, and that is exactly what SB 214 provides. This bill would correct the acreage cap issue, leveling the playing field so that premium adjustments don't disproportionately squeeze family farms. 

I urge you to reach out to our state legislators and ask them to support SB 214. We cannot control the spring rains, but our representatives can control how our risk management tools are structured. setup: A home baker is reviewing the Corlane SM6 mixer for blog readers deciding whether to buy it.

a.text:
# Corlane SM6 Stand Mixer: An 8-Month Review

I've been running the Corlane SM6 nearly every day for eight months now, mostly on the sourdough and bagel doughs I sell at the market on weekends. That's a lot of hours on a heavy mixer, so I feel like I can finally give you a real answer on whether it's worth the money.

## The Good: The Motor Is a Beast

This is the reason to buy this machine. I regularly throw a double batch of stiff bagel dough at it — the kind of low-hydration dough that makes most home mixers whine, walk across the counter, or overheat — and the SM6 doesn't stall. It doesn't even sound stressed. Eight months of this abuse and the motor performs exactly like it did on day one. If you've ever smelled hot motor coming off a mixer mid-knead, you know what that peace of mind is worth.

## The Annoying: Two Real Flaws

**The bowl lift lever squeaks.** Not a dealbreaker, but about once a month it starts squeaking badly enough that I hit it with WD-40. It's a two-minute fix, but on a $429 machine, I shouldn't have a monthly maintenance ritual for a lever.

**The included dough hook is too short.** This one genuinely baffles me. The bowl is deep — great for big batches — but the stock hook doesn't reach far enough down to engage the dough properly, especially with smaller batches. Dough just sits at the bottom getting nudged instead of kneaded. I ended up buying a third-party hook, which solved it completely, but budget an extra $20–30 for that because you'll want it.

## The Price

$429, which is about $80 more than the comparable KitchenAid. That's a real gap, and the KitchenAid is a fine machine. But I've killed a KitchenAid motor on bagel dough before, and I have not come close to killing this one.

## Verdict

**If you knead heavy dough every week — bagels, stiff sourdough, big batches of bread — buy the SM6.** The motor alone justifies the $80 premium, and the squeaky lever and hook swap are minor annoyances against a machine that never quits under load.

**If you're mostly making cookies, cake batter, and the occasional loaf, skip it.** You'd be paying extra for torque you'll never use, plus inheriting the quirks. Get the KitchenAid and put the $80 toward good flour.

For me, doing market volume weekly? It's earned its spot on the counter.

b.text:
# Corlane SM6 Stand Mixer Review: 8 Months In, Used Almost Daily for Market Sourdough

I bought the Corlane SM6 in February and have put it through roughly 240 bakes since. Most of those are sourdough loaves and bagels for my Saturday farmers market stall, with the occasional batch of sandwich bread or brioche thrown in on slower weeks. Here's the honest rundown.

## What it does well

The motor is the star of the show. Corlane rates it at 500W, but the spec sheet is less important than what it actually does in the bowl, which is chew through a double batch of stiff bagel dough (about 1,500g flour total) without slowing down, walking across the counter, or triggering the thermal cutoff. My old 4.5-quart KitchenAid would have tap-danced itself off the edge of the island on that load. The SM6 weighs about 28 pounds and sits flat. I never lock it to the counter, and it has not moved once.

It also handles wet doughs cleanly. Hydration levels above 80% get scraped down once at the four-minute mark and that's it. The 6-quart bowl is genuinely useful for anyone scaling up beyond home portions, and the head tilts back far enough that I can get a full hand in to scrape without removing the bowl.

## What's annoying

Two real issues, both fixable but worth knowing before you buy.

**The bowl-lift lever squeaks.** It's a metal-on-metal contact point and it started chirping around month three. A shot of WD-40 on the pivot clears it for about four weeks, then it comes back. It's a 30-second job, but it's the kind of thing that shouldn't be a recurring maintenance item on a $429 machine.

**The included dough hook is too short for the deep bowl.** It clears the bottom fine, but the gap between the hook and the sides of the bowl means unmixed flour collects in the corners on stiff doughs. I had to buy a third-party spiral hook (a $22 replacement from a small-batch maker on Etsy) and the difference was immediate. The stock hook is fine for cake batter. For real bread work, plan to swap it.

## Corlane SM6 vs. KitchenAid

If you're cross-shopping the SM6 against something like the KitchenAid 6-Quart Pro 600, the comparison is straightforward:

- **Power and torque:** The Corlane wins, and it's not close. This is the only category that actually matters for heavy dough.
- **Build and finish:** KitchenAid still has the edge on fit and finish. The Corlane is mostly metal, but the knobs and switches feel a step below.
- **Attachments and ecosystem:** KitchenAid wins by a mile. If you care about pasta rollers, meat grinders, and the full attachment universe, KitchenAid's catalog is bigger and more proven.
- **Price:** The equivalent KitchenAid runs about $349 on sale, so you're paying roughly $80 more for the Corlane. That premium is buying you a better motor and bowl-lift design, not better aesthetics.

## Final verdict

**Buy the Corlane SM6 if** you knead stiff or heavy dough more than once a week and your old stand mixer has ever let you down mid-batch. The motor is genuinely best-in-class at this price, and for serious bread bakers it earns its premium.

**Skip the Corlane SM6 if** you're mostly making cookies, cakes, and the occasional loaf. You'll pay $80 extra for capability you'll never use, and you'll be annoyed by the squeaky lever. A KitchenAid Artisan will handle that workload for less money, and the accessory ecosystem is worth real money if you bake beyond bread.

For me, the SM6 is a clear yes. Eight months in, it has not flinched at anything I've thrown at it, and the two complaints I have are both $25 fixes. If you sell bread or bake for a family of gluten enthusiasts, you'll get your money out of it in the first year.

setup: A high school girls' soccer and track coach is writing an op-ed urging turf funding for the girls' field.

a.text:
Nine games. That's what we lost to water in the last two seasons. Nine games where I told my girls the field was unplayable, or worse—where we played on it anyway because there was nowhere else to go and they'd been training for it since August. I watched a midfielder try to cut left in a mud pit in November and just... keep sliding, losing three yards, getting up angry and soaking. I watched a sophomore tear her ACL in October stepping into a rut I'd flagged to the athletic department three times. She's got a surgery on her calendar and a semester off the pitch. Her senior season is over.

I'm not telling you this for sympathy. I'm telling you because next week the school board votes on the facilities budget, and I need you to look at what "facilities" means when half your athletes can't play on them for half the fall.

Let's be plain about the geography here. Our grass field—our *only* grass field for girls' soccer—floods because the drainage was never adequate and the grade is wrong and every November we play on what is functionally a creek bed with grass sticking out of it. You could argue we've made it work. I've made it work. My assistant and I have spent more November afternoons pushing water off the pitch with brooms than I care to admit. But "make do" has a body count, and right now it's one blown knee per season minimum, and nine cancelled games means nine fewer chances to be scouted, to compete, to not forfeit a match on a Tuesday because some other field opened up on short notice.

Now. Here's the thing I want the board to answer to their own faces: the boys' football field got turf in 2019. Same athletic budget. Same drainage problem. A decade of complaints about mud, about ruts, about kids blowing out a knee in November—and they fixed it. Six figures, done, problem solved. And I'm glad, genuinely, I'm glad for Coach Daniels and his players. But I have to ask: why does the fix require four years and three budget cycles when the players are girls in cleats instead of pads? Why does a girl's ACL cost less to prevent than a boy's?

I don't want to make this a fight. I don't want parents pitting one team against another at a board meeting in a fluorescent-lit room in March. But I will not pretend the timeline is an accident. The drainage report for the football field was the same report—*the same report*—that listed our field as the second priority. Second priority. We are still second priority six years later.

What I'm asking for is not a favor. Turf installation on the girls' field is roughly in line with what was spent on the football field in 2019. It is a line item. It is a one-time cost that stops me from spending October writing rain-out notices and stops a girl's parents from getting a phone call from me at 6 a.m. saying their daughter is going to the hospital. It means my track kids get a dry warm-up area in the spring. It means the JV game against Whitmore next November actually gets *played*.

The board gets to vote on the budget. The voters get to call them. I just want my girls to have a field that holds a game.

I'll be at the meeting in March. I'll be there with two of my assistants and at least three players' parents. You can talk to us after, if you want. We'll be the loud ones in the gymnasium with our cleats still muddy.

—Coach [Name], Head Coach, [High School] Girls Soccer & Track

b.text:
# The Girls Deserve a Field That Doesn't Hurt Them

We've had nine games rained out or relocated in the last two seasons. Nine. That's not bad luck or a rough patch. That's a field that doesn't work.

Our girls soccer field sits at the bottom of a slope and floods anytime we get more than a drizzle. The grass turns to mud, the mud turns to puddles, and the puddles sit there until someone cancels the game or moves it to a campus we have to bus to. Our girls end up playing "home" games twenty minutes away while their parents and classmates stay home. Last October, one of my sophomores planted her foot in a rut left from a previous flooding and tore her ACL. She's had surgery. She missed the rest of the season. She'll miss track this spring. A rut in the grass did that.

The boys football field got turf in 2019. I'm not going to pretend that doesn't matter to these girls, because it does. They walk past that field every day on their way to practice on a surface that floods, wears unevenly, and actively injures them. They're not asking for anything the boys don't already have. They're asking for the same.

I've coached girls soccer and track at this school for eleven years. I do it for the stipend and because I care about these kids, not because I want to write op-eds. But I've watched two seasons of games wash out, watched a girl get hurt on a field we knew was a problem, and watched the school board approve turf for football while the girls play in mud. Something's wrong with that math.

The facilities budget vote is coming up. Turf for the girls soccer field is in the proposal. I'm asking the board to approve it. Not as a luxury, not as a "nice to have if we can afford it," but as the bare minimum for giving these girls a safe place to play the sport they signed up for.

Nine rained-out games. One torn ACL. One field that doesn't work. The fix is sitting in the budget. Approve it.

setup: A third-year electrical apprentice is writing an argumentative essay for the union newsletter against a 15% cut to apprenticeship funding.

a.text:
# Cutting Apprenticeship Funding Is Cutting the State's Best Investment

I'm a third-year electrical apprentice with our local. I'm not a writer, so I'll keep this simple: the state's proposed 15% cut to apprenticeship funding is a bad deal for taxpayers, a bad deal for workers, and a bad deal for anyone who wants their lights to turn on when they flip the switch. Here's why, with real numbers.

## The numbers from my own cohort

My apprenticeship class started with 24 people. Twenty-one of us finished. That's a completion rate of nearly 88%. All 21 are working journeyman jobs right now. Not looking for work. Not sending out resumes. Working.

Compare that to the four-year college route. Plenty of good people go to college, and I'm not knocking them. But a lot of students don't finish, and plenty of the ones who do are still hunting for work in their field years later. My cohort went 21 for 21 on employment. Show me another training program with that record.

## Apprentices get off public assistance fast

Apprentices in our trade start around $19 an hour. That's a real paycheck from day one, not a loan you pay back later. It means a first-year apprentice with a family can start coming off assistance programs almost immediately instead of leaning on them for four more years while they train.

By the time we top out as journeymen, we're making around $46 an hour. That's a wage that buys a house, raises kids, and pays a whole lot of taxes back into the state. Every apprentice who finishes stops being a cost on the state's books and becomes a contributor. Fast.

## The math the legislature should be looking at

Here's the number that matters most. The total public cost per apprentice who completes the program is about $14,000. The average public subsidy for a four-year college graduate who finishes is around $48,000.

That's more than three times the cost for a result that's less certain. I'm not saying defund colleges. I'm saying if you have two programs and one of them delivers a working, taxpaying skilled tradesperson for $14,000, you don't cut that one. You'd have to look hard to find a better return anywhere in the state budget.

Cut apprenticeship funding by 15% and you don't save money. You just push more people toward the expensive path, or worse, toward no path at all. Then the state pays anyway, in assistance programs, in lost tax revenue, in contractors who can't find qualified electricians.

## The state needs us more than ever

Ask any contractor in this state how easy it is to find a licensed electrician right now. The answer is: it isn't. We've got an aging workforce, a construction backlog, and more electrical work coming with every new building, every EV charger, every solar install. The pipeline for skilled trades is the apprenticeship system. There isn't a backup plan.

A 15% cut means fewer apprentices accepted, fewer instructors, fewer classes. That's fewer journeymen in five years, right when the state will need them most. This isn't a cut you feel next month. It's a cut you feel for a decade.

## What I'm asking

To my brothers and sisters in the local: contact your state legislators. Tell them your story, your wages, your career. The numbers speak, but they speak louder coming from the people who lived them.

To any legislators reading this: I was one of 24 people who got a shot. Twenty-one of us finished and are working right now, paying taxes, off assistance, building the state's infrastructure. It cost the public about $14,000 each to get us here. That's not spending. That's the smartest money the state puts out. Don't cut it.

b.text:
The state should not cut apprenticeship funding by 15%.

I’m a third-year electrical apprentice with the local IBEW, and I see what this funding does every day. It gives people a real path into a good job without crushing them with student debt. It also helps local contractors and the whole economy by creating skilled workers who are ready to work.

My own cohort started with 24 apprentices. Twenty-one finished and are now working journeyman jobs. That is a strong return on the state’s investment. These are not people who got trained and then sat on the sidelines. They are working, paying taxes, and building things this state needs.

The numbers speak for themselves. Apprentices start around $19 an hour. By the time they finish, they can top out around $46 an hour as journeymen. That means they move off assistance programs fast and become taxpaying workers instead of staying dependent on public aid.

The cost is also much lower than people might think. The total public cost per apprentice who finishes is about $14,000. Compare that to something like $48,000 in average public subsidy per four-year college graduate who finishes. If the state wants to spend money wisely, apprenticeship is one of the best deals out there.

A cut to apprenticeship funding would hurt working people, hurt contractors, and hurt the state’s future workforce. It would also make it harder for young people and adults trying to build a better life with their hands and their heads.

We should be growing apprenticeship programs, not cutting them. Keep the funding in place and keep investing in a system that works.

setup: A family plumbing company owner is writing a blog post for Minneapolis homeowners about winterizing outdoor pipes.

a.text:
# How to Winterize Outside Spigots in Minneapolis

Winterizing your outside spigots helps prevent frozen pipes, water damage, and emergency plumbing repairs. In Minneapolis, outdoor faucets can freeze quickly when temperatures drop, especially if water is trapped in the spigot or the pipe behind it.

Follow these steps before the first hard freeze.

## 1. Shut off the interior water valve

Find the interior shutoff valve that controls your outdoor spigot. It is usually located in the basement, utility room, crawl space, or near where the pipe passes through the foundation wall.

Turn the valve clockwise until it is closed. If your home has more than one outdoor faucet, check for a separate shutoff valve for each one.

If you cannot find an interior shutoff valve, call a Minneapolis plumber for help. Some homes do not have a dedicated valve, and forcing or incorrectly closing the wrong valve can create additional problems.

## 2. Disconnect the garden hose

Remove every hose, splitter, timer, nozzle, and other attachment from the outdoor spigot.

This is the most important step—and the mistake we see most often. Leaving a hose connected can trap water inside the faucet and the pipe. When that water freezes, it expands and can crack the spigot or the water line inside your wall.

A connected hose is responsible for many of the burst-pipe calls we receive in January.

Store the hose indoors or in a protected garage space after draining it.

## 3. Open the outside spigot

Once the interior shutoff valve is closed, open the outdoor faucet completely. Let any remaining water drain out.

Leave the spigot open through the winter. This gives trapped water a place to expand if it freezes and helps relieve pressure in the pipe.

If your shutoff valve has a small bleeder cap or drain screw, place a bucket underneath and open it carefully to drain water from the section of pipe between the valve and the outside faucet. Close the bleeder cap after the line has drained, but leave the outdoor spigot open.

## 4. Install a foam faucet cover

After the spigot has drained, install an inexpensive foam faucet cover. These covers typically cost around $3 and are available at most hardware stores.

To install one:

1. Place the cover over the outdoor spigot.
2. Secure it according to the manufacturer’s instructions.
3. Make sure it fits snugly against the wall.

A foam cover adds insulation and helps protect the faucet from cold air. It does not replace shutting off and draining the water line.

## What if you have a frost-free spigot?

Frost-free or freeze-resistant outdoor faucets are designed to drain when they are shut off. However, they still require the hose and attachments to be removed. A hose can prevent the faucet from draining properly and may cause the pipe to freeze.

If a frost-free spigot leaks, does not drain, or continues running after you shut it off, have it inspected by a plumber.

## What to do if you cannot find the shutoff valve

Do not assume the outdoor faucet is safe just because it has a foam cover. If you do not have an interior shutoff valve—or cannot locate it—contact a professional plumber before freezing weather arrives.

A plumber can help identify the correct valve and determine whether the outdoor water line needs to be drained or repaired.

For Minneapolis homeowners, the basic winterization checklist is simple:

- Shut off the interior valve.
- Disconnect all hoses and attachments.
- Open and drain the outside spigot.
- Install a foam faucet cover.
- Call a plumber if there is no interior shutoff valve.

Taking a few minutes to winterize your outdoor spigots can help prevent a burst pipe and costly water damage during a Minneapolis winter.

b.text:
**How to Winterize Your Outside Spigots in Minneapolis**

Shut off the interior valve that feeds your outdoor faucet. You’ll usually find it in the basement or crawlspace near the wall where the pipe exits the house. Turn it fully closed.

Open the outside spigot and let it drain until nothing comes out. Leave it open for a minute so any remaining water can escape.

Disconnect every hose. This is the step most people skip—and it’s the reason for most of the burst-pipe calls we get every January. A connected hose traps water in the faucet and pipe. That water freezes, expands, and splits the line inside the wall. Pull the hoses off and store them.

Screw on a cheap foam faucet cover (about $3 at any hardware store). It adds a little insulation and keeps wind and snow off the fixture.

That’s it. The whole job takes five minutes per spigot.

If you can’t find an interior shutoff valve—or your house was built without one—call us. We’ll locate the right valve or install one so you can protect the line properly. Don’t wait until the first hard freeze.

setup: A fourth-generation soybean and corn farmer is writing a newsletter commentary on crop insurance costs and SB 214 for county readers and state legislators.

a.text:
# Prevented Planting Premium: A Reminder That Family Farms Need Fair Policy

This spring, my fields stayed underwater through late May. By the time the soil dried enough to plant, I'd crossed the prevented planting deadline. I ended up getting only 60% of my usual acreage in the ground.

That's the reality of farming in our region some years. What's less inevitable is the policy that followed.

The USDA raised prevented planting insurance premiums by 22% in our area this year. For my operation, that's roughly $46,000 in additional costs annually. I'm paying more to insure against the same weather risk I've always faced.

But here's what really stings: the way the acreage cap is structured, operations like mine—family farms running four, five, maybe six thousand acres—get hit proportionally harder than the larger operations nearby. A 22% increase on capped acreage means I eat a bigger percentage loss than neighbors farming 20,000 acres or more. We're all paying more, but the formula punishes scale differently depending on where you fall.

This isn't about complaining. It's about asking our state legislators to act. Senate Bill 214 addresses exactly this problem by fixing how the acreage cap works. It's straightforward policy that would level an uneven playing field.

Family farming operations deserve insurance structures that don't inadvertently force consolidation. I'd ask everyone reading this to contact your legislators about SB 214. Tell them family farms matter—not just as nostalgia, but as the businesses they still are.

b.text:
By late May this spring, I had only gotten 60% of my acres planted. The rain would not quit, and like a lot of growers, I was forced to look hard at prevented planting coverage.

Then the bill came due.

USDA raised the prevented planting base rate 22% in our region this year. For my farm, that increase adds about $46,000 in extra premium cost. That is not a rounding error. It is a major hit to a family operation that already has to make every acre, every bushel, and every dollar count.

What makes this especially hard is the way the acreage caps work. Large operations can spread that increase over far more ground. Family farms like mine cannot. The result is that the same policy change lands much harder, proportionally, on smaller and mid-sized farms that are already trying to do everything right and still manage risk in a year when the weather simply will not cooperate.

Prevented planting coverage matters. It is one of the tools that helps keep farms afloat when spring conditions turn against us. But when the premium jumps this sharply, and when the cap structure treats family farms so differently, it needs to be fixed.

That is why I am asking readers to support SB 214. This bill would address the acreage cap and make the system fairer for family operations that are carrying the same weather risk, but not the same scale.

If you are a farmer, or if you care about keeping family agriculture strong in this state, please let your legislators know SB 214 deserves their support.

setup: A retired Army staff sergeant is writing about coming home after his second deployment for readers of the veterans' writing workshop anthology.

a.text:
Cereal Aisle

Twenty-three years in, and I still can't tell you why the cereal aisle got to me. I'd been shot at. I'd carried a man to a helicopter with his leg gone below the knee. But it was a grocery store in Clarksville that put me on my heels.

I went in for cereal. Just cereal. My wife had a list and that was one of the things on it, and I told her I'd handle it, I wanted to feel useful, wanted to feel like I could still walk into a building and get something done. So I found the aisle and I stood there.

There were forty kinds. I counted, sort of, though I lost track after a while because I kept losing my place and starting over. Cinnamon this and honey that and a dozen versions of the same three cereals just in different boxes, cartoon animals looking at me like they were waiting on an answer. I stood there for twenty minutes. A woman with a cart full of kids came down the aisle, grabbed a box without slowing down, and kept going. I envied her more than I've envied anybody in a long time.

Over there, you didn't have forty of anything. You had what came on the truck. If it was oatmeal that day, it was oatmeal, and you ate it and were glad to have it. Nobody stood in front of a shelf trying to decide between them. I think that's what did it — not that I was overwhelmed by cereal, but that I'd forgotten how to choose things that didn't matter. A year of only the choices that mattered — go left or right, call it in or wait — and then somebody hands you your whole self back and says pick a breakfast.

I ended up with the same kind I always used to buy, the plain toasted oat kind in the yellow box. Took me twenty minutes to walk in a circle and land back where I started.

***

My daughter was six when I came home the second time. Same daughter, same wife, same airport terminal I'd walked through before, except this time when I came around the corner she didn't run at me. She stepped back. Got behind her mother's leg, one hand gripping the fabric of my wife's jeans, and just looked at me.

I hadn't thought about how long a year is when you're six. A year for her was a sixth of her whole life. My face in photographs is not my face in person, not to a six-year-old — the person in the pictures didn't have this much gray in his beard, didn't stand like this, didn't smell like plane and sweat instead of whatever she remembered.

I crouched down. I didn't reach for her. I'd read somewhere, or somebody told me, don't grab, let them come to you. So I just crouched there in my uniform with my duffel on the ground beside me, in the middle of that terminal, other families around us doing the version of this reunion where the kid comes running and everybody cries the good kind of tears. Ours wasn't that. My wife put her hand on our daughter's back and said, "That's Daddy. That's your daddy," like she was reminding her of something she'd only half-learned.

It took maybe a full minute. Might not sound like much. It was the longest minute I've spent, and I've spent some long ones.

Then she came around her mother's leg, slow, and put her hand out like she was going to shake mine, this very serious, formal little gesture she must've picked up from somewhere, and I took her hand and shook it, and something in that made her laugh, and after that she let me pick her up.

***

The door thing took longer to fix than either of those.

For a year I'd slept in a bunk facing the door. Everybody did. You don't think about it as a decision, it's just how you set yourself up, so that if something happens you see it coming a half second sooner. Half a second matters. You'd be surprised how fast you can go from asleep to upright with a rifle in your hands if you've had enough practice and enough reason to practice.

Home, our bedroom door was on the wrong wall for that. I moved to my wife's side of the bed for a while without really saying why, just so I'd be facing the right direction, and she let me, didn't ask about it for a couple weeks. And I needed the door open. All the way open, not cracked. She was used to sleeping with it shut, always had been, but for months she didn't say anything about that either.

I'd wake up at every sound. House settling, cat on the stairs, ice maker dropping a load of ice into the bin at two in the morning — I was up, sitting, before I even knew what had woken me. Some nights I didn't wake her. Some nights she was already awake because I'd woken her sitting up like that, and she'd just wait until I lay back down and not say anything.

It took the better part of that first year home before I could sleep facing away from the door. Longer before we could close it again. I remember the night we finally did — my wife asked, kind of careful, if I minded, because she gets cold and likes it shut in the winter, and I said no, go ahead, and I lay there afterward waiting to feel that old alarm go off in my chest. It didn't. Or it did, a little, but not enough to get me up. I noticed that, lying there. I noticed I'd noticed it, if that makes sense. Like checking a wound to see if it still hurts and being surprised, a little disappointed almost, that it doesn't hurt as much as you remembered.

We still sleep with the door shut now. Most nights I don't think about it at all.

b.text:
**Coming Home**

When I came home from my second deployment, my wife and daughter met me at the airport.

My daughter was six. I had been gone a year, which is a long time when you are six. Before I left, she used to run at me full speed and expect me to catch her. At the airport, she stood behind her mother’s leg.

I could see one eye and part of her face. My wife put a hand on her shoulder and told her, “It’s Daddy.”

I was still in uniform. I had my bags with me. There were people all around us hugging and taking pictures. I wanted to kneel down and open my arms, but I did not want to make it worse. So I stood there and said hello.

She looked at me for a few seconds. Then she came out from behind her mother, but she stayed close to her. I hugged my wife first. After that, my daughter let me hug her, though her arms stayed at her sides.

By the time we got to the car, she was talking to me. Mostly she told me what had changed. She had a different teacher. Her friend had moved away. She could ride her bike without training wheels. There was a new restaurant near our house. She had lost two teeth.

I sat in the passenger seat and listened. The roads looked familiar, but not exactly. There were new buildings and new signs. My wife drove. My daughter talked from the back seat. Every so often, I turned around to look at her, just to make sure she was there.

A few days later, I went to the grocery store by myself.

My wife had given me a short list. Milk, bread, eggs, cereal. It should have taken twenty minutes.

I got to the cereal aisle and stopped.

There were cereals from one end of the aisle to the other. Bright boxes, plain boxes, family size, low sugar, high fiber, chocolate, cinnamon, fruit, marshmallows. Some were supposed to help your heart. Some were shaped like little cookies. Some had cartoon animals on the front.

I did not know what to pick.

Before I deployed, I had bought cereal plenty of times. I must have. But standing there, it felt like somebody had asked me a question with forty correct answers and forty wrong ones.

I picked up a box and read the side. Then I put it back. I picked up another one. A woman pushed her cart around me, reached past my shoulder, grabbed a box, and kept going. She did not even slow down.

I stood there for about twenty minutes.

Finally, I bought the cereal my daughter used to like before I left. When I brought it home, she told me she did not like that kind anymore.

At night, I had trouble sleeping.

For the past year, I had slept facing the door. I did it without thinking. Even when there was no reason to worry, I wanted to see the entrance. I wanted to know what was on the other side.

At home, my wife slept on the side of the bed closest to the door. She always had. I did not want to ask her to switch, so I lay on my side and looked past her.

She liked the bedroom door open. That way she could hear our daughter if she called during the night. I wanted it closed.

The first few nights, I got up after my wife fell asleep and shut it. In the morning, she opened it again. Neither of us said anything about it.

One night, she woke up while I was standing beside the door.

“What are you doing?” she asked.

“Nothing,” I said.

I left the door halfway open and got back into bed.

For a while, every sound in the house woke me up. The refrigerator kicked on. Pipes knocked in the wall. A car drove past. Our daughter got up to use the bathroom, and the floor creaked under her feet.

Sometimes she came into our room after a bad dream. She would stand in the doorway until one of us noticed her. Then she would walk around to my wife’s side of the bed.

After a few weeks, she started coming to my side.

The first time, she tapped me on the shoulder and whispered, “Dad.”

I opened my eyes. She was standing there in her pajamas, holding a blanket.

“Can’t sleep,” she said.

I moved over and let her climb in. She lay between us, taking up more room than a six-year-old should be able to take. Her foot pressed into my leg. My wife stayed asleep.

I looked at the open bedroom door. The hallway beyond it was dark.

After a while, my daughter’s breathing slowed. The house made its usual noises. I stayed awake a little longer, facing the door. Then I closed my eyes.

setup: A high school girls' soccer and track coach is writing an op-ed urging turf funding for the girls' field.

a.text:
Nine games in two years. That’s how many times my girls’ soccer team has had a game rained out, postponed, or moved to an away field because ours turned into a swamp. This isn’t a minor inconvenience—it’s a pattern. And last October, it cost us more than a schedule shuffle. One of my starting defenders planted her foot in a deep rut that had been hidden by standing water the day before, heard a pop, and tore her ACL. That surgery, that recovery, that lost season—it all traces back to a grass field that can’t handle a hard rain.

I’m not a writer. I’m a coach. I do this for a small stipend because I care about the kids. So I’ll say it plainly: Our girls’ soccer field is dangerous and unfair. The boys’ football field got turf back in 2019. It drains perfectly, plays fast, and doesn’t chew up ankles when the weather turns. Meanwhile, my team dodges puddles and ankle-breakers every spring. We’ve had girls slide into a tackle and come up with mud in their mouths because the ground can’t take another step. We’ve had goal kicks that stop dead in a pool. The conditions are messing with our development—and our safety.

The numbers don’t lie. Over the past two seasons, nine games lost or relocated because of flooding. That’s nine fewer chances for these athletes to compete, to be scouted, to learn how to win and lose on their home soil. The football team hasn’t missed a single home game due to field conditions since their turf went in. They get a reliable, consistent surface. We get a lottery.

I’ve heard the argument: Grass is softer, cheaper to maintain. But our grass isn’t soft in October—it’s sodden and rutted. And the “cheaper” math ignores the cost of rescheduling buses, officials, and staff when we lose a home game. It ignores the cost of a knee surgery and months of PT. It ignores the simple message we send when we pour money into the boys’ Friday night lights while the girls’ soccer team is an afterthought.

The school board votes next month on the facilities budget. I’m asking them—and this community—to look at the facts, not the gender of the athletes who use the field. Turf for the girls’ soccer field isn’t a luxury. It’s a safety fix, an equity fix, and a long-overdue investment. We don’t need a new grandstand or a fancy press box. We need a surface that doesn’t flood, doesn’t rut, and doesn’t send my players to the emergency room.

One field. Two years. Nine lost games and one torn ACL. That should be enough. Fix the field. Fund the turf. It’s that simple.

b.text:
**Our Girls Deserve a Field They Can Actually Play On**

Over the last two seasons, our girls’ soccer team has had nine games rained out or moved because our grass field floods.

Nine games. That means players, families, officials and opposing teams have made plans, only to have them canceled or relocated because the field cannot handle ordinary weather. It means lost home games, lost revenue and lost opportunities for our athletes to compete in front of their classmates and families.

It also means we are asking students to play on a surface that can become unsafe.

Last October, one of our players tore her ACL after stepping into a rut on the field. I am not going to pretend that a new surface eliminates every sports injury. It does not. Soccer is physical, and injuries happen. But we should not be putting our athletes on a field with ruts, standing water and uneven footing when we have the ability to provide something safer and more reliable.

The school board is considering next year’s facilities budget. Installing turf on the girls’ soccer field should be part of that budget.

This is not a request for luxury. It is a request for a basic athletic facility that works.

The boys’ football field received turf in 2019. That investment made sense. Football needed a dependable field, and the school made the decision to provide one. But girls’ soccer deserves the same consideration. Our athletes work just as hard. They practice in the same weather, represent the same school and compete under the same academic and athletic expectations.

This is also a fairness issue.

We should not have one group of athletes playing on a dependable, all-weather surface while another group is routinely displaced by rain. We should not tell girls that their games can be moved, shortened or canceled because their field is not a priority. If the school is willing to invest in facilities for one program, it should be willing to invest in facilities for another program with a demonstrated need.

The current field does not just create inconvenience. It affects the quality of the season. When games are moved, families have to rearrange work schedules and transportation. Opposing teams have to travel again. Coaches have to rebuild practice plans. Senior nights and other events become harder to schedule. Players lose the experience of playing at home, in front of their community.

And when a game is moved to another field, that field may not be ideal either. We end up scrambling for space instead of giving our athletes the stable, well-maintained facility they deserve.

A turf field would allow us to keep more games at home and make better use of the schedule. It would provide a more consistent playing surface and reduce the damage caused by wet conditions. It would give the school a facility that can serve students more reliably instead of sitting unusable after every heavy rain.

I understand that the district has competing needs. Facilities budgets are not unlimited, and every project has to be examined carefully. But fairness should be part of that examination. So should safety. So should whether students are actually able to use the facilities we already ask them to depend on.

Our girls are not asking for special treatment. They are asking for equal treatment.

They show up early. They stay late. They play through heat, cold and pressure. They represent this school with pride. The least we can do is give them a field that drains, holds up and does not turn a season into a series of weather-related cancellations.

The school board should put turf for the girls’ soccer field in next year’s facilities budget. It is the fair decision, the practical decision and the responsible decision.

setup: A small dog grooming salon owner is writing a how-to for dog owners about preventing coat matting between grooming visits.

a.text:
I get it. Life gets busy, and keeping up with a thick double coat or tight curls between my appointments can feel like fighting a losing battle. But if you’ve ever tried to untangle a knot that’s already set in, you know exactly why prevention matters so much. The mistake I see constantly is people bathing their dog first because they think warm water and shampoo will somehow loosen those mats. It doesn’t. Wet matted fur just turns into a felt pad that locks everything in tighter, making what could have been an easy job suddenly very difficult—and painful for your pup. That’s why, every single time at home, you need to brush before the bath, never after.

Grab a good slicker brush and focus on using short, line-by-line strokes rather than big circular motions. Circling sounds natural, but it actually twists the hair around itself and speeds up tangle formation. You want to gently skim through the topcoat and get down into the undercoat in those same quick, forward-and-back passes. Work in sections starting behind the ears and under the front legs, since that’s where mats start first. Those are high-friction zones where movement, loose hair, and everyday wear all collide. Take your time clearing out any loose tumbleweeds in those specific spots before they have a chance to weave themselves into something solid. Once those areas stay clear, the rest of the coat usually follows along pretty easily.

Now, let’s say you do spot a little lump forming before your next visit with me. Don’t reach for the comb yet. Instead, work a little dog conditioner into it with your fingers before you ever touch it with a brush or comb. Rub it in thoroughly, let it sit for a couple of minutes, and only then will you gently guide your tools through that spot. That tiny bit of slip completely changes how the hairs slide past each other. Once it’s softened up with conditioner, you can carefully use the slicker brush, still sticking to those short line strokes, and you’ll likely catch it before it ever becomes a real issue. 

It really is just about catching it early and keeping the right technique consistent. Your double coat or curly breed wasn’t built to mat if you give it a little daily attention, and it’ll make both of your lives infinitely easier until we’re back in the salon chair together.

b.text:
As a groomer, I love nothing more than sending your pups home looking fluffy, clean, and smelling amazing. But I also know how much work goes into keeping those coats looking that way between your visits to the salon, especially if you have a curly-coated doodle or a thick, double-coated breed. It can feel like a losing battle against tangles, but I want to share a few insider secrets that will make your at-home brushing sessions so much easier—and much more comfortable for your dog.

First, let's talk about the single biggest mistake I see dog parents make. You notice your dog is getting a little tangled, so you think, *I’ll give them a bath to loosen things up.* Please, step away from the tub! Bathing a matted dog actually does the exact opposite of what you want. When wet matted fur dries, it shrinks and tightens, turning those loose tangles into a solid, felted pad. Once that happens, it’s incredibly difficult—and often painful—to brush out. 

The golden rule of home grooming is to always brush *before* the bath, and never, ever after. 

When you sit down to brush, the tools and the technique you use make all the difference. Grab a slicker brush—the one with the fine, slightly bent wire bristles. Instead of brushing in big, sweeping circles, which actually winds the hair into tighter knots, you want to use short, straight "line" strokes. Gently pat the brush into the coat and pull out away from the skin in short, straight motions. 

It helps to work in small, manageable sections rather than trying to tackle the whole dog at once. I always recommend starting in the areas where mats love to hide first: right behind the ears, and deep under the front legs. These are high-friction areas where the legs rub against the body and collar straps rub against the neck, so they tangle first. If you can keep those trouble spots clear, you’re already winning the battle. 

If you do run into a mat that has already started to form, don’t try to force your brush or comb through it. Instead, take a little bit of dog-safe conditioner or detangling spray and work it directly into the knot with your fingers first. Massage it in gently to help lubricate the hair shafts and loosen the grip of the tangle. Once the conditioner has sat for a minute, use your fingers to gently tease the mat apart before you ever let a brush or comb touch it. 

A few minutes of this routine a couple of times a week will keep your pup's coat healthy, pain-free, and beautiful. Plus, it makes their professional grooming appointments a breeze for both of us! Next time you bring your pup in, feel free to ask me to show you the line-brushing technique in person—I’m always happy to do a quick demonstration to help you out.
