setup: A high school junior is writing an argumentative essay to her English teacher and classmates arguing for open campus lunch for juniors and seniors.

a.text:
**Open Campus Lunch for Juniors and Seniors**

Lunch is supposed to give students a break in the middle of the school day, but right now it is also one of the most crowded and stressful parts of the schedule. Our school should allow juniors and seniors to have open campus lunch because it would reduce cafeteria overcrowding, reflect what students actually want, and follow the example of nearby districts where the policy has worked. Allowing older students to leave campus for lunch would be a reasonable change that benefits both students and the school.

The most immediate reason to consider open campus lunch is overcrowding. Our cafeteria only seats 220 people, but one lunch wave has 340 students. That means there are more students than seats before even considering how long lines move or how much space people need to actually eat comfortably. When the cafeteria is that full, students have trouble finding seats, the noise level increases, and lunch becomes rushed. If juniors and seniors were allowed to leave campus, fewer students would need to eat in the cafeteria at the same time. This would make lunch more manageable for the students who remain and for the staff supervising them.

Students also strongly support the idea. In a survey I conducted with 80 students at our school, 71 said they were in favor of open campus lunch for juniors and seniors. That is almost 89 percent, which shows that this is not just a small preference but a clear opinion among the student body. Students are the ones most affected by lunch policies, and their views should matter when the school is deciding how to improve the daily schedule. Juniors and seniors are also older and more experienced students, so they can be trusted with a limited privilege like leaving campus for lunch.

Another reason to support open campus lunch is that similar schools have already tried it successfully. Nearby districts such as Fairmont, West Linn, and Cascade already allow open campus lunch, and their published statistics show no rise in tardiness. This is important because one of the biggest concerns about open campus lunch is that students will not return to class on time. However, the evidence from other districts suggests that students are able to handle the responsibility. If those schools can make the policy work without creating a tardiness problem, our school can do the same with clear expectations and consequences.

Some people may argue that open campus lunch is a bad idea because students might leave the allowed area, return late, or make poor choices while off campus. Those concerns are understandable, but they do not mean the policy should be rejected. Instead, the school can create rules to prevent problems. For example, open campus lunch could be limited to juniors and seniors who have signed permission forms. Students could also lose the privilege if they are late or break the rules. Since nearby districts have not seen an increase in tardiness, it seems likely that these concerns can be managed.

Open campus lunch for juniors and seniors would be a practical solution to a real problem. It would reduce overcrowding in the cafeteria, give students more independence, and follow the successful example of nearby schools. The evidence shows that students support it and that it does not have to create the problems people fear. Our school should consider open campus lunch as a responsible and reasonable change.

b.text:
The modern high school day is often structured like a marathon with poorly timed stops. For juniors and seniors, the midday meal period rarely functions as intended. Instead of a restorative break, lunch frequently becomes a logistical bottleneck that forces older students into cramped spaces and rushed schedules. Restricting campus access to underclassmen while treating upperclassmen as younger siblings overlooks the reality that students in grades eleven and twelve possess the maturity and planning skills to make responsible midday choices. Our district should implement an open campus lunch policy for juniors and seniors. Doing so would resolve severe cafeteria overcrowding, align with regional precedents that prove punctuality can be maintained, and provide the focused mental break that students consistently report needing.

The most immediate problem with the current lunch structure is spatial. Our cafeteria was designed to accommodate roughly 220 students per wave, yet we currently seat 340 juniors and seniors during the same period. That leaves over a hundred students without adequate seating, pushing them into hallways, empty classrooms, or out the door entirely just to secure a place to eat. Forcing everyone to remain on campus under these conditions breeds congestion, increases noise levels, and wastes valuable minutes between periods. Opening the campus to older students would instantly reduce the headcount during peak lunch hours, allowing the remaining population to sit comfortably, finish meals without rushing, and transition back to afternoon classes with less friction. Administrative control does not require sacrificing basic comfort, and alleviating a documented overcrowding crisis is a straightforward reason to adjust the policy.

Beyond logistics, concerns about open campus lunch often hinge on the assumption that older students will abuse the privilege and cause chronic tardiness. Historical data from comparable districts directly contradicts this worry. Three neighboring school systems—Fairmont, West Linn, and Cascade—already allow open campus lunches for upperclassmen, and each has publicly reported attendance figures showing no measurable increase in tardiness. These districts share similar geographic layouts and demographic profiles, which means physical access to nearby businesses is equally feasible here. When schools establish clear check-out expectations and monitor arrival times, students generally return promptly. Trusting juniors and seniors to manage their own time yields consistent results, whereas blanket restrictions only reinforce an outdated, paternalistic approach to scheduling.

Student perspectives further strengthen the case for this shift. In a survey of eighty students across both grade levels, seventy-one responded positively to the proposal. Respondents consistently noted that after two consecutive hours of morning instruction, staying in a crowded, loud cafeteria drains attention rather than restoring it. Many pointed to quieter off-campus locations as opportunities to decompress, complete light assignments, or simply step outside between periods. A predictable midday reset improves concentration for afternoon coursework, particularly in subjects that demand sustained focus. Ignoring nearly nine out of ten surveyed students in favor of maintaining a congested status quo undermines the very purpose of a healthy school environment.

Critics will inevitably raise safety and truancy concerns, arguing that releasing older students off campus creates liability risks or opens doors to missed periods. While these worries warrant thoughtful management, they do not justify preserving an inefficient system. Proper implementation requires standard administrative protocols: digital sign-out logs, verified emergency contacts, and clear academic consequences for unexcused absences. Districts that have adopted similar frameworks report minimal incidents because accountability measures pair effectively with student responsibility. Removing a restriction based on hypothetical worst-case scenarios prevents all students from benefiting, including those who follow the rules consistently.

The current lunch arrangement treats a routine daily transition as a containment exercise rather than an opportunity to build independence. Implementing open campus lunch for juniors and seniors would immediately relieve cafeteria overcrowding, follow a tested regional model that maintains punctuality, and honor student feedback regarding mental fatigue and focus. High schools should prepare students for adult decision-making, not restrict movement solely to simplify supervision. By adopting a more flexible lunch policy, our district can demonstrate confidence in its older students, streamline daily operations, and ultimately foster a calmer, more productive academic atmosphere.

setup: A retired Army staff sergeant is writing about coming home after his second deployment for readers of the veterans' writing workshop anthology.

a.text:
**Coming Home**

When I came home from my second deployment, my wife and daughter met me at the airport.

My daughter was six. I had been gone a year, which is a long time when you are six. Before I left, she used to run at me full speed and expect me to catch her. At the airport, she stood behind her mother’s leg.

I could see one eye and part of her face. My wife put a hand on her shoulder and told her, “It’s Daddy.”

I was still in uniform. I had my bags with me. There were people all around us hugging and taking pictures. I wanted to kneel down and open my arms, but I did not want to make it worse. So I stood there and said hello.

She looked at me for a few seconds. Then she came out from behind her mother, but she stayed close to her. I hugged my wife first. After that, my daughter let me hug her, though her arms stayed at her sides.

By the time we got to the car, she was talking to me. Mostly she told me what had changed. She had a different teacher. Her friend had moved away. She could ride her bike without training wheels. There was a new restaurant near our house. She had lost two teeth.

I sat in the passenger seat and listened. The roads looked familiar, but not exactly. There were new buildings and new signs. My wife drove. My daughter talked from the back seat. Every so often, I turned around to look at her, just to make sure she was there.

A few days later, I went to the grocery store by myself.

My wife had given me a short list. Milk, bread, eggs, cereal. It should have taken twenty minutes.

I got to the cereal aisle and stopped.

There were cereals from one end of the aisle to the other. Bright boxes, plain boxes, family size, low sugar, high fiber, chocolate, cinnamon, fruit, marshmallows. Some were supposed to help your heart. Some were shaped like little cookies. Some had cartoon animals on the front.

I did not know what to pick.

Before I deployed, I had bought cereal plenty of times. I must have. But standing there, it felt like somebody had asked me a question with forty correct answers and forty wrong ones.

I picked up a box and read the side. Then I put it back. I picked up another one. A woman pushed her cart around me, reached past my shoulder, grabbed a box, and kept going. She did not even slow down.

I stood there for about twenty minutes.

Finally, I bought the cereal my daughter used to like before I left. When I brought it home, she told me she did not like that kind anymore.

At night, I had trouble sleeping.

For the past year, I had slept facing the door. I did it without thinking. Even when there was no reason to worry, I wanted to see the entrance. I wanted to know what was on the other side.

At home, my wife slept on the side of the bed closest to the door. She always had. I did not want to ask her to switch, so I lay on my side and looked past her.

She liked the bedroom door open. That way she could hear our daughter if she called during the night. I wanted it closed.

The first few nights, I got up after my wife fell asleep and shut it. In the morning, she opened it again. Neither of us said anything about it.

One night, she woke up while I was standing beside the door.

“What are you doing?” she asked.

“Nothing,” I said.

I left the door halfway open and got back into bed.

For a while, every sound in the house woke me up. The refrigerator kicked on. Pipes knocked in the wall. A car drove past. Our daughter got up to use the bathroom, and the floor creaked under her feet.

Sometimes she came into our room after a bad dream. She would stand in the doorway until one of us noticed her. Then she would walk around to my wife’s side of the bed.

After a few weeks, she started coming to my side.

The first time, she tapped me on the shoulder and whispered, “Dad.”

I opened my eyes. She was standing there in her pajamas, holding a blanket.

“Can’t sleep,” she said.

I moved over and let her climb in. She lay between us, taking up more room than a six-year-old should be able to take. Her foot pressed into my leg. My wife stayed asleep.

I looked at the open bedroom door. The hallway beyond it was dark.

After a while, my daughter’s breathing slowed. The house made its usual noises. I stayed awake a little longer, facing the door. Then I closed my eyes.

b.text:
The plane touched down at Fort Bragg, and just like that, I was home. Again. The first time, I’d come back from Iraq with a duffel bag full of dirty uniforms and a head full of things I didn’t want to talk about. This time, Afghanistan. Different sand, same weight.

I stood in the cereal aisle at the commissary, staring at the shelves like they were a puzzle I couldn’t solve. Forty kinds of cereal. Forty. Back in the FOB, we got whatever was in the MREs—peanut butter, crackers, maybe some Skittles if you were lucky. Here, there were boxes with cartoon characters, organic labels, granola that cost more than a six-pack. I picked up a box of Frosted Flakes, put it back. Grabbed the Raisin Bran, set it down. Twenty minutes later, I walked out with a loaf of bread and a jar of peanut butter. Old habits.

The airport was worse. My wife had texted me a picture of our daughter a few weeks before I left—missing her two front teeth, grinning like she’d just won a prize. I’d kept that picture in my pocket the whole deployment. Now, standing there in the terminal, I saw her peeking out from behind my wife’s leg, eyes wide like she wasn’t sure who I was. She was six. I’d been gone a year.

“Hey, kiddo,” I said, crouching down. She didn’t move. My wife gave me that look—the one that said *give her time*. So I did. I sat on the floor and pulled out the little wooden camel I’d carved for her in the downtime. She took it, turned it over in her hands, then finally stepped forward and hugged my neck. I held on tight.

Sleeping was the hardest part. For a year, I’d slept with one eye open, always facing the door, always ready. Now, back in our house, my wife left the bedroom door open like she always did. I lay there, staring at the ceiling, listening to the quiet hum of the fridge, the occasional car passing outside. No mortars, no generators, no guys talking in their sleep. Just silence. I got up and shut the door. The next night, I left it open for an hour before closing it. The night after that, two hours. Eventually, I stopped noticing.

Some mornings, I’d wake up and forget where I was. Then I’d see my wife’s hair spread out on the pillow next to me, hear my daughter laughing in the other room, and remember. Home. Again.

setup: A high school junior is writing an argumentative essay to her English teacher and classmates arguing for open campus lunch for juniors and seniors.

a.text:
Every day during fourth period, a collective anxiety builds. When the bell rings, it is a mad dash to the cafeteria—not just out of hunger, but out of a survival instinct to secure a plastic chair. Our school's lunch period has become a daily exercise in overcrowding. To solve this logistical bottleneck and grant upperclassmen a step toward independence, our school should implement an open-campus lunch policy for juniors and seniors. This policy is not just a student wishlist item; it is a practical solution backed by spatial reality, strong student consensus, and the proven success of our neighboring districts.

The most immediate argument for an open campus is simple math. Our cafeteria is officially rated to seat 220 people. However, during our designated lunch wave, there are currently 340 students trying to eat, socialize, and decompress. This leaves over one hundred students displaced every single day. Teenagers are forced to eat sitting on hallway floors, crowded on stairwells, or crammed into classroom doorways. This is not only uncomfortable and noisy, but it also creates a safety hazard and a supervision nightmare for staff. By allowing juniors and seniors—the oldest, most responsible segment of this wave—the option to leave campus for lunch, we would immediately alleviate this pressure, bringing the cafeteria back down to a manageable, safe capacity.

Furthermore, there is an overwhelming demand for this change among the student body, reflecting a readiness for greater responsibility. In a survey I conducted of 80 students at our school, 71 were in favor of an open-campus policy. This represents nearly 89% of the surveyed population. While critics might dismiss this as teenagers simply wanting to escape school grounds, the reality is that juniors and seniors are at a transitional stage in their lives. We are preparing for college and the workforce, environments where we will be expected to manage our own time, logistics, and safety. Giving upperclassmen the agency to choose where they eat is a small, controlled way to foster that necessary maturity. 

The primary opposition to an open campus usually centers on reliability, with opponents worrying that students will not make it back in time for fifth period. Fortunately, we do not have to guess how this policy would play out in reality; we can look to our neighbors. Three nearby districts—Fairmont, West Linn, and Cascade—already allow open-campus lunches for their upperclassmen. According to their published district statistics, none of these schools experienced a rise in tardiness after implementing the policy. When students are trusted with a privilege, they respect it, knowing that irresponsible behavior will result in losing their off-campus access. 

Ultimately, transitioning to an open-campus lunch policy is a win-win scenario for both the administration and the student body. It resolves a physical capacity crisis in our cafeteria without requiring a single dollar of construction budget, matches the overwhelming desire of the student population, and carries zero statistical risk of increased tardiness. It is time for our school to trust its juniors and seniors, ease the lunchtime crowd, and open the doors.

b.text:
High school is often described as a bridge to adulthood, yet for most of the day, students are treated like children. We are told when to sit, when to speak, and when to eat. But for juniors and seniors, who are only a year or two away from managing their own schedules in college or the workforce, an open campus lunch would be a meaningful step toward independence. Our school should allow juniors and seniors to leave campus during lunch because other districts have already shown it can work safely, our own students overwhelmingly support the idea, and our current cafeteria is simply too small to serve everyone comfortably.

One of the strongest arguments for an open campus lunch is that it is not a risky experiment. Nearby districts have already tried it and succeeded. Fairmont, West Linn, and Cascade all allow juniors and seniors to leave campus during lunch, and their published statistics show no rise in tardiness after the policy was introduced. This matters because the most common objection to open lunch is that students will return late to class. But if three separate districts, with different student bodies and different campuses, all report the same result, that objection starts to look more like a fear than a fact. Juniors and seniors are old enough to understand that losing the privilege would mean losing it for everyone, and the data from nearby schools suggests they are capable of meeting that responsibility.

It is also worth listening to the students who would actually be affected by the policy. I surveyed eighty students at our school, and seventy-one said they were in favor of an open campus lunch for juniors and seniors. That is nearly ninety percent. When such a large majority of a group supports a change that directly affects them, their voices should carry real weight. Students are not asking for a shorter school day or fewer classes; they are asking for thirty minutes of trust and autonomy in the middle of the day. The survey results show that this is not a fringe opinion held by a handful of students who want to skip class. It is the mainstream view of the student body, and it deserves to be taken seriously.

Finally, there is a practical problem that open lunch would help solve immediately: our cafeteria is overcrowded. The cafeteria seats 220 students, but one lunch wave contains 340 students. That means more than one hundred students have nowhere to sit during their designated lunch period. Some sit on the floor. Some stand against walls. Some try to squeeze onto benches that were not built for that many people. This is not a minor inconvenience; it is a daily reminder that the school’s facilities have not kept up with its enrollment. Allowing juniors and seniors to leave campus would reduce the number of students in the building during lunch and make the cafeteria a more comfortable place for everyone who remains. It is a solution that costs the district nothing and helps students immediately.

An open campus lunch for juniors and seniors is not an act of rebellion. It is a reasonable policy that recognizes students’ maturity, reflects the success of neighboring districts, answers the clear wishes of the student body, and relieves a real overcrowding problem in our cafeteria. The school has asked us to act like adults in our classes and our extracurriculars. Letting us leave campus for lunch is a simple way to show that trust beyond the classroom walls.

setup: A general contractor is writing a short X thread to contractors, homeowners, and architects about a hidden joist problem and the lesson learned.

a.text:
1/4 Just wrapped up a kitchen remodel on Maple Ave and found something that’s worth sharing—because it could save you a ton of time, money, or both. Pulled up the old flooring and discovered the joists weren’t just sagging… they were *split* under the original load-bearing wall.

2/4 Home was built in the ‘50s, and the previous layout had a non-load-bearing wall running parallel to the joists. At some point, someone moved it—right onto the weakest point of the span. No sistering, no extra support. Just… hope? Cost to fix: ~$2,800 in labor/materials to sister 8 joists and add a beam.

3/4 The real lesson? **Don’t assume the last guy knew what they were doing.** If you’re moving walls, even non-load-bearing ones, check the framing underneath. A $200 inspection before demo could’ve saved this homeowner thousands. And if you’re a homeowner? Ask your contractor how they’re verifying structural integrity.

4/4 Bonus: If you’re in an older home and see cracks in drywall or doors that stick, don’t just patch it—get under the floor or in the attic. Those “cosmetic” issues might be your only warning. Stay safe out there.

b.text:
1/4 On the Maple Ave kitchen, demo exposed a floor joist that had been cut nearly through for an old plumbing run. From above, the floor only showed a slight dip. Once the ceiling was open, the problem was obvious.

2/4 We stopped work, brought in the engineer, rerouted the plumbing, and repaired the framing to his detail. Added cost: about $3,200 between engineering, labor, materials, and the plumber coming back.

3/4 That wasn’t a “contractor markup surprise.” It was concealed damage that couldn’t be confirmed before demolition. We documented it, priced it separately, and got approval before proceeding.

4/4 The lesson isn’t just that old houses hide problems. A solid remodel needs a contingency, clear change-order terms, and enough schedule flexibility to fix what’s behind the walls instead of covering it back up.

setup: A retired Army staff sergeant is writing about coming home after his second deployment for readers of the veterans' writing workshop anthology.

a.text:
Coming back from my second deployment was different than the first. I didn’t know what to expect, but I didn’t expect the airport. My wife was waiting by baggage claim, and our daughter was with her. She was six years old. I dropped my duffel bag and took a knee to give her a hug, but she didn’t move forward. She took a step back and hid behind her mom’s leg. She didn’t recognize me at first. I had been gone a long time. My wife just rubbed her shoulder and looked at me. I nodded, picked my bag back up, and we walked out to the truck.

A few days later, my wife asked me to run to the grocery store. We needed milk and cereal. Over there, you eat what’s in the chow hall or whatever is in the MRE box. You don’t make decisions about food. I walked into the cereal aisle at the store and just stopped. There must have been forty different kinds of cereal. Both sides of the aisle, top to bottom. Flakes, puffs, frosted, plain. I stood in the middle of the aisle for twenty minutes. I couldn't make a choice. People pushed their carts around me and went about their day. I finally grabbed a yellow box of Cheerios just to have something in my hand and went to the register.

The nights took longer to figure out. For a year, I had slept on a cot facing the door. You always sleep facing the door so you can see who is coming in. It's just a habit you build. At home, my wife likes to keep our bedroom door open so she can hear if our daughter wakes up in the middle of the night. The first week back, I couldn't close my eyes if that door was open. I just lay there in the bed, staring out into the dark hallway. I ended up getting up and shutting it just so I could pass out, which meant my wife didn't sleep well. 

We had to work on it. After a few weeks, I tried leaving the door cracked an inch. A month after that, we opened it halfway. It took a long time before I could finally fall asleep with the bedroom door wide open, with my back turned to the hall.

b.text:
When I got back from my second deployment, I landed at the airport on a Tuesday. I had my A-bag slung over my shoulder and my uniform was stiff from thirty hours of travel. When I came off the terminal ramp, I saw my wife standing by the stairs. My daughter, Maya, was right next to her. She was six years old. I dropped my bag and walked toward them, but Maya didn't run out to meet me. She pulled back and hid behind her mother's leg, clutching the denim of Sarah’s jeans and peeking out with one eye. She didn't recognize me. To her, I was just a tall man in camouflage with a shaved head and a heavy voice she had only heard through a bad laptop speaker once a month. It took a while and a pack of gum from my pocket before she let me touch her shoulder.

A few days later, Sarah sent me to the store to get something for breakfast. I walked down the cereal aisle and stopped. I just stood there. There were forty different kinds of cereal stacked from the floor to the top shelf. Red boxes, blue boxes, boxes with cartoon characters, boxes with dried fruit. Down range, you ate whatever MRE was in the crate or you took the tray they handed you at the chow hall. You didn't make a choice, you just ate. I stood in front of those shelves for twenty minutes, looking at the options until my throat felt tight and my hands started to sweat. A woman pushing a cart asked if I was in line, and I couldn't answer her. I grabbed the first red box my hand touched and walked straight to the register.

The nights were the hardest part. For a year, I had slept in a CHU with my cot positioned so I was facing the door. If the handle moved or the light changed, I wanted to see it before anything else happened. 

At home, Sarah liked to leave our bedroom door cracked open a few inches so we could hear Maya if she woke up in the night. The first night back, I laid in the dark and felt like the room was spilling out into the hallway. Every instinct I had told me to get up, pull the door shut, and turn the bed around. I laid on my back for hours, looking at the thin strip of hallway light cutting across the carpet, trying to train my mind to leave it alone. 

It took months to get used to it. Some nights I still woke up in a sweat, stood up in the dark, and walked over to touch the wooden doorframe just to make sure where I was. Then I would leave it open and go back to bed.
